stories.title: Krishna Drains the Demoness Putana's Life
stories.story:
Gokul slept. The cowherd settlement lay dark, its doors shut, its cattle folded into their pens, and the night itself seemed to hold its breath. Through that darkness a woman moved from house to house, stopping at each doorway and looking in at the sleeping families, and no dog barked and no watchman stirred as she passed.

She was not a woman. She was Putana, a demoness known in many villages only as a name spoken in whispers — a child-killer who moved through the world the way sickness does, quietly, at night, drawn to the very young. She had come to Gokul to find a child, and she went from house to house, searching.

By chance, or by some darker purpose, her wandering brought her to the house of Nanda. There, in a dim room, an infant lay asleep — a child the whole settlement held dear. Putana lifted him from where he lay, cradled him against her, and gave him her breast.

There was milk in it, and there was something else as well. A poison lay there, meant for just such a child, laid to reach him through the very act that should have nourished him, and to still him as he fed.

The baby's eyes stayed closed, as if in sleep. He did not wake. He did not cry. He closed his mouth over her breast and began to drink, and it must have seemed to her, in that quiet room, the easiest thing she had ever done.

But what he drew from her was not milk alone. He drew out her life along with it, and she felt it going.

"Let go," she cried. "Let go of me."

The child did not let go. He drank on, and her cry rose out of that quiet house, terrible and deep. It rang across the settlement, and the earth shook with it, and the mountains, and the sky, and the very stars and planets in their slow paths trembled at the sound of it.

Then the life went out of her, and she fell.

As she fell, she was no longer the woman who had moved so quietly through the dark. She crashed down in her own form — monstrous, vast, her hair flung loose, her arms and legs thrown wide — and lay sprawled on the ground of Gokul like a great demon struck down out of the sky by a thunderbolt.

The child lay where he had been thrown, whole and unharmed. When the household woke and ran out, they found them there together: the baby they loved, and the dreadful thing that had come for him in the night.

They could make no sense of it. A demon had crept in to feed the child death, and the child had turned the feeding back upon her, and now she lay fallen in the yard while he lay beside her, whole and unharmed, as if the night's horror had never touched him at all. By daylight they carried the great body away, and the settlement slowly returned to its work; but the child fed and slept as on any other day, as if the whole night had been no more than a bad dream.

Long afterward, when the boy had grown and gone from the world, Uddhava would speak of Putana with a strange tenderness. The very demoness, he said, who had pressed her poisoned breast to the child with murder in her heart — even she had been received, by that same act, as a nurse, and granted a mother's place. What she had meant to do was not undone by this. But in the memory of it, it was not the last word either.
stories.reflection: Putana came to destroy the child, yet the tradition remembers her with tenderness: the very act of violence, offered to him, became her path to a mother's place. The story does not soften her cruelty, but it refuses to make cruelty the last word.
stories.content_note: A demoness attempts to poison an infant and dies; her death is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: Putana was not the last danger to find the baby in Gokul.

stories.title: The Fragrant Smoke
stories.subtitle: The villagers burn Putana's body
stories.story:
The woman who had come to Gokula was gone. In her place lay something that no one in the village could look at for long.

Putana's body, released from the lovely form she had worn, lay where she had fallen — enormous beyond belief, so vast that as she fell she had crushed the trees for a long stretch around her. Her mouth gaped wide, its teeth like the shafts of a plow; her nostrils opened like caves in a mountain; her eyes were deep pits a man might fall into. The cowherds and their women, gathered at a distance, trembled at the sight of it, and none of them would draw near.

And there, in the middle of all that horror, was the child. Krishna lay playing on the corpse's chest, utterly unafraid, as though he had been set down in his own courtyard on an ordinary morning. The very thing that made the grown men step back could not trouble him at all.

Yasoda and Rohini came forward and gathered him up. The women bathed the child, first with cow's urine and then with the fine dust of the cow pen, as was their custom of cleansing. Then, touching water and sprinkling it over him, they passed their hands over his body and chanted over each part of him in turn — his feet, his hands, his waist, his heart, his throat, his head — calling on the Lord to guard every part of him. They asked the one who holds the discus to stand before him and the one who holds the mace to stand behind, the bow and the sword to guard his sides and the conch to sound above him, the great bird Garuda to watch the ground and the Lord of all to stand around him everywhere. They named every spirit that preys on children, and they bade them all stay far away.

Meanwhile Nanda and the other cowherds were on the road back from Mathura. They reached the village to find the great body stretched upon the ground and the child safe, and they marveled. Surely, they said to one another, this was no ordinary boy. Surely he was a great sage, or a master of yoga, to have come through such a thing untouched.

Then they took up their axes. They cut the vast body to pieces, and they carried the pieces away and set them alight.

And here was the strangest thing of all. As that body burned, the smoke that rose from the fire was not the smoke of burning flesh. It carried a fragrance like aloe — sweet, and clean, and almost holy — drifting up over the village of Gokula. The demoness who had come to kill a child had been granted the reward of a mother, and the very air above the fire seemed to say so.
stories.reflection: The fragrant smoke is the story's quiet astonishment. The one who came to destroy a child is granted a mother's reward, and the text marks it not with a lecture but with a sweetness rising from the fire — grace offered even to the one who meant harm.
stories.content_note: The cowherds cut up and burn a demoness's corpse; described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But the danger to the child was not yet over.

stories.title: The Infant Who Overturned a Cart
stories.story:
A cart is a heavy thing, made to carry pots and grain and the whole weight of a household's goods. It does not fall over on its own. And yet, on the day of a certain child's birth-rites in Gokula, a loaded cart overturned for no reason anyone could see, and the only one near it was an infant too small to lift a single one of its pots.

The day had begun with ceremony. Yasoda, Nanda's wife, had bathed and purified herself, and the brahmins had come to recite the benedictions over her newborn son and had been honored with gifts. The women of Vraja had gathered for the rite of the child's first rising, and Yasoda moved among them, greeting each one, for a mother performing such a ceremony has many duties and her mind was full of them. In the press of it all, the child was set down for a moment in the shade of a cart that stood in the courtyard, heaped with vessels.

He was hungry, perhaps, or simply tired of being still. He began to cry, and as infants do when they cry, he kicked.

One small foot struck the underside of the cart above him. A foot as soft and tender as a new leaf, as a fresh sprout of the season, striking wood and iron.

The cart went over. Not tipped gently, but overturned, its wheels wrenched from the axle and its shaft and yoke broken, its vessels spilled and shattered across the courtyard.

The crash brought everyone running. Yasoda came, and the women of Vraja, and Nanda and the other men, and they stood around the wreckage in a ring of wonder, agitated by a sight they could not explain. How, they asked one another, could a cart turn over by itself? No wind had stirred. No animal had been near it. There it lay, upended and broken, and in the middle of it all sat the child, crying.

The cowherd boys and girls, who had been playing close by, said what they had seen. The child did it, they said. It was the baby who kicked it, with his own foot. But the grown men shook their heads. That was child-talk, the sort of thing children invent. How could an infant's foot overturn a cart that strong men could hardly shift?

Yasoda did not stay to argue. She was afraid, afraid of the evil eye and of whatever unkind influence might be drawn toward a child who had been part of such a wonder. She gathered up her crying son and held him to her.

The cowherds, strong men all, set the cart upright again and gathered up what remained of its goods. Then Nanda, troubled and unable to explain what had happened, did what a father does when the world will not give an answer. He gathered the brahmins skilled in the mantras and had the protective rites recited over his son, with the words of the three Vedas, and he brought out his finest cows and adorned them with cloth and garlands and gold, and stood with a steady heart while the blessings were spoken over the child.

But no prayer could undo what the courtyard had seen that day, and no one who was there could forget it. A cart overturned by the kick of a child too small to lift a single one of its pots, and the child himself, unhurt, reaching up to be held. The men went back to their herds and the women to their houses, but the question went with them, unasked and unanswered.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is not only the overturned cart but the way the village receives it: the children tell the plain truth and the adults refuse it, because the truth is too large for their idea of what a child can do.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha sets this episode while Yasoda is away bathing at the river and Nanda returns from the forest to find the cart overturned; the Bhagavata Purana places it during the child's birth-rites. The miracle at the heart of both is the same.
stories.next_story_tease: Kamsa's servants were not finished with Gokula, and the next would come not in a human shape but as a storm.
stories.hero_scene: The infant Krishna lies beneath an overturned cart, one small foot raised in a kick, while the cart's wheels lie torn away and pots and vessels scatter across the courtyard as the cowherd men and women stare in astonishment.

stories.title: The Whirlwind That Stole a Child
stories.story:
The day had been quiet in Gokula, and Yasoda sat with her son on her lap, dandling him and looking into his face, the way a mother does when there is nothing to do but be with her child and be glad of it. The village hummed around her, the cows lowing in their pens and the women calling to one another down the lanes. There was no sign of the storm to come, nothing in the clear air to warn her.

And then, without any warning, the child grew heavy in her arms. She felt it plainly, the small body suddenly pressing down on her as though its weight had doubled, so heavy that she could hardly hold him. Astonished, she set him down on the ground to see what it could mean.

Before she could think further, the air changed.

A wind came tearing through the lanes of Gokula, a dry and violent wind that lifted the dust of the earth and set it spinning in a harsh wheel of grit. This was no storm. This was Trinavarta, a demon in the service of Kamsa, the king who had sworn to see the child dead, and he had come in the shape of a whirlwind, sent by his master to do what the king could not. He came the way such servants come — with no face to remember and no warning to give, nothing but the wind and the dust he wore like a body. The spinning dust filled the whole settlement, and it stole the light and the sight of everyone in it.

For a long moment Gokula went dark. No one could see the person beside them, and no one could see their own hand before their face, for the dust had thrown a cloud over the entire settlement. The wind tore at the thatch, the pens lowed in panic, and the darkness itself seemed to move, spinning where the storm stood. The cowherds stumbled and called out, and mothers reached into the brown air for children they could not see, their voices thin and frightened, and everywhere there was confusion and a fear with no shape to it.

When the dust began to settle, Yasoda looked for her son, and he was gone.

For a moment she did not move. He had been in her arms only moments before; the weight of him was still in her arms. But the ground where she had set him down was empty, and she stood looking at it, unwilling to believe what her eyes were telling her.

She searched the spot where she had set him down, and the ground was empty. She searched for his path, for any trace the small body might have left on the earth, but the wind had scoured the ground clean and there was nothing to follow. She called his name, and the sound of it was lost in the settling dust. She looked this way and that through the thinning haze, but she could not find him anywhere, for the whirlwind that had passed through was already receding, carrying with it the child she had held a moment before. The other women of Gokula, hearing a cry, came running with their faces wet with tears, for the village's dearest child had been taken, and no one could say where the storm had gone.

And somewhere high above the blinded village, the whirlwind rose with its small captive, a demon going up into the sky with a child who, a moment ago, had been too heavy for his own mother to hold — rising, as it believed, to carry out the errand it had been sent on.
stories.reflection: The detail that the child suddenly felt heavy in Yasoda's arms, just before the whirlwind came, is quietly ominous: the thing that will undo Trinavarta is already present in the very weight that surprised his mother.
stories.content_note: A demon snatches an infant away in a blinding whirlwind; the episode is brief and ends on the moment of loss.
stories.next_story_tease: But the whirlwind had not counted on the weight of the child it carried.
stories.hero_scene: A towering whirlwind of dust and grit sweeps through the lanes of Gokula, blinding everything, while Yasoda reaches through the choking brown air toward the spot where her child had been.

stories.title: Trinavarta Is Crushed by the Child's Weight
stories.story:
One afternoon the sky over Gokul turned strange.

It began as a wind — a dry, rising wind that lifted the dust of the lanes and set the doors to banging. The cattle stirred in their pens and lowed uneasily, and the women at their churning looked up and shaded their eyes. Then the wind thickened and darkened and began to spin, and those who looked up saw that it was not a storm at all. There was something inside it, and it was moving toward the house of Nanda.

It was Trinavarta, a demon who came as a whirlwind, and before anyone could cry out he swept down, snatched the baby from the courtyard where he lay, and carried him up into the spinning air.

The child vanished into the dust. The settlement was plunged into a choking darkness. Mothers groped for their own children and called their names, and no one could say where the boy had gone. High above, Trinavarta rose, clutching his prize, and the earth fell away beneath him.

But something was wrong.

The child in his arms was growing heavy. He had been nothing — a feather, a leaf — and now he pressed down on the demon like a stone. Trinavarta climbed, and the child grew heavier. He strained to rise higher into the sky, and the child grew heavier still, until the whirlwind demon found that he could not move at all. A child is the lightest thing in the world, and yet the sky could not hold this one; the demon who had risen like smoke now hung motionless, pinned by something he could not see or understand. It was as though he were holding up a mountain. As though he were holding up the whole weight of the world.

The wind, which a moment before had borne him aloft so easily, now held him fast; he could neither rise nor turn. His flight stopped. Then the baby's small hands closed around his throat, and Trinavarta could neither move nor breathe. His eyes started from his head.

And he fell.

He fell out of the sky onto a rock below, and the rock shattered him — the whirlwind broken to pieces on the stone. The cowherds ran to the place, expecting the worst, and found the child lying safe upon the demon's chest, as if the fall had been a cradle and the monster his bedding. The mothers who had lost sight of him in the dust came running too, and found him not only alive but unmarked, and they pressed him close and wept with relief. They passed him from hand to hand, turning him over to look for a wound, and found none.

They could not believe their eyes. A demon had carried the boy off to his death, and here he was, back among them, unhurt, as though the whole thing had been no more than a game of the wind. "What penance have we done?" they asked one another. "What worship, what good deeds, what kindness to other beings, that the child who was taken from us has been given back alive?"

They lifted him up and carried him home, and for a long time the men of Gokul would speak of the wonders they had seen in that broad forest. Nanda, the cowherd chief, kept his own counsel, but he had begun to notice how many wonders gathered around this quiet child — and how, one after another, they all ended the same way: with the boy safe, and the danger gone. He did not speak of it, but he began to watch the child more closely.
stories.reflection: The demon meant to carry the child off into the sky, and instead he was brought down by the very thing he tried to steal — a smallness that held the weight of the world. The rescue is not a struggle of equals; it is the unmasking of what the child already carried.
stories.content_note: A demon is crushed in a fall; the description is brief and not graphic.
stories.hero_scene: A demon in whirlwind form crashes out of a dark, dust-choked sky onto a rock, shattered, while the infant Krishna lies safe and unharmed upon his chest in the aftermath.

stories.title: The Universe in Her Son's Mouth
stories.story:
There is no hour more ordinary in a mother's day than the hour she feeds her child. It was in just such an hour, the child on her lap and nearly done with his milk, his drinking slowing, that Yasoda saw what no one had prepared her to see.

She was looking down at him the way mothers do, at the small face with its lovely, contented smile. And the child yawned.

It was only a yawn, the kind every tired infant makes. But as his mouth opened, Yasoda looked into it, and instead of the pink of a child's gums she saw the sky. The wide sky, and the earth spread out beneath it, and the heavens beyond, and the hosts of stars turning in their courses, and the directions, and the sun and the moon and fire and wind and the great oceans, and every living thing. The whole universe, moving and unmoving, arranged inside the open mouth of the child she was nursing.

She saw all of it, suddenly and at once, and she trembled. Her limbs shook, and her breath caught in her throat, and she trembled the way a leaf trembles in a strong wind, for she understood, in that instant, that the small mouth before her opened onto everything.

It lasted only as long as a yawn lasts. But in that small space of time, Yasoda saw more than the sages spend whole lifetimes seeking, and it was offered to her without a word, in the open mouth of the child she was feeding, for no reason but that she was his mother and happened to be looking.

What must that have been like? A mother bending over her baby, and in the space where his small mouth opened, the turning of the worlds. A woman who has churned butter and mended cloth and sung her baby to sleep, suddenly given the whole of creation to look at. The child who could not yet speak a word held the sky and the sea and all that lives, and he offered no explanation and asked for none. He only yawned, and let her look, and then, as quickly as it had opened, the moment passed, and he was only a child again, warm and drowsy against her, his mouth once more too small to kiss without bending down.

The source does not say how long she sat there afterward, or what she said when the trembling stopped. It says only that she saw, and that she shook. Perhaps that is enough. Some things are too large to be spoken of, and are carried instead, silently, in the heart of a woman who once looked into her own child's face and saw everything.
stories.reflection: The vision is given to a mother in the most domestic of moments, while she is nursing, and it is not sought or asked for. The infinite does not interrupt her love; it shows itself through the very child she is holding.
stories.hero_scene: Yasoda, the child on her lap, stares into his yawning mouth and sees the whole universe within it, the sky and oceans and sun and moon and stars, while she trembles.

stories.title: Garga Secretly Names Rama and Krishna
stories.story:
Most ceremonies are made to be witnessed, but a naming can be a dangerous thing. When the family priest Garga came to Nanda's house in Gokula, he asked that the rites be done in secret.

Garga had not come on his own. He had been sent by Vasudeva, the man from whose arms the child had been carried to Gokula as a newborn, to perform the rites that every child must receive. The reason for the secrecy waited a few days' journey away, in Mathura. There a king named Kamsa was hunting for Vasudeva's children, and he would not have wanted a single one of them to live.

Nanda had not expected the old priest, and the sight of him at the door filled Nanda with joy. He rose at once and pressed his palms together. He washed Garga's feet and seated him with honor, and offered him the welcome due to a guest, and only then, with careful and pleasant words, did he make his request. It was no small thing to ask a priest to one's home, and Nanda asked it with the courtesy of a man asking a great favor. Of all those who know the things beyond the senses, he said, it is you who should perform these rites. For Garga could read the course of the stars as they moved through the sky, and he saw with a knowledge that did not come through the eyes.

Garga answered him plainly, and in a low voice. Kamsa, he said, is a man of evil mind, and he knows of your friendship with Vasudeva. If a naming in Gokula were spoken of, word would travel, and questions would follow, and the child would be in danger. Let this be done quietly, with no one to see and no one to tell.

So it was. There, in that room, without the knowledge of the other cowherds, Garga performed the rites. To the elder boy, the son of Rohini, he gave the name Rama — the boy who would also come to be called Balarama. And to Nanda's son he gave the name Krishna. The two names sat lightly on the two sleeping children, as if they had been waiting for them all along.

Then Garga spoke of what he could see, and his words fell soft in the quiet room. This child, he said, has not come into the world for the first time. In age after age he appears, and in each age his form takes a different color; he comes under many names, for the names and forms of this boy are beyond counting. And before this birth, Garga said, he was born of Vasudeva. The cowherds and all of Gokula would find their welfare in him. Through him the good would be shielded from those who did them harm, and the wicked would be kept at bay. He would be the delight of the cowherds and of all Gokula, Garga said, and the source of every good thing that came to them. Those who set their hearts on him, Garga said, are fortunate indeed. He is equal, Garga said at last, to Narayana himself in his qualities.

When the rites were done, Garga left as quietly as he had come, and Nanda spoke to no one of what had been said in that room. The two names were given in secret and held in secret.

And yet they did not stay secret. The name Krishna, first spoken behind a shut door in Gokula, would one day be spoken in every home and every temple, and on the lips of the whole world.
stories.reflection: Garga's secret naming holds the whole shape of Krishna's early life in miniature — the fear of Kamsa that forces concealment, and the quiet certainty that what is hidden now will not stay hidden.
stories.hero_scene: The sage Garga, seated in Nanda's dim home, performs the naming rites in secret, the two infants before him, as Nanda looks on with his palms pressed together.

stories.title: The Butter Thief of Gokula
stories.story:
The trouble in Gokula did not begin with butter. It began with two boys learning to crawl.

Krishna and his brother Rama had grown quickly, the way children do when no one is watching, and in a short time they were dragging themselves across the ground on their little legs, churning up the mud of the cowherd lanes. They babbled as they went, and the whole settlement seemed to brighten at the sound, for there was nothing the cowherds loved more than the sight of those two small boys in motion. When they had crawled far enough, they would turn and creep back toward their mothers with puzzled, half-frightened faces, as if they had traveled a great distance and were surprised to find themselves home.

Their mothers would gather them up, two small boys caked in mud with their limbs stained the color of the lane, and press them to the breast, and look into their faces with their sweet smiles and their first little teeth, and be filled with joy. There was no resisting it.

Soon the boys were up on their feet, and then the real play began. They would catch the calves of the herd by the tail and let themselves be dragged this way and that across the yard, and the women of Vraja, seeing it from their doorways, would leave whatever they were doing and come out to watch, laughing. The two mothers could only try to keep their restless sons away from horns and fire and a boar's tusks and open water and swooping birds and thorn bushes, and they could not. The boys were too quick and the mothers too fond, and in the end the women gave up trying and simply watched, their minds never quite at rest.

And then Krishna discovered butter.

It began innocently, as these things do. He and his band of cowherd friends would slip into a neighbor's house and set the calves loose at the wrong hour, and stand laughing at the confusion. Then he found where the curd and the milk were kept, and the games turned to theft, but theft of a kind that made the gopis want to laugh even as they scolded. He worked with tricks and contrivances, and he chose his moment well, when the women were busy with their housework. When the pots hung high out of reach, in slings among the rafters, he would drag a stool or a mortar beneath them and climb. In the dark of a storeroom he needed no lamp, for the jewels on his own small body caught what little light there was and showed him where the pots were. He would eat the sweet curd and butter, and feed the monkeys who were his constant audience, and if a monkey refused to eat, he would smash the pot in a temper. And when he could not reach a pot at all, he would march off angry and shout curses at the little boys of the house.

The gopis complained to Yasoda, of course. They came with their lists of outrages, and their eyes, even while they complained, were soft with the sight of him, his face so lovely it undid their anger, and their scolding came out half-laughing. And Yasoda, who had seen a cart overturn beneath that same small foot, listened to it all with a smile on her face, and could not bring herself to scold him. And so it went, day after day, the butter missing and the mischief unpunished, and Gokula learned to live with a thief no one truly wanted to punish.
stories.reflection: The charm of the mischief is that everyone is in on it except the scolding: the gopis complain with delight in their eyes, and Yasoda hears them out and does nothing. The village loves the very trouble it reports.
stories.next_story_tease: And one of those pranks would soon send every cowherd boy running to Yasoda with news.

stories.title: Krishna Shows the Cosmos in His Mouth
stories.story:
One day Krishna was playing with his brother Rama and the other cowherd boys, tumbling in the dust of the lane the way small boys do, and when the game was done the boys came running to Yasoda with news.

"Krishna ate mud," they told her, all of them at once, their faces bright with the importance of the news. "We saw him. He ate dirt while no one was looking." They were certain of it; they had been playing with him all afternoon, and they knew what they had seen.

Now, whether he had eaten it or not, Yasoda was his mother, and a mother must ask. She took him by the hand and drew him to her, and scolded him, but gently, the way a mother scolds a child she is trying to keep safe — not so much angry as wanting the truth.

"Why did you eat mud," she asked, "in secret, when no one was looking? You know it is not good for you."

"I did not eat it, mother," Krishna said, meeting her eyes. "They are all saying what is not true."

Yasoda looked at him. There was a simple way to settle it, the oldest trick a mother knows.

"Then open your mouth," she said. "If you have eaten nothing, there will be nothing to see."

And Krishna opened his mouth.

What Yasoda saw there is beyond telling, and yet it has been told for thousands of years. In the small mouth of her small son she saw the whole universe. She saw the earth with its mountains and its oceans, and the sky, and all the directions, and the slow turning circle of the stars and planets. She saw water and fire and air and the vast space between them. She saw every living thing, and time itself, and the endless tangle of deeds and their results, and all the hidden differences between one being and another, moving together inside a child's open mouth — the whole world, moving and unmoving, held in the span of a few small teeth. She saw it all, and yet his mouth was small enough to kiss.

The same vision that the sages spend whole lifetimes seeking through the Vedas and the Upanishads and the long, patient disciplines of knowledge — she saw it in a single moment, freely given, in her son's open mouth.

She stood still, overwhelmed, and her own mind asked the only questions it could form. Is this a dream? she thought. Is it some divine illusion? Or is it a delusion that has come over my own mind?

And because she could not hold the vision, she reached for the ordinary truths that had always held her. I am Yasoda, she told herself. This is my husband Nanda. This is my son. I am the wife of the lord of Vraja, the mistress of all his wealth. And the child in front of her was only her child again.

Then the vision was veiled from her, as gently as it had come. Her memory of it slipped away, and she did not remember that she had ever seen the universe. She bent down, lifted her son onto her lap, and was simply his mother again, and the world, for that hour, was small and ordinary.

She would not remember. That, perhaps, was the mercy of it — that after seeing everything, after holding the whole of creation in a single glance, she was given back the one thing that mattered most, and it fit, again, in her two arms. And that, in the end, was enough.
stories.reflection: The story shows the infinite and then gently takes it back. Yasoda is not denied the vision because she is unworthy, but because her love needs him small; the mother who has seen the whole cosmos in his mouth is given back the child she can hold, and that is presented not as a loss but as a mercy.
stories.next_story_tease: And the days went back to being ordinary again — which, in that house, meant mischief.

stories.title: Krishna Breaks the Butter Pot
stories.story:
Yasoda was churning. She sat at the churn, working the rope with both arms, and the whole of her told the story of a mother's long morning: the cloth bound at her waist with its cord, the garland of jasmine slipping from her hair, the sweat on her face, the small rings at her ears swinging as she pulled, her bangles shifting with every strain of the rope. It was the kind of morning that promised to be long and uneventful, and Yasoda was glad of it. The curd turned in the pot, and the butter was nearly ready.

Then her son came to her. He was hungry, and he came and stood close, pulling at her and wanting to be held, and she could feel the churn slow as she turned to him.

She lifted him onto her lap and nursed him, and as he fed she looked down at his face and smiled. It was the still, warm moment of the day.

It did not last. Behind her, the milk she had set to boil — forgotten in the warmth of that moment — climbed the sides of its pot and began to spill, hissing onto the coals. Yasoda had to set the child down and run to it. She left him there beside the churn.

He did not take well to being put down. One moment he had been warm and fed and held; the next, he was alone on the floor.

His lower lip began to tremble. He bit it with his small teeth, angry, and looked at the churn-pot — the pot full of fresh butter — and then he broke it. The pot fell apart, and all the butter of the morning's churning lay open before him.

He took up the butter, and, being a child left to his own devices, he did not eat it all himself; with no one there to tell him otherwise, he ate only what he pleased and shared the rest. He climbed up on the upturned mortar where it stood, and there, out of Yasoda's sight, he held out the butter, and a monkey — one of the creatures that wandered freely through the cowherd lanes — came and took it from his hand, and ate it with as much delight as if it had been a feast.

When Yasoda came back and saw the broken pot and the butter gone, she understood at once who had done it. She picked up a stick.

The boy saw the stick. He scrambled down and ran — as if he were afraid, though anyone watching would have seen that his fear was a game. And his mother ran after him.

It was a curious chase. The same child whose mind, the scriptures say, even the yogis in their long austerities cannot reach or enter — he was running through his own courtyard, and his mother was gaining on him. She ran with her full, swaying burden, her waist slender above it, her breath coming short, and still she could not quite catch him.

At last he let himself be caught. And when she had him, he did the thing that undid all her anger: he rubbed his eyes with his small, sooty hands — hands black with the collyrium and ash of the morning — and he cried, with tears that left black smears down his cheeks, the very picture of a wronged and sorry child. And Yasoda, who had come running with a stick, found the stick hanging loose in her hand, her anger already gone. The butter, the chase, the broken pot — none of it mattered now.
stories.reflection: The comedy is gentle because it turns on a real child's logic: interrupted at the breast, he takes the next sweet thing and shares it, then runs and pretends to cry. Even the line that the yogis cannot reach him lands lightly — the point is not his power but that a mother's chase is the one pursuit he never really outruns.
stories.next_story_tease: Yasoda's anger would not last, and soon she would go looking for a rope.

stories.title: Yashoda Binds Krishna to the Mortar
stories.story:
Yashoda's anger had cooled as quickly as it had come. She had run after her son with a stick in her hand, meaning to teach him a lesson for the broken butter pot; but the moment she caught up with him and saw the fear on his small face, the stick dropped from her fingers and lay in the dust. She could not strike him. Her anger was a brief, hot thing, and it always died the moment it met his eyes.

But the boy had done wrong, and something had to be done. So she put the stick aside and reached instead for a rope. She would tie him up — a gentler punishment, she told herself — and then she could finish her work in peace.

She took the rope and wound it around his waist. It came up short. However she pulled, the rope ended a little short of the knot, short by two fingers' width, no more. She frowned and joined another length of rope to the first. Still two fingers short. She joined a third, then a fourth, fetching coil after coil from the store of her own house, tying rope to rope, and still the gap would not close. All the rope in the house, joined end to end, could not make a loop that would hold him.

She worked on, and the morning grew warm. The sweat stood on her face and along her arms; the hair she had braided at dawn came loose; the garland slipped from it and hung crooked. Still she tied, and still the rope fell short by those same two fingers.

And then, at last, Krishna looked at his mother. He looked at her wet face, her loosened hair, her hands worn raw from tying ropes for his sake alone, and something in him softened. He was not a child whom any rope could hold. No one in all the worlds could reach him or bind him — not the greatest of the gods, not the mightiest of beings. And yet here was his mother, wearing herself out over a length of rope, for no other reason than that she was his mother and he was her son.

So he let it happen. Of his own accord, moved by nothing but her striving and her love, he stood still and let the rope close around his waist at last. Yashoda bound him to the great wooden mortar, the heavy block on which the household pounded its grain, and this time the knot held.

She wiped her face, satisfied, and turned back to her work. And the child sat bound to the mortar, as quiet as if he had chosen it — because, in the end, he had.
stories.reflection: The wonder is not that Krishna could not be bound, but that he chose to be — that the effort of a mother's love accomplished what the strength of the whole world could not.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana fold this rope-binding into the later uprooting of the twin trees; the Bhagavata gives it as a separate episode.
stories.next_story_tease: Bound at last to the mortar, the child would soon drag it out toward the two great trees at the forest's edge.

stories.title: Krishna Uproots the Twin Arjuna Trees
stories.subtitle: How he came to be called Damodara
stories.story:
Krishna was still a crawling child, too young to walk, when the people of Gokula learned that he could not be kept still. He went into the cow sheds and came out gray with ash and dust. He rolled in the cow dung and only laughed. With his small body pasted in ashes and powdered cow-dung, he shone like a little prince of fire. He wandered into every corner of the village, and Nanda could not check him, and his mother Yashoda could not keep pace with him. When she caught him and began to scold him, he looked back at her with such innocent eyes that the scolding died on her lips, and she laughed in spite of herself.

One day, though, the mischief went too far, and Yashoda's patience ran out for good. Worked up with real anger, she took up a length of rope. She fastened it around the boy's waist and tied the other end to a heavy wooden mortar, the great block on which the household pounded its grain. Now go, she told him, go where you will — if you can. Then she turned back to her work, certain the matter was settled.

It was from that day, and from that rope, that he came to be called Damodara, the one bound by a rope around his belly. But a rope could not hold him. Dragging the mortar after him, Krishna left the courtyard and made his way toward the edge of the forest, where two great arjuna trees stood side by side — twin trees, tall and straight, grown huge with years, their branches laced together in the canopy. He went out meaning to surprise the people of Gokula and to play a game that only he understood. The mortar scraped behind him over the packed earth, heavier than he was, yet he dragged it as if it weighed nothing at all. At the edge of the forest the two trees rose up before him, straight as two pillars of an unseen gate.

He crawled between the trees, pulling the mortar through the narrow space. The mortar caught against their roots and held. Krishna pulled, and pulled again, harder. And with a single tug the two trees tore up out of the earth, roots and branches and all, and came crashing down with a sound that carried through the whole of Gokula. Birds burst from the fallen branches. Dust rose in a pale cloud and hung in the air, and for a long moment no one moved. The earth where the trees had stood lay torn open, and their long roots, thick as a man's arm, pointed up at the sky.

The cowherds came running at the noise, and they stopped short at what they saw. There stood no great trees now, only two fallen trunks, their great crowns thrown across the path. And Krishna, still tied to his mortar, only laughed, as if to show them all what a child could do.

But those two trees had not always been trees. They were two sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth, who had been cursed by a divine sage to stand rooted in the earth until someone set them free. Tall as they were and broad as their branches spread, they were prisoners, and no one in Gokula had ever guessed it. The sage's word had been waiting all those years to come true. Year after year the two had stood in their green stillness, leaf and branch instead of arms and legs. It was to make that word good that Krishna passed between them. A child too small to be trusted out of the yard had, with one pull, ended their long imprisonment and drawn the two of them back into the light.

When the dust settled, the two great trees lay still upon the ground. And between them sat a crawling child, a rope still at his waist, laughing.
stories.reflection: The story holds two wonders in one image: a child too small to walk brings down two great trees, and beneath their crash two cursed beings are set free. The binding meant to restrain him becomes the very thing that liberates.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana fold the earlier rope-binding into this episode; the Bhagavata opens with Krishna already bound — Damodara.

stories.title: The Two Devotees Are Liberated from the Trees
stories.story:
The sound of the two trees falling was still rolling across the fields of Gokula when the cowherds heard it and came running. They found the child — the crawling boy with a rope still tied about his waist to the great mortar — sitting beside the two uprooted arjuna trees, their trunks laid out on the earth and their roots torn up into the air.

Then something rose out of the fallen trees, and the cowherds stopped where they stood.

Two figures climbed up from between the roots, and they were not men of any village. Light seemed to cling to them; they shone like fire just kindled, and the whole clearing was brightened by them. They were Nalakuvara and Manigriva, and the curse that had held them within those trunks was over at last.

The two beings walked to the child and bowed their heads to the ground before him, their palms joined. And they spoke to him — not as men speak to a small boy, but as servants to their Lord.

They called him by name, again and again, and praised him. They called him the great yogi, the first and highest of all persons, the one who was there before all things, the one Lord who dwells within every living body, the self of every self. He is the great and subtle source of all that exists, they said, and yet nothing of this world — none of its changing qualities — can ever grasp or hold him. To that Vasudeva, the maker of all, they offered their obeisance. Obeisance to the supreme goodness, they said; obeisance to the supreme blessing.

And then they asked for the one thing they had waited so long to ask. Let our voices always be given to singing of your deeds, they said. Let our ears always hear of you. Let our hands always work in your service, our minds rest at your feet, our heads bow before the worlds where you dwell, and our eyes look upon those who are devoted to you. Grant us leave, Lord — we are your servants, and we are yours.

Krishna heard them, and his answer was simple. You are both mine, he told them, and your hearts are fixed on me. Go now to your own home.

They bowed once more, and then they went — the two radiant beings rising and passing away toward the north, free at last.

The cowherds stood in the clearing a long while, staring from the uprooted trees to the child who sat calm among the roots. They had heard the crash of the falling trees, and they had seen what came out of them. They could not explain any of it. But they understood enough to be afraid, and enough to know that the child in their midst was not simply a child.
stories.reflection: The liberation is quiet on Krishna's side and vast on theirs: they do not ask for riches or revenge, only that their senses be turned forever toward him — and that, once granted, is enough to set them free.

stories.title: The Fruit-Seller Receives a Gift of Jewels
stories.story:
In those days Krishna was still small enough to be carried, and his days in Gokula were full of play. He danced whenever the cowherd women clapped and coaxed him to dance. When his father asked, he would fetch the stool and the weights and the wooden sandals and carry them, pleased to be of use. To anyone with eyes to see, the Lord of all things was going about the lanes of a cowherd village like an ordinary child, happy to be asked, happy to serve. He was learning the weight of a stool in his arms the way any child learns it, and the women of the house laughed to see him trot off at an errand and come back beaming.

One morning a fruit-seller came through the lane, a woman with a basket of fruit and a voice that carried down the street. Come, buy fruits! Sweet fruits! she called. The cry rolled ahead of her through the little village, and heads turned at the sound of it.

Krishna heard the cry and hurried at once. He snatched up a fistful of grain to barter — grain was what a village that kept no coins gave and took — and ran toward the fruit-seller, eager for the trade. He had seen the fruit-seller's trade before, baskets carried from lane to lane, and the exchange was a small boy's idea of the world's business: you give, you get, everybody is pleased.

But his hands were small, and his eagerness was greater than his grip. Before he reached the woman, the grain began to run out through his fingers and spill onto the ground, a thin white trail marking where he had run. By the time he stood before her, his two fists were nearly empty.

The fruit-seller looked down at the child — at the grain scattered in the dust and the two small, empty hands held up to her — and her heart turned over. She did not scold him. She laughed, softly, and bent down and began to fill his small hands with fruit, heaping them with what she carried, until no more would stay. Whatever anyone else might have done with an empty-handed bargainer, she did the one thing that costs nothing and means everything: she gave.

And then she saw her basket.

Where her fruit had been, the basket now gleamed. In place of the fruit she had emptied into the child's hands, it was full to the brim with jewels — gems that caught the morning light and threw it back in every colour. The fruit was gone, and in its place shone a treasure beyond anything her life of selling fruit had ever held. The basket that had weighed in her arms like a day's honest work now weighed like a king's ransom.

She stood still, the heavy basket in her hands, and looked from the jewels to the small boy before her, and back again. She understood, in that moment, that she had not been selling fruit to a child at all. She had been giving it, without knowing, to the one who gives everything back a hundredfold.

But she said nothing of what she understood. She only looked at him, and he looked back at her — a child with his arms full of fruit, and a woman with her basket full of light.
stories.reflection: The exchange turns on a small, human generosity: the woman is not asked for anything but fruit, and she gives it to a child who has already dropped his payment. What comes back is beyond measure, because grace answers the open hand.

stories.title: The Cowherds Decide to Migrate to Vrindavan
stories.story:
Gokula had begun to feel like a place under siege, and no one could say quite why. The signs had come one after another, and each of them had touched the children — above all, one child.

The elder Upananda was the oldest of the cowherds and the one whose judgment the others trusted, a man long in years and long in sense. He had watched the recent days with a growing unease, and at last he called the cowherds together. When they had gathered — Nanda at their head, and all the men of the settlement around him — he spoke plainly.

We who wish Gokula well, he said, must leave this place.

He reminded them of what they had all seen with their own eyes, one wonder and one terror after another. The boy had been delivered, almost beyond hoping, from the demoness who came to kill children. A whirlwind demon had caught him up and carried him into the sky, and yet he had come down alive. And he had passed between the two great trees, and he had not died. Before even those, the waggon he had lain beneath as an infant had been overturned by a kick of his foot, its pots and pans flung across the ground. Set out in a row, as Upananda made them set it out, the pattern could not be mistaken: everything that came near the child was broken or undone, and the child remained. Each time the child had been saved by what could only be called a miracle. But Upananda saw in these narrow escapes something more than fortune. He saw a warning.

Before another evil omen falls upon Vraja, he told them, we should go. And there is a place to go: a forest called Vrindavana, fresh and green, new pastureland good for the cattle. New ground, he said — groves that had never been grazed, grass that had not been cropped, a place where the omens of Gokula had no hold. There, perhaps, the prodigies that had marked this settlement would not reach them. Let us go there at once. Yoke the carts, and do not delay.

The cowherds listened, and they did not argue. One after another they nodded, and the word went round: well said, well said. They had seen too much to dismiss the old man's fears, and the thought of a new forest, thick with fresh grass and safe for the herds, came as a relief after the days they had just passed through.

So the order was given, and the settlement began to move. The carts were yoked. The old men climbed up, and the children were lifted in, and the women gathered what the household would need, and the whole colony — every family, with all their belongings and all their cattle — made ready to leave the only ground most of them had ever known. Whatever could be carried went onto the carts; a village, once moved, does not send back for what it left behind.

It was no small thing, to uproot a village. But the cowherds did it in a single day and in a single mind. The elders led, the herds followed, and the carts rolled out of Gokula toward the new forest by the river, where the grass was said to grow deep and the danger, they hoped, had not yet found them.
stories.reflection: Upananda's wisdom is practical and communal: he does not claim to understand the wonders, only to see that they have become omens, and that the right answer to a sign one cannot read is to move the whole community out of its path.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana attributes the decision to the elders with Nanda at their head, alarmed by Putana's death, the overturned waggon and the trees; the Bhagavata has Upananda speak of the omens. Both agree on the departure for Vrindavana.

stories.title: The Wolves That Moved a Village
stories.story:
The forest that had held their childhood was nearly gone.

Krishna and his brother Balarama had passed seven years in Vraja, playing through these woods. They had gone out among the cattle in dark-blue and yellow clothes, their bodies painted with yellow and white paste, crow feathers in their hair, and filled the forest with the music of their pipes. Some days they wore crowns of leaves and garlands of wild flowers, and looked like two young trees walking; other days they crowned themselves with lotuses, hung gourds on a string, slung a rope over one shoulder like a sacred thread, and played their flutes as they went. They had lain down on beds of leaves and slept, and run about like two young horses, and in their play they had beautified the whole forest.

Now, standing in it, Krishna saw what those years had cost. The grass was gone, the twigs stripped, the trees pulled up by the milkmen. Fires from the cow-sheds had scorched the trunks, and the birds had flown from the bare branches. Even the wind that had once blown sweet through the leaves seemed not to stir here anymore. The forest, Krishna said, had become like rice served with no dish to go with it — there, but giving no pleasure.

He turned to his brother. They could not play here any longer, he said; there was no place left even to rest. And the cows suffered too — where droppings fell on the grass, the grazing soured and the milk turned poor. It was time to move.

Then he told Balarama of the place he had heard of: a forest on the bank of the Yamuna called Vrindavana. Grass grew thick there, he said; the ground was free of thorns and insects, and the trees bore fruit. Cool winds blew there all the year, as if every season had made its home in that one place. Kadamba trees stood in the groves, and close by rose the great mountain Govardhana, its summit high like the celestial mount Mandara. In the heart of that mountain grew an enormous fig tree, the Bhandira, its branches spreading for a yojana, dark against the sky like a rain-cloud. And the river Kalindi, the Yamuna herself, flowed through the middle of it all, as straight as a parting drawn through hair. There, Krishna said, they would look upon the mountain, and the tree, and the river, with joy.

There was only one difficulty. The milkmen would not willingly leave the home they knew. So Krishna made his decision. Let us create some calamity, he told his brother, and frighten the milkmen into going.

And as he spoke, the thought became the thing. From the hairs of his body there arose wolves — hundreds of wolves, creatures that live on fat and blood and flesh, dark-faced, each bearing on its body the mystic mark called Srivatsa. They poured out of him and ran in every direction, as if the whole village of Vraja was to be overrun. They fell upon the calves and the cows and the women, and a great fear seized the milkmen. The wolves gathered themselves into groups of five and ten and twenty and thirty and a hundred, and ranged through the settlement, and the terror of them spread everywhere.

That terror was the whole point. Krishna did not mean to harm his own people; he meant to move them, as a herdsman moves a herd that has grazed one field down to the root. The fear the wolves carried would loosen the milkmen's grip on the ruined forest and carry them, at last, toward the green land on the Yamuna, where the grass still grew deep.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not argue the milkmen out of their home; he frightens them out of it. The wolves are not a punishment but an instrument — a gentle violence aimed at carrying his people from a spoiled place to a better one, the same hand that had beautified the forest now loosening its hold on them.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells this migration as Krishna conjuring wolves to frighten the milkmen into moving; the Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana instead attribute the move to omens and portents.
stories.hero_scene: Hundreds of dark-faced wolves streaming from the body of the seven-year-old Krishna, fanning out across the settlement of Vraja, as milkmen, cattle and women scatter in fear.

stories.title: Uddhava Remembers Krishna's Cowherd Childhood
stories.story:
Years later, when Uddhava looked back, what he remembered first was not a god but a boy.

He remembered the calves. There had been a time, he said, when Krishna went out among them day after day, surrounded by the young ones as he herded them, and sported in the groves along the Yamuna. The river lay green and quiet behind them, and the child moved at the heart of the herd while the calves pressed close around him, as if they knew him and had no wish to be anywhere else. To the people of Vraja he showed his childhood play, and they found it lovely to watch, the way one watches something that will not come again.

He remembered, too, the way Krishna had been in those days. A child who wept and laughed in the same hour, whose glance, when he looked up, had the bright boldness of a lion cub. It was not one mood but the whole of childhood that lived in him at once — tears and laughter turning into each other the way they only do in the very young. The cowherds never tired of watching it, because in him their own children's days seemed lit from within.

And he remembered the flute. When Krishna played, the cowherds forgot their work and stood listening. The sound gathered the people around him the way the calves gathered at his feet, and no one wanted the tune to end; it seemed to hold them all in one place, under the trees, until the last note let them go.

But the memory that stayed with Uddhava longest was the strangest one. Kamsa — the Bhoja king, Krishna's own cruel uncle — had never stopped sending his agents against the boy. They came as shape-shifters, demons who could take any form they chose, and they came into the groves of Vrindavan meaning to destroy him. Krishna dispelled them, Uddhava remembered, in sport — as easily as a child knocks aside his toys. There was no battle in it, and no fear. The same boy who herded calves and played the flute simply brushed aside whatever darkness came looking for him, and then went back to his play, as if nothing had come at all.

That was what Uddhava could not put out of his mind: that the tenderness and the power had been one thing. The child who wept and laughed among the calves was the same one before whom the demons melted away. It was the oldest memory he had of him, and it never dimmed. Whenever Uddhava spoke of Krishna in the years that followed, it was this boy he spoke of first — the child in the grove, with the calves and the flute, before the world knew him as anything else.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's memory holds the childhood and the godhood in a single breath: the same boy herding calves, weeping and laughing, and dispelling demons 'in sport, like toys.' The recollection finds the divine not in the miracles alone but in the tenderness of the ordinary day.
stories.next_story_tease: And among those remembered days was one that began more quietly than the rest, with a child left alone in a courtyard and two trees standing in the yard.

stories.title: Krishna Notices the Twin Arjuna Trees
stories.story:
The house was quiet, and for once the child was on his own.

His mother was deep in her household work — the endless round of churning, sweeping, tending the fire, keeping the day in order — and in the lull she had no eye to spare for him. So Krishna was left to himself, a small boy with the whole courtyard open before him and nothing to do but look.

And what he looked at, in that stillness, were the two arjuna trees.

They stood side by side at the edge of the ground, tall and straight, their trunks grown thick with years and their branches lacing together high overhead. To anyone else they were only trees — part of the furniture of the village, as ordinary as the wall or the well, the kind of thing no one ever really sees. But the child's eyes lingered on them, the way a child's eyes will linger on the one thing in the yard no one else notices, as if the trees were speaking to him in a language just below hearing.

They had not always been trees.

Once, long before, they had been two young men of the highest birth: Nalakuvara and Manigriva, sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth. They had moved among the guhyakas, the celestial attendants of their father's realm, rich and favoured beyond anything the earth could offer, and they had grown proud on that fortune. And then, in a single act of heedless pride, they had thrown it all away. A curse — the curse of the sage Narada — had brought them down from that height and fixed them here, rooted to the earth as two arjuna trees, their names and their story buried deep inside the wood.

That is what stood in the courtyard that day, though no one in the village knew it. The two trees were a secret wearing the shape of the ordinary, waiting, as trees do, with a patience no person could match.

And the child — the one child in all the world who could undo such a curse — stood looking at them, not yet knowing what he saw. Or perhaps, in the way children understand things without being told, knowing a great deal more than anyone around him guessed.

For now, the moment asked nothing of him. The trees stood, and the boy looked, and the house went on with its quiet work behind him. But something had been set between them, a recognition waiting for its hour. Whatever was to come — and something would come — would begin in that still, unremarkable moment, with a child and two trees and the space between them.
stories.reflection: The whole weight of the episode rests on a child's idle glance. The drama is built from stillness — a boy left alone in a courtyard, two trees, and a hidden history that will not stay hidden. What looks ordinary can carry a long past, waiting only to be seen.
stories.next_story_tease: What the two had done to earn such a fate — and whose curse had fixed them to the earth — was a story of its own.

stories.title: Narada Curses Nalakuvara and Manigriva
stories.story:
The two young men could not have chosen a worse moment to be proud.

Nalakuvara and Manigriva were the sons of Kubera, the lord of wealth, whose home was on Mount Kailasa, and they had never known a day of want. One day, drunk on the celestial wine called varuni, their eyes rolling with intoxication, they wandered down to the Ganga and into the water, where lotus groves grew thick along the bank. There they sported in the river with the celestial women, careless of everything but their own pleasure.

It happened that the divine sage Narada was passing that way. The women saw him first, and shame swept through them. Naked as they were, and dreading what a curse from such a sage could do, they drew their garments close and made themselves decent in an instant. But the two brothers, blinded by wine and by the pride of their riches, did not cover themselves. They saw the sage and did not bow. They stood where they were, as if their wealth made them untouchable.

Narada looked at them, and what he felt was not anger but a kind of grief. He began to speak.

The body, he said, that these two were so proud of — people call it divine, but in the end it is worms, and filth, and ashes. It comes from a father and a mother, common as any, and it returns to the unmanifest from which it arose. For a man whose eyes are blinded by the pride of riches, poverty is the best medicine, the sharpest eye-salve. A poor man is free of the stiff neck of ego; his body is lean with hunger, and he does not stand on his dignity. It is to the poor that the sages, who look on all beings with an equal eye, are drawn. And it is in that company that a man learns to want only the feet of Krishna.

Then Narada turned his words upon the two before him. These two, he said, are the sons of the world's protector, and yet they are sunk in darkness. Therefore let them stand as trees — rooted, motionless, unable to move a single step. But he did not wish them lost forever. It would not be for all time, he said. After a hundred years of the gods, they would come into the very presence of Krishna himself, and at his touch their long stillness would end and they would be set free.

So it fell out as the sage said. The two proud young men became twin arjuna trees, and their curse was also their cure — a long rooted silence in which the pride that had blinded them could slowly drain away, until the day a child came near them in a courtyard in Gokula.
stories.reflection: Narada's curse is framed not as revenge but as treatment. Pride, in his telling, is a kind of blindness, and poverty its sharpest cure; the sentence of tree-ness is softened by the promise of Krishna's touch, so that the punishment is turned toward release before it is even carried out.
stories.content_note: The episode involves intoxication and references to unclothed figures; it is told with restraint.

stories.title: The Cowherds Settle in Vrindavan
stories.story:
The road to Vrindavan was full long before the people reached it, because the cattle went first. A whole herd moved out ahead, hundreds of broad, slow backs, and behind them came the cowherds with their families and their carts, every horn and conch they owned blowing as they went, so that the dust of the track and the sound of it rose up together. It was not a flight, and not a festival. It was a village on the move.

The women rode in the carts, freshly adorned for the road, and in one cart Yasoda and Rohini sat side by side, the two mothers together. Krishna and Balarama were somewhere in the procession — among the boys who ran ahead and fell behind, or perched on the tail of a wagon, or lost in the warm dust beside the cattle. No one could say where they were at any given moment. That was simply the way of it with those two.

The carts carried more than people. They carried the whole weight of a household — cooking pots and bedding and bundles of grain, the old people who could not walk the whole way, and the small children too young to walk at all. But a cowherd's true wealth moved in front, on four legs, and no one drove the herd hard and no one left it behind.

They were bound for Vrindavan, a place the elders knew, a forest that stayed green and pleasant in every season. The journey was not long, and there was no ceremony about its end. The carts rolled in, the horns blew once more and fell quiet, and the cattle came to a stop.

Then the cowherds looked around, and understood why they had come.

The trees stood thick and cool, their shade lying across the ground like cloth. The hill of Govardhana rose to one side, low and broad, like a guardian set down to watch over the country. And the Yamuna ran past the edge of it all, its banks smooth with sand, the water moving quietly in the light. The old verses remember each of these things by name, because each of them mattered: the forest, the hill, the river.

They made their camp in a crescent of wagons, the way travellers have always made a wall of their carts and called it home. The cattle were loosed to drink, and settled into the grass with deep, satisfied sounds. The fires were lit, and their smoke went up straight into the still evening. The children, set down from the carts at last, ran the length of the new ground as though it had always been theirs.

And in a way it had. In Vrindavan the cowherds set down everything they owned and everything they loved. No one made a speech, and no one raised a flag. The wagons, the herds, the mothers and the boys and the two who were somehow more than boys — all of it came to rest inside that crescent, and the forest, the hill, and the river received them without a word.
stories.reflection: The settling of Vrindavan is told almost without event — a journey, an arrival, a camp — and that quietness is the point. Before any miracle or battle, there was this: a whole people on the road, and a place that received them without ceremony.
stories.next_story_tease: Settled in their new home, the boys would soon take up the herding of calves — and find an enemy waiting among them.

stories.title: Krishna Slays the Calf-Demon Vatsasura
stories.story:
Not long after the cowherds had settled in Vrindavan, the boys of the village were given a new piece of work. The calves had grown old enough to leave the pens, and it was time for them to be taken out to grass with the older herd. So the boys were set to watch over them. It was light work, and it suited them. Krishna and Balarama went out with the rest, and the days settled into an easy rhythm of sun and river and slow-moving cattle.

The pasture lay on the bank of the Yamuna, where the grass grew thick and the water was always near. All day the boys moved through it, and they did not keep watch in silence. The old verses remember how they passed the hours. Sometimes one of them played the flute while the others drifted closer to listen. Sometimes they flung their throwing-ropes at a mark on the ground, testing who could strike truest. And sometimes the two brothers squared off against each other, pawed the earth, and roared, and wrestled like a pair of young bulls while the other boys made a ring and shouted first for one side and then the other. It was play, and it held the long day together.

And it was into this quiet, sunlit routine that the demon came.

He was called Vatsasura. He did not come as himself. He took the shape of a calf — so young, so harmless-looking that no one would look twice — and he stepped in among the herd as though he had been born to it. Among all those grazing backs and twitching tails, one more calf was nothing at all. He moved through them slowly, waiting.

But Krishna saw him. It is the strange and wonderful thing about these early stories that he always sees. The moment the false calf edged close, he reached out, caught it by the hind legs, and took the tail in the same grip. Then he lifted the creature clean off the grass.

He whirled it. Around his head he swung it, once and again, gathering speed, and then he let it fly, and the creature in its stolen calf's body went tumbling through the air and struck a wood-apple tree with a force no living calf could have survived. It fell lifeless to the ground and lay still beneath the tree, in the very shape it had borrowed, and it did not rise again. Whatever the demon had meant to do to the boys, he never did it.

The boys stood astonished for a long, still moment. Then the wonder broke, and they shouted together, "Well done! Well done!"

The verses close on a line worth pausing over. These two, they say, had become calf-herders — and those same two were the keepers of all the worlds. The day's work looked small: a single false calf among a hundred real ones. But the hand that threw it was the hand that held everything. The herd went on grazing as though nothing had happened, and the boys went back to their watching, a little quieter than before.
stories.reflection: Krishna's strength shows itself first in the most ordinary work — watching calves on a riverbank. The story does not separate the boy who plays the flute and wrestles like a young bull from the keeper of all the worlds; they are the same pair of hands.
stories.content_note: A demon in calf form is flung against a tree and killed; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Kamsa had more than one creature at his command, and a greater one was already winging toward the pasture.

stories.title: Krishna Slays the Crane-Demon Bakasura
stories.story:
The days in Vrindavan had taken on a pattern by then: the boys led out the calves, the sun climbed, the river ran. But one morning they came to the pasture and found that it was not empty. Something stood there, huge and still, and as they drew near they saw what it was — a crane, but no crane that belonged to the river or the reeds. It was enormous, tall as a thing that had grown up out of the ground, and it stood planted on the grass, watching. The boys stopped where they were, and the calves bunched behind them and lowed, and for a long moment nothing moved on the riverbank. Then they understood that it was not a bird at all, but a demon who had taken the shape of a crane. Baka, the old verses call him, and they add that he was a friend of Kamsa's.

They had no time to warn one another. The great bird struck, and in a single motion it opened its long beak and swallowed Krishna whole.

The boys cried out. Balarama stood frozen, and the rest of them could only stare at the place where their friend had just been standing, and at the throat of the monstrous bird. They thought, in that black moment, that they had lost him. A demon had taken the child who never seemed afraid of anything, and the riverbank felt suddenly enormous and empty.

But inside the crane's belly, Krishna did not burn like a swallowed morsel. He burned the other way. He grew hot, like a fire set at the very root of the creature's palate, and the scorching spread upward, and the great crane, which had swallowed the boy to be rid of him, found it could not bear him for even a moment. Its beak gaped wide, and it flung him out again onto the grass — whole, unharmed, not even scorched himself. The boys' cries turned, in an instant, to something else.

Then the demon came at him, enraged and beating its wings, and Krishna did not wait for it to reach him. He took hold of the bird by the two halves of its long beak, one in each hand, and tore it apart the way a child splits a stalk of grass. The crane that had swallowed him fell broken to the ground, and did not move again.

The boys could hardly believe what their eyes had seen. They ran to Krishna as though he had come back to them from far away, and the verses say it with a simple, perfect image: it was as if their very breath, which had left their bodies when he vanished down that throat, now returned to them. And from the sky above, the dwellers of heaven — who had watched it all — let fall a shower of flowers, the blossoms drifting slowly down over the children, over the fallen demon, over the quiet water of the Yamuna. The herd grazed on as before, and the boys sat down in the grass to catch their breath, and after a while they led the calves home in the long, level light of evening.
stories.reflection: Bakasura swallows Krishna and discovers, too late, that he has taken in what he cannot contain. But the story's real center is the image of the boys' breath returning — what the demon meant to take, Krishna gives back.
stories.content_note: Krishna is swallowed by a demon crane and tears it apart; the violence is brief and not described in detail.

stories.title: Aghasura Becomes a Giant Python
stories.story:
There is a kind of grief that only wants to make more grief, and Aghasura had it. He was the younger brother of Putana and of Bakasura — the first of them had come to the cradle long ago and been destroyed, and the second had come to the pasture not many days since and been torn apart — and the loss of them sat in him like a splinter. The old verses say that Kamsa put him up to the deed. But they also say he needed little urging. He wanted revenge, and he knew exactly where to find it.

He did not go down to the village in his own shape. He grew. He stretched his body out and out until he was a python a yojana long and as thick as a hill, and he lay down across the path the boys took each day to the pasture, and he opened his mouth.

It was no ordinary mouth. His lower lip rested on the earth and his upper lip touched the clouds. The space between them was a cave, dark and deep, and his teeth rose like the peaks of a mountain range, so that the whole monstrous thing looked less like a living creature than like a piece of the country itself — a gorge, a cavern, a ridge of stone — lying open in the afternoon light.

That was his trick, and it worked. The boys came down the path with their calves and stopped short at the sight of it, and not one of them was afraid, because not one of them saw a snake. They saw a marvel.

"Look," they said to one another, "a mountain has lain down in the forest." And they argued over it the way children argue over a wonder. Was it a cave cut into the rock, or a cloud that had come down to rest, its edge reddened by the sun? The verses remember the whole happy, foolish debate — how they measured the thing with their eyes and gave it a hundred wrong names, how they stepped closer to peer into the deep shadows of it — while the creature they were praising lay silent and waiting. They even said, in their play, that if it tried to swallow them it would die as Baka had died. And they said it laughing, because they did not believe for a moment that it was alive at all.

Only Krishna knew. He heard their guesses, and he knew in the same instant what the thing was, and whose brother it was, and what it meant to do to him and to Balarama. And he made up his mind, there on the path, that the mouth which had opened to swallow his friends would not close on them.
stories.reflection: The horror of Aghasura lies in how well his disguise works: the boys praise the very mouth that would eat them. Deception here is not a lie told but a truth too strange to be believed, and only Krishna sees through the loveliness to the danger beneath.
stories.content_note: A demon takes the form of a vast python and lies in wait to swallow the boys; the danger is described, but no one is harmed in this episode.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna had recognized the demon — and he was about to step into its open mouth.
