stories.title: Krishna Kills Aghasura and Revives His Friends
stories.story:
Aghasura was a demon, and he had come to the forest in the shape of an immense python. The forest had gone quiet around him, as though the birds had understood before anyone else what lay stretched along the ground. The cowherd boys of Vrindavan, out with their calves, had gone into his open mouth, and now they lay inside him, alive but trapped, not yet swallowed. What had drawn them in, the account does not say; only that they had gone in, and not come out.

Krishna saw it, and the sight pierced him with pity. These were his friends, his own companions, and they were inside the belly of a demon, helpless, with no one in the world to turn to but him. He was amazed, too, at what fate had done. What use, he reasoned, was the life of this wretch? And how could the harm to these innocent ones be undone? Could both be accomplished at once, the death of the evil one and the saving of the good? He saw that it could, in a single stroke, and he did not hesitate. He walked into the demon's mouth.

The gods, watching from behind the clouds, cried out in fear. They had seen what a demon could do to a child, and they did not yet know that they were watching a god undo it.

Inside, Krishna grew. He grew until the demon's throat was blocked, until the great serpent could neither swallow nor breathe. He grew past its teeth and its throat, and the darkness inside it gave way before him. Its eyes bulged, and it writhed this way and that, and its vast body thrashed against the earth as the air was cut off from it. It had meant to hold the whole herd in its belly, and instead it found that it could not even draw a breath. And as its last breath left it, the boys and their calves, who had lain lifeless inside, Krishna raised up and led them out into the open air, alive again.

As the demon died, a great light rose from its body and stood blazing, filling all ten directions with its splendour, like a second moon or the sun coming up at night, and the light entered Krishna.

Then the sky broke into sound. The gods rained flowers down. The gandharvas sang and the apsaras danced, and the brahmins raised their hymns, and all of heaven celebrated the boys' return. And where the demon had fallen, only its dried skin remained, stretched across the ground of Vrindavan, a wonder that would not soon be forgotten. The boys looked at it for a long time before they gathered their calves and started for home.
stories.reflection: The story's emphasis falls not on the killing but on the great light that leaves the demon and enters Krishna, and on the boys walking out alive. Even for an enemy, the account holds out release rather than destruction.
stories.content_note: A demon in python form swallows the cowherd boys and calves; he is overcome without graphic detail.

stories.title: Brahma Steals the Calves and Boys
stories.story:
Brahma, the lotus-born, had seen it all. From beyond the world he had watched a small cowherd child walk into the open mouth of a python-demon, and he had watched the same child lead his friends out again, alive. He had seen the great light leave the dead demon and enter the boy. The wonder of it would not leave him.

He was the maker of the worlds, the firstborn. He had shaped the stars and set the seasons turning, and nothing in his creation was supposed to surprise him. And yet here was a thing in Vrindavan that his own handiwork could not explain — a village child who had stepped into death and come out holding his friends by the hand. Could it be what it seemed to be? The verses say he wanted to see the beauty of that greatness again, and more besides, and that he wanted to be certain.

So he waited, and the chance came quickly. One day the boys were at their play on a sandbank by the river. It was an ordinary day of the kind Vrindavan knew well — the calves grazing near at hand, the boys spreading out their meal and eating together, the sun warm on the water. In a careless moment the calves strayed, and Krishna went after them alone, to bring them back. The sandbank lay quiet behind him, and the boys, whose sudden fear Krishna had just quieted with a word, were at ease. What was there to fear, with Krishna only a little way off?

And into that quiet Brahma moved. It was not a violent thing. One moment the cowherd boys were there, and the next they were gone, and the calves with them — gathered up and hidden away by a power no one in Vrindavan could see or name. No footfall, no sound; the river went on running as if nothing had been there at all. The creator carried them off as easily as a man gathers a handful of seeds, and set them down in a place beyond the reach of any searching eye. Then he waited to see what the child would do.

When Krishna came back to the sandbank, the river was the only sound. No boys. No calves. The food they had been eating lay where it had been set down, and no one was left to eat it. He knew at once what had happened, and who had done it, for nothing is hidden from him. And yet, the old verses say, he searched. He went into the deep forest and looked for them, and he did not find them, because they were not there to be found. The all-knowing one went looking for what he already knew, and let the question hang unanswered in the air.

So the day ended with the sandbank empty and the Lord of all worlds standing alone at the water's edge, knowing everything and letting the thing play out a little longer. The mothers of Vrindavan were about to learn that their sons had vanished. And Krishna was about to show the creator something he had not thought to look for.
stories.reflection: Brahma's test is born not of malice but of wonder: the maker of the universe, unable to account for what he has seen, hides the children away simply to understand what is standing before him. The episode quietly reverses the roles, so that the one who tests is himself the one about to be taught.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna would not leave the boys' mothers to grieve for long.
stories.hero_scene: An empty sandbank by the river at dusk, with the boys' half-eaten meal spread on the ground and the boy Krishna standing alone at the water's edge — the only figure left in a landscape from which every calf and cowherd boy has vanished.

stories.title: Krishna Becomes Every Calf and Boy
stories.story:
One day the calves and the cowherd boys of Vrindavan vanished, and no one could say where they had gone. The boys had walked out to the pasture that morning with their staffs and their flutes, driving the calves before them, and they simply did not come back. As the afternoon stretched toward evening the mothers stood in their doorways, listening. The cows shifted in their pens and lowed into the quiet for calves that did not answer. The whole village seemed to have lost its young at once.

Krishna had been with the boys, and he knew exactly where they had gone. He could have undone the thing in a moment, set every child and every calf back in its place with a word. But he chose a gentler way, one meant not merely to repair what was missing but to fill the waiting hearts of the mothers and the cows.

He became them. Standing at the edge of the pasture, Krishna expanded himself into every vanished calf and every vanished boy. Into each small body he entered, taking on not only the face and the limbs but everything that made that child that particular child — his staff and his horn, his flute and the leaf he carried, his ornaments and his clothes, and deeper than these, his temperament, his speech, his name, his age, the very way he walked and played. All of it, the old verses say, became full of the Lord.

Then each boy gathered his own calf and walked home to his own house. In the cow-pens the cows hurried forward, calling to their calves with a lowing that filled the evening air, and the calves ran to them as though they had never been away. In the houses the mothers rose at the first note of a flute, ran out, and lifted their sons into their arms. They held them close and would not put them down, kissing them, washing them, dressing them, marking their foreheads with tilak and setting food before them, asking nothing, needing no answer. The lost thing had come back, and that was all they required.

And the strange and tender thing was this: their love did not simply return. It grew. The cows loved their calves, and the women loved their sons, with a warmth greater than they had felt before — because what they held in their arms was not their own child but the Lord himself, playing the part of each one, and not a soul suspected it.

So it went, not for a day or a week, but for a full year. Morning after morning the boys who were Krishna drove the calves who were Krishna out to the pastures, and evening after evening they came home to mothers who, without knowing it, were loving God as their own. The affection in those homes climbed daily, the way a vine climbs, leaf by leaf, in a season no one counts. By the end of that year the mothers had been given something no one could have asked for: a whole year of loving, without knowing it, the very one for whom their love had always been meant.

It is a strange and beautiful picture. The mothers believed they were pouring their love into their own sons, and in one sense they were; in another, they were giving it straight into the hands of the one who had come into the world to receive it. Krishna did not set the world right by snapping his fingers. He set it right by becoming the thing those mothers loved, and letting their love find him where he stood, hidden in a hundred doorways, smiling up at a hundred faces that had no idea who they held.
stories.reflection: The episode turns on a quiet paradox: the mothers' love deepened precisely when its object was Krishna, though they did not know it. Love, the story suggests, is not made less real for being offered in ignorance — it is simply received by the one who was always its true object.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet a wildfire was soon to sweep through the forest toward the herd.

stories.title: Brahma Falls at Krishna's Feet
stories.story:
To Brahma, only a moment had passed. In Vrindavan, a year.

When the creator came back to look for the calves and boys he had hidden away, he found them exactly where they had always been — playing on the sandbank, tending their calves, running home at dusk to mothers who held them as though they had been gone a long while. The cows hurried from their pens at the sound of lowing, and the calves ran to them, and the whole herd went about its evening as if nothing had ever disturbed it. And the love in those homes — the verses say it had grown deeper than before. The cowherd men and women doted on their children with a tenderness that surprised even themselves, and no one could have said why.

Brahma could not tell the difference between what he had hidden and what he saw now. The boys he had carried off — where were they? And these here, who were they? He stood a long while turning it over, and the more he thought the less he understood. He reached for the very power of illusion that had hidden the children in the first place, and tried to use it again — and the illusion merely looked back at him. It was, the verses say, like a firefly's light at noon, or a darkness trying to settle in the mist of a morning that is already gone.

Then, before his eyes, the children changed. Every cowherd boy on the sandbank appeared no longer as a boy but as a four-armed form, holding a conch and a discus, a mace and a lotus. On each chest shone the shrivatsa mark, and on each arm glinted armlets and bracelets, and from head to foot each form was draped in garlands of fresh tulsi leaves. Each face smiled like moonlight, with a sidelong glance full of kindness, and each form was pure being, pure knowledge, and pure, endless joy. Around them, the verses say, stood all the worlds and all the powers that move them, from the first gods down to the last blade of grass, and every one of them in its own form. Where a crowd of village children had been playing, there now stood an endless company of the Lord himself — and Brahma, who had made the universe, stood speechless before it.

Brahma's senses stood still. The verses say the eleven doors of his perception froze where they were, and he could do nothing but look, unable to say what he was seeing. It was too much for him, and then it was hidden — for Krishna saw what was happening, and gently, as one draws a curtain, he covered Brahma's sight. When the creator opened his eyes again, it was like a man waking from the dead. The vision was gone. He looked around, and there was the ordinary world, men and animals sitting together with no sign of their natural enmity. And there, before him, stood a small boy with a morsel of food in his hand, searching for his friends exactly as he had been searching before, playing the part of a cowherd child as if nothing at all had happened.

Brahma came down from his swan and threw himself on the ground like a golden rod. He touched Krishna's feet with the tips of his four crowns, and he bathed them with his tears.
stories.reflection: Brahma came to test, and found himself tested. The vision of countless four-armed forms is overwhelming, but what finally undoes him is the plainness that follows it — a child with a morsel of food, looking for his friends. Krishna's true hiding place, the story suggests, is not the spectacle but the ordinary.
stories.next_story_tease: But Brahma had not yet finished speaking.

stories.title: Brahma's Hymn of Forgiveness
stories.story:
Brahma did not rise quickly. He lay at Krishna's feet, and the words came out of him one after another, like water finding its way downhill.

"This body of yours," he began, "is made of your own will. It is not made of matter, as mine is. Who can understand it?" He said that those who set aside the struggle to know, and simply bow and listen, are the ones the truth comes to meet; while those who chase understanding alone, throwing devotion away, are like men threshing empty husks — all their labour, and nothing left in the hand. Even the purest-hearted, he said, even the great seers, cannot measure your greatness, for it is not the kind of thing that can be measured.

Then his voice changed, and he came to what he had really come to say. "Look at my foolishness, Lord," he said. "I was born of passion, and in my ignorance I thought myself a lord apart from you. Forgive me." He measured himself against what stood before him and found the measuring absurd. "Where am I," he asked, "a little body of seven hand-spans, shut inside this shell of a universe — and where is your greatness, in the pores of whose skin whole worlds drift, more worlds than I can count?"

He remembered the day's unfolding, and named it aloud. "Today you have shown me your maya," he said. "First you were one. Then you were all the cowherd boys and calves. Then you were an endless company of four-armed forms, and I worshipped you along with everything that lives. Then you were as many universes. And what remained, when all of it was seen, was only the one — the unlimited."

He spoke, too, of the world itself, and how strange it was. “This whole world,” he said, “is as unreal as a dream, and full of sorrow — and yet through your maya it shines as if it were real, resting on you alone.”

He called him by his oldest name. "You are Narayana," he said, "the Self of every being, the witness of every world. It was from your navel, when the worlds had dissolved into water, that all of this rose again. Who among gods and sages and men and beasts can say where you have come from?"

And then he marvelled, not at his own smallness but at the good fortune of Vrindavan. "How fortunate are the women who fed you at their breast as if you were their own child, tasting in your milk the nectar of the gods. How fortunate are the people of Nanda's pasture, where you have chosen to live — whose very dust, the dust of your feet, the Vedas go searching for and never find enough of."

At last he came to the end of the hymn, and to the one thing he had come to ask. He praised the one who is the joy of the Vrishni lotus, who makes the earth and the cows and the brahmins flourish. "Give me leave, Krishna," he said. "You know everything there is to know." And he walked three times around the child, and bowed, and went back to his own realm, leaving behind him a hymn that has not been forgotten since.
stories.reflection: The hymn is remarkable because it is the creator himself measuring his limits. It does not argue Krishna's greatness from above; it works from below, setting a seven-span body against pores that hold universes, and finding that the only honest posture left is praise and a request to be allowed to go.
stories.next_story_tease: And the boys, who had been hidden all the while, would sit down to their meal as if nothing had happened.

stories.title: The Year That Was a Moment
stories.story:
When Krishna had given Brahma leave and the creator was gone, the Lord turned back to the sandbank, and the boys and their calves were there again, just as they had been, as though no hand had ever carried them away.

He set everything back as it had been. He did not announce it, and there was no fanfare and no explanation. He simply returned what had been taken, and the world closed over the gap the way water closes over a stone.

And this is the strangest part of the whole affair. A year had passed — a full year, in which the cows had grazed and the seasons had turned and the mothers of Vrindavan had poured their love out over children who, though they did not know it, had never truly been away, and the calves had grown, and the river had risen and fallen again. But the boys knew nothing of it. The whole year sat upon them as lightly as a dream that vanishes the moment the eyes open. Their minds, the verses say, were covered by maya, and what they had lost, they could not remember losing. Even the days they had spent hidden away, and the friend who had hidden them, and the year that had gone by — all of it was gone from them, as if it had never been.

"Welcome back!" they cried when they saw Krishna, as if he had only just stepped away. "You returned quickly!" They did not ask where he had been, because as far as they knew he had never left them at all, and that certainty was its own quiet mercy.

The calves came wandering back to the boys as though they had only just strayed, and no one thought to wonder at it. Krishna smiled, and sat down among them, and ate. They finished the meal they had left unfinished, as though the afternoon had never been broken off. Then they gathered up their things and started home, and the forest went with them; he called to the calves as they went, and the calves followed the sound of his voice — Krishna decked in peacock feathers and flowers and the bright earth-colours of the woods, his flute sounding, the boys singing his praises as they walked, and the eyes of the gopis, watching from the doorways, turning glad at the sight of them.

And as they came into the village they had a story to tell — how, that very day, the son of Yashoda and Nanda had slain a great serpent. They carried its dried skin with them as proof, the way a hunter carries home the hide, and no one who saw it could doubt the tale.
stories.reflection: The tenderest detail is the return to the story the boys were telling before they vanished — the great serpent, slain 'that very day.' A year of their lives passed without them, and they pick up the thread exactly where they dropped it. Time, the story suggests, is not one thing for everyone, and what Krishna guards can be given back whole.
stories.next_story_tease: And soon the boys would set their hearts on a palm grove whose sweet fruit no one had ever dared to eat.

stories.title: The Fruit No One Had Ever Eaten
stories.story:
The cowherd boys had been out since morning, moving with their herds through the woods around Vrindavan, and the afternoon had settled into the slow, warm rhythm they knew well — the calves grazing, the boys at their games in the shade, the sun high and steady. It was an ordinary day, and it would have stayed an ordinary day, but for the wind. When it turned, it carried a scent they knew at once, and it stopped them in the middle of their play. The calves went on grazing, but the boys stood still, lifting their heads like animals catching a trail. Sweet, heavy, faint as a half-remembered dream, the smell drifted from the edge of the forest, from a place they all knew and none of them entered.

A little way off stood the palm grove, the talavana. In every season its trees let fall fruit so ripe and fragrant that the smell of it perfumed the air for a long way around. The verses say the fruit kept falling, and lay fallen, in such abundance that no one could have gathered it all — it never stopped coming. Yet it lay where it fell, season after season, untouched. The ground beneath the palms was littered with it, soft and over-ripe, and no hand had ever gathered a single piece. No one in Vrindavan had ever tasted it.

The reason was not hard to find. The grove belonged to a demon named Dhenuka, who had taken the form of a donkey, and his kin were there with him, as fierce as he was. He was immensely strong, and he had made men his food, and so people were afraid of him and kept their distance. Even the grown men, who grazed their herds across every other corner of the forest, gave that grove a wide berth, and no one would walk past it alone. The fruit ripened and dropped and rotted on the ground, and the boys looked at it only from far off, while the fragrance drifted over them and tormented them.

That day the torment grew too much to bear. The smell came again, sweet and insistent, and the boys could not turn away from it. They came to Krishna and Balarama and spoke all at once, their words tumbling over one another. "Rama! Rama, mighty-armed! Krishna, destroyer of the wicked!" they cried. They told them of the grove, of the fruit that fell and fell and was never eaten, and of the fierce donkey who guarded it and had made men his food. Their minds, the verses say, were greedy with the fragrance. "Give us that fruit," they begged.

Krishna heard his friends out, and heard the longing in their voices. He did not need to be persuaded, and he did not stop to weigh the danger. What the verses say of him is simple: hearing his friends' words, he wished only to do what would please them. So the two brothers set out for the palm grove, the boys following close behind, and the sweet smell of the forbidden fruit growing stronger with every step they took toward it.
stories.reflection: The boys do not try to take the fruit themselves; they know exactly where strength and protection lie, and they ask for what they want with a trust so complete it is almost childlike. The fragrance stands in for every desire that is lovely and safe-looking but guarded by something no one has dared to face.
stories.next_story_tease: But the guardian of the grove would not give up its fruit so easily.
stories.hero_scene: The cowherd boys clustered around Krishna and Balarama at the edge of the palm grove, pointing toward palms heavy with ripe fruit, the sweet fragrance hanging in the warm air as the brothers set out toward the forbidden trees.

stories.title: Balarama and the Donkey Demon
stories.story:
For a long while the two brothers had moved with the cowherds and their herds through the forests around Vrindavan, and the days had a settled, easy rhythm. But the palm grove had always stood apart from that rhythm — a place the herds were never taken, a place the boys had only ever pointed at from a distance and hurried past. Now, with the boys' request still fresh in the air, the brothers did not hesitate at its edge. The trees were loaded with ripe fruit, the smell of it hanging thick in the still air, and Balarama walked straight to the nearest palm and laid his arms to its trunk. He shook it, and the ripe fruit came down in a shower.

He moved from tree to tree, and each one he shook let go of its fruit, so that the ground began to fill with it, the fruit striking the earth in a steady, sweet rain. The boys must have laughed at the sound — the soft, quick drumming of fruit striking fruit, the first time in anyone's memory that the grove had given anything away. For a little while the grove seemed almost innocent, nothing in it but sunlight and palms and the smell of ripe fruit.

But the grove had a keeper, and he heard the noise. In that pleasing grove dwelt the fierce demon Dhenuka, who fed on the flesh of deer, and the crashing of the falling fruit called him out of the deep trees. He came rushing through the palms in a great passion, in his donkey's form, huge and furious, and he did not pause to measure his enemy or to cry a warning. He fell upon Balarama and struck at him with his hind legs, kicking out with all the strength in him.

Balarama caught him by the hind legs. The verses say he whirled the donkey round with a single hand, as easily as play, until the creature expired, and then dashed him against a great palm tree. The tree, struck by that huge-headed body, trembled from crown to root, and the blow shook down fruit like rain poured upon the earth by the wind. Dhenuka fell lifeless to the ground.

The demon who had made men his food, whose very name had kept the whole of Vrindavan out of this grove, lay dead at the foot of a tree he had guarded all his days. It was no wonder, the verses add, for the one who did it is the infinite Lord of all the worlds. The boys watched in silence, and slowly the grove grew quiet again, until there was nothing left stirring in it but the last of the falling fruit.
stories.reflection: There is a strange gentleness in how the verse describes it: Balarama does not labor against Dhenuka, he simply catches him and lets the demon's own fury carry him to his end. The thing that had kept everyone away for so long turns out to be no match for a boy's ease.
stories.tradition_note: The sources differ on the details: the Bhagavata Purana has Balarama shake down the palms and make the kill himself, while the Vishnu Purana has both brothers shake the trees and names Rama (Balarama) alone as the slayer.
stories.content_note: A demon in donkey form is whirled and dashed against a palm tree; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Dhenuka's kin came rushing to avenge him.

stories.title: The Grove Opened to Everyone
stories.story:
The grove did not stay quiet for long. Dhenuka's kin, the other demons who had shared his form and his appetite, heard what had happened, and they came rushing to avenge him. They came not one or two but in a body, the whole fierce kindred of Dhenuka, their hooves drumming on the earth as they poured through the palms. They must have seen the fruit scattered over the ground and the great tree still trembling, and still they came, rage pressing them forward where fear had kept everyone else away for so long. They had guarded this grove as fiercely as their fallen kinsman, and they meant to keep it.

They came all at once, charging at Krishna and Balarama from every side. The brothers did not retreat, and they did not prepare for a long fight. The verses say they moved as if at play, without effort or hurry, and flung the charging donkeys lifeless among the palm trees, one after another, until the last of them lay still. There was no battle to it, only a clearing away, the way a hand sweeps fallen leaves from a path — and the demons, who had been terror itself to everyone who lived nearby, were no more than leaves before it.

When it was over, the grove lay strewn with the lifeless bodies of the demons, and the ground, already deep in the fruit Balarama had shaken down, was thick with both. What had been a place of fear was only a quiet grove again, silent but for the wind moving through the palms. The terror that had hung over it for so long was gone, and in its place there was only the smell of ripe fruit and the shade of the trees.

The gods and the wise, the verses say, heard of the great deed and rejoiced at it. And below, in the grove itself, something simpler and longer-lasting began. The people, their fear gone, came in and ate the palm fruit at last — the fruit that had fallen year after year, untouched and uneaten, now gathered and tasted freely, by anyone who wished it, children and elders alike. The cattle, too, grazed where they had never before dared to venture, cropping the new grass in the shade of the palms, and the grove that had once been spoken of only in warnings became a place people walked through without a second thought.

There was no guardian left to keep anyone out, and so the grove, for the first time, belonged to everybody. Krishna, the verses close, stood among them with his eyes like lotus petals, and the sound of his name and his deeds went out into the world as something auspicious to hear.
stories.reflection: The abundance was always there, falling to the ground season after season; what had kept it out of reach was not scarcity but fear. Once the fear is gone, nothing else changes and everything changes — the same fruit, the same grove, now open to everyone.
stories.content_note: Several demons are flung lifeless among the palms; the violence is brief and not described in detail.

stories.title: Krishna Swallows the Forest Fire
stories.story:
Night had settled over Vraja, and the settlement slept. The cattle lay still in the dark, the cowherds and their families had given themselves to rest after the long day's grazing, and the forest stood quiet around them all, breathing its cool breath over the roofs and the sleeping herds. It was the deep, trusting sleep of people who had never had reason to fear the night, and the forest had always been their shelter. Nothing in that stillness warned of what was coming.

Then, from the dry heart of the woods, a fire rose. A blazing forest fire, feeding on the parched grass and the undergrowth, and it did not stay where it was born. It came toward Vraja from every side at once, a wall of flame closing in on the sleeping settlement, until there was no direction left to turn that was not burning. Wherever a frightened eye looked, there was the glow of it, and the crackle of it filled the night like a voice, and the heat arrived before the flames like a warning that came too late. The dry grass and the undergrowth went up as if the forest had been waiting to burn, and the smoke rose thick and black against the dark sky.

The people woke to heat and light and smoke. They were scorched where they lay, and terror seized them, and there was no path out, for the fire pressed in from every side. They did the only thing they knew to do. They cried out, all of them together, into the roaring dark: "Krishna! Krishna! O greatly fortunate one! O Rama of boundless power! We are your own people, your friends — save us from this terrible fire, this fire that no one can cross, this fire like the one that will end all things!"

The verses say the Lord of the world looked on the distress of his own people. He did not rebuke them for their fear, and he did not send them away. He simply took the fire into himself and drank it up, the whole of it, the flames that had closed around Vraja on every side, until nothing was left burning in the night but the memory of the heat. What had been a wall of destruction was gone, as if it had never risen. The people, who a moment before had stood helpless before the flames, now saw only darkness and the unchanged shapes of their own homes.

The village stood whole. The dark came back over the trees, cool and still, and the people found themselves alive in it, in the silence after the roar, breathing air that no longer stung, wrapped in a night that no longer burned.
stories.reflection: The villagers are shown in their ordinary fear, calling out like people who have nowhere else to turn, and the answer they receive is not a lesson but a rescue. Divine power here is not spectacle; it is the simple act of making a place safe again for the people who sleep in it.
stories.content_note: A forest fire threatens the sleeping settlement; the danger is real but no one is harmed.

stories.title: Pralamba Joins the Games in Disguise
stories.story:
The cowherd boys of Vrindavan were not unused to strangers. Travelers passed through the forest, and boys from the neighboring villages sometimes drifted over to watch their games. But there was something about the new boy that none of them could quite name. He appeared at the edge of their play without anyone noticing him arrive, smiling easily, and before long he was standing among them as though he had always been there.

Krishna and Balarama were tending the herd in the forest, and the days were full of the games cowherd boys invent to pass the time — running and leaping and wrestling, calling the cows by name, weaving little ornaments of grass and wild flowers. The stranger slipped into all of it without effort. He laughed at their jokes and kept pace in their races, and the boys, generous as children are, took him for a friend. There was no reason to look twice at him; he was only another boy with a garland of wild flowers, quick with a jest, easy in a race. That was the whole art of the thing.

He was no friend. He was a demon named Pralamba, an asura who had come in the shape of a cowherd for a single purpose: to seize the boys and destroy the two brothers whose growing fame had begun to trouble the powerful. Adorned with wild flowers and wearing the easy manner of a milk-boy, he moved among them studying their weaknesses, casting dreadful looks at the brothers when he thought no one was watching, and waiting for his moment. The other boys saw only a pleasant newcomer. Pralamba saw prey.

Krishna saw everything. The verses are plain on this point: though he knew the stranger for what he was, the all-seeing Lord welcomed his friendship. He did not cry out, did not warn the others, did not tear the disguise away. He returned Pralamba's smile with the same quiet friendliness, and let the demon believe his trick had worked. And in his heart he resolved what must be done with him.

So when the afternoon grew long, Krishna — who knew every game the cowherds played, and how to turn a game to his purpose — called the boys together and proposed something new. They would play the riding game, he told them, carrying one another on their shoulders and racing the way the cowherds did. The boys clapped and cheered and rushed to pair off, and Pralamba, delighted at the chance to draw close to the brothers, smiled his borrowed smile and took his place among them. The trap, had he known how to look for it, was already closing around him.

Krishna watched him move into position, and let him.
stories.reflection: What is striking is how unhurried Krishna is. He knows the demon for what he is and does not flinch or warn; he simply receives the danger as calmly as a host receives a guest, and lets the deception run its course until it turns against the deceiver. The disguised enemy is never as hidden as he believes.
stories.next_story_tease: In the game that followed, the demon would seize his chance — and meet the brother whose weight he could not carry.

stories.title: Balarama Slays the Demon Pralamba
stories.story:
The riding game was a simple one, the kind children everywhere have always played: one boy hoisted another onto his shoulders, and they raced, and the one who lost carried the winner. Krishna and Balarama joined in with the rest. The verses say that when Sridama and the other strong boys of the herd stood on Balarama's side, even Krishna was defeated, and good-naturedly he took Sridama on his back. Laughter spread across the clearing as the boys staggered under one another's weight.

Pralamba had chosen to carry Balarama. To anyone watching, it looked like an unlucky draw, for Balarama was no light burden. But the demon had made the choice himself, and for his own reasons. All through the games he had studied the two brothers, casting his dreadful looks at them, and he had concluded that Krishna was beyond his reach, too dangerous to touch. The elder brother, he decided, was the one to take. So with Balarama on his shoulders, Pralamba began to move — not back toward the Bhandira tree where the others were gathering, but away, quickly and quietly, in the opposite direction.

At first Balarama thought little of it. But the demon's steps were swift, and the laughter of the other boys faded behind them. Then the shoulders beneath him began to swell. The figure he was riding grew — hugely, hideously — until it was no longer a cowherd boy at all but a great asura in his true form, tall as a tree, dressed in gold and blazing with ornaments, his eyes like chariot wheels and a crown upon his head, and the earth sank under the weight of his feet. He had thrown off his disguise and was carrying Balarama away through the sky like a storm-cloud carrying the moon. For a moment even Balarama, the plow-bearer, was startled.

Then his mind steadied. "Krishna," he called, "I am being carried off by this great demon, who has thrown aside his illusion and shown his real form. How shall I overcome him?"

Krishna, watching from the clearing, answered him with a smile. He knew, he said, what Balarama truly was; the one being carried was not the weaker of the two. He told his brother to remember his own strength and not to fear.

So Balarama did. He let himself be carried a little longer, gathering himself, and then he raised his fist — a fist the verses compare to a thunderbolt — and brought it down once upon the demon's head. The skull shattered. Pralamba fell from the sky and lay dead upon the earth like a toppled mountain, blood running from his mouth, and the cowherd boys came running and saw him there, slain by Balarama's single blow.

The danger was over as suddenly as it had come, and the brothers turned back toward their herd and their friends, unhurried, as though nothing very remarkable had happened at all.
stories.reflection: Balarama's moment of fear matters. Even the strong are allowed a heartbeat of alarm before they remember what they are; what follows is not a struggle but a single, settled blow. The story keeps its power precisely because it does not pretend the danger was never real.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha adds that the celestials gave Balarama the name Baladeva in honour of this feat, and the Vishnu Purana tells the death somewhat differently — Balarama laughing as he squeezes the demon with his knees and beats his head and face with his fists. This account follows the Bhagavata Purana, where the demon falls to a single blow.
stories.content_note: The demon's death is described briefly; the fall is restrained.
stories.next_story_tease: But a fiercer danger than any demon was about to find the herd among the tall reeds.

stories.title: A Fire in the Munja Grass
stories.story:
The herd did not mean to wander. Cows and goats and buffaloes are creatures of appetite, and that day the cowherd boys were deep in their games — running and leaping and wrestling on the grass, their calls ringing through the trees — and no one was watching the grazing line. So the cattle drifted, from one grove to the next, cropping as they went, until the forest had closed behind them and the boys finally looked up to find the clearing empty.

Krishna, Balarama and the other cowherds called for the herd and heard nothing back. The afternoon that had been so full of games suddenly felt very large and very still. They spread out and began to search, the way people who know the land search — reading the ground itself. Here the grass had been cropped short by grazing mouths; there it had been cut and trampled by hooves. Here, pressed into the soft earth, a line of hoof-prints led away into the trees. The boys followed the trail the way one follows a dropped thread, deeper and deeper into the wood, and the longer they searched, the deeper the forest's silence grew around them.

The trail led them into a dense thicket of munja grass — tall, sharp-bladed reeds that grew higher than a man and hid whatever moved among them. Deep in that green tangle they found the herd at last: the cattle lost and lowing, turning in circles, no longer sure of the way back. The boys pushed in after them, and Krishna called out to the cows, his voice deep and full, like a cloud gathering before rain. The frightened animals pricked their ears at the sound and began to quiet.

And then the fire came.

Smoke rose first, a grey smudge lifting above the trees, and then the flames themselves, with the wind at their back. It began, the verses say, as if by accident — a wildfire with smoke for its banner, springing up around them on every side, the destroyer of all that lived in the forest. The wind drove it forward. It ate through the dry grass and raced from tree to tree, crackling and roaring, and the heat of it pressed in on the boys and the cattle from all directions. The cows lowed in terror and pressed together, and the boys, who a moment before had been searching and calling, now stood ringed by flame with nowhere left to run.

They did the only thing left to do. They cried out — "Krishna! Krishna! Great hero! O Rama, whose strength never fails!" — the names of the two brothers rising above the roar of the burning grass.

And the fire kept coming.
stories.reflection: The danger here is not a demon but something as ordinary as wind and dry grass — which is exactly what makes it frightening. The boys are not weak or foolish; they do everything right, and still the fire surrounds them. Sometimes the test is simply to be where there is no way out, and to know whom to call.
stories.next_story_tease: The fire was closing in — and then Krishna told them to shut their eyes.

stories.title: Krishna Swallows the Wildfire and Saves the Herd
stories.story:
The fire came without warning, and it came from every side at once. One moment the cowherd boys were out in the Vrindavan woods with their cattle, the afternoon hot and still around them, the grass dry from a long stretch of sun; the next the grass was alight, and the flames were running toward them like a closing hand. They had spent the day as they always spent it, driving the herd from one pasture to the next, the calves at the cows' heels, and now the woods themselves had turned against them.

The boys had nowhere to turn. The smoke bent the trees and darkened the sky, the cattle lowed and bunched together in the middle of the clearing, and the boys, who were only children, saw the fire lean in toward them from all around. It was not the slow, watchful fire of a hearth. It moved with a roar, and the dry grass fed it as fast as it could burn. They called out to Krishna, who was among them, and their cry was simple: surely those who belong to you, Krishna, do not deserve to perish like this.

Krishna did not argue with them and did not run. He told them not to fear. Close your eyes, he said, and do not open them until I tell you. And they did. They did not ask him how, or why, or whether it would work; they simply shut their eyes, the way a child shuts them when a game requires it, except that this was no game. They stood in the middle of the burning forest, the roar of the fire all around them and the heat on their faces, and not one of them opened his eyes. It was trust, plain and simple, and it was all he asked of them.

What happened next none of them saw. Krishna drew the raging fire into his mouth and drank it down, the whole of it, flame by flame, until the heat and the roar and the smoke were gone. When at last he told them to open their eyes, they were not standing in the burning forest at all. They were at Bhandira, safe, and their cattle stood with them, and not one of them was hurt. There was no smell of smoke left in the air, only the lowing of the cattle, settling.

The boys looked at one another, and at the trees around them, and then at Krishna, and they could find no words for it. They had walked into a ring of fire and had come out of it, and it had cost them nothing but the closing of their eyes. The account says only this: it was his yoga, his power, accomplished by his own maya. It does not explain it further, and perhaps no explanation is wanted.

And then, as if nothing at all had happened, the afternoon went on. The herd was whole, the boys picked up their day where they had left it, and they were home before dark. When they tried, later, to tell the elders what had happened, the words would not come out straight, and the elders smiled and let it go.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is that it is told almost without explanation. Krishna asks for nothing from the boys but the closing of their eyes, and the fire is gone before they open them; the story names the power behind it and then returns, without comment, to an ordinary afternoon.
stories.content_note: A forest fire briefly surrounds the cowherd boys and their cattle; no one is harmed.

stories.title: The Monsoon Pastures
stories.story:
The rains had come to Vrindavan, and the forest had answered them. Where the ground had been dry and tired, there was now green; the trees stood heavy with ripening dates and jambu fruit, and water ran bright in the hollows. For weeks the herd had moved through brown grass and dust; now every hollow held water and every tree threw shade. Everywhere the wood stirred back to life, and the creatures that lived in it moved about in a kind of quiet delight. The verses call it the best of forests in the rains, and the boys could see why. It was into this world, washed clean and full, that Krishna and Balarama led the herd.

The cows went slowly, and for a good reason — their udders were heavy with milk, so that they walked with the careful, swaying gait of creatures carrying more than they can give all at once. The forest itself seemed pleased to receive them: the trees let fall their honey-sweet blossoms as they passed, and the deer and the birds went about their own business without alarm, as though the boys and their herd were simply part of the season. There was no watchfulness in the wood that day, no sense of anything to guard against — only the season doing what the season does.

When a sudden shower broke, the boys did what anyone who knows the forest does — they took shelter under a spreading tree, or in the mouth of a cave where the rain could not reach, and stood there listening to the water on the leaves. And when the shower passed and the sun came back out over the wet foliage, the whole world smelled of earth and green things. The sweetness that dripped from the trees hung in the air with the freshness of the rain, and the delighted forest-dwellers went back to their business as though the boys were only more of the wood.

It was then that they ate. They had brought the simplest of meals — curd and rice — and they set it out on a flat stone at the water's edge and sat down around it together. They had been walking since first light, and the food tasted of the walking, and of being young and hungry in the open air. They sat on the green grass with the river at their backs, the cows grazing close by, and ate without hurry, the way boys eat when nothing in the world is waiting for them. There was nothing more to the feast than that: the food, the stone, the river, and the company. And afterward, with the meal done, they lay back on the soft green grass and watched the herd.

The cows stood nearby, chewing their cud with eyes half-closed in contentment, and the boys watched them in the same unhurried way, the way one watches a thing that asks nothing of you. All around them the monsoon showed itself — the shining leaves, the full streams, the ripe fruit bending the branches, the groves dripping with their own sweetness — and it was, the verses say, a beauty that brings happiness in every season, remembered long after it was gone.

No demon came that day. No fire, no danger, no test. There was only the rain-washed forest, the slow cows, the simple food on a stone, and two brothers resting among their friends as the afternoon wore gently on toward evening. They lay there until the shadows began to lengthen, and then, as the herd decided such things in its own time, the cows turned for home and the boys rose to follow — taking with them, without knowing it, one of the afternoons the verses would keep.
stories.reflection: After the demons and the fires, the story pauses for something that needs no rescue and teaches nothing — a meal of curd and rice on a stone, and the sight of contented cows. It is a reminder that the boy-god's life in Vrindavan was also made of such afternoons, and that joy is itself a kind of worship, needing no occasion.
stories.next_story_tease: But the cowherds had begun to wonder at all the boy had done.

stories.title: The Cowherds Wonder at Krishna's Deeds
stories.story:
The mountain was back on the ground, the storm had spent itself, and yet the cowherds of Vrindavan could not stop turning the matter over. They gathered in knots at the edges of the pastures, speaking in low voices and glancing now and then toward the boy who sat among the calves as though nothing at all had happened.

How could a child of seven hold up a mountain with one hand? They had seen it with their own eyes — the boy standing beneath the great hill while the rain lashed down and the people and the cattle sheltered beneath it — and seeing it had not made it any easier to believe. It was not a thing a boy could do. It was not a thing a man could do. And it was not the first strange thing, either. Not by a long way.

So they began to count, the way men count debts they cannot pay. There was Putana, the demon woman who had come to Vrindavan in the shape of a nurse and had taken the child to her breast to feed him, and from whom he, a babe whose eyes were barely open, had drawn out the life instead. There was the whirlwind that had snatched him up when he was a year old and carried him high into the sky. There was the morning his mother Yashoda had caught him stealing butter and, in her vexation, had bound him to a heavy grinding mortar. There were the demons of the forest — the one who had slipped among the calves in the form of a calf, the donkey demon and all his kindred, and Pralamba, whom Balarama had thrown down. And there was the serpent Kaliya, whose venom had poisoned the river, and whom the boy had subdued and driven out of the lake.

One by one they set these things down, and the counting only deepened their confusion. A boy of seven, they said, and a mountain lifted. The two things would not sit together in the mind. And yet beneath all the counting lay something else, harder to name — a love for the boy that none of them could set aside, a fondness that held them fast to him no matter what he did or what he was.

Nanda listened to all of it and said nothing for a long while. Then he spoke, and what he said did not explain the matter away. He gave them back the words of Garga, the family priest, spoken long ago and kept quiet ever since.

When the child had been born, Nanda had called Garga to Vrindavan to give him his name. The old sage had come, and he had known at once who the child truly was, and he had told Nanda in confidence what he could not say too loudly. 'This son of yours,' Garga had said, 'was once born of Vasudeva. He takes a body in each age, and many are his names and his forms. He is the delight of the cowherds and of the cattle, and he will be your welfare. In earlier times the good were harried by the wicked, and he will stand between you and every danger. This boy, Nanda, is the equal of Narayana in his qualities.' And having said it, Garga had returned to his own home.

This was what Nanda repeated to the cowherds now, and hearing the words of Garga from his lips, the people of Vraja felt their fear loosen. It was a strange comfort — not an answer to how a boy could lift a mountain, but a reason not to be afraid of the question. The wonder did not leave them; it found a place to rest. If the boy among the calves was truly what the old sage had said, then a lifted mountain was no contradiction at all, but only the first of the things that were owed to them. And they looked at him with new eyes.
stories.reflection: The cowherds' wonder is never answered with an explanation. Nanda gives them something older and stranger — the memory of a prophecy spoken in confidence years before. It does not explain how a boy lifts a mountain; it tells them who the boy is, which turns the impossible into something to be trusted rather than feared.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana gives a different turn to this episode: there the cowherds voice their doubt directly to Krishna, who answers that he is simply their kinsman, neither god nor Yaksha nor demon. The Bhagavata, followed here, has Nanda quiet their wonder by recalling Garga's prophecy instead.
stories.next_story_tease: But the wonder was not finished with them; soon Nanda himself would be taken from the river in the night.

stories.title: Nanda Is Seized by Varuna and Rescued
stories.story:
It happened at night, at the river. Nanda, the chief of the cowherds, had gone down alone to the Yamuna to bathe while the dark hours still lay over the water. The river was still, the stars lay scattered across its surface, and there was no one else about. The village slept, and the only sound was the water closing softly around him as he stood in the shallows.

He had not been long in the water when hands closed around him. A servant of Varuna — one of the god's attendants, a creature who could not tell that this cowherd chief, standing in the dark river at the wrong hour, was not a man to be taken — seized Nanda and drew him down beneath the surface, down through the cold and the silence, to the abode of Varuna, the lord of the waters, at the bottom of the world.

On the bank, the cowherds missed him. They had all bathed there a hundred times and thought nothing of it, but now the river seemed to have swallowed one of their own. They called his name, and no one answered. They searched the dark water with their eyes, and it gave nothing back. Fear took hold of them, and they cried out the only names that seemed to matter: "Krishna! Rama!"

Krishna came at the sound. He went to the edge of the river and understood at once what had happened. He did not hesitate, and he did not wait for help. Without a word he entered the water and went down after his father, down to the court of Varuna.

Now Varuna saw who had come into his presence. And the lord of the waters did not meet the boy as one meets an intruder. He rose and honored him with offerings and with worship, the way a host honors one far greater than himself. Then he bowed, and he spoke.

"Obeisance to you," he said, "who are the supreme Self. My servant was a fool, and did not know what he was doing; he did not understand what was right. Forgive him. And you who see all things, grant your grace to me as well."

Krishna accepted the honor without anger, and Varuna returned Nanda to him. The boy brought his father back up through the water, to the bank where the cowherds stood waiting with their fear.

When they saw Nanda step out of the river, whole and unharmed, the fear let go of them all at once. They pressed around him, asking what had happened, where he had been, whether he was hurt. But Nanda climbed out into the lamplight and the familiar faces, and for a long moment he did not speak. He had seen the lord of all the waters rise and bow to the boy he had raised as his own son, and he did not know how to begin to say it.
stories.reflection: The story turns on a strange reversal: the father is taken, and it is the son who descends to bring him back. Varuna's apology is not to Nanda but to Krishna, and the rescue is less a battle than an act of recognition — the great god honoring the boy before a word of force is spoken.
stories.next_story_tease: And what Nanda had seen beneath the water he would soon tell to all his kinsmen.

stories.title: Krishna Reveals His Supreme Abode
stories.story:
Nanda came back from the river with a story, and he could not keep it to himself. He had been seized in the dark water by a servant of Varuna and carried down to the lord of the waters; and there, before his own eyes, Varuna had risen and honored Krishna, and had bowed to him, and had begged his grace. Nanda told his kinsmen all of it, and the cowherds listened, and something quickened in them.

They had always loved the boy. They had carried him and fed him and scolded him, and all the while, beneath the ordinary love, a question had been waiting. Now it stirred. The cowherds' minds grew eager, and they turned the thought over and over. If the lord of the waters bowed to this child, then perhaps the child was more than a child. Perhaps the one they called their own was, in truth, the Lord himself. The thought took hold of them, and with it came a longing they could not have put into words: if he was indeed the Lord, they wanted to see where he truly dwelt.

Krishna knew. He sees everything, and he saw what was moving in the hearts of his people, and he was moved by it. He thought of how men and women live in this world — caught in ignorance, and desire, and the endless work of karma, unable by themselves to see past the shadows to the light that never fails. They could not see the eternal for the passing, and they could not reach the eternal by their own striving. And being full of mercy, he resolved to give them what they yearned for, though it was a thing that could not be shown in any ordinary way.

He led them to the water. He took them down into the lake of Brahman and let them sink beneath it, and there, beyond all darkness, he revealed to them his own abode — the eternal light of Brahman, which is truth, and knowledge, and the infinite. It was not the light of the sun or of the moon, which rise and set. It was the light from which all lights are born — a radiance before which no shadow could stand, and it had no beginning and no end. The cowherds saw it, and were lost in it, and were filled with a bliss beyond anything the world could give.

Then Krishna drew them up again, out of the water and back into the air of Vrindavan. They stood on the bank, blinking in the ordinary light, carrying inside them a sight they would never be able to say. And Nanda and the others looked at the boy who stood before them, wet from the river, small and familiar, and they knew, as they had not known before, who it was they had been loving all along. The vision did not push them away from him; it only deepened the wonder, and the wonder only deepened the love.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not take his people away to show them heaven; he lets them sink into the light and then brings them back to the riverbank. The vision is given not to detach them from the world but to answer a longing with a glimpse — and then to return them, changed, to the boy they had always known.
stories.next_story_tease: But the world they returned to still held its dangers, and a demon was watching their next night in the forest.

stories.title: Shankhachuda Abducts the Gopis
stories.story:
One evening, when the day's work was done and the heat had gone out of the air, Krishna and Balarama went into the forest with the women of Vraja. It was the kind of evening the brothers loved best, when they could forget the sun and the cattle and the long day, and simply be together with the people who loved them. The first stars were coming out, the moon was climbing above the branches, and the two brothers began to sing, honouring the face of the coming night.

It was not an ordinary singing. The verses say the song was sweet and slow, and that it was auspicious to the mind and to the ear of every living thing — a sound that could reach into whatever heard it and settle there. The gopis listened, and the song worked on them the way strong wine works: they went still, their thoughts left them, and they forgot where they were and what they held in their hands. The women, bound to the brothers in deep affection, stood as if in a dream, and the forest itself seemed to lean in to listen.

The brothers went on singing, freely and as if intoxicated by the night itself, half-lost in the music. And while every eye was on them and every heart was open, the demon Shankhachuda saw his chance.

Shankhachuda was a servant of Kubera, the lord of treasure — a demon, strong and watchful, of the kind that had troubled Vrindavan before. He had come there for no good purpose. He had seen the women and the brothers, and he had waited at the edge of the gathering, hidden in the dark beyond the firelight, patient as a shadow, biding his time for the moment when their guard was down. Now, in the hush while the song held everyone still, he moved. He seized the women — the gopis whom Krishna and Balarama regarded as their own people — and carried them off into the night.

The spell broke at once. The gopis screamed, and their cry cut through the singing: "Krishna! Rama!"

The two brothers turned and saw their own people being carried away into the dark. They did not stop to reason, and they did not think of weapons or of consequences. The only thought was the women being carried away, and the only answer was to run. "Do not fear!" they cried, and the cry itself was a promise. They tore up the trunks of two sal trees, hefted them like clubs, and plunged after the demon — two lions leaping into the night after the one who had dared to lay hands on what was theirs.
stories.reflection: The demon strikes at the one moment the gopis are unguarded — not in weakness, but in absorption, their attention given over entirely to the song. The brothers' answer is immediate and instinctive: a shout of reassurance before any thought of battle, and then a pursuit that will not be turned aside.
stories.next_story_tease: But the demon would not escape — and the jewel he wore was about to change hands.

stories.title: A Jewel for Balarama
stories.story:
The demon had taken the women of Vrindavan — the gopis, the cowherd women of the village — and he had not reckoned on being followed.

His name was Shankhachuda, and he had carried the gopis off into the forest as though they were his for the taking. For a little while the deed must have seemed to him to stand: the forest was deep, the village far, and no one, he may have told himself, would come after him so quickly.

But two had come after him, and they were not walking. Coming on together behind him were Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, and the verses say what the demon saw when he looked back at those two: Time and Death themselves, arriving side by side. The courage went out of him in a rush. He trembled, and he ran.

And Krishna, the verses say, ran after him wherever he ran.

It was not a long chase, but it was a certain one. The demon flung himself this way and that through the trees, branches catching at him as he went, and whichever way he turned, Krishna was there — never quite near enough to be seized, never far enough to be lost, matching him stride for stride, wearing him down. The demon's breath came hard. He had trusted the forest to hide him, and the forest had let him down; there was no path through it that did not carry Shankhachuda closer to the one thing he dreaded, and step by step the gap between them closed.

Not far off, Krishna overtook him. He came up on the fleeing demon and, with a single blow of his fist to the head of that wicked one, struck Shankhachuda down and put an end to him.

And then, with the demon lying where he had fallen and the women he had taken looking on, Krishna did a small and telling thing. From the fallen demon's crest he took the bright jewel that had shone there — the ornament Shankhachuda had worn at the crown of his head, the treasure that had gleamed above his brow even as he ran — and he did not keep it. He carried it to Balarama, his elder brother, and placed it into his hands. Balarama, who had come with him, received it; the verses record no ceremony, only that the gift was given, and that the women saw it given.

It was not spoil, and it was not for himself. Krishna wanted nothing from the demon. The bright thing he had lifted from the dead man's brow he laid in his brother's keeping, and the women who had been carried off saw it all — saw the terror leave their captor, saw him fall, saw the jewel pass from a demon's crest into Balarama's hands, a gift given openly, where everyone could see it given.

Then the forest was quiet again. The women were safe, the chase was over, and the jewel that had once ridden at a demon's crown belonged now, by Krishna's own hand, to his elder brother.
stories.reflection: The episode is brief, but its last image is the one that lingers: Krishna lifting the demon's one treasure and, without a moment's hesitation, giving it to Balarama. The victory matters less to the story than the gift — the spoils of the fight passing to the elder brother, in full view of the women who had been taken.
stories.content_note: A demon is struck down with a single blow; the violence is brief and not described in detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But a worse terror was already on its way to the herds, this time in the shape of a bull.

stories.title: A Bull the Colour of Rain
stories.story:
The first warning was a sound — a bellow that rolled over the grazing grounds of Vrindavan and set the herd moving before anyone understood why. Then the cattle saw what had made it, and they did not wait to be told. They scattered, leaving the herd behind, because standing at the edge of the pasture was a bull that was no bull.

He was the demon Arishta, come in the shape of a savage bull to break the cowherds' world. The Vishnu Purana describes him slowly, as if the terror of him had to be taken in one detail at a time: the colour of a cloud charged with rain, horns vast, eyes like two fiery suns. His tongue kept licking his lips, his tail stood erect, and between his shoulders rose a hump of enormous size; his dewlap hung low, and his face was scarred from butting against trees. Wherever he moved, his hooves ploughed up the earth. And this was no stray animal wandered in from the wild: the same source says he was a demon who haunted the forests in the shape of a bull, destroying hermits and ascetics wherever he went. Now he had come to Vrindavan.

The cows fled in fear, abandoning the herd, and the cowherds' cries went up. Krishna saw the herd scattered, the men and the cattle driven to flight by the brute, and he did not withdraw. He called the creature out — what is this, he demanded, terrifying the cowherds and their animals, you lowest of beings? — and he slapped his arms together, the sound ringing out, goading the demon on.

Arishta needed no goading. Enraged, he pawed the ground with his hoof, lowered the points of his horns, fixed his reddened eyes on Krishna, and charged.

Krishna did not step aside. The Vishnu Purana says he waited, smiling, for the bull to reach him. He met the rush and seized the bull by the horns, and flung him — the verses say he was thrown a full eighteen paces and landed in a heap on the earth. For a moment the cowherds must have thought it over.

But the demon rose again, and came again, more furious than before, and this time Krishna took hold of him by the horns and forced him down, pressing him to the ground with his foot. There the great bull lay, and there the demon in him died — vomiting blood, kicking out his feet, his eyes rolling and finding no rest, until at last he lay still.

When it was over, the herdsmen glorified Krishna. The gods, the verses say, praised him with a shower of flowers, and the cowherds sang of him the way the celestials of old had sung of Indra when he triumphed over the demon Jambha. The bull that had scattered the herd was finished, and the cowherds, who a moment before had scattered, gathered again around him, safe, and the cattle, one by one, came drifting back to graze.
stories.reflection: Arishta is not described as an army but as a single animal, and that is precisely what makes him frightening: he is terror of the ordinary, everyday kind, the thing that can scatter a herd in a heartbeat. Krishna meets him without weapons and without retreat, and the story's comfort is that the fear itself is what gets flung down and finished.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana describes the killing differently: Krishna tears off one of the bull's horns and beats him to death with it, after wringing his throat like a wet cloth. The Bhagavata, followed here, has him fling the bull aside and press him to the ground. The two agree on the essentials.
stories.content_note: A bull-demon is slain; the fight is described with some force but not graphically.
stories.next_story_tease: But Kamsa had not finished with Vrindavan, and his next messenger would arrive in the shape of a horse.

stories.title: The Empty Forest
stories.story:
Keshi came to Vrindavan in the shape of a horse, and he came with a purpose. Kamsa, the king who wanted Krishna dead, had sent word to the demon, and Keshi had obeyed: he went straight to the forest and set about the cowherds as his master wished.

He was no ordinary horse. His mane tossed like a storm-cloud, and his neighing was itself a terror. The Harivamsha says he was born along with Kamsa and was as dear to the king as his own life, a peerless fighter who had never met his equal. He killed the cows and the cowherds and fed on them, and wherever he ranged, the forest fell empty — the people who lived by the woods and the cattle withdrew from it, the paths the herds had worn went unused, and the animals could no longer travel the forest roads. For a while the woods seemed to belong to the demon alone.

Then, one day, following the sound of men, the horse came to the settlement of the cowherds. The moment the women and the boys and the men saw him, they set up a cry and fled — to Krishna, their refuge, calling out to him.

Krishna gave them his word and went out to meet the demon. Some of the cowherds cried after him, urging him back — you are only a boy, they said, and this one is beyond the strength of all — but Krishna had already made up his mind.

The horse saw him coming and charged, his mouth open wide, as if he meant to drink the sky, his eyes and teeth bared and his neck raised high. Krishna called out to the demon, roaring like a lion, and met the rush. The horse struck at him with his fore-hooves and bore down on him, and Krishna slipped aside from the first rush, caught hold of the demon, whirled him around, and hurled him to the ground.

Keshi rose, angrier than before, and came at him again, jaws stretched open to bite. This time Krishna did not dodge. Smiling, he thrust his arm into the horse's open mouth — the verses say it was like a hand thrust down a serpent's hole. The demon's teeth met that arm and dropped out, as though they had touched hot iron, and the arm, once inside, began to swell, growing until it filled the creature and stopped his breath. Keshi choked. He kicked out his legs and struggled, and then he was still, his body split open like a ripened gourd — one source says it was torn asunder like a tree struck by lightning — and Krishna drew his arm out again.

The gods, seeing it, showered flowers down upon him. And the sources say that from this deed Krishna took a name that would stay with him for good: because he had slain Keshi, the world would call him Keshava.
stories.reflection: The fight is decided by a strange, almost gentle gesture — Krishna does not strike the horse so much as fill it, letting his arm grow until the creature's own fury chokes it. It is a striking reversal: the demon that came to devour is itself devoured by stillness, and the victory leaves behind not only peace but a name.
stories.tradition_note: The name Keshava, 'slayer of Keshi,' is recorded in the Harivamsha and the Vishnu Purana; the Bhagavata tells the fight itself without pausing on the name.
stories.content_note: A horse-demon is slain as Krishna thrusts his arm into its mouth; the violence is brief and not described in graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: And the next danger would come wearing a friend's face.

stories.title: The Thief in the Game
stories.story:
The boys of Vrindavan were playing a game, and one of them was not a boy.

It was a game they loved: some of the boys would be the keepers of the calves, and some would be thieves, and they would steal and be caught and steal again, all through the long afternoon on the slopes of the hill where the herd grazed. It was a game that only pretended to danger, a game that began in laughter and usually ended in a tangle of dust and shouting. And into it, dressed as a cowherd boy, slipped something that did not pretend.

He was Vyoma, the son of Maya, a demon and a master of deception. He had taken the shape of one of the boys, and no one looked at him twice. One by one he began to lead the children away — the way a thief in their game would lead off a keeper he had caught — except that the boys he took did not come back. He came and went among them as one of them, and when he drew a boy toward the mountain, the boy went with him, because it looked like nothing so much as the game they were all already playing. Again and again he carried one off to a cave in the mountain and sealed him inside it, and the children he had stolen lay hidden in the dark, many of them, while the game went on around the empty places where they had been. One would be there a moment before, and then not there at all, and the laughter would go on as if nothing had changed.

Krishna saw what was happening. The verses call him the giver of refuge to the good, and this is what that meant: he understood at once what the demon was doing, and he did not let the game go on a moment longer.

Then Krishna left off the shape and size of a boy. He stood in his own form, the verses say, vast and strong as a king among mountains, and he turned on the deceiver. He seized Vyoma with both hands, threw him down upon the earth, and ended him.

And then, without pausing, Krishna went to the mouth of the mountain cave, broke through the covering that sealed it, and brought the boys out, one after another, from the darkness and the fear they had been shut into, and stood them blinking in the daylight again.

The game was over. The boys who had been stolen came out into the light and were counted one by one, and the thief who had hidden among them lay still, and the mountain gave back everyone it had taken.
stories.reflection: The most striking thing is where the demon chose to hide: not at the edge of the village but inside the boys' own game, wearing a friend's face. The story does not dwell on the violence; it hurries past it to the cave and the bringing of the children out, as if the rescue, not the slaying, is the point.
stories.content_note: A demon disguised as a cowherd boy carries children off into a cave; the danger is real but ends in their rescue, and the slaying is brief.
stories.next_story_tease: But the cowherds' greatest fear still waited, coiled in the waters of the Yamuna.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing huge as a mountain before the cave, breaking open its sealed mouth as the stolen cowherd boys come out into the light, the disguised demon cast down behind him.

stories.title: The Vow at the Poisoned Lake
stories.story:
One morning Krishna went into the forest alone. Not with Balarama, and not with the herd of boys who usually followed at his heels — only himself, dark as a rain-cloud, with a feather in his hair, garlands of new kadamba and arjuna buds around his neck, and a flute in his hand, walking where the cattle led him. The woods of Vrindavan that day seemed made for wandering. Peacocks called from the branches, and low thunder muttered among the hills, as if the season itself were leaning close to listen.

He had ranged here before, and the forest always answered him. Plantain groves stood thick and green, the ground was soft with new grass and studded with lotuses, and the air carried the scent of dark-blue lotus from the water. Fountains lay hidden among the trees, and the wind that came off the leaves fanned him as he walked. It was the kind of place, the old verses say, where a boy might sing to his cows and believe the whole earth was listening. Sometimes he would stop under the great Bhandiraka fig tree, tall enough to brush half the sky, its branches bowed with fruit, and let the other cowherd boys amuse him with their songs, and answer them on his flute.

Then one day, while the cattle grazed and the sun climbed, he came down to the bank of the Yamuna. The river lay before him like a woman decked for a festival — lilies and lotuses on her surface, swans and cranes calling over the water, her landing-stairs smooth, her current strong and sweet, her many little lakes catching the light, and the water-fowl ranging over her in pairs. It should have been the sweetest water in the world.

But the river was not well. There, in a lake along her side, lived Kaliya, the serpent-king, and his venom had seeped into the water until it was no longer fit to drink. Nothing that drank from it could live. The birds had gone quiet over the water, and for all its beauty the river carried a hidden bitterness that could kill.

Krishna stood at the edge and looked into the deep. He did not rage, and he did not turn away. Quietly, the way a boy decides to climb a tree for its fruit, he made up his mind. I should vanquish this king of serpents, he resolved. I shall climb the Kadamba tree, and jump into the lake, and vanquish Kaliya.

It was a small sentence for so great a deed, and he spoke it without raising his voice. But the resolve was set, and the water, as if it knew, seemed to darken under his gaze.
stories.reflection: The striking thing about the resolve is its quiet. Krishna does not rehearse a battle or boast of strength; he decides the way a boy decides to climb a tree, and the whole deliverance of the river hangs on that calm sentence.
stories.tradition_note: This moment of resolve is particular to the Harivamsha; the Bhagavata Purana moves more directly from the poisoning of the river to the leap.
stories.next_story_tease: But the poisoned water had already begun its silent work on the unsuspecting cowherds and their cattle.
