stories.title: The Brahmanas Refuse Krishna's Request for Food
stories.story:
The cows had been grazing since morning, and by afternoon the boys were hungry. Krishna and Balarama were pasturing the cattle not far from home, with the cowherd boys around them, and hunger came over them all alike. It was nothing dramatic — only the ordinary ache of boys who had been out in the fields since dawn, with the sun climbing and the evening meal still far off. The forest was still, the heat of the afternoon lay over everything, and the boys' thoughts kept straying home to the kitchens and to food.

Now, nearby, a company of brahmanas — learned men, well-versed in the Vedas — had gathered to perform a sacrifice. The smoke of their fire rose above the trees, and the sound of their chanting reached the pasture where the boys sat. A sacrifice in those days meant hospitality; a man who could feed gods at the fire should not find it hard to feed a few hungry boys. So the request Krishna made was not an unreasonable one. He knew the brahmanas were there, and he knew what they were doing, and he sent the boys to them. Go, he said, and ask them for food in my name.

The boys went, crossing the fields toward the smoke. They stood before the brahmanas with folded hands and spoke with all the respect they could summon. O gods of the earth, listen to us: we come at Krishna's bidding. While pasturing the cows not far from here, Balarama and Krishna have grown hungry, and they ask for food.

The brahmanas heard the request. And they paid it no mind. The verses say they neither said yes nor said no; they simply did not heed it. Their whole attention was given to the machinery of the sacrifice — the proper place, the proper time, the offerings, the mantras, the priests, the fires. Each detail had to be exactly right, and the work of keeping it right left no room for two herd-boys standing at the edge of the rite. They looked at the boys and saw only herd-boys; and behind the herd-boys, in the one who had sent them, they saw only a boy who herded cows. It is a strange blindness the verses describe. The brahmanas were worshipping the very one who now stood a field away, hungry, asking through two boys for a little food. They had spent their lives learning to know him, and yet, when he came asking, they knew him least of all. The rites were flawless and the fires correct, and the one the rites were for stood unrecognized a stone's throw away.

The text says it more sharply still. The supreme Brahman stood within their reach, hidden from them by their own learning. They did not recognize him.

The boys waited, and the silence stretched. They had come with a simple, courteous request, and they had received neither yes nor no — only the sound of mantras going on without them. There was no anger in them, only confusion. They had seen the smoke and heard the chanting and expected generosity; instead they had met a wall of rites that had no room for them. At last they turned and walked back across the fields, empty-handed, to where Krishna and Balarama sat with the cows.

And the brahmanas returned to their fires, satisfied that the rites had been kept correct, and did not know what they had turned away. Their learning had kept the rite perfect. It had also kept them from the one the rite was for.
stories.reflection: The refusal is not hostile; it is distracted. The men are so certain of the forms of worship — the place, the time, the mantras, the fire — that they cannot see the one the worship points to, standing just outside and asking for a little food. Their learning becomes the wall that keeps them from what they study.
stories.next_story_tease: But the brahmanas' wives would prove quicker to answer than their husbands.

stories.title: The Brahmanas' Wives Bring Food to Krishna
stories.story:
The boys came back empty-handed, and when they told Krishna what had happened — that the brahmanas had neither refused nor agreed, that they had simply gone on with their rites as though no one had spoken — the master of the whole world only laughed. There was no anger in it. He did not scold the men, and he did not repeat the request. He simply said: go to their wives, and tell them that I have come, with Balarama.

So the boys went a second time, now to the women's quarters of those same houses. There the wives sat, well-adorned in their own homes, going about the quiet work of the afternoon. The boys bowed to them and spoke with the same respect as before: Obeisance to you, wives of the brahmanas; listen to our words. While pasturing the cows with the cowherds, he has come from far away, with Balarama — and he is hungry.

The wives heard the name, and everything in them rose at once. They had always longed for the sight of Krishna; the verses say the longing was constant, something they carried every day without speaking it aloud. They had heard of him — the dark boy of Vrindavan whose name was on everyone's lips — and they had kept that longing lit like a lamp in a dark room. Now, without a word of hesitation, they began to fill vessels with food — food of four kinds, rich and fine, prepared with care — and they hurried out toward him. In that sudden movement there was something of a festival — doors flung open, feet hurrying, voices rising — as though the whole women's quarter had been waiting all along for exactly this summons.

Their husbands tried to stop them. Their brothers tried, their kinsmen tried, their own sons called after them from the doorways, asking where they thought they were going and before whom. They called it madness, or worse; they reminded the women of their duties, their good names, the scandal of it. But the women did not slow. A longing kept secret for years has a force that reproach cannot match, and the verses are clear that not one of them turned back. The text reaches for water to say what they were like: they went as rivers run to the sea, drawn by a pull that nothing in the house could answer.

It is worth pausing on what they left behind. Not small things — houses, husbands, the regard of kin, the settled shape of a whole life. And they left it all without a backward look, because the one thing they had wanted without daring to ask for it had finally come within reach. And yet the text gives the moment no weight of tragedy; there is only eagerness in it. The women are not fleeing a prison; they are running toward a light they have waited for, and the running itself is a kind of arrival. They did not need to be told the way; they had walked it a thousand times in their thoughts.

So through the groves of Vrindavan they went, their vessels bright in their hands, their veils and bracelets catching the afternoon light, their faces all turned one way — toward the place where Krishna waited with Balarama and the boys and the grazing cows. Some carried the food balanced high; others held it close against them, as though afraid the afternoon might end before they arrived.

It had taken the men an afternoon of silence to answer him. It took their wives no more than a breath.
stories.reflection: The contrast is the point of the story. The learned brahmanas saw only a herd-boy and sent him away; their wives, who had no learning to lean on and only longing to go by, saw what the longing had prepared them to see. They drop everything — home, kin, reputation — because the one they have wanted is finally near.
stories.next_story_tease: But when the wives reached him, they would refuse to go back at all.

stories.title: The Wives Refuse to Return
stories.story:
The women had crossed a line they could not walk back across. They had left their husbands' great sacrifice, carried food through the forest, and fed Krishna and his cowherd companions with their own hands. They had not come with any thought of returning; they had come only to see him. Now they stood before him in a grove on the banks of the Yamuna, where the ashoka trees were tipped with fresh young leaves, and they looked at him, and they could not look away.

The strange thing was that they had known him before they ever saw him. They had heard of the cowherd boy whose name was on every tongue in Vraja, until his image had taken up its place in their minds and would not leave. The verses say their hearts were already sunk in him, their ears filled with the nectar of hearing about him, long before they stood in the grove. So when they saw him, it was not a stranger they found but the one they had been carrying inside them all along.

He stood among his friends the way a dancer stands at ease — one hand resting on a companion's shoulder, the other slowly twirling a lotus. His skin was dark, his garments gold, a garland of forest flowers at his neck and a peacock feather in his hair. Earrings swung at his cheeks, and his face, bright as a lotus, wore a faint smile. The verses say the women drank him in through their eyes and held him there for a long while, the way the wise let go of their false ideas of who they are — and the sorrow that had followed them all the way from home quietly left them.

Then Krishna spoke. "You are welcome," he said. "Sit. Tell me what I can do for you."

But he did not stop at a welcome. The wise, he told them, see clearly what is best for themselves, and so they give to him all they have — breath and mind and intelligence, wife and children and wealth, everything a person holds dear. And therefore, he said, they should return now to the place of sacrifice. Their husbands were brahmanas; their place was there.

The women did not lower their eyes. "Do not speak such cruel words," they answered. "We have left everyone — fathers, husbands, sons, brothers, every bond we had — so that we might carry on our heads the tulasi garland that has fallen from your feet. Neither our husbands nor our fathers nor our sons nor our brothers nor any of our people will take us back now. How much less any stranger? For us, who have fallen at your feet, there is no other refuge. Grant us this."

It was the truth, and Krishna saw it. They had staked everything on him, and there was nothing left to return to. He was pleased — the verses are plain about this — and he granted them the grace they had asked for. But he also taught them something to carry back with them. It is not bodily nearness, he told them, that binds a person to him. He is won by remembrance — by hearing of him, and seeing him, and holding him in the mind, and speaking of him. Then he sent them home, and they went, their hearts fixed on him, the way the wise carry what they love with them wherever they go.
stories.reflection: The wives' refusal is not defiance of their husbands but the plain statement of a fact: they have already left everything, and there is no going back. Krishna's answer turns their longing away from his physical presence toward something they can carry anywhere — remembrance.
stories.next_story_tease: But the husbands they returned to would soon see, in their wives' faces, exactly what they themselves had refused.

stories.title: The Brahmanas Repent
stories.story:
The sacrifice had everything a sacrifice should have: the right place, the right hour, the right offerings, the right mantras, and fires tended by priests who knew every rule. The brahmanas had given themselves to it completely — so completely, the verses say, that when a young cowherd came to them asking for food, sent by his companion Krishna, who waited hungry in the forest with his friends, they had waved him away. There were rules to follow. There was no time for a cowherd's errand.

It was their wives who had gone instead, carrying food through the woods to Krishna and his friends while their husbands stayed behind with the fire. Now the women came home, and the brahmanas looked at them, and something in their faces stopped the men where they stood. Even the one wife whose husband had held her back by force had not been stopped; she had simply closed her eyes and gone to Krishna in her mind, meditating on the Lord exactly as she had heard of him. And Krishna, for his part, had fed the cowherds with the very food the women had carried through the woods.

Then the full knowledge of it reached them, the way a slow truth reaches a man who has been busy elsewhere. The one they had refused was Vishnu himself — the Lord, standing in the forest in the shape of a cowherd boy, and they had turned him away for the sake of a ritual. The verses record what they said to one another, and it is not a proud speech. "Shame on our birth," they said, "and on its threefold aims. Shame on our vows. Shame on our great learning." For the Lord's power to delude, they understood, could bewilder even the wise, even the yogis. And look — look at these women. They had no initiation into the brahminical way, no long years of study in a guru's house, and yet they loved Krishna, the teacher of all the worlds, with a love so complete it shamed everything the men had spent their lives acquiring.

So the brahmanas spoke of what they now saw. The place of the sacrifice, the hour, the separate offerings, the mantras, the priests, the fires — these were not separate things, not tools to be arranged. They were all Krishna himself. He it was whom the goddess of fortune serves, turning away from all others, ever longing for the touch of his feet. He it was who needs nothing and yet grants liberation to those who ask. "Salutations to the Lord Krishna," they said, "whose wisdom never falters. He is Vishnu himself, the lord of all lords of yoga, the first being of all — and it is his own power that keeps our minds deluded." They remembered their own fault, the insult they had offered him, and they wanted, more than anything, to look upon him.

But they did not go. They did not dare. Kamsa ruled nearby, and they were afraid. So the men who knew every verse of the ritual sat at home and longed for the boy they had turned away, praising him in words they had never once thought to speak beside the fire.
stories.reflection: The brahmanas' lament is really a confession that their ritual had become an end in itself — something performed without remembering whom it was for. The women, who knew none of the rules, had found the one the rules point to.

stories.title: Krishna Vanishes
stories.story:
It began on a night when the moon rose full and calm over Vrindavan, painting every corner of the sky with its red light, the way a beloved long away brightens a face at the moment of return. The forest took the light softly — the leaves, the paths, the water of the Yamuna all touched with that red glow — and it was a night made for beauty and for longing. When Krishna's flute sounded through the forest, the women of Vraja heard it in the middle of their ordinary tasks and set them down. One left off milking, another left the milk half-boiled over the fire, another turned from a husband she was serving, another from a child she was feeding — and they came, each one slipping away unnoticed, their earrings swinging as they hurried to where their beloved stood. Some came with their clothes and ornaments half arranged, so great was their haste; and some who found themselves shut inside their houses, unable to slip out, stood where they were and closed their eyes and held him in their minds. Their families called them back, but they did not turn. Their minds were no longer their own; Krishna had taken them, and the women went where the music led.

He received them, and for a while the forest held only what they had all come for. It is easy, in such a moment, for a small and secret thought to take root: that the joy is theirs, that they have earned it, that the one they love is somehow their own.

The verses put it plainly. Pride rose in the gopis out of their good fortune — the sense that they, of all people, possessed him. It was a small thing, the way such pride always begins: a certain warmth in the heart, a certain sense of having been chosen. And Krishna saw it.

There was no word, no warning. Where he had been, there was nothing. He vanished then and there, in the middle of the night, in the middle of their happiness, leaving the women he loved standing suddenly alone among the trees.

But the verses are careful to say why. He did not leave them to punish them. He left them to humble them, and to favor them. The pride that had begun to grow in them was the one thing that could have spoiled what they had found; and so the Lord, who had come so close, stepped back, so that what they felt for him could grow deeper than the thing they felt for themselves.

In the silence he left behind, the night was suddenly very large, and the gopis understood, in a way they had not understood before, how much of what they loved was simply him. The flute had stopped. The place where he had stood still held the warmth of him, and that was all that was left. They looked at one another in the red moonlight, and none of them could speak. They had asked the night for so much, and the night had given it, and now, in an instant, it had been taken back — not to hurt them, but to teach them what it was they had been given. The moon had not dimmed, and the forest had not changed. Only he was gone; and without him, the same night was a different place.
stories.reflection: Krishna's disappearance is the opposite of abandonment. He removes the one thing — pride — that would have soured the gopis' love, so that what remains is only the love itself.

stories.title: The Gopis Abandon Their Homes
stories.story:
The moon came up full over Vrindavan, and it washed the eastern sky with a red that was almost the colour of fresh kumkum. The forest stood soft in that light, and the whole of it seemed to wait. The river below carried the light in broken pieces, and the air smelled of the year turning. It was one of those autumn nights when the heat of the day has gone and the earth gives back its warmth. Krishna looked at the night and at the forest, and he raised his flute and began to play.

The song did not call out to anyone by name. It was simply the flute on an autumn night, low and sweet, and it did not ask; it drew. It did not soothe; it quickened, the way a single note can set a whole evening leaning. It was the kind of song that makes a listener restless in her own house. It was the sound they had been waiting for without knowing it. It crossed the fields and the lanes and the courtyards of the village, and it made the quiet of the evening feel like a promise. The women of Vraja heard it, and their minds went out of them.

One of them was milking, and she left the cow standing with the pail half full and did not look back. One was serving the evening meal, and she set the dish down while it was still warm and walked out. One had a child at her breast, and she put the child down and went. One was anointing herself for the evening, and she stopped where she sat. One had kohl half applied to her eyes, and she left it there, one eye dark and the other bare. Each of them was in the middle of something, and each of them left it unfinished. The evening tasks lay where they had dropped, and the houses stood half-done, as though time had stopped inside them.

Husbands caught at their arms, and fathers and brothers called after them, and the hands of their kinsfolk closed over their wrists. It made no difference. Their voices rose and fell behind them, and were lost under the sound of the flute, which went on and did not hurry. They went, heedless of every restraint, because the sound of the flute had taken them and would not let them go.

Some of them could not go at all. The door was watched, or the house had closed in around them, and no way out could be found. Those women shut their eyes where they stood, some of them before they had even reached the door. The ache of being apart from the one they loved had grown unbearable and fierce, and in the shutting of their eyes it burned itself out, and whatever else had been in them went with it. With their eyes shut they went to him, and they found him as surely as the women who had crossed the fields.

By the time they reached him, the moon stood high over the Yamuna. Krishna saw the women of Vraja come near to him, the milkmaid with the pail half full, the one with kohl on a single eye, and those who had never left their courtyards at all but had come to him with their eyes closed. The night, which had begun so quietly, had gathered them all to one place on the riverbank, and behind them the village went on sleeping, unaware of who had slipped away from it. The Yamuna was there to meet them, dark and slow under the moon.
stories.reflection: What stays in the mind is the inventory of unfinished things, the milk half-milked and the eye half-painted. The gopis are not shown renouncing anything with ceremony; they simply drop what they are doing mid-task because the flute interrupted a normal evening and they answered it. The detail that some could not leave at all, and still reached him by closing their eyes, quietly widens the story: the going is outward, but the meeting is not limited by walls.
stories.next_story_tease: But the night was far from over; the dance had not yet begun.

stories.title: Krishna Tests the Gopis
stories.story:
When the gopis finally reached Krishna that autumn night, he greeted them with a smile and a question that was not at all what they had come for. "You are welcome," he said. "What can I do for you? Is all well in Vraja? Tell me why you have come."

Then, before they could answer, he went on. "This night is fearsome," he said, "and full of fierce creatures. It is not right for women to be here. Go back to Vraja. Your mothers and fathers, your sons and brothers and husbands, are searching for you, and they cannot find you. Do not bring such distress on your own family."

He pointed to the forest around them — the flowering trees lit by the full moon, the Yamuna's breeze moving through the leaves — as if to say: you have seen it, now go. "Return to the settlement without delay," he said. "Serve your husbands. The calves and the little ones are crying; go milk the cows and feed them."

And then he softened, just a little. "Or," he said, "if it is love for me that has bound your hearts and brought you here, that is only fitting — for every living thing finds its joy in me. But hear me: the highest duty of a woman is to serve her husband faithfully, to do good to her own people, and to care for those who depend on her. A wife must not leave her husband — not even one who is ill-tempered, or unlucky, or old, or dull, or sick, or poor. A love outside marriage brings no heaven and no honor; it is trifling and painful and feared, and it disgraces a woman of good family. And besides — love for me is born of hearing about me, and seeing me, and meditating on me, and speaking of me. It is not born of standing near me. So go back to your homes."

The gopis stood very still. The verses say their hopes broke, and a grief they could not cross settled over them. They stood with their faces turned down, their lips gone dry with sighing, tracing lines in the earth with their toes, wiping away the tears that streaked the vermilion on their chests, saying nothing.

Then one of them found her voice, and the rest followed, their words coming out choked with feeling. "Do not speak such cruel words," they said. "We have left behind every pleasure we had, and come to your feet. Accept us, your own devotees. Do not cast us off — the way the ancient Lord receives those who long for freedom."

"You, who understand duty, have told us that a woman's dharma is to serve her husband and her children and her people. Let it be so. But you are the dearest of all who have bodies; you are our friend, our very self. Those who are wise give their love to you, who are forever dear — of what use to us are husbands and sons, who bring only sorrow? Be gracious, Lord. Do not cut down the hope we have carried for you so long, O lotus-eyed one."

Their voices gathered strength. "Our minds have been carried away by you; they cannot go back into our houses. Our hands no longer do the work of the house, and our feet will not move from the foot of your feet. How shall we go back to Vraja? What would we do there? Quench the fire that your smiling glance and your sweet songs have lit in our hearts — or else we will be burned up by the pain of missing you, and reach your feet only through our meditation on you."

And at last they asked for the one thing they had come for. "What woman in the three worlds, hearing the song of your flute, could keep to the path of the good and not come running? Seeing your face, with its smiling eyes and its dark curls, your arms that grant fearlessness, your chest that is the home of fortune herself — we are your servants. Place your lotus hand upon our heads. You are the one who takes away the fears of Vraja, the friend of the afflicted. Give us your service."
stories.reflection: Krishna's test is a strange kind of kindness: he argues against the gopis with every duty the world recognizes, so that the only answer they have left is the truth — that he is not one more claim among their duties, but the self to which all duties return.
stories.next_story_tease: And Krishna, who had argued against them with every duty in the world, would answer their plea with something far gentler.

stories.title: Krishna Relents and Sports with the Gopis
stories.story:
The sound of them reached him before anything else. Across the dark water of the Yamuna the gopis were calling his name, and Krishna — who needed nothing from anyone, who was already complete in himself — listened for a long while before he moved. The night was full of their voices, and he let it be full for a little longer.

These were the milkmaids of Vrindavan, the ones who had left their homes at the sound of his flute and followed him to the river on a full-moon night. Earlier that evening he had tested them, sending them back with words meant to turn them away, to see whether their devotion could survive his refusal. It had. They had not turned back and gone home. They had only grieved, and gone on calling for him, their longing unbroken by his absence. It was that grief, more than anything else, that moved him at last.

Now, hearing how they grieved, he could hold back no longer. The verses are careful to say he was already self-satisfied, already full, and that nothing he did that night came from any need of his own. Yet he smiled — not the smile of a man who has been won over, but a smile that meant favor — and he came to them, and he showed them grace. The gopis had asked for nothing but him, and that was exactly what they received.

He came down to the cool, sandy bank of the river, into the soft light of the full moon. The moment they saw him, their faces opened like flowers. They began to sing to him, and he sang with them; one voice answered another across the pale sand, a hundred voices braided together in the night. They sang to him, and he answered with his own song, and for a little while there was nothing in the world but the two sounds answering each other, grief turning to gladness without a single word being changed.

Then he spread his arms wide and drew them near, and the gopis pressed in around him. The verses say he embraced them, holding each of them close the way a person holds what he loves, and that he returned their affection with the light play of his fingertips. There was laughter, a hand at the fold of a garment — the breathless, easy joy of a long parting ending. The text touches all of it lightly and does not linger, as if to say that some happiness is too simple to describe.

There was no audience to that night, and no proof of it afterwards. The verses record only that it happened, and that it happened on the bank of the Yamuna, on sand that stayed cool through the heat of the night. The gopis asked for nothing more, and they received everything.

What the text insists on is quieter still. These women, who moments before had believed themselves abandoned, now felt themselves the most blessed women alive. Not because they had earned him — they would have said they had not. But because he had chosen to come back to them, and his coming was enough.
stories.reflection: The source is careful to say Krishna was self-satisfied, complete, in need of nothing — and that the favor he showed was therefore pure gift. The gopis' happiness is not a reward for endurance but the answer to longing that asked for nothing but him.
stories.next_story_tease: But the night's joy would not hold; Krishna was about to slip away from among them.

stories.title: The Gopis Search the Forest
stories.story:
One moment he was there among them; the next, the gopis turned and he was gone. No word, no warning — only the empty place where Krishna had stood.

They did not go home. They went into the forest, the way the verses say it: like women out of their minds, searching from wood to wood and singing his name aloud so that all of Vrindavan could hear it. The moonlight fell in pieces through the leaves, and still they went on, their bare feet finding the paths between the trees, their voices lifting and falling in the dark.

And as they searched, they began to take on his very manner. The verses say his walk, his smile, the way he glanced, the sweet way he spoke — all of it rose up in them as they went, until each gopi seemed to carry a little of him in her own step and voice. To see them was to see him, scattered among a hundred women.

And because they had no one else to ask, they questioned the trees. They stopped before the ashvattha and the plaksha and the great banyan, the holy fig trees of the forest, and asked: have you seen Nanda's son? They turned to the flowering trees — the ashoka, the kurabaka, the champaka, the nagakesara and the punnaga — and to the tulasi plant, which they called the one beloved of Govinda's feet, and put the same question to each of them. Have you seen him, the one who stole our hearts with his smiles?

They asked the mango and the jackfruit and the kadamba, the bilva and the bakula and the nipa, the jasmine and the creepers that twine up the trunks of the forest trees, the creepers the verses picture throwing their arms around a great tree like a friend embracing a friend. They even turned on the earth itself and demanded to know what penance it had performed, that the mere touch of his feet should make it blossom the way it did — whether it was his stride or the touch of his feet that had set the whole ground breaking into flowers. And they asked the doe, wondering whether Krishna had come this way — his arm resting on a beloved's shoulder, a lotus in his hand, the garland of tulasi around his neck and the bees following him, drunk on its scent, the jasmine garland carrying a faint perfume of the one he loved — and whether the trees had bowed to him as he passed, honored by one long, loving glance.

But the forest kept its silence. The trees held their branches still. The gopis went on from tree to tree, calling the question again and again, because asking was the only thing left to do.

They were not looking for news of him. They were looking for him. And somewhere in the middle of it the search stopped being a search for a lost person and became the only way they knew to keep him near — to keep saying his name, to keep his walk and his smile before their eyes, even when he would not show himself.
stories.reflection: The gopis address trees and creepers as if they could answer, which is the whole heart of the passage: when the beloved vanishes, love turns the whole world into a possible messenger. Their grief does not sit still; it moves, questions, and fills the forest with his name.
stories.next_story_tease: And when the trees gave no answer, their searching turned to something stranger still.

stories.title: The Gopis Enact Krishna's Lilas
stories.story:
Still searching, still calling Krishna's name through Vrindavan, the gopis began to do the one thing that made their loss bearable. They began to become him.

Each of them took up one of his deeds — the deeds they had heard sung since he was a baby in the cowherd village — and played it out there in the forest, for no audience but the trees and the moon. The forest lay still around them, silvered with moonlight, and the only sound was their own voices. The verses call their words the words of the frantic, and they were; but it was a frenzy that knew exactly what it was doing. It had a shape, and the shape was him.

One woman lay down on the forest floor and played Putana, the demoness who had once come to the village disguised as a wet-nurse, her breast smeared with poison, meaning to kill the infant Krishna as he fed. Another became Krishna himself and drank at her breast as he had done, and — so the story they had all heard went — he had drawn out the demon's very life with the milk. They played it through, there under the trees.

Another took the part of a demon again, this time the one who had come as a wooden cart to crush the sleeping child. She carried off a third gopi who had become the baby Krishna, and the baby kicked out with a small foot and overturned the cart, the way the real Krishna once had.

Two of them stood side by side and became Krishna and Balarama, the two brothers, and around them other gopis became the cowherd boys, keeping watch over cattle that were not there and calling to one another the way the herders did at pasture, their voices soft among the trees.

Then one of them raised her arm high above her head, the way Krishna had raised the whole hill of Govardhana on a single finger to shelter the village from the storm, and she called out in a voice that carried through the trees: do not fear the wind or the rain; I have made you a shelter.

One climbed up onto another and stamped down with her foot, as Krishna had once danced upon the hoods of the serpent Kaliya in the river's poisoned waters. Another pointed into the distance and cried: O cowherds, see the fierce forest fire — the fire Krishna had once swallowed whole to save them. One slim gopi sat down and let herself be tied with a garland of flowers at a grinding mortar, the way the child Krishna had been tied by his mother to the mortar for his mischief, and had slipped free even then.

Through all of it they went on asking the trees and the creepers of Vrindavan: have you seen him? And even as they asked, they kept moving, because motion was the only thing that kept the ache from settling. Every part they played was only another way of calling him back — as if, by wearing his deeds, they could hold some piece of him until he returned.
stories.reflection: The gopis' imitation is not mockery but memory made physical. In their frenzy they rehearse the whole of Krishna's childhood — Putana, the cart, Govardhana, Kaliya, the mortar — as a way of keeping him present. Devotion here is not a feeling but a performance, an enactment of everything he has been to them.
stories.next_story_tease: Then the earth itself laid a trail before them.

stories.title: The Favored Gopi's Pride and Krishna's Second Vanishing
stories.story:
On the forest floor, clear in the soft earth, the footprints stopped them. They knew them at once: these were the marks of Nanda's son.

The gopis stood over them the way you stand over a letter you did not expect. And then they saw what made their breath catch. Beside Krishna's footprints ran another set, smaller and lighter — the steps of one of their own. And where the two sets went on together, the ground was pressed deeper in places, as though he had carried her.

Suddenly the trees they had been questioning had no answers they wanted. The gopis read the story from the earth instead. Here, flowers had been gathered — picked for her, by him, the way a lover gathers blossoms. Here, a woman's hair had been dressed and arranged by careful hands. The gopis looked down at the dust of those footprints and called it blessed: blessed is the dust of Govinda's feet.

One of them had been chosen. The verses do not say the others were angry; they say they marveled, and ached. This woman, they told one another, must have worshiped him as no one else had, for him to single her out. He had taken her aside, away from all the rest, and kept her to himself in the deep of the forest. The verses add a strange and tender note: though he is self-delighted and self-satisfied, whole in himself and undivided, he had enjoyed her company all the same. The thought of it turned in the others like a splinter. They asked themselves what they had done, and what she had done, that he should choose her while the rest of them wandered the wood in the dark. And still they could not look away from the footprints, because the footprints were all of him they had left.

And the one he had chosen felt it too. Standing there, reading what the footprints told, she began to think herself the greatest of all women. Pride crept in where the wonder had been. So when she found Krishna waiting in a farther part of the forest, she did not fall at his feet. She told him, the text says, that she was tired — that she could not walk — and that he should carry her wherever he chose.

Krishna answered her gently. Climb onto my shoulder, he said, and I will take you.

She reached for him. She climbed. And at the very moment she would have settled onto his shoulder, Krishna was gone — vanished into the air, leaving her with nothing under her hands.

The verses give her cry: O lord, O my beloved, where are you, where are you, mighty-armed one? The forest gave back no answer. She had been lifted to the highest place of all, and she had thought it was her own. Now she stood alone, and understood.
stories.reflection: Krishna vanishes at the exact point of pride, not in anger but as a lesson that cannot be spoken — the favored gopi had begun to possess what could only ever be received. Her cry in the empty forest is the turning: what pride had claimed, loss hands back as longing.
stories.next_story_tease: But her remorse would not go unanswered for long.

stories.title: Krishna Reappears Among the Gopis
stories.story:
For a long while the gopis had searched the forest, and their grief had seemed to have no end. Krishna had vanished — twice now — and the second vanishing had taken from them even the thin comfort of hoping that searching would bring him back. Then, when they had nearly stopped looking, he was simply there before them: smiling, his face bright and open as a lotus.

The verses say only that he appeared. One moment the grove held nothing but their own sorrow; the next he stood among them, and the sorrow was not reasoned away — it left them all at once. They rose as if life itself had come back into their bodies. Their eyes, a moment before downcast and searching, bloomed open with joy.

And because no two of them loved him in the same way, no two of them received him in the same way. One took his hand in her two folded palms and held it, as you would hold something too precious to let fall. One, slender and quick, bent and lifted from him the betel he had been chewing, and kept it cupped in her own palms like a gift she would not share. Another knit her brows at him, flushed with an anger that was really love, silently reproaching him for having left her to such grief. Another did not blink at all, drinking in his face as if afraid that the moment she closed her eyes he would be gone again. And one more did not look with her eyes; she gathered him into her heart through the narrow opening of her closed lids, and kept him there, where he could not leave.

The verses linger on this, because it is the whole meaning of the scene: all of them, every one, overjoyed at the sight of him, their grief of separation washed clean. They pressed around him, and he stood among them.

Then he led them away from the place of their grief to the bright sandbank of the Yamuna. It was autumn, and the moon was full; its light lay on the water and the sand like something poured out, and the verses say that light drove away the darkness of all that was wrong. There, in that light, the ache in their hearts was dispelled, and their longings came to rest — the way, the verses say, the ancient scriptures themselves come to rest when they have carried a person all the way home.

He sat down among them. He was the master of every master of yoga, and yet the seat he accepted was the one they had already prepared for him — not any throne, but the seat they had made for him inside their own hearts. They welcomed him with smiles, with sidelong glances, with the small glad play of their brows: the language of people who have been given back what they thought was lost.

There is no rebuke in the scene, and no explanation. Krishna does not say why he had vanished, and the gopis do not ask. Whatever they needed to hear, they would hear soon enough. For this one moment, the answer was simply that he had come back.
stories.reflection: The scene is made of small, individual gestures — a hand held, a bit of betel kept, an unblinking gaze — because the verses want the reunion to be felt one gopi at a time and then all at once. Here grief is not dispelled by argument but by presence.
stories.next_story_tease: But the gopis still carried a question they needed to ask him.

stories.title: Krishna Teaches About Love
stories.story:
In the moonlight on the sandbank, with the Yamuna moving quietly nearby, the gopis found the courage to ask what had been troubling them. They had just been given back what they thought they had lost, and in the relief of it the question they had carried for so long rose at last to the surface. They had given up everything for Krishna — home, family, the quiet duties the world expected of them — and they wanted to understand the way he loved them in return. Why, they asked, does he love those who love him, and yet seem to hold something back, to give and then to vanish?

He did not answer with a doctrine. He answered with the way love actually behaves.

Some people, he said, serve those who do not serve them back — the way a father and mother serve a child, not because the child can ever repay them, but out of compassion. The parents keep no account of what the child owes. They give because the giving is its own reason, and that is one kind of love, whole and complete, asking nothing in return. And there are others, he went on, who even when they are served with everything do not serve back at all. So from those, he asked, how could anyone expect love, when even a gift freely given wins nothing from them?

But he, he told them, was like neither. When people served him, he did not simply return the favor, the way one trader settles accounts with another, weighing what was given against what is owed. That kind of repayment would end the matter, and he did not want anything to end. What he gave back, he gave in order to draw them further in — to deepen the very love that had reached for him, so that it would not stop, so that its roots would go down and hold.

And then he turned the question around and set it before them. You, he said, have cast aside the world and its claims, even the obligations the scriptures lay down, all for my sake — and still you follow me. There is no repaying that. He told them plainly that even if he lived as long as the gods themselves, he could not repay what they had done for him. So there would be no settling of accounts, no balancing of the ledger, not ever.

The verses say it more beautifully than any of them could have: their own goodness returned to them of itself. The love they had given was not an investment to be recovered with interest. It had already done its work, and its reward was simply itself. The love was already theirs, the way a flame is already warm without needing to be warmed in return.

And so he had answered their question by dissolving it. They had asked how he would repay their love, and he had told them there was no question of repayment — because what they had given could not be repaid, and did not need to be. It had already come home.
stories.reflection: Krishna refuses the arithmetic of love. He will not settle accounts with the gopis the way a trader settles a debt, because that would end the matter; instead he deepens the devotion they have already offered. Their love, he tells them, is its own reward — it has already returned to them.
stories.next_story_tease: That night, under the same autumn moon, the answer would be danced rather than spoken.

stories.title: The Great Rasa Dance
stories.story:
The moon that rose over the Yamuna that autumn night was full and whole, and the forest lay silver beneath it. The river moved quietly, and the air was mild, and the whole of Vrindavan seemed to have settled into the kind of night that asks nothing of anyone. It was the season of clear nights, when the year turns and the moon hangs low and white. Krishna looked at the night and found it good for dancing. So it was that, on the bank of the river, he began the rasa dance, and the gopis of Vraja gathered around him.

He did not dance alone at the centre of the circle. He became as many as the women themselves, so that between every two gopis there stood a Krishna, and each one felt him near and no other beside her. In him they had found the one they loved beyond all others, and for those hours nothing else existed. The circle was bright with sound before it was bright with anything else, bangles and anklets and little bells keeping time in the dark.

They danced with the whole of themselves. Their feet found the beat and kept it; their arms swept and lifted; they bent at the waist, and their garments swayed, and their earrings swung against their cheeks. Their faces glistened with the effort, and their throats flushed as they sang aloud, and their hair came loose, and the flowers slipped from it without anyone stopping to notice. They sang of him as they danced, their voices rising above the water, and their songs, as much as their steps, belonged to the season, full of the clear night and the turning year. One of them sang with him in a single blended voice, as though the same note came from two throats. Another, weary from the dance, leaned on his shoulder for a moment and did not fall. One, as she moved, kept only the tinkling of her anklets and her girdle for company, and still she sang. In the ring they shone, it is said, like lightning moving within a circle of clouds.

High above, the women of the sky leaned out to watch, and the sight bewildered them: a ring of mortal women on a riverbank, and at every turn a god beside each of them. The gods rained flowers down on the dance. Petals fell on the water, on the grass, on the dark heads of the gopis as they circled, and the night filled with their fragrance.

As the night wore on, the gopis grew tired, and some of them, in the middle of their joy, put on a small show of pride, yet still they sang of his deeds, delighting in the touch of his hands. Where a face was hot from the dance, his hand was there, and the weariness of them seemed to matter to him more than the dance itself. He led them to the river to wash the heat of the dancing away. They went with him the way a herd follows its lord, and in the water they splashed him, laughing, and he let them. From the bright chariots above, more flowers came down, and with them the praise of those who watched, and Krishna, rejoicing in his own nature, took his ease among them.

In this way the moonlit nights of autumn passed, one after another, and Krishna, who wanted for nothing, kept the company of the women of Vraja under the moon, and the women kept his. The dance ended as it had begun, not with a word but with the moon high over the water.
stories.reflection: The multiplication is striking not as a display of power but as a form of attention: Krishna becomes many so that no gopi in the circle is left without him. What the sources linger on is not the miracle itself but the moonlight, the music, and the nearness.

stories.title: Uddhava Arrives Bearing Krishna's Message
stories.story:
The stranger who came into Vrindavan was no cowherd. The settlement had been quiet since Krishna left it, the cows still grazing and the flute silent, and into that quiet a man walked who did not belong to it. The gopis saw him from across the grove and stopped what they were doing, because there was something about him that made them stare: his dress, his ornaments, even the way he carried himself seemed to belong to someone else — to Krishna, who had gone away from them to the city, and who had not come back.

They surrounded him at once, astonished. Who is this, they asked one another, so beautiful to look upon, and from where has he come, wearing Achyuta's dress and ornaments? And their astonishment was not only at his beauty. It was at the sudden, aching nearness of the one they had been pining for — as though Krishna had come back to them wearing a stranger's face. For months they had lived in the stillness of his absence, and now here was a man who wore his very clothes, as if the one they longed for had reached out and touched their world again.

They honored him before a word was spoken. They received him with humility, with shy smiles and sidelong glances and gentle words — the same tenderness they would have given Krishna himself. Then they said what they had already understood: we know you have come as the attendant of the lord of the Yadavas, sent out of love for the home he left behind. Otherwise, if it were not for him, we can see nothing else in this cowherd settlement worth your remembering. What would bring a man like you to Vraja, except him?

And there, in that greeting, the grief they had been carrying began to speak. The world, they said, makes friendship for a purpose, and when the purpose is served, the friendship is served too. A woman of the street leaves a man the moment his purse is empty; the kindness she showed him was never for him, only for his money. Subjects abandon a king the moment he can no longer rule; their loyalty was only the price of his protection. Birds forsake a tree the moment its fruit is gone, and guests walk away from a house the moment the meal is done. Everyone, it seemed, loved only while there was something still to be had.

But they did not. Their love was the one thing in Vrindavan that had not gone looking for something to be had. Krishna had left them, and still they spoke of no one but him; there was nothing left to gain from him, and still they would not let him go. The verses say it plainly: with speech, body, and mind fixed on Govinda, they went on singing the deeds they loved, and weeping, with all shame gone — because grief for him was not a thing to hide.
stories.reflection: The gopis greet Krishna's messenger with their own hard-won knowledge of the world — that most friendship lasts only as long as its usefulness — and measure their own love against it. Theirs is the one attachment that did not break when the object of it went away.
stories.next_story_tease: And as they spoke, one gopi, seeing a honeybee, would pour out her grief to it as though it were Krishna's own messenger.

stories.title: The Gopi's Lament to the Bee
stories.subtitle: Bhramara-gita
stories.story:
One of the gopis sat a little apart from the others, and while she sat there, turning over her grief for Krishna, a honeybee came humming and settled near her feet. Her mind was so full of him that she did not see an insect. She saw a messenger, come from far away, and she spoke to it as though it could carry her words back.

O bee, she said, friend of the cheat — do not touch my feet. She knew what it was, she said, the moment she saw it: a courier wearing the saffron of the garlands that had been crushed against other women's breasts, come to mock her before the assembly of the Yadavas. Let Krishna carry his favor to those proud women who now have him, she said; I have no need of a messenger from such a place.

Her anger was grief with nowhere else to go. He made us drink once, she said, the nectar of his lips, and it bewitched us — and now he casts us aside like flowers, the way a garland is thrown down when the evening is over. How is it, she asked, that the goddess of fortune waits upon his feet, though she too has lost her heart to him? Why does the bee sing of the lord of the Yadavas here, before us, who have nothing left to offer it? Let it sing instead before his new loves, the ones whose pain he has already eased.

She did not stop. She remembered how he had always charmed and then wounded — taking what was offered and then binding the giver, the way a hunter calls and then strikes — and she said, enough of friendship with the dark one, though his stories are the one thing we can never let go of.

And even as she said enough, she could not leave him. Others, she said, had heard a single drop of the nectar of his pastimes and had abandoned home and family to wander like birds. We trusted him, she said, the way a deer trusts a hunter's call — and we have felt the sharp hurt of longing again and again. Dear friend, she said to the bee, if you are truly sent by the one I love, choose what you want and take it, for you are to be honored by me. But how will you carry us back to him, whose side no one can bear to leave, and on whose chest the goddess of fortune sits as his wife?

Then all her reproach collapsed into a single, helpless question. Does he still dwell in the city of Madhu? Does he remember his father's house, and his kinsmen, and the cowherds? Does he ever speak of us, his maidservants? And when — when will he place on my head that arm of his, fragrant with aloe?

She did not expect the bee to answer. The question was not really for the bee at all. It was the same thing she had been asking the empty air every day since he left, and it would go on being asked until he came back.
stories.reflection: The lament's power is that reproach and longing are the same act. The gopi accuses Krishna of abandoning her precisely because she cannot imagine a world without him; every bitter word is only another way of keeping him near.
stories.next_story_tease: The messenger who had come to Vrindavan would soon carry her words, and Krishna's answer, back between them.

stories.title: Uddhava Delivers Krishna's Message and the Gopis Reply
stories.story:
A real messenger had come at last. For months the women of Vrindavan had poured their grief into the empty air; they had even pleaded with a bee, mistaking it for a courier from Mathura. Now a man stood before them who had actually travelled from Krishna, carrying words from his own mouth. His name was Uddhava, and the verses say he had been sent for this one purpose — to bring the women of Vraja some word from the friend who had left them.

Uddhava was Krishna's friend and counsellor, a man of learning and restraint, and the verses make a point of what he did first. Before he spoke a single word of the message, he praised the gopis. Through gifts, vows, austerities, sacrifice, study and self-control, he told them, they had offered up sons, husbands, homes and their own bodies to a single love, and that love had made them peerless — no one on earth had done what they had done. Only then, having honored them, did he speak Krishna's words.

The message was not an apology, and it was not a promise to return. Krishna asked them to see that he had never truly been far from them at all. As ether and air, fire, water and earth pervade every living being, so he pervaded all things; he was the one who creates, preserves and destroys by his own self alone, the self made of pure knowledge, untouched by the world's qualities. There was nothing outside him to be lost. A beloved who is far away, he said, remains close in the mind of the one who loves; so let them fix their minds wholly on him, and they would soon attain him. This, he said, was the whole conclusion of the scriptures, of yoga and of the wise. And then, almost a memory spoken aloud: it was he who had played with them at night in this very forest of Vraja.

The gopis did not accept it, and they did not refuse it. They answered with a grief so steady it had become its own kind of truth.

Does he remember us? they asked. Does Govinda, who understands every shade of love, remember the nights when the moon hung bright over Vrindavan, the groves white with jasmine and kunda blossom, and he danced among us, his ankle-bells ringing, while we praised him with our songs? Will the Dasarha ever come back here, scorched by a sorrow of his own making? He has won a kingdom now and slain his enemies; why would he return to us, women of the forest? What are we, who live in the woods, to that great soul? And then the heart of it, the question behind every other question: who could bear to give up the memory of him? These rivers, these hills and forest paths, these cows, the sound of the flute — everything in this place calls back the son of Nanda, again and again. O lord, O lord of Rama, O lord of Vraja, remover of sorrows.

So the exchange ended not in comfort but in a strange completion. Krishna had asked them to fix their minds on him; they answered that they could not do otherwise — that the world around them would not let them forget, and that forgetting was the one thing their love could not manage. What he had called a path to union, they had already been walking, without choosing it, from the day he left. Uddhava, who had come to teach them, stood silent, and something in the learned man began to turn.
stories.reflection: The gopis cannot be consoled by argument because what they carry is not ignorance but love. Krishna asks for a mind fixed wholly on him, and their reply — that rivers, hills and a flute will not let them forget — is that very fixing, already accomplished. Their longing is the union he describes.
stories.next_story_tease: But their reply undid the messenger, and Uddhava would soon wish to trade his learning for a place in the dust of their feet.
stories.hero_scene: Uddhava standing before the gopis in a Vrindavan grove at dusk, the women gathered around him, their faces lifted as they answer that every river, hill and the sound of the flute will not let them forget Krishna.

stories.title: Uddhava Praises the Gopis and Departs
stories.story:
The learned man who had come to teach stood humbled, and the wish that rose in him was one no teacher was supposed to make. Uddhava had listened to the gopis answer Krishna's message, and what he had seen in them rearranged everything he thought he knew about worth.

He did not leave at once. The verses say he stayed some months in Vrindavan, easing the sorrow of the women who had become his teachers. Day by day he walked the country, looking at the rivers, the forests, the valleys and the flowering trees, and day by day he watched the gopis in their state — wholly absorbed in Krishna, their minds carried away by him, so agitated with love that the place itself seemed to shake with their longing. And as he watched, the praise poured out of him. Wherever he looked — a river bend, a stand of trees, a hill in the distance — he saw how thoroughly the place and its people belonged to Krishna, and how thoroughly Krishna belonged to them.

These cowherd women, he said, have reached the highest place any living being can reach. Their hearts are fixed on Govinda, the soul of all things; what good are even brahmana births, he asked, compared to the taste of the endless stories about him? Consider the distance between the two — where are these simple forest women, and where is the supreme self? — and yet the Lord has made them his own. The favor of being held in Krishna's arms at the rasa dance, the embrace that even the gods long for, was freely given to these women of Vraja. This blessing, he said, is not granted even to the goddess of fortune herself, nor to the lotus-scented women of heaven; how then could anyone lesser hope for it? And the Lord bestows his highest good even on the ignorant who serve him, the way a king of medicines heals one who takes it without understanding what it is. These women had thrown away their families and the straight road of duty for the path that the scriptures themselves search for.

And then the wish that turned the whole order upside down. May I become any shrub, any creeper, any herb at all in Vrindavan, blessed by the dust of these gopis' feet. Again and again he bowed to that dust — I bow to the foot-dust of the women of Nanda's Vraja, again and again — the man of learning wanting nothing more than to grow from the roadside where they walked.

When the time came to go, he had one more duty. He comforted Nanda and Yashoda and the cowherds, speaking to them of Krishna, and they honored him as they would a brother, coming to him with offerings in their hands. Their one wish, spoken plainly, was that their minds might rest forever at Krishna's lotus feet, wherever the wandering of their lives might take them. Uddhava bowed toward Krishna, wherever he was, and set out on the road back to Mathura, carrying the news of how the people of Vraja loved him still — a devotion he could now measure, because he had felt a share of it himself. When he reached Mathura he told Krishna plainly of the fullness of the devotion he had found among the cowherds.

He had gone to console, and had been the one changed. A counsellor of kings had asked to be a roadside shrub, and no one who heard him thought the wish foolish.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's wish to become a shrub in Vrindavan quietly reverses every ranking he brought with him. The man of learning envies not the gopis' knowledge but their totality — they gave away everything the world calls secure and gained the one thing the scriptures point toward but cannot hand over.
stories.next_story_tease: Not long after Uddhava returned to Mathura, another envoy set out for Vrindavan — a man named Akrura, sent by the king.

stories.title: Akrura Journeys to Vrindavan
stories.story:
The man on the road was the envoy of a tyrant, and yet the nearer he came to Vrindavan, the lighter his errand felt. Akrura had been sent by Kamsa, the king of Mathura, to fetch Krishna and Balarama to the city. But in his own heart Akrura was no servant of Kamsa, and as his chariot moved through the country he began to speak to himself, not as a messenger but as a pilgrim.

What good have I ever done, he wondered, that I should have this? What great austerity have I performed, that the rare sight of Krishna — the sight the sages and the gods long for — should be coming to me? He turned the thought over and over, and it kept returning the same answer: it was not a thing he had earned. Even Kamsa, by sending him, had unwittingly shown him grace; the very man who meant harm had handed Akrura the chance to behold the lotus feet of Hari. Feet worshipped by Brahma and Shiva, by the goddess of fortune and the sages, feet that had wandered the forest herding cows, marked with the dust of the gopis' love — feet that give shelter to those fleeing the great serpent of time, and at which Indra and Bali once placed their offerings and won the lordship of the three worlds.

He let himself imagine the meeting, and the imagining became its own kind of prayer. He would see the face at last — the fine cheeks and nose, the smiling glance, the eyes like red lotuses — the Lord who had descended of his own free will into the line of the Yadus to lift the earth's burden, whose praises mingle with every auspicious word spoken of his deeds and his births. He pictured himself falling at Krishna's feet, and Krishna's own lotus hand resting on his head in blessing. He saw the embrace: the two strong arms closing around him, and the voice — that voice — saying, "O Akrura." And if that word were ever spoken to him, he thought, then his birth — every birth — would at last be fulfilled. He imagined Krishna looking at him with a smile and eyes soft with kindness, and the thought alone, he felt, would wash away every wrong he had ever carried. He dared to hope Balarama would embrace him too.

And then the fear that every sincere heart knows. I am Kamsa's messenger, he thought. What if Krishna, who sees everything within and without, reads the errand and turns away? But the fear dissolved as quickly as it rose. Krishna is no partisan, he told himself; he has no favorite and no enemy, no one he despises and no one he avoids. He would not hold against a man the chariot he happened to arrive in, or the errand he happened to carry.

So he rode on, his thoughts no longer on the message he carried but on the feet he was travelling toward. The sun sank low, and at Gokula, as the day ended, he came down from the chariot. There in the dust of the road he saw them — the footprints of the Lord, marked with the lotus and the other signs, the feet whose dust adorns the crowns of all the protectors of the worlds. He stood before them a long moment, and the journey was already over, because the errand had already become something else.

He had set out to carry a king's order. He had arrived carrying only a longing, and it was enough.
stories.reflection: Akrura's fear that Krishna will read his errand and turn away is the fear of anyone who comes to the divine with mixed motives. The story answers it not with reassurance but with a truth about Krishna himself — that he holds no one as enemy or favorite — which makes the road, and not the message, the real point of the journey.
stories.next_story_tease: The footprints were only the beginning; ahead, at the cow-pens of Vrindavan, the Lord himself was waiting to be seen.
stories.hero_scene: Akrura standing beside his chariot on the road into Gokula at sunset, gazing down at the footprints of Krishna marked with the lotus and other auspicious signs in the dust.

stories.title: Akrura Arrives in Vrindavan and Beholds Krishna
stories.story:
Akrura reached Vraja at the hour when the day gives way to night — the sun's rays grown weak, the moon rising tawny in the crimson sky, the birds gone to their nests, and the cows come home lowing to be milked, their calves bound to the stakes, the milkmen calling the kine in by name and kindling the evening fires. It was at this hour that he came down from his chariot and walked in.

At the cow-pens, among the milking cows, he saw them, and he could not stay on his feet. There were two youths — one dark, one fair, both big-armed and garlanded, their feet marked with the flag, the thunderbolt, the goad and the lotus. The dark one was Krishna, dark as the leaf of a full-blown lotus; the fair one was Balarama, white as jasmine. They stood at the milking place in the midst of the calves, at the meeting point of boyhood and youth, and their very radiance, the verses say, scattered the last of the evening's gloom. Akrura's face opened with delight.

He did not walk toward them; he fell. Jumping down from the chariot, overwhelmed with love, the hair on his body standing on end and his eyes brimming, he threw himself into the dust where the Lord's feet had been, crying out again and again over the blessed foot-dust that crowns the heads of all the protectors of the worlds. This, he knew, was the highest thing any embodied being could hold — to lie there in that dust, free at last of pretence and fear and grief. Within himself he praised the Lord again and again, remembering who this was — the lotus-eyed one who had once lain on a fig-leaf at the dissolution of all things, and who had once stepped over the three worlds as a dwarf.

Krishna saw him coming and understood everything at once. He and Balarama came forward, and as Akrura lay prostrate at their feet, the two of them lifted him up and embraced him. They asked after his welfare, gave him a seat of honor, and offered him a cow as a guest is offered. Balarama, who knew every courtesy, washed his tired feet from the road. The envoy of a cruel king was received as a brother come home.

Only when he had eaten and rested did the questions begin — and they came not from the youths but from Nanda, the cowherd chief. Nanda received the stranger as family, and then asked, gently, how the Yadavas fared — living as they did under a king with no grace in him, the wretch who had killed his own sister's children while she wept. There was no anger in Nanda's voice, only the concern of one kinsman for others far away under a cruel roof.

And so the man who had arrived as the agent of that very king was received, not as an envoy to be suspected, but as a friend to be fed and questioned with kindness. No one demanded his business. No one asked what message he carried, or pressed him to speak. The cowherds honored him, and he in turn honored Krishna, and for that one evening at least, the errand that hung over them all could wait.

Akrura had expected to look upon Krishna from a distance, as a servant looks upon his lord. Instead he was pulled to his feet, embraced, and seated at the table as kin. The sight he had longed for became a welcome, and the welcome became the message he had really been sent to learn.
stories.reflection: The story turns on hospitality rather than drama. A man who came as the envoy of a tyrant is met with food, a seat of honor and a kinsman's question, before any errand is spoken. In that welcome the fear Akrura carried on the road dissolves — he is received not for what he represents but for who he is.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana also describes this meeting, likening Krishna to the leaf of a full-blown lotus and Balarama to jasmine, a swan or the moon; the Harivamsha sets the arrival in a richly described evening in Vraja and adds the image of Krishna among the calves like a bull. The core event is the same across all three.
stories.next_story_tease: But the errand could not wait forever, and before long Akrura would have to speak the truth of why Kamsa had really sent him.

stories.title: Akrura Reveals Kamsa's Plan
stories.story:
The man Kamsa had sent was, of all things, an honest one. Akrura had come to Vrindavan to carry out his king's orders, but the moment he beheld Krishna he had bowed to the ground, and the errand no longer sat easily in his mouth. Now he stood before Krishna and Balarama, and Krishna welcomed him as a kinsman, though his greeting carried an edge. Why do you ask after our welfare, Krishna said, when the trouble in our own family only grows? And then he asked what message had brought Akrura all this way.

Akrura gave it to him, all of it. He told of Kamsa's long enmity toward the Yadavas, the hatred the king of Mathura had nursed for years. He told of Kamsa's resolve to kill Vasudeva, their father. And he told them the reason he himself had been sent as a messenger: the king meant to use this errand to draw the two brothers to the city.

Then, because he was a Yadava himself and could not keep it in, he spoke of their parents. Your father, he said, has grown old in sorrow; his limbs have wasted away, and Kamsa of sinful designs oppresses him still. Out of fear for the king and grief at your absence, his mind burns with anxiety day and night. And Devaki — he would not soften it — your mother is growing lean with grief, like a cow separated from her calf. Her sons never lay at her breast. Her eyes have sunk into their sockets like the moon seized by Rahu, and she wears soiled garments and spends her days poorly. Since your infancy she has been parted from you, never once hearing your child's talk, never once seeing your moon-like face. If, by giving birth to you, she must only repent, what need had she of a son at all? A woman without children suffers but one grief; a woman whose sons do not accomplish their purpose knows no end of sorrow. As the earth bears you, so Devaki deserves your reverence — save her, a goddess sunk into the water of sorrow.

You vanquished Kaliya in the waters of the Yamuna, Akrura went on. You lifted Govardhana for the sake of the cows. You destroyed Arishta and the wicked Keshi. Now make one more exertion, with the same care, and save your aged parents from their grief. You are the saviour of even your enemies, your prowess like Indra's, your accomplishments without equal — and yet the mother who bore you lives in a grief she never asked for. Though they are aged, your parents now serve another master, and Kamsa insults them on your account. Those who saw your father insulted in Kamsa's own court are all shedding tears. A son is born owing his parents a debt, one the scriptures set down, and it is paid only by care. If you show them this favour, they will lay down their grief — and you will have done your duty.

Krishna had known all of it before Akrura opened his mouth. He took no offence at the words. He simply said, "So be it."

Hearing that, the cowherds led by Nanda resolved to obey Kamsa's summons: they would go to Mathura. They dressed themselves and set about arranging their tributes — buffaloes and bulls, curd, milk, and clarified butter — and the heads of the cowherd clans made ready their offerings. Akrura spent the night without sleep, speaking with Krishna and Balarama, and in the dawn, when the birds began to sound and the last stars faded, Vraja stirred and prepared to travel.
stories.reflection: Akrura's honesty is the quiet centre of this episode: sent as Kamsa's messenger, he speaks the truth of his own mission and pleads for the parents left behind in Mathura, while Krishna, who already knew it all, listens to the end before he answers.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana (5.18) has Krishna answer with a specific vow, that within three nights he would slay Kamsa and his adherents; the Bhagavata Purana, followed here, records the revelation and the reason for the mission without that promise.
stories.next_story_tease: But when Nanda proclaimed the journey to the whole village, the gopis heard it — and their grief would not be silenced.

stories.title: The Gopis Grieve at His Leaving
stories.story:
Nanda gave the word, and it fell on the gopis like a blow. Gather all the milk and its products, he told the cowherds; tomorrow we go to Mathura, and we will carry the king his tribute. The gopis heard it, and their world tilted.

Some of them lost the light from their faces, their breath coming short. Others stopped in the middle of whatever they were doing, lost in the thought of him. Others stood remembering him — his smiles, his way of walking, his laughing glances, the softness of his look — and were afraid of the separation that was coming. They turned on Akrura.

You showed us his face, they said, framed by those dark curls, the cheeks so fair, the fine nose, the little smile that chased away every sorrow — and now you are doing us a cruel wrong, carrying him out of our sight. You are called Akrura, "not cruel," and yet you are cruel indeed: you gave us these eyes, and now you steal away the very thing they were given to see.

Others thought of the city, and their fear sharpened. The night will pass pleasantly for the women of Mathura, they said; their wishes have come true. Today the eyes of the city clans will feast on him, and we will be left here with nothing. He will hear their sweet and polished speech, and he will never again endure our rustic words. He captured our hearts with words sweeter than honey, and then he wanders off to be charmed by the bashful smiles of those simple city women. Nanda's son is new to affection, and his friendship breaks in a moment. We gave up our homes, our kin, our children, our husbands, to serve him — and now, how will he ever look at us again?

Let us go and stop Madhava, one of them said. What can our elders and kinsmen do to us now? There he stands, the dry-hearted one, already mounting the chariot, while the proud ones urge him on.

And they remembered the evenings, which were the worst of all to remember. At the close of day, when Krishna came back into Vraja with the cowherds around him, the dust of hooves on his hair and garland, playing his flute and casting his smiling, sidelong glances, he would steal their hearts all over again. His smiles and his sweet words, his playful glances and his embraces, had made their nights pass by like a moment. Without him, they asked one another, how were we ever to cross the darkness that now stretched ahead?

They wept, their bracelets hanging loose upon their wasted arms, and the thought of his going sat on the whole village through the night.
stories.reflection: The gopis' grief is remarkable for how precise it is. They name exactly what they will lose — his face, his smile, his flute at evening, the dust of hooves on his hair — and they fear, with reason, that the polished city will outbid their rustic love. Their sorrow is not vague; it is a catalogue of a life.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna would not leave them to their weeping without a word.
