stories.title: The Citizens Rejoice in the Arena
stories.story:
Krishna walked into the arena still holding the elephant's tusk, Balarama at his side, and the city looked down at the two of them and forgot, for a moment, that it had come to watch them die. They shone as they entered — the two of them great-armed, in bright garments and garlands and ornaments, the tusk carried like a staff of proof — and the crowd's eyes followed them across the sand.

The galleries were full — townsmen and countrymen, kings and commoners, wrestlers and merchants, women at the screened windows — all of them standing on the tiers and leaning forward over the rail. The verses say they drank the two young men in, with their eyes and as if with their tongues, unable to look away from what stood below them.

Then they began to speak to one another, and what they said was the same and yet different, for each person saw the two according to his own heart. To the wrestlers, they whispered, this one is a thunderbolt. To ordinary men he was the best of men. To the women he was love itself given a form. To the cowherds of Vrindavan he was one of their own, come in from the pastures. To the wicked among the kings he was a chastiser, come to call them to account. To the ignorant he was the highest truth; to the yogis, the end of all their striving; to the line of the Vrishnis, their own supreme deity. To his parents he was still only a child. And to the lord of the Bhojas — to Kamsa, seated high above them — he was death walking in through the gate.

And as they looked, the people began to remember aloud what they had heard of this boy. They told how he was born to Devaki and carried away in the night to Gokula. How the demoness Putana had been brought to an end by him, and the whirlwind demon after her. How he had saved the cows and the cowherds from the forest fire, and how he had held up a great hill on one hand for seven whole days. They spoke of the gopis, who never tired of his smiling, glancing face, and of how he had made the line of Yadu famous in every land. And this one beside him, they said, is his elder brother — the glorious Rama, with the lotus eyes.

The trumpets were still sounding, but above them rose another sound: the murmur of a crowd realizing, all at once, who it was that had walked into its arena. The two they had come to see as victims were being named, from every side and in every way, as something far older and far larger than the sport of an afternoon. The rejoicing filled the galleries before a single blow of the wrestling had been struck.
stories.reflection: The verse does not pick one of the crowd's descriptions as the true one. It says Krishna is all of them at once — thunderbolt and kinsman, child and death — and that each person, for a moment, is given the sight he or she is ready for. Recognition is the whole event here, and it happens before the fight.
stories.next_story_tease: But the rejoicing did not last; Chanura was already stepping forward.

stories.title: Chanura Challenges Krishna and Balarama
stories.story:
The rejoicing had not yet settled when a wrestler walked out into the centre of the arena and raised his hand for quiet. His name was Chanura, the strongest of Kamsa's champions, and the crowd, which had been chanting only a moment before, knew at once what was coming.

He called out to the two brothers by name, and his words were smooth. "Son of Nanda," he said, "and Rama — you two are counted among heroes. And those who do what pleases the king find their own welfare in it. The cowherds, after all, are always cheerful, as everyone can plainly see. So let us, both you and I, do what will please the king today."

It was an invitation dressed as a courtesy, and everyone in the arena understood what it really asked. Chanura was leading the two boys toward a match with the king's wrestlers — men trained to kill, men for whom the ring was not sport but work. He spoke of pleasing the king as if pleasure and death were the same thing in that place, and the crowd's noise fell away as it waited to hear how the two would answer.

Krishna's reply, the verses say, was fitted to the place and the moment, and it was more careful than Chanura's challenge deserved. He did not refuse the fight, and he did not call it a trap, though it was. He simply stated what was true. We are subjects of this lord of the Bhojas, he said, but we are forest-dwellers — boys who grew up among the cows. We are children. A boy plays with boys of his own strength; that is what is proper. Let it be a fair match, and we will gladly make sport.

There was a weight in that answer that Chanura, for all his size, did not seem to feel. He was a wrestler who had made his name by breaking the men he was set against, and he would not be turned aside by the word of a boy. He answered that the fight must go forward, that the strong ones were waiting, and that there was no injustice in any of it — he himself would meet Krishna, and Mushtika would face Balarama.

High above the ring, Kamsa did not speak. He had arranged this whole day, and now his champion was arranging the last of it for him, pressing the two boys toward the match that was meant to end them. He leaned forward on his throne and watched, and said nothing.

So the terms were set, not by the two young men but by the man who could not see what he was asking for. Chanura had framed the match as a favour to the king and a kindness to the crowd. In pressing it on two boys who had asked only for equals, he had done something simpler and more dangerous: he had made it plain, to everyone watching, which side had begun with the unfairness. The wrestlers took their places, and the arena held its breath.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer is a small lesson in restraint. He does not refuse the fight; he names its rules — that they are boys, that equals should meet equals. It is Chanura, the champion, who insists on the unfair match, and in doing so he only tells the whole arena whose cause is the just one.
stories.next_story_tease: The match itself was about to begin.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Slay the Wrestlers
stories.story:
Kamsa had called the brothers to Mathura for a festival of arms, meaning all along to destroy them, and now, in the great arena before a packed assembly, he set his champions against them. Chanura and Mushtika were not ordinary men. They were grown wrestlers, hardened in every limb, and the two who stood opposite them were boys, barely arrived in the city, their faces soft and their eyes bright. The crowd saw the mismatch the moment it was announced. There was nothing festive about it; everyone in that arena understood what the king intended, and no one dared say it aloud until the match was under way.

The match began. Hand to hand and foot to foot they gripped, elbow to elbow and knee to knee. They whirled and threw and grappled, lifted and shook and dropped, rose and circled and set again, each reading the other's strength. It was, the verses say, a contest of equal against equal in skill, but the bodies could not have been more unequal. The women of the assembly could not keep silent. "What injustice is this," they cried to the royal court, "for these honored ones? The wrestlers are hard as diamond in every limb, like mountains — and look at the faces of these two boys. Do you not see Krishna's lotus face as he moves about his enemy, and Balarama's eyes gone red? Fortunate indeed is the land of Vraja, where such boys grew up tending cows and playing the flute with garlands of wild flowers in their hair. What penance did the gopis of that place perform, that they may drink in such a face each day — at the morning milking and the churning and the sweeping, at dawn when the herd goes out and at dusk when it comes home again, when they run out to the road to see that smiling face and its compassionate glance?" But the fight went on, for the king had willed it, and the two wrestlers, hearing the women's fear, only pressed in harder.

Krishna heard their words and, moved by that motherly concern, turned fully to his task. He sprang at Chanura with the speed of a hawk, both fists clenched, and struck. Chanura did not so much as flinch — the blow fell on him the way a garland falls on an elephant, light and unregarded. But Krishna would not be shaken off. He seized the wrestler, whirled him through the air, and dashed him to the ground, and Chanura's life left him there in the dust of the arena.

Beside him Balarama met Mushtika, and his fist found its mark until Mushtika sagged and fell, undone. Then the others came forward in turn, and the two brothers dealt with them the same way. Kuta went down before Balarama, and Shala fell to a blow from Krishna's foot, and after them Tośala, until not one of the king's champions was left standing.

The assembly sat stunned. What they had watched was not the sport Kamsa had promised. Two boys had walked into an arena built to break them and had walked out untouched, while the men who were meant to break them lay still. The two brothers stood breathing easily in the middle of it all, as though the morning had cost them nothing. The women who had cried out against the injustice did not cheer; they had simply been proven right, and the court that had let the match proceed sat silent under the weight of it. And somewhere above it all, the king who had arranged this fate was already reaching for a crueler command.
stories.reflection: The women's protest is the moral heart of the scene: the crowd recognizes the injustice before the fight is decided, and says so aloud. Their outcry does not stop the contest, but it records for the reader exactly who understood the truth of what was being arranged.
stories.content_note: The death of the wrestlers is described briefly; the Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana give a more graphic account than the Bhagavata, which this telling follows.
stories.next_story_tease: But the king's fury was not spent — the death of his champions only stoked it.

stories.title: Krishna Slays Kamsa
stories.story:
The arena had gone quiet. The last of Kamsa's champions lay where he had fallen, and for a long moment the king of Mathura sat on his high dais staring down at the two brothers who had just unmade his every plan. The crowd, which had cheered and protested and held its breath all morning, now waited in a different silence, afraid of what the king would say. Then, before the whole assembly, his fury found its voice. He gave his orders in a rush: drive the two sons of Vasudeva out of the city, bind the cowherd chief Nanda, and put the evil-minded Vasudeva himself to death. He meant to end in one morning what he had spent years failing to prevent.

Krishna heard him from the arena floor, and something in him kindled. He did not wait for the guards to move, did not give the king time to rise. He crossed the floor and sprang, and in one motion he was on the high dais where Kamsa sat. The king reached for his sword, but Krishna was on him like a hawk sweeping left and right across the sky, too quick for the hand that groped for the hilt. He seized Kamsa by the hair, and the crown slipped from the king's head as Krishna dragged him from the seat and hurled him into the arena below. Then Krishna fell upon him, and before the eyes of all the people the reign of Kamsa came to an end.

The account does not linger on the killing. What it remembers instead is the strange mercy hidden inside it. All his life Kamsa had lived in dread of Krishna, seeing him everywhere — in what he drank, in what he ate, in every walk he took, in every sleep, in every breath. The prophecy that Devaki's child would be his death had followed him so completely that he could not turn anywhere without meeting the one he feared. By day and by night the face he dreaded stood before him, so that there was not a single unguarded hour in all his reign. And so when the end finally came, it was not a stranger who struck him down. It was the very face he had spent every hour trying to forget, coming for him at last.

Krishna and Balarama had not come to Mathura for the sport of an arena. As one old account puts it, they had come to set their parents free — and the man who had held Devaki and Vasudeva captive for so many years now lay still before their son. What Kamsa had feared for a lifetime had come to pass in a single morning, and it had not required more than a boy's two hands. A long dread was over, not only for Kamsa but for the whole city that had carried his fear through all those years.

The dais stood empty. The crown lay where it had fallen. The tyrant was gone, and the city he had ruled with fear could look up without weighing his next command. Somewhere in the stands a long-held breath went out of the crowd, the way a storm loosens all at once. Krishna stood over the fallen king in the silence of the arena, and Mathura did not yet know what to call the thing that had just happened. But the man who had waited his whole life to destroy Krishna had, in the end, received exactly what he had spent so long fearing — and even that, the story insists, was a kind of grace.
stories.reflection: The verses refuse to make the slaying purely a victory. Kamsa, who could not stop seeing Krishna in everything, is remembered as a man whose constant dread became, at the last, a form of constant remembrance — so that even his death brought him to the one he had fled.
stories.content_note: The death of Kamsa is handled with restraint, as the source itself does; the tyrant is struck down without graphic detail.

stories.title: Balarama Slays Kamsa's Brothers
stories.story:
Kamsa lay dead, and the arena that had rung with the crowd's cheers only moments before had gone still. The wrestlers had fallen, the elephant's tusk was still in Krishna's hand, and the great shout that went up at the king's death had died in the air. Then, into that stillness, his eight younger brothers came rushing at Krishna, fury where their king's careful plan had been.

They were not soldiers come to avenge a lord; they were a house in its last rage. The verses give them no long introduction, only a line of names — Kanka and Nyagrodha and the rest — and the single motion of their charge. Eight men of one blood and one purpose, and no plan behind the rush — only the blind momentum of a house that has nothing left to lose. They had watched their brother fall, and they came at Krishna as a family comes at what has undone it, all at once and without thinking.

Balarama did not let them reach him. He was the elder, the son of Rohini, and he had stood through the whole long day at his brother's side — patient while Krishna met the elephant at the gate and the wrestlers in the ring, content to let the younger take the field. But there was a limit to that patience, and the eight charging men crossed it. He stepped between them and Krishna and raised his club.

The fight was not a contest. Balarama moved through the eight brothers the way a lion moves through cattle — not with anger, but with the swift, certain work of one who is stronger than everything coming at him. The verses keep the moment short, and there is a mercy in that: one club, eight men, and then silence. He took the proudest of them in his two hands and felled him as easily as the rest. The house of Kamsa, which had spent so many years sending its killers after a child, sent its last strength and found that the child's brother was enough.

When it was over, Balarama stood in the centre of the ring as he had stood all day — unhurried, unmarked, his work done. The brothers who had rushed at Krishna lay where they had fallen. The arena, which had come to see a king's triumph, had seen instead the end of a king's house.

Nothing in the crowd moved for a long moment. The elephant was slain, the wrestlers were slain, Kamsa was slain, and now his brothers with him. The day that had been planned to finish two boys had finished everything Kamsa had built — and the two boys still stood at the centre of it, alive and unharmed.
stories.reflection: The eight brothers rush at Krishna in the moment after Kamsa's fall, and Balarama meets them before they can reach him. The speed of it — eight men, one club, over almost at once — is the point: the house of Kamsa does not surrender, and so it is finished in a single motion.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha folds into this episode the later meeting with Vasudeva and Devaki, and names one of the slain brothers Urgita; the Bhagavata keeps the parents' greeting separate, and this story follows it.
stories.content_note: Includes the slaying of Kamsa's eight brothers, told with restraint.

stories.title: The Widows of Mathura Weep
stories.subtitle: Kamsa's funeral rites are performed
stories.story:
The arena fell quiet in a way no crowd's silence could explain. Kamsa lay dead, his brothers with him, and the men of Mathura stood stunned among the fallen. But already another sound was rising over the field, thin at first and then everywhere at once — the weeping of women.

The wives of the slain warriors had found their husbands where they lay, on the field where heroes sleep their last sleep. They knelt in the dust and gathered the bodies into their arms, and their cries rose together and tangled in the air. They called to the fallen men by every name love keeps for the dead — lord, beloved, knower of righteousness, kind to the shelterless — and asked the question that all such grief asks: who will protect this city now that you are gone? The men who had died that day were not all loved, but they were all mourned. Even Kamsa's widows wept, and the sound of it reached the palace and the streets.

Krishna did not turn away from the grief he had caused. He walked among the royal women and comforted them, and his gentleness there was the same hand that had broken the bow and struck the king down. He had the customary funeral rites prepared for all the dead, so that no wife would be left to burn her husband's pyre without honor.

Then Ugrasena came to him. The old king, Kamsa's father, approached burning with grief for his son, breathing like a man who had drunk poison, and in the assembly of the Yadavas he reproached himself aloud. "By my childish folly and my anger," he said, "I have made widows of these thousand women. They bewail their husbands so piteously that even the regent of the dead would pity them. And yet — Kamsa was sinful, hated by the pious, ruthless of temper. Death is better than such a life, and what pity should there be for him? The wicked are constrained by death to reap their fruits; the pious reach auspicious ones." Then he made his request. "Let me perform the after-death rites of my son. Let me build his pyre, put fire to it, and offer the water-oblation, and so discharge my debt to him. After that, with my wife and daughters-in-law, I will range in the forest with the animals. This is my only prayer."

Krishna heard him out and was filled with surprise, and there was something like tenderness in the answer he gave. "What you have said befits your age, your family, and your nature. But the inevitable work is done — why speak as if it were not? Though dead, Kamsa will receive funeral honors befitting a king. You are born of a great race and know everything that should be known; understand that destiny is inevitable." He did not refuse his grandfather the rites he asked for.

So they placed Kamsa's body in a palanquin, as the ritual law required, and carried it through the city to the northern bank of the Yamuna. There they raised the pyre, and set the fire, and performed the obsequial rites for the dead king while the smoke rose slow over the river. The widows' mourning went on into the evening, until grief had worn itself thin enough to let the city begin its long work of living again.

The day that had begun with a wrestling match had ended with a funeral. Mathura had its freedom, but freedom, too, must bury its dead before it can be enjoyed.
stories.reflection: The episode is grief without vengeance: the man who slew Kamsa comforts the widows and sees that the funeral rites are done, and even the king who hunted him for years is buried with the honors of a king. Krishna's power over the city is shown not in what he takes but in how he lets it mourn.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata keeps this episode brief; the Harivamsha expands it into a long exchange in which Ugrasena reproaches himself for his son's death and begs Krishna's leave for the funeral rites. This story follows both, keeping the Bhagavata's shape and the Harivamsha's detail.

stories.title: The Prison Doors Open
stories.subtitle: Krishna and Balarama free their parents
stories.story:
The prison gates of the palace stood open, and the two brothers walked through them as though they had been waiting to do so all their lives.

All the years of Kamsa's reign those gates had held Vasudeva and Devaki — the couple whose children Kamsa had feared so much that he killed them one by one, and whose last two sons had been smuggled out of that very prison on the night of their birth. Krishna had been carried across the Yamuna in his father's arms while the rain fell and the river rose; Balarama had been taken to safety before him. The brothers had grown up in Gokula knowing their parents only as names, as a story, as the reason their lives had taken the shape they did. Now the arena was won, Kamsa was dead, and nothing stood between them and the cell where their mother and father had been bound all those years.

They found them still in bonds. Krishna and Balarama released Vasudeva and Devaki from their chains themselves, and then, before the parents could speak, the two brothers bowed and touched their feet — the full prostration of children before their elders, done with a care that made the guards who had held those cells for years look away.

Devaki had spent her life afraid of these sons. She had been told, on the night of her wedding, that her eighth child would be the death of Kamsa, and she had watched Kamsa take her children from her, one after another, as they were born. She had lived with the terror that her sons would be found and killed, and with the stranger fear that if they lived, they would have to kill a king. Every fear she had carried through all the years of her imprisonment had been about these two young men who now knelt at her feet. And when she and Vasudeva raised them and held them, there was no fear left in the embrace. The parents knew, in that moment, who their sons were — that these were no ordinary boys, but the lords of the world — and knowing it, they embraced them without the smallest hesitation.

They remembered, too, the words Krishna had spoken to them at his birth, when the chains fell from their hands and he told them he would return when the time came. The promise had been kept. The child who had been given away in the night had come back a man, and he had come back to them first, before the throne, before the city, before anything else that victory might have claimed.

Vasudeva said little; there are reunions that words cannot carry. The chains lay on the floor of the cell, and the room that had been a cage for so many years had become, in the space of a few breaths, the place where a family stood whole. Outside, Mathura was still learning what freedom meant. Inside the prison, four people who had been parted by a tyrant's fear held one another, and the tyrant could not reach them anymore.
stories.reflection: The parents know their sons are the lords of the world, yet they embrace them simply as sons — knowledge does not make the reunion less intimate. And Krishna's first act after winning the city is not to claim it but to return to the prison his parents were kept in, as if that debt came before every other.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana places the meeting with Kubja the maidservant on the way to the palace and tells the parents' release more briefly, adding that Vasudeva and Devaki bowed to Krishna, recalling what he had said at his birth. This story follows the Bhagavata's account.
stories.next_story_tease: Freedom was given, but there was an older debt the brothers still had to confess.

stories.title: A Debt No Son Can Repay
stories.subtitle: Krishna begs his parents' forgiveness
stories.story:
Of all the scenes the arena had prepared for that day, no one had foreseen this one: Krishna, who had broken the great bow, felled the wrestlers, and ended Kamsa, standing bowed before his mother and father and asking their pardon.

He spoke first, with Balarama at his side, and his words were not the words of a conqueror. "Mother, father," he said, "you were ever longing for us, and fate struck you down — we could not have our dwelling near you, though you wished it with all your hearts. Whatever a man is, he is born from his parents and nourished by them; the very body that becomes the seat of every purpose is theirs. The debt owed to a mother and a father, to an aged parent, to a devoted wife, to a young son — no one can repay it, not with his own self, not with all his wealth. And we, kept from you by Kamsa, our minds never at peace — we could not serve you as sons should serve. Forgive us, father; forgive us, mother. We were in the power of another."

The plea is astonishing when you consider who made it. He had just taken back from Kamsa everything Kamsa had stolen — the city, the throne, the years — and the first thing he did with it was kneel before two people who had been helpless in their bonds for all those years and ask their forgiveness for a childhood he had never been allowed to give them. He did not excuse himself. He did not say that he was a child, or that Kamsa had forced it, or that the long separation had not been his fault. He simply named the debt — a debt no son can repay — and asked pardon for having been unable even to try.

Vasudeva and Devaki could not answer at first. They had spent so many years imagining this moment, rehearsing all the things they might say to the sons who were taken from them, and now the sons stood here, grown, asking pardon of them. The parents reached out and held them, and their tears fell on their sons' heads like rain, and the old rope of affection bound the four of them together in the middle of the prison that had held two of them for so long. Whatever they had suffered — the children taken one by one, the years of chains and dread — dissolved in that embrace, because the children who had been taken had come back, and they had come back asking forgiveness rather than giving it.

There was no anger in the prison that day, no settling of accounts. Kamsa had built his reign on the fear of these two boys, and the boys had grown into men who, given the whole of Mathura, chose first to kneel. The tyrant had stolen their childhood; they did not ask for it back. They asked only that their parents forgive them for having missed it.

The chains that had bound Vasudeva and Devaki lay on the floor where the brothers had dropped them. And in the room where a king's cruelty had once done its work, there was only the sound of weeping — but it was the weeping of a family that had found one another again, and it was not grief.
stories.reflection: Krishna's plea inverts the ordinary order: the one who freed the city asks his own parents' pardon for a childhood he could not choose. He frames it as a debt no son can repay — and asks forgiveness not for having done wrong, but for having been prevented from doing right.
stories.next_story_tease: But the throne of Mathura could not stand empty, and there was an old king still waiting in his cell.

stories.title: The Throne That Was Never Meant to Be
stories.subtitle: Krishna crowns Ugrasena king of the Yadavas
stories.story:
Mathura had a king all along — he had simply been in prison for years.

Ugrasena, Kamsa's father, had been pushed aside and locked away by his own son, who had taken the throne and ruled the city through fear. In all the years of Kamsa's reign, through the killings, the taxes, the arena, few had dared to remember the old man in the cell. But when Krishna had freed his parents and the dust of the arena had settled, he did not sit on the empty throne himself. He went to the prison, released his grandfather from confinement, and led him out into the light of the city his son had stolen from him.

Then, before the assembled Yadavas, Krishna declared that Ugrasena would be king. And he explained why the throne had to pass to him, and not to the young conqueror whom every hand in the city would have raised up. Long ago, he said, a curse had been laid upon the Yadava line: because of Yayati's curse, no Yadava was to sit on the throne. The kingship of the Yadavas was a charge to be held, not a prize to be taken, and it could not be held by one who was born under that curse. So the man who had actually won the city would serve, and the man the curse allowed would rule.

Ugrasena did not want it. He had seen what the throne had done to his son; he had spent years in a cell because of it. He spoke of performing the rites and retiring to the forest with his wife and daughters-in-law, and pressed Kamsa's kingdom and wealth upon Krishna; but Krishna refused, saying he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne, and instructed his grandfather to place himself on the throne and win glory by becoming king. But Krishna, who knew the law, would not be moved. The Harivamsha remembers his reply in the form of an instruction: place yourself on the throne, and acquire victory by becoming the king. And so Govinda, well read in the laws, installed his grandfather on the throne that his son's death had left vacant.

There was a strangeness in the coronation that the city felt without quite understanding. The boy from Gokula, who had arrived in Mathura that morning as a stranger and left it the master of everything, stood at the foot of the throne and placed an old man upon it — an old man who had been robbed of that very seat by the tyrant Krishna had just slain. He did not take the crown, the wealth, or the army; he gave them all to the man Kamsa had wronged. The Yadava chiefs and the citizens looked at the old king, and at the young man who refused to be king, and understood that they had been given something stranger than a victory — they had been given justice.

Ugrasena took his seat, and Mathura had a king again, and the king was the man Kamsa had tried to erase. Krishna had said that while he served at his grandfather's side, the very gods themselves would pay tribute to the throne. The city could not see the gods, but it could see this: the tyrant's line was over, the old king had come home, and the boy who had done it all asked for nothing — not the throne, not the crown, not a single measure of the wealth lying in Kamsa's halls.

The yoke of the Yadava kingship had been carried by a usurper for years. Now it rested on the shoulders it had always belonged to, and the man who had won it back stood below it, content to serve.
stories.reflection: Krishna wins Mathura and immediately gives it away — to the grandfather Kamsa had imprisoned. His power is expressed as service: he refuses the throne not out of modesty but out of law, honoring the old curse on the Yadava line by letting the lawful king rule while he himself stands below the throne.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells the same crowning in its chapter on Kamsa's funeral rites, folding the consolation of the widows into the same episode; the Bhagavata keeps the coronation and the mourning separate, and this story follows it. The Yayati curse is given only in summary in the sources.
stories.next_story_tease: With a king at last upon the throne, there remained the wounded city and the Yadavas to be gathered.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna placing his grandfather Ugrasena upon the throne of Mathura in the great hall, the assembled Yadavas and citizens watching, the old king seated while Krishna stands below him with folded hands.

stories.title: Krishna Restores the Yadava Kinsmen
stories.story:
For years the name Yadava had meant exile. Scattered by fear, the kinsmen of Krishna's own house had slipped out of Mathura one family at a time — uncles and cousins and in-laws, the Vrishnis, the Andhakas, the Madhus, all of them relatives of the child the tyrant Kamsa had hunted since birth. They had gone in every direction, into foreign kingdoms where they could be nobody's kin and nobody's target, and there they had grown thin and grey, worn down by years of borrowed roofs and borrowed names.

With Kamsa dead and Ugrasena crowned king, Krishna sent word to every corner of the earth: come home. The old texts say he brought back all his own kinsmen and connections from every direction — the very people Kamsa's fear had scattered. They came as they had left, by twos and threes, dusty from long roads, their faces lined by the same years that had emptied the city. Some had been gone so long that the grandchildren they brought had never seen Mathura. They stood at the gates uncertainly, exiles returning to a home that might not remember them.

Krishna met them himself. He honored each one, spoke to them as a kinsman, and comforted them in their exhaustion. He settled them in their own houses, the houses their families had abandoned, and gave them back their wealth — fields, cattle, jewels, everything Kamsa's rule had made them flee. Whatever they had lost in those foreign lands, he restored. The verses say that protected by the arms of Krishna and Balarama, they obtained everything their hearts had desired for years.

Then the city began to breathe again. Courtyards that had stood silent filled with voices. And the rejoicing that the years of exile had deferred broke out at last in every courtyard. And day after day, the rejoined clans gathered where they could see the young lord's face — the sight of him, the texts say, was delight enough. Morning and evening they came to look at him, and the looking healed them. It is said that even the oldest among them, the men who had fled in their prime and returned stooped, became young again in Mathura — their strength restored until they seemed as vigorous as the sons beside them.

There was no war in this homecoming, no enemy defeated at the gate. The enemy had been fear itself, and it had been defeated years ago, quietly, by a boy growing up in another village while his kinsmen scattered across the world. What remained was the slower work: gathering the scattered, returning what had been taken, and letting a city that had been emptied by tyranny fill up again with the sound of family.

When the last of the exiles was settled in his father's house, Mathura was whole in a way it had not been since before Kamsa seized the throne. The clans were one again under one king. And Krishna, who had restored them all, turned with his brother toward the next task — a quieter one, and stranger to the storytellers: the education of two young men who already knew everything.
stories.reflection: Krishna's restoration of the scattered clans is quiet compared to the battles around Kamsa's fall, but it is the real work of kingship: gathering rather than conquering, and healing the long damage of fear. The detail that even the aged grew young again suggests that returning home — and being welcomed by the one who sent for you — restores more than wealth.
stories.next_story_tease: But there was a debt of another kind still to be paid: the education of the two brothers.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Study Under Sandipani
stories.story:
The two boys who had just emptied a palace of its tyrant were sent, of all things, to school. Vasudeva had watched his sons bring down Kamsa with their bare hands, but in the days that followed, the father's mind turned to something quieter: the rites that would make them twice-born, and the education owed to them as princes.

He summoned the brahmins of Mathura and had them perform the sacred-thread ceremony for Krishna and Balarama. The boys received the initiation, took up the vows, and became students in the proper order of the world. For the brahmins who officiated, Vasudeva gave a generous teacher's fee — cows adorned with golden necklaces, richly decorated, the very cattle he had mentally pledged at the ceremonies that followed the births of his two sons. The gift was no afterthought; it had been promised in his heart for years.

The old texts pause here to say something strange: the two who now stood before the brahmins were already the lords of all knowledge, all-knowing, the masters of the world itself. And yet they desired to live in a guru's house, like any boy learning his letters. So, having taken up the student's vows, they went to the teacher Sandipani, in the city of Avanti.

At the gurukula they asked for nothing special. They served as humbly as the poorest of Sandipani's students — fetching, running errands, living under the teacher's roof, keeping conduct so blameless that no master could find fault with them. Their patience and purity of heart pleased the brahmin teacher, who saw in these two extraordinary pupils only humility. So Sandipani taught them in earnest: the science of the bow with all its secret doctrines, the codes of duty and right conduct, the paths of justice and reasoning — everything he knew, he gave them.

And the learning took. In sixty-four days and nights, the brothers mastered all the arts and sciences that Sandipani could teach. What took other students years, they absorbed in two months of days and nights — the texts are precise about the number, as if marking how the ordinary pace of learning was overturned entirely. The guru who had accepted them as ordinary boys found himself teaching students who were already the originators of every branch of knowledge, and who had attended his school simply because the form of the world required it.

When the sixty-four days were done, Krishna and Balarama had completed their education. They stood before Sandipani as finished students, ready to take their leave of the guru's house and return to the duties of their city. The brothers had mastered the bow, the law, and the arts — but no student leaves a teacher without settling what is owed, and the teacher's fee had not yet been spoken of.
stories.reflection: The striking detail is that the two described as lords of all knowledge still went to school — the teachers of the world sitting at a mortal's feet, not to learn but to honor the form of learning itself. Sixty-four days to master every art suggests that for them, study was never about acquisition; it was about reverence for the teacher and the vows.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana (5.21) combines this episode with the later recovery of Sandipani's son, whereas the Bhagavata keeps the study and the payment of the guru's fee separate; this story follows the Bhagavata.
stories.next_story_tease: But no student leaves a guru without a fee — and Sandipani had a price that no gold could pay.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna and Balarama sitting cross-legged before the teacher Sandipani in the gurukula of Avanti, bows laid aside, the aged brahmin teaching while the two brothers listen with quiet, complete attention.

stories.title: Krishna Retrieves Sandipani's Son
stories.story:
When Krishna and his brother Balarama had finished their years of study, they went to their teacher, the sage Sandipani, and asked what fee he would take. A student's debt to a teacher is not discharged with words, and the two brothers, who had learned the whole Veda at his feet, meant to pay it in full. They had come to him not as princes but as students, and he had taught them as he would teach any boy, holding nothing back. It was the custom that a student, at the end of his studies, offers his teacher whatever is asked of him, and the two brothers had come prepared to give anything. What Sandipani named was not gold or cattle or land.

Long ago, he told them, his young son had died in the sea at Prabhasa and had never come home. The sage had consulted with his wife before he spoke, for the request was not a small one; it reached back into a grief that had never healed. “Give me back my son,” he said. It was a fee no one else in the world could pay. Krishna agreed at once.

He and Balarama mounted their chariot and drove to Prabhasa, to the very shore where the boy had been lost, and there they sat down at the water's edge. It was a long road, but they did not linger on it; a teacher's word had set them moving, and they meant to see it done. The shore was empty, and the waves came up the sand and fell back again, as if the sea were waiting to see what they would ask. The ocean itself, knowing who had come, rose and brought them an offering and asked what they sought. “The son of our teacher,” Krishna said. “Give him back to us.”

But the sea answered that the boy was not in its keeping. “A demon named Panchajana,” it said, “who lives in these waters in the form of a conch shell, carried him off. It is Panchajana who has him.” The sea spoke plainly, as one who did not wish to be blamed for what another had done.

At these words Krishna went down into the water without a moment's hesitation, down into the cold and the dark where the demon lay coiled in his shell, while Balarama waited on the shore above. He found Panchajana in the depths and slew him, and from the demon's body — for Panchajana was a monster shaped like a conch — he took the great shell itself, the conch the world would come to know as Panchajanya, named for the demon from whose form it was made. Then he climbed back into the chariot, the conch in his hand, and with Balarama beside him he drove to the city of Yama, the lord of death.

The city of the dead is not reached by any road of the living, but at its gates Krishna raised the conch and blew it, and the sound of Panchajanya rolled through the realm of the dead like a summons no one there could refuse. Yama himself came out to meet them and honored them with deep reverence, and the boy — the teacher's son, dead and lost — was returned to the two brothers, brought back from death itself. Death, which had held him so long, gave him up without argument.

They drove back to the hermitage with the boy alive again, seated in the chariot between them, and laid him in his father's arms — the boy restored in his former person, as he had been before the sea took him, with no mark of death upon him, so that a father's long grief was ended in a single afternoon. Sandipani, receiving his son from death, blessed the two brothers and sent them on their way. “Go home, heroes,” he said, “and may your fame be pure.”
stories.reflection: The story is unusual among the tales of Krishna's deeds because he appears in it as a student repaying a teacher, not as a king or a warrior. The fee Sandipani names — the life of his son — is one that no wealth could settle, and Krishna treats it as a debt he is glad to pay, going as far as the realm of death itself to honor a teacher's word.
stories.content_note: Krishna slays the sea-demon Panchajana; the death is described briefly and without detail.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna stands at the gates of Yama's dark city, raising the great conch Panchajanya to his lips, while Balarama waits at his side and the sound of the conch rolls out through the realm of death.

stories.title: Krishna Visits Trivakra and Grants Her a Boon
stories.story:
There was one house in Mathura that Krishna had not yet entered — the house of the woman whose crooked back he had straightened on his first morning in the city. She was called Trivakra, and though her body had been made straight, her heart had been bent toward him ever since that first meeting. The old texts call her the Sairandhri, the serving woman, and they say Krishna knew her longing — the love that burned in her and would not let her rest.

So, one day, he went to her. He took Uddhava with him, and the two of them walked through the streets of Mathura to the house of the woman who had once offered him perfume. Her home was rich, furnished with splendid things, arranged with care for the one she hoped would come. When she saw him approaching her door, she rose from her seat at once, flustered, the calm of her day scattered in a moment. Uddhava, honored for his goodness, sat down on the ground, touching the seat that was offered, leaving the place of honor for his lord.

Then Trivakra prepared herself as one prepares for a festival. She bathed, anointed her skin with fragrant oils, dressed in fine silk and ornaments, wove garlands into her hair, and set out betel and sweet drinks and everything her house could offer. She took Krishna by the hand — his hand adorned with bangles — and drew him close, shy at the newness of his nearness, trembling at what she hardly dared to hope.

And then she embraced him. She pressed him to her breast with both arms, held him as though she would not let him go, and in that embrace her long torment ended. The verses say she had been burning with love for so long that the ache had become her constant companion; and now, holding the blissful form before her, she let the fire at last burn out. She had obtained what the whole world calls hard to obtain — the lord of liberation himself, standing in her small house, letting her hold him.

When she could speak, she asked only one thing: "Stay with me, beloved, for a few days. That is all I ask." She did not ask for wealth, or power, or a place in his court. She asked for his company, for a few days of his presence in the house she had arranged for him.

Krishna, who honors those who honor him, gave her the boon she wished for. He stayed. And when he left, he returned to his own abode, having honored her devotion in the way that mattered most to her — by giving her himself. The serving woman of Mathura, the once-bent Trivakra, had worshipped the lord of all lords, and her worship had not been in vain.
stories.reflection: Trivakra asks for nothing but a few days of Krishna's company, and that is the boon he grants. The story is striking because her longing is not rebuked or spiritualized away — it is met, gently and completely, as devotion that takes the form of love and is answered in kind.
stories.tradition_note: This is the later visit to Trivakra, described in Bhagavata 10.48; her first meeting with Krishna, when he straightened her back, is told in its own episode (10.42).
stories.next_story_tease: Years later, an old classmate from the gurukula would arrive at Dwaraka carrying memories of those student days.

stories.title: Memories of the Gurukula
stories.subtitle: Krishna and Sudama recall their student days under Sandipani.
stories.story:
When Sudama, his old classmate from the gurukula, came to Dwaraka, Krishna did not speak of the kingdom, or of armies, or of the affairs of state. He spoke of the forest. "Do you remember, brahmin," he asked, "our days in the guru's house?"

It was a question that carried both of them back to another life — to Avanti, to the teacher Sandipani's ashram, to the years when they had been two boys under one roof, bound by the same lessons and the same small duties. Krishna spoke of what that time had meant. The guru's house, he said, was the true birth of a twice-born, the direct root of all good deeds; it was there, in service and study, that a man came into himself. He was not to be reached by sacrifice, nor by sons, nor by austerity, nor by a mind merely quieted — but by such days as those, spent at the feet of a teacher.

And then he asked: "Do you remember what happened when we were sent to gather firewood?"

Sudama remembered. The guru's wife had sent them into the great forest to bring back wood, and the two boys had gone in together, as they did everything in those days. They had walked deep into the trees, gathering what they could, until they realized that the light was failing. The sun had already set; darkness was covering every direction of the sky. And then the storm came — a violent wind, sheets of rain, water rising around them until the forest floor was a flood. They were struck again and again by the wind and the rain, drenched, shivering, unable to see the path by which they had come. Lost in the blackness, they held each other's hands and walked, and walked, hoping only that dawn would find them.

It was the longest night either of them had known. They wandered through the flooded darkness, two boys holding on to each other, until at last the rain ceased and the first grey light came. And there, when the sun rose, stood their guru — Sandipani himself, who had known where they were and had come through the storm to find them.

The old teacher looked at his two soaked, exhausted students, and his eyes filled. "Ah, my sons," he said, "you have suffered so much for my sake. This is exactly what true disciples must do — this is the repayment of the guru. I am pleased with you. May your wishes come true."

Krishna finished the memory quietly. "Such were the days we spent in the guru's house," he said. "There were many like that one."

For a moment the two men sat in silence — the lord of Dwaraka and the brahmin from the south, both of them boys again in that dark forest, holding hands against the storm. It was the memory Krishna chose to share with his old friend: not a lesson from the scriptures, not a feat of arms, but a night of fear and cold and a teacher who came at dawn. And it was enough — more than enough — to show what the years under Sandipani had made of them.
stories.reflection: Krishna recalls not a triumph but a night of fear, and the detail he treasures is the guru who came at dawn. The memory defines discipleship as shared hardship and gratitude — the debt a student repays not with gifts but with the very act of having served.
stories.next_story_tease: But the peace of Mathura would not last — an army was already marching toward the city.

stories.title: The City Without Walls
stories.story:
Mathura had thrown back the armies of Magadha, and the city had cheered. The elders of the Yadava line did not join in the cheering. They had watched King Jarasandha come against the city once and then again, and they knew the arithmetic of such wars: every repulse bought a season, and the host that returned was always larger than the one that had fled. The two brothers had stood at the head of the defense and scattered his forces with their own hands, and the city trusted them utterly. But the elders had begun to ask a harder question — what would happen when the brothers alone were no longer enough?

It was that question that brought the clan together in council. The hall filled with the older men of Mathura, the counselors and kinsmen who had seen more sieges than they cared to count, and for a long while the talk moved in circles: the pride of the Magadhan king, the size of his host, the strength of the brothers. Then Vikadru rose. The clan counted him its foremost speaker, and when he stood, the others fell quiet and let him put into words what all of them had been circling.

"Mathura cannot withstand another siege," he told them, plainly and without ornament. The city's supply of food and fuel, he reminded them, was limited. What the storehouses held would not carry the town through a long investment. And beyond the granaries lay the larger truth: the city was not protected by a fort. No ring of walls, no citadel, no gates built to stop an army. Mathura was a city of cowherds and traders, grown rich on the river and the pastures, and it had never been turned into a stronghold. Whatever the valor of its defenders, Vikadru said, a city with thin stores and no walls could not stand attack for even one day.

The words fell on the room like a cold wind. Someone protested that the brothers had beaten Jarasandha twice. Vikadru did not argue the point; he answered it. An army could be met in the field and scattered, and the brothers had proven that twice over. But a siege was not answered in the field. A siege was answered with grain and with stone, and Mathura had neither in plenty. Jarasandha did not need to win a single battle; he needed only to sit before the gates and let hunger do his work for him.

The council turned at last to Krishna, because everything in Mathura turned to Krishna. He had listened to the whole of it without once interrupting — the way he heard every counsel, weighing each word before he answered it. And when the elders had finished, when Vikadru's plain assessment hung in the air, Krishna did not answer at once. He sat a long moment in the silence, and the elders watched him, waiting for the reassurance they had come to hear: that the city was safe, that the brothers would scatter the next host as they had scattered the last.

He did not give it. There was no defiance in his face and no fear in it either, only that still attention — the look of a man measuring a road he has not yet begun to walk. Whatever he was thinking, he kept it behind his eyes, and the council ended with the truth spoken and no decision made.

That night the lamps of Mathura burned late over a city that had cheered its defenders and slept without walls around it, trusting to two brothers and to the hope that Jarasandha would grow tired. Only Krishna, standing at a window above the un-walled streets, seemed to be looking past the city altogether — toward the south, where the mountains stood blue and far, and where the answers to Mathura's trouble might be waiting.
stories.reflection: The elders' counsel is honest about what courage alone cannot do: Jarasandha does not need to win a battle, only to wait. Their warning that the city could not stand even one day of siege is itself a kind of loyalty — telling Krishna the truth they would rather not believe, because he must hear it.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna sat with the counsel in silence; the answer he carried out of that hall would take him far from Mathura.

stories.title: The Art of Withdrawal
stories.story:
When the council had ended, one more voice had yet to be heard, and it belonged to the senior of the Yadava house. Vasudeva rose and gave Vikadru's counsel his full assent before the assembly. What the foremost of royal speakers had said, he told them, was true and well meant; it agreed with royal duty and looked to the good of all. "Do what he has said," he told his son.

Krishna had heard his father, and he had listened to the elders, and he had weighed the whole of it — the course of events, the words of reason, what the scriptures taught of a king's duty. And now he answered, and his answer began with a lesson in statecraft. A king, he said, meditates daily on peace and on war, on alliance and on dissension, on when to advance and when to draw back. The learned king does not place himself before a powerful enemy and wait to be destroyed; he withdraws, and when the time is proper, in proportion to his strength, he engages in battle again.

Then he said the thing the council had not dared to ask of him. "Therefore, although I am capable, I shall, at this very moment, fly away with the worshipful Baladeva — like one incapable, saving my life." The words were chosen with care, and they carried his whole meaning: this flight would look like fear, would read as the retreat of a beaten man, and that appearance was the weapon he intended to use.

He laid the plan out plainly. They would go south, ascend mount Sahya, and enter the Deccan. They would see the charming cities of Karavira and Krouncha, and the foremost of mountains, Gomanta. And when Jarasandha heard that the two of them had fled, he would not turn aside to sit before Mathura's gates — elated with success, he would pursue them in pride, following the brothers with his followers into the forests of Sahya. "This departure is conducive to the well-being of the race of Yadu," Krishna said. "By this, the province, the city, and the citizens will fare well."

It was a strange thing to hear, and the elders heard it in silence: the two men who had been Mathura's defense proposing to become its bait. But the logic stood firm. Jarasandha's war was against Krishna; if Krishna was not in Mathura, then Mathura was not the battlefield. The enemy would follow the enemy.

And so they went. That very day the two brothers — though no one in the city doubted their strength — set out for the south without the least anxiety in their minds. They passed through kingdom after kingdom, hundreds of them, the two travelers taking on different forms at will as they moved through strange lands. They climbed the slopes of mount Sahya and found the road that led south, and the farther they went, the more they discovered that they were not among strangers. Long ago, in the time of the old king Yadu himself, his five sons had gone out to found cities across the land; Padmavarna had raised Karavira on mount Sahya, and Sarasas had laid out Krouncha in its groves of trees. The brothers came at last to Karavira, a city presided over by members of their own family, standing in the shadow of the mountain.

They had left the un-walled city behind. Ahead lay the southern heights, and somewhere behind them, in his pride, came Jarasandha — exactly as Krishna had said he would, exactly as the plan required. On the bank of the river Vena stood a great fig tree, and under its shade the two brothers paused to rest.
stories.reflection: Krishna frames his retreat as the flight of one "like one incapable" — a king who withdraws not from fear but from calculation, and who makes his own seeming defeat the instrument of the city's safety. The plan turns flight into bait: Jarasandha's pride will follow the brothers and leave Mathura alone.
stories.next_story_tease: Under the great fig tree on the bank of the Vena, someone was waiting.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna and Balarama setting out on the southern road, Mathura's low un-walled houses behind them and the blue mass of mount Sahya on the horizon, the two brothers calm and unhurried, leaving the city to safety by their absence.

stories.title: The Hermit with the Axe
stories.story:
On the bank of the river Vena stood a great fig tree, and under it the two brothers found a sight that stopped them mid-stride. An old ascetic sat at the root of the tree milking a cow — a cow white as the milky arani tree, her calf beside her, giving milk whenever it was wished. The man himself was white as a flame of fire, dressed in bark with matted locks, worn thin by offering the three sacred oblations day after day, and still as the ocean. Across his shoulder lay an axe.

Krishna recognized him at once, though he had never set eyes on him: Rama, the son of Jamadagni, born in the race of Bhrigu — the one the world called the destroyer of the Kshatriyas. Everything that was said of this man ran through Krishna's greeting: how he had agitated the ocean with the speed of his shafts and laid out the city of Surpara on its shore; how, remembering his slain father, he had gone out with this same axe and cut down the thousand arms of Kartavirya like a forest; how the earth's mud was still said to be stained with the blood of the warrior kings he had slain. The fiercest figure of an older age sat here in the shade of a fig tree, quiet as the preceptor of the gods, milking a cow.

Krishna approached him with respect and addressed him in sweet words. Perhaps, he said, the great sage had heard of two Yadavas living on the bank of the Yamuna. "We are those two." He told him their story without embellishment: from the very beginning of their birth, their father Vasudeva, afraid of Kamsa, had placed them in Vraja, and there they had grown up without fear. When they came of age they entered Mathura and destroyed the haughty Kamsa in the assembly; they set his father Ugrasena back on the royal seat; and then, as before, they returned to the work of cowherd boys. And after all of that, Jarasandha had come against their city, again and again, until the two of them had left Mathura to draw him away.

The old sage listened to the whole of it. This, at last, was a story he understood — the same story he had lived in his own terrible way: the kings of the earth coming against one man, and one man deciding how the kings would fall. And when Krishna fell silent, Parasurama gave his counsel. It was not the counsel of a hermit who counsels peace; it was the counsel of a warrior who had spent his life choosing his ground. Get up, he told them, onto that high summit. If you obstruct Jarasandha by fighting with him from the fort there, you will be able to conquer him. On the heights, where an enemy must climb to reach you, the host of kings would spend itself against stone and against two men who did not tire.

So the mountain was named: Gomanta. The brothers received the counsel as they had received the elders' warning in Mathura — weighing it, turning it, finding the sense of it. It answered the question that had traveled south with them since they left the un-walled city: where, in the end, would the stand be made? Not behind Mathura's missing walls, not on the open road, but on the heights, where a fort could be made of the mountain itself.

They stayed a while with the sage on the bank of the Vena, and when they left, they turned their faces toward Gomanta. Behind them, the old man with the axe went back to his cow, and the river went on past the fig tree, carrying nothing of the war.
stories.reflection: The fiercest hermit in the tradition, who spent his life bringing down warrior kings with his axe, counsels Krishna not destruction but position — the choice of ground. It is an older age handing its wisdom to a new one: the enemy is not to be exterminated but out-thought.
stories.next_story_tease: On the heights of Gomanta, the brothers would find the host of kings waiting — and the sky would open with weapons.

stories.title: The Weapons Descend on Gomanta
stories.story:
The kings' soldiers saw the two brothers coming down from the mountain, and terror ran through the host. The beasts stamped and shied; the ranks went rigid; for the two who descended carried no weapon at all — nothing but their arms — and they moved across the field like two makaras, the great creatures that churn the ocean, angry and unhurried.

Then, before the eyes of the assembled kings, the sky opened. The weapons the brothers had received once before, in their encounter at Mathura, came down from the heavens like burning flames — huge bodily weapons, adorned with celestial garlands, lighting up the ten quarters with their brilliance, descending as if thirsting for battle. Four Vaishnava weapons came down for the two Yadavas: the plough-share Samvartaka, the mace Saunanda, the discus Sudarshana, and the club Koumodaki.

Balarama, the foremost of the Satvatas, took up the plough-share in his left hand — moving obliquely like a serpent, wreathed in celestial garlands — and the mace Saunanda in his right. Krishna took up the discus Sudarshana, worthy of being looked at by all the worlds and effulgent like the sun, and his other hand closed around the club Koumodaki. Thus armed, the two brothers — one in Vishnu, divided into two for the sake of men — began to withstand the enemy.

The battle that followed was not a contest but a harvest. Balarama raised the plough-share and dragged the cars of the Kshatriyas from their courses, venting his anger on their horses and elephants, churning mountain-like elephants with his mace as if churning them in a vessel. Around him, the leading Kshatriyas, on the point of being slain, abandoned their cars in fear and fled to Jarasandha.

Jarasandha met them with contempt. "Fie on your conduct as Kshatriyas grown tired of battle," he said. Did they not know that the sages say those who, albeit powerful, fly from the battlefield leaving their cars behind are visited by the sin of destroying an embryo? "Why do you flee in fear of a milk-herd of limited power who fights on foot?" Let them return to the field and fight, or wait as spectators — for he himself, he vowed, would dispatch those two cowherd boys to the abode of Yama.

The words stung them back into courage. Rallied, the Kshatriyas returned to the fight with a downpour of arrows — coats of mail, swords, quivers, horses with golden reins, cars of moon-like lustre, cloud-like elephants driven by their keepers. Covered by rising umbrellas and fanned with chowries, the kings shone on their cars in the field. And the brothers received them. Thousands of arrows shot by the kings struck the two descendants of the Yadu race, and the two bore them like mountains sprinkled with rain; assailed by heavy clubs and maces, they did not tremble.

Then Krishna, like a cloud swollen with wind, increased his body, and with the discus effulgent like the sun he began to cut down men and horses, elephants and mighty car-warriors. On the other side, Balarama dragged the kings with his plough-share and struck them with his club until they lost consciousness and could not stand; the variegated chariots of the kings broke down, their car-wheels obstructed, and could not move across the field. In the thick of the slaughter, king Darada fell before Balarama — one more among the kings who had come to end the cowherd boys, ended in turn.

When the field grew quiet at last, the host that had marched against the two brothers lay scattered and broken. The mountain Parasurama had named had held, as he had promised it would, and the brothers stood on the heights as they had come down from them: armed, unmarked, unhurried. But the war was not finished. Jarasandha was still somewhere beyond the broken ranks, and the two brothers knew, standing among the wreckage of his host, that he would come again.
stories.reflection: The weapons come down of their own accord, garlanded and blazing, as if they had been waiting for the moment — and they are taken up as naturally as the brothers' own arms. Jarasandha's contempt is the other face of the same scene: he sees only a cowherd fighting on foot, and cannot see that the arms of Vishnu are already in the brothers' hands.
stories.content_note: Battle episode: the rout of the assembled kings, told with restraint; includes the slaying of king Darada.
stories.next_story_tease: From the broken ranks of the kings, one ruler came forward with friendship instead of a weapon.
stories.hero_scene: The four divine weapons descending from the open sky like burning flames — the plough-share Samvartaka, the mace Saunanda, the discus Sudarshana, the club Koumodaki — garlanded and blazing, as Krishna and Balarama raise their arms to receive them before the terrified host of kings on mount Gomanta.

stories.title: The King of Chedi Offers Friendship
stories.story:
When the last chariot of the routed army had vanished beyond the plain, the foot of Mount Gomanta fell quiet. For days the kings had pressed the mountain, their archers and elephants and great war-cars, and for days two men had held it. Now the field lay strewn with broken axles and abandoned standards, and the soldiers who remained stood far off, watching the two sons of Vasudeva walk down from the slopes with nothing in their hands but the weapons that had dropped out of the sky.

Jarasandha himself had fled. The king of Magadha, who had bound the kings into his siege and sworn he would despatch the two cowherd boys to the abode of Yama, had ridden away with the rest when the battle turned. It was he who had rallied the faltering Kshatriyas with bitter words, fie on their conduct, fleeing from a milk-herd who fought on foot, and for a while his fury had held the line. The kings had come back to the fight in a downpour of arrows, and Krishna and Balarama had stood under it like two mountains sprinkled with rain. But no rally could outlast what they had seen that morning: the four weapons blazing down from the sky like flames, the ploughshare and the mace in Balarama's hands, the sun-bright discus and the club in Krishna's, and the war-cars of the kings breaking up beneath them. So the alliance that had besieged Gomanta scattered, and the mountain stood.

Then, out of the silence, a single chariot rolled forward across the field, unhurried, banners high, and stopped at a courteous distance. From it stepped the king of Chedi, a man of years, remembered by the Yadavas as kin, for his house was bound to theirs by marriage. He walked to where Krishna and Balarama stood, and before the watching remnants of two armies he remembered that kinship aloud.

Long before this war, he said, our families were one. This war was never mine by choice. I came where the kings came, and I have seen what your arms can do. I want no more of it. Let us go together, my army and my followers and I, to the city of Karavira. Let the road know us as allies.

It was a strange offer to make in the wreckage of a battle, and perhaps only a man who had been on the losing side could have made it with such simplicity. Krishna accepted him at once, with the ease of a man who had never truly counted him an enemy at heart. Balarama, who an hour before had dragged kings from their chariots with his ploughshare, stood by without objection, and the king of Chedi, the fear of the field gone out of his eyes, looked almost young again.

They set out the same day, the small army of the Chedi king and the two sons of Vasudeva riding together where they had lately fought. The country people who had hidden during the siege came to the roadside as the column passed, women and children and old men, and the word ran ahead of them: the war is over, and the king of Chedi rides with Krishna. It was, the soldiers muttered to one another, the strangest peace they had ever seen concluded, no plunder and no tribute, only a kinsman's word given and accepted. Dust rose behind the chariots, and Karavira lay somewhere beyond the horizon, a city that knew nothing yet of what was coming toward it, or of the kindness that had turned a routed king into a friend.
stories.reflection: The king of Chedi had come to Gomanta as part of the siege, but he was the first to remember, once the fighting was over, that his house and the Yadavas were family. The war had not created the enmity; it had only hidden the kinship, and the moment the king chose to recall it, the enmity had nothing left to stand on.
stories.next_story_tease: But at Karavira, the king Shrigala had heard how the armies had fared at Gomanta, and he meant to meet Krishna himself.
stories.hero_scene: On the battlefield plain at the foot of Mount Gomanta, the king of Chedi steps down from his chariot and offers his hand to Krishna in friendship, his army and banners gathered behind him, while Balarama stands at Krishna's side and broken war-chariots litter the field.

stories.title: The Heir of Karavira
stories.story:
The gates of Karavira opened before the column had even reached them, and the king came out to meet it as a storm comes out of a clear sky.

King Shrigala drove out on a chariot that shone like the car of Indra, quick-coursing horses and golden axles, quivers inexhaustible, and at the sight of him the earth itself was said to sink a little under his wheels. He had heard how the armies of the kings had fared on Mount Gomanta, and the report had not frightened him. It had offended him. In the middle of the open field, with his army ranked behind him, he reined in before Krishna and called out so that all could hear.

"I have heard of your work against the stupid kings at Gomanta, who had no leader," he said. "I am the emperor of the world. You are alone, and I am with my army, so I should not fight you with all these men. Come, I will fight you alone, and one of us will meet his death in a fair fight. If you are slain, I shall be the only Vasudeva in the world. And if I am slain, you shall be the only one."

Krishna heard him out without changing expression. "Strike me as you wish," he said.

Shrigala's answer was a net of arrows. He showered Krishna with shafts and maces and weapons covered with flame, and Krishna stood where he was, motionless, like a mountain taking rain. Only when the assault had spent itself did his wrath rise, and then he lifted the discus that had come to him at Gomanta and hurled it. It struck the king of Karavira in the breast, pierced him through, and returned to Krishna's hand as a hawk returns to the wrist. Shrigala, who an hour before had been the emperor of the world, fell from his chariot like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, and lay bleeding on the field.

His army broke. Some fled, some entered the city weeping, and some would not leave their fallen king and stood bewailing him where he lay. And Krishna, raising the hand that bore the discus, spoke to them all in a voice like the rumbling of clouds: "Do not fear! Do not fear."

It took a moment for the words to mean anything. Then the people of Karavira, looking from their slain king to the man who had slain him and yet told them not to fear, began to weep, the ministers and the citizens, and the queens who came out of the city with their sons, striking their breasts and crying over the king who would not rise again.

Among them came the queen Padmavati, and with her the boy prince Shakradeva, Shrigala's son. She did not come to curse. She came to the victor of the field and pleaded for her son.

And Krishna, looking at the boy who had lost everything in one afternoon, said: "This son of Shrigala is as my own. I declare safety to you all."

Then, in the sight of the weeping city, the victor did what no conqueror in that land was expected to do. He lifted the prince onto the throne of Karavira, the throne his father had been so sure of defending, and sprinkled him with celestial water, and anointed him king of the city that an hour before had been his enemy's.

The young king sat very straight on the great seat, his mother's hand on his shoulder, and the people of Karavira, who had come out prepared only to mourn, found themselves staring at a boy who was now their king and at the man who had given him the crown. Whatever they had feared from the fall of Shrigala, it was not this.
stories.reflection: Shrigala had staked everything on the idea that one of the two men on that field must cease to exist: if Krishna fell, Shrigala would be the only Vasudeva, and if Shrigala fell, Krishna would be. Krishna answered the wager not by wiping out the loser's line but by adopting it, making the slain king's son his own and placing him on the throne, so that in the end neither Vasudeva was destroyed and the boy inherited his father's crown instead of his father's war.
stories.next_story_tease: Far away at Kundina, the kings were gathering for the swayamvara, and Jarasandha had a warning for them all.

stories.title: A Warning for the Swayamvara
stories.story:
The kings of the earth were gathered in the golden assembly hall of Bhishmaka at Kundina, come for the swayamvara of the king's daughter, and when Krishna arrived with Garuda and the Yadavas at his back, the brightness of the gathering dimmed. The leading kings, well-read in the science of polity and expert in counsel, exchanged glances and fell silent, stricken with an anxiety they could not quite name.

Jarasandha rose to speak, and the hall attended as the gods attend the king of gods.

He began quietly, with a warning dressed as counsel. This Krishna who has come to Kundina, he said, is the well-known son of Vasudeva, endued with great energy and prowess. He has come for the maiden, and forsooth he will set forth mighty exertions to win her. You should behave according to the rules of polity, weighing your own strength and weakness.

Then his voice changed, and the kings heard what he really thought.

You know well what these two sons of Vasudeva did on Mount Gomanta, without Garuda's help. I cannot say how Krishna will fight now that the mighty car-warriors of the Yadava, Bhoja and Andhaka races stand with him. But when Vishnu sits on Garuda and sets forth his exertions for the maiden, even Indra, assisted by all the celestials, will not be able to stand in the battle-field.

And then, to the kings who had come to choose a husband for a princess, Jarasandha began to recite what this suitor had been. When the universe lay under one all-spreading ocean, Vishnu took the form of a boar, raised the drowned earth from the nether region, and killed the Daitya king Hiranyaksha. The unconquerable Hiranyakashipu, who had not met his death in the three worlds, in sky or earth or nether region, in day or night, by anything dry or wet, was slain by Hari in his man-lion form. He bound the mighty Bali, foremost of Asuras, with a noose of promise, and sent him down to the nether region as a dwarf. At the junction of the ages he took birth in disguise from Jamadagni and Renuka as Rama with the axe, and cut down the thousand-armed Kartavirya, elated with the pride of his kingdom. He was Dasharatha's son Rama, born in the race of Ikshvaku, who killed Ravana, the conqueror of the three worlds. In the war whose root was Taraka, eight-armed and seated on Garuda, he killed the Asuras who were elated with their boons, and with his discus, effulgent like the sun, he killed the demon Kalanemi who terrorized the gods.

The hall was very still now. And nearer still, Jarasandha went on. As a boy in the forest he slew the demons Dhenuka, Arishta and Pralamba. In his cowherd form, Devaki's son sported there and slew Putana, Keshi, the elephant Kuvalayapida, the wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika, and Kamsa with all his followers. In disguise he performed these superhuman feats.

"This is my sure understanding," Jarasandha said, "and I acquired it at Mathura. I consider Devaki's son Keshava the first cause of the celestials, the destroyer of the Asuras, Narayana, the ancient Purusha, the prime cause of the universe, Truth, the creator of all creatures manifest and unmanifest, unconquerable, unborn, eternal, the lord of the three worlds. Can Garuda be the carrier of a mere man, even a mortal lord paramount? When Janarddana displays his prowess for the maiden, what powerful man will be able to stand before Garuda? Forsooth I tell you that Vishnu himself has come for this swayamvara. Mighty is the calamity that will befall you on his arrival here. Do whatever you think proper after this."

He sat down, and for a long moment no one moved. Then Sunitha rose and gave his voice to the king of Magadha's words, and the kings knew that the warning would not be argued away.

Outside the golden hall the evening drew in, and in the city of Kundina the lamps were being lit for a festival that suddenly felt less like a festival. The kings sat on among the variegated coverings of their seats, each man alone with the name Jarasandha had spoken aloud in council, the name none of them had wanted to say and none of them could now forget.
stories.reflection: It is Jarasandha, Krishna's declared enemy and the man who had bound the kings into war against him, who names Krishna plainly before the assembled princes: not a rival suitor but Vishnu himself. Hatred here produces a clarity the indifferent kings do not share; the enemy sees exactly whom he is fighting, even as he resolves to fight him anyway.
stories.next_story_tease: But the kings did not answer with one voice, for Dantavakra would speak for peace and Salwa for war.
stories.hero_scene: In Bhishmaka's golden assembly hall at Kundina, Jarasandha stands among the seated kings, one hand raised, speaking with heavy certainty, while the assembled monarchs lean forward in alarm beneath the hall's lamps.
