stories.title: The Council Divides
stories.story:
When Jarasandha sat down and Sunitha had given his voice to the warning, the kings of the earth looked at one another across the golden hall of Kundina. Into that silence rose Dantavakra, the king of Karusha.

He did not quarrel with the warning. What the king of Magadha and Sunitha have said for our well-being, he said, appears to me proper. I cannot blame these nectarine words out of malice, pride, or any desire for victory of my own. Who else could speak, in the midst of kings, words grave as an ocean and sanctioned by the science of polity?

What wonder is it that Vasudeva has come here? He has come for this maiden, as we have all come. We all unitedly laid siege to Gomanta; why do we find fault with that battle? Because of Kamsa's foolishness, those two heroes first lived in Vrindavana. To slay them, Kamsa invited Rama and Keshava and set an infuriated elephant against them. They slew the elephant and entered the arena, and by their own prowess slew Kamsa, king of Mathura, with his followers. What offence did they commit thereby, that we all, elderly in age, came to Mathura at another's instigation?

The hall stirred uneasily, for Dantavakra was describing their own war back to them. Terrified at our huge and overwhelming army, he went on, Rama and Keshava left their own city and their soldiers and fled to Gomanta. We pursued them there, and though we are expert in the art of fighting, we were defeated in the battle-field by those two boys. We laid siege to the hill, as Kshatriyas should, and set fire to it. Had they given up their lives quietly in that conflagration, taking it for a forest fire, we would have considered them humbled. We blame Janarddana because he fought against us. As matters now stand, wherever we go, we shall pick up a quarrel. Let us therefore contract friendship with Krishna.

Krishna has not come to this city of Kundina to pick a quarrel. He has come for the maiden; why should he fight with another? He is not an ordinary human being: the foremost of men in the land of mortals, the foremost of gods in the land of celestials, the Deity and the Creator of the worlds. In God there is no malice, pride or crookedness. The gods do not grow stupified or lean and are not visited by calamity, and they remove the calamities of those who bow unto them. Vishnu, the king of gods, has come here with Garuda to show his true form. And know this: Krishna never goes with his army to slay his enemies. That he has come accompanied by the leading Bhojas, Vrishnis, Andhakas and Yadavas indicates his desire of contracting friendship with you. Let us go, O kings, and offer the high-souled Keshava hospitality with arghya and water to rinse his mouth. If we make peace with Keshava, we shall be able to live freed from anxiety and fear.

Then Salwa, the foremost of speakers, rose, and the temper of the hall changed. What is the use of this fear? If we had trembled at the thought of Krishna and judged it proper to make peace with him, we would have left our weapons at that time. Why speak ill of our own army and extol another? That is not the duty of Kshatriya kings. We are all born in great royal families and have glorified our respective races; why should our sense be poor, like that of a coward?

He did not deny the warning. He embraced it and drew a different conclusion from it. I know Devaki's son Krishna as the immortal, eternal Prime Deity Vishnu, invincible unto the kings, powerful, adored of all the worlds, Vaikuntha, the preceptor of the entire world. I know all the objects of Vishnu: he has in view the destruction of king Kamsa, the relieving of the earth of her burden, our destruction, and the protection of the worlds. A great battle will take place between Vishnu and all the kings. I know truly that, consumed by the fire of his discus, we will go to the abode of Yama. Yet no one meets with untimely death, and no one survives when the proper time comes and the lease of his life runs out. Therefore a man should not entertain fear. When the ascetic virtue of the Daityas is annihilated, the divine Vishnu, conversant with yoga, brings about their destruction in due time. He sent down the mighty Bali to the nether region. He has performed many other feats like this; do not question the subject of fighting.

The debate broke against that rock and scattered. And through it all, Bhishmaka, king of Kundina, host of the council and father of the maiden and of the arrogant young Rukmi, had listened in silence. He had heard the warning of Jarasandha, the plea of Dantavakra, the defiance of Salwa, and weighed each against the one thing he could not bear to lose. Rising from his seat among the gathered princes, Bhishmaka resolved to go himself to Krishna, to propitiate, before any war began, the suitor the whole earth had gathered to deny. The council still rang with argument behind him as he stepped out into the evening, and Kundina, unknowing, went on lighting its lamps.
stories.reflection: Every king in the hall seems to know who Krishna is; what divides them is what to do with the knowledge. Dantavakra reads the same facts as a summons to peace, Salwa as a summons to courage, and Bhishmaka, who alone among them is not deciding for an army but for his own children, reads them as a reason to bend. The council's war of words ends not with a king convinced but with a father moved.
stories.next_story_tease: But the kings were not done debating, and soon Shalya would propose summoning the Yavana king Kalayavana.

stories.title: Shalya Proposes Inviting Kalayavana
stories.story:
The kings had come to Kundina to win Rukmini, and they were going home with nothing. Krishna had carried her off from the swayamvara before any of them could move, and now the defeated suitors gathered one last time in the assembly hall of her father Bhishmaka, restless on their beautiful seats, before scattering to their own kingdoms.

Bhishmaka, well read in the laws of conduct, rose and asked their forgiveness. "You all know the calamity that has befallen the swayamvara," he said. "Forgive me for the fruit that is the outcome of my misconduct." He honored them duly and sent away the monarchs of Central India and of the east, west, and north, who departed delighted. But a circle of kings remained, desirous of listening to the mystery: Jarasandha of Magadha, Sunitha, the energetic Dantavakra, Shalya the king of Soubha, king Mahakurma, Kaishika, the leading kings of the Pravara race, the royal sage Venudari, the king of Kashmir, and the kings of the Deccan.

To them Bhishmaka spoke again, aiming his words at his own son. "Observing the movements of my son, my eyes are agitated with fear. I consider all now as mere boys. Krishna alone is the foremost of beings — the incarnation of glory, the partaker of fame — and he has established his fame and the might of his arms in this land of mortals. Blessed is Devaki, the foremost of damsels, who has conceived as her son the lotus-eyed Krishna, identical with the sum total of beauty, the greatest of all in the three worlds, adored of all the immortals."

When he had spoken, Shalya of Soubha rose and answered in sweet words. "O lord of kings, do not lament for your son. Kshatriyas meet either with success or defeat in battle — that is the inevitable course and the eternal religion of mortals. Save Baladeva and Krishna, what third person can withstand your highly powerful son? When by the might of his arms he handles the Bhargava weapons, difficult of being used even by the celestials, what man is capable of bearing it? This eternal being Krishna is without birth or death. In this land of mortals even the holder of the trident cannot defeat him. Knowing Keshava as Ishana, your son did not engage in fight with him."

Then Shalya paused, and said what he had really come to say. "It is not that there is none who can defeat him." The great sage Gargya, desiring a son, had adored Rudra for twelve years, living on powdered iron and practising dreadful and highly difficult penances. When Shankara, pleased, offered him a boon, Gargya prayed for a son whom the kings of Mathura would not be able to slay, and Rudra granted it. By virtue of that boon, Gargya's son Kalayavana is unslayable by the kings of Mathura in the battlefield — and especially in the city of Mathura itself. Though Krishna is highly powerful amongst the princes of Mathura, if Kalayavana comes to battle and fights with him, he will be able to defeat him. "O kings," Shalya said, "if you accept my words as becoming and sound, send an emissary to the capital of the king of the Yavanas."

The leading kings heard him out and were delighted. "We will do it," they said. Only Jarasandha lost heart, recollecting the words of Brahma. "Alas!" he said. "Formerly, assailed by the fear of a foreign king, all the chiefs, seeking refuge with me, used to get back their lost kingdoms, their servants, their armies and conveyances. Now, on account of their bad feelings towards their lord, they excite me to seek another's shelter, like a damsel coming in contact with a stranger. Alas! Even I, who stand afraid of Krishna —" and there his voice died away.

But the will of the kings prevailed, and the emperor who had once sheltered the princes of the earth sent Shalya of Soubha as his envoy to the capital of the Yavanas.
stories.reflection: Shalya's counsel turns the kings' defeat at the swayamvara into a plan against Krishna, and the plan is clever enough that everyone accepts it at once. It is Jarasandha, the mightiest of them, who recoils — because he understands that calling in an ally is also an admission of fear.
stories.next_story_tease: Shalya of Soubha, dispatched as envoy, set out for the capital of the Yavanas.

stories.title: Shalya Delivers Jarasandha's Message to Kalayavana
stories.story:
A wind came up in the capital of the Yavanas that day — cold and fragrant, delightful and strange — and the assembled court wondered at it. Whence had it come? And then they saw the answer riding out of the south.

The king of the Yavanas, Kalayavana, governed his city in pursuance of royal duties. He was wise, conversant with the threefold objects of life, proficient in the arts of policy, innocent of the sevenfold calamities, endued with every accomplishment, well versed in the scriptures, pious, truthful, a master of his senses, acquainted with the rules of war, an expert in capturing forts, heroic, and accustomed to honor his ministers. That day he sat at ease encircled by his ministers, while the learned Yavanas, discoursing among themselves on celestial themes, adored him.

The car that came from the south was golden and white, lighted up with the lustre of jewels, adorned with celestial flags and pennons, drawn by horses fleet like the mind or the air, decked with tiger-skins — a terror to enemies, an enhancer of joy to friends, built by the celestial architect, effulgent like the sun. On it sat the powerful and beautiful king of Soubha: Shalya, the friend of Kalayavana.

Delighted to see his friend, Kalayavana rose from his throne, took the arghya offering and water for washing the feet, and went out to wait at the landing stair of the car. Shalya descended alone, with a confident heart, and joyously entered the palace. But seeing the offering in the Yavana king's hands, he drew back. "O you of great effulgence," he said, "I am not now worthy of arghya. I am an envoy of the kings, dispatched to you by the intelligent Jarasandha. I therefore do not deserve arghya from the kings."

Kalayavana smiled. "O you of large arms, I know that you have been dispatched here as an envoy by the king of Magadha on behalf of the kings. I adore you duly with water to wash the feet, a seat, and every means of welcome, because you have been sent by the entire circle of kings. By adoring you, I worship the whole host of kings; by honoring you, all of them are honored. Therefore, O king, sit with me on this throne."

So they shook hands, asked after each other's welfare, and sat at ease on the sacred throne. Then Kalayavana put the question that lay beneath the courtesy. "What has become impossible for him, depending on the might of whose arms you kings are all living without any anxiety as the gods do under the protection of Indra, that he has sent you to me? Tell me truly, O king, what mandate the powerful king of Magadha has issued to me. Even if it be very difficult, I shall carry out his command."

Shalya spoke. "O king of the Yavanas, hear what the king of Magadha has deputed me to communicate to you." And he delivered the message as it had been given to him.

"The irrepressible Krishna has been oppressing the world from his very birth. Informed of his wicked deeds, I attempted to slay him. Accompanied by a number of kings along with their fourfold forces and conveyances, I besieged the mount Gomanta with a huge army. There, listening to the highly sensible words of the king of Chedi, I set fire to that best of mountains for the destruction of Rama and Krishna. Beholding that fire, consisting of hundreds and thousands of flames and resembling the fire of dissolution, Rama, holding the golden-hilted sword, leaped down from the mountain summit into the midst of the ocean-like army of the kings. He killed the car-warriors, the infantry and the cavalry; he moved about like a serpent, and catching elephants, horses and soldiers with his ploughshare, he ground them with his mace. In that battlefield abounding in hundreds of kings he destroyed elephants with elephants, car-warriors with cars, and cavalry with horses. After him Krishna, taking up his discus effulgent like the sun and his black iron club, forcibly leaped down into the enemy's army, shaking the mountain with the force of his feet as a lion attacks the poor deer. And the mountain, whirled about and bathed with a shower, extinguished the fire and entered into the earth as if dancing."

Shalya paused, and the tale of defeat turned into a plea. "Enter the city of Mathura with your army," Jarasandha had said, "and establish your glory there."

When the envoy fell silent, the court of the Yavanas was still. The mandate lay before the king: Mathura was his for the taking, if he dared.
stories.reflection: The embassy moves by courtesy: Kalayavana honors the envoy and, through him, the whole circle of kings, and only then does the appeal arrive. Jarasandha's message is a confession of defeat at Gomanta turned into an invitation for another king to finish what he could not.
stories.next_story_tease: Kalayavana would answer the appeal by marching on Mathura that very day.

stories.title: Kalayavana Marches on Mathura
stories.story:
Of all the honors Kalayavana had ever received, none weighed like the message he held that day — the kings of the earth had asked him to vanquish Krishna.

"Happily honored and blessed am I," he said, "and my life is crowned with success, since numberless kings have requested me for vanquishing Krishna. The kings have appointed me in the work of subduing Krishna, who is invincible in the three worlds, even unto gods and Asuras. And they have blessed me so that I will achieve victory. While the kings, with delighted hearts, have declared my victory, I shall, by the very pouring of their water-like words, achieve success. Whatever it may be, I shall carry out the command of the Emperor Jarasandha, issued at the request of the kings. Even my discomfiture in it will be tantamount to my success. O king, today the day and the stars are auspicious, and in this auspicious moment I shall even today start for Mathura, to defeat Keshava in the battlefield."

He honored Shalya of Soubha duly with highly precious gems and dresses. For acquiring unstinted blessings he gave away various riches to his guest and to the brahmins, and duly offered libations to fire. Then, after the performance of benedictory rites, he set out with his army for vanquishing Janarddana. And Shalya, his desire fully achieved, embraced the lord of the Yavanas and set out with a delighted heart for his own city, carrying the answer of the Yavanas back to the kings.

Few in the host that marched behind Kalayavana knew the story of their king's birth, though all of India would soon learn it. The sage Gargya, called impotent by his brother-in-law in an assembly of the Yadavas, was deeply offended by the laughter that followed and repaired to the shores of the western sea, where he engaged in arduous penance to obtain a son who should be a terror to the tribe of Yadu. For twelve years he propitiated Mahadeva, living upon iron sand, until the deity at last was pleased with him and gave him the desired boon. The childless king of the Yavanas became Gargya's friend, and by the king's wife Gargya begot a son as black as a bee — whose breast was as hard as the point of the thunderbolt — and the child was therefore called Kalayavana. The old king placed his son upon the throne and retired to the woods. Inflated with the conceit of his prowess, Kalayavana demanded of Narada who were the most mighty heroes on earth, and the sage answered: "The Yadavas." It was an answer the king of the Yavanas never forgot, and it named the only enemies he thought worth marching against.

Accordingly Kalayavana assembled many myriads of Mlechchhas and barbarians, and with a vast armament of elephants, cavalry, chariots and foot, advanced impatiently against Mathura and the Yadavas — wearying every day the animal that carried him, but insensible of fatigue himself, and driving the whole host on at the pace of his own restlessness. The name of Kalayavana ran ahead of that army like fire: the king of the Yavanas was coming to Mathura, he had vowed not to turn back until Keshava was defeated in the battlefield, and he had sworn that even his own defeat would not count as failure.
stories.reflection: Kalayavana's boast contains its own admission — even his discomfiture, he says, will count as success. A king who sets out expecting that nothing he does can be failure has already stopped weighing his chances.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells this march differently: there, Kalayavana learns from Narada that the Yadavas are the mightiest heroes on earth and advances on his own, with no embassy from Jarasandha. This account follows the Harivamsha.

stories.title: The Serpent-Jar Stratagem Against Kalayavana
stories.story:
They saw the host before they understood what it was — a swarm of kings and barbarians covering the plain like locusts, and behind it a river that had never flowed before, born of the urine and dung of its horses and camels, which men afterward called Aswasakrit.

The story of its leader was known now across the land. The sage Gargya, dishonored by his own brother-in-law before the king, had given up his wife in anger and engaged in hard penances for a son; living on pounded iron for twelve years he worshipped Mahadeva, and Rudra conferred on him a boon — an all-powerful son who would be able to discomfit in battle the descendants of the Vrishni and Andhaka races. The childless king of the Yavanas heard of the boon, brought Gargya into his own kingdom, and consoled him; and by an Apsara in the guise of a milk-woman, Gopali by name, Gargya begot the highly powerful hero Kalayavana, who was brought up in the king's inner apartment like his own son and, after the old king's demise, became king. When he grew exceedingly powerful, the Shaka, the Tukhara, the Darava, the Parava, the Tangana, the Khasha, the Panhava, and hundreds of Mlechcha kings living near Himavan took shelter under him. Encircled by those Dasyu kings, assuming various dresses and holding various weapons, the king of the Yavanas set out for Mathura. He agitated the surface of the earth with innumerable horses, elephants, asses, camels and a huge army; the path of the sun was covered with the dust raised by his soldiers; and the river that followed him took its name from the beasts that made it.

Krishna had taken no notice of Kalayavana while he grew up in the midst of the Yavanas, for he had heard from Narada the story of his obtaining the boon. But now, hearing of the approach of this huge army, the leader of the Vrishnis and Andhakas addressed his kinsmen. "Great is the calamity that has befallen the descendants of the Vrishni and Andhaka races," he said. "This enemy is unslayable by us, on account of the boon conferred on him by the holder of the trident. I employed all other means — conciliation and the rest — to win him over. But he wishes for battle, worked up with pride. 'I am to live here,' Narada said to me; and I tell you the same. The emperor Jarasandha is not forgiving towards us, and the other kings, assailed by the Vrishni discus and on account of the destruction of Kamsa, have been displeased with us and sought refuge with the Magadha king. Under his protection they want to obstruct us, and many kinsmen of the Yadavas have been slain by them. What more shall I say? We will never acquire prosperity if we live in this city."

Saying this, and desirous of retreating, Keshava sent an envoy to the king of the Yavanas. To terrorize him, the highly intelligent Madhava put a highly dreadful black serpent — resembling a collection of collyrium — into a jar and sealed it up, and sent it to the king of the Yavanas through his own emissary. "Krishna is like a deadly serpent," the emissary said, and showed the jar to Kalayavana.

The king of the Yavanas looked at the sealed jar and understood at once what the Yadavas meant to say. Without a word, he had the jar filled with dreadful ants. The black serpent, eaten by the innumerable ants having sharp beaks, was reduced to ashes; and the jar, sealed anew, went back the way it had come.

So the warning returned to Mathura devoured — a serpent turned to ashes, and a king of the Yavanas who could not be frightened. Whatever answer Krishna meant to send next would have to be stronger than fear.
stories.reflection: The exchange of sealed jars is a conversation without words, each side answering a threat with a sharper one. Krishna's warning is devoured before it is even delivered — a reminder that a terror meant for the proud may only harden them.
stories.next_story_tease: But the exchange of warnings was not over; Jarasandha's mace was already hurtling toward Mathura.
stories.hero_scene: The emissary unsealing the jar before Kalayavana's court to reveal the black serpent coiled within, like a stroke of collyrium, while the king of the Yavanas watches unafraid.

stories.title: Jarasandha Hurls His Mace toward Mathura
stories.story:
From the heights of Girivraja, the king of Magadha lifted a mace and began to whirl it — once, and again, and ninety-nine turns in all — until the iron seemed less a weapon than the shape of his anger. Then, with everything he had behind it, he hurled it toward Mathura.

The enmity between Jarasandha and Krishna had begun some time before, when Kamsa was slain. It was not a grudge to be taken lightly. Jarasandha was the son of Vrihadratha, and the story of his rise was known wherever kings gathered. When the great ascetic Chandakausika had come into the country of the Magadhas, King Vrihadratha, filled with joy at the sage's advent, had gone out to receive him with his ministers, his priest, his wives, and his son, and had offered the Rishi his whole kingdom along with the boy. The sage, well pleased, accepted the worship and gave the king a prophecy instead: this son would grow in prosperity and prowess; other monarchs would never be able to equal his energy; weapons hurled at him even by the celestials would fail to cause him the least pain; he would blaze forth above the heads of all that wore crowns, and, like the sun dimming the lustre of all luminous bodies, rob all monarchs of their splendour; and all the kings of the earth would live in obedience to his commands. Vrihadratha installed the boy on the throne, and, having come to feel a great distaste for worldly pleasures, retired into the woods with his two wives. The prophecy kept its word. Jarasandha ruled like a father, and by his valour brought numerous kings under his sway.

And this was the man whose mace now flew toward Mathura, where Krishna of wonderful deeds was residing. The weapon fell near the city, at a distance of ninety-nine yojanas from Girivraja, and the place where it struck came to be called Gadavasan, adjacent to Mathura itself. The citizens, beholding the whole circumstance well, went to Krishna and informed him of the fall of the mace.

There was no mistaking the message. Jarasandha had two supporters, Hansa and Dimvaka, both incapable of being slain by weapons, both foremost among intelligent men in the science of politics and morality; together with Jarasandha, they were held to be more than a match for the three worlds. It was for this reason that the powerful Kukkura, Andhaka, and Vrishni tribes, acting from motives of policy, had never deemed it proper to fight with him. And now that strength had been hurled across the country and left lying near Mathura — a line drawn on the earth between Girivraja and the city where Krishna lived.

Krishna heard the citizens out. The mace lay at Gadavasan, close to the city's edge, and the warning was complete in itself: the king of Magadha had measured the distance to Mathura with his own arm, and a weapon that could cover that distance could be followed by the army that owned it. Whatever came next, the citizens had done what they could. They had brought the news to Krishna, and the weight of what it meant now rested with him.
stories.reflection: A mace hurled across the country was a king's way of drawing a line: the distance from Girivraja to Mathura, measured by his own strength, as a notice that the enmity over Kamsa's death would not quietly fade. The weapon itself was a warning, and it was also an announcement of the long conflict to come.
stories.next_story_tease: But the king of Magadha was only beginning; the time would come when Krishna proposed meeting that strength directly.

stories.title: Krishna Proposes Slaying Jarasandha as Prelude to the Rajasuya
stories.story:
There was one obstacle left between Yudhishthira and the Rajasuya, and it could not be conquered in battle.

In the assembly, Krishna stated it plainly. Both Hansa and Dimvaka had fallen; Kamsa, with all his followers, had been slain. The time had come for the destruction of Jarasandha. But Jarasandha was incapable of being vanquished in battle even by all the celestials and the Asuras fighting together. They thought, however, that he could be vanquished in a personal struggle with bare arms.

Then Krishna divided the work in a single sentence: in him was policy, in Bhima was strength, and in Arjuna was triumph. Therefore, as a prelude to performing the Rajasuya, they would certainly achieve the destruction of the ruler of Magadha. When the three of them approached that monarch in secret, he would without doubt engage in an encounter with one of them; and from fear of disgrace, from covetousness, and from pride of strength, he would certainly summon Bhima to the encounter. Like death himself, who slays a person however swollen with pride, the long-armed and mighty Bhimasena would effect the destruction of the king. "If thou knowest my heart, if thou hast any faith in me," Krishna said, "then make over to me, as a pledge, Bhima and Arjuna without loss of time."

Yudhishthira, beholding both Bhima and Arjuna standing with cheerful faces, answered. "O Achyuta, slayer of all enemies, say not so. Thou art the lord of the Pandavas. We are dependent on thee. What thou sayest, O Govinda, is consistent with wise counsels." The one who stayed under Krishna's command, he said, could already regard Jarasandha as slain, the monarchs confined by him already set free, the Rajasuya already accomplished. Then Yudhishthira spoke of leadership itself: troops, when properly led, always do excellent service; a force without a leader has been called inert by the wise; the wise conduct water into low places, and even fishermen drain tanks through holes. For the successful accomplishment of one's purposes, one should ever place Krishna in the van — that foremost of persons whose strength consists in wisdom and policy, and who possesses a knowledge of both method and means. Let Arjuna follow Krishna, and let Bhima follow Arjuna; policy, good fortune, and might would bring success in a matter requiring valour.

Thus addressed, the trio — Krishna, Arjuna, and Bhima, all possessed of great energy — set out for Magadha attired in the garb of Snataka Brahmanas, their resplendent bodies blessed by the agreeable speeches of friends and relatives. Inflamed with wrath at the sad lot of their relative kings, those bodies, already like the sun, the moon, and the fire, became much more blazing. And the people, beholding Krishna and Arjuna — both never before vanquished in battle — with Bhima in the van, all ready to achieve the same task, regarded Jarasandha as already slain.

Their road ran long. They passed from the country of the Kurus through Kuru-jangala and arrived at the charming lake of lotuses; they crossed the hills of Kalakuta, the rivers Gandaki and Sadanira, and the Sarkaravarta; they crossed the delightful Sarayu and saw the country of Eastern Kosala; passing over that country they went to Mithila, crossed the Mala and Charamanwati, and then the Ganges and the Sone, going on toward the east. At last they arrived at Magadha, in the heart of the country of Kushamva. Reaching the hills of Goratha, they saw the city of Magadha, always filled with kine and wealth and water, and handsome with its innumerable dwellings.

From the hillside they looked down on the stronghold of the man they had come to meet — with nothing but their bare arms. Three Brahmanas stood at the edge of the enemy's country, and the great enterprise lay spread below them.
stories.reflection: Krishna's plan rested on reading Jarasandha's character: a king certain that no weapon can harm him will still step down to meet bare arms, summoned by his own pride. Policy, strength, and triumph each had a man assigned to it, as if the victory were already divided into its parts before the journey even began.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana (10.71) presents this same plan as Uddhava's counsel to Krishna rather than Krishna's own proposal; the Mahabharata version, followed here, attributes it to Krishna himself.
stories.next_story_tease: In Girivraja, the three disguised Brahmanas would announce themselves in a way no one expected.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna in the simple garb of Snataka Brahmanas standing on the hills of Goratha, looking down across the wide, cattle-rich plains at the great walled city of Magadha in the distance.

stories.title: Krishna and the Pandavas Break the Chaityaka Peak
stories.story:
They had come to Girivraja to humble the pride of Jarasandha, and they began by breaking a mountain.

Krishna showed Arjuna the capital of Magadha standing in all its beauty — filled with flocks and herds, its stock of water never exhausted, adorned with fine mansions in excellent array, free from every kind of calamity. Five large hills protected the city of Girivraja: Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri, and the delightful Chaitya, all of high peaks, overgrown with tall trees of cool shade, and connected with one another, their slopes concealed by forests of delightful and fragrant Lodhra trees covered with flowers. It was here that the illustrious Gautama of rigid vows had begotten Kakshivat and other celebrated sons, and here that the mighty monarchs of Anga and Vanga and other countries had come in olden times to Gautama's abode and passed their days in joy. Owning such a delightful and impregnable city, Krishna said, Jarasandha was ever bent on seeking the fruition of his purposes, unlike other monarchs. "We shall, however, by slaying him today," he said, "humble his pride."

They entered the city of Magadha and approached Girivraja, full of cheerful and well-fed inhabitants belonging to all four orders, where festivities were perennial. And on arriving at the gate of the city, the brothers — instead of passing through it — began to pierce the heart of the high Chaityaka peak, the hill worshipped by the race of Vrihadratha and by the citizens, the hill that delighted the hearts of all the Magadhas.

There, long ago, Vrihadratha had slain a cannibal called Rishava, and from the monster's hide he had made three drums and placed them in his own city — drums of such making that once beaten, their sound lasted a full month. It was at that point, where those drums covered with celestial flowers used to yield their continuous sound, that the brothers broke the Chaityaka peak down. Attacking with their mighty arms that immovable, huge, high, and old and celebrated peak, always worshipped with perfumes and floral wreaths, those heroes broke it down. And desirous of slaying Jarasandha, they seemed by that act to place their feet upon the head of their foe. With joyful hearts they entered the city.

But the city read the omen before it saw the men. The learned Brahmanas residing within Girivraja saw many evil omens and reported them to Jarasandha. The king's priest made him mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him; and Jarasandha, possessed of great prowess, with a view to warding off those evils, entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts. The sacred hill of his ancestors had fallen at his gate, and all his rites could not undo what the portents promised.

Meanwhile the brothers — unarmed, or rather with their bare arms as their only weapons — entered the capital in the guise of Brahmanas. They beheld the extraordinary beauty of the shops, full of various edibles and floral wreaths, supplied with articles of every variety that man can desire. Those best of men, Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna, passed along the public road, and, endued with great strength, snatched forcibly from the flower-vendors the garlands they had exposed for sale. Attired in robes of various colours, decked in garlands and ear-rings, the heroes entered the abode of Jarasandha like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds. Their arms, besmeared with sandal paste, looked like the trunks of sala trees. The people of Magadha, beholding those heroes looking like elephants, with necks broad like those of trees and wide chests, began to wonder much.

Those bulls among men passed through three gates crowded with men, and proudly and cheerfully approached the king. And Jarasandha, rising up in haste, received them with water to wash their feet, with honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya, with gifts of kine, and with other forms of respect. "Ye are welcome," the great king said. And both Arjuna and Bhima remained silent at this.

The welcome hung in the air unanswered. Two of the three guests had said nothing at all, and the king of Magadha stood waiting amid the honours he had just given them.
stories.reflection: The broken peak was the first move of the whole enterprise, and it was deliberate: a king's own sacred hill, torn down at his gate, announced that these strangers had not come to beg but to humble him. The omens the priests read afterwards only told the city, in another language, what its own eyes had already seen.
stories.next_story_tease: The silence of the two disguised brothers would need an explanation.

stories.title: Krishna Speaks for the Silent Disguised Brothers
stories.story:
The king of Magadha had done everything a host should do. He had risen in haste when the three Brahmanas were brought before him, and he had received them with water to wash their feet, with honey and the other ingredients of the Arghya, with gifts of kine, and with every other form of respect his court could offer. "Ye are welcome," the great king said.

And both of his two younger guests remained silent.

The king had come to this meeting in a season of ill omens. The learned Brahmanas of Girivraja had seen many evil signs and reported them to him, and Jarasandha, to ward off the evils, had entered upon the celebration of a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts, his priest making him mount an elephant and whirling lighted brands about him. The broken mountain had promised him trouble; now three strangers stood where the trouble had arrived, and one of them was about to speak for all three.

The moment stretched. The three strangers had passed along the public road of the capital, past the shops full of various edibles and floral wreaths, supplied with articles of every variety that man can desire, and had snatched forcibly from the flower-vendors the garlands they had exposed for sale — as if the city itself were already theirs to help themselves from. The people of Magadha had wondered at them: heroes looking like elephants, with necks broad like those of trees and wide chests, their arms, besmeared with sandal paste, like the trunks of sala trees. Passing through three gates crowded with men, proudly and cheerfully they had come at last to the king. Now they stood before him, and his welcome had fallen into a silence he had not expected.

Krishna spoke for the three of them. "O king of kings," he said, "these two are now in the observance of a vow. Therefore they will not speak. Silent they will remain till midnight. After that hour they will speak with thee."

The explanation was simple and absolute. The king had received guests who could not answer him: not a single word until the hour of midnight, when the vow would end. Whatever questions Jarasandha might have wished to ask — who these Brahmanas were, whence they had come, what errand had brought them to the capital of Magadha — would have to wait for the night hour, and for the guests themselves to choose the moment their silence broke.

Until then, they were simply guests under his roof, owing him nothing but their presence while the hours of the night ran down. The court of Girivraja settled into waiting. The king had offered his welcome; the vow had answered for the two silent brothers; and the first words between Jarasandha and the disguised trio would come only when midnight released them.
stories.reflection: A vow of silence was a clever shield: it let Krishna's party enter the enemy's court, accept its honours, and give away nothing — not a word, not a name — until the hour they themselves chose. Jarasandha's hospitality was turned into a waiting game, and the waiting belonged to the host.
stories.next_story_tease: When midnight came, Jarasandha would question the strangers about their disguise.

stories.title: The Rules of an Enemy's Gate
stories.story:
The five hills of Girivraja ringed the capital of Magadha like the fingers of a cupped hand: Vaihara, Varaha, Vrishava, Rishigiri, and Chaitya, the last of them best loved of all, worshipped by the citizens and by the royal line of Vrihadratha. Krishna had pointed them out as the three brothers drew near, and had shown Arjuna the city the way a man shows a treasure he means to take. Filled with flocks and herds, its water never failing, adorned with fine mansions standing in excellent array, free from every kind of calamity — a city, he said, that its king believed impregnable. "We shall, however, by slaying him today, humble his pride."

They did not enter by the gate. At the foot of the Chaityaka hill the brothers had set their hands to the rock and torn down the peak the whole city honoured, at the very point where the great drums of Vrihadratha used to sound, once beaten, for a full month. Then, in the guise of Brahmanas, with their bare arms as their only weapons, they had walked through the crowded streets, past shops heavy with edibles and wreaths, snatched garlands from the flower-vendors, and gone in decked like princes of the road. Their arms, smeared with sandal paste, looked like the trunks of sala trees. Passing through three gates that were crowded with men, they had come on proudly and cheerfully, like Himalayan lions eyeing cattle-folds, and the people of Magadha, seeing these giants in mendicants' robes, had wondered much.

Within the city, the learned Brahmanas had already seen evil omens and reported them. Jarasandha's priest had made the king mount an elephant and whirled lighted brands about him, and the king had begun a sacrifice with proper vows and fasts to turn the portents aside. Yet when the three strangers presented themselves at his abode, he rose up in haste and received them with every honour — water to wash their feet, honey, the offerings of the arghya, gifts of cattle — and bade them welcome. Bhima and Arjuna stood silent, and Krishna spoke for them. But the king was not a man to let a strange entry pass unremarked, and when the ceremony of welcome was done, he looked at his three guests and asked what they meant by coming into his city by no proper gate.

Krishna answered without heat, as though stating a rule of grammar. "These are the rules of the ordinance," he said. "An enemy's abode should be entered through a wrong gate, and a friend's abode through the right one." Then he added what no guest in that hall could have expected: "Know, O monarch, that this also is our eternal vow — that having entered the foe's abode for the accomplishment of our purpose, we accept not the worship offered to us."

The water for the feet stood untouched. The gifts lay where they had been laid. The king of Magadha, who had risen to greet these men as guests, had just been told, in the most courteous words imaginable, that they were his enemies: that they had entered his house the way one enters an enemy's house, and that they refused his friendship outright. Whatever courtesy had passed between them was over. What remained was the purpose for which they had come.

He heard it in silence. And in that silence, the three brothers stood in the hall of the king they had crossed a mountain to kill, their errand spoken aloud at last, with nothing left between them and it but the word of a king who had not yet given his answer.
stories.reflection: Krishna answers a charge of bad manners with a precise code of his own: a friend's house and a foe's house are not entered the same way, and a guest who refuses the offered worship is declaring, openly and without rudeness, that he has come as an enemy. The courtliness of the reply only sharpens the threat beneath it.
stories.next_story_tease: But Jarasandha, certain of his own innocence, would demand to know what injury he had ever done them.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing calm in Jarasandha's hall, the untouched water for the feet and the gifts of welcome lying between him and the seated king, with Bhima and Arjuna silent behind him in mendicants' robes.

stories.title: The Hand Krishna Held Back
stories.story:
The hospitality had been refused, the challenge all but spoken, and now the king of Magadha asked his own question before anyone else could. He did not recollect, Jarasandha said, ever acting injuriously toward his guests; even searching his memory with care, he could not find the injury he was supposed to have done them. "When I have never done ye an injury, why do ye regard me, who am innocent, as your foe? Answer me truly, for this is the rule followed by the honest."

Krishna's answer changed the air of the hall. It was not of his own will that he had come, he said; a certain person, at the head of a royal line, had sent him and his companions against the king. "Thou hast brought many of the Kshatriyas of the world as captives to thy city. Having perpetrated that wicked wrong, how dost thou regard thyself as innocent?" He spoke of kings treated with cruelty, gathered together and kept for a sacrifice to the god Rudra. "The slaughter of human beings as sacrifice unto the gods is never seen. Why dost thou seek to perform a sacrifice unto god Sankara by slaughtering human beings? Thou art addressing persons belonging to thy own order as animals fit for sacrifice."

Then he told them plainly who stood before him. "Know that we are certainly not Brahmanas. I am Hrishikesha, otherwise called Sauri, and these two heroes among men are the sons of Pandu. O king of Magadha, we challenge thee. Fight standing before us. Either set free all the monarchs, or go thou to the abode of Yama." He spoke of what waited for warriors who died in open fight — heaven, the sure consequence, the triumph of Indra himself won by vanquishing the Asuras — and of kings like Damvodhava, Kartavirya, Uttara and Vrihadratha, who had met destruction along with all their forces for disregarding their superiors. "Don't disregard others, O king. Valour dwelleth in every man. There are many men whose valour may be equal or superior to thine. Cast off thy superiority and pride in the presence of those that are thy equals."

Jarasandha's answer was unshaken. He never made a captive of a king without first vanquishing him, he said; every one of the monarchs kept in his city had been defeated in open war. It was the duty of his order, as he understood it, to bring others under sway by the exhibition of prowess and then to treat them as slaves. "Having gathered these monarchs with the intention of offering them as sacrifices unto the god, how shall I, from fear, liberate them today?" He would not bargain, and he would not bend: troops against troops, he said, or alone against one, or against two, or against three.

Now came the moment when the brothers might have fallen on him together. Krishna alone was more than a match for the king of Magadha; the strength of the descendants of Madhu could have ended the matter there and then. But the lord Sauri, ever devoted to truth, kept in view the command of Brahma, and remembered that the ruler of Magadha was destined to be slain in battle by Bhima, and not by a descendant of Madhu. He desired not to slay the king himself. He drew back his own hand, and left the king to Bhima.

The son of Pandu stepped forward to meet the king of Magadha, and the long duel began — a fight in which Krishna would take no part, because destiny had written this death with a particular name on it, and he would not write over it with his own.
stories.reflection: The hinge of the episode is Krishna's restraint — the king of Magadha stands within his reach, yet he will not take what destiny has assigned to another hand. His power shows itself as much in what he refuses to do as in what he does.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as the duel began, a new enemy was already marching against Mathura — the Yavana king Kalayavana.
stories.hero_scene: Bhima stepping forward to face Jarasandha in the middle of the great hall, while Krishna stands back with arms folded, deliberately refusing a fight that destiny has assigned to another.

stories.title: The Captured Host of Kalayavana
stories.story:
The cave breathed out the smell of ages when Muchukunda stirred. He had slept through the turning of whole eras, and when he walked out into the daylight and looked at the men he met, they seemed small to him — diminished in stature, somehow, and in spirit. He understood then that the world he had known was long gone, and that the Kali age had arrived.

He had woken to find himself before Krishna, and had praised him as the sovereign of all things, the eternal lord, Hari — he who is praised by the wise. Krishna, in turn, had granted him his wish. "Go to whatever celestial regions you wish, lord of men," he said, "possessed of might irresistible, honoured by my favour. When you have fully enjoyed all heavenly pleasures, you shall be born in a distinguished family, retaining the recollection of your former births, and you shall finally obtain emancipation." Muchukunda prostrated himself before the lord of the world, went out from the cave, and from that new and shrunken world departed to Gandhamadana, the shrine of Nara-Narayana, to perform penance. And in time it came about exactly as Krishna had promised: he enjoyed the celestial regions, was born again in a distinguished family with the memory of his former births intact, and at last obtained emancipation.

Muchukunda was not the only one to come out of that mountain changed. By that same stratagem Krishna had destroyed his enemy — Kalayavana, the Yavana king who had marched against Mathura. The foe who had entered that affair had not come out of it, and now, free of the man who had threatened them, the Yadavas gathered what he had left behind.

Krishna returned to Mathura and took captive the army of Kalayavana — rich in horses, in elephants, in cars — and conducted it to Dwaraka, and delivered it to Ugrasena. It was a strange procession: the host that had marched out to destroy the Yadus now filed into their city at Krishna's command, its banners furled, its weapons turned to new masters. The Yadu race was relieved, from that day, of all fear of invasion. The war-elephants that had carried the invasion stood in the stalls of the city they had meant to sack.

With hostilities at an end, Balarama grew restless to see his own people, and went to Nanda's cow-pens. He moved among the herdsmen and their women with affection and respect: the elders embraced him, he embraced the younger ones, and with those of his own age he talked and laughed. The cowherds made him many kind speeches. But the gopis spoke to him with the affectation of anger, and beneath the teasing there was something real. "Is all well with the fickle and inconstant Krishna?" they asked. "Does the volatile swain, the friend of an instant, amuse the women of the city by laughing at our rustic efforts to please him? Does he ever think of us, singing in chorus to his songs? Will he not come here once again to see his mother?"

And then the questions turned inward, and the pretence fell away. "Father, mother, brother, husband, kin — what have we not abandoned for his sake?" they said. "But why talk of these things? It is a different tale to tell for him without us, and for us without him."

Balarama carried that message back with him when he left the cow-pens — the enemy's host captured, the city made safe, the war finished; and in Vraja, the women who had loved Krishna first still waiting for the song he no longer sang there.
stories.reflection: The episode pairs a great victory with a small, human wound: the safety Krishna wins for the Yadavas costs Vraja his presence. The gopis' jealousy is teasing, but their last words carry real pain — a reminder that the price of a kingdom is sometimes paid in the homes it leaves behind.
stories.next_story_tease: The Yadavas' relief would not last, for Jarasandha, hearing of his daughters' widowhood, was already gathering his armies.

stories.title: Twenty-Three Armies Against Mathura
stories.story:
The two widows came to their father's court the way grief comes: slowly, and with everything already known. Asti and Prapti, the daughters of Jarasandha, had been given in marriage to Kamsa of Mathura; now they stood before the king of Magadha and told him of their widowhood. Jarasandha heard the unwelcome news, and grief and anger rose in him together.

He had owed Kamsa a debt. The dead king had been his son-in-law and his ally — the son of Ahuka who, chaining his own father, had ruled Mathura with Jarasandha's backing, depending on his help and disregarding the Yadavas. He had been the one man who held the Yadava race in check while Jarasandha gathered the world's kings into his prisons. Now the debt was unpaid, and the Yadavas had killed the man with whom he had shared it; and when the vicious-souled Kamsa was slain by Rama and Krishna, Ugrasena, encircled by the Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, had become king in his place. Jarasandha resolved to make the earth free of Yadavas — to wipe the whole race of the Yadus away in a single campaign. Burning like fire in anger, and making every possible arrangement, the king of Magadha started for Mathura in no time at all.

And the kings he had conquered came with him — out of jealousy toward Janardana, or out of fear of Jarasandha, or simply because he had beaten them and they had nowhere else to stand. All the highly energetic warrior kings who had been defeated and subjugated by his prowess, and all who were his friends, relatives, kinsmen and allies, followed him with their own armies, each encircled by his own forces and eager to please him. Dantavakra of Karusha, the powerful king of Chedi, the king of Kalinga, Bhishmaka and his son Rukmi, the kings of Anga and Vanga, of Koshala and Kashi and Dasharna, Bhagadatta the lord of the Yavanas, Suvala of Gandhara, Duryodhana and the other sons of Dhritarashtra — king after king, mighty car-warriors every one, followed him, each encamping in his own order. They entered the province of Shurasena, a country of barley and fuel, and the command went out: let the armies of the kings united lay siege on all sides to this city.

Twenty-three akshauhinis ringed Mathura — armies measured not in men alone but in chariots, elephants and horses, so many that the horizon turned to dust and metal, and the ground under the city's walls seemed to shake with the weight of them. From the walls, Krishna looked at that host as it settled around them like a sea risen over its banks, an ocean driven past its shore.

And the blessed Hari, who had taken a human body as his means of working in the world, thought long and carefully. The old scriptures call him kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ — the one whose humanity is an instrument, chosen for this work. He did not turn the siege away with a gesture, or wish the army gone. He looked at it the way a man looks at a problem he means to solve, weighing the twenty-three armies, and the kings behind them, and the city, and the people inside it.

Around the walls, the fires of the besieging host burned through the night, ringing Mathura like a second horizon. The siege had begun, and the first night of it belonged to the besiegers. And in the city, Krishna was still thinking — because he had come to this world to act in human ways, and a human king, seeing such an army, must first decide what he is willing to do.
stories.reflection: Krishna meets the greatest army ever raised against him not with a miracle but with deliberation. The old phrase kāraṇa-mānuṣaḥ — one whose humanity is his instrument — is the point: he refuses to solve the siege by sheer divinity, choosing instead to think, plan, and act as a man among men.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana compresses this whole conflict into one line — Jarasandha attacked eighteen times and was routed each time — while the Harivamsha narrates the march and the siege separately and gives the invading force six divisions. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana's number of twenty-three akshauhinis.
stories.next_story_tease: And as Krishna thought, a divine chariot with celestial weapons was descending from the sky toward Mathura.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna on the walls of Mathura gazing out at Jarasandha's encircling army of twenty-three akshauhinis, spread across the plain like a risen sea, its campfires already burning against the dusk.

stories.title: A Divine Chariot and Weapons Descend for Krishna
stories.story:
From the walls of Mathura, the horizon had vanished. Where fields and woodlands had lain, there now stretched an army: the twenty-three divisions of King Jarasandha of Magadha, camped in rings around the city, so many men, horses, chariots and elephants that the plain seemed to heave like a sea overflowing its banks. Jarasandha had come to avenge his son-in-law Kamsa, and he had sworn to leave no Yadava alive beneath the sun.

Krishna stood looking out at it all, and while he looked he reflected. The weight of these warring kings lay heavy on the earth, he thought; this gathering itself was another burden laid upon her. "I will destroy this force," he said within himself, "this weight that has been heaped upon the earth. It was to remove the earth's burden that I came down; and for the protection of dharma, another form of mine is ever maintained."

And as he thought this, the sky answered him.

Out of the empty air above Mathura two chariots descended, bright as the sun itself. Each had its driver at the reins, and each carried the ancient divine weapons of a warrior — bows, quivers, maces, armor, things old beyond memory yet gleaming as though made that morning. No one had sent them and no one had summoned them. They came of their own accord, sinking out of the light like the answer to a question not yet spoken aloud, and came to rest before the two brothers.

Krishna turned to Balarama. "Look, Arya," he said. "Calamity has come upon the Yadavas, who look to you. It was for this that we two were born — to bring ease to the good."

The brothers armed themselves, and the ancient weapons fitted them as if they had been shaped for them all along. Then the two chariots rolled out through the gates of Mathura, past the citizens who had come running into the streets, and out onto the open ground between the walls and the enemy host.

Krishna's chariot was driven by Daruka, his charioteer. As the wheels cleared the gate, Krishna raised to his lips the great conch at his side and blew it once. The sound rolled across the plain like thunder walking the earth, deep and unhurried, filling the whole space between the city and the camps.

In the tents of the Magadha king, in the ranks of the allied kings, in the hearts of the soldiers who had come to wipe the Yadavas from the face of the earth, terror entered and took hold. Men looked at one another and did not know why their hands trembled.

Two chariots stood before the greatest army the age had seen, and the army, for a moment, did not move. The sun stood high over Mathura. The conch's echo went on fading over the fields.

Then the battle began.
stories.reflection: The chariots come down of their own accord, at the exact moment Krishna resolves to act — as if heaven had been waiting for his decision. His weighing of the earth's burden is described in wholly human terms, and the divine answer arrives only when the human resolve is complete.
stories.next_story_tease: Jarasandha's host rolled forward to meet the two chariots, and the greatest battle of the age began.

stories.title: The Yadavas Rout Jarasandha's Army and Spare Him
stories.story:
The two brothers rode out to meet an ocean. Jarasandha, seeing them come, cupped his hands to his mouth and shouted abuse across the field — insults for Krishna, and for Balarama a challenge: if you have any courage, come and fight; summon your fortitude and show it.

Behind the brothers, on the towers and terraces of Mathura, the women of the city had gathered to watch, and more than one swooned where she stood, overcome with grief and fear at the sight of that enormous host.

Krishna's chariot drove into the thick of it, and there he fought as he alone could. Like a wheel of fire that burns in an unbroken circle, his arrows streamed out — nock, draw, loose — without pause and without gap. Elephants with split foreheads crashed down among their own ranks. Horses fell with their necks severed. Chariots splintered like dry branches under a storm. Jarasandha's army was an ocean, dark and without a shore, and men said afterward that no one could have crossed it; but the one who waded into it, though he chose to fight in mortal form, was not measured by mortal measure. In the sky above, out of sight of the armies, the gods and the celestial singers gathered from all quarters to watch, and the field shone under their gathered light like the night sky.

In the middle of it all Balarama sought out Jarasandha himself. The Magadha king had spent his chariot, his horses and his charioteer in the press, and stood alone on the field — and Balarama seized him the way a lion seizes a lion, by the shoulders, so that the king of Magadha hung helpless in his grip. His army lay in ruins around him; his allies were dead or fled. The Vrishni soldiers closed in, and ropes were brought, and Jarasandha, the enemy of the house, was bound where he stood.

Then Krishna stayed the binding. "The Magadha is not to be slain," he said. "He will gather forces again."

Balarama's hands went still. Krishna spoke to the captive with words whose meaning was pure and plain, and then let him go. Jarasandha, released by the two lords of the world, stood a long moment in the shame of it — a shame softened only by the knowledge that every hero on the field counted him worthy of such handling. Then he turned and walked off the field, and no one stopped him.

All around him his host was gone. Krishna, his own strength unbroken, had crossed that ocean as if it had been a pond. As the news ran ahead of him, the people of Mathura poured out through the gates to meet him, free of their fever, carried on a wave of joy. Conches and kettledrums sounded from the walls; the streets were sprinkled with water and hung with banners; women stood on the rooftops and showered the returning chariots with garlands, curds and unbroken rice. The sun set on a city that had braced itself to die at dawn and could not stop celebrating at dusk. And the weapons that had come down from the sky for the battle were seen no more, as if they had never been.

Seventeen times after that day Jarasandha came again to Mathura, each time with an army reckoned in akshauhinis, and seventeen times the Vrishnis, by Krishna's splendor, destroyed his host and sent him home. He returned to Magadha with his life, and that was all he carried back.

The city sang on into the night. The king who had sworn to leave no Yadava alive had been spared by the very men he had come to destroy — and spared, as he himself suspected, for a purpose none of them could yet see.
stories.reflection: Krishna lets Jarasandha walk away at the height of victory, knowing the man will return seventeen times. His mercy is not softness but strategy: Jarasandha's death belongs to a design larger than this one day's battle, and the release is the first move of it.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha splits this episode differently: there the fighting runs twenty-seven days, and it is a voice from the sky — not Krishna — that stays Balarama's hand and declares that Jarasandha must not yet die. The Bhagavata Purana, followed here, has Krishna himself release the captive.
stories.content_note: Battle scene: the rout of an army is described with restraint, but includes slaughter imagery.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as Mathura celebrated, a new enemy — one protected by a boon no weapon could break — was already marching out of the north.

stories.title: Kalayavana Is Burned by Muchukunda's Glance
stories.story:
There is a cave in the mountains above Mathura where a king lay sleeping, and had been sleeping for longer than the oldest tree. It was toward that cave that Krishna ran one afternoon, with an army at his heels that no one in the world could defeat.

The army belonged to Kalayavana, king of the Yavanas, and his story had begun long before, in the house of a teacher. Gargya, the preceptor of the Andhaka and Vrishni races, had kept the vow of celibacy all his life; he had a wife, but he had never known her. And because of this his brother-in-law mocked him before the king and named him impotent. Stung beyond bearing, Gargya left the city, gave up all thought of his wife, and turned to penance. For twelve years he lived on pounded iron and worshipped Mahadeva, the holder of the trident, until the god gave him a boon: he would have a son, all-powerful, who would discomfit the descendants of the Vrishni and Andhaka races in battle.

The king of the Yavanas had no son. He heard of the boon, brought Gargya to his own kingdom, and set women to attend on him; and an Apsara named Gopali, taking the form of a milk-woman, conceived through him. The child was Kalayavana. He was raised in the palace like the king's own son, and when the king died, Kalayavana reigned in his place.

He grew, and his name grew with him. The kings of the Shakas and the Tukharas, the Daradas, the Paravas and the Tanganas, the Khashas and the Panhavas — hundreds of mlechcha kings from the lands near the great mountains — took shelter under him. When he finally marched on Mathura, his host covered the earth like a swarm of locusts, and the dust raised by his soldiers hid the path of the sun.

Krishna had heard from Narada the story of the boon, and so he had never met the Yavana head-on. Now he called his kinsmen together. "Great is the calamity that has befallen the Vrishnis and Andhakas," he told them. "This enemy cannot be slain by us, because of the boon the trident-holder gave him. I tried every means short of war — conciliation and the rest — and he will have battle, for pride has made him deaf. Narada said to me, 'You are to live here,' and I say the same to you. Jarasandha does not forgive, and the kings who shelter under him have not forgiven the death of Kamsa. We will never prosper if we stay in this city."

Still, he tried one last ruse. He sent an envoy to Kalayavana with a sealed jar, and inside the jar a dreadful black serpent, coiled like a stroke of darkness. "Krishna is like a deadly serpent," the envoy said, and showed the jar. Kalayavana understood the threat at once. He filled the jar with ants — innumerable, sharp-beaked — and they devoured the serpent and reduced it to ashes.

Then Krishna did the thing that looked like flight. He left Mathura, and Kalayavana pursued him, and the pursuit was exactly what Krishna intended.

The Yavana had heard Narada describe the marks of the one he sought: the chest marked with the Shrivatsa, the Kaustubha jewel on the neck, the face that was always glad, the pure smile. When he saw Krishna before him he knew him at once, and knew that no other could be. He ran at him; Krishna turned and ran before him, and at every step the Yavana felt his prize within reach. "Flight is not proper for one born in the Yadu clan!" he shouted after him. Krishna did not answer. He went on, and entered a mountain cave.

Inside, in the dark, a man lay asleep.

Kalayavana looked at him and laughed. "This one has led me far," he said, "and now lies here like a virtuous man, pretending to sleep." He was certain it was Krishna — for who else would lie in a cave while a king hunted him? He walked up to the sleeper and kicked him.

The sleeper had been asleep for a very long time. Slowly, as if rising from the bottom of a deep well, he opened his eyes. The glance that fell on the Yavana was angry — angry at being woken, angry at being kicked, angry at the presumption of a world that had forgotten to leave him alone.

Where the glance fell, Kalayavana caught fire, and in a moment he was ash.

The king who had hidden the sun with his dust left nothing behind in that cave but a small mound of ashes. And the sleeper, awake at last, sat up in the darkness and looked at the young man standing quietly before him.
stories.reflection: Krishna wins this battle by running, and the boon that made Kalayavana unbeatable in war means nothing against a power he never thought to guard against. The enemy who could not be slain by any weapon is undone by a sleeper's opened eyes.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana tells the cave episode briefly, without the story of Gargya's penance and Kalayavana's birth; that background comes from the Harivamsha, which is followed here.
stories.content_note: Includes a death by burning (a character reduced to ashes by a glance), described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But who was the sleeper whose glance could burn a king to ashes?
stories.hero_scene: In the darkness of the cave, Kalayavana's foot still lifted from the kick, frozen before the great slowly-opening eyes of Muchukunda; a single glance blazing across the dark, while Krishna watches from the cave mouth.

stories.title: Muchukunda's Story
stories.subtitle: Muchukunda, an Ikshvaku king who once guarded the gods against the asuras, was granted deep sleep as his reward.
stories.story:
The man who had burned a king to ashes sat up in the darkness of the cave and looked at Krishna, and Krishna looked back at him. For a long moment neither spoke. The sleeper had been asleep so long that waking felt like a birth; and the man standing before him was not the one who had kicked him.

This was Muchukunda, son of Mandhata, of the Ikshvaku line — a king of an age that had long since passed.

Long ago, when the gods fought the asuras, the hosts of heaven led by Indra had asked this mortal king to stand guard for them. They asked him because he was strong, and because when a king of the Ikshvaku line gave his word, he kept it. Muchukunda fought for the gods in their war against the asuras, and he guarded them through battles longer than the lives of ordinary men.

When the war was over, the gods released him. They met him at the mouth of the cave — Indra and the hosts of heaven — and they told him the truth gently, the way one tells a friend something hard. The world he had left was gone. His kingdom, with its enemies cut down, no longer waited for him. His sons, his queens, his kinsmen, his ministers and his counselors — all were scattered or sleeping. "Time is mightier than the mighty," they said. "The Blessed Lord is the immutable sovereign, and nothing stands against him."

Then they offered him a boon, as they had promised. "Choose whatever you wish," they said, "and good go with you. Ask anything except liberation — that is not ours to grant."

A man who has guarded heaven, and come home to find his whole world gone, may ask for anything. Muchukunda bowed to the gods, and he asked for sleep.

Not the sleep of a night or a season. He asked to lie down in the earth and sleep without waking, undisturbed, until the proper time came round for him to wake. The gods granted it, and Muchukunda, son of Mandhata, the king who had guarded heaven, lay down in the cave and slept.

And he slept. The years turned to ages, and the ages turned to yugas. Kingdoms rose and fell; Mathura was besieged and delivered; kings came to his cave and were burned to ash at his feet. Through all of it Muchukunda lay in the dark, breathing slowly, dreaming of nothing, waiting for a time he had not been told about.

Now he was awake. He sat in the cave with the ashes of a king before him and a young man with a quiet face standing in the dark, and he understood, without being told, that the one who had woken him was not the one who had kicked him.

He opened his mouth to ask who the stranger was.
stories.reflection: Muchukunda chose sleep when he could have chosen anything — a king who had spent his strength guarding heaven asking only to rest until the world needed him again. The boon he took was patience itself, a waiting for the right time.
stories.next_story_tease: When Muchukunda finally opened his eyes, he found Krishna standing before him.
stories.hero_scene: Muchukunda lying down to sleep in the mouth of the mountain cave while the ages prepare to pass over him; behind him the gods of heaven fade into the light, and the dark of the cave swallows the sleeping king.

stories.title: Krishna Grants Muchukunda His Boon
stories.story:
Muchukunda woke slowly, the way a man surfaces from a sleep that has lasted for ages. The cave smelled of smoke and ash, and near its mouth lay a heap of ashes where something — or someone — had been burned away. He had slept through the turning of the world, but he knew enough of what he saw to know that the one who had pursued Krishna into this mountain was gone now, consumed, as it seemed, by his own wickedness.

What stood before him was a young man such as he had never seen: dark as a laden rain cloud, dressed in yellow silk, four-armed, glowing as though light came from within him, a garland of forest flowers looped across his chest, and a smile of pure affection on his face. Muchukunda pressed his palms together. The long watch he had kept for the gods against the asuras had worn his senses thin, but he could still ask the question that mattered. "Are you the fire that burns within all things?" he said. "I think you must be the best of the three who rule the worlds. I cannot even look at you steadily — your splendor is more than my eyes can bear."

The young man spoke, and his voice was easy, as if he were telling an old story. Through many births, he said, he had measured the dust of the earth and known the deeds of all three times. But let the king hear about today. For the relief of a world grown heavy with evil kings, Kalanemi had been slain, and Kamsa, and Pralamba, and the others who hated the good. "And for your sake," Krishna said, "I came into this cave. Ask me for a boon, best of kings — whatever you desire, I will give it."

A gift, offered freely. Muchukunda had once conquered the four directions and sat on a golden throne while lesser kings bowed before him. He had been young and drunk on kingship, and the years of that drunkenness had passed like a bad dream. He had seen what became of it all: the body that is praised as a king's is only a jar of clay, and at the end it is called worms and ashes and dust. "When a man is ready to leave the turning world," he said, "it is then that he meets the good. I count it your grace, Lord, that the kingdom fell away from me of its own accord, for I desire no boon but the service of your feet — the one gift even the poorest may ask. Blessings bind. They are woven of desire and fear and the dull pride of having, and they keep a man tethered to what fades. Give me none of them. Only take me as your refuge."

Krishna heard him out, and when he answered there was something like pleasure in his voice. "That you were not tempted by the boons I offered," he said, "know that to be your true wakefulness. Men who are not devoted may discipline their breath and their minds for years and still not reach me. Wander the earth as you please — only keep your mind resting in me. You lived by the warrior's law and slew creatures in the chase; that debt is settled. In your next birth, king, you will be born a brahmana, the friend of all beings, and you will attain me alone."

Muchukunda had asked for nothing, and so he had received everything there was to receive. He rose from the stone floor of the cave and went out into a world that looked new to him — a wanderer now, with nothing to carry but the one thing he had chosen. Behind him the ashes in the cave settled into stillness, and the long sleep of the king of the Ikshvakus was over at last.
stories.reflection: Muchukunda asks for nothing, and that refusal is the whole of his request. A man who once conquered the directions has learned that every earthly gain ends as ordure, worms, and ash, so the only boon he wants is to be released from wanting. Krishna names that refusal itself a kind of wakefulness: the king who slept for ages is, at last, fully awake.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as Muchukunda walked out into the light, the king of Magadha was marching on Mathura once more.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Elude Jarasandha
stories.story:
The king of Magadha had come against Mathura before, and every time he had been turned back. Jarasandha could not forgive it. He had sworn to take the city that sheltered the two brothers, and now he marched on it again with an army so vast that it covered the plain like a rising flood. This time, he told his generals, there would be no third campaign. This time the Yadus would learn what it cost to defy him.

And this time the two brothers did not wait to meet him. Krishna had already set the city's wealth moving — the herds and the treasure, carried away with the men he had chosen for the task. Then, with the enemy's vanguard in sight, he and Balarama abandoned whatever remained and ran. The two of them, who had faced every host the Magadha king could bring and never given ground, fled on foot as though terror had finally caught them. They did not look back. They did not slow down. They ran as men run when everything is lost.

The king of Magadha laughed out loud when he saw it. This was the pair who had broken his armies season after season; now they were running like startled deer, and their flight told him the long quarrel was ending at last. Jarasandha gave chase, and his soldiers chased with him, sure that the day of reckoning had come. The brothers ran until their breath burned and their legs would carry them no farther, and when they reached the great mountain that stood alone above the plain — Mt. Pravarshana — they climbed, exhausted, and hid themselves among its rocks and trees.

Jarasandha's men ringed the hill. They searched the slopes for footprints, for any trace of the two who had vanished into the scrub, and they found nothing at all. The king of Magadha did what besiegers do when the quarry will not come out: he set the mountain on fire. Flames raced up the grass and the dry brush, and the smoke rose in thick columns until the whole flank of Pravarshana burned like a torch. Let them burn with it, Jarasandha thought, and he turned his army toward home, already telling himself the story of how the Yadus had died on the hill.

But on the burning slope, Krishna and Balarama were not waiting for the fire to reach them. They sprang from the blazing hillside — eleven yojanas they leapt, so far that no eye could follow their landing — and came down beyond the ring of Jarasandha's soldiers, unseen, in the quiet darkness at the mountain's foot. While the smoke still climbed behind them, they made their way across the country and back to their sea-girt city, where the Yadus had made their home behind walls of water that guarded them better than any wall of stone.

Jarasandha returned to Magadha believing the brothers had burned in his fire. He told the story of how he had smoked the two Yadus out of Pravarshana and left them ashes, and he was satisfied. What he did not know — could not know — was that the whole pursuit had been shaped from the beginning: the flight that looked like fear, the hill that looked like a trap, the fire that looked like an ending. Krishna and Balarama had chosen to be thought dead, because a king who believes his enemy is gone will stop looking. And so the brothers walked the streets of Dwaraka, unharmed and unlooked for, while the king of Magadha celebrated a victory that had never happened.
stories.reflection: Jarasandha's laughter is the hinge of the episode: he believes he has won because he saw the brothers run, and Krishna lets him keep the belief. The whole escape is a lesson in how an enemy defeats himself — the fire, the ashes, the triumphant return home all belong to a story that was never true, while the brothers slip, unseen, toward a city the sea will guard better than any army.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata shows the brothers reaching their sea-girt city after eluding Jarasandha; the Harivamsha places the resolve to abandon Mathura and the founding of Dwaraka at this point in the story.
stories.next_story_tease: But in the fortress of Girivraja, twenty thousand captive kings were still waiting on their release.
