stories.title: The Captive Kings Appeal to Krishna
stories.story:
One morning in the assembly at Dwaraka, when brahmanas were seated at ease and the business of the court had quieted, a man was brought in whom no one had seen before. His appearance was extraordinary — he was not a merchant or a soldier or a king's man, and there was dust on his clothes that spoke of a long road and hard traveling. The guards let him pass because he asked, with a stranger's urgency, to see Krishna. He crossed the hall, bowed low before the Lord of Dwaraka, and pressed his palms together.

He had come, he said, from the kings of the earth. When Jarasandha of Magadha had set out to conquer the directions, he had demanded that every king bow to him. Those who submitted kept their thrones; those who refused were taken by force and shut away in his fortress at Girivraja, in the heart of Magadha. Twenty thousand kings, the man said, lay imprisoned there — kings who had once commanded armies of their own and now sat in darkness, waiting for something that no army could bring them.

Then he delivered their words, and the hall grew still. "This world," the captive kings said, "is a place where the strong cut short the hopes of the weak whenever it pleases them. We have learned it at last. The happiness of a king is only a dream that depends on others; we carried its burden in bodies that knew fear from dawn to dawn. Now, Lord, we have given all of that up. We take refuge in you from the terror of this world. Your feet remove the sorrow of those who bow down — free us from the bond of Magadha. Jarasandha holds us with the strength of ten thousand elephants and keeps us shut in his house like a lion penning sheep."

And they reminded Krishna who Jarasandha was. Eighteen times, they said, this king had been broken by Krishna in battle, with his discus raised, and still he swelled with pride; still he oppressed the people who looked to Krishna for protection. "You have come down into this world for the sake of the good and the restraint of the wicked," the kings said. "If a man may cross your command and nothing follows, then we do not know what this world is. Ordain an end to it, unconquered one."

The messenger fell silent. Twenty thousand kings — every throne between the seas, it seemed — had sent their plea in the mouth of one unknown man, and the plea lay now at Krishna's feet. The brahmanas looked at one another, and the courtiers looked at the floor, and no one spoke. The assembly waited for the Lord of Dwaraka to answer, and in the stillness of the hall, twenty thousand prisoners hung on a single word.
stories.reflection: The captive kings speak in the language of total dependence: rulers who once commanded armies now own nothing but their fear and their choice of refuge. Their appeal carries a quiet inversion — the strong, they say, decide who lives in this world, so the weak can only choose where to turn. That they turn to Krishna is itself a claim about where true strength lies.
stories.next_story_tease: Uddhava, however, would counsel that no army could break Jarasandha — only a single combat could.

stories.title: Uddhava's Counsel to Slay Jarasandha
stories.story:
Uddhava was the man Krishna trusted with his mind — a friend who could say things plainly, and he said them now in the quiet of Dwaraka. The Rajasuya, he began, was no common sacrifice. It was the imperial rite, and the scripture was clear about who might offer it: only a king who had conquered the circle of the directions, who had brought every quarter of the earth to bow before him. And there was one direction that had never bowed. Magadha stood across the path of every conqueror, and at the heart of Magadha stood Jarasandha, holding twenty thousand kings in his prison at Girivraja and calling himself lord of all the earth.

For Krishna, Uddhava said, this was one deed that served two ends. Bring Jarasandha down, and the directions would lie open for the sacrifice; bring him down, and the captive kings would go free. There was no need to choose between the rite and the rescue — they were the same road, and it led to the same gate.

But how? Jarasandha was no ordinary enemy, and Uddhava did not pretend otherwise. His strength, he reminded Krishna, was the strength of ten thousand elephants. Send a hundred armies against him — a hundred akṣauhiṇīs, the full war-machines of kings, with their chariots and elephants and foot-soldiers — and he would still not fall. His like could not be overwhelmed; he could only be met. He was the match of one man alone, and the one man who could match him was Bhima. In a duel of two chariots, on a field with no army to hide behind and no retreat to run to, Bhima could finish what no host on earth could finish. That was the only way: not war, but single combat, man against man, and the stronger man would walk away.

And here was the shape of it. Bhima would go to Girivraja in the dress of a brahmana, as though he were a mendicant come to ask alms of the great king. He would beg Jarasandha for a duel, the way a brahmana begs what he needs — and Jarasandha, who prided himself on his strength and had never in his life refused a challenge, would grant it. Let the two fight it out, chariot against chariot, while Krishna was there to see it done.

Uddhava's voice carried no heat. He was not proposing a gamble; he was reading a map. The slaying of Jarasandha, he said, would serve a great purpose — for the kings he held in prison, for the sacrifice that waited on a conquered world, for the peace of every kingdom between the seas. The women of those captive courts already sang of the day their enemy would fall and they would be set free; the gopis sang of it, and the daughter of Janaka, and the sages who had found their refuge in Krishna. All the world that looked to him was waiting on this one deed. The man who could not be broken by armies would be broken by the one thing he had never learned to fear: an equal.

Krishna listened, and the plan settled into place like a stone dropping into still water. Bhima would go in a brahmana's guise; Krishna and Arjuna would be there to see it through; and the long quarrel with Magadha would end where Jarasandha had made his strength a prison — on a field of single combat, with no one left to save him but himself.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's counsel is precise rather than clever: it matches the one man who can fight Jarasandha to the only kind of contest in which the king can fall. The advice also binds two aims into one deed — the rite demands a conquered world, and the conquest here is a rescue. Strategy, duty, and mercy turn out to be the same road.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata (2.20) attributes this plan to Krishna himself; in the Bhagavata it is Uddhava who counsels it. The two versions are kept separate here, as the attribution difference is material.
stories.next_story_tease: Soon, to the sound of drums and conches, Krishna would set out from Dwaraka for Indraprastha with a vast host at his back.

stories.title: The Road to Indraprastha
stories.subtitle: Krishna leaves Dwaraka with a vast procession for Yudhishthira's Rajasuya.
stories.story:
The morning Krishna left Dwaraka, the conches sounded before the sun cleared the sea. They began at the palace and were answered from the gates, and by the time the first light touched the city's white towers, every street knew that the lord of the Yadavas was going out on a journey — and that no one remembered a departure like it.

He had spoken of it the evening before, quietly, the way he did everything that mattered. Yudhishthira, the eldest of the Pandavas, was preparing the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice that would confirm his rule, and had sent for Krishna to come to Indraprastha. There was more in the invitation than ceremony. The sacrifice asked that every king of the land acknowledge Yudhishthira's eminence, and one king, Jarasandha of Magadha, would never bow — the same enemy Uddhava had named in council, the one who could only be met in single combat and who stood between them and the sacrifice. But that was for later. First came the road.

Krishna entrusted Dwaraka to Balarama, who would guard the city and its people while he was gone. Then he mounted his chariot, the one that flew the Garuda banner, and gave the word.

What followed was less a departure than the city turning itself inside out. The army came first — chariots by the hundred, horsemen, elephants in their ornaments, foot soldiers in ordered ranks, so many that the plain beyond the gates could not hold them. The drums began: mridangas, bheris, the deep anaka, with conches and the curved gomukha horns joining in, until the sound rolled back against the walls and out over the sea. Banners climbed the morning air, and the sun caught on weapons, armor, and the crests of the allied kings who had chosen to ride with Krishna.

Behind the army came the inner procession. The women of the palace followed in their palanquins — Krishna's queens, with their children and attendants — borne on gilded litters with silk curtains drawn against the dust, and after them the long trains of oxen, camels, mules, and she-elephants carrying the household's goods. The whole mass of it shone and moved and sounded, like an ocean stirred by great fish, and at its head rode one chariot with a Garuda banner, and in that chariot Krishna himself, calm as the eye of the storm.

Halfway down the road, the sage Narada met them. He was the tireless traveler of the gods, welcome everywhere, and when he came before the Yadu lord he bowed and paid his homage, and Krishna returned the honor with words that pleased him. Then Narada rose through the sky, carrying the sight of Krishna in his heart, and the procession went on.

Krishna had also sent a royal messenger ahead of him, to the kings whose lands the road would cross — a courtesy, and a signal too, so that no ruler along the way would mistake an army for an invasion. The messenger carried his word from court to court, and the kings made ready to receive their guest.

The land rolled past them: Anarta, where Dwaraka stood, then the dry country of Sauvira, the wastes of Maru, and Vinashana, where an old river was said to vanish into the earth. They crossed the Drishadvati and then the Sarasvati, rivers of the older stories, and everywhere they passed, towns emptied into the streets to watch — the local kings riding out to greet Krishna and ride a stretch of the way beside him, children running alongside the elephants, women watching from the rooftops.

It took many days. But the road was the easy part; what waited at its end was not. Indraprastha lay ahead, and the Rajasuya, and the question of Jarasandha — and Krishna was going there with the whole weight of his city at his back, to settle all of it.
stories.reflection: The scale of the procession is not vanity. A king does not travel so heavily when his journey carries other kingdoms' fates; Krishna leaves his own city guarded and goes as a guest to another king's sacrifice, and the grandeur of the march says plainly how much is at stake — a sacrifice that could crown Yudhishthira's rule, or open a war with Magadha.
stories.next_story_tease: But the sacrifice would wait; there was an older imprisonment in Magadha to break first.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna in his golden chariot beneath the Garuda banner at the head of an immense procession leaving Dwaraka's gates — elephants, chariots and horsemen behind him, the queens' palanquins following, banners and fly-whisks stirring in the sea wind while drums and conches sound against the city walls.

stories.title: A Son Crowned, the Kings Freed
stories.subtitle: After Jarasandha's fall, Krishna sets his son on the throne of Magadha and opens the prison.
stories.story:
The city of Girivraja was still settling after the fall of its king when Krishna did something the court had not expected. Jarasandha was dead — Bhima had slain him in single combat outside the city, after a duel long enough to shatter two great maces — and in the hush that followed, everyone waited to see what the victors would do with a conquered capital. Magadha had been the terror of kings for a generation: its armies had marched across the world and carried its enemies home in chains. Some braced for fire, or plunder, or a war carried into the houses of the defeated. What they got instead was a coronation.

Jarasandha's son was a young man named Sahadeva. He had not chosen his father's wars, had not dragged kings from their thrones, had not filled the dungeons beneath the city. Krishna called him forward before the assembled court and installed him as lord of the Magadhas — the house of Jarasandha set back on the seat its king had made terrible. The ministers and elders of Magadha, who had expected a reckoning, watched the crown come down on the head of the one man in the city whose hands were clean of all of it. A conquered capital does not often get its own line of kings back, and the court did not quite know what to make of the mercy.

But the crowning was only half of what Krishna had come to do. The other half lay underneath their feet.

For years Jarasandha had kept his prisoners in Girivraja: kings he had vanquished in battle and carried away from their own thrones — the Kshatriyas of many lands, men who had ruled their own courts and now sat in darkness. He had not held them for ransom. He had gathered them with the intent of offering them, one great day, as a sacrifice to Rudra, the kings of the world led up like animals to feed a god who had never asked for them.

Krishna went down to them himself, and the prison was opened. One by one the captive kings came out into a light they had not seen in years: blinking, leaning on one another, slow to trust that the doors were truly standing open and that no guard would drag them back. Some wept. Some knelt. There is no long account of that release — the old text gives it a single line — but release after that long a captivity was not a small thing. It was the undoing of Jarasandha's whole design: the kings of a hundred lands walking free out of the city that had swallowed them, no condition asked, no oath extracted, no price set on their freedom.

Girivraja that day saw both halves of a victory arranged side by side: a new king crowned in the hall above, and in the courtyard below, the old king's prisoners taking their first free steps. The kingdom of Magadha did not fall — it was handed back to its own people, with a son of their own line on the throne. It was the cruelty of the old reign that ended, not the kingdom itself.

And with the kings freed, the last obstacle on the road to the Rajasuya was gone. The captives who had been meant to die for a sacrifice would instead return to their own kingdoms, and when they reached their courts they carried a story with them: that the man who had conquered their lands had been answered at last, and that the man who had freed them had asked nothing for it but their freedom — and that on the day Magadha lost its terrible king, it found a gentler one.
stories.reflection: The crowning of Sahadeva is the quieter half of a victory. Bhima's duel ended Jarasandha, but it is Krishna who decides what comes after — a son restored to his father's throne and prisoners walking free. Justice that removes a king's cruelty without erasing his kingdom is the harder kind, and this story shows it being chosen on purpose.
stories.next_story_tease: But how Jarasandha came to that duel had not yet been told.

stories.title: Three Brahmanas at the King's Door
stories.subtitle: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna come to Girivraja in disguise to ask alms of Jarasandha.
stories.story:
Three brahmanas came to the gate of Girivraja at the hour of hospitality, when a householder's door was open to any guest, and asked to see the king. They wore the marks of their calling, carried themselves like men of peace, and asked only for alms — the oldest, simplest request a traveler can make. But the king they had come to see was Jarasandha, lord of Magadha, and the three brahmanas were not brahmanas at all.

They were Krishna, Bhima, and Arjuna. Jarasandha was the one king who stood between them and the Rajasuya, and they had already learned what every army in the world had learned: he could not be beaten in open battle. His strength and his hosts were too great for any force to carry his walls. But a duel — single combat, one man against one man — was a different matter, and it was for that that the three had set out, disguised as wandering brahmanas, on a plan Krishna had argued and Yudhishthira had finally accepted.

The road had been long. From the country of the Kurus they had crossed Kuru-jangala, passed the lake of lotuses and the hills of Kalakuta, forded the Gandaki and the Sarayu, walked through the eastern lands and past Mithila, and crossed the Ganges and the Sone before the hills of Goratha rose ahead of them. There, at last, they saw the city of Magadha standing on its height, filled with cattle and grain and water — the seat of the man they had come to meet.

At the hour of hospitality they presented themselves at his house, and Jarasandha received them as he received every suppliant. He was a king famed for his giving, the sort of generosity that becomes a story in its own right — a man of whom it was said he would part with anything a guest asked of him, even his own head. The three made their request in the proper form. Know that guests have come to you, they said, suppliants from far away. Grant us what we desire, and may it be well with you.

Jarasandha looked at them as they stood before him, and something in the looking changed. He was no fool. He studied their voices, their bearing, the marks on their forearms — the scars a bowstring leaves on a man who has spent his life drawing one. These were no brahmanas, he understood. These were royal men wearing a brahmana's guise.

He did not turn them away. Instead he thought of Bali, the great king who had given the earth itself to Vishnu when the god came to him as a dwarf brahmana asking for a step of ground, and who had lost his kingdom and kept his fame. A Kshatriya's life is brief, Jarasandha reflected; the body falls like a thing discarded. What is a king's life worth if it is not spent winning fame that outlives him — and what fame is greater than a gift given to brahmanas? He had heard how such men as Harishchandra and Rantideva, and even a hunter and a pigeon in the old tales, had won eternal honor with perishable bodies by giving.

So when he spoke, his answer was large. Ask, he told them. Choose whatever you desire, and I will give it — I would give you my very head.

The three brahmanas heard the words of the king of Magadha, and if any of them felt the weight of being offered everything by a man who did not know what they meant to ask, they did not show it. The boon had not yet been named. Jarasandha stood at his own door, generous as his fame promised, and waited to hear what three strangers who were no strangers would demand of him.
stories.reflection: The story gives Jarasandha his due: he recognizes the three men by voice and by the bowstring scars on their arms, and still offers them whatever they ask. His famous generosity is not a mask — it is the very quality the disguise relies on, and the tale lets him see through one deception while standing openly inside the other.
stories.next_story_tease: The masks would not stay on much longer.

stories.title: The Disguise Cast Off
stories.subtitle: Krishna names himself and his companions, and Jarasandha chooses his opponent.
stories.story:
Jarasandha's promise hung in the air of his own hall: ask, and it is yours — even my head. The three brahmanas had come a long way for those words, and now the moment had come to say what they had crossed half the world to ask. What they asked was not alms.

Give us battle, said Krishna. That is our request. If you think fit, let it be single combat, man to man — we are not suppliants for grain or gold. We are warriors, and we have come desiring war, and nothing else.

And because the time for masks was over, he went on and named them, one by one, in the king's own hall. This man is Bhima, Vrikodara, a son of Pandu — and this is his brother Arjuna. And know me: I am Krishna, their cousin, and your enemy.

It was a revelation delivered plainly, as if he were introducing guests at a feast, and it did what a revelation in such a place always does: it stripped the courtesy from the room. These were not three wandering brahmanas who had come to test a king's charity. They were the men who had crossed his lands, walked through his gate, and stood in his hall to tell him they had come to fight him. And Krishna did not soften it. You have brought the Kshatriyas of the world here as captives, he said — kings of every country your armies reached — and you keep them to offer in sacrifice to Rudra. The slaughter of human beings as an offering to the gods was never seen among the virtuous. Set those kings free, or go yourself to the abode of Yama.

Jarasandha threw back his head and laughed aloud. It was not a small laugh, and it was not kind. He answered that he could not recollect ever having wronged the three; that even searching his memory he found no injury done to them. A Kshatriya, he said, does not make a captive of a king who has not first been vanquished in fair war. Every man in his prison had been beaten in battle before he was chained — that was the law of his order, to bring others under sway by prowess and then hold them. And if he were to free them now because three men came to his door and asked, what would remain of the duty he had kept all his life? Then he turned on Krishna, and his words went for the throat.

I will not fight you, he said. You are a coward. When the pressure came, you abandoned your own city of Mathura and fled to the sea — you hid yourself in the salt water and called it a kingdom. Your valor fails you in the field; there is no honor in crossing blades with a man who ran from his own capital. You are not worth my mace.

But the other two he measured differently. Arjuna, he judged, would not be a fighter for him — not his match. Bhima, though: Bhima was his equal in years and his equal in strength. That was the one he wanted, the fight that would mean something. So the king of Magadha made his choice. He had a great mace brought and handed it to Bhima, and took a second mace for himself, and without another word he walked out of his hall and through his city gates, down to the level ground outside the walls where kings settled such accounts.

Bhima followed him. Behind them came Krishna and Arjuna, and behind them, gathering as word spread through the streets, the city of Girivraja itself — to see the strongest man in Magadha meet the man who had come for his prisoners, with nothing left between them but the duel.
stories.reflection: Jarasandha's taunt — that Krishna fled Mathura and hid by the sea — is the insult of a man who measures courage only by what he would do himself. Krishna does not answer it; he has already answered it by walking into Girivraja disguised, which is the kind of nerve that gets a man inside an enemy's gates without losing a single soldier.

stories.title: The Duel of Equal Champions
stories.story:
On the open ground outside Girivraja, two men faced each other with maces in their hands, and the dust between them might as well have been a battlefield. Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had ruled that city for years on a strength no one had ever matched. Bhima, the second of the Pandava brothers, had come there with Krishna and Arjuna, and when Krishna revealed who they were and demanded the duel that would settle an old feud, Jarasandha had looked the three of them over and chosen Bhima. It was the choice of a man who wants to break the strongest one first.

Now they stood facing each other, and for a long moment neither moved. Then both raised their great maces and closed in. The first blows were enough to have finished lesser men: the clubs came down with the full weight of both arms behind them, and the sound of their meeting rolled across the field like the clash of a thunderbolt, sharp and dry.

The two champions began to circle, moving in wide, intricate patterns, turning now left, now right, like wrestlers who had spent a lifetime reading each other's feet. Each watched for the instant the rhythm would break, the instant a shoulder would dip too far or a heel slide in the dust. Neither found it. Every step was answered, every rush met, every opening closed the moment it appeared.

Then the maces began to give way. Blow after blow, the great clubs of both men shattered under the force of the exchange, splintering like brittle twigs, until each champion was left holding a ruined staff in his hands.

Anger did the rest. Dropping what was left of their weapons, the two men fell on each other with their bare hands, striking with fists hard as iron. The blows landed on shoulders and chests and sides, and the sound of fist on flesh was harsh and rolling, like the crash of a thunderbolt over the plain. Neither man gave ground. Bhima's strength had never met its match; Jarasandha's had never met its equal. They were matched in skill, matched in strength, matched in the fire that drives a fighter, and every advantage one of them seized, the other answered before it could be pressed.

By the time the light began to slant over the city walls, the duel had still not been decided. Both champions stood breathing hard, bruised and battered, their ruined maces lying in the dust where they had dropped them. Neither had fallen, and neither would fall. Every blow had been answered, every feint read, every rush of strength met by a wall of equal strength.

And so the great duel of the two champions remained unfinished. Not for lack of fury, but because fury alone could not break the balance between them. Bhima looked across at his enemy and saw something like himself: the same pride, the same iron fists, the same refusal to fall. The fight could have gone on until the next dawn, and the one after that, and still neither man would have yielded.

Only one person on that field knew that the duel could not end this way. Krishna had not crossed the country to watch two equal champions wear each other down. He had come to end a threat, and he was watching with the patience of a man who already knows how the story must turn.
stories.reflection: The duel is left unfinished not because either man weakens but because they are exactly matched; Bhima's strength meets a strength like his own, and endurance alone cannot break the deadlock. Krishna watches, knowing that a fight this even can never be won by fighting.
stories.content_note: A sustained mace and fist duel; intense but described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna had not come to Girivraja to watch a duel that could never end; he knew the one secret that could finish it.

stories.title: The Twig That Ended a Duel
stories.story:
By the time the maces had shattered and the two champions had fallen to trading blows with their bare hands, everyone who watched understood the same thing: this duel had no end in it. Bhima and Jarasandha were too evenly matched. Skill for skill, strength for strength, fury for fury, neither could finish the other, and both were too proud to stop.

Krishna watched it all. He had not come to Girivraja to watch two champions wear each other down. He had come to end a threat, and he knew something no one else on that field knew: Jarasandha could never be killed by the ordinary means of war.

The secret lay in the king's birth. Jarasandha had been born in two halves, and the demoness Jara had joined the halves together; the joining was what gave him life, and it was the same joining that left him vulnerable. A body so put together could not be felled by any blow, however mighty. It could only be undone along the seam where it had been joined.

So instead of watching, Krishna acted. While the two champions circled each other in the dust, he bent down and picked up a twig from the ground. Then, in Bhima's sight, he snapped it in two, cleanly, and let the halves fall. It was a small gesture, the kind no one else would have marked. But Bhima's eyes caught it, and understanding broke over him like daylight.

He turned back to Jarasandha. The king of Magadha came at him with a rush, fists raised, expecting the same iron exchange as before. This time Bhima did not meet the rush head-on. He dropped low, caught Jarasandha by one leg, and pinned the other foot to the earth with his own. His arms closed around the great body like iron bands, one leg held fast, the other pressed down, and he heaved with all his strength.

It was not a blow, and that was the whole point. No blow could have done it. Bhima tore the joined king apart along the seam of his birth, from the leg and the thigh through the loins and the hip and the back, up to the shoulders, and the king of Magadha, who had seemed unkillable, was killed at last.

A great cry of lamentation rose up, a cry of horror and grief that rolled over the city like thunder: the lord of Magadha was dead. The cry spread from the field to the streets, and the earth of Girivraja seemed to settle under the news.

When it was over, Bhima stood over the body of the man he could not have beaten in a fair fight, and understood at last what Krishna had shown him with a broken twig. Some enemies are not defeated by the hardest blow a man can throw. They are defeated by being known truly.
stories.reflection: The duel of equal strength could never be won by strength; the king who seemed unkillable is undone not by a harder blow but by a secret known to one man. Krishna does not fight the battle himself. He sees the truth that ends it, and shows Bhima how to act on it.
stories.content_note: Jarasandha is killed by being torn in two; described with restraint, without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: Behind the mountain walls of Girivraja, twenty thousand eight hundred imprisoned kings heard the cry of lamentation and dared to hope.

stories.title: The Kings Emerge From the Mountain
stories.story:
For years the mountain at Girivraja had held more kings inside it than many kingdoms could count. Jarasandha, the king of Magadha, had not killed every ruler he conquered. Some he carried home and sealed inside a prison carved into the rock, where men who had once commanded armies and sat on thrones wasted away in the dark, forgotten by the world that had feared them.

Then Jarasandha fell in the duel, and Krishna opened the prison.

The men who came out were hardly recognizable as kings. Hunger had eaten the flesh from their bodies and dried the color from their faces, and long confinement had worn them thin, so that they walked out into the daylight like men who had forgotten what a crown feels like. Twenty thousand eight hundred of them. More kings than most of the world had ever seen gathered in one place. And every one of them stopped at the sight of the dark figure waiting outside the gate.

Krishna stood before them in his own form, and the sight of him was a kind of medicine. He was dark and four-armed, with the mark of Srivatsa curled on his chest, and his eyes were like the heart of a lotus in bloom. His lotus hands held the mace, the conch and the discus; a jewel blazed at his throat; a garland of wildflowers hung over his shoulders. The kings drank him in. They breathed him in through their noses, they reached for him with their arms, and the long weariness of their captivity dissolved in the joy of seeing him. Then, one after another, they bowed and pressed their heads to his feet.

When they spoke, they did not speak of revenge. "We do not resent the king of Magadha," they said. "A ruler swollen with the pride of power does not find what is good for him. Such men mistake a mirage for a pool of water and die of thirst staring at it. We were the same. Our fortunes blinded us, and we fought each other for conquest. See what has become of those fortunes now. You have shaken them away. What is a kingdom, after all, to this body that falls and suffers and ends? Teach us the way to your lotus feet, for that alone is worth having."

And with a single voice that rose from the dust of the prison yard, they praised him: Krishna, Vasudeva, Hari, the Supreme Self.

Krishna answered them. "It is well that you have resolved rightly, you who speak the truth. Haihaya fell, and Nahusha, and Vena, and Ravana, and Naraka. Pride undid them all. Know that this body and everything born of it come to an end. Return to your people and carry on their line, taking happiness and sorrow, birth and death as they come, indifferent to the body, content in yourselves, firm in your vows."

Then he turned to Sahadeva and had the kings attended to. They were bathed and fed fine food and dressed in fresh garments and ornaments. Mukunda himself honored them, and the kings stood before him clean and adorned, their dull eyes bright again. Chariots were brought, yoked with good horses and decked with jewels and gold, and onto those chariots the kings were lifted.

So the twenty thousand eight hundred kings were freed at last from their long hardship by Krishna, and they rode home through the country that had forgotten them. And when they reached their people, they told them everything: the years of darkness in the mountain, the duel outside the gates, and the dark four-armed figure who had stood waiting for them in the light.
stories.reflection: The kings' first words are not curses on Jarasandha but confessions of their own pride; captivity has taught them what their crowns could not. Krishna sends them home not as subjects but as kings again, and what they carry back is not wealth but a story.
stories.next_story_tease: Soon after, with enemies pressing on Mathura, Krishna would begin looking for a new home for his people.

stories.title: Krishna Chooses the Site of Dwaraka
stories.story:
Krishna called the Yadus together in the assembly at Mathura and told them what most of them had been unwilling to say out loud: the city of their birth could not hold them much longer.

"This city is the home of the Yadus," he said. "We were born here and brought up in Vraja. Our griefs have ended and our enemies have been defeated. But our hostilities with the kings have begun, and our battle with Jarasandha has commenced. Our army and our animals are beyond counting, and we have jewels and friends in plenty. Yet Mathura is limited, and an enemy can enter it too easily. If a crore of princes and soldiers live crowded together here, dissension will find its way among them. It is time we laid out a city elsewhere."

The Yadavas heard him out and answered with one delighted voice. "Krishna," they said, "do what you think proper for us all."

When the elders of the Vrishnis consulted among themselves, they spoke of the danger openly. Jarasandha, they said, was destined to be unslayable by them, and his power was very great. Many armies of many kings had been destroyed at Mathura, and still his soldiers were so many that the Yadus could not hope to destroy them even in a hundred years. And then word came that made the decision for them: Jarasandha was marching on Mathura with Kalayavana at his side and a great, irrepressible army behind him.

The Yadus resolved to retreat. Krishna rose in the assembly and said: "Today is an auspicious day. We leave Mathura this very day, with our army and our followers."

They left the city in a flood of gold and dust, headed by Vasudeva, with wives in the chariots and elephants swaying under their burdens, the noise of the column rolling out like the waves of the ocean. They carried their wealth, their kinsmen and their friends; golden chariots, infuriated elephants, horses trotting with gold on their harnesses. They set out toward the west, Vasudeva and the elders guiding the army from the front, and they marched until the ocean rose on the horizon.

The shore they reached was beautiful enough to feel like a reward. It was variegated with creepers, rich in coconut trees, covered with ketaki and palmyras and climbing vines, and the Yadavas looked around them as if they had stepped into a celestial region.

But Krishna had not come there merely to camp. He walked the shore searching for the place where a city could stand, and he found an extensive tract of land on the bank of the ocean. Its soil was coppery and mixed with gravel, well suited for beasts of burden, and it carried every favorable mark a city could want, as if the Goddess of Prosperity herself had chosen to preside over it. The sea breeze fanned it and the ocean watered it. And near it, shining like Mount Mandara, rose the charming mountain Raivata, its slopes rich with gems, a place great men had long resorted to. There the sage Drona had lived for many years, and there the king Ekalavya had dwelt; and on its flank lay a level sporting ground, laid out square like a board of dice, that men called by the name of Dwaravati.

Krishna chose that site for his city. The Yadavas, who had wanted nothing more than to encamp their soldiers there, pitched their tents for the night, and the shore filled with the smoke and voices of a people making themselves at home.

That night Krishna walked among the tents without a trace of anxiety. He thought of the city that would rise on that coppery ground, of the houses that would line its streets and the names he would give them, one by one.

And so the Yadavas secured Dwaravati, and lived there happily with their friends, the way the gods live in their own city: a city still to be built, but already a home.
stories.reflection: Krishna chooses the new city the way a gardener chooses ground, reading the soil, the breeze and the mountain. But he does not seize the land as a conqueror; he puts the proposal to the Yadus first, and the city is founded on their consent as much as on his vision.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana places the founding of Dwaraka after the slaying of Jarasandha. This Harivamsha account, followed here, tells the move differently: the Yadus leave Mathura because Jarasandha and Kalayavana are advancing on the city.
stories.next_story_tease: The tents were barely pitched before Krishna set about making the new city worthy of the name Dwaravati.

stories.title: Krishna Enriches Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: Wealth rains on every house, and the gods' own assembly hall is brought down from heaven.
stories.story:
The city was rising from the shore of the western sea, but the people raising it had almost nothing of their own.

Krishna had brought the Yadavas to this coast after years of wandering and enmity, and now the walls were going up on the coppery tract near Mount Raivata. He had risen with the sun, performed his morning ablutions at the forest's edge, and surveyed the ground himself before a stone was laid. On an auspicious day under the star Rohini he had offered presents to the brahmanas and asked their blessings, and then the work had begun: courtyards and promenades, well-levelled roads and inner apartments, the four gates with their names — Shudraksha, Aindra, Bhallata, Pushpadantaka — and temples for Brahma, for the god of sacrifices, for Indra, and for the presiding deities of fire and water. When the ocean would not yield enough room, Krishna had asked it to withdraw twelve yojanas, and the sea had obeyed, so that the city could spread itself along the shore.

Even the celestial architect had come down to help, and the city was taking shape as something that could be spoken of beside Amaravati itself. Krishna had set the old king Ugrasena at its head. "Take Ugrasena before you," he told the Yadavas, "and enjoy this place without anxiety, like the celestials."

But as he watched the city rise, Krishna's thought kept returning to his people. They were building themselves a home out of nothing, and they were poor. The verses put it plainly: he felt a desire to gratify his own people, who were poor, with profuse riches.

He acted without delay. He summoned Sankha, the guardian of treasure, and gave him a single command: shower heaps of wealth into every house of Dwaraka. Not a treasury at the centre, not a storehouse behind guarded walls — every house. Sankha obeyed, and wealth came down on the new city like rain, filling courtyards and granaries, until no household in Dwaraka stood empty-handed.

Then Krishna's thought turned higher. The kings of heaven held their councils in a great assembly hall called Sudharma, and no city on earth had anything to match it. The Yadavas, who had so lately been wanderers, had no place of their own where the whole clan could gather to take counsel. So Krishna sent the wind itself on the errand: Vayu, the god of the air, was to go to the celestial region, beg the assembly hall Sudharma of those who kept it, and bring it to Dwaraka.

The wind went, and the wind returned, and the hall of the gods came to rest above the city of the Yadavas. From that day, when the elders of the Yadu race gathered to decide their affairs, they met in a hall that had once held the deliberations of heaven.

The city on the sea had begun as a refuge; it was becoming a capital. Wealth lay in every house, the gods' own assembly hall stood among the people, and the clan that had arrived at the shore with little more than its courage could now be spoken of in the same breath as the cities of the celestials. Krishna had asked for the city to be a place where his people could live without fear, and what he had fetched from heaven was not a throne for himself but a hall — a place where the whole community could sit together and decide its own affairs.

So Dwaraka grew rich in a single season, and the wealth did not gather at one door. It lay scattered through every household, like seed sown where the city meant to stand for a long time.
stories.reflection: Krishna's first concern in his new city is not the height of his own walls but the emptiness of his people's hands, and so the wealth is not hoarded at the centre but showered into every house. The one treasure he fetches from heaven is not a throne but an assembly hall — as if a people who had lived as wanderers were being told they would now deliberate like gods.
stories.next_story_tease: But Indra had not finished with Dwaraka — he sent the celestial architect to make the beautiful city more exquisite still.
stories.hero_scene: Heaps of gold and gems raining down into the courtyards of the newly built Dwaraka while Krishna watches from the ramparts, and far off over the sea the wind-god Vayu descending out of heaven carrying the celestial assembly hall Sudharma in his wake.

stories.title: Vishwakarma Adorns Dwaraka for Krishna
stories.subtitle: At Indra's bidding, the celestial architect remakes the city in the image of Amaravati.
stories.story:
He came back to his city on Garuda's back, and even from the air Dwaraka looked like a place from the other world — sporting-houses and gardens, turrets and courtyards spread across the ground the sea had surrendered, the whole city filled with echoes on every side. And Krishna had not yet seen it at its best, because the king of heaven had plans for his city.

When Indra learned that Krishna had returned to Dwaraka, he sent for Vishwakarma, the architect of the gods. "If you wish to do what pleases me," Indra said, "make Krishna's beautiful city more exquisite, for his sake. Encircle it with hundreds of gardens and build Dwaraka after the city of the celestials. Adorn it with all the gems you will find in the three worlds — for Krishna, who rises up for all the works of the gods, is forever plunging into the dreadful ocean of war. His home should shine like his deeds."

Vishwakarma went to Dwaraka and did as he was asked, and when his work was done the city had been remade in the image of Amaravati.

Krishna entered, and the verses keep turning over what he saw, as though even they could not take it all in at once. The city stood ringed by ditches full of lotus-stalks, like the Ganges and the Sindhu, with swans sporting on the water. The walls that ran along the rooftops were of gold, so that the city looked the way the sky looks when it is covered with gold-hued clouds. On the east shone a gate of gold and jewels, and beyond it the hill Raivataka with its charming table-lands and caves; to the south the bushes were draped in creepers of five colours, to the west in creepers the colour of a rainbow, while the yellow mountain Venuman stood guard in the north, like Mandara among mountains.

Forests crowded around the city on every side — Chitrak, Panchavarna, Panchajanya, Sarvartuka, and the great woods of Bhargava and Pushpaka, huge as Mount Meru, their creepers running down to the very roots of the trees, with ashoka and mandara flowering among them. And the sacred river Mandakini, bright with lotus leaves and gems, came down and entered Dwaraka with fifty mouths, gladdening every inhabitant.

Within the walls, eight thousand cars stood hung with nets of bells and flying banners. The city measured eight yojanas in length and twelve across, with double that number of colonies, eight great highways and sixteen crossings, and seven high roads that Vishwakarma had laid out for the movement of soldiers — a city so well made, the verses say, that even the women could easily defend it. The palaces of the Yadavas rose with golden and jewelled stairs; their turrets carried flags, their domes were of gold, and their tops, covered with golden flowers and colours of five kinds, imitated the beauty of mountains with charming summits and caves. They shone like forest-fire and filled the sky with an effulgence like the sun's and the moon's, and the whole city, with its cloud-like houses, stood under the sky like a heaven filled with variegated clouds.

And there, at the heart of the splendour, Vishwakarma built the house of Krishna himself — four yojanas long and four broad, adorned with palaces and false mountains — and beside it a golden palace of surpassing beauty, the most beautiful of all, which he built for Rukmini.

Everything the architect did at Dwaraka he did under the orders of the king of heaven. And Krishna, beholding the palaces of his people and the city the gods had adorned for him, was highly pleased, and having accomplished all that he had set out to do, entered it.
stories.reflection: What is striking is that Dwaraka's beauty is not Krishna's boast but Indra's gift — the king of heaven sends his own architect to adorn the city of a mortal king, as though heaven itself could not bear that Krishna's home should lag behind its own. The verses catalogue the splendour almost breathlessly, and among all the golden houses the one they pause on is Rukmini's.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells of Vishwakarma and Dwaraka more than once; in this passage he comes at Indra's request to beautify a city that already stands.
stories.next_story_tease: And the celestial architect was not done with Dwaraka yet.

stories.title: Vishvakarma Builds Dwaraka for Krishna
stories.story:
Mathura could not hold forever. That was the arithmetic Krishna carried with him as he looked out from its walls, and it was not the fear of a soldier but the calculation of a ruler.

A foreign king named Kalayavana had marched on Mathura with an enormous army of foreign soldiers, numberless as the dust, and now ringed the city, its soldiers stretched to every horizon. Krishna knew that if he stayed to fight, a second enemy would fall on them from behind — Jarasandha, whose armies would arrive the moment the battle began. Two wars at once, and Mathura's people would pay the price. A ruler who loved his people could not spend them so cheaply. There was no shame in retreat, if retreat saved the people for whom a king exists at all.

So Krishna made a different kind of choice. He would not meet two armies with one. He would move his people to a place no army could easily follow. He chose a site in the sea and asked the ocean to withdraw its waters over a stretch twelve yojanas wide, and the ocean gave way, leaving the seabed bare for the work to come.

On an auspicious day, chosen under a favorable star, he made offerings to the brahmanas and had them perform the rites of blessing, and then he set the work in motion. He summoned Vishvakarma, the divine architect, in his mind, and the architect came to him there by the water, ready to build. By his art the city rose from the water — Dwaraka, a fortress in the sea, twelve yojanas wide, with high ramparts, turrets of silver and gold, and gardens of celestial trees and vines, and courtyards laid out with a craftsman's care. It was a city so skillfully made it seemed the work of a god, because it was. Every wall showed the divine architect's craft; nothing in it was ordinary, and nothing was wasted. Indra, king of the gods, sent the Sudharma assembly hall and the Parijata tree; Varuna, lord of the waters, sent swift white horses. So the new city was furnished with the best of heaven and of the deep.

Then, by his mystic power, Krishna conveyed all the people there — the whole of the Yadava clan, with their families and their goods — from Mathura to the new city by the sea. In a single day the city was full of life, and Mathura stood behind them, quiet at last. They had left their old home not in flight but in good order, and they took up the new one in the same spirit.

Krishna had planned it as carefully as any battle. He told the Yadavas that the site he had chosen was like the very abode of the gods, and that the city would be known by the name of Dwaravati, as Indra's city is known as Amaravati. He laid out the courtyards and the promenades and the well-levelled roads, and he gave each family land for a house. Nothing was left to chance; a city, like a battle, is won in the planning. Temples were raised for the gods in their proper places, and four great gates opened onto the sea and the land, and the Yadavas marked out their plots with ropes and measured their streets, until the fort began to look like a home. The people took up their measuring ropes and their rites. What Krishna built was not merely a wall. It was a place where his people could live without looking over their shoulders — and it would shelter them for years to come, through every storm that gathered against them.
stories.reflection: Krishna's choice is a statesman's, not a warrior's. Faced with two enemies at once, he does not seek the glory of a great battle; he withdraws his people to a fortress in the sea and asks the divine architect to raise a city. Protection, the story suggests, can be built as surely as it can be won.
stories.hero_scene: The sea-fortress of Dwaraka rising from the withdrawn waters — golden domes and high ramparts gleaming above the sea — while Krishna looks on from the shore as the divine architect Vishvakarma raises the city into being.

stories.title: News of Rukmini's Swayamvara
stories.subtitle: Spies bring word from Kundina, and Krishna sets out with the Yadava host.
stories.story:
The spies came to the house of Balarama and found there what they had hoped to find: all the leading Yadavas, gathered in assembly at Krishna's word, in a house that stood like the home of a patriarch. They had come to sow the topic of future events, and they found the whole clan ready to hear them.

What they carried was news that would set the kings of the earth in motion. At the call of the king of the Bhoja line, a great meeting of kings was to be held at the city of Kundina, and rulers from every province were already hurrying there. The word passing from mouth to mouth was this: Rukmini, the sister of Rukmi, would hold her swayamvara. Adorned with golden ornaments, the fairest woman in the three worlds, she would choose a husband on the third day from that day.

The emissaries did not spare the Yadavas the scale of the gathering, and their words carried an edge of prophecy: this meeting of kings, they announced, would be the future destruction of those same kings. The rulers were coming on elephants, horses and cars, elated with pride like lions and tigers, bent on injuring one another, gifted with the gait of infuriated elephants, fond of battle and highly powerful. The plain before Kundina would soon hold hundreds of their encampments, and the kings who feared the Yadavas would sit there in safety like immortals in the land of the celestials, under the protection of numbers.

"The kings of all the earth are assembling," they said. "Why should we remain depressed alone? Let us all, encircled by our armies, set out for victory."

The verses say the words struck Krishna like a dart to the heart. He did not deliberate long. He set out immediately at the head of his army, and the Yadavas of fierce prowess mounted their cars and followed him like the gods in their pride. Krishna shone at the head of that host, his discus and mace uplifted, he whom even Ishana held dear; and the car-warriors behind him made his beauty greater still, a stream of cars effulgent like the sun and echoing with the tinkling of bells.

But before he left, he stopped to give counsel to Ugrasena, the king. "Wait here with my brother," he said. "When this city is emptied by our departure, those kings of deceitful conduct who fear us but enjoy themselves in Kundina may attack it at Jarasandha's desire. The city must not be left unguarded."

Hearing this, the old king replied in words that trembled with affection. "O Krishna, if you go and leave us behind, we shall not be able to live here happily, or anywhere else — like a woman without her husband. Under the shelter of your arms we do not fear even Indra and the gods, much less the kings of the earth. We shall follow you wherever you go for the sake of victory."

And Krishna, hearing the king's words, smiled. "I should do whatever you wish," he said. "There is no doubt about it."

So the departure became a shared journey — the old king refusing to be left behind, and Krishna, who had begun by guarding the city, yielding to the affection of his people. The army moved out of Mathura, car after car falling into line with banners streaming until the whole might of the Yadava clan was on the road behind him, and the way to Kundina lay open before them, where the fairest woman in the three worlds was waiting to choose.
stories.reflection: The verses say the news struck Krishna like a dart to the heart, and they do not explain why — the restraint is part of the art, as though something more than politics had been touched. The scene is doubled by Ugrasena's refusal to be left behind: the old king's devotion answers Krishna's care for the city, and a planned departure becomes a journey they take together.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna reached Kundina as the sun was turning red, and the assembled kings saw who had come.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna setting out from Mathura at the head of the Yadava host, discus and mace uplifted, the army streaming behind him in sun-bright cars, while the aged king Ugrasena follows — refusing to be left behind.

stories.title: Krishna Summons Garuda at Bhishmaka's House
stories.subtitle: The king of birds appears at a thought, and the assembled kings learn who has come to the swayamvara.
stories.story:
Krishna reached Bhishmaka's house at the hour when the sun, low in the west, turned the colour of heated iron. He had come to see the swayamvara, and what he saw first was the gathering itself: the spacious arena crowded with camps, the tents of a hundred kings filling the plain before Kundina, the smoke of their fires rising into the evening air.

For a moment he was moved by what the verses candidly call a rajasika inclination — a restless stirring of pride, the desire to make the assembled kings understand who had arrived. It was not a sinful impulse, the text is careful to say; it was the wish to display his own prowess. And Krishna had a way of displaying prowess that no king in that arena could match.

He thought of Garuda.

Not a messenger, not a summons — a thought was enough. As soon as Vinata's son was in his mind, the king of birds took a form that could be seen easily and came to Krishna. He came with the strokes of his wings, wings that could agitate even the wind itself, and every man gathered there — kings, warriors, servants, all of them — trembled, bent over, and fell to the earth, writhing like serpents deprived of the power to rise.

Krishna alone stood firm, like a mountain. He knew, before he saw, that the king of birds had arrived. Then he saw him: Garuda, adorned with celestial garlands and unguents, shaking the earth with the flapping of his wings; golden-feathered, bright as a mountain made of minerals; the weapons on his back lying with their faces downward like licking serpents seeking the touch of Vishnu's hand; black serpents dragged in his talons as he came. This was the bird who had brought ambrosia for Krishna, the destroyer of serpents and the terror of the Daityas, whose emblem stood on the flagstaff above Krishna's car — and now he stood before his lord, like a god bringing a gift.

Krishna welcomed him with pleasure. "O foremost of birds, you are welcome," he said. "We are going to the swayamvara at the house of Kaishika — come with us. Hundreds of powerful kings have gathered there with their elephants, horses and cars. We shall behold those high-souled ones."

So the car set out again, with Garuda beside it and the mighty car-warriors of the Yadavas following, and when they reached the city of Vidarbha, all the kings who had come for the swayamvara were filled with delight at the sight of them. Holding all manner of weapons though they were, they hurried to make arrangements for Krishna's quarters, as though the terror of the king of birds had already passed and left only wonder behind.

Bhishmaka himself rose from among the kings and came to welcome him. The king, well read in the moral laws, brought water to wash Krishna's feet and rinse his mouth, offered the ritual arghya, and placed him in his own city. And as Shankara is said to enter the hill Kailasa, Krishna entered with his army the house that had been kept ready for him from before. He was honoured there with edibles and drinks, with jewels and affection, and Vasava's younger brother Krishna lived happily in the house of Bhishmaka.

The kings who had fallen before the king of birds — the same kings who now pressed forward, delighted, to make room for Krishna — had been shown, without a single word of threat, what stood beside him. The swayamvara had not yet begun, and already the assembly knew who had come to it.
stories.reflection: The verses are candid that this is display — a rajasika impulse, pride without sin. Krishna arrives at the swayamvara and announces himself with the king of birds, so that every king in the arena understands, before a word is spoken, who has come. And the scene ends in the quietest possible key: Bhishmaka washing Krishna's feet and honouring him, and Krishna at rest in the house prepared for him.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha names Rukmini's father both Bhishmaka and Kaishika; this retelling follows the title of the episode and uses Bhishmaka throughout.
stories.next_story_tease: But in Bhishmaka's house, Rukmini had her own counsel to give Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: Garuda appearing before Krishna among the encamped kings of the swayamvara — wings shaking the earth, golden feathers bright as a mountain of minerals, black serpents dragged in his talons — while warriors lie fallen and trembling on the ground and Krishna alone stands firm like a mountain.

stories.title: A Swayamvara That Was Never Meant to Be
stories.story:
The king of Kundina had agreed to a swayamvara he did not want. Bhishmaka had let his son Rukmi send out the invitations — every throne in the land summoned to choose a husband for the princess Rukmini — and now the kings were arriving by every road: chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry pouring into the city until the streets seemed to dance with armed men. And the more the kings assembled, the more Bhishmaka felt the whole affair slipping out of his hands.

He had come to Krishna with his trouble, seeking him out as a man seeks the one person who might set a disaster right. "My son, out of his childish nature, wishes to give away his sister in a swayamvara," he said. "I do not like it. I wish my daughter to choose the one person she sees and no other. Forgive my son's bad conduct, O Lord; be propitiated."

Krishna's answer was not gentle. "If your son is this arrogant while still a boy, how arrogant will he be when he grows old?" he said. "A king who speaks a falsehood, even before a single king, consumes himself with the fire of Yama's tortures. Truthfulness is the foremost religious duty of kings; Brahma himself pointed it out in the days of yore. So how can your son now utter a lie before all these kings assembled in your city?" And then his voice sharpened further. "You say you know nothing of this great gathering — yet kings like the sun and moon sit at your tables, and cars, elephants, horses, and infantry have made a wild dance through Kundina. How can you not know of your son's work? Perhaps you thought my arrival was not conducive to your well-being, and so you offered no hospitality to one you deemed unworthy. Manu and the law-givers have ordained that he who puts obstacles in the way of a maiden wastes himself in hell. That is why I did not enter your assembly hall, nor accept your welcome. Kaishika, ever fond of guests, gave rest to my followers; and I, with Garuda beside me, live here as in the city of the gods."

Bhishmaka bowed low under the force of those words. "Be propitiated, O Lord of the celestial region," he said. "Forgive me, lord of the land of mortals. I am possessed by the darkness of ignorance; give me eyes of wisdom. We are men of perverse understanding with fleshy eyes. But now we have obtained you, who are the God of gods. Having obtained your shelter, I entertain no fear."

Then Krishna softened, and what he said next changed everything. "O king, the goddess-like form of Rukmini has brought me to this place," he said. "I will not tell you to give her to me and to no one else. But listen to what the gods decreed long ago. When they assembled on the summit of Mount Sumeru, in the days of yore, they said to her: 'Go with your husband to the world of men. Having been born in the house of Bhishmaka in the city of Kundina, be united with Keshava.' I tell you this plainly, king; do whatever you think proper after due consideration."

"But know this," he went on. "Truly, your daughter Rukmini is not a woman. She is the goddess Lakshmi herself, born among mortals at the words of Brahma. She must not be given away in a swayamvara where all the kings will be assembled. Invite one bridegroom, and confer her on him with proper rites — that is a Kshatriya's duty. You cannot give Lakshmi away in a swayamvara." He paused, and when he spoke again there was something almost like a smile in his voice. "To put impediments in the way of that swayamvara, Garuda, son of Vinata, has been sent here by the king of the gods. And I too have come — to witness the festival of the kings, and to see your daughter, the beautiful lotus among women."

Bhishmaka heard it all in silence: that his daughter was not his to give at all, that the gods had decided her fate on a mountain before she was born, that the ceremony his son had announced across the land could never bind her. He had come to Krishna fearing a disaster; he left knowing that what he had feared was the will of the gods themselves.
stories.reflection: The revelation reframes the entire swayamvara: Rukmini is not a prize to be contested but a goddess whose destiny was fixed before her birth, and so no assembly of kings can undo it. Krishna's sternness with Bhishmaka — about falsehood, hospitality, and the law — clears the ground for the gentle truth he then delivers.
stories.next_story_tease: Before he left Kundina, Krishna would show Bhishmaka what he truly was.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, facing King Bhishmaka in the quiet of Kundina, one hand raised as he speaks the revelation — that Rukmini is the goddess Lakshmi, born to be united with Keshava — while Garuda waits behind him in the fading light.

stories.title: A Farewell of a Thousand Arms
stories.story:
The conversation was over, and Krishna rose to take his leave. He had told King Bhishmaka what the gods had decreed on the summit of Mount Sumeru — that Rukmini was Lakshmi herself, born into the house of Kundina to be united with Keshava — and the king had bowed and asked only for wisdom. It was time to go. The kings who had come for the swayamvara were stirring in the city, and Krishna had a journey before him.

But as he stood to go, something happened that Bhishmaka would carry with him for the rest of his life.

The man who had stood before him and spoken of his daughter was suddenly not a man at all.

Bhishmaka looked, and the form before him was vast and quiet and older than the world: the prime and self-sprung Krishna, the one who existed before every beginning, with eyes like red lotuses. He had a thousand feet. A thousand eyes. A thousand arms. The shape of a man, and inside that shape, the shape of everything — every direction at once, every being that breathed, every star the sky had ever held. The king of Kundina stood in the presence of the universe wearing a human face, and he understood, in one blinding instant, who had been sitting in his house and asking for nothing.

Bhishmaka did not speak of his daughter then. He did not speak of the swayamvara, or of his son, or of the kings outside the walls. All of that fell away from him like dust. He bowed low — lower than he had ever bowed to any king, lower than he had bowed even a moment ago when he had begged for forgiveness — and he began to praise.

He praised the glory that stood before him: the self-sprung one, who had no beginning and no cause, who had made himself known in the house of a mortal king. He praised him as the first of all beings, the source from which everything else flowed, the one who was already there before the first dawn and would remain after the last one. The words came out of him slowly at first, then faster, as if the vision had unlocked something in his chest that had been waiting all his life to be spoken. He had thought he was entertaining a guest, a young prince from Mathura who spoke well and carried himself like a king. Now he knew he had been sheltering the Lord of all that exists, and his praise rose and broke over that knowledge like a wave.

And then it was over.

Krishna stood before him again as he had stood before — a young man, gracious, ready to leave. The thousand arms were one pair of arms. The thousand eyes were two. The vision had not been taken away so much as folded back up, the way a vast sky folds into a single point at nightfall.

Bhishmaka straightened slowly, and said nothing. There was nothing left to say. He had been shown what his daughter was, and now he had been shown what her destined husband was, and the two truths together had rearranged his entire world. His son had wanted a grand swayamvara; the gods had wanted something else entirely; and the king, who had spent days anxious and afraid, found that he was no longer afraid of anything.

Outside the palace, the assembled kings were waiting. As Krishna came out of Bhishmaka's presence, they rose and followed him — the kings of the earth, who had come to Kundina to compete for a bride, now following the young man who had claimed her as if drawn by something they could not name. They did not know what Bhishmaka had seen. But they had seen Krishna, and even that was enough to move them.

Bhishmaka watched them go from the doorway of his palace, and what he had seen stayed with him: the self-sprung one, the thousand arms, the red-lotus eyes that held the whole of creation. A king does not forget the day the universe visited his house.
stories.reflection: The cosmic form appears not as a spectacle for a crowd but as a private revelation to one anxious father — the divine answering Bhishmaka's plea for 'eyes of wisdom' by literally showing him what he could not otherwise see. That the vision is followed by Krishna quietly returning to human shape suggests the form is a gift of sight, not a display.
stories.next_story_tease: Once the kings had gone, the swayamvara's true decision passed to Rukmini herself.
stories.hero_scene: Bhishmaka on his knees before Krishna, who stands revealed in his universal form — a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, eyes like red lotuses — filling the dim hall of Kundina with light while the mortal shape he wore moments ago seems to hang over him like a garment.

stories.title: The Choice Rukmini Made in Secret
stories.story:
After Krishna left Kundina, the kings who had come for the swayamvara gathered one last time in Bhishmaka's assembly hall, anxious to be on the road to their own kingdoms. Bhishmaka, foremost of kings and well-read in the moral laws, stood before them and asked their forgiveness. "You all know the calamity that has befallen this swayamvara," he said. "Forgive me for the fruit that has grown out of my misconduct."

He honored them, welcomed them, and sent them on their way — the monarchs of central India, and the kings of the east, the west, and the north. Those kings, mighty car-warriors, returned his honors gladly and rode off delighted, glad to leave a ceremony that had come to nothing. A few remained behind with Bhishmaka — Jarasandha among them, and Sunitha, and Dantavakra, and the king of Soubha, and others of the Deccan, lingering as if they sensed that the mystery of Kundina was not yet finished.

But the true decision of that swayamvara was not being made in the assembly hall at all. It was being made in the women's quarters, where the princess at the center of everything had heard what the kings had not.

Rukmini had never set eyes on Krishna; she knew him only through the reports of his beauty and virtues that had reached Kundina, and her heart had already answered them. Everything her brother Rukmi had planned — the invitations, the gathering of kings, the grand ceremony where she would walk in and choose — had been built on the idea that she was a prize to be won, a question to be answered by the world. Standing in the shadow of that enormous plan was a girl who had already answered the question herself, and who had answered it the way her father's heart had, and the way the gods had: with Krishna.

Now she approached her friends, her face bent down in shame — not the shame of wrongdoing, but the burning shyness of a girl confessing a feeling too large to keep inside. The chaste and wise Rukmini, whom the kings of the earth had come to court, stood among the women who had grown up beside her and spoke the plainest words she had ever spoken.

"I tell you truly," she said, "I do not wish to be the spouse of anyone else save Krishna, who has lotus eyes."

That was all. She did not argue, did not explain, did not defend. She had seen the one man in the world, and every other suitor who had ridden into Kundina for her sake had become, in a single moment, impossible. Her friends heard the quiet certainty in her voice and knew there was nothing to say against it — that the princess who had drawn half the kings of the earth would stand before none of them and place a garland on his neck, because her choice was made, and it was made in the only way such choices can ever truly be made: by herself, in secret, with no ceremony to help her.

The swayamvara her brother had announced across the land would still be held, or would not; the kings would still come, or would not; none of it mattered now. What mattered was that Rukmini had chosen, and the one she had chosen was Krishna. Whatever happened in the assembly hall, whatever her brother arranged and whatever the kings demanded, the bride had already decided — and a bride's decision, made like this, is the one thing no assembly on earth can overrule.

In the quiet of the women's quarters, with the evening settling over Kundina and her friends around her, Rukmini sat with her secret and held it close. The greatest event of her life had begun, and no one in the city knew it yet.
stories.reflection: The story turns on the contrast between the public machinery of the swayamvara and a private word spoken among friends: all the kings, invitations, and ceremonies are scaffolding around a choice that Rukmini makes alone, for herself. Her shyness is not hesitation — the certainty is already complete before she speaks it aloud.
stories.next_story_tease: What Rukmini declared in the women's quarters, Krishna would answer with a chariot before the eyes of the assembled kings.
stories.hero_scene: Rukmini among her friends in the women's quarters of Kundina, her face bent down in shyness as she confesses that she will accept no husband but the lotus-eyed Krishna, evening light falling through the lattice onto the circle of young women.

stories.title: Two Weddings in One Memory
stories.subtitle: Uddhava recalls how Krishna carried off Rukmini and won Satya
stories.story:
Years later, when Uddhava — who had served Krishna and loved him — remembered the great days of his Lord, two weddings came back to him in a single memory, the way a man recalls two victories of a long-ago war in one breath.

The first began with a summons. Bhishmaka's daughter had sent for Krishna, and he had answered. She was the princess Rukmini, the one the kings of the earth had gathered in Kundina to compete for; but she had already chosen, and her choice was known only to her and to the man she had called. So when Krishna came to Kundina, he came as a bridegroom answering a bride, not as a suitor entering a contest.

The kings who had ridden to the swayamvara saw none of that. They saw only what they had come to see: the ceremony, the crowd, the chance to win a princess. And while they looked — while the suitors watched and waited, sure that the day would end with one of them crowned — Krishna carried off his bride.

It was a gandharva marriage, the old rite by which a man and a woman take each other with no priest, no fire, no assembly: a marriage of consent alone, the simplest and oldest binding there is. In the sight of all the assembled kings, who could only look on, he took Rukmini and made her his own by that rite, and the swayamvara that had drawn half the thrones of the earth ended without a single garland being placed. The kings had come to compete; Krishna came, and took, and the competition was over before it began. It was his share — the bride the gods had destined for him — and he claimed it openly, with the whole gathering of suitors as his witness.

But Uddhava's memory did not stop there, because Krishna's life did not stop there. The same recollection that held Rukmini held another bride as well: Nagnajiti, the princess called Satya, whose swayamvara was held in her own kingdom, in a hall ringed by the proudest kings of the age. There was no summons for Satya's hand, no secret message carried to Dwaraka. She was offered as a prize to the strongest, and the kings who came for her were arrogant and sure, each of them certain the garland would be his.

Krishna came to that swayamvara too, and he did not need to be summoned. When the proud kings pressed forward, he met them and humbled them — defeated them, one after another, until the pride of that assembly lay broken at his feet. The kings who had come to win a princess left having lost something of themselves, and Satya, Nagnajiti, went with Krishna as his bride.

Two weddings, remembered together: one a secret answered openly, one a contest won by strength. In the first, a princess chose him in the dark and he came for her with a chariot while the suitors stared; in the second, he walked into the hall of the proud and took what was his by defeating them in front of their own eyes. The rites were different — one the whispered consent of a gandharva marriage, the other a victory before a crowd — but the shape was the same: Krishna married the women the gods had joined to him, and the kings of the earth, for all their armies and their pride, could not stop him. They could only watch.

That is how Uddhava remembered it, years afterward in the palace at Dwaraka, with the two brides of his Lord ruling that great house beside him: the carried-off princess and the won princess, Rukmini and Satya, two weddings folded into one shining memory of a man who could not be opposed.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's recollection deliberately pairs the two marriages, and the pairing says something about Krishna: Rukmini is taken by the quiet rite of consent while the suitors watch, Satya is won by openly humbling the proud. One is a whisper, the other a conquest — yet in both, the initiative is entirely his, and the assembled kings are reduced to spectators.
stories.tradition_note: This account comes from Uddhava's recollection in the Bhagavata Purana, which condenses Rukmini's carrying off and Satya's swayamvara into a single memory; the Harivamsha tells each of the two marriages at length.
stories.next_story_tease: But the story of that summons goes back further — to the day in Kundina when Rukmini first made her choice and entrusted it to a brahmana messenger bound for Dwaraka.
stories.hero_scene: Uddhava, in the palace at Dwaraka, remembering: Krishna lifting Rukmini onto his chariot before the staring assembly of suitors at Kundina, and in the same memory standing victorious in the swayamvara hall of Nagnajiti with the humbled kings around him.
