stories.title: A Princess Chooses Krishna
stories.story:
The princess of Vidarbha settled her own marriage before anyone thought to ask her, and she settled it without ever having set eyes on the groom.

Rukmini was the daughter of Bhishmaka, king of Kundina, and she was known for her intelligence, her beauty, and her character. Her brother Rukmi had decided her future for her: he meant to give her in marriage to Shishupala, the king of Cedi, and as far as he was concerned the matter was closed. The girl herself was told that her hand was spoken for, and the household began to move toward the wedding as toward something already decided.

But Rukmini had been hearing other names. Word of Krishna of Dwaraka reached Kundina, and she listened to it closely, the way a thirsty field listens for rain. Travelers and brahmanas spoke of his beauty, of a valour that had grown into legend, of virtues and a glory that seemed to deepen with every telling. The more she heard, the more one conviction settled in her and would not be moved: he alone was a fitting husband for her. Not the prince her brother favored, not any of the alliances her family counted — Krishna.

She knew better than to take her wish to her family. Her brother had set his heart on Shishupala, and a princess who argued with him would only have tightened his grip on the plan. So Rukmini chose a different road. Among the brahmanas who traveled freely between the courts, carrying news and messages and blessings, she found one she trusted completely. To him she entrusted a message meant for Krishna and for no one else, and she sent him out swiftly and in secret, so that no word of her decision would reach her brother before the message reached its destination.

The brahmana took the long road from Vidarbha to Dwaraka and made it quickly, carrying the princess's secret like a flame cupped in his hands. At the city's gates he was admitted past the guards who kept them and brought to Krishna's presence.

And here the story turns on a small thing that says everything. When Krishna saw the travel-worn brahmana, he did not wait for the man to state his business. He rose from his own seat, a king rising for an unknown visitor, and received him as a guest of the first rank. For Krishna held the brahmanas in the highest honor; a man who had given his life to study and prayer came before any crown in his regard, and everyone in Dwaraka knew it.

The court watched the traveler be welcomed, given his place, spoken to with courtesy. And then the two of them spoke quietly together, and the message that had crossed the whole country on a princess's behalf passed out of the messenger's keeping and into Krishna's.

The brahmana had done what Rukmini asked of him. He had brought her decision to the one man in the world she had chosen — and what happened next would depend on Krishna's answer.
stories.reflection: Rukmini chooses Krishna on report alone, before she has ever seen him, and she acts with startling practicality: where she cannot persuade her brother, she quietly arranges the matter herself through a trusted messenger. In this story the devotion begins with her, and it moves her to take her future into her own hands.
stories.next_story_tease: What the brahmana had brought was no ordinary embassy: Rukmini had chosen her husband, and she meant for Krishna to know it.
stories.hero_scene: A travel-worn brahmana standing before Krishna in the hall of Dwaraka while Krishna rises from his seat to receive him, the court watching in surprise as the unknown visitor is welcomed like a guest of the first rank.

stories.title: The Jackal and the Lion's Share
stories.subtitle: Rukmini's secret message to Krishna
stories.story:
The message had crossed half the country to reach him, but Krishna asked after the messenger before he asked after the message.

He received the brahmana from Vidarbha with honor and with questions that showed he had thought about the man before him. Was his dharma still what the elders approved? A brahmana, Krishna said, should be content with whatever comes to him by chance; an unsatisfied man, even if he were a lord of the gods, would wander from world to world and never find rest. He asked after the brahmanas of Vidarbha — whether they were well, those good men content with their own gains, friends to all beings — and he asked how the traveler had managed to cross the difficult road that lay between their lands. The brahmana answered fittingly, and then he gave Krishna what he had carried so far: Rukmini's words, delivered as she had spoken them.

"Having heard your virtues, O beauty of the three worlds," her message began, "my heart has entered into you, and it is not ashamed. Your virtues, entering through the ear, take away the body's distress; your form is the whole reward of a seeing eye. What wise girl of a good family would not choose you as her husband — you, who have no equal in family, conduct, beauty, learning, youth, and wealth, you who delight the minds of men? You are the one I have chosen. I have given myself to you. Do not let the king of Cedi touch the hero's share — do not let Shishupala, like a jackal, seize the lion's prey."

Then her words turned practical, and the princess of Kundina laid out her whole heart and her whole plan in the same breath. "If the Lord, worshipped with sacrifices, gifts, and vows, honored in gods, brahmanas, and elders, is pleased with my devotion, let him come and take my hand — not Damaghosha's son, not any other. Tomorrow they will marry me. Come to Vidarbha in secret, surrounded by your warriors; crush the forces of the king of Cedi and the king of Magadha, and carry me off by the rakshasa rite — the old rite in which a bride is taken by force — as the prize of your valour. But how could you take me while I live within the inner apartments, without killing my kinsmen? I will tell you the way. The day before the wedding there is a great procession of the family goddess, and in that procession the new bride goes out to the temple of Girija."

She ended where she had begun, with the one thing that mattered more than any plan. "If I do not obtain your grace, O lotus-eyed one, I would give up this body, weakened by my vows; even a hundred births would not change my choice."

The brahmana fell silent. Krishna had listened without moving, taking in the princess's love and her strategy as one single thing, as she had meant them to be. The message had found its home. What he said in answer, and the journey that followed, would belong to the night.
stories.reflection: What is striking about Rukmini's message is that adoration and strategy are one and the same in it: she offers herself to Krishna and then, in the same breath, tells him exactly how to come and claim her. Even her fear — that Shishupala, like a jackal, would seize the lion's share — is expressed as devotion.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana also tells the story of Rukmini's marriage; the message as rendered here follows the Bhagavata Purana.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna heard the message out in silence, and before the night was over he was on the road to Vidarbha.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna seated in the lamplit hall of Dwaraka, listening without moving as the brahmana delivers Rukmini's words, her message hanging in the quiet air between them.

stories.title: The Night Journey to Kundina
stories.story:
The road from Dwaraka to Kundina usually took days. Krishna crossed it in a single night.

He heard the brahmana out, and he did not hide what the message had done to him. "I too," he said, "cannot sleep at night for her sake." And he said plainly what he meant to do: he would bring her back, crushing in battle the wicked kings who stood in his way. There was no council called, no army mustered. The chariot was made ready, the four horses — Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa, and Balahaka — were yoked, and Daruka his charioteer took the reins. Krishna seated the brahmana beside him, and they went out through the gates of Dwaraka while the city slept.

Through the dark they flew, over river and plain, the princess's words still hanging in the air between them. By the time the sun rose, Krishna was within the borders of Vidarbha, and no one in Kundina knew he had come.

In Kundina, no one had slept either, but for a different reason. The city was being made ready for a wedding. Bhishmaka, led by love for his son, had ordered the streets swept and sprinkled, the roads and crossings cleaned; garlands, perfumes, and bright garments appeared on every side. He worshipped the ancestors, the gods, and the brahmanas according to the rites. The bride was bathed and adorned with the auspicious ceremonies, and the foremost brahmanas chanted the mantras of the Sama, the Rig, and the Yajur over her for her protection; gifts of gold and silver cloth and sesame mixed with jaggery were distributed, and the whole city put on its finest face for the day to come.

The guests who arrived made the purpose of the gathering plain. Damaghosha, the king of Cedi, came for his son with herds of rutting elephants and chariots garlanded with gold, and the lord of Vidarbha went out to receive him with honor. With him came Shalva, and Jarasandha of Magadha, and Dantavakra, and Viduratha — kings who hated Krishna and his brother Balarama, and who were determined to give the bride to the prince of Cedi. "If Krishna comes," they resolved among themselves, "we will fight him, and we will fight him together."

Word of that muster traveled the roads, and it reached Balarama. Flooded with love for his brother, he gathered a great force and set out after him, so that the Yadava who had ridden ahead with a single chariot now had an army on the road behind him.

And all the while, in the inner apartments of Kundina, the bride-to-be was counting the hours toward a wedding she had never wanted — hoping, with everything in her, that the man she had written to had heard her message in time.
stories.reflection: The line that stays with the reader is Krishna's admission that he, too, could not sleep for her. The great dash to Kundina is easy to read as rescue or romance; the source quietly makes it mutual, and lets the two longings answer each other across the country.
stories.next_story_tease: In Kundina the bride-to-be had heard that Krishna had come — but the wedding was still a night away, and she had not yet seen him.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna's chariot flying across moonlit plains at full gallop, Daruka driving, the brahmana holding on beside him, the four horses — Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa, and Balahaka — stretched to their limit through the night.

stories.title: The Vow at Ambika's Temple
stories.subtitle: Rukmini's silent prayer as her wedding dawns
stories.story:
A single night lay between Rukmini and her wedding, and the man she had chosen had not come.

Her mind, stolen away by Govinda, would not rest. She thought: only a night remains before my wedding, and I am a girl of little fortune. Will the faultless one find something blameworthy in me? The creator is not favorable to me, nor Maheshvara. Tears came as she prayed, with everything in her, that Krishna alone might be her husband.

Then, at last, came the messenger. The same brahmana she had sent to Dwaraka returned to her, sent back now by Krishna himself, with a bright face and news that made her heart lift: he had come. The darling of the Yadus had reached Vidarbha. Krishna was here.

News travels in a wedding city. Bhishmaka heard that Krishna had arrived among the gathered kings, and he offered the madhuparka, the honeyed welcome kept for honored guests, with fresh garments, and had a splendid residence made ready for him. And the townspeople of Vidarbha, hearing that Krishna walked among them, said openly what everyone felt: "Rukmini deserves to be his wife, and no other. What good deed did we do, that the maker of the three worlds should be pleased with us?" Love bound the whole city; they spoke of nothing else.

Then came the day of the family goddess's procession — the day Rukmini's own message had pointed to. Wrapped in a vow of silence, she went out on foot to see the lotus-petal feet of Bhavani, her mothers and her companions all around her. Thousands of women followed with offerings; singers sang and musicians played; and the city poured out to watch the bride go to the temple of the goddess.

At the shrine she washed her hands and her feet. The elderly brahmana women who knew the rites worshipped the goddess with water, perfume, unbroken rice, incense, fresh garments, garlands, and ornaments, and the married women of the household joined them in the worship. Then they gave Rukmini the remainder of the offerings and pronounced their blessings over her. And Rukmini, bowing before the goddess, prayed the one prayer she had carried in her heart across all those miles: may Krishna, the Lord, alone become my husband. Bless this.

She rose, laid aside her vow of silence, and came out of Ambika's temple. And the assembled heroes who saw her — slim-waisted, her face bright with earrings, her smile pure, her lips like bimba fruit, her teeth like jasmine buds — stood struck silent, struck with love, as if the goddess's own enchantment had stepped out into the daylight.

Only one man in all that crowd did not stare. Krishna had come, as she had asked him to. And the procession that was to have delivered her to Shishupala was about to deliver her to Krishna instead.
stories.reflection: Rukmini's prayer at the temple is both worship and the final move of her own plan: the procession she had described in her message is what brings her out of the inner apartments, into the open, where Krishna can reach her. The goddess is asked to bless what the princess has already resolved.
stories.next_story_tease: Beyond the temple door, the hour she had written to him about had come.
stories.hero_scene: Rukmini kneeling in silent prayer before the image of Ambika in the incense-filled shrine, her hands joined, her mothers and friends around her, the lamp of the goddess lighting her bowed head as the brahmana women chant blessings.

stories.title: Krishna Carries Off Rukmini
stories.story:
Krishna loved a woman, and she was about to be given to another man. Rukmini, the princess of Vidarbha, was the daughter of Bhishmaka, the king of Kundina, and her beauty was spoken of across the kingdoms. Krishna had asked for her hand, but her brother Rukmin, who hated him, refused the match. Then, at the suggestion of Jarasandha, her father affianced her to Sisupala, the king of Chedi. Her father was a powerful king, and her brother Rukmin was proud, and between them her future had been settled. Now the wedding was near, and the kings of the earth had gathered in Kundina for it, Sisupala's allies among them, an armed ring of princes who had come to see the princess given away.

Krishna, too, had come to Kundina, with Balarama and many of the Yadus at his side. The city was full of banners and of soldiers, for half the kings of the earth had arrived, and the roads were thick with their chariots and elephants.

On the day of the ceremony Rukmini went to the temple to pray, as a bride does before she is given. The temple stood at the edge of the city, and the princess went up its steps alone while the noise of the assembled kings gathered like a storm behind her, and the whole court waited outside the doors. When she came out and stepped toward her chariot, the assembled princes fell silent. She was radiant, and the kings who had come to take part were wounded by the sight of her, struck still on their elephants and horses and chariots, some of them slipping from their seats in their daze. She pushed back a strand of hair with her left hand and glanced shyly over the gathered princes — and her eyes found Krishna, waiting in the crowd. For a long moment no one moved, as though the whole assembly understood at once what was about to happen.

Before anyone could move, Krishna swept her up. He set her on his own chariot, the one flying the banner of Garuda, and drove through the ring of kings as a lion drives through a pack of jackals, carrying off the share that was his. The princess made no move to stop him. All the banners and the ceremony and the armed guests had come to nothing in the space of a single breath.

The proud kings could not bear it. Jarasandha and the rest stood shamed, their honor torn away, and cried aloud that their fame, won with their bows, had been snatched from them by cowherds — like a lion's kill stolen away by deer. They surged after the chariot, and Rukmin himself swore he would never set foot in Kundina again until he had slain Krishna. But Balarama and the Yadus met the pursuers and threw them back, holding the road while Krishna rode on.

When Rukmin overtook the chariot alone, Krishna scattered his army as if in sport and flung him to the ground, and would have ended him then and there. But Rukmini begged for her brother's life. “He is my only brother,” she said. “Do not kill him. Give him to me.” And Krishna, who is not ruled by anger, spared Rukmin at the entreaty of the woman he had just carried off, and granted her the gift of his life. Rukmin, keeping his vow, never returned to Kundina; he founded a city of his own, Bhojakata, and dwelt there ever after.

And Krishna married Rukmini in due form, having won her as a warrior wins a bride — the woman he loved, carried away on his chariot from the midst of her enemies. And in time she bore him a son, Pradyumna, born of the god of love himself, so that the taking of the bride opened onto the next chapter of their lives.
stories.reflection: The episode is often called an abduction, but what Krishna does is openly claim a bride in front of the very kings who had gathered to give her to another. There is no concealment in it; the drama is that every armed prince in the assembly watches it happen and none of them can stop it.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata places the carrying-off at Rukmini's svayamvara, as she came out from the temple; the Vishnu Purana sets it on the eve of her betrothal to Sisupala and adds the pursuit and defeat of her brother Rukmin. This telling follows the Bhagavata for the abduction and draws the closing detail of Rukmin's defeat from the Vishnu Purana.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, driving a chariot flying the banner of Garuda, sweeps Rukmini up from beside her own chariot and turns to ride through a ring of stunned, falling kings as the princess looks back over her shoulder.

stories.title: Spared for Rukmini's Sake
stories.story:
The road to Dwaraka stretched ahead, and behind it hung a wall of dust. Rukmini sat close beside Krishna in the chariot, and she did not need to turn around to know who rode at the head of that pursuit. She knew her brother's temper, and she knew what he had sworn before he left Kundina.

The kings who had gathered for her svayamvara had not accepted their loss. They had come to Kundina to win her, and now she was gone, carried off in a stranger's chariot, and their pride would not let the matter end there. The whole assembly took the road after Krishna — the allies of Jarasandha, the kings of the Deccan, the princes of every house that had hoped to claim the princess of Vidarbha.

Krishna's warriors — Balarama, Gada, and the best of the Vrishni heroes — wheeled about to meet them, and the battle was short. Standards came down, chariots broke apart, and one after another the pursuing kings fell back and scattered across the plain, leaving it littered with broken wheels and fallen banners. Shishupala of Chedi rode up burning with rage, and Krishna met his fury with calm words, telling him to put aside his grief. "I have been defeated by you seventeen times in battle," Shishupala answered, "and I have never grieved, and never rejoiced." It was the answer of a man who had learned to lose, and with it the heart went out of the pursuit.

But one man had not come to win a bride. Rukmi, Rukmini's brother, had sworn before his father Bhishmaka and before all the assembled kings that he would not re-enter Kundina until he had slain Krishna and brought his sister back. When he saw the allied army fall back, he did not fall back with it. He came on alone, his chariot cutting through the rout, straight at Krishna's banner.

The chase ended where the chariots met, and what followed was a lesson in what one bowman could do. Every weapon Rukmi raised, Krishna shattered: the bow broke in his hand, and the heavy mace, the spear, the javelin, the shield — arrow after arrow found each in turn and split it. Krishna's shafts brought down the horses and wrecked the chariot, and Rukmi leapt from the wreckage, sword in hand, to finish the fight at close quarters. His sword and his shield went the way of the rest, cut to splinters, and the prince of Vidarbha stood weaponless in the open field.

Krishna moved to end it, and Rukmini cried out. She slipped from the chariot and threw herself at his feet, shaking with fear, and begged for her brother's life. "He is my only brother," she pleaded. "Give me my brother in charity."

The plea stopped his hand. Krishna spared Rukmi — but he did not send him home untouched. He bound the defeated prince, shaved his head and his beard, and disfigured him, so that the man who had sworn to return to Kundina in triumph carried a mark no court could miss. Then he lifted Rukmini up, held her, and comforted her, and promised her brother his life and his safety.

Rukmi lay senseless on the field, and his own men carried him away. But he could not go home. His oath was broken, and he would not show his face in the city he had sworn to enter in triumph. He built a new city in Vidarbha, Bhojakata by name, and ruled the southern districts from it, while his father Bhishmaka remained in Kundina. The vow he had made to shame Krishna had become the sentence that kept him from his own house.

Balarama and the Vrishni army, having scattered Jarasandha and the rest, turned for Dwaraka. And Krishna, who had spared the brother and kept the sister, set his face toward the city as well — toward a wedding that the whole of Dwaraka was already preparing to celebrate.
stories.reflection: Rukmini's plea is the hinge of the scene: the brother who tried to destroy her happiness is saved by her, and Krishna's mercy is not softness — he spares the life but leaves a mark of the humiliation, so the victory is complete and the life is kept at once. The greater irony lands on Rukmi himself: the oath he swore to shame Krishna becomes the sentence that exiles him from his own home.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha places the duel near the river Narmada, with Rukmi struck unconscious and later carried off the field; the Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana have him pursue Krishna and be spared at Rukmini's entreaty, the Bhagavata adding the shaving and disfigurement.
stories.content_note: Contains a battle scene and the humiliation of the defeated Rukmi (his head and beard shaved, his face disfigured), told without graphic detail.

stories.title: A Festival in Every House
stories.story:
Rukmi never went back to Kundina. His oath lay broken on the battlefield where Krishna had spared his life, and a man who had sworn to return in triumph could not bear to return in defeat. He built a new capital in the province of Vidarbha, a city called Bhojakata, and from there he ruled the southern districts, while his father Bhishmaka stayed on in Kundina. The wedding his sister had chosen for herself had cost him his home.

The Yadava host came home to Dwaraka — Balarama at its head, having settled with Jarasandha and the pursuing kings — and Krishna entered the city with Rukmini at his side. What had begun on the open road, in the old manner of kings, was to be completed before the whole city: Krishna wed Rukmini in due form, with the full rites, before the fire and the witnesses of the Yadu court, and Rukmini, who had chosen him before she ever saw him, at last became his queen. The rush of the escape, the dust of the chase, the fury of her brother — all of it receded, and what remained was the moment she had staked everything on.

Then Dwaraka gave itself to festival. Every house in the Yadu city held its own celebration, from the great mansions to the smallest homes, and the poorest lane kept festival as eagerly as the palace. The streets were sprinkled with water to lay the dust of the procession; the doorways were hung with mango-leaf garlands and ropes of fresh flowers, with strings of gems and woven toranas; auspicious pots stood at the thresholds; and the air carried incense and the glow of lamps. Banners bearing Indra's emblem rose above the gates, and from every quarter of the city came the sound of conches and drums and singing. Men and women put on their finest — jewels and earrings, fresh-washed cloth, bright colors — as if the whole city had dressed for the bride.

Guests came from every quarter: kings of the Kuru, Srijaya, and Kaikeya lands, of Vidarbha, of the Yadu and Kunti houses. And wherever they gathered, the story was told and retold — how Rukmini had been carried off from her own svayamvara, from under the eyes of the greatest kings of the age. The tale that had sent those kings chasing in fury across the plain was sung in Dwaraka as a love story, and the city rejoiced at every telling of it. Great joy filled every house, and the marriage of Krishna and Rukmini was celebrated from the palace to the waterfront, with singing and music and blessings rising into the evening air.

The sources add what came after. The Vishnu Purana says Rukmini bore Krishna a son, Pradyumna, a portion of the god of love himself, who would grow into one of the Yadus' greatest warriors; the Harivamsha names her Krishna's first wife, foremost among his queens.

Night fell on Dwaraka, and the lamps burned in every window, and singing drifted through the streets. A marriage that had begun in a stolen moment on an open road had ended in the oldest and grandest of things: a city keeping festival for its prince and its princess.
stories.reflection: Rukmini's marriage is one of the few tales that begins in open conflict and ends in unalloyed festival: the abduction that enraged the kings is sung in Dwaraka as a love story. And Rukmi's exile is entirely his own work — the oath he swore against Krishna turns out to be the very thing that keeps him from his home.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana closes its account of the marriage with the birth of their son Pradyumna, while the Harivamsha names Rukmini Krishna's first wife and lists ten sons. The Bhagavata keeps its focus on the wedding itself and the city's celebration.

stories.title: The Vow at the Yamuna
stories.story:
Krishna was a guest at Indraprastha, the Pandavas' new city on the Yamuna, and the days passed in friendship — feasts, long talks, the easy company of Arjuna. One morning the two of them mounted Arjuna's chariot, the one that flew the monkey banner, took up their bows and armor, and rode out into the great forest to hunt. It was the pastime of princes, and they were good at it: tigers, wild boars, buffaloes, and antelope fell to their arrows, and the servants carried the best of the kill back to the city, for the king's table on the coming festival day.

The hunt ended at the river. The two friends bathed in the clear, slow water of the Yamuna, drank from it, and rested on the bank — and there, near the water's edge, they saw a maiden. She stood alone, graceful and lovely, with the stillness of someone who had been waiting a long time and had grown patient with it. Krishna sent Arjuna to her, to ask her name, and her family, and what it was she hoped for.

"I am Kalindi," she said, "daughter of the Sun, and I live in the waters of the Yamuna. I have no other choice to make: I will take no husband but him in whom all beauty dwells."

Arjuna carried her words back to Krishna. She had not asked to be rescued, or claimed, or taken away. She had simply declared — with the calm of a vow kept for years — that she had chosen her husband long before he came. Her penance, her waiting in the river, had been for Vishnu himself, for the one her heart had already settled on, for Krishna. The question he had sent Arjuna to ask had been answered before it was even spoken.

So Krishna went to her, took her onto his chariot, and in time, at an auspicious hour when the season and the stars were favorable, married her. The sources record the marriage as quiet and complete: no armies, no svayamvara, no chase, no envoys, no long negotiation — a meeting by the water, a vow spoken plainly, and a wedding. She had chosen him with no expectation of being chosen in return, and her choice was honored. The daughter of the Sun came out of her long penance and into the Yadu household, and she is remembered by the river's own name, Kalindi, the maiden of the Yamuna.

The Yamuna kept its part of the story. It had sheltered her through the years of waiting, held her in its waters, been the place where her resolve lived; and it was the place where the waiting ended. Some vows are answered by battles and miracles; hers was answered by a chariot stopping on a riverbank, and a question asked kindly of a stranger.
stories.reflection: Kalindi's vow is striking because it is entirely one-sided: she decides on a husband she has never met and then waits for him to appear. Her penance is not performed to earn a reward but to declare a choice, and the Yamuna, where she made her home, becomes the quiet witness of a devotion that asked for nothing but the chance to give itself.

stories.title: Seven Bulls and a Bride
stories.story:
The road from Indraprastha to Dwaraka was long, and it passed through kingdoms where Krishna's name was spoken with hatred. In Avanti, the princes Vinda and Anuvinda had long been devoted to Duryodhana, and their sister Mitravinda — the daughter of Krishna's own aunt — was to be given in svayamvara. The kings who gathered for it were his enemies, and the assembly had been arranged, it seemed, to leave Krishna out of the reckoning entirely.

He did not stay out. Before the assembled kings could decide anything, Krishna carried Mitravinda off — forcibly, as the Bhagavata puts it — and set her in his chariot. The svayamvara that had been designed to keep her from him ended with the bride already gone, and the kings who had come to claim her were left shouting after a departing chariot. It was not a wooing; it was a taking, swift and complete, and Avanti learned that its gates and its alliances were no shield against Krishna's will.

Word of it ran ahead of him. In Kosala, a different kind of test was waiting. King Nagnajit, a righteous king, had a daughter named Satya, and her fame had spread across the kingdoms because of the condition her father had set: no man could win her without first subduing seven bulls — fierce, untamable beasts that had already broken every suitor who had tried them.

Krishna, hearing that Satya was to be won by taming bulls, went to Kosala. King Nagnajit rose from his seat and came forward to receive him with honor, and Satya herself, seeing Krishna, chose him in her heart — this, she knew, was the husband she had hoped for, the one her prayers had described. But her father was bound by his own promise. "We made this agreement before all the world," Nagnajit said. "These seven bulls are fierce, and beyond control. Subdue them, and my daughter is yours."

Krishna bound up his garment and stepped into the pen. The bulls that had broken every suitor came at him — and the old telling adds that he seemed to be everywhere at once, as if seven Krishnas stood in that pen, one for every bull. Ropes closed around them, and their pride and their strength gave way, until all seven stood roped and quiet, and the kings who had failed before him stared in silence.

The king of Kosala, amazed, gave Krishna his daughter. The queens of the palace rejoiced; conches and kettledrums sounded; there was singing and music, and the blessings of the brahmins rose over the courtyard. Krishna gave gifts in return — ten thousand cows, nine thousand elephants, and chariots in plenty — and then he placed Satya on his chariot, and with a great army around them, set out for Dwaraka.

The kings who had lost did not let them go quietly. When they heard that the bride was being led away, they raised a cry and loosed volleys of arrows at the chariot as it passed. Arjuna, riding with Krishna as a friend does, turned every shaft aside, and the bridal procession rolled on unharmed.

So Krishna came home to Dwaraka with two new brides: Mitravinda, carried off from the svayamvara of Avanti, and Satya, won fairly in the bull-pen of Kosala. One kingdom had barred its gates to him; the other had set a test no man could pass. The gates were opened, and the test was passed, and the seven bulls of Kosala stood behind the chariot like a strange honor guard — proof of the strength of the man who had come for Satya.
stories.reflection: The two brides are won two different ways: Mitravinda is taken by force from an assembly built to exclude Krishna, while Satya is won openly, by meeting a test announced to every suitor. Nagnajit's condition shows a king who does not refuse Krishna but simply holds him to the same bargain as all the rest — and Krishna's answer to seven untamable bulls is not to kill them but to rope them, the quietest possible proof of strength.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata presents Mitravinda's carrying off and Satya's bull-trial as one journey, though they were separate svayamvaras in separate kingdoms; the Harivamsha recalls the Satya episode separately.
stories.next_story_tease: At home in Dwaraka, Rukmini was about to hear a strange account of the husband she had chosen.

stories.title: The Jest That Felled Rukmini
stories.story:
In the inner chamber of the palace in Dwaraka, the air was soft with the scent of parijata blossoms, and bees moved lazily through garlands of mallika. Krishna lay at ease on a couch white as milk foam, and Rukmini sat beside him, fanning him with a fan whose handle was set with jewels. She had taken it from a friend's hand a moment before; her anklets kept a soft, unhurried time. It was the kind of quiet in which a single careless word can do the most damage.

He began lightly enough, smiling. Great kings had sought her, he said — Shishupala, Shalva, Jarasandha, Dantavakra, princes of every kind of strength and wealth. And whom had she chosen? A man with nothing. He was penniless, he told her; he had always been, and the penniless were the only people he could call his own. He kept company, he said, with folk who walked hidden roads that the world never saw. He was not the sort to run after wives and sons and household splendor. So let her think again, this jewel of a bride: let her choose some worthy kshatriya, a bull among kings, and leave her empty-handed husband to his own devices.

He meant it as play. A jest, a game, the kind of teasing a man gives the woman who loves him, expecting her to laugh and scold him. His smile was real; his delight in her was real. That was the terrible part — the jest came wrapped in exactly the love it seemed to deny.

But from the lips of the lord of the three worlds, Rukmini had never heard an unkind word before that day. She heard this one as a sentence.

She had not chosen him in a market or a council hall. She had chosen him across the ruin of her own life — she, the princess of Vidarbha, who had sent him word against her own brother's wishes, who had climbed into his chariot at her svayamvara while the kings of the earth looked on and Rukmi raged behind her, and who had crossed half of India to reach Dwaraka with him. Every king he now named had been gathered in that hall. She had turned from all of them, and the whole world had approved her choice. The one person whose approval she had never thought to need was Krishna himself.

His words struck where nothing else could reach. She said nothing; she could not. Her eyes filled, the tears dark with collyrium, and she traced the floor with her toe as if writing out the shape of her failure there. The jeweled fan slipped from her hand and struck the floor with a small, final sound, and the chiming of her anklets stopped all at once. Then she fainted outright, collapsing where she sat, her hair loosening and scattering around her like a plantain tree struck down by the wind.

Krishna saw the fall, and in that instant the game was over for him. He rose from the couch, bound to her by the very love he had been teasing, lifted her in his arms, and wiped the tears from her eyes and the grief from her face. He had meant a jest and found a wound. There in the ruined quiet of the chamber he began to comfort her, holding her like a man who had suddenly understood what he had almost thrown away.

But the jest itself was still between them — unconfessed, unmade — and Rukmini, waking into his arms, did not yet know that it had never been true at all.
stories.reflection: Rukmini, who defied kings and her own brother to choose Krishna, faints at a single word from him: the story measures trust by what one voice can do to it. His jest is playful, but her collapse is real, and the comfort he gives shows the game had already gone further than he intended.
stories.next_story_tease: But the jest was not yet unmade — and Rukmini's answer, when it came, would be the most serious words she ever spoke to him.

stories.title: The Jest Unmade
stories.story:
Rukmini came to herself in Krishna's arms, and the first thing she understood was that the world had not ended — only her certainty in it.

He had lifted her from where she fell and was wiping her tears, and now, seeing her eyes open, he told her the truth at last. He had spoken in jest. He had wanted to see her face, he said — the face of a woman who loved him, trembling between love and anger. That face, he told her, was the supreme gain of a householder; no treasure in any house could equal it.

She looked at him for a long moment. Then Rukmini, who had been silent, spoke — and she did not scold him. She answered the jest as if it were the most serious question ever put to her.

She knew, she said, whom she had chosen. The kings he named were mortal lords with mortal power, and she had seen what became of such kings: Anga and Vainya, Jayanta, Nahusha and Gaya — men who had held the whole earth and, wanting only him, had laid their kingdoms down and walked into the forest. Even the guardians of the worlds, she said, carried tribute to his feet; sages who had laid aside punishment worshipped him in silence. At her own svayamvara his bow had spoken once and the kings had scattered like animals before a lion — and he had carried her off the way a lion carries off its share. Who else, after that, could she shelter under? Having once breathed the fragrance of his lotus feet, the fragrance that releases the sorrowful, what woman would choose any other refuge?

Let her be a servant, she said, in the house of even one of his devotees, and she would count herself richer than any queen. A woman who does not love his feet is a living corpse — skin and bone dressed in finery — and she had no wish to be such a one. Let her love for him stand, in this world and the next. And as for his words: she did not hold them false. A wanton's heart runs after every new thing, but hers, once given, did not wander.

Krishna heard her out, and when she finished he praised her — not her beauty, which every king at her svayamvara had already praised, but her faithfulness, and the vow she had kept. He had seen no wife like her, he said. At her own wedding, with all the kings of the earth gathered to claim her, she had ignored them and sent a brahmin to him in secret. She had never once complained of her brother's enmity, fearing that her words would wound him. She had sent a messenger to win her own husband; she had crossed a kingdom for him. And now, when he teased her, she had believed him — because she could not imagine that he would lie, even in play.

Whatever she desired, he told her, she already held; he was hers, and his desire had nothing left to ask of her. Those who seek him only for the gifts of marriage, he said, are poor in fortune even when rich; but the devotion she had given him, given again and again, was of the kind that frees a soul from the world.

Then the quiet returned to the chamber, and this time it was the right kind of quiet. The jest was unmade, the tears wiped away, and the two of them sat together in the peace that follows a storm — the peace of a house where everything has been said and forgiven.

And the old account adds one last thing: as Krishna lived with Rukmini, so he dwelt in the homes of his other wives — the Lord of the universe, in each of their houses, simply a husband at home.
stories.reflection: Rukmini's long reply never argues with the jest; it simply tells who Krishna is, as if the teasing had asked her to say it aloud. And Krishna's answer is the rarer thing — he praises her not for beauty or rank but for the faithfulness of a choice made against the world.

stories.title: The Dice Game at Bhojakata
stories.story:
The wedding of Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson, to Rukmi's granddaughter had gone off in perfect peace — which was remarkable, because Rukmi had spent years as Krishna's enemy. He had sworn to destroy the man who carried off his sister Rukmini, and had been defeated instead; the defeat had never sat well with him. But for the sake of his daughter and his granddaughter he had swallowed the old grievance, and the two families had feasted together in his city of Bhojakata as if there had never been a quarrel.

Then the ceremony was over, and the kings fell to sport.

It was the Kalinga king who first saw the opportunity. Balarama, everyone knew, loved a game of dice and played it like a cowherd — which, the gathered kings reminded one another with smiles, was exactly what he was. Rukmi was expert at the game. So a word passed among them — the king of Ashmaka, Rukmi's own son Shrutarva, Chanura, Kratha, Anshuman, Jayatsena, and half a dozen princes of the Deccan — and they urged Rukmi to sit down with Krishna's brother and teach him the difference between a plow and a pair of dice.

The hall was a beautiful one, with golden pillars and a floor strewn with flowers and sprinkled with sandal water, and the kings took their golden seats. Rama joined them gladly, saying he was only sporting, and the dice were shaken out. The wagers climbed — a hundred coins, a thousand, ten thousand — until Rukmi set a stake of a hundred thousand and Rama matched it, and lost. The glorious Rama's anger rose like the sea at high tide, but he mastered it, as the old account notes he was master of his wrath, and he calmly offered one final wager: everything, on a single throw. This time, though Rukmi cheated, it was Rama who won. The game was fair, and the victory was his.

Then a voice spoke from the sky, clear enough for the whole hall to hear: the stake had been won by Balarama, and by Balarama alone.

Rukmi, stung to the heart, refused to hear it. Urged on by the very kings who had set the trap, he stood up and jeered at the guest he had just feasted. "Cowherds who live in the forest," he said, "know nothing of dice." The kings laughed with him, and the Kalinga king laughed loudest of all, showing every tooth.

It was the last laugh any of them had that evening.

Balarama rose from his seat. He seized the Kalinga king where he sat and dashed him to the floor, and the teeth that had gleamed in that laugh were struck out of his head. The kings who had mocked him he broke where they stood — arms, thighs, skulls — until the flower-strewn hall ran red. And Rukmi, the author of it all, the man who had staked his honor on a rigged game, he struck down dead with his iron club.

In the sudden silence, Krishna said nothing — neither good nor ill of it. The dead man was Rukmini's brother, and there was no word he could speak that would not wound her. He said nothing then, and that silence was remembered longer than any word spoken at the feast.

The wedding party gathered itself and left Bhojakata the same night, Aniruddha and his bride placed in the best of the chariots, the long road to Dwaraka stretching ahead of them. Behind them the gaming hall stood empty among the marriage garlands — the place where a family had made peace, and a game of dice had unmade it.
stories.reflection: Rukmi is destroyed not by the dice but by the taunt: the game was lost, the voice from the sky had named the winner, and one sneer about cowherds turned a defeat into a funeral. The wedding that was meant to heal the family's old wound reopens it — and Krishna's silence, out of care for Rukmini, is the most telling detail in the scene.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata says Balarama killed Rukmi with his iron club; the Vishnu Purana instead says he struck him dead with the very board the game was played on. Both agree a heavenly voice declared Balarama the true winner, and the Harivamsha adds that the Kalinga king's teeth were knocked out.
stories.content_note: Contains violence: Balarama kills Rukmi and injures the other kings at a dice game. Described with restraint, but may warrant parental awareness for younger listeners.
stories.next_story_tease: For Krishna himself another svayamvara was already waiting — this one with a fish for a target and a bow that no king of the earth could string.

stories.title: The Fish at the Svayamvara
stories.story:
Years afterward, when Draupadi asked Krishna's queens how each of them had come to marry him, Lakshmana answered with a story about a fish.

But before that story, there was a quieter one. On the way, Krishna had married Bhadra, the daughter of his aunt Srutakirti, given to him by her brothers — a marriage of kinsmen, arranged and blessed, with none of the swordplay that seemed to follow him everywhere. That wedding passed without incident, and it is remembered mostly because of what came next.

In the kingdom of Madra, the king had set his heart on finding his daughter Lakshmana a husband worthy of her. He had done it in the old way, the way that tested more than beauty: he proclaimed a svayamvara, and for its test he hung up a fish — a target so placed that no archer could see it directly, only its reflection in the water far below. The king who could string the bow and pierce that fish would take his daughter home.

The kings of the earth came to Madra. They arrived in procession, each one expecting to leave with the bride. They tried the bow one after another, and the hall watched them fail. Some could not string it at all; it stood unbent before them, mocking their arms. The kings of Magadha, Ambashta and Cedi — the strongest of the suitors — managed to draw it, but the fish hung high and its image trembled in the water, and every arrow they loosed at the reflection missed the truth of it. One by one the kings set the bow down, their pride broken, until the arena stood empty.

Krishna had watched in silence. He took up the bow, and the great weapon bent in his hands as if it had been waiting for him. He looked once at the water, where the fish's shadow wavered, and fitted a single arrow. It flew; the fish fell; and from the sky the drums of the gods rolled out while shouts of victory rang across the earth. As the old verse puts it, he carried off the fair daughter of Madra the way Garuda seizes nectar from the gods.

In the crowd, Lakshmana was already moving. She came into the arena with her anklets chiming, a garland of golden-gleaming jewels in her hands and a shy smile half-hiding her face. She looked once at the kings who had failed and once at the man who had not, and then she set her garland on Krishna's shoulder. Conches and drums and bheris answered; the svayamvara was over before anyone could object.

Not everyone let it end there. The kings who had lost her to a stranger's arrow did not take their defeat kindly, and as Krishna turned to leave they surged forward to stop him. Daruka, his charioteer, lifted Lakshmana into the waiting chariot, drawn by four fine horses; and Krishna met the kings with arrows from Sharnga, and where his arrows passed, arms and legs and necks were cut down, until the road to Dwaraka lay open. He entered his own city like the sun entering its home, through gates hung with banners, and the king of Madra — his daughter already gone — did the only thing left to him: he honored the guests Krishna had left behind with serving women, wealth, elephants, chariots and horses, as if the wedding had been held in his own hall after all.

That was Lakshmana's story, told years later to Draupadi. She ended it with a strange, quiet line. "We are only servants," she said, "in the home of that self-satisfied Lord." A queen of Dwaraka, won by arrow and garland before all the kings of the earth — and in her own telling, nothing more than a servant in a house whose master needed nothing at all.
stories.reflection: Lakshmana's closing line is the quiet heart of the story: every king at the svayamvara was competing to possess her, and she describes herself as a servant in the home of a Lord who is complete in himself. The fish, the bow, the fleeing kings — in her telling it was never a contest in which she was being won, but a service she was entering.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata tells this twice: a brief list of Krishna's marriages (10.58) and Lakshmana's own full account years later (10.83). The details of the fish target come from her telling; the brief version adds only that he carried her off like Garuda seizing nectar.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, a missing jewel — the Syamantaka — would soon turn even Krishna's own kinsmen against him.

stories.title: Suspicion Falls on Krishna
stories.subtitle: The Vrishnis and Andhakas believe he stole the Syamantaka jewel
stories.story:
Prasena rode out of Dwaraka on a bright morning wearing the Syamantaka jewel on his breast, and no one in the city saw him alive again. When the news of his death reached the clan, the Vrishnis and Andhakas did not mourn long in silence. Before the rites were over they had begun to speak of Krishna.

It was easy to see why. The Syamantaka had come to Dwaraka as a gift of the sun, and its worth was beyond reckoning: gold welled up in the palaces of the Vrishnis and Andhakas while it was among them, the rains fell in their season, and there was no fear of disease in the city. Satrajit, who had received the jewel, had in his delight given it to his brother Prasena, and Prasena wore it everywhere he went. And everyone in Dwaraka knew that Krishna had wanted it. He had never reached for it — he was more than capable of taking it by force or by stealth, and he had done neither — but he had wanted it, and in a city of kinsmen that was remembered.

Then Prasena went out hunting, wearing the jewel. A lion slew him in the forest for its sake; a bear slew the lion, took the jewel, and carried it away into its den. But the members of the two great families heard only that Prasena was dead and the Syamantaka gone. They knew their Krishna had a fancy for that jewel. Some said it openly; others let the words hang in the air whenever he passed. Suspicion settled over him like a shadow, and no one spoke of the lion, or the bear, or the forest at all.

Krishna heard what was being said, and he did not answer with denials. Knowing himself innocent, he made a resolve: I must bring the jewel. He set out with his followers for the forest where Prasena had hunted, and they searched the mountains Rikshavan and Vindhya until Krishna himself was worn with fatigue. At last he came upon Prasena's body, his horse lying dead beside it — but no jewel. Near them lay the lion, killed not by any hunter but by the great bear, and the truth of what had happened was written plainly in the tracks. Krishna followed them through the forest and up the mountain, until he stood before a vast den.

From inside came a woman's voice, gentle and unhurried — a nurse, playing with a child. "Do not weep," she was saying. "The lion killed Prasena, and the lion was killed by Jamvavan. This jewel belongs to you now." Krishna stood at the mouth of the den and understood the whole of it.

He left the Yadavas there, with Baladeva, at the entrance. Showing his face and speaking softly, with the Sharnga bow in his hand, he moved alone into the dark of the den, into the house of the bear-king. And there, in the belly of the mountain, Krishna wrestled with Jamvavan — without rest, day after day, for twenty-one days.

Above, the waiting ended. The Yadavas, headed by Baladeva, turned back to Dwaraka, and when they reached the city they announced what they believed: that Krishna had been slain. The rumor ran through the streets, and in the very city where the clan had whispered that he had stolen the jewel, the word now went around that he was dead.

But in the darkness under the mountain the struggle went on. Twenty-one days the bear-king and the man who had come for the jewel fought on, while above them the clans of Dwaraka were left with nothing but their suspicion, and their grief, and a treasure that belonged to neither.
stories.reflection: What damns Krishna in this episode is not evidence but appetite: the clan knows he wanted the jewel, and wanting is enough. He answers the accusation in the only way that can silence it — by going to recover the very thing he is suspected of stealing — and even then the story twists against him, so that the rumor that follows him into the den is not of guilt but of death.
stories.next_story_tease: But the recovered jewel would not end the trouble: before long it would turn Krishna's own brother against him.

stories.title: Balarama Departs to Mithila in Anger
stories.subtitle: Demanding the jewel Krishna does not have, his brother turns his back on Dwaraka
stories.story:
The quarrel began over a jewel that neither brother was holding.

By the time the Syamantaka's story reached this pass, the jewel had already cost a life. Krishna had recovered it from Jamvavan's den and had conferred it on Satrajit, whose daughter Satyabhama had become his wife. Then one night Shatadhanwa, a kinsman of the Bhoja line, murdered Satrajit in the dead hours — a crime in the dark of a kinsman's own city, the kind that sets every household of a clan on edge — and carried the jewel off, not for himself alone. He made a present of it to Akrura, who had long desired Satyabhama and the jewel both, and Akrura exacted from him a promise: he would never reveal where the jewel had gone. If Krishna attacked, Akrura swore, he would stand beside Shatadhanwa; the whole of Dwaraka, he said, was under his control.

Satyabhama, stricken with grief at her father's murder, came to her husband and told him everything that had been done, and stood weeping at his side. Krishna hurried to his elder brother Balarama. "Prasena was killed by a lion," he said, "and Satrajit has been slain by Shatadhanwa. The jewel is mine by right now. Mount your chariot — we will kill this Bhoja, and the Syamantaka will be ours."

There was a terrible encounter between Krishna and Shatadhanwa. Akrura, who could have helped the man he had sworn to stand beside, watched from nearby and, out of wickedness, did nothing. Fear seized Shatadhanwa and he fled on his mare Vijnatahridaya, a horse that could cover a hundred yojanas in a single stretch of running. Mounted on her he fought with Krishna as he fell back, and the chase carried them over plain and hill for all that distance, until at last the great mare, spent with exhaustion and misery, sank beneath her rider and her breath went up into the sky. Krishna turned to Balarama. "Wait here," he said. "I have seen the mare's wretched plight. I will go on foot, and I will carry away the jewel myself."

He walked on, caught Shatadhanwa on the road to Mithila, and killed him there. But when the fallen man was searched, the Syamantaka was not on him. Krishna came back to his brother with empty hands.

Balarama held out his hand. "Give me the jewel."

"I have not got it," said Krishna.

At that, Rama's anger broke. "Fie on you, fie on you!" he cried. "I forgive you because you are my brother. Farewell — I am going away. I have nothing to do with you, or with the Vrishnis of Dwaraka." And he turned and entered the city of Mithila.

The king of Mithila rose to receive him, honored him as he deserved, and pressed on him gifts after his own heart — feasts, honors, and presents chosen for the guest himself, until the angry visitor wanted for nothing. And among the princes who came to wait upon the famous guest was Duryodhana of the Kurus, and from Balabhadra, Duryodhana received the most excellent instruction in the use of clubs. Of all the honors paid to Balarama in Mithila, that lesson would be remembered longest of all.

But Dwaraka would not let the estrangement stand. All the mighty car-warriors of the Vrishni race gathered, and Krishna himself went at their head to Mithila to propitiate Balarama, and they brought him home to Dwaraka. The quarrel that had begun over a jewel no one could produce ended not with the jewel, but with the brothers together again.
stories.reflection: Balarama's anger is startling because it is so human: he demands from Krishna the very jewel Krishna went to recover, and when the answer is denial he walks away from his brother and his city over it. What repairs the breach is not proof of innocence but the clan's insistence on bringing him home — which suggests the quarrel was never really about the jewel at all.
stories.content_note: Includes Satrajit's murder in the night and Shatadhanwa's killing in pursuit; both are described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But Akrura, who knew where the jewel truly was, would soon carry that secret out of Dwaraka — and the rains would go with him.
stories.hero_scene: On the road before Mithila's gates, Balarama turns his back on Krishna with a furious gesture, walking away into the city, while Krishna stands behind him with empty hands.

stories.title: The Drought That Left with Akrura
stories.subtitle: After Akrura leaves Dwaraka, Indra withholds the rain; when he returns, the showers fall again
stories.story:
The rains stopped the day Akrura left Dwaraka, though no one in the city would have connected the two things at the time.

Akrura was the foremost of the Vrishnis, a man whose liberality was famous among the clans, and he carried a secret. When Shatadhanwa had murdered Satrajit and fled with the Syamantaka jewel, it was to Akrura that the treasure had been given; Akrura had bound the murderer to silence and kept the jewel hidden, and his own riches had grown, year after year, on the secret. Krishna suspected where the jewel lay, and the suspicion soured the air of Dwaraka. At last the estrangement broke open: Akrura, with the Andhakas, left the city. Krishna did not call him back — among the kinsmen it was said that the neglect was deliberate, a calculated breach meant to set the clans at odds — and the foremost man of the Vrishnis rode away into the west. The city watched him go, and told itself that the trouble had gone with him.

After his departure, the sky changed. Indra, the thousand-eyed, withheld the rain. The clouds came up from the sea and passed over the land, and Dwaraka's fields dried under an unchanged sun. The drought spread and bit deep: the earth cracked, the wells failed, the herds grew thin, and the whole country was devastated. The grain stores shrank, and the cattle stood listless in the empty riverbeds. Day after day the people watched the sky and found nothing in it but heat.

It was then that the Kukuras and Andhakas, the very clans who had let him go, turned back toward Akrura. They began to propitiate him — to send to him, to honor him, to call him home — having learned in their need what his presence had meant to the land. They sent their elders to find him, and offered him honor as one who carried the land's fortune with him. The old account does not explain why the sky had closed when he left; it records only the connection, as plainly as it records the drought.

When the liberal Akrura returned to Dwaraka, the change came at once. The thousand-eyed Indra began to pour showers down on the bank of the ocean, and the rain fell on the thirsty country as if the sky had been waiting for his coming. The drought ended as abruptly as it had begun, and the city breathed again. The rain came down on the shore first, and then over the city, and the smell of wet earth returned to Dwaraka.

With the rains came reconciliation. To please Krishna, the intelligent Akrura gave him his sister Sushila in marriage, binding the two houses together once more. And then, in the midst of the assembly of the clan, Krishna spoke. He had guessed the truth, he said, by Akrura's endless riches and his liberality — no man could give so freely without a hidden fountain behind his giving. "The jewel is in your keeping," Krishna told him. "Give it to me. Do not cheat me of it, O giver of honors. The anger that possessed me sixty years ago is now ended."

He did not speak as an accuser. He spoke as a kinsman closing an old account: the rain was falling, the brotherhood was whole, and the long anger was spent. Whether the jewel passed back into Krishna's hands that day, the sources do not say; what they record is the return, and the rain, and the words spoken in the assembly.
stories.reflection: The land's fortune is bound to a single man's presence: while Akrura was away the sky closed itself, and when he returned the rain came back to the ocean's edge. The story does not excuse his secret — but it insists that a community's wellbeing is tied to its members, and that reconciliation, not punishment, is what finally brings the rain.
stories.tradition_note: This drought episode appears only in the Harivamsha; the Bhagavata Purana does not tell it.
stories.next_story_tease: The jewel that had cost so much had not begun its life in Dwaraka at all — it had been a gift from the sun himself.
stories.hero_scene: Akrura riding back into Dwaraka as the first rain of the long-awaited monsoon breaks over the city and the ocean, while the Kukuras and Andhakas come out to meet him on the shore.

stories.title: The Sun's Gift to Satrajit
stories.subtitle: Surya gives his devotee the Syamantaka, a jewel that shines like a second sun
stories.story:
The people of Dwaraka saw the sun walking through their streets, and it was only Satrajit.

He came in from the coast in the early morning, and the jewel at his throat blazed so fiercely that anyone who looked at him from a distance felt his sight dim and blur. Children cried out, elders shaded their eyes, and for a moment the whole city believed that the sun-god himself had come down from the sky to walk among them. Then they saw that the blazing figure was Satrajit, their own kinsman, wearing on his breast a jewel that shone like a second sun. The wonder of it ran through Dwaraka before he had reached his own door. Word raced ahead of him through the streets: the sun has come down to Dwaraka.

The jewel was the Syamantaka, and it had come to Satrajit as a gift. He had worshipped the sun all his life, with a devotion so steady that the god had become his friend. The Harivamsha tells how it happened on the shore of the ocean: at dawn, when Satrajit went down to the water to bathe and offer his prayers, the sun-god stood before him in his own effulgent form — blazing, yet familiar, a friend paying a visit. "You have come to me as a friend," Satrajit said, "but I have received no gift from you. Give me the jewel with which you light the worlds." And the sun took the Syamantaka from his own neck and placed it in Satrajit's hands. The king carried it back to the city with the light of the sky at his throat, and the people followed him through the streets, certain they were watching the sun itself go by.

The Bhagavata Purana tells the same gift more briefly: pleased with his devotee Satrajit, the sun-god gave him the jewel, and the dazzled citizens, seeing him blaze, were certain the sun was abroad in their streets. However it is told, the result was the same. Wearing it, Satrajit shone like the sun; and the jewel was no mere ornament. Each day it yielded eight loads of gold, and while it remained in Dwaraka the city knew no calamity — no disease, no misfortune, no fear. In the older telling, gold welled up in the palaces of the Vrishnis and Andhakas while the jewel was among them, and the rains came in their season.

The splendor of the Syamantaka filled the city with wonder, and with something else. Among those who looked on it was Krishna, and he grew desirous of the peerless jewel. He was capable of taking it — there was no one in Dwaraka who could have stopped him — yet he did not take it by force, and he did not steal it. He simply wanted it; and in a city of kinsmen who could read one another's hearts, wanting was as visible as wearing. He spoke of the jewel openly, as a man speaks of what he admires, and the clan heard the want in his voice.

In time Satrajit, delighted with his treasure, conferred the jewel on his brother Prasena, who wore it proudly wherever he went. And a treasure that shone like the sun could not be hidden, and could not be kept quiet. The Syamantaka had come to Dwaraka as a gift of light; it was about to become the most desired, and the most dangerous, thing in the city.
stories.reflection: The Syamantaka is a gift of pure light: it dazzles, it enriches, it protects. Yet the very splendor that made it a blessing made it a danger — wealth that shines draws every eye, and the jewel that lit Dwaraka would soon light the desires of those who wanted it.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha tells the gift in greater detail — the sun appearing to Satrajit on the ocean bank at dawn — while the Bhagavata Purana records it in a single stroke; the two accounts agree on the essential fact of the gift.
stories.next_story_tease: Not long after, Prasena would ride out into the forest wearing the jewel on his breast — and the forest would keep him.
stories.hero_scene: Satrajit walking through the streets of Dwaraka blazing like the sun itself, the Syamantaka at his throat, while citizens shield their eyes and bow, mistaking him for the sun-god come down to earth.

stories.title: The Rumor Against Krishna
stories.story:
The Syamantaka had been in Dwaraka only a few seasons, and already it had changed how the city kept account of its people. The jewel — a gift of the sun god — was said to fill its owner's coffers with gold, to summon rain in its season, to keep disease from the house that held it. Everyone knew where it had come to rest: around the neck of Satrajit, a noble of the Yadu clan, who walked through Dwaraka glowing like a second sun.

Krishna asked for the jewel. He did not demand it, though he could have taken it; he did not scheme for it; he simply asked. Satrajit refused. He was a covetous man, and the Syamantaka was the finest thing he had ever owned, and he could not bear to part with it. Krishna let the matter rest. But the refusal did not rest; it lay in the city's memory like a seed, and the seed had ears.

Then Prasena went hunting. Prasena was Satrajit's brother, and one morning he rode out into the forest wearing the Syamantaka at his throat. He did not ride back. A lion had brought him down — killed him and his horse together — and then the lion itself had been struck dead in turn, by a great bear, who took the jewel from the kill and carried it into the mountains.

When the news reached Dwaraka, no one spoke of lions or bears. The city remembered that Krishna had asked for the Syamantaka and had been refused, and a whisper began to move through the streets like wind through standing grain: Krishna had killed Prasena. He had wanted the jewel; now Prasena was dead and the jewel was gone; who else could have done it? The whisper grew, and every retelling sharpened it.

Krishna heard what the city was saying. He did not rage, and he did not answer with speeches. He knew he was innocent, and he knew that words would not prove it — only the jewel would. "I must bring the jewel," he resolved, and with his followers he set out for the forest where Prasena had gone.

The trail was written plainly on the earth for anyone who knew how to read it. Krishna followed the tracks of horse and rider through the forest, up into the Rikshavan mountains and across the flanks of the Vindhya ranges, searching every path and hollow until weariness began to pull at his limbs. Then he found Prasena — Prasena and his horse, both dead in a clearing, and no jewel on either. Near them lay the lion, killed by something greater than itself. The footprints around the kill told the rest of the story: a bear had taken the jewel from the lion's body and carried it away.

Krishna followed the bear's trail to the mouth of a den in the mountainside — a vast, dark opening that breathed cold air. From inside came a woman's voice, low and coaxing, the way a nurse speaks to a child. She was playing with the jewel, offering it to a little one, saying, "Do not weep." Then her words floated out of the den, and Krishna heard the whole truth of what had happened in the forest: "The lion killed Prasena, and the lion was killed by Jambavan. So do not weep, my good boy — this Syamantaka belongs to you."

There it was. No one in Dwaraka had spoken a word in Krishna's defense, but the den had just cleared his name: the bear king Jambavan had taken the jewel from the lion, and the jewel now lay in the hands of Jambavan's own cub, kept as a plaything.

Krishna left Balarama and the Yadavas at the mouth of the den. Then, alone and silent, his bow in his hand, he stepped into the darkness. The rumor had driven him out of Dwaraka. The truth was waiting for him inside.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer to the rumor is not a defense but a search: he lets the truth travel the same ground the accusation did, from the city to the forest to the den, and it vindicates him without a single argument. The city was ready to believe the worst; the evidence was ready to prove otherwise.
stories.next_story_tease: In the darkness of the den, the king of bears rose to meet him.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, alone at the mouth of Jambavan's vast dark den, stepping into the shadows with his bow in hand while Balarama and the Yadavas wait behind him at the entrance.

stories.title: Krishna Wrestles Jambavan for the Jewel
stories.story:
There was a jewel called Syamantaka, a gift of the Sun himself, so bright that it lit whatever room it entered like a lamp and drew the eye of every man who saw it. It had come into the keeping of a Yadava named Prasena, a man to whom the Sun had been a friend as dear as life. The Sun, appearing before him, had taken the jewel from his own neck and placed it in Prasena's hands, and its light had made Prasena a wonder in his own city. One day Prasena went out with the jewel and did not come back. In the forest they found him, and his horse beside him, both killed by a lion — and the jewel was gone.

Then the ill report began to spread through Dwaraka, quietly at first and then aloud. The jewel, men whispered, had gone into the keeping of Krishna. It was the kind of rumor that spreads in a city where a great man lives — easier to believe than to question, and hard to shake off once it has settled. His name was stained with it, and he could not let it stand. To clear himself, he went out to find the truth.

He traced Prasena's trail into the forest and found the man and his horse, slain by the lion. But the trail did not end at the body. He read the broken branches and the marks of hooves, and followed them on through the trees, where the light grew thin and the birds fell silent, until the ground opened into the mouth of a dark and terrible cave — the den of Jambavan, the king of the bears. Krishna entered it, and there in the dimness he saw the Syamantaka itself, the priceless, sun-bright jewel, lying where it had been tossed aside as a plaything for a child.

A nurse keeping watch over the cave saw this strange man standing in the bear's den and cried out in fear. At the sound, Jambavan came charging from the dark and threw himself upon Krishna, and the two began to fight, each resolved to win.

It was no brief contest. For twenty-eight days they wrestled, fist against fist, night and day without rest. The cave shook with it, and neither of them would yield. There was no audience and no reprieve, only the two of them and the thunder of their blows. Day followed day in the dark, and they fought on, locked together, while outside the world went about its business unaware. Krishna's blows fell like thunderbolts, and slowly the old bear's limbs and joints were crushed beneath them, until Jambavan could barely stand.

And in his exhaustion, Jambavan suddenly understood who stood before him. “I know you,” he said. “You are the life and strength and power of all living things — the maker of the makers of the world. By the glance of your anger the ocean once churned; by you the bridge was built and Lanka set ablaze; the heads of the rakshasas fell before your arrows.” The old bear had known this Lord in another age, and he knew him now.

The fight was over. Krishna laid his hand gently on the bear-king and said, “We have come to this cave for the jewel, O king of bears.” And Jambavan, his anger gone, rose and gave Krishna the Syamantaka, and with it his own daughter, the maiden Jambavati, to be his wife. So Krishna came out of the dark cave into the light of day, the jewel glowing in his hands, and turned toward Dwaraka — and the truth went before him, so that no one there could ever say again that the jewel had been taken by his hand.
stories.reflection: The story turns on a strange resolution: the accusation Krishna refuses to answer with denials he answers by walking into the dark and finding the truth. The fight itself becomes a kind of recognition — only when Jambavan is spent does he see who has been wrestling with him, and an enemy yields at once a vindication and a wife.
stories.tradition_note: The duration of the wrestling differs between sources: the Bhagavata gives twenty-eight days, the Harivamsha twenty-one. This telling follows the Bhagavata.
stories.hero_scene: In the dim mouth of a cave, Krishna and the towering bear-king Jambavan are locked together in a wrestling hold, while the bright Syamantaka jewel lies glowing on the cave floor behind them.

stories.title: Krishna Returns the Jewel and Clears His Name
stories.story:
Dwaraka had given Krishna up for dead. He had walked into the bear king's den and not come out, and the days had passed, and the city had begun to mourn. Devaki and Rukmini wept for him; and the people of Dwaraka, in their grief, turned on Satrajit — it was his refusal, they said, that had sent Krishna into the forest after the jewel, and his pride that had cost the city its prince. From every quarter, citizens cursed the man who had once been the envy of them all, and the curses followed him through the streets he had once walked in triumph.

Then Krishna came home, as if risen from the dead. He emerged from the forest with the Syamantaka restored and a bride at his side — Jambavati, the daughter of the bear king who had kept the jewel. The city that had mourned him filled the streets to see him return, and the talk that had cursed Satrajit fell quiet, waiting to see what Krishna would do.

What he did was summon an assembly. In the presence of the king, before all of Dwaraka, Krishna told the whole story in order: how Prasena had fallen to the lion, how the lion had fallen to the bear, how the jewel had gone into the bear king's den and been given to his cub as a plaything, and how Krishna had entered the den and wrestled Jambavan day after day in the dark, until the bear king yielded both the jewel and his daughter in marriage. He held nothing back, and he asked nothing for himself.

Then he took the Syamantaka and placed it before Satrajit, and gave the jewel back to its owner — the very stone he had asked for once and been refused, now returned without a word of reproach.

The assembly went silent. Every whisper that had followed Krishna — that he had killed Prasena, that the jewel had been his true motive, that a man who wanted a thing that much could not be trusted — had been answered, not with denials but with the jewel itself, carried back across the mountains and laid at the feet of the very man who had refused him. Satrajit took the Syamantaka with his face bowed, deeply ashamed. He had suspected Krishna, had denied him, and now Krishna had returned the jewel to him freely, before the whole city.

Shame turned to resolution. Satrajit thought of the enmity his refusal had caused, of the curses the city had heaped on his name, of his brother dead in the forest, and of what he could do that would ever undo it. He could not give back the dead, and he could not silence the talk with words. But he could give everything he had left. He offered Krishna his daughter — Satyabhama, a jewel among women — and with her, the Syamantaka itself, both together as reparation.

Krishna accepted Satyabhama and married her according to the rites, before the same assembly that had watched his name be cleared. But the jewel he refused. "We do not accept the jewel, O king," he said. He had not crossed mountains and wrestled a bear king to own the Syamantaka; he had gone to clear his name, and his name was clear. The jewel had come from the sun, and it belonged with the man the sun had chosen to hold it.

So Satrajit stood in the assembly with the jewel in his hands and his daughter married to the man he had wronged — richer in kinship than he had ever been in gold, and, for the first time in months, at peace.
stories.reflection: Krishna accepts the bride but refuses the jewel — the very prize he had once asked for. By the end, possession has ceased to matter: the Syamantaka's only value was the truth it could prove, and once the truth was out, the jewel could go home. Satrajit's gift is an apology in the only coin he had left.
stories.next_story_tease: But there were men in Dwaraka who still wanted the Syamantaka — and one of them had already begun to plan.
