stories.title: Satadhanva Murders Satrajit for the Jewel
stories.story:
Krishna was away from Dwaraka, visiting the elders of the Kuru court in Hastinapura, when the plan was made. In his absence two men of the city found their moment — Akrura and Kritavarma, who had watched Satrajit's fortunes rise with the Syamantaka and had never forgiven him for it. Akrura had long wished for Satyabhama herself, and once the jewel came to Satrajit's keeping he had begun to desire that as well; the beautiful daughter and the brilliant stone, he felt, had both been denied him unfairly. Satrajit had broken his word to them, they claimed; he had promised them a jewel among women and then scorned them, and now the Syamantaka hung around his neck while they went without. Envy, in Dwaraka, had learned to dress itself as a broken promise.

They did not act with their own hands. They found Satadhanva, of the Bhoja line, a man of strength and little conscience, and they put the thought into him as one sharpens a blade and hands it over. Satrajit had broken his word, they said; the jewel should be seized; the deed would be easy, and the reward beyond price. Satadhanva listened. He was a man who had always wanted what belonged to others, and the Syamantaka was the most beautiful thing in Dwaraka.

That night, while the city slept, he crept into Satrajit's house. He slew the sleeping Satrajit, took the jewel from its place, and was gone before the household could gather itself. The women of the house cried out into the empty dark like orphans, their wailing swallowed by the stillness of the night, but the deed was done. The city's wealthiest man lay dead, and the Syamantaka had changed hands for the second time.

Satadhanva did not keep the jewel for himself. He carried it to Akrura — the man who had always wished for Satyabhama and had long desired the jewel as well — and Akrura received the Syamantaka as his due. But he was a cautious man. He made Satadhanva swear he would never reveal where the jewel had gone, and he promised in return: "If Krishna attacks you, I will follow you. The whole of Dwaraka is now under my control." So the oath bound the two of them together — the murderer and the man who had set him on, each holding the other's secret, each believing himself the cleverer.

Through the long night the Syamantaka lay hidden in Akrura's keeping, and in Satrajit's house the women wept. By morning the theft was known and the murderer was not — the jewel had simply vanished with the life it had cost. Only two men in Dwaraka knew where it was, and they had sworn to carry the secret to their graves.

But the house they had robbed was not empty. Satrajit had a daughter, and she was already making ready for the road.
stories.reflection: The murder is dressed in grievance — a broken promise, a seized prize — but underneath it is simple greed: Akrura wanted what Satrajit had, and Satadhanva was willing to take it for him. The jewel that had raised Satrajit's fortunes drew the blade that ended them; nothing about the Syamantaka ever stayed neutral.
stories.content_note: Satrajit is murdered in his sleep; the violence is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: Satyabhama would find her father before the city did — and her grief would carry the truth to Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: At dead of night, Satadhanva moving through the dark house of Satrajit with the Syamantaka in his hand, the city asleep outside and the deed already done.

stories.title: Satyabhama Reports Her Father's Murder
stories.subtitle: She finds her father slain and hastens to Hastinapura to tell Krishna, who laments with Balarama.
stories.story:
Satrajit's daughter found him first. Morning came into the house, and Satyabhama found her father dead — slain in the night, the Syamantaka gone from its place. She cried out, "Father, father!" and the sound of her own voice told her it was true; she felt herself slain along with him, as though the grief had cut her down where she stood. For a long moment the world was only the body on the floor and the emptiness where the jewel had been.

But the shock did not leave her helpless. Her husband was far away in Hastinapura, the city of the elephant, and the man who had done this had the whole night's start on her. There was no time to wait for the city to wake and the rites to be prepared. So Satyabhama did for her father what could be done: she laid his body in a great vat of oil, to keep it safe until proper rites could be performed, and then she left Dwaraka and rode for Hastinapura. The road was long, and she rode it as though the news would spoil in her keeping — as though, if she reached her husband quickly enough, the telling would hurt less. The dust of the road rose around her, and she did not slow for it. When the gates of Hastinapura finally rose before her, she passed through them without stopping, and asked for her husband before she had even caught her breath.

She found Krishna and told him everything — how Satadhanva had come in the night, how her father lay dead in Dwaraka, how the Syamantaka had been taken from the house, and how she had left the body in oil and ridden through the dust to bring the word herself. Standing by his side, she wept; and Krishna heard the news, and the news broke him too. He who had held the world's sorrows in his hands wept for this one as though it were the only grief that had ever touched him.

He grieved, and Balarama grieved with him. The two lords, who held the worlds in their keeping, wept for their kinsman — following the ways of human beings, mourning as a son-in-law and a brother mourn. There was nothing distant about that weeping, and everything human in it; the lords of the universe grieved with the same tears as any family in Dwaraka that morning.

The mourning did not last long. When it was done, something else had entered Krishna's eyes — the quiet of a man who has been handed a name he will not forget. Satadhanva had taken a life and a jewel. He would be allowed to keep neither.
stories.reflection: The detail that Krishna and Balarama wept "following human ways" is the heart of the episode — the lords of the universe grieve without distance, as any family would. Satyabhama's journey carries the story forward: she becomes the bearer of her own loss, and the grief she brings will not go unanswered.
stories.next_story_tease: When the mourning was over, Krishna and Balarama set out in pursuit of Satadhanva.

stories.title: A Hundred Yojanas and No Jewel
stories.story:
Satadhanva rode as if the road were endless and the distance nothing. His mare, Vijnatahridaya, could carry him a hundred yojanas without rest, and behind him came the two men he feared most in the world: Krishna and Balarama, bent on avenging the murder of Satrajit and recovering the Syamantaka jewel.

Days earlier, Satyabhama had returned to her father's house to find him slain in the night, and the great jewel — the same gem Krishna had once bestowed on Satrajit — was gone from his home. Every sign pointed to Satadhanva of the Bhoja race, and there was no time for counsel: Krishna and Balarama mounted their chariot and gave chase at once, determined to run the killer down before he could reach a friendly court and slip beyond their reach.

The flight took them beyond the borders of the Vrishni lands and onto the long roads that led toward Mithila. A hundred yojanas the mare covered, mile after mile, with the brothers pressing close behind, and the road itself grew strange to them — for neither had ever had cause to ride so far from Dwaraka before. But no creature can outrun exhaustion forever. At last, in a grove on the approach to Mithila, Vijnatahridaya stumbled and stood motionless, her strength spent, her breath failing; and there the rider and the horse came to a stop, with the chariot still closing in.

Krishna looked at the trembling mare and turned to his brother. "Wait here," he said. "I will go on foot and take the jewel from him myself." Balarama held the chariot, and Krishna went forward alone, on foot, with the discus in his hand — the same discus that had ended the lives of greater demons than Satadhanva.

The fugitive had no fight left in him. Krishna overtook him on the outskirts of Mithila and struck him down with the discus, and the murderer of Satrajit was dead, cut down in the very field where he had hoped to find safety. Krishna bent over the body and searched it. He searched the folds of the fallen man's garments and the saddle of the dying mare. There was no jewel. The Syamantaka was not on Satadhanva.

Krishna returned to his brother with empty hands. "Give me the jewel," said Balarama, and Krishna answered simply: "I have not got it."

The words fell between the two brothers like a stone. Balarama's face darkened, and his anger rose as it rarely did. "Fie on you, fie on you," he said. "I forgive you because you are my brother. But I will go away from here. I have nothing more to do with you, or with the Vrishnis of Dwaraka." And with that, the elder brother turned his back on the chariot and entered the city of Mithila alone.

There King Janaka received him with honor, rising from his seat at the sight of the beloved guest and loading him with gifts worthy of a king's affection. Balarama stayed on in Mithila for months, and in that time he found a pupil: the young prince Duryodhana of Hastinapura, who had come to Janaka's court and received from Balarama the finest instruction in the use of the mace that any teacher could give.

Krishna returned to Dwaraka alone, the murderer punished and the jewel still lost. The pursuit that had begun with a murdered father-in-law ended with a dead fugitive, a parted brother, and a gem that seemed to have vanished into thin air. Somewhere in Dwaraka, someone was keeping a secret about the Syamantaka — and Krishna, who knew all things, had already begun to suspect where the jewel had truly gone.
stories.reflection: The chase that spans a hundred yojanas ends in nothing: the killer is dead, but the jewel is not on him, and Balarama walks away rather than ride home empty-handed beside his brother. Krishna's pursuit was just, yet justice alone does not return what was stolen — the story turns on the gap between punishing the thief and recovering the loss.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata has Balarama simply go on to Mithila to visit King Janaka, his dearest friend; the Harivamsha presents the parting as a rift, with Balarama angry that Krishna could not produce the jewel. Both agree that Satadhanva was killed near Mithila and that no jewel was found.
stories.next_story_tease: Somewhere in Dwaraka, a secret was being kept about the missing jewel.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, alone on foot on the road near Mithila, his discus back in his hand, standing over the fallen Satadhanva beside the collapsed mare, while Balarama waits far behind with the chariot.

stories.title: The Jewel in Akrura's Keeping
stories.story:
The rains stopped when Akrura left Dwaraka, and they returned when he came back — or so the old men said, and the Kukuras and Andhakas, watching the earth grow dry and the sky harden, were ready to believe it. Krishna had come home from Mithila with the killer of Satrajit dead and the Syamantaka jewel still missing, and in the weeks that followed he had seen to it that the fallen Satadhanva received the rites due to the dead, for even an enemy of the Bhoja line was kin to Dwaraka's house. But the jewel was the thing the city spoke of in whispers. Satadhanva had died with empty hands; the gem had not been on him. So where was it?

Krishna, who knew all things, had asked himself the same question — and he had found the answer in a promise made in the dark. Satadhanva had not acted alone. The night Satrajit was slain, the jewel had passed from the killer's hands into the keeping of Akrura, who had sworn to the dying thief that he would never reveal what he held.

And Akrura had kept his word so well that his prosperity itself gave him away. He had thrown himself into a vast undertaking, gathering jewels and goods for a sacrifice so long and so lavish that men called it the Akrura Yajna, and he had entered a vow of armor as though expecting danger. To most of Dwaraka it was the piety of a great lord; to Krishna it was a confession in another language.

Now Krishna did what he always did with secrets: he brought them into the light. He honored Akrura before the assembly, greeted him with friendship, and spoke to him of old times; and then, gently, he put the matter before him. "O lord of gifts," he said, "was the jewel not entrusted to you by Satadhanva? Satrajit had no son, so the gem would pass to his daughter's sons; yet no one else can hold it. Let it rest with you, virtuous one — but show it to the kinsmen, and bring peace to this house."

And Akrura, moved by the gentleness of the words, brought out the Syamantaka and showed it to the assembled kinsmen. Krishna held the jewel up before them all, letting its light fall on every face, and the stain of suspicion that had clung to him since Satrajit's death — the whispered talk that he had taken the gem for himself — dissolved in that light. Then he returned the jewel to Akrura, who received it back with wonder; and the Harivamsha records that Krishna gave it up with a delighted heart, as though the treasure had never been the point at all.

The city breathed again. Balarama, who had been living in Mithila in high honor as King Janaka's guest, was brought home by the car-warriors of the Vrishni race, with Krishna himself among those who went to fetch him; and brother and brother were reconciled. Akrura, confirmed in Krishna's friendship, gave his own sister Sushila to Krishna in marriage. The rains, the old men noted with satisfaction, continued to fall.

The Syamantaka had returned to Dwaraka — not to Krishna's keeping, but to the man who had hidden it, trusted because he had been trusted.
stories.reflection: Krishna's way with the jewel is characteristic: he does not seize it or expose the hider. He asks, in public, with honor intact, and lets the truth do the work — clearing his own name not by force but by bringing the secret into the light, then giving the treasure back so that reconciliation matters more than possession.
stories.tradition_note: In the Harivamsha, Akrura had long coveted the jewel and had sworn to Satadhanva never to reveal where it lay; Krishna returns it to him with a delighted heart, and Akrura seals the reconciliation by giving his sister Sushila in marriage.
stories.next_story_tease: But while the jewel was being restored, a demon far to the east was stealing the earrings of the mother of the gods.
stories.hero_scene: In the assembly of Dwaraka, Krishna holds up the Syamantaka jewel for all his kinsmen to see, its light falling across their faces, while Akrura stands quietly at his side.

stories.title: Indra's Plea at Dwaraka
stories.story:
The wind that afternoon carried a fragrance no garden of Dwaraka had ever produced, and flowers fell from a sky that had been clear a moment before. In the great assembly hall called Dasharha — whose golden doors opened onto a courtyard a full yojana across — the leading Yadavas sat at their daily business. Then a great noise filled the air, and through a net of light they saw the king of the gods descending on his white elephant Airavata, the celestials gathered about him.

Rama and Krishna went out at once, with King Ugrasena and the chiefs of the Vrishni and Andhaka houses, to receive him. Indra came down from the elephant, embraced Krishna and Balarama and the king in order of age and rank, and, honored by both brothers, entered the hall and accepted the offerings of hospitality. When he was seated, he reached out and touched Krishna's face with his hand — the auspicious countenance of his younger brother, as the old telling has it — and he spoke.

"By you, Madhusudana," said Indra, "the world's oppressors have fallen one by one — Arishta, Dhenuka, Chanura, Mushtika, Kesin, Kamsa, Kuvalayapida, and the child-killer Putana. By your valor the three worlds are preserved, and the gods receive their share of the sacrifices. But hear now why I have come. The demon Naraka, son of the Earth, king of Pragjyotisha, has grown swollen with a boon granted him by Brahma. He has stolen the earrings of my mother Aditi, which drip nectar. He has taken Varuna's umbrella, which no water can wet, and the jewel-crest of Mount Mandara. He has carried off the maidens of gods, saints, demons, and kings — sixteen thousand and a hundred of them, wearing a single braid — and shut them in a house he built for them on Mount Mani. And now, O Govinda, he demands my elephant Airavata."

The hall was silent. Indra went on: "He is unslayable by any creature — but not by you, O Upendra. Garuda will bear you to his city. Slay the sinful wretch, and come back."

Krishna smiled gently. He rose from his throne, took Indra by the hand, and thought of Garuda; and the great bird, who could range anywhere and take on any strength, was there in the courtyard. Krishna seated Satyabhama on his back, mounted behind her, and rose into the sky, turning east toward Pragjyotisha, where razor-edged nooses defended the demon's walls and four terrible guardians — Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada, and Muru with his thousand sons — kept watch. Indra mounted Airavata and, in the sight of all Dwaraka, returned to the abode of the gods.

The city stood looking after them: the lord of Dwaraka flying out to war with his queen at his back, against a demon who had robbed the mother of the gods — and who would soon learn that Brahma's boon had a limit.
stories.reflection: The king of the gods does not come to Dwaraka as a commander but as a supplicant, listing the oppressors Krishna has already removed and then naming the one he cannot. Indra's visit makes plain what the Yadavas have always suspected: their city is where heaven itself sends its hardest battles.
stories.next_story_tease: But before the demon's fall, a quiet gift at a mountain festival would stir a storm in Krishna's own household.

stories.title: A Flower for Rukmini
stories.story:
Mount Raivataka had never seen such a gathering. Krishna had come there with Rukmini for the festival that closed the vow she had undertaken, and with them had come his sixteen thousand wives, each in splendor befitting her rank, along with his sons and brothers, who had been sent on ahead by Narada's own arrangement. For days the mountain had rung with the sounds of giving: the twice-born received what they desired, beggars were loaded with gifts, and those who kept religious rites went away satisfied. Krishna, the lord of subdued senses, gratified everyone who sought his goodwill, and at the end of the fasting he honored Rukmini, the daughter of Bhishmaka, before them all.

While he sat there with Rukmini at his side, encircled by the other queens, the ascetic Narada arrived. Krishna rose and received the sage with the rites laid down in the scriptures; and Narada, adored in turn, gave his host a single flower — a blossom of the Parijata, the heavenly coral tree, which no earthly garden could ever produce.

Krishna took the flower, and because Rukmini sat beside him, he placed it in her hand. She understood at once; raising the blossom, she set it in her hair, and the daughter of Bhishmaka — already the very collection of the beauties of the three worlds — was doubly beautiful with the celestial flower among her tresses.

Then Narada spoke, and his words were a praise of Rukmini and of the flower he had brought. It never withers, he said; for a full year it breathes whatever fragrance she wishes. It gives heat and cold as she desires, and from it flow juices of every taste. Whatever flowers she longs for, the Parijata will give her; whatever color she wishes to see, it will assume; it will grow thin or plump at her will. It serves her as a lamp in the night, drives off unwholesome smells, and grants her garlands of Santanaka flowers and garments that never decay. When she wishes, it sings with musical instruments; and it keeps hunger, thirst, and weariness far from her. It is the root of good luck and of piety, and it will not let the mind that wins it wander toward any evil path. Only when a year is complete will it leave her — for such is its nature, ordained by the Creator — and even the wives of the gods, Uma and Aditi and Sachi and Savitri and Sri herself, wear it for no longer than a year.

Then came the words that changed the mood of the gathering. "O goddess," said Narada, turning to Rukmini, "among the sixteen thousand wives of Vasudeva, I consider you the foremost and the most beloved."

The queens around them heard it. Some bowed their heads; others felt the praise land like a blow, and the bright air of Raivataka turned a shade cooler for them. Rukmini kept the flower in her hair, and the festival went on. But the flower, which never withered, had been given its year; and the words of the sage, which never fade, had been spoken once — and would be remembered longer than any blossom.
stories.reflection: Narada's gift honors Rukmini, but the praise is public, delivered before all sixteen thousand queens, and the episode quietly sets the stage for the jealousy that follows. The flower is described as inexhaustible in its powers yet limited to a single year — a reminder that even heaven's gifts are bounded, while the words spoken over them are not.
stories.next_story_tease: But in another part of the mountain, a proud queen had heard every word.

stories.title: The Queen Who Cast Off Her Jewels
stories.story:
Every ornament she owned lay in a heap at her feet. Satyabhama had barely let her maids finish their report before her hands were at her clasps, and now the necklaces and bangles that had gleamed on her at dawn lay discarded on the floor, and she had shut herself into the loneliest room in the mansion.

The festival at Mount Raivataka had been for Rukmini. Krishna had brought his first wife there for the ceremony that ended her vow — a great gathering in which he had satisfied the twice-born Brahmins with every desired object, given to the beggars, to those who practiced religious rites, and to all who sought his well-being, and had honored his kinsmen according to their rank. To it had come all his sixteen thousand wives, each with the splendour befitting her station, and on the day the fasting ended, the Lord had honored his beloved Rukmini, the daughter of Bhishmaka, before them all.

It was there that the sage Narada had arrived, and Krishna had adored him with rites laid down in the scriptures. The sage, pleased, had given Krishna a single Parijata flower, and Krishna — Rukmini at his side — had passed it to her. Following her husband's hint, that blameless lady had set the celestial flower in her hair, and Narada had declared her worthy of it: the flower never withered, it gave fragrance for a full year, it granted heat and cold as the wearer wished, it served as a lamp at night, it could assume whatever color she desired, it gave garlands of Santanaka flowers and undecaying clothes at a thought, and it sang songs to good music when she wished it. The goddesses of heaven themselves — Sachi, Aditi, Savitri, Uma — wore such flowers, though even for them the flower's stay lasted no more than a year.

And in another mansion on the same hill, Satyabhama's maids had brought her the news, word for word. The daughter of Satrajit was proud, and her pride stood on a single foundation: that she was the wife Krishna loved best. Now a flower from the gardens of heaven had been set on Rukmini's head, and the greatest of sages had praised the co-wife in her husband's presence, and the whole festival had turned on a fortune that belonged to someone else. The accession of such good fortune to the other wife of her husband was more than she could bear. Worked up with anger like the flame of fire, the proud queen rose, cast off her ornaments where she stood, and retired to the apartment of anger — the room kept in the mansion for exactly such a mood, as if the palace itself expected this of its queens.

She sat there in the midst of her handmaids, who knelt silent and did not dare to speak. Through the windows the sounds of the festival drifted up the hill — the songs, the blessings of the Brahmins, the laughter of guests who had come to honor a happiness that was not hers. The apartment of anger was far from all of it. There Satyabhama sat, her jewel boxes empty, her anger burning slowly like a fire that has been fed and left to itself.

She did not know — how could she? — that in the hall below, Krishna had already noticed her absence from the circle of his wives. The festival went on without her; the praises of Rukmini continued. But the queen who had cast off her ornaments sat waiting in her anger, and it was only a matter of time before someone who loved her came looking for her.
stories.reflection: Satyabhama's jealousy is the shadow side of her love: she measures Krishna's regard by what can be seen, and a flower on another queen's head becomes a verdict on her own worth. The pride of being loved best is a fragile crown, and this is the first moment it slips — a small, human crack in the grandeur of Dwaraka.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna, reading the storm in her silence, slipped away from the festival toward her mansion.

stories.title: The Fan and the Falling Tears
stories.story:
Krishna read the change in the air before anyone spoke of it. Narada was still seated with Rukmini, the sage's voice still praising the flower, but one face was missing from the circle of his wives, and he knew, as he knew everything, where it had gone. Under some pretext he rose and left the festival.

His steps carried him quickly toward the spacious mansion on the Raivataka hills that Vishvakarma himself had built for Satyabhama. He was aware, as he walked, that the daughter of Satrajit — dearer to him than his own vital breaths — was under the influence of jealous resentment, and the slayer of Madhu went the slower for it, with greater fear. He left Pradyumna to entertain and attend upon Narada, told his servant Daruka to wait at the gate, and entered the palace alone.

From a distance he saw her, inside the apartment of anger, in the midst of her handmaids, sighing hot and frequently. She laughed a derisive laugh mixed with sighs at a lotus she had brought near her own lotus-like face and was nipping with her nails. Sometimes she described figures on the ground with the tip of her slightly bent toe. Sometimes she sat in deep thought, her face resting on her left palm. Sometimes she took the sandal from her maids' hands, smeared it on her breast, and then cruelly threw it aside. She rose from her bed and fell into it again. He watched all of this — the theater of a woman who wanted to be angry at the one man she loved — and did not announce himself.

Then she laid her head on her pillow, drawing her veil over her face, and Krishna thought: this is my opportunity. By signs he commanded the handmaids not to speak of him. With faltering steps he approached Satyabhama, took up the fan, and standing by her side began to fan slowly, and to laugh gently.

His contact with the Parijata flower had perfumed him, and the fragrance spread through the chamber — divine, supernatural, rare. Satyabhama smelled it and was taken with admiration. She uncovered her face. "What is this?" Rising from her bed, without bestowing a single glance on her godly husband, she began to question her maids about the cause of the fragrance. The maids could say nothing; they knelt on the ground with their faces to the earth and their palms joined in supplication. Not finding the source, Satyabhama wondered whether the earth herself had emitted one of her excellent scents. Then, looking on all sides, her glance suddenly lighted on Kesava, the creator of the worlds.

"Ah! right," she said — and suddenly her eyes were dimmed with tears, the intensity of love filling her all the more with jealous anger. With her delicate lips pouting and herself sighing, she turned her downcast countenance away in another direction and remained so for a while. Then, contracting her brows in a disapproving frown and placing her face on her palms, she said to Hari with her eyes upraised: "Thou lookest beautiful." The tears of jealous passion flowed down from her eyes like drops of dew falling from a pair of lotus petals.

The lotus-eyed Krishna, seeing the tears stream down his wife's lotus-like face, approached her in haste and held them in his hands. Wiping with his own hands the tears that were falling on her breast, the wearer of the Srivatsa mark spoke gently. Why did tears flow from her eyes like dew from a pair of lotuses? Why did her face and body wear the look of the full moon in the morning sky, or the full-blown lotus at noon? Why, today, did she wear plain white garments and not the ones sprinkled with safflower and gold-dust that she loved — white being the dress ladies wear only when they worship the gods?

And then his protest, the whole answer to everything she had not yet said: "Just as flame is in fire, so my love resides in thee, and thee only."
stories.reflection: Krishna does not meet Satyabhama's jealousy with correction or a defense of his conduct; he slips past her guards, takes up the fan, and asks her why she is sad — the question of a lover, not a lord. The protest that his love dwells in her alone is all the more tender for coming while she is still turned away, still unwilling to look at him.
stories.next_story_tease: The flower, it turned out, was not the wound; the wound was being left out — and Krishna answered it with a promise far larger than a single flower.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, fan in hand, catching Satyabhama's falling tears in his cupped hands as she sits on the edge of her bed with her face turned away and half-hidden in her veil, her handmaids kneeling silent with joined palms in the shadowed apartment of anger.

stories.title: The Promise of the Whole Tree
stories.story:
Then Krishna asked her to name the thing itself. Sitting close to his queen, who still would not lift her eyes from the ground, he said that her sorrow seemed to burn through all his limbs. What was the cause of her grief? If there was no harm in it, if it was proper for an affectionate husband to hear it, he entreated her on his life to reveal it to him.

And Satyabhama, seated with her countenance cast down toward the earth, spoke in a voice choked with the vapour of grief. "It was your own self that established my honor and my prosperity in days gone by," she said, "and that honor and that prosperity have become famous in the world. That I was most beloved of thee among all thy wives — that is what prompted me to raise my head with pride above all others. But my maids have told me, as they have heard it said, that today I have been laughed at by my co-wives and by other people. I hear that the Parijata flower that Narada gave thee, thou hast given to thy dear one, totally neglecting my poor self. By presenting her with that best of precious things thou hast given unmistakable expression to thy regard for her. Narada eulogized her in thy presence, and thou surely wert gratified hearing that praise of thy dear wife. But even if the sage had his reasons for praising her, why was the name of this unfortunate one uttered in that connection?

"If I am to repent for having tasted the sweet liquor of thy love," she went on, her voice rising, "it is better I should have nothing to do with it. Be kindly pleased to accord me thy permission. I could not have believed even in a dream that thou wouldst honor somebody else more than myself — but alas, it has come to pass in real life, even before the eyes of others. Perhaps the sage Narada has conceived a love for her; my grief is that thou wert present in the scene. Thou hast told me that people live for honor only. So, thus dishonored, I do not desire to live any longer. My source of protection has turned today into my source of fear.

"Renounced by thee, I shall be reduced to the condition of the white lily. How could I, who was thy beloved wife and am now discarded, look upon these Raivataka hills decked with the flowers of spring? How could I breathe this pure breeze, ringing with the notes of the cuckoo and fraught with the fragrance of flowers? How could I, who once sported on thy lap inside the waters of this ocean, glance at it again in my unhappy condition? Thou didst tell me in days gone by: 'O daughter of Satrajit, know that there is no wife of mine dearer to me than thyself.' What of that assurance now? Who cares to remember it?" Her voice broke into a kind of bitter laughter. "I did not know thee before to be so much of a cheat and a knave, but now I have come to know thee as fickle, deceiving, and partial to my rival. I have read thy secret thoughts by thy articulations and thy features, O thief, although thou triest to conceal them. Thy tongue only is honeyed, but thou art too guileful."

When the resentful daughter of Satrajit had spoken, Krishna consoled her. "Say not so, O lotus-eyed one, dearest ruler of my heart. What shall I tell thee more, my darling? Know me to be thine entirely. To please me, the sage Narada of unimpeachable deeds gave that flower to her out of generous feeling or regard for her — but I did not give it with my own hands."

Then he made the vow that changed everything. "What to speak of a single flower — I shall fetch that best of all trees, the Parijata tree itself, from the gardens of paradise, and keep it in thy mansion. So be it, then; this shall be my foremost concern."

The storm in Satyabhama's eyes faltered. She had asked, in her grief, to be remembered; he had answered by promising her a tree from heaven — not the flower that had wounded her, but the whole tree it had come from, uprooted and planted in her own courtyard. Whatever she had expected from her accusation, it was not this.
stories.reflection: Satyabhama's long accusation is a precise anatomy of a wounded pride, and its sharpest lines are those of a woman testing whether she is still loved. Krishna's answer is not to argue with any of it but to outbid the wound: against one flower he sets a whole tree of paradise, as if the only way to prove where his heart lives is to give more than the rival received.
stories.next_story_tease: But the tree belonged to Indra's heaven, and to bring it down Krishna would have to ask a king of gods who had no wish to part with it.

stories.title: A Message Carried to Heaven
stories.story:
Narada was preparing to take his leave of Dwaraka when Krishna stopped him with an errand to heaven. The sage who moved freely between the worlds had come, as always, at the right moment — for Krishna had made a promise to Satyabhama, and the promise required the one thing no man could simply take: the Parijata tree itself, which grew in Indra's paradise.

"Go to heaven," Krishna said, "and there interview the courtiers of the slayer of Tripura. Remind Pakasasana — Indra — of all our ancient brotherly love, which thou knowest. Inform him of it not as my command but as my request. The Parijata tree, which the illustrious Kasyapa created in days gone by for the sake of Aditi's happiness, that best of all trees which bestows religious merit and unbounded prosperity, and which was given as a gift to the very virtuous goddesses in fulfillment of their vows — my wives, hearing of the presentation of that tree, desire to give it away in their turn, for earning virtue and merit consequent on munificent deeds, and for my gratification. Ask him, therefore, to send down to Dwaraka that best of all trees, the Parijata. And it shall be restored to heaven after the ceremony of presentation is over."

He paused, and added what sounded almost like a compliment. "Thou shalt so put forth thy endeavors that the lord of the immortals be persuaded to give over the excellent tree. This will also bring into prominence what ambassadorial abilities thou dost possess — and I know that it is possible for all thy acts to be attended with success."

Narada smiled. "Very well," he said. "I shall speak to the lord of the gods in this manner, O foremost of Yadus. But I am sure he will never part with the Parijata tree." And then the sage, who had seen everything, told Krishna why.

The gods and the Danavas had obtained the Parijata when they churned the ocean with the Mandara mountain. At that time the creator of the worlds had desired to take the tree away together with that best of mountains — and Indra had gone personally to Shankara, to Mahadeva himself, and entreated him: "This is Sachi's sporting tree; may it be allowed to remain in her gardens." Mahadeva granted the boon — "Let it be so" — and did not bring the Parijata to the Mandara. Later, to please his wife Uma, Hara created on the dales of the Mandara a forest of Parijata trees extending over a full four miles: a self-luminous wood into which neither the rays of the sun, nor the cool beams of the moon, nor even the breath of the wind could penetrate, where heat and cold reigned at the pleasure of the mountain's daughter. None could enter it but the mighty god and goddess, their followers, and Narada himself. There the Parijatas showered gems and jewels at a mere thought, and the attendants of Shiva enjoyed the forest with their lord's permission.

"Once," Narada said, "a mighty and dreadful Daitya named Andhaka, puffed up with the arrogance of a boon he had obtained, ventured to transgress into that forest — and Hara slew him, though he was ten times as powerful as Vritra and incapable of being slain by any created being. I tell thee truly, O lotus-eyed god: the thousand-eyed Indra will never give thee the Parijata tree, obtained with such great difficulty. That best of trees always bestows on the goddess Sachi all her desires, and it fulfills the wishes of the highly powerful Indra himself."

Krishna heard the sage out, and then gave him his answer. "O sage, if that lord of the immortals does not give the Parijata tree at thy request, I shall then hurl my mace at his breast."

The request, it appeared, had carried an ultimatum in its pocket all along. Narada set out for heaven carrying both — the brother's plea, spoken in the ancient friendship between the two houses, and the warrior's warning, spoken in the same breath. Whether Indra would hear the first or the second was now the only question.
stories.reflection: Narada's long recollection shows how dearly the Parijata was won — the gods churned an ocean for it, and Shiva himself was talked out of taking it — so Indra's grip on the tree is old and possessive. Krishna's message is a masterpiece of two registers: he asks as a brother first, and warns as a warrior only at the edge, leaving heaven's king to choose which Krishna he will meet.
stories.next_story_tease: In heaven, Indra listened to the message with gathering anger — and answered it with a challenge.

stories.title: A Challenge Sent to Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: Indra refuses to part with the Parijata tree
stories.story:
In the court of heaven the sage Narada stood before the king of the gods, and the message he carried was not the one Indra had hoped to hear. His brother Krishna, the lord of Dwaraka, wanted the Parijata tree — the tree that bloomed in Indra's own pleasure garden, the Nandana forest, where its blossoms were said to scent the very air of heaven.

The request had been made as one brother makes to another. Krishna, Narada reported, expected indulgence because he was Indra's younger brother, and he had sent his words with courtesy. But he had also sent a warning. Neither gods nor Gandharvas, neither rakshasas nor asuras, neither the foremost of serpents nor any power in the worlds, would turn him from his pledge. If Indra refused the tree when it was asked in friendship, Krishna had said, he would come to heaven himself and hurl his mace at the breast of the king of the gods — the breast on which queen Sachi lays her fragrant ointments.

Indra heard him out, and the grievances of a lifetime gathered behind his eyes. Had he not forgiven Krishna again and again, remembering only that the boy was his brother? When the Khandava forest burned, Krishna had driven Arjuna's chariot and kept Indra's rain clouds away, letting the great fire rage on. When Krishna lifted the Govardhana hill to shelter the cowherds of Vrindavan, he had done it by setting aside the worship that belonged to the lord of rain. When Indra had asked Krishna's help against the demon Vritra, Krishna had answered only that he was impartial and looked on all creatures equally — and so Indra had slain Vritra with the strength of his own arms. And in every war between the gods and the asuras, Krishna fought as his own will pleased, never troubling himself about the authority of the king of heaven.

Narada listened, and then spoke plainly. He had tried to turn Krishna from this course, he said; he had shown him reason after reason, and the lord of Dwaraka had paid heed to none of them. To Indra he offered the counsel of a friend: it seemed better to allow the Parijata to be transplanted to Dwaraka than to let a quarrel split the house of heaven.

But Indra's mind was already made up. Let the sage carry this answer to the wielder of the discus. Their father Kashyapa and their mother Aditi had gone into the waters on a sojourn, and the matter should rightly have been laid before them — for what had his brother done but abuse his elder brother, and at the urging of his wife? "Fie on women," the king of the gods said, "and fie on the influence of arrogance, when even Vishnu, led by his wife, insults me this day." He recalled what his parents and Brahma himself had taught him — that there is no friend like a brother, that a wise and well-behaved brother is dearer to a man than thousands of sons. The asuras fought him because they were not his brothers; only a brother could wound him so. He would not be the one to begin a rupture among kin, and so let his brother's challenge be set before their parents when they returned.

Narada waited for the king of the gods to finish. When Indra had said all he meant to say, his answer stood clear and final. "Until I am conquered in a battle by Krishna, the wielder of the discus," he declared, "I will not, O foremost of sages, part with the Parijata tree. Go, and tell Achyuta that I am prepared for the quarrel."

So Narada bowed and left the court of heaven, carrying the challenge back to Dwaraka. And the king of the gods, who had once unleashed storms on the world for the sake of his pride, sat waiting for the brother who had promised to come.
stories.reflection: The quarrel is framed entirely in the language of kinship: Krishna asks as a younger brother, Indra refuses as an elder one, and each grievance Indra recites is a memory of being set aside by someone he loves. The refusal is less about a tree than about a brother who has never once deferred to him.
stories.next_story_tease: The challenge reached Dwaraka, and Krishna prepared to come to heaven in person.
stories.hero_scene: In the great court of heaven, the sage Narada stands before the seated king of the gods, who listens with gathering anger as the messenger relays Krishna's demand for the Parijata tree, the air of the celestial hall heavy with the weight of the coming quarrel.

stories.title: Battle at Heaven's Eastern Gate
stories.subtitle: Indra challenges Krishna for the Parijata tree
stories.story:
Krishna came to heaven the way daylight comes to a garden — openly, and before the eyes of everyone.

He had left Dwaraka that morning under the pretext of a hunt, riding out to the Raivataka mountain with Satyaki beside him. There he handed his chariot to his charioteer Daruka, told him to wait and groom the horses, and promised to re-enter the city on that very car by evening. Then, with Satyaki, he mounted the back of Garuda, and his son Pradyumna followed behind in a car swift enough to course over hills. Within the twinkle of an eye the lord of Dwaraka stood in the Nandana forest, the pleasure park of the gods, where hosts of celestial warriors kept watch with their weapons and the finest trees of heaven grew in long, ordered avenues.

He did not linger. Before the guards could gather themselves, Krishna tore the Parijata tree from the earth and set it on Garuda's back. And then a strange thing happened: the tree itself seemed to awaken, to bow before the lord who had taken it, as a living thing might bow in prayer. Krishna spoke to it gently. "Do not fear, O tree." When he was sure it was firmly placed, he circled the stronghold of the gods once, the great tree riding behind him on the king of birds, its branches still heavy with blossoms.

The keepers of the garden did not wait to see more. They ran to Indra with the news, and the sound of their running reached the court of the king of the gods before their words did: the finest tree in heaven was being carried away.

The king of the gods came out mounted on his great elephant Airavata, with his son Jayanta following on a chariot, and found Krishna at the eastern gate of heaven. "O slayer of Madhu," Indra called out, "what is this going on?"

Krishna, seated on Garuda, bowed his head in salute to his elder. "I am only taking away this excellent tree," he said, "for a ceremonious observance for your sister-in-law."

But Indra had given his answer to Narada, and he would not soften it now. "O lotus-eyed one, you should not take away this tree without challenging me to fight. Deal the first blow on me, O mighty-armed Kesava — let your promise be fulfilled by hurling your Kaumodaki mace at me."

So the brothers began. Krishna loosed arrows fierce as thunder at the great elephant; Indra loosed arrows of heavenly make at Garuda and cut off Krishna's shafts as they flew. Krishna, smiling, cut off Indra's in turn, and the two lords of earth and sky stood in the air severing each other's arrows, bowstring answering bowstring. At the twang of the Sharanga and the thunder of Indra's bow together, the inhabitants of heaven themselves swooned away.

While the duel raged, Jayanta slipped toward Garuda and tried to pull the Parijata from the bird's back. "Prevent him," Krishna said to Pradyumna, and instantly his son turned and barred the way. The two young warriors faced each other from their chariots, Jayanta piercing Pradyumna with sharp arrows, Pradyumna answering shaft for shaft, until a fierce combat blazed between the son of Indra and the son of Krishna, as though the quarrel of the fathers had passed whole into the hands of the sons. The gods and the sages, the Siddhas and the Charanas, all looked on, struck with wonder at what they saw.

And then, from the host of heaven, a new champion began to advance — a messenger of the gods named Pravara, of great strength, making straight for the tree on Garuda's back. Krishna marked him and spoke one quiet word to Satyaki. "Even from this place, oppose him." Satyaki, who had never refused his lord, moved to meet the champion of heaven.
stories.reflection: The battle begins with courtesies — Krishna salutes his elder before trading arrows with him — and what follows is a family quarrel fought with divine weapons, watched by all of heaven. The courtesy makes the rupture more striking: neither brother wants to begin the enmity, and neither will step back.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells this episode differently: there, Krishna disarms the gods with his discus and spares Indra, while the Harivamsha has Indra ride out on Airavata and demand a formal battle. This story follows the Harivamsha.
stories.content_note: An archery battle between Krishna and Indra and their sons; described without gore.
stories.next_story_tease: But the gods had one more champion — a warrior whom no weapon could slay.

stories.title: The Warrior Who Could Not Be Killed
stories.subtitle: Satyaki duels Indra's champion Pravara
stories.story:
Among the warriors of heaven there was one whom no weapon could slay. His name was Pravara, and his story was strange for a fighter of the gods: he had been born a Brahmana on Jambu island, had won his way to heaven through the merit of penances, and had earned the friendship of Indra himself. Brahma had granted him a boon — that he could never be killed. In the service of the king of the gods he had become a messenger of heaven, accomplished in mighty weapons, able to subdue all foes, and now, in the battle over the Parijata tree, he came forward to earn his keep.

He moved straight for the tree on Garuda's back, and Krishna marked him at once. "O Satyaki," he said, "even from this place, oppose him."

Satyaki was no stranger to impossible work. He had stood beside Krishna through the wars of Mathura and Dwaraka, and he had never yet refused his lord. He nocked an arrow and rode to meet the champion of the gods, while the celestial host fell back on either side to give the two warriors room.

The duel that followed was like no other in that long morning. Pravara was a master of the bow, and the boon of Brahma hung over him like a second skin. Shaft after shaft Satyaki loosed, and shaft after shaft Pravara met in mid-air, cutting the arrows down before they could reach him. When Satyaki's bow sang, Pravara's answered; and again and again the champion of heaven struck the bow from Satyaki's hand, disarming him before the eyes of the watching gods.

A lesser man would have been broken by the shame of it. Satyaki only bent, retrieved his bow from the air or the dust, and returned to the fight. His arrows flew straighter for each humiliation, and though he could not wound the immortal champion, he gave him no rest, closing the ground between them again and again so that Pravara had no moment to look past him. The gods and sages who had gathered to watch the brothers' quarrel found themselves watching this instead — a mortal warrior holding his own, by pure refusal to yield, against a man who could not lose. They saw the bows flash and the chariots turn in the narrow sky, and not one of them could say when Satyaki had last given ground.

Then Pravara tired of the game. He had not come to heaven to trade arrows with a mortal, however stubborn. Turning his mount, he made for the Parijata, reaching for the tree that rode on Garuda's back.

And the king of birds, who had borne the tree through the whole battle without moving, moved at last.

One blow of Garuda's wings — one vast, sweeping stroke — and the champion of heaven was gone. Pravara and his chariot together were hurled a full four miles back through the sky, tumbling end over end, until they struck the ground and lay still. The warrior whom no weapon could slay had been felled not by arrow or mace, but by a wing; his chariot lay where it had struck, and he lay senseless within it.

The gods stared. The duel between the brothers paused, as if heaven itself needed a moment to understand what it had seen. And Satyaki, bow still in hand, took his place beside the tree — the one guard of the Parijata that no champion of heaven, it seemed, could pass. And while heaven still stared at its fallen champion, the king of birds was already turning his eyes toward the elephant below.
stories.reflection: Pravara's boon protected him from every weapon in creation, and Garuda's wing was not a weapon in any sense the boon had imagined. The duel is a reminder that Satyaki's loyalty is as much a part of this story as any god's power — he holds the line not because he can win, but because he will not stop.
stories.content_note: A duel with arrows and a blow from Garuda's wing that hurls Pravara and his chariot four miles; described without gore.
stories.next_story_tease: But the king of heaven's great elephant was still on the field.

stories.title: The Fall of Airavata
stories.subtitle: Garuda brings down the king of elephants
stories.story:
Through the long morning the duel of the brothers had filled the sky above heaven — Krishna on Garuda's back, Indra on his elephant, the air between them crossed and recrossed with arrows. But the great elephant Airavata was more than a mount. He was the banner of the king of the gods, the beast that had carried Indra through a hundred wars with the asuras, whose very presence in a battle line was said to mean that heaven would not lose. His tusks were the pride of the celestial world, and the sound of him was like the sound of a storm coming.

Krishna had marked him early. In the first exchange of the fight, the lord of Dwaraka had driven arrows into the elephant's flanks — sharp arrows, fierce like thunder itself — and Airavata had only stood, shaking them off as a mountain shakes off rain. Against the boon-crowned champions of heaven, against Indra's own thunder, the elephant had never once given ground.

But there was one on the field who was not a god, and who owed nothing to the orders of heaven. Garuda had carried the Parijata tree on his back through the whole battle, patient as the sky, while arrows rattled against his feathers like hail on a roof. He had seen the warrior Pravara hurled four miles through the air by a single sweep of his wings. Now he turned his attention to the elephant.

The king of birds did not waste time with arrows. He struck Airavata on the head with his fierce claws, and the great talons sank deep — fearful talons, made for tearing, that had once held serpents large enough to drink rivers. The elephant screamed and reared, the wound afflicting him sorely. He shook his vast head, trying to throw the bird off, but Garuda held, striking again, until the greatest beast of heaven began to stagger in the heights.

And then the heights gave way.

Airavata, wounded and reeling, lost his footing in the sky itself. The king of elephants fell from the heights of heaven, turning slowly as he dropped — past the gates and the gardens of the gods, past the very avenues of the Nandana forest where the tree had stood that morning — down and down through the blue air, until he struck the top of the Parijatra mountain and lay there, the pride of heaven brought to earth at last.

For a moment the battle seemed to stop. The gods stared at the mountain where their banner had fallen; the sages and the celestial hosts fell silent. Indra remained with his great elephant Airavata, who now lay fallen on the top of the Parijatra mountain, and even the arrows between the brothers ceased to fly. The sound of the elephant's fall seemed to ring on in the air long after the dust had begun to settle. The tree still rode on Garuda's back. The champions of heaven lay scattered or senseless. And the lord of Dwaraka, who had come for a single tree, had somehow brought the king of the gods down to the level of ordinary warriors — no longer enthroned, but standing in the air like any fighter, with nothing left between him and his brother but the distance of a bowshot.

The day was not yet done. The sun still stood high, and the quarrel was far from settled. But something had changed in the sky over heaven, and everyone who watched knew it: the might of the king of the gods had been measured against the might of the bird who carried Krishna, and it was the bird who had prevailed.
stories.reflection: Airavata was the visible power of the king of the gods, the beast whose presence promised victory — and he is brought down not by a divine weapon but by claws, by the older strength of the bird who carries Krishna. In the quarrel between the brothers, the measure of power belongs not to the thunderbolt but to the one who bears it.
stories.content_note: Garuda wounds Indra's elephant with his claws and the elephant falls from heaven; described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: When nightfall ended the day's fighting, Krishna turned to the Ganga and to Shiva.

stories.title: A Boon Won in the Night
stories.story:
The truce at nightfall was Krishna's doing.

All day, over the Parijata — the wish-giving tree of heaven, uprooted from Indra's own garden — the king of the gods had fought from the back of his elephant Airavata, and Garuda had met him with beak and claw until the great beast swayed, bleeding, in the sky. Now the sun had gone down behind the Parijatra mountain, the battle had begun again, and Krishna, looking across at the wounded elephant, raised his hand.

"Airavata is sorely wounded," he called to Indra, "and night grows apace. Let us refrain from fighting now. Do as you wish tomorrow morning."

The king of the gods saw the sense in it and agreed.

The mountain on which they camped had made itself small when Krishna came, sinking into the earth until it was no bigger than a stone for grinding sandal — a bow of reverence from a peak that knew whose weight it carried. Indra raised a shelter of stones for the night near the sacred Pushkara lake, and there Brahma came to him, and the sage Kashyapa with Aditi, and the hosts of heaven: the Sadhyas and the Vasus, the Ashwini twins, the Adityas and the Rudras. Krishna stayed on the far side of the mountain with his son Pradyumna and the warrior Satyaki, and behind them, resting on Garuda's back, stood the great Parijata itself, its blossoms pale in the failing light.

Before the night settled, Krishna turned to the mountain under him. It had bowed itself for his sake, and he would not let such reverence pass unmarked. "You shall be called Sanapada," he said, "and you shall be auspicious and holy as the Himalaya. Abound in gems; outvie Meru itself. I shall be glad to see you, always, full of precious stones."

Then, saluting the god whose emblem is the bull, Krishna thought of the Ganga — and at his thought the river that has its source in Vishnu's own feet came flowing up the mountain to him. He worshipped her, bathed in her water, and taking up that sacred water and leaves of the bilva tree, he offered them and invited Rudra, lord of all lords, to be present.

Shiva came. He appeared there with Uma at his side and his followers around him, manifest upon the surface of the Ganga's water and upon the bel leaves themselves. Krishna worshipped him with flowers of the Parijata — the very tree that had set heaven and earth at war — and then, in a voice that carried across the dark water, he eulogized the lord of lords.

"You are Rudra," he said, "for you bind beings in maya and release them, and you manifest through the sound that pervades the universe at birth; you are self-manifest. You are Pasupati, lord of all creatures, of those who hold to life and those who have renounced it. You are the performer of all acts; no master of the universe is your superior. You are the beginning, the giver of life, the cause of contentment of all the great masters, and so the learned call you the God of gods. Because all manifest creation is begotten of you, you are Bhava, the source from which all is born — self-created, creator of all creators. The defeated gods and asuras crowned you, and so you are Maheswara, the maker of the universe. I resign myself entirely to your protection. Crown me, who am devoted to your devotees and beloved of your beloved, with fame."

The night held still. When the hymn was done, the god of gods looked on Krishna and spoke.

"O best of gods, you shall obtain the things you desire. You shall carry away the Parijata tree. And you shall be invincible."

Then Shiva and Uma faded back into the night from which they had come, and Krishna was left on the moonlit bank with the water moving at his feet. The war over the tree had been fought with arrows and with claws; it would end, he knew now, with the tree going home with him.
stories.reflection: Krishna spends the pause in the fighting not in readiness but in worship, saluting the god whose devotee he declares himself to be. The boon he wins is quietly telling: he asks that the Parijata be carried away and that he remain invincible — as though the night's devotion, not the day's arrows, were the real weapon in the quarrel.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shiva had not finished speaking: before the night was over he would tell Krishna what lay hidden beneath the mountain.

stories.title: The Stronghold Beneath the Mountain
stories.story:
The mountain had one more secret, and Shiva had not yet finished speaking.

The night on the Parijatra had turned to worship. Krishna, staying on the mountain with his son Pradyumna and the warrior Satyaki, had thought of the Ganga — and at his thought the river that rises from Vishnu's own feet had come flowing up to him. He had bathed in her waters, offered her the bilva leaves and the sacred water, and eulogized Shiva until the god of gods appeared with Uma upon the river and the leaves, and had won from him the boon that he would carry away the Parijata and remain invincible. The hymn had ended; the boon had been spoken. And still Shiva lingered on the dark water, and still he spoke.

"On the summit of this mountain," he said, "there is a stronghold of the Danavas, called Satpura. Hidden inside that fastness live mighty Danavas of wicked soul. By the boon of Brahma they are invincible to the gods — no weapon of the celestials can touch them, and no god can prevail against them. Do you, O Krishna, slay them."

The words fell into the night like a stone into still water. Here was the truth behind the mountain's reverence, the reason it had bowed itself into the earth at Krishna's coming: it was not merely holy — it was a gate. Beneath its summit, in the stronghold of Satpura, an army of Danavas waited, shielded from every god by a boon older than the quarrel over the Parijata. The day's war had been fought in the open sky, arrow against claw, for a tree. This was a different kind of war — one the gods could not fight at all, hidden under the very ground where Krishna now stood. The charge was one no god could carry out, and it was given to Krishna alone.

Before dawn, on the summit where the stronghold's gate was hidden, a shrine was raised, and Krishna was enshrined within it. The mountain that had made itself small as a grinding stone at his coming kept his presence from that night forward — a place of worship now, as the god of gods had made it holy, and a watch kept over the fastness in its heart. Whatever the Danavas had plotted in their invincible hiding, they would do it now under the eye of the one being their boon did not bind.

When morning came, the fight with Indra would resume on the slopes below, and the Parijata would still be the prize. But the night had given Krishna more than a boon. It had given him a task — and the mountain itself, with its hidden enemy, now stood under his eye.
stories.reflection: The revelation sits oddly against the boon of the night before: Krishna is promised the Parijata, yet the stronghold he is shown is one the gods themselves cannot enter by Brahma's boon. The shrine on the summit reads like a claim — the mountain that bowed to Krishna now holds his presence, as though the hidden enemy were answered by an equally hidden protection.
stories.next_story_tease: Dawn would bring the fight with Indra again — and Krishna carried the night's promise that the Parijata would go home with him.

stories.title: The Parijata Comes to Dwaraka
stories.story:
The Parijata was coming to Dwaraka — on loan from heaven, and with a mother's condition attached.

The quarrel between Krishna and Indra over the tree had been ended by the elders of the gods: the sage Kashyapa and his wife Aditi, who were parents to both. When the night had passed, Aditi spoke to Krishna. "Take this Parijata," she said. "Go to Dwaraka and perform the auspicious festival so longed for by your wife. But when that ceremony is over, you are to bring this tree back, and place it as before in the garden of Nandana."

Krishna accepted the tree and its condition together. Satyaki and Pradyumna, who had guarded the Parijata through all the fighting, kept their watch as it traveled, and Garuda bore the great tree without complaint, its blossoms swaying above the clouds. On the way home Krishna set the tree down at Raivataka, the mountain that looked out toward the sea and the city, before carrying it the last stretch into Dwaraka itself.

Word of the tree ran ahead of them. When Krishna arrived over the city, he blew his conch, and the sound delighted every inhabitant of Dwaraka. He alighted from Garuda, and with Satyabhama at his side he walked to her garden and planted the great Parijata there, where its roots would hold the earth of the city and its branches rise toward the sky it had come from.

Then the wonder of it began to spread. The fragrance of the tree perfumed the earth for three furlongs in every direction, drifting through the streets of Dwaraka like a rumor of another world. Anyone who came near it could recall the events of a prior existence, as if the tree held a mirror to the lives behind this one; and when the Yadavas looked into its blossoms, they contemplated themselves in their original celestial forms — the forms they had worn before this world, remembered now at the sight of their own faces in the tree. Heaven, it seemed, had come to earth with its roots in Satyabhama's garden.

Satyabhama received the tree joyfully. This was the auspicious festival she had longed for, the rite she had spoken of; and here was the tree of heaven itself, planted at her door, blooming in the air of Dwaraka. Whatever the ceremony required — flower, shade, or fragrance — the Parijata would provide.

Only the condition hung over the joy, soft as the tree's own scent: the tree was a loan, not a gift. When the rite was done, it was to return to the garden of Nandana, to the heaven from which it had been uprooted. For now, the city had its wonder — a tree from the gods' own garden rooted in mortal earth, filling three furlongs of Dwaraka with the scent of another world.
stories.reflection: The tree is a gift with a return address: Aditi lends what Indra could not keep by force, and Satyabhama's joy is framed by a condition. The wonder of the tree — past-life memory, celestial forms — belongs to the Vishnu Purana's telling, while the loan belongs to the Harivamsha's; both agree on the marvel itself, heaven rooted in a mortal garden.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha has Aditi grant the Parijata on condition that it return to the garden of Nandana after Satyabhama's rite, while the Vishnu Purana has Indra himself consent to the tree remaining on earth as long as Krishna abides there.
stories.next_story_tease: The battle that had uprooted the tree, and the parents who stopped it, were yet to be told in full.

stories.title: A Mother's Hands Between Two Brothers
stories.story:
Before the Parijata could be carried home to Dwaraka, the quarrel over it had to be settled — and the settling came close to unmaking the world.

On the Parijatra mountain, in the first light, the battle over the tree began again, and this time the world itself reeled. Krishna and Indra fought from their cars, and though neither struck the other directly, their weapons sought everything around them: Krishna's arrows scattered Indra's soldiers, ten shafts apiece for the horses of the king of gods; Indra's arrows covered the horses of Krishna's car and buried Garuda's wings in a storm of shafts; a thousand arrows cloaked the great elephant. And as the two heroes fought, the earth shook like a boat adrift in water, the quarters blazed with an unnatural lustre, mountains trembled, hundreds of trees were uprooted, and pious mortals fell where they stood. Hurricanes tore the sky. Rivers turned and ran backward. Fire burned even in water, planets clashed in the heavens, hundreds of stars dropped from the sky, and the elephants of the quarters quivered in their stalls. Cranes wheeled overhead crying dreadfully, and it seemed that earth, heaven, and sky had all vanished from view.

In that breaking world, the ascetics recited their mantras and the brahmanas gave themselves to meditation, praying for the sake of all creatures.

Then Brahma spoke to Kashyapa. "Go, with your wife Aditi," he said, "and prevent your two sons."

The sage obeyed, and came with Aditi to the battlefield. The moment Krishna and Indra saw their parents, the fury fell away from both of them. They climbed down from their cars, laid down their arms, and saluted the feet of Kashyapa and Aditi.

Aditi took them both by the hands. "Born of the same parents," she said, "you are trying to slay each other as if you were not brothers. Let pass what has happened. If you think you should obey the words of your mother and your father, lay down your arms and hear what I say."

"Let it be so," they said, and the two of them walked together to the bank of the Jahnvi river.

There, at the water's edge, Indra spoke. "O Krishna, you are the Lord and Creator of the universe, and I have been placed by you in my kingdom. Having yourself established me here, why do you disregard me? Having accepted me as your elder brother, why do you wish to destroy me?"

Krishna did not answer with weapons. The two bathed together in the Jahnvi, and returned to Kashyapa and Aditi; and the ascetics gave that place a name — the union ground of dear ones — for there the two lotus-eyed brothers were united with their parents. Before the assembled celestials, Krishna promised safety to Indra; and the gods, shining in their true forms, repaired to heaven, with Kashyapa, Aditi, Indra, and Krishna riding together on one car. Sachi, Indra's queen, adored the sage and his wife.

The battle was over; the quarrel was healed. And when the night had passed, Aditi, who had seen her sons almost destroy the world over a tree, took the tree itself out of the quarrel and gave it to Krishna — to carry to Dwaraka for his wife's festival, on the condition that it return to the garden of Nandana when the rite was done. The war that had shaken the three worlds ended not with a victor but with a mother's gift: the tree was given, not taken, and the brothers went home at peace.
stories.reflection: The battle ends not with a victor but with a mother's hands holding both her sons'. Indra's question — you placed me in this kingdom, you call me elder brother, why would you destroy me? — is the real resolution: the quarrel was never about power but about kinship, and once the brothers bathe together in the Jahnvi, the war simply stops being possible.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, Satyabhama was readying a rite that would put even the gift of the Parijata to a stranger test.

stories.title: The Garland That Bound and Released
stories.subtitle: Satyabhama's Punyaka rite and the gift to Narada
stories.story:
The garland Satyabhama lifted over Krishna's head was not meant as decoration. Flowers and all, it was a binding — the knot of a rite that would hand her husband to a wandering sage and then buy him back again, all within the same afternoon.

It began with a summons. Krishna thought of Narada, and the sage appeared as though the thought itself were a road. Satyabhama invited him to accept the Punyaka ceremonies, and when the appointed hour came, she and Krishna bathed the great muni, anointed him with scents, hung garlands on him, and fed him with their own hands. Then the rite proper began. The lucky damsel set a garland of flowers around Krishna's neck and bound him to the Parijata, the heavenly tree that grew in Dwaraka. With his permission she dedicated him to Narada, and then she gave away her gifts: sesame seeds that gleamed like jewels, gold mixed with rice and other plants, mountains of gold, and a thousand cows — wealth poured out in such measure that the ceremony looked less like worship than like a festival of giving. The women of the household looked on as the sage accepted it all, and the joke that was already forming hung in the air.

Narada accepted everything, delighted. "O Keshava," he said, "given by Satya together with water, you have become mine. Follow me, and do what I say."

"This is the first stage," Krishna answered, and began to follow him.

The sage walked a few paces, cut various jokes, and said, "Wait here, I am going." Then, instead of going, he lifted the garland from Krishna's neck. "To release yourself," he said, "give me a Kapila cow with her calf, and the skin of a black antelope filled with sesame seeds and gold. This means of release has been laid down by the god whose emblem is the bull."

"So be it," said Krishna, and offered the fee on the spot. Then he smiled at the muni. "Narada, you who are conversant with religion, I have been greatly pleased with you. Ask for a boon, and I will grant it."

Narada asked that the eternal Vishnu might always remain pleased with him, and grant him habitation with him; and that if he were ever born again, he might be born of no woman, and as a Brahmana. "So it will be," said Krishna, and the sage was content — for the lord's promise to the wandering singer of heaven had been spoken, and everyone who heard it knew that it would hold.

The rite did not end with the release. Satyabhama had invited all sixteen thousand of Krishna's wives to the Punyaka ceremony, and when it closed she distributed among them the celestial garments and ornaments that Shachi, Indra's queen, had once given to Vasudeva — finery from the very court of heaven, handed out in Dwaraka as a bride's gift to a household. And the Parijata, at Krishna's command, began to display its own accomplishments, flowering and working its wonders while friends and relations gathered to witness the power of the tree.

It became a festival. Krishna brought the Pandavas, with Pritha, Draupadi and Subhadra; Shrutasrava came with her son, and Bhishmaka with his; and other friends and relations arrived as well. For a year Krishna stayed in Dwaraka, happy in the company of Arjuna and the ladies of his household, the days turning gently around the blooming tree, which flowered in Dwaraka as though it had never left heaven.

At the end of that year he carried the Parijata back to the city of the celestials — returning the tree to heaven, and with it, in some measure, the peace between the two brothers who had lately faced each other in battle.
stories.reflection: The whole rite runs on a divine joke: the lord of the universe is bound by a garland, sold for gold and cows, and ransomed back at a price fixed by Shiva. Krishna plays along without once breaking the mood, and the ceremony ends in generosity instead of solemnity — devotion, in this telling, is not afraid to laugh at itself.
stories.next_story_tease: When the tree came home to heaven, Krishna would make a vow before Indra that set a ten-day countdown to war.

stories.title: The Vow Before Indra
stories.subtitle: Krishna returns the Parijata to heaven
stories.story:
When the Parijata returned to the city of the celestials, it was more than a tree coming home. It was the same tree that had nearly set brother against brother — the battle over it had ended only when Kashyapa and Aditi, sent by Brahma, halted the fight, and the two who had quarrelled bathed in the Jahnvi and made peace. Now Krishna carried the tree back up from Dwaraka after a year of festival, and in heaven he saluted Indra, Aditi and Kashyapa, one after another — the gesture of a son arriving at his parents' door, the heavenly tree settling back into the garden it had left. The court that had seen them fight now saw them stand together before their parents, and the sight carried its own peace.

Aditi received it exactly that way. After Krishna had bowed to her, she spoke. "May you both always entertain such brotherly feeling," she said. "O Janardana, you are to satisfy this desire of mine."

"It shall be so," said Krishna.

Then, having honored his parents, he turned to the king of gods, and his words changed the mood of the meeting. "O king of gods, giver of honor," he said, "I have been commanded by the high-souled Shiva to destroy all the unslayable Danavas who live on earth. From today, within ten days, I will kill all those Asuras. At the time of that battle, Pravara, together with the heroic Jayanta, must wait in the sky to slay the Danavas. Of them, one is a god in human form, and the other is the son of a god."

It was a strange vow, and Indra knew why it was strange. These Danavas were unslayable by the gods. They carried a boon from Brahma, and no weapon of heaven could touch them; that was why they had lived so long on earth, proud and untroubled. Yet here was Krishna promising to finish them within ten days, and asking that the two sons of the gods stand ready in the sky when he did — waiting, as though the slaughter of the invincible were a thing that could be scheduled. The gods gathered closer at the words, for it was not every day that the lord who lived among mortals set a date for war. Indra had long known these Danavas as a burden heaven could not lift; now, for the first time, he heard someone promise to lift it.

Krishna explained it plainly. "Although those Danavas, proud of the boon conferred on them by Brahma, cannot be killed by the gods," he said, "we will kill them, for I am now a man."

There was the whole secret, and it turned the vow from a boast into a promise. The boon that shielded the Danavas from every god left them helpless against a man — and Krishna, who had just spent a year being bound with garlands and ransomed with cows, spoke of that human form as his weapon. He was the man who would do what heaven could not, and the gods had only to watch the sky when the killing began.

Indra, pleased, answered, "So it will be." And then the king of gods and the lord of Dwaraka embraced each other — the quarrel over the Parijata finished, at last, with an embrace; and a different war agreed upon in the same breath, one to be fought on earth within ten days. And somewhere below, on the earth he had chosen, the Danavas went on living as though no such promise existed. The ten days had begun to run, and the world below did not yet know it.
stories.reflection: The vow's logic is the striking thing: the Danavas' invincibility is a gift from Brahma, and it is precisely that gift which makes them killable — by a man. Krishna speaks of his human form not as a weakness but as the one door the boon left open, and the embrace with Indra seals both reconciliation and war in a single moment.
stories.next_story_tease: Within those ten days, Krishna would be drawn to a sacrifice at Shatpura where the Danavas were already making demands.
