stories.title: The Demand at the Sacrifice
stories.subtitle: The Danavas of Shatpura claim a share of Brahmadatta's yajna
stories.story:
"Give us our share in the Yajna. We will drink Soma, and Brahmadatta must give us his daughters."

The demand reached the sacrificial ground of Shatpura in the middle of a year-long rite. It came from Nikumbha and the other Danavas of the city, who assembled on the bank of the sacred river Avarta, a place resorted to by the munis — and they came proud of the boon that made them fearless. They did not frame their words as a request. They claimed a share of the sacrifice, the most valuable of the jewels Brahmadatta possessed, and his daughters, who they had heard were many and beautiful. "If he transgresses this order," they announced, "we will not allow him to celebrate this Yajna. This is our order."

Brahmadatta was a Vajasaneyi Brahmana, a disciple of Yajnavalkya, well-read in the four Vedas and the six Angas, a man of morality — and he answered the Danavas the way his learning taught him. No portion of sacrificial offerings had ever been laid down for them in the Vedas; if they doubted it, they could ask the great munis who sat at the rite. His daughters he would give in marriage to proper bridegrooms, following the same Vedas; that was his resolution. "If you come to terms," he said, "I may give you my entire collection of jewels. If you show your force, I will not give even that — for Devaki's son is my supporter."

The Danavas chose force. They scattered the articles of the sacrifice and began to carry away his daughters.

It happened that Vasudeva and Devaki were themselves at Shatpura, for Brahmadatta was a class-friend and preceptor of Vasudeva, and Krishna's father had come with his wife to protect the rite — just as Indra guards Brihaspati, his own preceptor. Around them sat the greatest of the sages, Vyasa, Yajnavalkya, Sumantu, Jaimini, Dhritiman, Jajali, Devala, and others of firm devotion; and Devaki, by the grace of her son, went among the beggars of the yajna distributing whatever each one asked, in proportion to the wealth of Vasudeva. Such was the household the Danavas had chosen to challenge: the preceptor of Vasudeva, guarded by the mother of Krishna. The sacrifice was rich in food and in gifts — and it was precisely that richness the Danavas meant to tear apart.

When Vasudeva saw the sacrificial articles being robbed by the Asuras, he thought of Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada. And the moment he thought of them, Krishna knew everything. "Proceed, O my son," he said to Pradyumna, "and save the maidens by virtue of your illusive powers. I myself will soon go to Shatpura with the Yadava army."

Pradyumna, ever obedient to his sire, was there within a moment. By his illusive power he took the maidens away, created figures of them to leave before the Daityas, and told Devaki, "Be not afraid." The Danavas, satisfied, carried off the illusory maidens and entered their city in triumph, while Brahmadatta's real daughters were safe. The deception had saved the maidens and bought the sacrifice its peace — for a little while.

The great yajna went on according to proper rites, and its fame spread. All the kings invited by Brahmadatta arrived and encamped near Shatpura: Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the Malava and Tangana kings, Rukmi, Ahvriti, Neela, Narmada, Vinda, Anuvinda, Avantya, Shalya, Shakuni, and other heroic warrior kings besides. The sacrifice that had begun as a year of offerings now wore a ring of armies around it, and every new arrival made the encampment thicker and the air heavier.
stories.reflection: Brahmadatta's defiance rests on one sentence: no share of the offerings was ever laid down for the Asuras in the Vedas, and his daughters will be given to proper bridegrooms, not to force. He stakes everything on the order of the rite and on the name of Devaki's son — and the rescue comes not as a miracle but as a son obeying his father's summons.
stories.next_story_tease: Narada, watching the kings gather around the sacrifice, decided that the assembly needed a conflict — and set out for Nikumbha's house.

stories.title: The Sage Who Brought the War
stories.subtitle: Narada incites the kings against the Yadavas
stories.story:
"At this Yajna all the Kshatriyas and the Yadavas have assembled. Surely this will lead to a conflict. I shall therefore try to bring it about."

That was Narada's thought as he looked over the encampment at Shatpura. The kings had come from every quarter — Jarasandha, Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the Malava and Tangana kings, Rukmi, Shalya, Shakuni, and many more — and camped around the sacrificial ground where Brahmadatta's year-long rite still burned. On one side of that circle stood the Yadavas, and on the other the kings; and in the city itself the Danavas nursed the grievance of the maidens they had thought to carry off. The sage who had lately been honoured in Dwaraka and rewarded with a boon now looked at this gathering and saw not a sacrifice but a stage. Where another sage might have foreseen bloodshed and spoken a warning, Narada walked straight to Nikumbha's house. He moved among gods, kings and Asuras as though they were rooms of a single house, and in every room his words carried weight.

The Danavas received him with worship, seated him, and waited. Narada wasted no words. "Having caused a dissension with the Yadavas," he said, "how are you sitting here at ease? Do you not know that Brahmadatta is the friend of Krishna's father?"

Then he told Nikumbha what was coming to the sacrifice. The five hundred wives of Brahmadatta had been brought to the sacrificial ground to honor Vasudeva's son — two hundred of Brahmana origin, one hundred of Kshatriya origin, one hundred of Vaishya, and one hundred of Shudra. All of them had worshipped the sage Durvasa, and the sage had granted them a boon: each would bear, one by one, a son and a daughter. And so, by virtue of that boon, they had all given birth to fair daughters — of matchless beauty, tender, ever youthful, chaste, their bodies carrying the fragrance of all flowers. He let the picture hang in the air, then drew the conclusion for them: jewels would open the ears of the kings, and maidens would seal the bargain.

The point was not lost on Nikumbha. These were the maidens who would come with the Yadavas — more of them, and lovelier, than the daughters the Danavas had failed to seize.

"O hero," Narada went on, "invite in proper order the help of the other kings." The Asuras understood the lesson. If the kings who had come for the sacrifice could be turned — bought with jewels, promised maidens — then the Yadavas would find no friends at Shatpura, and the Danavas would meet them with an army of their own. The Danavas set about their work, and Narada, his errand at Nikumbha's house done, passed back through the encampment.

There he did the other half of his work. The great sage prevented the heroic sons of Pandu — he held the Pandavas back, so that when the trouble came, they would not stand with the Yadavas. It was a careful mercy, or a careful cruelty: whatever came to pass at Shatpura, the sons of Pandu would be spectators.

So the stage was set at Shatpura. The Danavas had their allies among the kings, the kings had their price, the Pandavas had been set apart, and the Yadavas were walking toward a sacrifice that had quietly become a trap. Nothing had been decided by battle, and yet everything had been arranged for one — which was exactly the kind of work Narada did best. And he had done it all without ever raising his voice.
stories.reflection: Narada here turns the blessing he received in Dwaraka toward the opposite end: he does not merely foresee the clash at Shatpura, he resolves to bring it about. The same gifts that let him joke with the lord of the universe let him arm the Asuras and disarm the Pandavas.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the assembled kings could act, Nikumbha would use his illusive powers to carry the Yadava heroes one by one into a cave beneath Shatpura.

stories.title: The Cave That Swallowed the Heroes
stories.subtitle: Nikumbha's illusion empties the Yadava ranks, one hero at a time.
stories.story:
As the clear sun rose over the plain, the mountain gave birth to an army. From the mouth of Shatpura cave the Danavas came roaring, a host spilling out on asses, elephants, crocodiles, hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises, with chariots drawn by the same wild beasts, and the sound of trumpets, wheels and conches rising like a storm that had learned to march.

The war that had begun at the crowded sacrifice had carried the Yadava host to this plain, and they had come prepared for everything but this. Krishna, Baladeva and Satyaki had ridden to the field on Garuda's back, bathed in the waters of the sacred river Avarta, and worshipped Shiva before the first arrow flew. Pradyumna stood at the head of the army, and the Pandavas kept guard over the sacrifice ground behind them. At Krishna's mandate the war-bugles sounded, and Samba and Gada drew the host up in the shape of a great crocodile, while Sharana, Uddhava, Viprithu, Prithu, Sudangshthra, Vichakshu and the rest held the rear with Aniruddha. And above, where only Krishna could see them, hovered Jayanta and Pravara, summoned by a single thought.

The kings of the earth had chosen sides. Among those who came to aid the Asuras stood the followers of the Chedi king Shishupala, the hundred brothers of the Kuru house headed by Duryodhana, and rulers such as Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni and Jarasandha, drawn into the gathering storm. At the head of the whole host came Nikumbha, as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host, only darker; and behind him the Asura ranks filled earth and sky with their leonine cries.

The battle opened with arrows like serpents. Nikumbha's shafts fell on the Yadava army like a rain of poison, and Anadhrishti, commander-in-chief of the Yadu host, could not bear it. He answered shaft for shaft, his feathered arrows clearing the enemy ranks, until the air grew so thick with missiles that Nikumbha himself, with his chariot, his standard and his horses, disappeared from sight. It was an insult the great Asura would not bear: anger kindled in him, and with it the decision to fight with what no arrow could touch.

That was when the field learned its true enemy. Nikumbha, foremost of those who wield illusion, was not hiding. He was working. By his illusive powers he bewildered Anadhrishti where he stood, carried him to the cave of Shatpura, and imprisoned him there. Then he returned to the field and did it again. Kritavarma. Charudeshna. Vaitarana of Bhoja's race. Sanatkumar. Arksha, the son of Jambavati. Nishatha and Ulmukha. And after them, one by one, countless more Yadava heroes, each led dazed and helpless into the dreadful cave while the shape of Nikumbha himself was so completely hidden that no one could see him come or go.

It was a war fought by subtraction. The Yadava ranks did not fall. They vanished. A captain would be standing there shouting orders, the dust would shift, and he was gone, swallowed by the mountain. The army could answer spears and arrows; it could not answer a man who was never where it looked.

When the truth of it sank in, rage came to the Yadava side such as the plain had not seen. Krishna, Baladeva, Satyaki, Samba, the irrepressible Aniruddha, and Pradyumna above them all, who had watched their kinsmen led into the dark, were filled with anger. They had come to fight a war; they found themselves watching a prison being filled.

Krishna looked at the cave, and then at the host that had done this. He set string to his Sarnga bow, and the note it made silenced the battlefield.

The fire was about to range on grass.
stories.reflection: The battle turns on an enemy who fights by theft rather than slaughter, taking warriors whole instead of killing them. Against a power that hides itself, no formation avails, and the story's edge is that the fury which finally answers it belongs not to the army but to Krishna alone.
stories.content_note: Battle violence with restraint: warriors are captured and imprisoned rather than killed.
stories.next_story_tease: But the Sarnga bow was already strung.

stories.title: Fire Ranging on Grass
stories.subtitle: The Sarnga bow answers the Asura host at Shatpura.
stories.story:
When Krishna set string to the Sarnga bow, the Asuras saw their death approaching, and being Asuras, they charged straight into it.

Anadhrishti and the other captains had been swallowed by the cave of Shatpura, taken one by one through Nikumbha's illusion. The Yadava army still stood, but its heart was inside the mountain. There was only one answer left, and Krishna gave it. He drew the Sarnga and began to move among the Danavas.

He moved as fire ranges over dry grass: not running, not pausing, simply advancing, and everything ahead of him burned. The comparison was no ornament. Fire does not fight the grass; it passes through it, and the grass is gone. The Sarnga's arrows flew before him in sheets, and wherever he stepped, the Danava host found itself standing in the path of a blaze.

The Danavas did not understand what they were seeing. To them he was one man with a bow, and they had a mountain's worth of weapons. They took up thousands of sataghnis and parighas, fiery lances and burning axes; they tore up dreadful rocks and great stones; they hurled infuriated elephants, chariots and horses; and they ran at him with all of it, like locusts driven by the noose of Death into a burning fire. The whole arsenal of the mountain came down on Krishna in one tremendous shower.

The Narayana-fire consumed it all. The flung weapons, the stones, the maddened elephants, the chariots, all of it met the blaze of his arrows and was gone. And Krishna, smiling, baffled them all, standing under the downpour as a bull stands in autumn rain, patient and unhurried and untouched. He had been smiling since he strung the bow, and the smile, in the end, was more terrible than the fire.

Then the host tried to run. Some broke for the sky, rising on whatever dark power they had left, seeking the one direction an army believes is safe: upward, into the open air.

It was not safe. The sky was not empty. Above the field, hidden where only Krishna could see them, waited Jayanta and Pravara, called up by a thought before the battle began. As soon as any Asura rose into the sky, their arrows met him, and every one of them fell. The Asuras who remained looked up and understood, too late, that the one direction they had left unguarded was guarded. The sky became a wall.

And so the Danava host was caught between two deaths: the fire ranging on the ground, and the silent archers who owned the air. The Danava host was not beaten yet, it was burning: the numbers they had trusted, the weapons they had trusted, the fury they had trusted, all of it ash in the path of one smiling archer. The plain filled with the wreck of their courage. Their roar died into the dust, and the rout that Nikumbha's illusion had postponed came at last, in full.

Krishna lowered the Sarnga bow. The fire had done its ranging, and the grass was gone. Beyond the smoke stood the cave of Shatpura, still holding its prisoners.

The battle was won. The cave was not.
stories.reflection: The rout has the shape of a parable about fear: the host that charges a burning fire, and the few who escape, are met by the one force they forgot, the sky, where Jayanta and Pravara have waited unseen all along. Krishna's calm throughout, smiling and bearing the shower like a bull in rain, is the story's true wonder.
stories.content_note: Battle violence described with restraint; no graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: The rout was complete, and only the question of what would be done with the conquered city remained.

stories.title: Shatpura for Brahmadatta
stories.subtitle: After the victory, the conqueror gives the city away.
stories.story:
The kings who had gambled on the Asura side sat in the victor's camp as prisoners, and when the Danavas saw it, fear finally entered their hearts.

They had been routed by Krishna and the Yadavas and had fled in every direction. Now their allies were captives and their stronghold surrounded, and the war they had promised to win was lost. Nikumbha alone refused to accept it. Filled with anger, he turned on his own fleeing host: "Why do you break your promise and run? You swore to avenge the destruction of your kinsmen. If you are slain in battle, you will live happily in the region of the celestials. But if you flee, whose face will you look upon in your own house? What will your wives say? Shame on you, all of you!"

The Asuras, burning with shame, turned back and threw themselves at the Yadavas with double fury. It did not save them. At the sacrificial ground, where the ritual pavilions still stood, the Pandavas, Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva, cut down all who came; and those who tried to escape by rising into the sky were slain by Indra's son Jayanta and the brahmana Pravara, still on watch above the field. The field ran red; a river of blood flowed down from the mountain Govinda, its fish the swords of the fallen.

Only Nikumbha kept the old courage. Seeing his comrades slain and the enemy's power growing, he leaped up and fought on, and Jayanta and Pravara met him with arrows like thunderbolts. The great Asura struck Pravara down with his iron club, and the brahmana fell to earth; but Indra's son caught him up in his arms, embraced him, found him still alive, and set him down before turning on the Asura. Arrow after arrow he buried in Nikumbha's body, until the wounded Daitya, thinking of the kinsman-killer he had sworn to avenge, broke off the fight and vanished, going where Krishna stood. And Indra himself, seated on Airavata, came down with the gods to witness the battle, and embracing his victorious son and Pravara, had celestial trumpets sounded over the field.

When the last Asura had fallen or fled, the plain fell silent. The war was over.

Krishna then did what conquerors are not expected to do. He gave the victory away. The kings who had been taken with their followers, the rulers who had chosen the Asura side when Narada's incitement and Asura gold had swayed them, were brought before him. Instead of punishment they received jewels and fine raiment from his hand. For them the war ended not in chains but in gifts.

To the Yadavas, his own people, he gave the hundreds of Daitya maidens of the conquered city. To the Pandavas, who had guarded the sacrifice and fought beside him, he gave six thousand chariots with their horses, a gift that made the five brothers wealthy beyond any campaign.

And then came the last and strangest gift. In the conquered city of Shatpura, the lair from which the Danavas had poured out to war, there lived a brahmana named Brahmadatta. Krishna summoned him and granted him the city itself, caves, walls and all.

The warriors around him must have wondered. They had bled for this ground, watched their captains vanish into that mountain, seen their friends carried off. And Krishna placed it all in the hands of a priest. Yet perhaps the explanation lay in the gift itself: he had not conquered Shatpura to hold it. He had conquered it to give it away.

So the Asura city, which had known only war, passed into the keeping of a man of peace, while the Yadavas, laden with honor and chariots, turned their faces toward home.
stories.reflection: The distribution is the true conquest: after a war fought with bows and illusions, Krishna's first act is to undo what wars do, restoring captives, honoring the kings who opposed him, enriching the allies, and handing the enemy's stronghold to a brahmana. Spoils in his hands become gifts, and the conquered city becomes a bequest.
stories.next_story_tease: Aboard the boats that carried them onward, the Yadavas were about to learn a song from heaven.

stories.title: Heaven Sings at Sea
stories.subtitle: The celestial Chhalikya song comes down to the Yadava fleet.
stories.story:
After the battles, the Yadavas took to the sea. The war at Shatpura was done, the fleet that carried the Yadava court sailed out into open water, and on those boats, at Krishna's command, a celebration began such as the world had never heard.

It started with Balarama. Warmed by Kadamvari wine, his eyes gently reddened, fair as the moon in his cloud-dark raiment, he sat sporting with Revati, the daughter of King Revata, looking at her face and finding in it all the delight he needed. Seeing his brother so content, Krishna summoned the Apsaras, the dancers of heaven, and the beautiful women came to the boats to please Rama and Revati. They had dressed themselves as the women of the Yadava country. They saluted Revati and Balarama first, and then, as the couple wished and the Yadavas asked, they danced in time and displayed gesture after gesture of the celestial dance, singing, in the Yadava tongue, songs set to thousands of tunes.

And the songs they sang were the deeds of Krishna himself. They sang of Kamsa's destruction and the fall of Pralamba and Chanura; of the child tied to the mortar, who earned the name Damodara; of Putana's end and the great trees pulled up by the roots; of the serpent Kaliya pressed down in the lake; of Govardhana held aloft on one hand for the sake of Gokula; of the hump-backed woman cured, the dwarf form assumed, the wolves sent against the forest, the flying city Saubha brought down, Subhadra carried away from her brothers, the battle with Valahaka and Jamvumali, and the jewels taken from Indra himself. Every wonder of his life came back to him as song, sung before the whole company, and Balarama, delighted, began to sing with Revati, clapping the time.

Krishna, to please his brother, sang with Satyabhama. Arjuna, who had come aboard for the sea-voyage, joined his sister Subhadra and Krishna in the singing. And then the whole fleet joined: Gada and Sarana, Pradyumna, Samba and Satyaki, Charudeshna; Balarama's sons Nishatha and Ulmukha; the commander Akrura, Sankha, and all the leading heroes of the Yadava house sang together in one great chorus. By Krishna's power the boats themselves grew to hold them all, and the music carried over the water until the whole world was filled with joy and the sins of those who listened were washed away.

Then Narada came down, the guest of the celestials, the wandering singer of heaven, and took up his vina. He played, and he sang for Krishna with such intensity that a portion of his matted hair melted away in the heat of his own devotion. He composed songs on the spot and sang them again and again with every gesture his body could make. He smiled on Baladeva and Revata's daughter, on Krishna and Pritha's son Arjuna, on Satyabhama and Subhadra; and though the wives of Krishna were patient by nature, the sage who loved a joke made them laugh whether they wished to or not. He sang tunes high and low, laughed aloud, and wept tears of joy.

And Krishna himself danced. To the music of his own flute he performed the Hallishaka before them all, and the Apsaras answered him step for step, the beautiful Rambha rising to dance before Rama and Keshava, and Urvashi with her.

The celestial song called the Chhalikya, which until then had been heard only in heaven, was brought down that day and sung for mankind, and the world listened from its rooftops and its boats.

When the music finally ended, the damsels moved through the company at Krishna's command, giving away the best jewels of the earth, beautiful raiments and garlands, until every guest was laden with gifts. And the fleet sailed on, singing: heaven's song riding on mortal water, where a boy's deeds were remembered, and the war was, for one night, nothing but a song.
stories.reflection: The soiree turns the war's end into a festival of memory: every great deed of Krishna's life is sung back to him, and the celestial Chhalikya is brought down to human ears. Heaven does not stay above, it comes aboard the boats, dances, and weeps with joy, and the story's quiet point is that the divine rejoices to be remembered by the world it saved.
stories.next_story_tease: The celebration ended, and Nikumbha still lived.

stories.title: A Thousand Nikumbhas, One True Head
stories.story:
The garden attached to Bhanu's women's quarters was supposed to be unapproachable. That was precisely why, on the afternoon the Yadava heroes were busy with their sports, it stood unguarded — and why the demon Nikumbha chose that hour to strike. Years before, Pradyumna had carried off Prabhavati, the daughter of Nikumbha's brother Vajranabha, and the demon had never forgiven the insult. Now he slipped into the garden, seized Bhanumati, the beautiful daughter of Bhanu, and was gone before the weeping could even begin.

When the lamentation reached the men's quarters, Vasudeva and Ahuka rushed out in fury and found only an empty garden. They went straight to Krishna. He asked no questions and called no council: with Arjuna beside him he mounted Garuda, ordered Pradyumna, whose banner bore the makara, to follow in his chariot, and set off in pursuit. They caught Nikumbha long before he could reach the city of Vajra and the safety of his kinsmen.

The fight that followed was stranger than any of them had expected. Nikumbha fought smiling, a heavy club in his right hand and the weeping Bhanumati in his left, and because of her no one could strike him in earnest. Krishna, Pradyumna and Arjuna could have killed the demon a dozen times over; none of them could bear to wound the maiden. Arjuna, the finest of archers, solved the riddle the way a skilled man handles a serpent coiled around a camel: he struck the serpent and left the camel alone. His arrows, thin as reeds, found the demon again and again without ever touching the girl.

Then Nikumbha changed the game. Illusion was his art, and in a single breath he and the maiden vanished so completely that even his pursuers could not tell where they had gone. A yellow vulture crossed the sky, and Arjuna's arrows bit into it — the demon, transformed, was fleeing. The chase carried them across all seven continents of the earth, until at last Nikumbha dropped onto the summit of Mount Gokarna, on the bank of the river Chela Ganga, a mountain guarded by the energy of Mahadeva himself, which no god, Asura or ascetic could cross.

He had chosen well — but not well enough. Pradyumna, himself a master of illusion, slipped past the demon's guard and snatched Bhanumati away while Krishna and Arjuna drove Nikumbha back with arrows, until he fled from the northern slope of the mountain to the southern. With Krishna's permission Pradyumna carried the maiden home to Dwaraka, and returned at once to find Krishna and Arjuna waiting at the mouth of the cave into which Nikumbha had disappeared — the entrance to Shatpura, the city of his own people.

All night the three kept watch at the cave's mouth. At dawn the demon came out to fight. Arjuna's arrows from the Gandiva sealed the passage, but Nikumbha broke through them, seized his thorn-covered club and struck Arjuna full on the head. Blood poured from the hero's mouth and he fell senseless; the master of illusions snatched him up and carried him off. And then, all at once, the earth and the sky were full of demons.

Thousands of Nikumbhas filled the heavens — on the earth and in the welkin, in every direction, identical faces, identical clubs, identical smiles. Every eye saw a thousand demons. Krishna saw only one. With a sight older than the world and its illusions he perceived the true form of the creator of illusions, standing among his own echoes, and the discus left his hand and flew true. It cut off the head of the real Nikumbha, and in that instant every false Nikumbha dissolved like mist at sunrise. The demon who had filled the sky with himself was gone, and Arjuna, whom he had abducted, was free.

The gates of Shatpura stood open and empty behind them. Krishna gathered his friend up onto Garuda, and they turned toward Dwaraka — leaving behind a city whose master had been destroyed by the very illusion he had trusted.
stories.reflection: The thousand Nikumbhas are defeated not by force but by perception: Krishna wins the moment he sees through the illusion to the single true form behind it. Notice too that the whole pursuit was shaped by compassion — the heroes refused to strike until the maiden could be spared, so the killing blow came only when the fight could be finished cleanly.
stories.content_note: Mild battle violence: a hero is knocked unconscious and a demon is beheaded by the discus; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Nikumbha had a brother, and that brother had already begun to ask the universe for a gift that would threaten all three worlds.

stories.title: Vajranabha Demands the Three Worlds
stories.story:
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, an Asura sat in austerities so severe that the grandfather of the worlds himself took notice. Vajranabha was no ordinary demon, and he wanted no ordinary power: he wanted to be unkillable, and he wanted a home that nothing could enter. When Brahma, pleased by his penance, appeared before him and offered a boon, the Asura asked for two gifts — that even the gods might never be able to kill him, and that he might possess the city Vajra, where even the air could not enter without his will, a city that gave its lord whatever he desired before he had even thought of it, ringed by gardens and walls, surrounded by branch cities, full of peerless gems.

Brahma granted both, and Vajranabha moved into Vajra. Millions of demons came to live there under his protection, filling the central city, its gardens and its many charming branch cities, healthy and well-fed and contented, while their king enjoyed the boon he had demanded. No enemy had ever been known to pass those walls, and no one in the three worlds had found the door.

For a time that satisfied him. Then pride finished what penance had begun: the king of the Asuras decided the three worlds were not the gods' to keep. He stood before Indra, the king of heaven, and announced: "All the three worlds are the common property of the high-souled sons of Kashyapa. I wish to govern the three worlds. If you do not approve of my proposal, give me battle."

Indra answered with patience instead of war. He consulted Brihaspati, the priest of the gods, and then said: "Our father, the ascetic Kashyapa, is now engaged in a sacrifice. When it is finished, he will do what is fair." Vajranabha carried the same demand to Kashyapa himself, and heard the same words: go back to Vajra, live self-controlled, and wait for the sacrifice to end.

The demon returned to his city to wait — and while he waited, the gods were not idle. Indra went secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything Vajranabha had said. Krishna's answer was calm and complete: "My father's horse-sacrifice is at hand. When it is over, I will kill Vajranabha. But even the wind cannot enter his city unless he wishes it, so we will find our own way in."

The way in was already taking shape. During the horse-sacrifice, a wandering actor named Bhadra so charmed the assembled sages with his art that they offered him any boon he desired. Prompted — the text says it plainly — by Krishna's wish and the goddess of learning herself, Bhadra asked for strange gifts: to range freely over the earth and the sky, to be slain by no creature mobile or immobile, to take any form he pleased, to be never touched by age, and to find the sages always pleased with him. The Munis said "So be it," and Bhadra became the one being in all creation who could go anywhere and be welcomed everywhere. He began to wander the cities of the demon kings, performing for the Danavas, and on every festival day he came to Dwaraka, where the Yadavas received him as a guest of honour.

The plan was quiet, and it was already complete. And in heaven, Indra was speaking to the swans — the celestial birds who, though they carried the gods and the pious across the sky, were his own brothers, begotten by Kashyapa. To them he spoke of the great duty that now lay before the gods: the destruction of their enemies.
stories.reflection: The boon that made Vajranabha untouchable also made him predictable: a king who cannot be killed and a city that cannot be entered will be defeated through exactly that logic — by someone who can go anywhere and take any form. Boons answer words, not intentions, and pride read his own wish as a promise of safety.
stories.next_story_tease: The actor's boon was the key to Vajra — and soon the Yadavas would carry it through the city's unbreachable gates disguised as a company of players.

stories.title: The Play That Drained a City
stories.story:
By the time the company of actors reached the lands of the demons, their fame ran ahead of them. Everywhere they performed, the Asuras rose from their seats, delighted, and pressed jewels into their hands; in the city of Supura the citizens were so enchanted they begged for more. What the demons never guessed was that the troupe's newest players were not actors at all. They were Pradyumna, Gada, Shamba and the other Yadava heroes in the costumes of the stage, led by Bhadra — the actor who had been granted the boon to wander freely through all the three worlds.

The city of Vajra was supposed to be impossible to enter. Even the wind could not pass its walls unless the demon king Vajranabha willed it. But kings have appetites, and when Vajranabha heard of the marvellous actors he did what any patron of the arts would do: he sent a messenger, and invited them in. The demons of the branch cities brought the troupe to the charming city of Vajra, lodged them in a house built by the celestial architect, and supplied everything they could need by the hundred.

Vajranabha raised a beautiful pavilion and made a festival of the visit. The women of his family watched from behind a screen where they could see everything; the king himself sat among his kinsmen. And the actors began.

First the instruments — bells, flutes, drums — and then the women of the troupe sang the celestial song Chhalikya, the very music the Yadavas had brought down from heaven. They sang of the descent of the Ganga in seven scales and three modes, in the raga Vasanta and its kin, so sweetly that the Asuras rose again and again to heap rewards on them. Then came the Ramayana itself: the birth of Vishnu for the destruction of Ravana, and how the sage Rishyashringa was brought to King Dasharatha. The demons were startled by the likeness of the players — it seemed impossible that actors should resemble Rama and Lakshmana and Bharata so closely — and they rose from their seats, called out their praise, and gave away necklaces of gold and vaidurya, bracelets and cloth.

After the Ramayana, Pradyumna himself, still in the guise of an actor, conducted the prologue with Gada and Shamba, and Rukmini's son sang the hymn of the descent of the Ganga with beautiful gestures. Then came the drama Rambhabhisara: Shura played Ravana, Monovati played Rambha, Pradyumna played Nalakuvara and Shamba his jester. By their illusory powers the Yadavas conjured the very scene of Kailasha, and acted how the furious Nalakuvara cursed the wicked Ravana, and how Rambha was consoled.

The Danavas were enchanted. Costly garments, jewelled necklaces, sky-going chariots and celestial elephants, cool sandal and aguru and rare scents, and at last the fabled gem Chintamani, which grants whatever its owner thinks of — all of it rained upon the actors, scene after scene, until the treasuries of the demon lords ran dry. Even the women of the Danava chiefs gave away their jewels. The demons were deprived of their riches, the text says, precisely in the act of trying to spend them.

Only slowly did they understand. They had paid their enemies to entertain them — and the Yadavas, welcomed through gates that no army could ever have breached, had walked into the unbreachable city of Vajra.

Behind the screen, where the women of the Asura's own family sat watching, Vajranabha's daughter Prabhavati had received a message carried from Dwaraka. Her friend Suchimukhi whispered that she had seen Pradyumna himself, and that he had appointed this very evening to meet her. The Bhaimas never speak untruth — and so, the goose assured her, that night she would see her love.
stories.reflection: The city that no army could enter was entered by applause: the demons paid their enemies to entertain them and never suspected that the pleasure they bought was their own ruin. There is something almost courteous in the way the Yadavas take Vajra — not by storm, but by invitation.
stories.next_story_tease: The emptied treasuries were only the beginning, for Vajranabha had already set his heart on conquering heaven.

stories.title: A Father's Warning, a Son's March
stories.story:
The great sacrifice of Kashyapa had ended, and the gods and the Asuras had returned to their own worlds. All of them, that is, except one — and Vajranabha had not gone home to rest. He had gone home to prepare for war.

The lord of the unbreachable city Vajra had decided that the three worlds belonged to him, and he came to his father Kashyapa to set the conquest in motion, expecting perhaps a blessing. He received a warning instead.

"Sakra is the eldest of you all," said Kashyapa, "and the foremost in accomplishments. He is endued with great ascetic power, strong by nature, devoted to the Brahmanas, grateful, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good and the pious. He holds his sovereignty because he works for the well-being of all creatures. You will not be able to vanquish him, Vajranabha — you yourself will be killed. As a man who rouses the anger of a serpent meets his own destruction, so you will be destroyed in no time."

Vajranabha heard the words as a man hears medicine when he is already in love with death: as one whose limbs are bound by the noose of Death refuses the remedy, so the king of the Asuras refused his father's counsel. He saluted Kashyapa, turned away, and began to gather his kinsmen, his warriors, his friends. He would conquer the three worlds — and he would begin with the region of the celestials.

But the gods were already ahead of him. Indra and Upendra had sent the swans, the celestial birds who are brothers of the gods, begotten by Kashyapa, to bring about Vajranabha's destruction; and when the swans carried word that the Asura was marching on heaven, the Yadavas held a worried council. "Vajranabha will be killed by Pradyumna," they said. "But Vajranabha's daughter and the daughters of Sunabha are the devoted wives of our heroes, and they are all with child, their time near at hand. What are we to do?"

They sent the swans back to Indra and Krishna with the question, and the gods answered with a promise: "Do not fear. You will have beautiful sons, like Kama himself in accomplishments — even in the womb they will master the Vedas with their auxiliaries. Your sons will grow to youth at once, and they will be masters of every future topic and every scripture."

The swans carried the promise to the city of Vajra, where the Yadava heroes waited with their wives. Prabhavati bore Pradyumna a son, omniscient and youthful like his father; after a month Chandravati bore Chandraprabha, who resembled Gada; and Gunavati bore Gunavan — all of them youthful, omniscient, wonderful. The boys mastered every shastra as they grew, and they moved freely about the turrets of the palaces, shown to the Daityas, the text says, by the very desire of Indra and Upendra.

The Daityas stationed in the sky saw them and carried the news at once to Vajranabha, who was making ready to conquer heaven. "Arrest them!" cried the irrepressible king of the Asuras. "They have trespassed into my house!" Soldiers ringed the quarters, and cries arose on every side: "Seize them, kill them!" The mothers, who loved their sons, began to weep.

Pradyumna stood firm among them. "So long as we are alive and steady, you need not fear. The Daityas will not be able to do anything to us." Then he turned to the bewildered Prabhavati. "Your father, your uncles, your brothers and your kinsmen are waiting with clubs in their hands. For your sake they deserve our respect and honour — but the time is dreadful. If we endure this, we shall die; if we fight, we shall succeed. Consult with your two sisters, and tell us what we should do, for we are under your orders."

Prabhavati knelt, her hands on her forehead, weeping. "Take up your arms and protect yourself. If you survive, you will see your wife and your sons. Remember the honourable Rukmini and Aniruddha, and save yourself from this peril. A great rishi conferred a boon on me: that I would lead a blameless life forever, never be a widow, and my sons would live. I have hope that his words will not be falsified." She rinsed her mouth, and placed a sword in her husband's hands.

Beyond the city, the armies of Vajranabha were gathering for the march on heaven. Within it, a woman who carried a rishi's promise armed her husband for the war that would test whether that promise would hold.
stories.reflection: Kashyapa's warning is not a threat but an account of how sovereignty actually works: Indra rules because he serves the well-being of all creatures, not because he is the strongest. Vajranabha hears only the prophecy of death and marches toward it. Set against his pride is Prabhavati, a daughter of the enemy who arms her Yadava husband on the strength of a rishi's word — boon against boon, promise against promise.
stories.next_story_tease: Meanwhile Dwaraka was preparing a different kind of return — one that would bring the parijata tree and the captive maidens of Naraka's house back to Krishna's city.

stories.title: Homecoming with the Parijata
stories.story:
From Garuda's back, Krishna looked down on Dwarka, and the city looked back at him like a long-awaited answer.

He saw his own house rising among hundreds of palaces, the sable-hued palace of the Yadavas, its gates bright with a million white jeweled pillars, gems lustrous as fire, a number of effulgent golden seats set here and there for his court. For his reception a great palace had been raised entirely of gold, with pillars of crystal, ringed by lakes full of lotuses and fragrant red lotuses, where maddened peacocks and coels called from the trees and golden stairways led down to the water. Viswakarma, the celestial architect, had enclosed the whole with stone walls a hundred yards high, girded with ditches, a plot half a yojana on every side, measured, men said, against the palace of Indra himself.

Then Krishna raised the Panchajanya to his lips and blew. The sound made the hairs of his enemies stand on end; the ocean was stirred to its depths and the sky resounded, and to those who heard it in Dwarka it was the most wonderful sound in the world. At the note of the conch, and at the sight of Garuda circling down, the Kukuras and the Andhakas, his own kinsmen, felt their sorrow fall away. There he was, Keshava, shining like the sun, conch, discus and club in his hands, seated on the great bird. The citizens' joy spilled over: trumpets sounded, bugles blew, and men raised leonine shouts of triumph. Beholding the slayer of Madhu before them, the Kukuras, the Andhakas and the other Dasharhas began to approach him with great delight, crowding toward him, their joy overflowing.

King Ugrasena, placing Vasudeva before him, made his way to Vasudeva's palace to the sound of conches and trumpets. In their houses Devaki, Rohini and the wives of Ahuka moved about with joy. A few moments later Hari, he whom Indra and the other gods serve, arrived at the house prepared for him.

He alighted at the entrance and showed proper respect to all the Yadus. Balarama honored him, and Ahuka, Gada, Pradyumna and the rest; and so welcomed, Krishna entered his residence with the mountain of jewels beside him. Pradyumna, Rukmini's son, carried in the Parijata, the tree that was Indra's own favorite. By the power of that celestial tree the heroes saw their own forms made beautiful and took great delight. Eulogized by the rejoicing Yadu chiefs, Krishna passed into the house Viswakarma had built, placed the mountain of jewels with its shining summits in his inner apartments, and then, with the Vrishnis about him, worshipped the celestial tree and planted it in its proper place.

There remained one more homecoming. With his kinsmen's permission, Krishna honored every maiden he had brought back from Naraka's house, the women the demon king had held captive, giving them raiments, ornaments, maid-servants, riches and every object of enjoyment. Devaki, Rohini, Revati and the wives of Ahuka had already received them with honor. By his good fortune Satyabhama ruled over all the women of the household, while Rukmini, Bhishmaka's daughter, was in charge of the relatives. And to each of those women Krishna allotted her own house, her own tank, her own garden.

So the city that had sent him to war received him home with trumpets and gold; and the women Naraka had hidden away came out into the light of Dwarka, each with a place to call her own. The Parijata, planted in its proper place, began to change the air of the city, and the mountain of jewels stood in the inner apartments like a promise kept.
stories.reflection: The return to Dwarka is complete only when the women Naraka had kept captive are given homes of their own. The treasure Krishna brings back is not measured in jewels but in the shape it gives to freedom: separate houses, tanks and gardens, one for each of the maidens.
stories.next_story_tease: But beyond the rejoicing city, the war was not over: Rudra's terrible fever-demon, Jvara, still waited on the field where the Asuras had fled.

stories.title: When Fever Consumed Baladeva
stories.story:
The Asura army broke before the four of them like water against rock, and then the battle showed its true face.

Balarama, Rohini's son, grew dreadful in the fight, his form like Kala himself at the end of a cycle, as if he meant to consume everything that stood before him. Ranging over the field, he drew the enemy close with his ploughshare and ground them down with his mace. Mighty Pradyumna held the Danavas at bay with his arrows. Krishna, dark as a mass of collyrium, blew his conch and fought in a hundred ways, conch, discus and club always in his hands. Garuda himself joined them, striking the Daityas with his wings and tearing them with beak and nails, sending them to the abode of Yama. Assailed by that downpour of arrows and overpowered by those four heroes, the dreadful Asura army turned and fled the field.

Seeing his host routed, and wishing to protect them, Rudra's follower came walking onto the field: Jvara, the fever-demon, sighing again and again like a madman. He had three legs, three heads, six arms and nine faces, and he carried a weapon that consumed whatever it touched. He was like Yama himself. He roared like thousands of muttering clouds, yawned and dozed as he came, his hair standing on end, his eyes filthy and terrible. Making his face still more terrible, he called out in anger to the wielder of the ploughshare: "Why are you so proud of your strength? Do you not see that I have come to this field? Wait a few moments. You came before me in battle, but you will not return with your life."

Smiling, showing a fist dreadful as the fire of dissolution, Jvara ran at Balarama. But Rohini's son moved too quickly, wheeling in a thousand swift circles, and the demon could not find his opening. At last, aiming at that body huge as a mountain, Jvara hurled his consuming weapon. It struck Balarama's breast; then, dropping from his breast, it fell on the summit of Mount Sumeru and shattered the great mountain into pieces. But a remnant of the burning weapon stayed where it had fallen, and it began to consume Krishna's elder brother.

The warrior who had stood unshaken against armies now sighed and yawned without cease, reeling about the field, his eyes dilated, his hair on end, his senses bewildered. Almost losing consciousness, he cried out to Krishna: "O Krishna, O large-armed Krishna, giver of protection, I am being consumed, I am being consumed completely. How shall I be saved?"

Krishna smiled. "No fear," he said.

And he embraced his brother. By that embrace, by the touch of loving Krishna, Balarama was saved from the burning. The fever that had begun to eat him went out in his brother's arms.

Then the slayer of Madhu turned, angered, to the demon. "O Jvara, come and fight with me. Show me the full extent of your strength and power in this battle."

The fever-demon raised his burning weapon again, and the field grew still for what came next.
stories.reflection: The mightiest warrior on that field is not laid low by an army but by fever, something small and formless; and the cure is not a weapon but an embrace. Krishna answers his brother's despair with two words, 'No fear,' and the burning goes out at his touch.

stories.title: The Grapple with the Fever-Demon
stories.story:
The fever-demon Jvara had come to the battlefield to protect the routed Asura army, and in one terrible stroke he had nearly destroyed the mightiest man on the field: his burning weapon had fallen on Balarama's breast and begun to consume him. Krishna had saved his brother with an embrace, and the fire had gone out. Now Krishna turned to the demon himself. "Come and fight with me," he said. "Show me the full extent of your strength and power in this battle."

Jvara, the follower of Rudra, three-legged, three-headed, six-armed, with nine faces and a consuming weapon, answered with a weapon already burning. The field had emptied around them: the Asura army had fled, and only the two of them stood face to face in the middle of it.

With his right hand he discharged his great burning weapon straight at Krishna's body. It struck home, and Krishna, the foremost of strikers, felt the burning for a few moments. Then the fire went out. It had touched him, spent itself against him, and died, the way fire dies when it meets what it cannot consume.

Then Jvara, his long arms like serpents, struck Krishna on the neck and dealt a blow to his breast. Thus there took place a great encounter, in the middle of that field, between the fever-demon and the foremost of men. The sound of their striking arms rolled across the plain like thunder striking a mountain summit: blow after blow exchanged by the two most powerful beings on that field, strokes that would have felled armies. Krishna returned each stroke; the demon, who could range the sky, met a man who would not be shaken from his ground. And in the midst of it, strange to hear above the din, came words as if one fighter were instructing the other: "Do not strike this way. Strike this way."

For a long moment the Lord of the Universe, hidden in the guise of a man, wrestled with the sky-ranging Jvara, who gleamed with golden ornaments. He fought as a man fights, as if his own end were possible, as if this one body were all he had. And then he caught the fever-demon in his arms and ground him down, grinding the golden-adorned, sky-ranging Jvara with his arms, the way a pestle grinds grain in a mortar, until the demon's strength ran out of him like water from a broken jar. In that great battle the two had fought for a moment, and that moment had decided everything.

At last Krishna threw the broken Jvara down upon the earth, and for a moment he believed the field was won.

But the fever-demon, released from that crushing embrace, did not flee the field. He did what no beaten enemy had done before: he entered Krishna's body.
stories.reflection: In the midst of the duel come strange words of instruction, 'Do not strike this way, strike this way,' as though the fight itself were a lesson being given and received. And Krishna, wearing a mortal body, lets the burning touch him for a few moments before it goes out: even what wounds him is held within his own order.
stories.content_note: A wrestling duel between Krishna and the demon Jvara; described without gore.

stories.title: Fever Driven Out by Fever
stories.story:
He thought the demon was finished. He was wrong, and the mistake cost him more than any blow had.

Krishna threw Jvara down upon the surface of the earth, considering him dead from the grinding of his arms. But released from that grip, the fever-demon of incomparable energy did not leave the field. He entered Krishna's body.

Possessed by fever, Krishna's movements slackened. The victor of enemy cities, the great yogin, had to steady himself again and again with his hand on the ground. Sleep pressed upon him; his steps faltered; his hair stood on end; he sighed and yawned without ceasing. The man who had just crushed a demon in his arms was brought low by the demon's last trick, and it was a long time before he regained his natural state.

Then, knowing himself possessed, Krishna did what no one else could have done: he created a fever of his own. From his own energy the dreadful lord brought forth a second Jvara, a fever terrible to all creatures, made for the destruction of the first. The created fever seized the first Jvara by force, dragged him out of Krishna's body, and presented him before his maker. Thus the fever that had entered Krishna was driven out of him by fever itself.

The angry lord struck Jvara down upon the ground and was about to tear him to pieces. Bewildered, the demon cried out: "O Janardana, it behooves you to protect me!"

And as Krishna's hand was raised, a voice without a body spoke from the sky: "O Krishna, O large-armed Krishna, the delight of the Yadavas, do not kill this Jvara. O sinless one, he is worthy of being protected by you."

So Hari, the lord of the past, the future and the present, the great preceptor of the world, let the fever-demon go. Jvara prostrated himself, his head bowed at Krishna's feet, and said: "O descendant of Yadu, O Govinda, hear what I have to submit. Grant me this one boon, that I alone be the fever in this world, and no other flourish beside me."

"It is proper," said the lord, "to confer a boon on one who prays for it. And you have sought my protection. So be it, Jvara. As before, you will be the only fever. And he whom I have created, let him dissolve back into me."

The fever Krishna had made, the cure that had driven out the disease, dissolved into its source and vanished, as everything made from him returns to him. Then Krishna told the demon how he would range through the world, and gave him one more promise: the man who, having saluted Krishna, attentively reads this account of the great battle will be freed from fever. "So be it," said Jvara, delighted, and saluting his master, he left the battlefield.
stories.reflection: The episode turns on a strange symmetry: fever is driven out by fever, the cure created from the same energy as the disease and then dissolved back into its source. And even the demon who had possessed him, once he asked for protection, was spared: in Krishna's world, even fever is answered when it prays.
stories.next_story_tease: But Jvara was not done: before he left the field, the spared demon would receive the terms of his rule over every living thing.

stories.title: The Only Fever in the World
stories.subtitle: Krishna spares the defeated Jvara and grants him dominion over fever
stories.story:
An invisible voice spoke out of the sky, and the great battle of Sonitpura came to a halt.

The war between Krishna and the thousand-armed king Vana had drawn the gods themselves onto the field. Vana was Shiva's devoted servant, and Shiva had sent his own creatures to fight for him — among them Jvara, the fever. The burning sickness had slipped inside Krishna's own body the moment it was struck down: for a while Krishna's movements had slackened, his steps had grown heavy, his hair stood on end, and he had yawned and sighed without cease, supporting himself with one hand on the ground until, after a long time, the great yogi shook the weakness off. He had drawn the demon out by creating from his own energy a second Jvara — a fever more dreadful than the first, terrible to all creatures — which had seized the original by force and dragged it from his body. Now the creature lay pinned in Krishna's hands, and Krishna, angry, threw him down on the earth and was about to tear him into pieces.

Then the invisible voice spoke from the sky: "O Krishna, large-armed Krishna, enhancer of the delight of the Yadavas, do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you."

Krishna, the lord of the past, the present and the future, the great preceptor of the world, heard it and let the fever go.

Jvara rose and prostrated himself at Krishna's feet with bent head. "O descendant of Yadu, O Govinda, hear what I have to submit unto you. I pray for this one boon only: that I may be the only Jvara in this world, and no one else may flourish."

"It is proper to confer a boon on one who prays for it," Krishna said, "and you have sought my protection. Fare well, Jvara. You will have what you pray for. As before, you will be the only fever — and may the one I created dissolve in me."

And the counter-fever that Krishna had made melted back into his own being, as frost melts into the morning.

Then Krishna told the fever how it would range through the world from that day on. "Divide yourself into three parts: with one, possess the four-legged animals; with the second, the immobile objects; with the third, human beings. And with the fourth portion of your third part, you will always live among the birds." Among mankind the fever would come in four forms, returning every day, after two days, after three days, and after four days. In trees it would live as the insect and the blight that withers the leaves and turns them pale; in fruits, as the disease called Aturya; in lotuses, as frost; in the earth, as drought; in water, as the weed Neelika; in peacocks, as the growing of the crest; in mountains, as mineral; in cows, as the sickness called Khoraka. "With your very sight and touch," Krishna said, "animals will lose their lives. Only gods and men will be able to withstand you."

Jvara was delighted. With folded hands he saluted Krishna. "I am blessed, Madhava, that you give me sovereignty over all creatures and objects. I wish to carry out any other order of yours — order me what I am to do. I was created long ago by Hara, the slayer of Tripura. Now, vanquished by you in battle, I have become your servant. You are my master."

"Then hear the resolution I cherish," Krishna said. "Any man who salutes me and attentively reads this account of the prowess of my arms in the great battle will be freed from fever."

"So be it," Jvara said.

Having received his boon and given his promise, the fever saluted Krishna and left the battlefield — carrying with him, in the very shape of his existence, the mercy that had spared him.
stories.reflection: Jvara asks not for safety but for supremacy — he wants to remain the only fever in the world — and Krishna grants the wish while redrawing its limits: the fever may range everywhere, but it returns in measured forms, and the telling of its defeat is promised to free men from it. Mercy, here, is not the erasure of an enemy but the reshaping of his power.
stories.next_story_tease: But the fever was only one of Vana's defenders — Shiva himself was already riding toward the battlefield.
stories.hero_scene: On the Sonitpura battlefield the defeated Jvara, a gaunt burning figure, prostrates with bent head at Krishna's feet while Krishna, radiant, raises a hand in blessing and the counter-fever he created dissolves into mist behind him.

stories.title: The Lion-Drawn Car Enters Battle
stories.subtitle: Shiva and Kartikeya ride out to protect Vana
stories.story:
Half of Vana's army was running, and the rest was burning.

Riding together on the back of Garuda, Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna — three heroes who blazed like three fires — swept down on the Danava host with a downpour of arrows. The fire kindled by Krishna's discus burned among them like the fire of the world's dissolution and consumed thousands; the survivors scattered, dropping their coats of mail, their swords, their daggers, their darts, their leathern protectors and their axes.

Vana galloped after his own soldiers, shouting them back. "Born in the race of the Daityas, why do you, overwhelmed with fear and displaying your weakness, fly away from the battlefield? Think of your birth, and of the life you have lived with Hara, and then decide whether you should fly. I stand before you now." But the Danavas, beside themselves with fear, paid no heed and fled. Kumbhanda, Vana's powerful minister and friend, tried his own appeal: "O leading Danavas, behold Shankara, Kartikeya and Vana himself in the field. Give up hope of your lives and fight." The words were still in the air when the last of them vanished. Of all that great army, only the Pramathas, Shiva's own attendants, stood firm and wished to fight again.

Then Shiva's anger rose. Seeing his soldiers routed by Krishna, the great god's eyes reddened, and to protect Vana he mounted his lustrous car and prepared himself for fighting. Kartikeya too ascended a car that burned like fire. And Rudra's own chariot — drawn by lions, making a great sound, as if devouring the sky — came rolling onto the field like the full moon freed from clouds.

It was surrounded by ghosts. Some had the faces of lions, some of tigers, some of serpents, some of horses, camels, asses, peacocks, rams, cats, sheep. Some wore matted locks, some had their hair bound up, some went naked, some were dressed in bark or in the skins of lions and tigers; some had beautiful faces and were adorned with celestial weapons and flowers, while others were dwarfish and grim-visaged, their faces covered with blood, their teeth huge, their hunger for flesh never satisfied. They blew conch-shells and bugles as they came, and they stood encircling Shankara, the destroyer of great enemies, waiting at ease while the lion-drawn car bore the god of gods toward Hari.

Krishna, seeing that car approach, rode Garuda into the battle. Hara, who always stood at the head of a fight, struck him in anger with hundreds of winged arrows; and Hari, irate, took up the excellent weapons given him by Indra and answered. The earth shook under the exchange, the elephants trembled and raised their heads, the mountains were covered with the water of streams and scattered their summits on all sides. The quarters, the sky and the earth were as if ablaze; fire-brands fell from every side, and dreadful jackals began their inauspicious cries. Indra himself sent down showers of blood and fire-brands over the rear of Vana's army, the wind blew high, and the luminous bodies and herbs, shorn of their lustre, flew about in the sky.

Brahma, the Grandfather, knowing that Rudra, the destroyer of Asuras, had entered upon a battle, came there encircled by the celestials; the Apsaras, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas and Charanas stood in the sky to witness the encounter.

Then Vishnu discharged Indra's weapon at Rudra. Burning, it flew straight at the car where the god stood — and the very next moment hundreds and thousands of arrows dropped before Hara's car in answer. Seeing it, and filled with anger, Hara discharged his dreadful fiery weapon in return, and it appeared indeed highly wonderful. Krishna and the three other heroes were entirely covered with arrows, and the sky above Sonitpura turned the colour of the end of the world.
stories.reflection: The moment Shiva enters, the war stops being a siege and becomes a confrontation between gods themselves. The ghosts with their animal faces and their conch-shells are a reminder that Shiva's power is not tidy — it is wild, old, and loyal — and Krishna rides out to meet it without hesitation while the whole sky gathers to watch.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet before that duel could be decided, a strange figure would step between Krishna and his discus.

stories.title: The Goddess Who Stood Between
stories.subtitle: Kottavi intervenes, and Krishna puts away his discus
stories.story:
After the high-souled Krishna and Rudra had retired from the field, the hair-stirring battle of Sonitpura did not end — it changed hands. The war between Krishna and Vana, the thousand-armed king who was Shiva's devotee, had drawn the gods onto the battlefield, and now the younger commanders took it up.

Kartikeya, mounted on the car that Kumbhanda had brought him, drove straight at Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful, sharpened arrows. Bathed in blood, the three heroes fought back like three fires. When they struck Kartikeya with the three weapons given by the Wind-god, the Fire-god and Indra, he counteracted them with three weapons of his own — Shaila, Varuna and Savitri — and the Yadavas, by their illusory power, devoured even those, though the holder of the burning bow and shaft shot them swiftly.

Then Guha, burning with effulgence and biting his lips, took up the dreadful weapon called Brahmashira, like the Destroyer himself. When it was discharged — blazing with the effulgence of a thousand suns, destructive of the world — creatures lost consciousness at its warmth and fled on all sides, and the whole universe bewailed. Keshava, the slayer of Keshi, saw it and raised his discus, the destroyer and counteractor of all weapons; and as clouds in the rainy season cover the rays of the sun, so that discus covered the lustre of the Brahmashira and left it shorn of its power and energy.

Kartikeya's eyes reddened in anger, and he blazed up like fire to which clarified butter has been offered. He took up the golden Sakti — the celestial spear, set with bells, sure of aim, destructive of enemies, effulgent like a fire-brand and resembling the fire of dissolution — and hurled it with a shout that struck terror into his enemies. The spear flew into the sky, yawned, and moved about with great force, as if it desired to slay Krishna. The gods and their king were greatly depressed: "Perhaps Krishna will be consumed." But as the great spear appeared before him, Madhava shouted — as if remonstrating with it — and struck it down to the ground. "Well done! Well done!" rose from all sides, and Indra together with the celestials sent up a leonine shout.

Then Vasudeva, powerful, took up his discus to kill the Daityas. And he was about to discharge it when the beautiful Kottavi came before him — naked, at the command of Mahadeva, to protect Kumara. Lamva, the eighth portion of the goddess, intervened between them like a beautiful golden spear.

Seeing the goddess stand before Kartikeya, the large-armed Krishna was baffled. "Fie on you! Fly away soon from this place. Why do you throw obstacles in the way of certain destruction?"

Kottavi heard him — and for the sake of protecting Kumara, she did not put on her cloth.

"Take Guha with you," Krishna said, "and fly away soon from the battlefield. It will be well for us today if you do this. Or else, if I refrain from fighting, he will fight with me."

And beholding the naked goddess in the battlefield, the divine Hari put away his discus.

Then the goddess brought Guha before Hara, and the great danger passed. When Vana saw Kartikeya released from Krishna's discus and retiring from the field, he felt the inclination to fight Madhava himself. His ghosts, his Yakshas and his soldiers fled away on all sides; of that broken army only the Pramathas remained. And with them, and with his great Daitya commanders, Vana marched out to battle — while his priests and other elders, well read in the Shrutis, performed benedictory ceremonies on his behalf with mantras, recitations and herbs, chanting the destruction of his enemies.
stories.reflection: Krishna's discus has never hesitated before a weapon, but it stops before a woman who stands unarmed. The episode turns on a strange kind of strength: the goddess does not fight, she merely refuses to move, and in that refusal the shape of the battle is changed.
stories.content_note: The episode centers on the goddess Kottavi appearing unclothed on the battlefield; the source treats this matter-of-factly, and the story describes it with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: With Kartikeya withdrawn, Vana himself now took the field, roaring of his thousand arms.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, discus raised to strike, frozen mid-throw as the goddess Kottavi stands unclothed and unafraid before the young Kartikeya, her form gleaming between them like a golden spear.

stories.title: The Boast of a Thousand Arms
stories.subtitle: Vana vaunts, and Krishna answers with the Sarnga bow
stories.story:
"Wait! Wait!" Vana shouted across the field of Sonitpura. "You will not escape me today alive to Dwaraka, to see your friends there. O Madhava, you have been urged on by Death. Vanquished by me in battle, you will look on the golden leaves of the trees on the eve of your death. O Garudhwaja, you have eight arms — how will you fight with me, who have a thousand? Slain with all your friends in the city of Shonita, you will remember Dwaraka. Today you will see my thousand arms, adorned with various weapons and ornaments, multiply into a million."

His words travelled over the field like the dreadful waves of an ocean raised by wind, and his eyes, filled with anger, shone like two suns rising in the firmament.

From the top of the palace, Narada laughed aloud — so loudly that the sky seemed sundered in twain. Seated on his yoga seat, the ascetic moved about on all sides, filled with curiosity to see the battle.

Krishna answered with the patience of a man who had heard many boasts. "O Vana, why do you roar thus out of foolishness? Heroes do not vaunt. What is the use of vaunting? Come and fight with me in the battlefield. O son of Diti, you have given vent to many unconnected words. If victory were accomplished by words in a battle, you would no doubt be victorious already. Come, Vana — either defeat me, or, vanquished by me, lie down on the earth for good, with your face down."

And with that he struck Vana with arrows that cut him to the quick. Vana, in turn, covered Krishna with burning arrows, with parighas and nisthringsas, with clubs, tomars, shaktis, maces and pattishas, until the holder of the conch, the discus and the club was buried beneath them. Proud Vana, with his thousand arms, fought easily; and Keshava, who had eight, fought on. Seeing Krishna's superior training, the son of Bali grew greatly worked up with anger, and he discharged the celestial great weapon that Brahma, by his ascetic powers, had created long ago for Hiranyakashipu. All the quarters were enshrouded with darkness; thousands of dreadful omens appeared on every side; everything went beyond the range of perception. The Danavas applauded Vana — "Well done! Well done!" — while the cries of the gods, "Alas!", were heard. A dreadful downpour of burning arrows was caused by the force of that weapon, and while Keshava was being burnt, wind, storm and clouds did not move.

Then the divine slayer of Madhu took up Indra's weapon, like unto inevitable death. The moment it was ready, all the worlds were shorn of darkness, the fire was extinguished, and the Danavas completely lost their hearts. Seeing their weapon counteracted as soon as Indra's weapon was drawn, the gods began to laugh and roar like lions.

Beside himself with rage, Vana spoke harsh words to Keshava on Garuda's back and covered him with maces and pattishas. Keshava, the slayer of his enemies, counteracted his uplifted weapons, smiling. Then, with arrows like thunderbolts shot from his Sarnga bow, he sundered Vana's car, with its horses and standards, into pieces. The very next moment he separated from Vana's person his lustrous crown, his coat of mail, his bow and his shield — and, smiling, struck him on the breast with winged arrows. Cut to the very quick, Vana lost consciousness and swooned away.

From the top of the palace, Narada rose up clapping. "O great fortune! Great fortune! Blessed is my life and my birth, since I have witnessed today this wonderful prowess of Damodara. O large-armed one, adored by the gods, accomplish that for which you have incarnated yourself — destroy soon Diti's son Vana."

And as the armies watched, even the standards fought their own battle: the horses of the gods and of the Danavas clashed, and Garuda and the peacock struck at each other with wings, beaks and talons, until the great bird, leaping up in anger, seized the peacock's head in his beak.
stories.reflection: Narada's laughter at the boast and his applause at the defeat frame the whole duel as a spectacle: the ascetic watches from the palace rooftop, and the mightiest warriors of the universe perform for him. The hundred arms multiply into a million only in Vana's own telling — in the end, it is one bow that dismantles them.
stories.next_story_tease: But Vana's life was not yet decided — the goddess would step between them once more.
stories.hero_scene: Vana's thousand arms spread in fury as Krishna's arrows from the Sarnga bow shatter his chariot, crown, mail, bow and shield, while Narada claps from the palace rooftop and Garuda battles the peacock overhead.

stories.title: Kottavi Stands Between Krishna and Vana
stories.story:
The war had come to Sonitpura because Krishna's grandson Aniruddha had been taken from Dwaraka and bound with serpent-nooses in the palace of Vana, king of the thousand arms. Now the city had fallen, the young man was free, and the last of the fighting was being done out on the open field.

High above it, the standards themselves were fighting. Garuda and the great peacock of Vana's banner clashed in the air, striking with wings, beaks and talons, until the eagle caught the peacock's head in his beak and flung it down. Beneath them, Vana had risen for the second time that day. His chariot lay in splinters, horses and standards shattered by arrows from Krishna's Sarnga bow; his crown, his coat of mail, his bow and his shield were scattered in the dust. He came on anyway, a thousand arms, and every one of them holding a weapon.

Krishna faced him from Garuda's back. "Wait, wait!" Vana roared, and the anger in his eyes burned like two suns rising. "You will not escape me alive to Dwaraka today. Being of eight arms, how will you fight me, who have a thousand? You will see my arms multiply into a million."

"Heroes do not vaunt," Krishna answered. "If words could win battles, you would have won already. Come, Vana — either defeat me, or be vanquished and lie down on the earth for good."

The exchange that followed shook the field to its edges. Vana loosed the great weapon that Brahma had created by his ascetic power for Hiranyakashipu, and darkness covered all the quarters; burning arrows fell like a dreadful rain, and even wind and cloud held still. The Danavas applauded, and the gods cried out in alarm. Then Krishna took up Indra's weapon, and the darkness was shorn away, the fire went out, and the gods watching laughed like lions. Beyond reason now, Vana buried Krishna under maces and spears; and Krishna, smiling, struck him on the breast with winged arrows, and the thousand-armed king of Sonitpura lost consciousness and fell.

Narada, watching from the palace roof, rose up clapping. "Great fortune, great fortune!" he cried. "Blessed is my birth, for I have witnessed the prowess of Damodara today. Destroy Diti's son, Vana."

The discus was already in Krishna's hand when the goddess appeared. Kottavi — Lamva, she was also called — stepped between them unclothed, with nothing to protect her but the fierce dignity of an old promise. "I gave this boy my word long ago," she said. "I conferred on him a boon, saying that I would protect him. I will not see that boon broken now."

Krishna looked at her, and the discus did not move. "Then hear my vow, goddess. I will cut off Vana's thousand arms today, every one of them. Let them fall to the earth. Your son will live, even if Vana is left with only two arms."

She could not find fault with mercy that came shaped like that. And so it was done: the discus passed through the field of arms like light through a forest, and where it went, weapons fell and arms fell with them, until the king who had fought with a thousand hands stood at the end of it with two — alive, breathing, shorn of his terrible power but not of his life. The goddess's boon was honoured, and Krishna's vow was honoured too.

The field fell silent, watching Vana stare at his two empty hands. And high above, unseen by any, Shiva was watching the battlefield as well — and Shiva, too, had once promised Vana his protection.
stories.reflection: Krishna's mercy here is exact and strange: he takes away the thing that made Vana terrible, the thousand arms, and leaves the life. Kottavi's boon and Krishna's own vow meet in a single act of measured severity, and both promises are kept in the same stroke.
stories.content_note: Depicts a battle and the severing of Vana's thousand arms; described with restraint, not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shiva, too, had promised Vana his protection — and he was watching the field.
