stories.title: The Serpent of Ambika Forest
stories.subtitle: Nanda is swallowed and freed
stories.story:
A cry cut through the Ambika forest in the small hours of the night, and every cowherd of Vraja woke at once. "Krishna! Krishna!" Nanda's voice rang through the trees. "A great serpent has taken me!"

There was no mistaking that voice, or the terror in it. The cowherds had come to the forest of the goddess Ambika to keep a vow, and they had lain down to sleep under the great trees, their cattle grazing at the edge of the clearing. Nanda, the chief of the herdsmen, slept at the centre of the camp — and when the cowherds came running with burning firebrands snatched from the campfire, they saw why he had cried out.

A serpent of impossible size lay coiled across the clearing, and Nanda was wrapped inside its folds. The creature had not eaten in a long time; hunger had driven it from the deep parts of the forest toward the sleeping men, and it had taken their leader like a mouse in a nest. It was already swallowing, its jaws working over Nanda's shoulders, and its coils tightened with every breath it drew.

The cowherds did not stop to think. They fell on the serpent together — beating it, scorching it, pressing the smoking ends of the firebrands into its scales, shouting all the while. The great snake shuddered and hissed; the smell of burning scales filled the clearing. But it did not let go. The fire that made the cowherds flinch back only made the serpent draw Nanda deeper, and Nanda's cries grew fainter as the great jaws worked.

Then Krishna came through the ring of desperate men. There was no weapon in his hand, no anger in his face. The cowherds fell back to let him pass, and he walked up to the serpent as if it were a stray calf, and touched it with his bare foot.

The touch undid what all their fire could not. The serpent released Nanda at once, its coils falling slack, and Nanda tumbled out onto the grass — shaken, breathless, alive. And where the monstrous body had lain, there now stood a being of molten light, as though the firebrands had finally taken hold and burned the beast away, leaving only what had been hidden inside it all along.

Krishna studied the radiant figure, which bowed low before him. "Who are you?" he asked. "You shine with a beauty that is wonderful to see."

"I was Sudarshana, a Vidyadhara," the being said, "one of the sky-farers. I was proud of my form and prouder still of my beauty, and one day I laughed at the sages of the Angirasa lineage to their faces. They cursed me — but theirs was a compassionate curse, laid on me as a grace I did not yet understand. It bound me in the body of this serpent, to crawl and to hunger until the touch of the blessed one should free me. That touch is yours, and this is the day. Your foot has burned away the evil of the curse, and I stand released."

"Then go," Krishna said. "The curse is finished."

Sudarshana praised him then — the one who takes away the fear of all who come to him for refuge, the great yogi, the lord of the good — and when his words ran out, he circled Krishna, bowed again at his feet, and rose into the dark sky until the night swallowed him.

The cowherds stood a long time in silence. The firebrands still smoked in their hands. Nanda sat on the grass, whole, drawing breath after breath. They had grown up with Krishna — had watched him graze the calves, had scolded him and loved him as their own — but they had never seen anything like this. What kind of boy was it whose foot could turn a devouring serpent into a shining god?

They finished their vow in the forest of Ambika as the sun rose, and on the road back to Vraja they told the story at every village they passed. Each telling made it more wonderful, and each telling left them more certain: the boy who walked with them was not merely a boy, and the night in the Ambika forest was only the beginning of what they would see.
stories.reflection: The curse the sages laid on Sudarshana had been a grace all along — punishment as a waiting-room for Krishna's touch. The same night reads three ways: terror for Nanda, astonishment for the cowherds, gratitude for the freed Vidyadhara, and all three are held together by one boy's bare foot.
stories.next_story_tease: The serpent gone and the vow fulfilled, Krishna's road was already turning another way — toward Mathura.

stories.title: The Weaver and the Garland-Maker
stories.subtitle: Two craftsmen of Mathura honour the brothers
stories.story:
Mathura had never seen boys like the two who walked its royal road that evening. Men and women stopped to look; children ran ahead to look again. They moved like young elephants, unhurried and easy, and the dust of the road only made them shine the more.

They had come from Vrindavan, brought by Akrura in his chariot, and Akrura had left them at the city's edge to enter on foot. Now they walked the royal road through the streets of Kamsa's city as if they had been born to them — Krishna and Balarama, cowherd boys in plain cloth, on the day before the city would learn what they were. Men and women regarded them with pleasure and went along behind them sportively, the way a town follows a festival it has not yet understood.

It was a weaver who first dared to stop them. He looked at the two brothers — at the homespun cloth they wore, at the road dust on their shoulders — and it grieved him that such forms should go so dressed. He brought out his finest cloth and, glad beyond measure, cut and fitted garments for them both, rich cloth of many colours, each garment marked with its own device. When Krishna and Balarama stood dressed in the weaver's work, they shone, and the weaver saw that he had dressed something more than two travellers. Krishna was pleased with him, and to the weaver he gave a rare gift: a form like his own, so that the man who had clothed the lord's body would bear the lord's likeness in his own.

From the weaver's shop they went on through streets that grew quieter as the evening deepened, until they came to the house of Sudama, the garland-maker. Sudama looked once at his two visitors and seemed to know at once who stood in his doorway. He brought them in, set seats for them, washed their feet, and offered them water and all the honours of a guest. He pressed garlands on them and sandal paste, and his hands trembled with delight as he worked.

"Our birth is made fruitful today," he said, standing before them with folded hands. "Our family is purified. You two are the supreme cause of this whole world — there is no partial glance in you, who are the soul of all that lives. Command your servant: what shall we do for you?"

Krishna and Balarama accepted the garlands and the paste, and were pleased. Then Sudama was asked what he himself wanted — and the garland-maker, who had given everything he had and asked for nothing, named one thing only.

"Unshakable devotion," he said. "A love of you that nothing can move."

"It is yours," Krishna said. "And with it, take this: fortune that never leaves you, prosperity that grows in your line for generations." The blessing, the older telling adds, would not end in this life either — at the end of his days a heavenly region awaited the man who had honoured the lord before he fully knew him.

Word of the two strangers spread through Mathura that night. The weaver told his neighbours, and Sudama told his customers, and the garland-scented shop carried the story out into the streets. Kamsa's city had been told to fear the cowherd boys from Vrindavan; instead it learned that they had walked its royal road like kings and blessed its craftsmen, that a weaver's needle and a garland-maker's flowers had been enough to earn the favour of the world's cause. The city waited, uncertain and wondering, to see what they would do next.
stories.reflection: The two gifts mirror each other: the weaver receives a form like the Lord's because he dressed the Lord's body, and the flower-seller asks only for devotion because he has already laid every other offering at Krishna's feet. Each man is answered exactly with what he offered.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells of the flower-seller alone, and frames his reward as fortune that never forsakes him and a heavenly region at the end; the Bhagavata adds the weaver and names Sudama's boon unshakable devotion.
stories.next_story_tease: But while Mathura wondered, in a dry well far away a king lay trapped in a lizard's body — and his long wait was almost over.

stories.title: Krishna Liberates King Nriga
stories.story:
This happened in the days when Krishna lived among the Yadus in Dwaraka, and the young men of the clan still played as boys play. One morning they ran out into the fields beyond the city walls and played until the sun stood high, chasing one another through the long grass and the dust. The games went on until their legs ached and their laughter ran dry in their throats. By afternoon their throats were dry, and they went looking for water, searching this way and that, calling to one another across the empty fields. In their searching they came upon a well. It was dry. But it was not empty.

At the bottom of the dry well lay a lizard, and it was vast — the size of a hill, a creature no such well should ever have held. It was a thing out of a story, too big to be real, and yet there it lay in the dark, still as the stone around it. Its hide gleamed faintly in the light from the well's mouth, and its stillness was the stillness of something waiting. The boys stood at the rim and stared down at it, astonished, and for a long moment no one spoke. Then, being boys and never ones to leave a wonder alone, they decided to haul it up.

They knotted together ropes of leather and thread, lowered them into the dark, and bound the great creature. Then they pulled — all of them together, setting their heels and calling out to one another — and the thing would not move. The great lizard did not so much as stir at their efforts. They pulled until their hands burned and their breath came hard, and still it lay where it was, patient as stone. In the end they had to stand back, breathless and baffled, and wonder what such a creature could be, and how it had ever come to rest in a dry well.

Word of it reached Krishna, and he came to the well, and the boys made way for him. He stood at the edge and looked down at the creature in the dark, and he did not trouble himself with ropes. He reached in with his left hand, took hold of it, and drew it up into the light. And the moment his hand touched it, the lizard was gone. The boys had strained and failed; his touch alone was enough.

In its place stood a man, and he shone. He stood in the sunlight with the brilliance of molten gold, a splendor that was not of this world, and the boys fell back from him, shielding their eyes. For a long moment no one could look at him directly. The whole morning's play was forgotten, and the well and the field and the dust of the road all seemed to stand still around him.

Krishna was not surprised. He knew already who stood before him and by what deed he had come to this. But he asked the question aloud, so that the answer would be heard not by him alone but by everyone gathered at the well. “What deed,” he asked, “has brought you to this state — you, who did not deserve such a thing?”

The radiant man lifted his head — for he was Nriga, a king of ancient days — and before the wondering crowd he began to speak, the boys pressing closer and forgetting, for a little while, their thirst. And the story he told, of how a king had come to crouch in a dry well, was one the whole city would learn.
stories.reflection: The scene withholds more than it gives. We are not told, here, why a king crouched in a dry well in a lizard's skin; we are shown only that the touch of Krishna's hand was enough to end it. Liberation, in this telling, does not wait for an explanation — it comes first, and only afterward asks, so that the telling can become a gift to everyone listening.
stories.tradition_note: This episode is told only in the Bhagavata Purana; it has no parallel in the other major sources.

stories.title: Nriga's Story of the Disputed Cow
stories.subtitle: How a king famed for giving fell into a lizard's body
stories.story:
The being who stood before Krishna had been a lizard until moments ago — a lizard the size of a hill, at the bottom of a dry well, drawn out at last by Krishna's left hand and transformed by his touch into a king of molten-gold splendour. The Yadu princes still stared. The people of Dwaraka pressed close. And Krishna asked the question everyone wanted answered: how had a being so evidently blessed come to spend his years at the bottom of a well?

The king bowed. "What is unknown to you, lord," he said, "you who are the witness of every being's heart? But if you wish the world to know, I will tell it. I am Nriga, of the line of Ikshvaku."

And Nriga told his story.

He had been a king famed above all kings for one thing: giving cows. As many cows as there are sands on the earth, as stars in the sky — so many had he given. Milch cows and young cows, gentle cows of fine colour and form, tawny cows with horns tipped in gold — he had given them to brahmanas of good conduct, to men who kept their vows, to households bowed down by want. And not cows alone: land and gold, houses and horses, elephants and maidens with their servants, sesame and silver and beds. His wealth had flowed outward his whole life, and the fame of it had travelled ahead of him into every kingdom.

Then, one day, the accident. A cow belonging to a leading brahmana of his realm strayed from its owner's herd and mingled with the royal cattle. In the great round of giving — one cow among thousands — it was led out and given to another brahmana.

"Its owner saw it as it was led away," Nriga said, "and he cried out: 'That cow is mine!' The brahmana who had received it cried out as well, that it was his by gift. Both stood before me, each seeking his own right, and both claimed the cow."

Nriga understood at once what had happened. He offered each brahmana recompense — whatever he had won by righteous toil — and begged them both to forgive a servant who had not known what he gave.

"Neither would accept," Nriga said. "The owner would not take another cow, or gold, or land, in place of his own. 'I will not accept it, king,' he said, and he walked away. The other would not give back the gift. The two could not be reconciled, and I could not undo what my own hand had done."

The story might have ended there, in a dispute no court could settle. It did not. In that very moment, Nriga said, Yama's messengers came for him. They took him from his palace to the court of Yama, lord of the dead, and Yama — who weighs every life — gave the king of givers a choice.

"You carry both merit and fault from this life," Yama said. "Your giving was vast; your error is real. Which will you taste first — the good or the bad?"

Nriga answered without hesitation. "Let me taste the bad first."

Why? He did not argue it. Perhaps because the merit of a life of giving could wait; because a king who had wronged two brahmanas, even unknowingly, would rather pay than postpone; because he trusted that what he had given with both hands would keep its own appointment. Whatever his reason, he chose the bad — and the bad took the shape of a lizard.

"I fell from my palace into this body," Nriga said, "and the dry well became my kingdom. Year after year I lay at the bottom of it — a king who had given away thousands of cows, unable to give anything at all, not even a prayer, in a lizard's throat. The merit waited. All those years, the merit waited."

He fell silent. The Yadu princes looked at the radiant king and tried to see the lizard in him. Krishna listened without moving.

"And now," Nriga said at last, "you have touched me. And I think — I hope — the waiting is over."
stories.reflection: Nriga is no villain: a famously generous king, undone by an accident that no compensation could repair. His choice to suffer the bad first is the quiet heroism of the tale — he would rather taste his error than postpone it, trusting that the merit of a life of giving would keep its own appointment.
stories.next_story_tease: His story told, Nriga bowed at Krishna's feet — and the ending the lizard-years had delayed was already descending from the sky.

stories.title: Nriga Ascends, and Krishna Warns the City
stories.subtitle: The lizard-king's merit claims its ending
stories.story:
Nriga stood in the light of Dwaraka, and for the first time in an age he was a king who could bow. He had told his story — the stray cow, the two brahmanas, Yama's choice — and now he stood before Krishna with the words running out and praise taking their place.

"What is there that you do not know, lord?" he said. "You are the witness of every being's heart. Yet how is it that I, who lived so long in blindness and in a lizard's body, have come to see you with my own eyes? You whom the yogis seek in the depths of their hearts, whom the scriptures only glimpse, the lord beyond the reach of the senses — you stand here before me, in this city. The very sight of you is the end of birth and of fear."

Then he asked for what he had been waiting to ask. "Permit me, Krishna," he said, "to go to the celestial world. Let me go where the merit of my giving has been waiting all these years." He bowed, circled Krishna, and touched the lord's feet with his head. Then he stood, and waited.

But Krishna did not send him off in silence. He turned instead to his people — the citizens of Dwaraka who had gathered to watch the wonder — and what he said to them was meant to outlast the day.

"The property of a brahmana," Krishna said, "even a little of it enjoyed, is fire that cannot be digested. I do not count the poison halahala the deadliest thing in the world — even that has an antidote. Poison kills the one who eats it, and fire is quenched by water. But the wealth of a brahmana, taken without leave, destroys three generations of the house that takes it."

The people listened, and Krishna went on, his voice carrying the weight of a warning meant for every king who would hear it: "Kings, blinded by their royal fortune, do not see their own fall. For every handful of dust they seize and for every tear shed by those they rob, they and their houses pay in years — unchecked, unrepentant, until the reckoning comes. Whoever takes the livelihood of a brahmana, whether it was given by his own hand or another's — may such wealth never come near me. Men who covet it become short-lived. And you, my people: never do harm to a brahmana, even one who has erred. As I bow to the brahmanas, attentive and well-disposed, so should you. Wealth torn from a brahmana drags the taker down."

The words fell on the gathered citizens and settled into them. Then, while the silence was still new, a celestial car descended — bright and fragrant, shining as if it were made of the morning itself — and came to rest before Nriga.

Nriga looked at Krishna once more. Then he stepped into the car, and the car rose. It climbed above the walls of Dwaraka, above the roofs and the upturned faces, Nriga's form growing small and bright against the sky until it was only a point of light — and then nothing.

The citizens stood looking up long after it was gone. Two teachings went home with them that evening, and both were told and retold in Dwaraka for a long time after. One was the warning that still hung in the air: the poison with no antidote, the wealth that destroys three generations. The other was the story of the king who had given away thousands of cows and still paid for one mistaken gift with a lizard's years — and of the touch that had finally, at the end of it all, set him free.
stories.reflection: Krishna's warning is carefully framed: he does not exalt brahmanas as a class so much as mark how the powerful consume what they never earned, and how a single unknowing wrong, even inside a life of great charity, still exacts its price. The poison metaphor — worse than halahala, because no antidote exists — carries the whole weight of the teaching.
stories.next_story_tease: But far from Dwaraka, in the kingdom of Karusha, a king had begun to call himself the true Vasudeva — and his claim would not go unanswered.

stories.title: Paundraka Demands Krishna's Insignia
stories.story:
In the kingdom of Karusha there lived a king who came to believe he was God.

It happened slowly, the way such things usually do. Paundraka's courtiers called him Vasudeva — the Lord descended to earth — and he liked the sound of it. Priests who wanted his favor agreed that he was the one Lord, that there was no other. One by one the voices of flattery closed around him, until the king lost all memory of his real self and accepted the title as simply true. He was Vasudeva. The whole world, in his mind, ran on his sufferance.

There was one difficulty, and it grew larger the longer he thought about it. The real Vasudeva was alive, and he wore the marks of the Lord openly, in the city of Dwaraka. Those marks — the discus, the conch, the other divine signs that the true Lord alone should carry — had become Paundraka's obsession. In his mind they belonged to him, and to him alone. That a Yadava prince named Krishna walked about bearing them was an insult too great to be endured. And so the king of Karusha did what any king certain of his own divinity would do: he sent a messenger to Dwaraka with a demand.

The journey from Karusha to Dwaraka was long, but the messenger made it in haste, and the demand lost nothing in the carrying. He entered Krishna's assembly, where the chiefs of the Yadavas sat with their lord, and delivered his master's words without flinching. Paundraka, king of Karusha, was Vasudeva, the one descended Lord; there was no other. The divine marks Krishna wore were Paundraka's marks, worn out of folly. Let Krishna give them up. Let him surrender the name of Vasudeva and the character that went with it, and come to Karusha to do homage — and he would be given means of subsistence.

The assembly laughed.

There is no gracious way to receive such a message, and the Yadavas did not attempt one. They laughed until the hall rang, at the thought of the king of Karusha demanding that Krishna hand over the signs of the Lord.

Krishna himself answered with a smile, in jesting words. Tell your master, he said, that the discus is already on its way to him. I will hurl these very signs at the fool and slay him. And he promised Paundraka one thing more: that his face would soon lie covered by cranes and vultures.

The messenger bowed and carried the reply back to Karusha — the whole of it, every word, with nothing softened. And Paundraka, who had been waiting for good news, heard the message out in silence. He had been certain of his own divinity, and the thought that the demand might be refused had never once crossed his mind. That was the nature of his delusion: it left no room for the possibility that the embassy had been absurd from the first word.

In the assembly of Dwaraka the laughter died slowly, and the chiefs of the Yadavas sat looking at their lord, because everyone in that hall knew that Krishna's promises were not the sort that fail. The discus would go to Karusha. The fool would meet it. The only question was when.
stories.reflection: The comedy of the episode is also its point: Paundraka asked Krishna to surrender the very marks that made him what he claimed to be. Divinity demanded as tribute reveals itself as costume, and the laughter of the assembly is the story's honest verdict on borrowed glory.
stories.next_story_tease: But the discus Krishna promised the messenger was already on its way — the impostor's borrowed glory was about to meet its end.

stories.title: Krishna Slays Paundraka and the King of Kashi
stories.story:
Somewhere east of Krishna's kingdom, a king began to wear another man's life. Paundraka had been an ordinary ruler once, no better and no worse than a hundred others, but he was flattered by people too eager to please him, until he forgot who he actually was. He began to believe that he — and not Krishna — was the true Vasudeva, the Lord come down to earth. It was a strange kind of theft, because the man he was stealing from was the very man he claimed to be.

He dressed himself in Krishna's yellow silk and marked his chest with the shrivatsa sign. He took up the conch, the discus, the sword and the mace, strung the great bow called Sharnga, and raised a banner bearing an eagle. In every particular he made himself look like Krishna, so that a man who saw him from a distance might honestly have mistaken one for the other. It was not a disguise worn for a single hour; it was a costume worn with total, settled conviction, until he could no longer tell where the pretence ended and he began.

Then he sent a messenger to Krishna with a demand. Relinquish the discus, he told him. Lay aside my insignia, my name, and the character of Vasudeva, and come and do me homage, and I will grant you the means to live. The impostor was offering, with perfect seriousness, to spare the man he was copying, and to keep him as a dependent.

Krishna heard the message and laughed. Go back to Paundraka, he told the messenger, and tell him I will send him my discus. He will rightly understand my meaning. I will come to his city with it, and I will deliver it to him, and there will be no delay. The discus, Krishna knew, could only be delivered in one way, and Paundraka would soon discover what that way was.

Paundraka was not alone in his delusion. The king of Kashi had made himself his friend and ally, a rear-guard at his back, and stood ready to defend him. So Krishna marched against them both, and the two armies met before the walls of Kashi, where the impostor and his ally would learn whether a borrowed name could stand in a real battle.

When Krishna saw Paundraka arrayed in the field — wearing the borrowed yellow silk and the borrowed banner, looking so like himself that the resemblance was almost a mockery — he laughed again. Then he fought. With mace and discus and a stream of arrows he scattered the combined army of Paundraka and the king of Kashi, the way a fire at the end of an age spreads through a field, until the ground before the city was cleared of everything that had stood against him.

He turned to Paundraka. O Paundraka, he said, I will now make you give up my name, which you, a fool, have falsely taken. With sharp arrows he struck Paundraka from his chariot, and with the discus he cut off his head. Then he turned on the king of Kashi, cut off that king's head with his arrows, and sent it flying over the walls and into the city, where it fell at the palace gate, its earrings still in place.

So the false Vasudeva died as he had lived, with his whole mind fixed on Krishna. And that, the old story says, was the strange mercy of it. Because Paundraka had spent his days absorbed in Krishna, even if only as an envious imitation, that constant thought had quietly burned away every bond that held him. The man who stole Krishna's name ended by arriving at the very place he had spent his whole life pretending to stand.
stories.reflection: Paundraka is the reverse of everything a devotee should be, yet the sources close his story with a startling grace: because his mind never left Krishna, even in enmity and imitation, the impostor was freed. The costume he wore in mockery became, in the end, the only true thing about him.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana extends the episode: after the two kings fall, the son of the king of Kashi sends a magical being against Krishna, and Krishna's discus destroys it and sets the city of Varanasi ablaze. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana, which ends with the two beheadings.
stories.content_note: Paundraka and the king of Kashi are beheaded in battle; the violence is described with restraint.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna on the battlefield before the walls of Kashi, seeing Paundraka arrayed in counterfeit yellow silk and an eagle banner that mirror his own, laughing as he raises the discus while the impostor's borrowed emblems glint in the dust.

stories.title: The Fire That Burned Varanasi
stories.story:
The fire that Sudakshina raised to burn Dwaraka fell instead on Varanasi — and on the man who had conjured it.

Krishna had recently struck down the impostor Paundraka, and with him the king of Kashi, who had sheltered the pretender. The queen and the kin of the fallen king mourned him, and his son Sudakshina performed the rites for his father's passing. But grief was not the only thing in the young prince's heart. When the ceremonies were done, he took his teachers with him and went to worship Shiva at Avimukta, the sacred heart of Kashi. He fasted, he chanted, he pressed his worship upon the Lord of that place with the single-mindedness of a man who has already chosen his request — and he prayed as a man who intends to be answered.

Shiva was pleased with him and offered a boon. Sudakshina asked for the southern fire — the fire of black magic, tended by brahmana priests, that would accomplish his purpose against the man he called impious: Krishna of Dwaraka. What he wanted was not wealth or protection but a weapon: a fire that would burn one enemy and spare everything else. The boon was granted. And from the fire pit there rose a demon of living flame.

It was terrible to look upon, the verses say — fangs set in a face of iron, brows knotted, a tongue that licked out like a serpent's, feet the size of palm trunks that shook the earth with every step. The priests who served that fire stood with Sudakshina and watched it take shape, and their own faces were white. The conjured thing set out across the country, walking toward Dwaraka — not like a beast, but like a purpose: unhurried, straight, and hungry. Everything in its path knew that it meant burning.

In Dwaraka the citizens saw it from the walls, and their courage failed. They ran through the streets to the assembly hall, where Krishna sat playing dice with his companions, and the cry went up: the fire of black magic is coming. Krishna looked up from the dice. The people of the city were afraid, and the household of Krishna trembled with them.

Krishna, who is witness within and without all things, needed no report. He heard the distress of the people and saw the fear of his own. The Sudarshana discus blazed into being — like ten million suns, like the fire that ends a world — and went to meet the demon.

It struck the conjured thing and broke it. Its face shattered, the demon turned and fled back along the road it had come — and fell upon the city of its making. It burned Sudakshina and the priests who had raised it, in Varanasi. The black magic consumed its own master.

But the discus was not finished. It entered Varanasi itself — through the ramparts, past the assembly halls and the markets, along streets that had never known an enemy — and burned the whole city. The city that had been inaccessible even to the gods was wrapped in flames, with all its princes and their followers. Where Varanasi had stood, there was ash and silence.

Those who raise fire for others should consider the wind. Sudakshina had asked for a fire to destroy his enemy, and the fire had destroyed his home, his priests, and himself — and the discus had done in a single night what no army, no god, had ever done to the city he loved.
stories.reflection: The story turns on a terrible symmetry: the fire raised for Dwaraka fell on its raiser, and the discus that broke the conjured demon then ended the city that had sent it. A harm intended for another comes home to the one who sets it in motion, and even a city inviolable to the gods could not stand against the power of Vishnu's weapon.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells the same episode without naming the Kashi king's son and gives the whole burning to the discus alone; the Bhagavata Purana names the prince Sudakshina.
stories.content_note: A conjured fire-demon and the burning of a city; described with restraint, but may warrant a word of context for younger listeners.
stories.next_story_tease: The embers of Varanasi had barely cooled when a new storm gathered far to the north — one that began at a svayamvara in Hastinapura.

stories.title: Samba Carries Off Duryodhana's Daughter
stories.story:
A svayamvara is supposed to end with the bride choosing her husband. Samba chose first.

Lakshmana, the daughter of Duryodhana, had come of age, and the roads to Hastinapura were crowded with princes gathered to offer themselves at her svayamvara. It is a festival of waiting: the princess moves among the assembled kings with a garland in her hand, and the choice is hers alone. For a young man with more pride than patience, it was an invitation to be bold — and among the waiting princes came Samba, the son of Krishna and Jambavati, a young Yadava of Dwaraka, handsome and headstrong, with more confidence than caution. Whatever moved him — love, pride, or the sheer pleasure of daring — he did not wait to be chosen. He lifted Lakshmana into his chariot and drove away with her, and before the guards could move, before the ceremony could recover, the chariot was gone through the gate.

The Kurus were furious. "This boy is ill-mannered!" "Bind him!" "What will the Vrishnis dare to do?" The house of Kuru had never thought much of the kings of Dwaraka; there were those at Hastinapura who said openly that the Yadu race had no claim to royal dignity. Now a boy of that house had treated their princess like plunder, and the insult was doubled. The great chiefs flung themselves into their chariots and gave chase — Karna, Shala, Bhuri, Yajnaketu, and Duryodhana himself, shouting "Stop! Stop!" as their wheels thundered over the ground after the abductor.

Samba was a great chariot-warrior, and he had not stolen a bride to be caught easily. He wheeled his horses, twanged his handsome bow, and shot into the pursuers — four arrows into the horses of each of the foremost chariots, a single arrow into each charioteer — and wounded them all. For a moment the might of the Kurus flinched before a boy.

But there were too many of them, and they came on in a ring, closing the open ground from every side. They cut down his four horses and brought his chariot to a halt. Chariot-less and ringed by enemies, Samba was seized and bound — the verses note that it cost the Kurus great effort — and led back to Hastinapura a prisoner, with Lakshmana taken from him.

The news of the capture flew to Dwaraka faster than any chariot. When the Yadavas heard that one of their princes had been bound by the Kurus, their wrath kindled, and the councils of Dwaraka grew hot with talk of war.

Samba had gambled everything on boldness and lost. The price of his audacity now lay in the hands of Duryodhana, and in Dwaraka proud men were already sharpening their anger.
stories.reflection: Samba's crime was not that he loved Lakshmana but that he treated her choice as his own — seizing her at the svayamvara as if a bride's hand were a prize to be taken. The Kurus' fury was genuine, and so was their contempt for his manners; the story leaves the question of who was right to the consequences that follow.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds Bhishma and Drona to the pursuing chiefs; the Bhagavata Purana names Karna, Shala, Bhuri, Yajnaketu and Duryodhana, which this story follows.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet even as the Yadavas' anger smoldered, Dwaraka was about to receive a guest who came with a question stranger than any war: how one man could fill sixteen thousand homes at once.

stories.title: Sixteen Thousand Homes, One Krishna
stories.story:
Narada had heard an impossible thing: that Krishna, with a single body, had married sixteen thousand women and kept a household for each. The sage, who wanders the three worlds and is astonished by little, was astonished by this. He came to Dwaraka to see it with his own eyes.

The city itself was the first marvel — adorned, the verses say, with nine hundred thousand palaces of crystal and silver, their streets laid out with care, their squares and marketplaces full of life. But the inner palace was something more: sixteen thousand mansions set with coral pillars and beryl floors, hung with canopies of pearls, lit by jeweled lamps that drove out all darkness, with peacocks calling from the roofs and maidservants moving through the rooms in gold necklaces and fine robes.

Narada entered the first mansion — the palace of Rukmini. There was Krishna, resting on a couch while his queen fanned him. The moment he saw the sage, he rose, bowed, and seated him with honor; he washed Narada's feet and took the water of that washing on his own head — he whom the worlds worship did reverence to a guest. And he asked what he could do for the sage.

Narada spoke his praise simply: nothing in you is wonderful, Lord of all worlds — friendship toward all beings, restraint toward the wicked; you have descended freely for the good of the world. I have seen your feet, the refuge of those fallen into the well of this world. Grant that I may keep the memory of you.

Then Narada rose and went to the second mansion — and there was Krishna again, playing dice with that wife and with Uddhava. "When did you arrive, sage?" they asked him, as if he had just come.

He went to a third, and found Krishna fondling small children in his lap. To a fourth, and Krishna was pouring oblations into the sacred fires, performing the five great sacrifices. To a fifth, and he sat in twilight meditation, chanting the brahman with his speech restrained. To a sixth, and he was riding out among horses, elephants, and chariots. To a seventh, and he sat in counsel with his ministers, Uddhava among them. To an eighth, and he gave adorned cows to the foremost brahmanas. To a ninth, and he laughed at a jest with his beloved. To a tenth, and he sat alone, absorbed in the Person beyond all nature. Elsewhere he made war with some kings and peace with others; elsewhere he performed the thread ceremonies and the weddings of his sons and daughters, and the festivals of his children; elsewhere he worshipped all the gods with great sacrifices; elsewhere he rode to the hunt on a Sindhu horse.

In all sixteen thousand mansions, the same. In every home Krishna was wholly present, and nowhere was he less.

After the first few mansions, Narada stopped being surprised at the sight of him and began instead to test what he saw. In one home the Lord was mid-sentence with a minister; in the next, mid-verse of a chant; and yet when Narada entered, each Krishna looked up as though the sage were the only guest in the world and greeted him with the same complete attention. The same Krishna. The same fullness.

At last he came before Krishna and laughed, like a man who has seen a trick he cannot explain. "I know your yoga-maya," he said, "which even the clever cannot see. Permit me to depart, Lord, to the worlds that are flooded with your glory."

Krishna let him go. And Narada left Dwaraka with his question dissolved. He had come to measure how one man could be husband to sixteen thousand wives, and he had learned that the question was wrongly put. In every home Krishna had been complete; nothing of him had been shared out thin, nothing diminished. The sage walked out of that city with his song already forming in his throat.
stories.reflection: Narada's wonder is the point: he comes to Krishna's sixteen thousand households as a puzzle of logistics and finds the puzzle itself dissolved — in each home Krishna is wholly present, and nothing of him is divided or lessened. The story does not explain yoga-maya; it shows it, room by room, and lets the seeing be the understanding.
stories.next_story_tease: But even as he took leave, Narada knew the wonder was deeper than he could name — and his song of Krishna's glory was about to begin.
stories.hero_scene: Narada stands at the threshold of a pearl-hung Dwaraka mansion and sees Krishna within — playing dice with a wife — while in the palaces behind him the same Krishna lifts a child, pours oblations into the fire, and rides out to the hunt, all at once.

stories.title: Narada Marvels at Krishna's Yoga-Maya
stories.story:
Narada had heard the reports of Dwaraka long before he ever saw the city, and he had come to test them with his own eyes. What he found there undid him.

He saw the city first — its sea walls, its markets, the wealth of the Yadava lords — and none of it surprised him. Then, for days, he walked among the palaces of Krishna's sixteen thousand queens, and in every palace he found the same thing: Krishna present, whole and unhurried, doing whatever the moment required. In one hall he sat at ease among his ministers. In another he listened to a singer in a garden. Here he stood beside a queen at the evening lamp; there he was laughing with children in a courtyard. In each palace it was the same Krishna — not a copy, not a shadow, but the same person, fully there, as though no other palace existed in the world.

The sage had wandered all the worlds. He had watched the gods at their councils and demons at their schemes, kings at their wars and ascetics at their penances. He had seen illusions that fooled even the wise. But this undid him. He could not keep it inside. He had come expecting to test a rumor; he found himself instead in the middle of a mystery he would spend the rest of his journeys trying to sing.

He found Krishna, and stood before him smiling in spite of himself. He had rehearsed nothing; the words came out the way wonder does, before he had decided to speak them.

'I understand your yoga-maya now,' he said. 'Even the masters of illusion cannot see it. Serving your feet has opened my eyes to it, and my mind can barely hold what it has seen.'

Krishna took the words the way he took everything — fully, and without a ripple of vanity. He was following the path of men, as he always did in Dwaraka: rising with the sun, ruling a city, living a mortal king's life among mortals. And yet the power he carried through those ordinary days was the power that holds every world in being. He did not argue with the praise, nor wave it away; he accepted it the way a lamp accepts the light it has always given. He looked at the sage standing before him, and what he said next was less an order than a release.

'Wander the worlds, Narada,' he said. 'Sing of these pastimes wherever you go. Let the telling of them purify whoever hears.'

So Narada departed, and Dwaraka saw the last of him for a long while. But the rest of the worlds saw more of him than they ever had. He went singing, and his songs carried the wonder he had found: that the lord of all could be in sixteen thousand places at once and be, in each, entirely himself — that the same hand which held a lamp in one palace reached for a child in another, and that no distance between them was real.

Wherever he went, people stopped to listen. Farmers in the fields and merchants at their stalls, women at the well and children on the road — all of them heard how the king of Dwaraka moved through his days like a man, yet held the worlds in his palm. And the old texts say of such telling what they say of few things: that whoever sings of these deeds, or hears them sung, or simply delights in them, finds his heart turning toward the path that has no end.

Krishna, left to his city, went on being what he was: a king among the Yadus, a husband to his queens, a man who met each morning the ordinary duties of a place that did not know it sheltered the wonder Narada had carried away, singing.
stories.reflection: Narada's wonder is the story's real subject: the lord of all worlds living the ordinary life of a king, and that ordinariness itself being the miracle. What he cannot explain, he carries out into the world as song — praise becomes the only adequate response to such a mystery.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna, meanwhile, was already living the next quiet chapter of his days — the ordered worship of a king's morning in Dwaraka.
stories.hero_scene: Narada, smiling in wonder with folded hands before Krishna in a lamp-lit hall of Dwaraka, as Krishna gestures him out into the world to sing.

stories.title: Krishna's Dawn Worship in Dwaraka
stories.story:
The birds of Dwaraka sang the sun up before it showed itself, a chorus at every window like heralds crying that the day belonged to Krishna. Inside the palace, in the deep quiet of the brahma-muhurta, Rukmini lay awake beside him, and could not bear the coming moment — the moment when her lord would rise from their bed and the night would be over.

But rise he did, as he rose every day. In the first grey light Krishna touched the water and cleansed himself for what came next. Then he sat, and turned inward, to the one reality that shines of itself, that has no second and no end, that no impurity can touch — and for a while the palace, the city, the sea beyond it, all fell away. It was not an escape from the day but the day's foundation; everything that followed stood on that stillness.

He bathed in clear water, according to the rite, performing each act as though it were the only act in the world — unhurried, complete, attentive. He put on fresh garments and performed the sandhya worship at the turning of night into day, feeding the sacred fire with oblations while his speech stayed still and his mind rode the chant. He saluted the rising sun, and offered the first worship of the day to his own senses, asking them to serve him rather than rule him.

Then the giving began. Every day, the texts say, Krishna gave away herds of milk-giving cows — cows with horns of gold and hooves of silver, strung with pearls, each with linen and sesame beside it, everything a household could need. The brahmanas came forward in turn, each receiving from the king's own hand, and his face showed no fatigue at the giving, only the same unhurried attention he gave to everything. He honored the cows and the brahmanas, the gods and the elders, his teachers, and every living being that came before him. He adorned himself, and those who saw him said the ornament of the human world had dressed itself in its own finery.

He looked into the mirror, as the custom of kings was, and saw the auspicious things set before him: clarified butter, cows and bulls, brahmanas, the images of the gods. He gave garlands, betel leaf and unguents to the brahmanas who waited on him, and they blessed him and went their way.

The sun was fully up. His charioteer brought the great chariot to the gate, and Krishna took his driver's hand and mounted, while the women of the inner palace watched him go with shy, loving glances. Through the streets of Dwaraka he rode, and the city rose around him like one living thing, until he came to the hall of Sudharma — the ancient assembly hall of the Yadus.

There the lords of the Vrishnis were gathered, Uddhava and Satyaki among them. Krishna took the highest seat, and the hall seemed to gather its light around him, as though the four directions brightened where he sat. The ministers brought their humor, jesting with their king as trusted friends do, and the sound of mridanga and vina, of flute and cymbals and conch, rose and filled the hall.

So the day of the lord of Dwaraka began — not in display but in order: water and fire, silence and song, gifts given and people heard. Those who watched him at his worship said he performed it not as a king performing for his court, but as a servant of the Lord within him — the same Lord whose service in Dwaraka meant the service of everyone who came before him.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the episode is its plainness: the lord of the universe performs the small disciplines of an ordinary king's day — ablutions, meditation, charity, court — and the disciplines are not beneath him but the very shape of his days. Devotion here is not spectacle but faithful repetition.

stories.title: Four Handfuls of Flat Rice
stories.subtitle: Sudama's Poverty and Journey
stories.story:
Of all the brahmanas who kept their vows in that poor village, none was more learned than Sudama, and none lived in greater want. He had chosen a life of the mind and the spirit, and the world had repaid the choice with hunger. His house stood at the edge of the village with empty stores. Whatever came to him by chance — a measure of grain from a harvest, a coin from a passing traveler — went to feed the fire and the family, and it was never enough. Some days there was no grain at all. His body grew thin, and his clothes wore thin with it, and his wife's face lost its color, the way faces do when they are always hoping and always short.

She bore it as long as she could. Then one day she came to him, her voice low and her eyes on the ground, and said what had been on her mind for months.

'You are a friend of the Blessed Lord,' she said. 'You know this. He is the lord of Shri herself — the lord of fortune — and you were his friend before either of you had anything. Go to him. He lives in Dwaraka now, lord of the Bhoja, Vrishni and Andhaka peoples. He will see you, and he will give us wealth, and this house will know ease again.'

Sudama heard her out and said nothing. He was a man who had long ago stopped asking the world for things; it was hard to begin again, even with a friend. But his wife did not stop. She asked again and again, day after day, and at last the thought took root in him. If Krishna was truly his friend, why should he not go? What harm could there be in one journey?

He resolved to go. Once the resolve was made, he did not linger over it; whatever waited in Dwaraka — a welcome or a door closed in his face — had to be better than standing still.

But he would not go empty-handed. A guest does not come to a king's door with nothing. Sudama went to the brahmanas of the village and asked — humbly, for he had never been good at asking — for something to carry. He asked for no gold and no fine cloth; the plainest gift would do. They gave what they had: four handfuls of flattened rice, the poor man's food, the kind of gift a neighbor brings a neighbor. He tied the four handfuls in a piece of rag and set out for Dwaraka.

The road was long and he was weak. He walked through country he had never seen, past fields and forests, resting where he could, and as he walked he turned one question over and over: how would he even gain sight of Krishna? The lord of a great city, surrounded by guards and ministers and queens — would such a man see a ragged brahmana standing at his gate? Sudama had no answer. He only walked, the little bundle in his hand, and trusted the friend he remembered — a boy who had shared his lessons and his hunger, and who had never once made him feel small.

At last the towers of Dwaraka rose on the horizon and the sea glittered beyond them. He crossed the outer groves, passed the three gates of the city, past merchants and chariots and men in armor, until he stood before the palace of the king who had sixteen thousand queens — the king who had once been a boy at their guru's house, hungry and ragged like him.
stories.reflection: Sudama's poverty is not merely hardship; it is also the condition that lets the story happen. The wife who refuses to let pride waste a friendship, and the poor man who would rather carry a gift of flat rice than come empty-handed, set the whole meeting in motion. The gift's smallness is the point — friendship is measured by the giving, not the gift.
stories.next_story_tease: Inside the palace, Krishna had already seen him — and was rising from his couch.

stories.title: Krishna Embraces His Old Friend
stories.story:
Sudama stood at the gate of the palace and knew he was out of place. The palace of Krishna housed sixteen thousand queens, and the building that held them was a city of its own — courtyards and corridors, gardens and lamps, guards who had seen every kind of man come and go but who looked at the ragged brahmana and saw something they could not place. But no one turned him away, and no one asked his business, as though the palace itself were waiting for him.

Sudama did not have to wonder what to do next. From somewhere deep inside the palace, Krishna saw him — saw him from afar, through rooms and walls and the whole long passage of years since they had been boys together. He rose from the couch where he sat with Rukmini and ran. Ran, the lord of Dwaraka, the husband of the goddess of fortune herself, ran to the gate to meet a beggar in a torn cloth.

He embraced him. The tears came to Krishna's eyes — the old texts say it plainly: the tears of joy — as he held his old friend, the best of brahmanas, thin and weary from the road. And Sudama, who had feared he might not be recognized at all, found himself wrapped in the arms of the lord of the three worlds. Krishna held him a long moment, and when he drew back his hands were still on Sudama's shoulders, as if he could not quite believe the road had brought him.

Krishna would not let him stand. He took him by the hand and seated him on his own couch. And then the servants of the palace could scarcely believe what their eyes reported: the king himself knelt and washed the feet of the ragged guest, and took the water and bore it to his own head, honoring it as the holiest of things. In all the palace, no one moved; the servants stood frozen, watching their king serve his guest. He had fragrant incense brought and rows of lamps lit, and he received his friend with joy, as though a treasure had come to the palace rather than a poor man. A poor man's gift, a king's welcome — somewhere between the two, the old friendship simply resumed.

The women of the inner palace saw it, and the wonder of it stopped them where they stood. Krishna, whose fame was spotless, whose word held the worlds together, had put a penniless brahmana on his own throne and washed his feet with his own hands. They had seen kings bow to him and learned men worship him; they had never seen him honor anyone like this. They whispered to one another: what merit has this man performed, this destitute beggar, that the guru of the three worlds should cherish him so? That the very abode of Shri should bow before him?

Rukmini herself came and stood beside them, and took up a fan, and fanned the emaciated brahmana — she, the goddess of fortune, cooling the man who had arrived at her palace with nothing but a rag of flat rice.

And the two friends sat and talked. Not of kingdoms, not of wealth. They talked of the old days, of the years when they had studied together in their teacher's house — the mornings, the lessons, the small adventures of boys — and the palace around them, for all its splendor, faded to nothing next to that.

The women of the palace watched the king of Dwaraka laugh with a beggar, and they understood, perhaps for the first time, what kind of king they served.
stories.reflection: The palace women's question — what merit has this beggar performed? — is the story's hinge. By every worldly measure Sudama deserves nothing, yet Krishna honors him as a treasure. The episode turns the usual logic of honor upside down: the king bows to the poor man, and the goddess of fortune fans him, because friendship, not rank, is what the lord of Dwaraka counts.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Krishna asked what gift his old friend had carried all the way from home.

stories.title: Krishna Eats Sudama's Flat Rice
stories.story:
Sudama was a poor brahmana, and he had set out for Dwaraka with very little in his hands — a single handful of flattened rice, tied in the fold of his cloth, the only gift he could bring to his friend Krishna, who was now lord of a city of gold.

Krishna had once been his friend; this much Sudama held to, though time and fortune had carried them far apart. Krishna had come into kingship and wealth — a palace, a household, a city that glittered on the sea. Sudama had stayed poor, with a wife at home and a house where the grain did not always last. The flattened rice was the food of the very poor, pressed flat and carried in a rag; it was all he had to offer, and he knew how small it would look in that place.

He had meant, somewhere in his heart, to ask for help. A poor man does not cross half the kingdom for nothing. But the nearer he came to Dwaraka, the smaller his request seemed, until it lodged in his throat like a stone he could neither swallow nor speak.

The city, when he reached it, was more than he had imagined — towers and gold and the sound of the sea against the walls — and he walked through it feeling smaller with every step, clutching the little knot of rice against his side. Krishna did not wait for Sudama to be announced. When he heard who had come, he went out himself and received his friend with the warmth of old affection, and led him in, and seated him where he himself sat. Sudama looked around at the splendor of that house and felt his poverty more keenly than he ever had at home.

Krishna, who sees into every heart, knew exactly why Sudama had come and what he carried. Gently he asked what gift his friend had brought him. Even a trifle offered with love pleases him, Krishna said — a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. Whatever is given with devotion, he accepts.

Sudama was ashamed, and he offered nothing. He could not bring himself to untie the knot in his cloth; the rice, so carefully carried all that way, now seemed too small to show and too poor to give. So Krishna reached over and took the handful of rice from the fold of his friend's cloth. What you have brought me, he said, is what pleases me most. He ate one mouthful, and it gave him the delight of a feast. He reached for a second.

Then the goddess of fortune, watching and pleased, stayed his hand. This much, she said, is enough to grant every riches in the world. She who is herself the source of all wealth was telling him that a beggar's handful of pressed grain was already enough.

Sudama did not understand what that could mean. He stayed that night in Krishna's house, and in the morning he set out for home. He had asked for nothing; not one word of his need had crossed his lips. He returned the way he had come, on foot and empty-handed, carrying only the memory of his friend's welcome — and to Sudama, that welcome was worth more than any treasure he might have been bold enough to name. Something had been given and received in that room, and though he could not put a name to it, he carried it home as surely as he had carried the rice. The shame that had walked with him all the way to Dwaraka did not walk with him back.
stories.reflection: The story turns on what Sudama does not say. Face to face with the friend he came to ask for help, he is too ashamed to speak of his need, and he offers only the handful of rice he carried in a rag. Krishna's delight in that handful — and the goddess of fortune's word that it already contains every riches — suggests that what is given with love is never small.

stories.title: Sudama Finds His Hut a Palace
stories.story:
Sudama walked the long road home from Dwaraka with empty hands, and his heart was strange with wonder. He had gone to see his old friend Krishna carrying a poor brahmin's gift, a single handful of flat rice, and Krishna had eaten it with delight, as if it were a feast prepared for a king. In the palace that night, any man in his place would have asked for help; his poverty had followed him all the way to Dwaraka, whispering of everything he lacked. But when he stood before Krishna, the words would not come. He could not ask for anything at all.

Now the villages of his own country were appearing one by one along the road, and he turned the marvel over in his mind. "Where am I," he asked himself, "poor and burdened with faults, and where is Krishna, the very home of fortune?" All his life he had measured the distance between them, and it had always seemed like the distance between mud and the moon. Yet Krishna had taken his handful of rice with love, and had given him back something he had not dared to imagine, and had done it without being asked, as though it were nothing.

Walking, he began to understand why. If he had asked for wealth and received it, would he have remembered? Wealth has a way of loosening a poor man's grip on everything else; it fills the hands and empties the heart. Krishna, who knew him through and through, had given him prosperity unasked, and in the giving had kept him still his friend. For the Lord, the wise say, does not hand his devotee the riches and glories that would pull the heart away from him; he gives what the heart can carry. And to Sudama he had given everything, because Sudama had asked for nothing but to remain his friend. "May this friendship, this companionship, this service to him," he prayed as he walked, "be mine in birth after birth."

He was still turning such thoughts when he came to the edge of his own village, and stopped, for he no longer knew it. Where his humble hut had stood there now rose a cluster of celestial mansions, ringed with gardens and clear lakes, their waters loud with the calling of birds. Well-dressed men and graceful women moved through the courtyards as though the place had always been theirs. Sudama stood in the road, a poor man in a worn cloth, and could not believe his eyes.

His wife heard that he had come, and hurried out to meet him, radiant as the goddess of fortune among her attendants. When she saw him her eyes filled with tears of love, and whatever hand had worked this change while he was away, she was still the same wife; she drew him, half laughing and half weeping, through the gates.

Inside, the wonder deepened. The beds were heaped soft as foam, spread with ivory and gold; jeweled lamps glowed in the rooms; the walls of crystal and emerald gave back the light of a hundred riches. Sudama, who had slept on a mud floor all his life, walked through his own house as though through a dream.

And there, among the golden couches, the truth of it settled on him at last. The Lord gives generously even to one who asks; how much more to a friend who asks for nothing? Krishna had accepted his single, meager handful of flat rice with joy, and had repaid it with a kingdom. It was not merely that Sudama had been given wealth, he realized. It was that Krishna had given it in such a way that the giving never came between them: unasked, unannounced, as natural as the return of an old friend.

That night, standing in the jewel-lit splendor of his own home, the poor brahmin who had gone to Dwaraka with empty hands found that he was rich beyond all measuring. Not in palaces, not in gold, but in this: that Krishna treasured even a handful of flat rice, and had turned an old friend's poverty into a palace without waiting to be asked.
stories.reflection: Sudama's poverty is not ended by the palace but redefined by it. The story's quietest point is that Krishna gives generously even to those who ask, yet gives most safely to the friend who asks for nothing, and Sudama's prayer is not for wealth but that the friendship itself should continue birth after birth.
stories.next_story_tease: The same grace was about to move on a grander stage, when Vasudeva himself would be initiated into a great sacrifice at Samanta-panchaka.

stories.title: Vasudeva's Sacrifice
stories.story:
The holy field of Samanta-panchaka lay open to the sky, a plain long consecrated by the rites of the wise, and on it that season the sages were doing something rare: they had chosen a man as their own. Vasudeva had come to them with a question about the highest duty, and the asking itself had pleased them. Now they took him as their disciple, and Vasudeva in turn chose them, as the dharma directs, to be his priests, and they prepared to initiate him into a great sacrifice.

The field itself had its own gravity. For ages the wise had come to Samanta-panchaka to offer their rites, and the very ground was held to be blessed, so that a sacrifice performed there stood in a place already full of offerings. The sage Narada was among the gathered rishis, watching the preparations take shape with quiet pleasure.

Word of the rite went out to every Yadava house, and the clans came. From every direction the great families of the Vrishnis and the Yadavas converged on the plain, filling it with color and the low murmur of a whole people gathered for one purpose. When the initiation began, the Vrishnis arrived wearing lotus garlands, and Vasudeva's queens came with them, delighted, bright with gold and fine garments. The air filled with the sound of mridangas and drums, conches and kettledrums, so that the whole field seemed to be singing. The priests anointed Vasudeva as the rite required, his body touched with unguents, and dressed him in silks and bracelets, necklaces, anklets and earrings, until the man who had come asking questions stood at the heart of the ceremony like a king at his crowning. His priests too were robed in jeweled silk, and the whole assembly shone under the open sky.

And among the kinsmen stood the two who made the gathering complete: Krishna and Balarama, each surrounded by his own family and his own sons. The account treasures this sight, not the theology of the fire, but the two brothers there, sons among their father's people, the extraordinary standing quietly in an ordinary family gathering.

Vasudeva performed the rites as the tradition prescribed, the subsidiary offerings of agnihotra and the rest, one after another, unhurried, with the great sages guiding every step. For days the fires burned, and the field breathed smoke and saffron and the scent of ghee, and the chant of the priests rose and fell with the sun. Then came the giving. At the proper time, as the scriptures direct, he gave the priests their dakshina, rich gifts of cows and land and maidens, so that the men who had conducted the sacrifice went away honored beyond anything they had asked. The sages completed the ritual with the offerings of the queens and the closing avabhritha bath, the final purification that brings a sacrifice to its end. When Vasudeva had bathed in that last water, he gave garments and ornaments to the bards and to the women who had graced the field; to his own kinsmen, with their wives and their sons, he gave abundant gifts, holding nothing back. Nor did he forget the wider circle: the assembled priests, the hosts of gods, men and ancestors and the celestial singers called caranas, all were honored in their turn, so that no one who had taken part went away empty-handed.

When the drums had fallen silent and the fires had received their last oblations, Vasudeva stood on that holy field, cleansed by the bath and crowned with the dust of the rite. He looked across the plain at his sons, Krishna and Balarama, each at the head of his own house, and it seemed to him that the sacrifice had already given him everything a man could ask. The field of Samanta-panchaka had seen many great rites; it had rarely seen one so simply complete: a father purified, his sons beside him, and nothing held back from anyone who had come.
stories.reflection: The account lingers not on the meaning of the rites but on the scene itself: the anointing, the music, the giving that leaves no one empty-handed. Its quiet center is the sight of Krishna and Balarama standing among their father's kinsmen, the extraordinary present in an ordinary family gathering.
stories.next_story_tease: But in Dwaraka, a mother's grief was waiting, older than any sacrifice and not yet healed.

stories.title: Devaki Asks for Her Slain Sons
stories.story:
In Dwaraka, everyone told the story of the boy who had come back from the dead. But for Devaki it was never a story.

Years before, when Krishna and Balarama had finished their studies, their teacher had asked for his fee: his own son, dead and gone, was to be brought back to him. The two brothers had gone to the world of the dead and done it, returning the boy to his father's arms. People marveled at the tale; it was told at feasts and retold to children. And Devaki heard it the way a woman hears a thing when it touches her own loss.

She had borne eight children, and six of them she had never seen grow. Kamsa, her own brother, had killed them one by one as soon as they were born, for he lived in fear that one of her sons would grow up to take his kingdom and his life. She had held each child only long enough to lose it. She had never watched one of those six take a step or speak a word; her whole memory of them was grief, worn smooth by years of silence. In Dwaraka, surrounded by palaces and grandsons, she had learned not to speak of them. The loss did not diminish with distance; it simply became the shape of her days, a room in the house of her mind she had learned to walk past quickly.

But the story of the teacher's son undid that silence. A father had wept for one dead boy, and his sons had brought him back. She had wept for six, and no one had ever brought them back, not the priests with their rites, not the years with their healing, not even the gods. The tale that made everyone else marvel made Devaki's old wound open again, and this time she did not turn away from it.

She went to Krishna and Balarama with tears on her face, and she did not demand; she asked. "You two are the lords of the masters of yoga," she said. "When your teacher commanded you, you went to the world of the dead and fetched back a son, long dead, and returned him to his father. That was the fee he asked, and you paid it. Grant my wish the same way. Bring back my sons, the ones the Bhoja king slew. I held each of them only long enough to lose him."

The two brothers looked at their mother. They did not tell her it was impossible. They did not say that the dead cannot be returned, that the years cannot be undone. They had fetched a dead son once, for a teacher's fee. She was their mother, and her wish was older than the palace she lived in, older than the kingdom, older than the grief she had carried all these years.

And in their silence Devaki understood that she had been heard. Whatever the two lords of yoga intended, they had not refused her; they had not turned away. Standing before her sons in the bright halls of Dwaraka, with the tears still on her face, she felt the weight of years lift just a little, like a door opening in that room of her mind she had walked past for so long. For the first time in years, she let herself hope.
stories.reflection: What is striking is how quiet the request is. Devaki does not rage or reproach; she reminds her sons of what they once did for a stranger's son and asks, almost gently, for the same for her own. In this telling, grief does not thunder; it remembers, and asks.
stories.next_story_tease: To answer her, the two brothers would descend beneath the world, to the kingdom of the daitya king Bali.

stories.title: Krishna and Balarama Visit Bali in Sutala
stories.story:
The two brothers did not travel by any road that day. Where they were going, beneath the world, no path led; they descended by their own mystic power into the vast, splendid realm called Sutala, the kingdom of the daitya king Bali.

Bali knew them the moment they appeared. He rose from his seat at once, for before him stood the soul of the universe, the lord of his own life, and he bowed low, his whole family bowing with him, his heart overflowing with the joy of the sight. He brought forward a noble seat and settled the two great souls upon it, and then he worshipped them with everything his kingdom held precious: garments of great worth, ornaments, cooling unguents, and all the riches of his realm laid out like an offering. He washed their feet with his own hands, his kin around him, and again and again he lifted those lotus feet to his head, his mind dissolved in love. It seemed to him that no king in any world had ever entertained such guests, and he did not intend to let the moment pass unhonored.

"Your sight is hard to obtain, even for the gods," Bali said. "Daityas and danavas, gandharvas and siddhas, vidyadharas and caranas, some approach you with enmity and some with longing, and none can comprehend you, O lord of the masters of yoga. From the dark well of this world, where no one thinks to seek you, you have drawn me up and set my feet upon your path. Instruct me, O lord. Make me sinless, master."

Krishna looked at the king of Sutala with the affection he gives to devotion, wherever it is found, in a palace above the earth or in a kingdom beneath it. And then he told him what he had come for.

"These six sons," he said, "were once the six sons of the sage Marichi. They laughed at Brahma, and for that fault they were cursed to be born as demons. Born in Devaki's womb, they were slain by Kamsa, the very children my mother weeps for. They dwell here, near your own city, waiting to be released from the curse. I will take them back with me, to end my mother's grief."

He said it without drama, as one stating what had always been true. The six sons of Marichi had passed through many births to arrive at this one waiting, in the shadows of a demon king's realm, for the two brothers to come and fetch them home. Their deaths at Kamsa's hands had never been an ending, only a pause.

Bali listened, and understood that the visit had never been about him, and yet he was not diminished by that understanding. It was enough that the Lord had entered his kingdom, enough that the Lord had sat on his seat and accepted his worship. The six sons of Marichi, waiting in the shadows of his realm, were about to be given back to the light, and Bali had been allowed to witness it.

So, having spoken, Krishna took the six sons into his keeping. Bali pressed his head once more to those feet that had descended into his kingdom, and the two brothers rose from Sutala with the six sons beside them, carrying a mother's grief, and its answer, back toward the world above.
stories.reflection: The descent to Sutala reads almost like a mirror of the world above: it is a demon king, not a mortal one, who shows what devotion looks like, asking nothing for himself and only to be made whole by the Lord's presence. The revelation of the sons' origin is given almost as an aside, as if to say that even their deaths were a thread in a longer design.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, a mother was waiting with open arms for the six sons she had lost.

stories.title: The Six Sons Restored to Devaki
stories.story:
Krishna and Balarama returned to Dwaraka carrying six small children, and the city that had witnessed every kind of wonder fell quiet at the sight. Two grown men — one dark, one fair — walking up the coast road with infants in their arms, six of them, small and silent, as though the brothers had gone down into the earth and come back with the morning held in their hands. Word of them traveled faster than their feet: children, the city whispered, they have brought children back from the underworld.

The children were Devaki's sons. Years before, her brother Kamsa had taken each of her first six children at birth and killed them, one by one, because a prophecy had warned him that a child of Devaki would one day end his reign. She had carried that grief ever since — a weight worn smooth by time but never lifted. She had borne Krishna and Balarama, the seventh and the eighth, and had loved them with all her strength; but the six were always there, six small absences standing in the shadow of her heart.

And now Krishna and Balarama had descended to Sutala, the netherworld kingdom where King Bali reigned, and had brought the six back to the world above. The journey home was long, and the brothers carried the children turn by turn, so that not one of them was ever out of someone's arms — as if the earth had once taken these children and they meant to be sure it did not take them again.

Word ran ahead of them through the streets, and Devaki came out of the palace as they reached the gate. She came forward slowly, the way people move when they are afraid to believe, and the women of the palace followed her with their hands pressed to their mouths. She stopped a little way off and counted them — one, two, three, four, five, six — and then her milk came, the body remembering what the heart had kept locked for so many years. She took them into her arms, all six at once, and nursed them, her breasts flowing, holding each small head to her, weeping and laughing together, while the courtyard stood silent around her. No one moved. The guards, the ministers, the women of the palace — they watched a mother receive her children, and there was nothing to say.

When the six had drunk their fill, they drew back from her and stood. Then, before the eyes of everyone gathered there, they bowed — first to Krishna, then to Devaki, then to Vasudeva, then to Balarama. And released at last from the curse that had taken them at birth, they rose from the ground and ascended, slowly, like light climbing a wall, until they reached the abode of the gods and were gone.

Devaki stood with empty arms, milk still on her lips, watching the sky where her sons had vanished. She had held them for a single evening — long enough to feed them, long enough to know them — and the old grief had gone out of her, the way a debt long owed is cleared. Beside her, Vasudeva watched his sons climb the sky and said nothing; there was nothing a father could add. The court watched her, and then looked up at the sky, and understood what they had seen: a debt of love, paid in full.

Dwaraka kept this in its memory for a long time after — six children carried down into the earth and carried back up again, and a mother whose arms were, for one night, the place where a curse was dissolved.
stories.reflection: Devaki is given her sons not to keep but to hold once: the restoration lasts a single evening of milk and touch, and then the children leave. The story honors a mother's love by letting it finish what a curse began — the six are freed through her embrace, not through any power, and her grief is answered by release rather than by possession.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna's journeys were not finished: in Mithila, two men were preparing for the same guest, each certain the visit was meant for him alone.
stories.hero_scene: The six sons, having drunk Devaki's milk, rising into the sky above the palace courtyard of Dwaraka as Devaki stands below with empty arms and milk still on her lips, while Krishna and Balarama watch and the whole court gazes upward in wonder.
