stories.title: Four Kings for a Conquered Land
stories.subtitle: Indra and Krishna divide Vajranabha's realm among four young princes
stories.story:
The war was over, and now came the harder question: what to do with what the war had won.

In the city of Vajra, where the streets had only just learned to be quiet again, Krishna and Indra moved as conquerors and guests at once. Vajranabha was dead, slain by the discus in Pradyumna's hand; his army was scattered, his allies fled — Nikumbha had gone to ground in the far city of Shatpura. In the streets, boys and old people were still recovering from the fear of the siege; Krishna and Indra had walked among them, consoling them, before turning to the question of the throne. The kingdom lay without a king, and kingdoms do not stay that way for long. So, following the advice of Brihaspati, the wise priest of the gods, Indra and Krishna consulted together about the present and the future.

Their answer was four. It was an answer with a shape: the kingdom would not be absorbed, not abandoned, not given to one conqueror. It would be divided — and divided among the young.

The conquered kingdom was divided into four parts. One fourth went to Vijaya, the son of Indra's son Jayanta, a boy of the divine line who could already range through the upper air. One fourth went to Pradyumna's son. One fourth went to Shamba's son. And the remaining fourth went to Chandraprabha, the son of Gada. Four young princes, each given a realm he had not had to conquer, each carrying a great name on young shoulders. Two houses, one protection: that was the design.

The division did not stop at the throne. The four koti villages of the kingdom were shared out, and a thousand prosperous branch cities like the town of Vajra itself. Warm clothing, deerskins, cloths, and jewels were divided into four parts as well, and Indra and Krishna took pleasure in giving it all away. No one was forgotten in the sharing; the wealth of the dead king became the wealth of the living. There was no grudging in the dividing; it was done openly, generously, in full view of the people.

Then came the crowning. Before the assembled Rishis, Indra and Krishna anointed the four young kings, pouring on their heads the water of the Ganga that issues from Vishnu's feet, while the music of celestial bugles sounded over the city. The Rishis blessed each prince in turn, and the sacred water ran down over the young crowns. Vijaya had already mastered the art of moving through the etherial region; the descendants of Madhava learned it too, inheriting the gift from their mothers, and in time they would travel the sky-road between the celestial region and Dwaraka, the city protected by the Bhaimas.

When the ceremony was done, Indra turned to Jayanta, whose son was among the four. "O heroic victor of armies," he said, "it behoves you to protect all these kings. One of them is a perpetuator of my race; the other three are born in the family of Keshava. By my command none amongst creatures will be able to kill them. Give them elephants born of the quarter-elephants, horses from the race of Ucchaisrava, and chariots built by the celestial architect." And the four kings, newly anointed, bowed and took their places, each in his share of the realm.

And so the city of Vajra, which a season ago had belonged to an asura king, passed into the keeping of four boys. Where one asura king had stood, four young kings now stood. The old king's realm became four realms, held by four young hands — and over them all, one protection, promised by the king of the gods himself.
stories.reflection: The division is not a dispersal: four shares are still one realm under a single protection, and the four young kings receive what they did not have to win. Indra's promise that no creature can kill them is the war, at last, saying it is finished — the children may grow.
stories.next_story_tease: But one member of the great family had still to come home.

stories.title: Yogamaya Comes Home
stories.subtitle: The illusory daughter of Yashoda appears before Krishna and Balarama
stories.story:
Krishna had come home from the mountain fortress of Naraka, and Dwaraka was still learning to believe it.

Naraka, the son of the earth, had been slain. The maidens he had kept locked in his inner apartments were free; the summit of Mount Mani, the jewel of his mountain kingdom, had been uprooted and brought home; and the wealth of his palace now lay in heaps before the Yadavas. "You are the masters of all these things," Krishna told them. The Bhojas, the Andhakas, and the Vrishnis heard it with their hair standing on end in joy, and they worshipped him. The streets of Dwaraka had not been so bright in years; the whole city seemed to be breathing out.

Then the women came. The wives of the Dasharhas and of Ahuka made their way to the hall to see Krishna with their own eyes, and with them came the seven queens of Vasudeva, headed by Devaki and by Rohini. There they saw Balarama and Krishna seated at ease, the two brothers together, and the sight of them seemed to complete something in the room. Rohini's face was soft with pride, and Devaki could not stop looking at her sons. First the queens saluted Rohini; then Balarama and Krishna rose and saluted Devaki. And those who watched thought that the goddess shone in the company of her two lotus-eyed sons as Aditi, the mother of the gods, shines among Mitra and Varuna.

Then a woman entered the hall whom no one had summoned — and yet everyone knew her. The women of the hall fell quiet as she passed; some of them had not seen her since she was a child.

She was the illusory daughter of Yashoda, the girl born at the very same moment as Krishna, the one for whose sake he had struck down Kamsa and all his kin. In the years since that night, the Vrishni family had adored her, brought her up, and kept her like a daughter. The people of the world knew her as the Yoga maiden, one and without parts, born for the protection of Keshava; and because she had guarded Keshava with her goddess-like celestial body in the days of his peril, the Yadavas worshipped her with joy.

As soon as she entered the hall, Krishna rose and went to her, the way a man goes to a beloved friend, and took her hand. And Balarama, the mighty one, took her by the hand as well, embraced her, and bent to smell her head, as a brother does. For a long moment the three of them stood there, the hall watching in silence.

And the Vrishni women who stood watching saw her then, standing between her two brothers, Balarama and Krishna, and she seemed to them like the goddess Shree herself — golden lotuses in her hands, seated upon a lotus. The women murmured her name like a prayer, and joy rose in the hall like a tide. They showered her with fried paddy and with flowers, a rain of blessing, and then they returned to their own quarters, carrying the sight of her home with them.

The Yadavas spent the rest of that day speaking of Krishna's wonders and honoring him, and Madhava, the enhancer of his city's joy, lived on happily among his people. The day had begun with a conqueror's return and ended with a sister in the house. And soon after, the sage Narada came to the hall, sent by the king of the gods, ready to tell the assembled Vrishnis the story of Krishna's boyhood. But that is another telling — and the hall was not yet done rejoicing over the daughter who had come home.
stories.reflection: The daughter who was left behind on the night of Krishna's birth comes back to the family that had to let her go, and is greeted not as a stranger but as a sister, with flowers and embraces. The Vrishnis had adored her like a daughter all along; her homecoming simply lets the family recognize what it already knew.
stories.next_story_tease: And elsewhere in Dwaraka, a young warrior was about to learn the truth of his own birth.

stories.title: The Secret Mayavati Kept
stories.story:
The boy who was called Shamvara's son had believed it all his life: that he was a prince of the demon city, and that the beautiful woman who raised him was his mother. Both were lies, and the night he learned the truth, the lying ended in fire.

The truth had begun on the seventh night of his life, far away in Dwaraka. He had been born Pradyumna, the son of Krishna and Rukmini; but the ancient Kama, the god of desire, had taken this birth for one purpose — to bring down the demon Shamvara. And the demon, as if urged on by death itself, crept into the lying-in room at the dark hour, lifted the week-old infant from the bed, and carried him across the night to his own city. Krishna, who follows the workings of celestial Maya, knew what had happened, and he did not strike the demon down. The theft was allowed; the child was part of a design larger than his mother's grief.

Mayavati had no children of her own, and Shamvara gave the stolen baby to his wife as though he were her son. She looked at the infant, and her hair stood on end; she gazed at him again and again with joy, and as she looked she remembered. In a life before this one he had been her husband — Kama, burnt to ashes long ago by the trident-bearing god in his sorrow for Sati. Now he had come again, into her arms, in another birth. "Being his wife," she thought, "and knowing him as my husband, how can I give him milk and call him my son?"

She could not bring herself to do it. She handed the baby to a nurse, and through the nurse's care the child grew up believing Mayavati was his mother. As the years passed she taught him every form of illusion, all the arts of Maya, until the stolen boy became a young man of striking beauty, expert in every weapon, quick to read the hidden intentions of the people around him.

Then Mayavati, who had carried her secret through all those years, came to him dressed as a beautiful woman and tempted him with her gestures. Pradyumna drew back, shocked. "What is this?" he asked. "Why do you cast off a mother's feeling and behave in this perverse way? Women's minds flicker like lightning. Am I not your son? Tell me the secret of what you are doing."

In a solitary place she told him everything. "You are not my son, and Shamvara is not your father. You are the son of Vasudeva and Rukmini, a prince of the Vrishnis. On your seventh night, when you were a helpless baby in the lying-in chamber, my husband stole you away. Your mother mourns you like a cow separated from her calf, and your father — mightier than Indra, the banner of Garuda on his flag — does not even know you are alive. I seek you as my lover, for I did not give birth to you, and my heart fails at your beauty."

Pradyumna had mastered every form of illusion, and the anger that rose in him now was like a weapon drawn. He spoke the demon's name aloud. "Shall I cower here, afraid of the wretch who stole the infant son of Keshava? I will do what makes him angry. I will break his standard and call him out; and when he comes to meet me I will kill him in battle and return to Dwaraka."

In one breath Mayavati's confession had given him back his name, his parents and his purpose. The boy who had believed himself a demon's son stood up a Vrishni prince — and the first thing he meant to break was the emblem of the power that had stolen him.
stories.reflection: What lingers is the silence between them: Mayavati has known who Pradyumna is since the night he was placed in her arms, and has carried that knowledge for years while raising him as her own. The love she finally declares is not a mother's confusion but a wife's memory — a devotion that waited an entire lifetime without once being spoken.
stories.content_note: Contains a woman's romantic pursuit of the young man she raised; the episode is handled with restraint and without explicit detail.
stories.next_story_tease: The first step of that resolve was a jeweled lion standard above the demon's gate.
stories.hero_scene: Pradyumna, a young warrior in the demon king's palace, stands frozen in a moonlit hall while Mayavati — beautiful, sorrowful, her hand raised — tells him he is not her son; the glittering towers of Shamvara's city visible beyond the window.

stories.title: The Lion Standard Comes Down
stories.story:
Above the gate of Shamvara's city stood a standard that seemed to hold up the sky: a jeweled pole with a flying pennon, and on it a lion worked in gold, so high that travelers measured the city by it. It was the pride of the demon king — a boast set in gold above his gate — and it was the first thing Pradyumna chose to break.

He had come to this city as a stolen child, carried out of Dwaraka on his seventh night, and for years he had been raised as a prince of the demon house. Now Mayavati had told him the truth: he was the son of Vasudeva and Rukmini, a Vrishni prince, and the demon whose name he had grown up bearing had lifted him from his mother's room. The knowledge burned in him. Every time he pictured his mother in Dwaraka, mourning him like a cow separated from her calf, the anger sharpened into a blade. He would not slip out of the city by night like a thief escaping with his life. He would make Shamvara come out and fight him openly, and he would return to Dwaraka only when the demon lay dead.

He was no ordinary youth to make such a vow. Mayavati had trained him in every form of illusion, and he had become expert in the use of all sorts of weapons, quick with bow and spear, quick to read the intentions of the men around him. What he had never been taught was fear of the demon house, and he did not feel it now.

"I will strike down the wonderful standard at his gate," he said, "the jeweled standard with the lion, standing like Mount Sumeru itself. When Shamvara learns that his banner lies broken, he will come out to me. I will kill him in battle, and I will go home."

He strung his bow, fitted an arrow, and loosed it at the jewel of a standard. The great pole shuddered, leaned, and came down across the gate like a falling tree; the gold lion tumbled into the dust of the road, and the pennon that had flown above the demon city for so long lay torn underfoot. The gate that had worn that banner like a crown looked suddenly bare, and the silence after the crash was the loudest thing in the city.

The city understood what it had seen. A prince of the house bringing down the king's own standard was not mischief — it was a declaration of war, written in one stroke, in the open, before every eye. Word reached Shamvara, and the rage that flooded him was exactly what Pradyumna had counted on. The demon's answer came fast. He called his hundred sons together and ordered them out. "Go quickly," he said, "and kill Rukmini's son." They came with their bows strung and their chariots ready, a hundred of them, to answer one insult.

They were good bowmen, those hundred brothers, and they had lived under the same roof as the stolen boy; they thought they knew his measure. They did not know him at all. He had been schooled in every form of illusion by Mayavati's own hand, and the blood of the Vrishnis ran in him — the same blood that had flowed in his father, whose banner bore the emblem of Garuda and who was mightier than Indra himself. Pradyumna stood in the open space before the fallen standard, his bow in his hand, and waited for the brothers of the demon house to come to him.

The lion lay in the dust behind him, and the war he had come for was beginning.
stories.reflection: Pradyumna chooses to be known before he chooses to be safe: he breaks the standard in the open so the war must come to him. There is a kind of honesty in it — the stolen prince refuses to leave his enemy's city the way he entered it, as a secret.
stories.next_story_tease: Shamvara's answer came with a hundred of his sons at once.
stories.hero_scene: Pradyumna on the wall above Shamvara's gate, bow drawn, sending the jeweled lion standard toppling — the gold lion tumbling against the evening sky while the demon city erupts below.

stories.title: One Hundred Sons Against One
stories.story:
A hundred sons of Shamvara came against him at once, and the young man from Dwaraka did not give ground.

They came on as a storm comes, showering him from every side with arrows, spears, axes, javelins and maces at the same moment, and the field before the gate turned dark with their shafts. Pradyumna, angered, answered each of them with five arrows of his own, and the field rang with bowstrings and the shriek of arrows. The sons of the demon were all good bowmen, and they wove a net of weapons over him to bring him down; Pradyumna cut straight through it. In the first exchanges he killed the ten strongest of the brothers; the next moment, with a broad-headed arrow, he took off Chitrasena's head. The last of them, seeing their brothers fall, united against him in a single rush, shooting as they came — and he cut off their heads, the old text says, as if in sport.

When it was over, all hundred lay on the field. Every one of them had been a good bowman; every one of them was dead. Pradyumna, the pride of Rukmini's heart, stood untouched among the fallen, and the field was quiet except for the wind moving in the fallen flags. He looked toward the city, still wanting battle.

In the palace, the news struck Shamvara like a blow: his hundred sons, gone in a single day. Wrath filled him, and he called for his charioteer, who saluted with his head touching the ground, brought the king's car, and roused the soldiers to readiness. The car itself was a thing out of nightmare — drawn by a thousand bears, bound with ropes of serpents, armored in tiger skin, hung with a net of small bells and painted over with stars, ringed with wooden fenders on iron axles, its deck reached by ten stairs, its flags bearing the figures of lions, its height like the summit of Mount Mandara, decked with waving chowries, gold flashing from every standard. Shamvara put on golden armor, took up his bow and arrows, and set out, as if urged on by death itself, with his four ministers around him — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramardana — and his army spread across the plain behind him: two hundred chariots, ten thousand elephants, eight thousand horses, and ten lakh foot soldiers.

The sky itself seemed to turn against the march. Cranes screamed overhead; firebrands fell among the columns; jackals howled at the army; vultures settled on the tops of the standards, already thirsty for the blood of Danavas. Headless figures seemed to drop upon the king's car. The moon was eclipsed and ringed with its dark disc; his left eye and left arm danced, presaging calamity; the horses' pace slackened of their own accord; Indra sent down a shower of blood mixed with live coals and cinders; the reins slipped from the charioteer's hands.

Shamvara paid no attention to any of it. Rage had closed his eyes to omens. He drove on, bent on slaying Pradyumna, and the earth shook under the sound of bugles, conch shells and drums blown together; beasts and birds fled in terror from the noise.

On the far side of the field, Krishna's son stood alone among the fallen, and he too was bent on slaying his enemy. He watched the horizon darken with the dust of an army, and at its head the monstrous chariot drawn by bears. He had called the demon out, and the demon was coming — and the boy who had mastered every form of illusion stood his ground and waited.
stories.reflection: The omens read the end before the battle begins — the eclipse, the vultures, the blood falling from a clear sky — and only Shamvara refuses to see them. Rage, the text suggests, is the one blindness no seer can cure.
stories.content_note: Battle violence: Pradyumna kills the hundred sons of Shamvara in a single fight; the deaths are recounted without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: The father himself was coming — and he did not come alone.
stories.hero_scene: The battlefield strewn with the fallen hundred; Pradyumna standing alone amid the wreck of bows and standards, bow in hand, as the horizon darkens with the dust of Shamvara's monstrous bear-drawn chariot and his army.

stories.title: The Four Ministers Fall
stories.story:
The war had begun with a broken standard and a hundred fallen princes; it had come down, now, to a single meeting between one young man and the four ministers of the demon king.

Shamvara's arrows came first — thousands of them, falling on Pradyumna like a season of rain — and the young man's hands moved faster than the eye could follow, cutting each shaft out of the air before it could touch him. Then he bent his own bow, and there was no man in the demon army who went unstruck.

The soldiers who survived that rain broke and ran back toward their king in fear, and Shamvara, watching his army scatter, was beside himself. He turned to the four ministers around him — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramardana. "At my command, go and strike my enemy's son," he told them. "Do not neglect him; kill him at once. A danger ignored at its beginning grows like a disease — leave this boy alone and he will ruin us all."

What followed was a meeting that lifted the hair of everyone who watched: Rukmini's son against the four greatest warriors of the demon court. The old text names him the enhancer of his mother's delight — and his mother was far away in Dwaraka, unaware that the son she had mourned for years was on a field in the demon country, cutting down her enemies. The ministers, filled with anger and eager to obey the king who had trusted them with this errand, drove their chariots out, wheel to wheel, with arrows showering from them, and the air between them and the young man filled with shafts. Pradyumna, quick as anger, took up his bow and stood his ground. He struck Durdhara with twenty-five arrows, Ketumali with sixty-three, Shatruhanta with seventy, and Pramardana with eighty-two. The four, in fury, covered him in a downpour of their own — and then the boy who had learned every form of illusion from Mayavati's own teaching finished the work.

He put an arrow through the breast of Durdhara, the short-lived one, and the minister fell. Before the eyes of the whole army he cut off Ketumali's head. The heart of the mighty Shatruhanta was cut out of him in the same breath. And Pramardana, the last of the four, was crushed beneath Pradyumna's club. He had measured out their doom by count — twenty-five here, sixty-three there — as if the numbers themselves were the sentence. The ministers lay dead in a ring around him, their chariots wrecked, their flags trailing in the dirt.

The demon army had watched its hundred princes fall, and now it had watched its four greatest warriors die in a single fight. It could bear no more. The rout was total: the soldiers threw down their weapons and fled the field in terror, abandoning their king, their banners, everything, and the field emptied like a tide going out. The omens that had darkened Shamvara's march were fulfilled at last — the vultures had been right, and the eclipsed moon had not lied.

Pradyumna stood among the wreckage and looked once more toward Shamvara — the demon who had stolen an infant from its mother's room and raised it as his own son, only to watch that boy cut down his hundred sons and his four ministers, one after another. Behind him the field lay under the torn flags of the four ministers. The father was alone now, with nothing left but his own weapons and the old arts of illusion that his own house had once taught to the stolen child.
stories.reflection: There is an exactness to Pradyumna's justice: each minister receives his counted share of arrows — twenty-five here, sixty-three there — before the end. The arithmetic of the field stands in place of mercy, as if the young warrior measures out doom the way his father measured out grace.
stories.content_note: Battle violence: the four ministers of Shamvara are slain in single combat; the deaths are recounted without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shamvara had not yet used the one weapon he trusted most — the art of illusion itself.
stories.hero_scene: Pradyumna astride his chariot in the turning chaos of battle, the four ministers falling one by one around him — Durdhara pierced through the breast, Ketumali's head taken, Pramardana crushed beneath the club — while the demon army breaks and runs.

stories.title: Illusion Against Illusion
stories.subtitle: Pradyumna meets Shamvara's magic on the battlefield
stories.story:
Across the field of battle came Shamvara's golden chariot, and the demon king rode it like a storm. "O hero," he told his charioteer, "take my car to the enemy soon. With arrows I will kill him who has done me wrong." He meant the youth who stood on the far side of the field with a bow already strung: Pradyumna, the son of Krishna and Rukmini, the baby Shamvara had once snatched away and meant to destroy, grown now into a man who had already cut down the demon's four chief ministers, one after another, until the army itself had fled from him.

Pradyumna watched the golden car approach and set a golden arrow to his string. His first shaft struck home, cutting to Shamvara's very vitals, and the demon king reeled in his seat, clutching the reins, and lost consciousness. When he came back to himself a few moments later, rage had made him reckless. He snatched up his bow and loosed seventy sharpened arrows at Krishna's son, and Pradyumna met them with seven shafts that cut all seventy into seven parts before they could reach him. Then seventy winged arrows flew back the other way, and then a thousand, until the sky was so thick with shafts that even the sun was hidden. Shamvara dispelled that darkness with his thunderbolt and showered arrows on Pradyumna's car; Pradyumna, light of hand, sliced them into pieces as they came. In the end it was the arrows that gave out first.

Then the demon changed his art entirely. By his illusory powers he showered the field with trees, and Pradyumna, beside himself with anger, burned them all to ash with fiery weapons. Shamvara answered with a downpour of stones, and Pradyumna swept them from the battlefield with weapons of air. Next came the beasts, lions, tigers, bears, monkeys, horses, camels, asses, and elephants like clouds, hurled at his car, and the Gandharva weapons cut the whole illusory herd into pieces. So Shamvara raised the stakes: elephants with sixty heads each, mad for battle, decked for war and ridden by expert drivers. Pradyumna answered illusion with illusion, calling up lions of his own, and the illusory lions destroyed the illusory elephants as the sun sends away the night.

Illusion followed illusion. Shamvara cast the Sunmohini Maya, the fascinating spell that the great architect Maya himself had fashioned, and Pradyumna checked it with his weapon of consciousness. Shamvara sent lions again; Pradyumna sent the sharabhas, eight-legged creatures of claws and teeth, and they pursued the lions as the wind scatters clouds. For the first time the demon king doubted himself. "Alas, how stupid I am," he thought. "Why did I not kill him in his infancy? Now he has attained to youth and mastered every weapon. Only one illusion remains to me, the dread illusion of serpents, which the great god Hara himself instructed me in, and which no one else knows. Let me spread it, and see whether this powerful magician can be consumed."

He spread it. Serpents full of burning venom coiled around Pradyumna, his car, his horses, and his charioteer, and bound them all fast. But Pradyumna thought of the garudas, the eagle-kings who feast on serpents, and at the very thought they came wheeling down and began to destroy the venomous illusion. When the last serpent dissolved, the gods and the asuras watching from the sky cried out together: "Well done! Well done! O mighty-armed son of Rukmini, the illusion is dispelled by you, and we are pleased."

Shamvara stood in his golden car with nothing left of his magic. But there remained one weapon that was not magic at all, a golden club shaped like the rod of Death itself, which the goddess Uma had conferred on him long ago, saying it could dispel all forms of illusion and kill all asuras. He had already sent many demons to the abode of Yama with it. Now, while the applause of the gods still rang over the field, his hand closed on it.
stories.reflection: The duel is a contest of knowledge as much as of strength. Shamvara's every illusion is genuine craft, and each one is met by a counter-craft in the boy he failed to kill, maya answered by maya, illusion by illusion, until nothing the demon knows is unknown to his enemy. What defeats him is not a larger army but a deeper mastery of the same art.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shamvara was reaching for the golden club that no weapon could withstand, and in the sky above the battlefield a figure was already descending to meet him.

stories.title: The Warrior Who Was Kama
stories.story:
A voice came from the sky over the battlefield, and for a moment even the arrows stopped. From the clouds a radiant figure descended, an ascetic with matted locks, a vina in his hand, his face bright as fire, and came to rest before Pradyumna's chariot on the field where the last illusions had just died. It was Narada, the wandering sage of the gods, and the king of the gods had sent him. He came without herald or escort, as he always came, and the armies on both sides knew him at sight: the sage who wandered between the worlds, carrying the news of the heavens in his vina.

Pradyumna's story had been hidden from Pradyumna himself. As an infant he had been stolen away by the demon king Shamvara, who had meant to kill him and somehow had not; the boy had grown to youth in the demon's household, had been trained in arms, and had come at last to stand against his kidnapper in open battle. He had slain Shamvara's four ministers and shattered every illusion the demon could cast, and still he did not know the simplest thing about himself: who he had been before this life began.

"Remember your pristine birth, O hero," Narada said. "You are Kama. In a former life you were the god of love, and you have been born again, in the house of Krishna, as Pradyumna. The demon who stole you never knew what he held." Then the sage gave him the Vaishnava weapons and a coat of mail. The weapons were not like anything in the demon's armoury, for they were consecrated to Vishnu, and the coat of mail settled on his shoulders as if it had been waiting for him. Then Narada told him the task the gods had set before him. "Having killed Shamvara in the battlefield with the Vaishnava weapons," he said, "take your own wife Mayavati and go to Dwaraka."

Pradyumna stood with the coat of mail on his shoulders and the Vaishnava weapons in his hands, and understood for the first time why Shamvara's magic had never held him. It had not been only a boy's quick hands that had cut the illusions to pieces. Something in him was older than the demon's art, older than the demon himself, and the illusions could not touch it.

His childhood in Shamvara's house had been a long apprenticeship in war and watchfulness, and no one had ever spoken of where he came from. Now the shape of his life rearranged itself in a few words. He was not an orphan of chance. He was Kama, born again, and every year of his stolen boyhood had been leading to this field. He thought of his mother Rukmini in Dwaraka, of his father Krishna, of a city he had been too young to remember; and he thought of Mayavati, a wife he had not known he possessed, waiting somewhere to be claimed. The battle that had begun as a boy's desperate contest had become something else. It was a return. He set his hand to the Vaishnava weapons, and their weight told him what no weapon of the demon's house ever had: he was not alone in this war.

Narada watched him a moment, then rose into the sky as suddenly as he had come, leaving the young warrior alone on the field with his new name and his new weapons. Pradyumna turned his chariot toward the golden car of Shamvara, who was reaching for his last weapon, the golden club that no god or demon could withstand, and did not understand why the boy's face had changed. But the gods watching from above understood. The stolen child had remembered himself, and the last battle of the demon king could now begin.
stories.reflection: Pradyumna does not change in the battle; he changes in a moment of recognition. He had fought brilliantly without knowing his own story, and the revelation adds not strength but meaning, the stolen child becomes the returning husband, and every blow from then on is struck toward a home he has never seen. Identity, the episode suggests, is what arms a person for the life they were meant to live.
stories.next_story_tease: And when the war was done, the same sage would appear before Krishna in Dwaraka with a riddle that left every king in the court speechless.

stories.title: Narada's Riddle: Who Is Truly Blessed
stories.story:
The storm broke over Dwaraka without warning, a hurricane, clouds charged with lightning, and the deep muttering of thunder over the sea-girt city. And in the heart of the tempest a figure appeared: Narada, the wandering sage, covered with matted locks, a vina in his hand, radiant as fire. The instant his feet touched the ground of Krishna's court, the foul weather vanished. The court went still.

All the kings of the earth had gathered in that hall. Duryodhana had undertaken a great sacrifice at Hastinapura, and every king who travelled to it had turned aside on the way to see Krishna, drawn by his fame, by the report of his sons, by the wonder of Dwaraka standing on the shore of the ocean. They had come in multitudes: Duryodhana himself and the sons of Dhritarashtra, the sons of the Pandavas, Dhrishtadyumna, and the kings of Pandya, Chola, Kalinga, Vahlika, Dravida and Khasa, with their armies. Krishna had welcomed each according to age and rank, had seated them in their proper places, and had taken his own golden throne, shining among them like the autumnal sun. The Yadus and the kings had talked of this and that, and then the storm had come, and then Narada.

The sage walked into the ocean-like court and went straight to Krishna's throne. "O thou of large arms," he said, "thou alone hast become an object of wonder to the gods. O Purusottama, there is none blessed like thee in the world."

Krishna smiled. "Yes," he said, "I am an object of surprise and good luck, especially in the matter of presents."

"I have got the proper reply," said Narada, and turned to go. "I depart for my wished-for region."

The kings looked at one another; the mystery of the words defeated them. "Narada said 'wonder and blessed,'" they said to Krishna, "and you replied 'presents.' We cannot decipher these celestial expressions. If we are worthy of the true import, we wish to hear it."

"You are the fit persons to hear it," Krishna said, "and the twice-born Narada will relate it. O celestial saint, describe to these kings the import of your question and my reply." Narada seated himself on a white golden seat and began.

"Once," he said, "I walked alone on the bank of the Ganga at sunrise, and I came upon a tortoise, huge as a mountain, four-legged, with two coatings, soaked with water and covered with moss, its skin hard as an elephant's. I praised it: what a wonderful body, what a fortunate life, to carry two invincible shells and range the water without a care for anyone. And the tortoise answered me like a man: 'What wonder is there in me, O sage? How can I be blessed? This Ganga, flowing downwards, is the blessed one, in whom hundreds and thousands of creatures like me range. What is more wonderful than she?'

"So I went to the Ganga and praised her in turn, the foremost of rivers, rich in lakes, thronged with huge-bodied animals, protecting the hermitages as she flows to the ocean. And the Ganga, in her turn, pointed me onward; and the ocean pointed to the earth, and the earth to the mountains, and the mountains to Brahma, and Brahma to the Vedas, and the Vedas to the sacrifices that keep them alive. Each one I praised turned and showed me something greater still, until the chain ran out at the yajnas, and great indeed is a sacrifice accompanied by presents. And above them all stands Vishnu alone, the great wonder, whom all these serve."

The court understood at last. The whole chain of creation, asked what was greatest, had pointed beyond itself, and the end of the pointing was Vishnu, and a sacrifice with gifts. So when Narada had called Krishna the wonder of the gods and blessed among men, he had been speaking the truth; and when Krishna had answered, smiling, that he was especially blessed in the matter of presents, the joke had carried the true answer all along, for the blessed one is the one whom all the giving of the world finally reaches. The kings murmured their wonder, and Narada, satisfied that the mystery was explained, rose and departed for his wished-for region, the storm not daring to return with him.
stories.reflection: The delight of the riddle is that every being in creation, asked to name what is greatest, points beyond itself, humility is the one thing the whole chain shares. And Krishna's odd reply about presents turns the loftiest praise into something warm and human, a god who answers an anthem with a smile about gifts.
stories.next_story_tease: But the peace of Dwaraka would not hold for long: soon the Yadavas would ride out against Bana, whose city burned with a fire that dimmed even Krishna's radiance.

stories.title: Garuda Quenches Bana's Fire
stories.story:
The gates of Dwaraka rang with conch shells and bugles, bards and panegyrists sang victory by the thousands, and men shouted blessings, as Krishna mounted the king of birds. With Balarama and Pradyumna behind him on Garuda's back, he rose into the sky, and his beauty, increased by the energy of Hari himself, became immense. Beneath them the city of Dwaraka grew small and vanished into the haze of the sea. They were flying to Sonitpura, to bring down Bana, and the flight itself was already a marvel.

Krishna, desiring to kill Bana, had taken a form like a mountain, with eight arms: in his right hands the sword, the discus, the club and the arrows; in his left the leathern guard, the Shranga bow, the thunderbolt and the conch, and his head had multiplied into innumerable heads. Behind him rode Balarama, holding a thousand forms, white weapons in hand, shining like the rising moon above the summit of Kailasha; and Pradyumna rode with them, radiant as the eternal youth Sanatkumara. The three of them together were a sight to stop the heart of any army, and the heavens themselves watched them pass. Beneath them the great wings beat, shaking mountains, obstructing the very course of the wind, crossing in moments the sacred route of the Siddhas and Charanas. And then, suddenly, the golden change.

They were high above the world when Balarama noticed it. "Krishna," he said, "what wonder is this, that we have on a sudden been shorn of our effulgence? We all wear a golden hue. What is the cause? Have we come to the side of Mount Sumeru?"

Krishna answered his brother. "Methinks Bana's city is near at hand," he said. "To protect him, the fire stationed in his city is coming out blazing. O holder of the ploughshare, we have been possessed by the effulgence of the fire of oblation; that is what has changed our colour."

"If by approaching the city of Bana we lose the lustre of our bodies," said Balarama, "do what you think proper afterwards."

Krishna turned to Garuda, the son of Vinata, who carried them. "Do what you think proper," he said. "When you have found out a means, I shall do what I think proper."

The king of birds answered with a thousand mouths. He spread them wide, leaped up from the path of his flight, and went to the etherial Ganga, the river that runs through the sky. He drank profuse water, until his great breast was heavy with it, and came back to the blazing fire of Bana's city and showered the water down. The water fell in great silver sheets, and the blaze that had stolen the lustre of three warriors dimmed, choked, and went out at once.

Even Garuda was astonished at what he had been asked to quench. "Oh! How powerful is this fire," he said, "like the fire at the end of a cycle. It disfigured the color of even the intelligent Krishna." Then he went on, beating his great wings, and the sound of them rolled across the plain like thunder.

Far below, in the approaches of Bana's city, the fires that served the demon king looked up. They were the fire-gods, the followers of Rudra, and they saw three dreadful men of many forms riding the king of birds through the sky. "Who are these," they asked one another, "and why have they come here?" They could not settle it among themselves, but they did not need to. The sound of Garuda's wings was already rolling toward them, and in Bana's city the chief of the fires had lifted his head. The riders were coming closer, and the road to Sonitpura lay open before them.
stories.reflection: The episode turns as much on trust as on power. Krishna names the problem, Balarama waits, and Garuda, the one among them who can fly, becomes the whole answer, drinking a river from the sky to do it. Greatness here is not hoarded but shared out: each does the one thing only he can do, and the fire dies.
stories.next_story_tease: But the fire-gods of Bana's city had marked the three riders, and their chief, Angira, was already taking up his mace.

stories.title: Angira Falls, and the Fire-Gods Flee
stories.story:
The fire that guarded Bana's city was out, and its keepers were coming to answer for it.

Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna were crossing the sky on Garuda, bound for Sonitpura, where the thousand-armed king Bana was gathering his defences for war. Along the way, the blaze that protected his city had leapt out at the travellers and burned away their natural colour, and Garuda had drowned it with water drawn from the celestial Ganga, taken in a thousand mouths at once. That was the insult. Now the fires themselves — the gods of flame, the followers of Rudra — rose out of the earth and air around the three riders and asked one another who these dreadful men of many forms were, riding the king of birds. They stared, and wondered, and could settle nothing. And so they did the only thing left to them: they attacked.

Garuda, who could change his shape at will, flew on with the speed of thought, crossing the sacred route of the Siddhas and the Charanas high above the world — but the fire-gods were swifter than that road, and they met the travellers before the city itself came into view. Krishna met them in the form he had taken for the journey — eight arms, a stature like a mountain, and in every hand a weapon of war: sword and discus, club and arrows, the great bow, the thunderbolt, the conch. Balarama rode beside him shining like the rising moon, and Pradyumna before them like the eternal youth of the gods. The noise of the clash rolled over the countryside like the roaring of lions.

In the city, Bana heard it and sent out a messenger fleet as thought to learn what was happening. Angira, chief of the fires, sent one of his own, urging the man to hurry to where the battle raged. What the messengers found was a field already burning with war: the five principal fire-gods — Kalmasha, Kusuma, Dahana, Shoshana and the powerful Tapana — fighting with all their armies, and beside them the five gods who preside over the offerings to the ancestors, Pithara, Pataga, Swarna, Agadha and Vraja, and the two effulgent gods in charge of the great sacrifices, Jyotisthoma and Vasatkara. At their head, on a chariot of flame, stood the great sage Angira himself, his blazing mace lifted high, shining over the whole field like a second sun.

Krishna watched them come, and he did not frown. He smiled — smiled again and again, the way a man smiles when a matter is already settled. “Wait patiently a few moments, fire-gods,” he said. “The time of your destruction is drawing near. Within a moment, consumed by the energy of my weapons, you will fly away on all sides.”

Angira heard the words and answered them by charging — running straight at Krishna with a burning trident in his hand, as if to take his life. Krishna bent his bow. Crescent-headed arrows sheared the great mace from Angira's hand, cutting it clean away, and one last arrow, death itself in flight, struck the chief of the fires on the breast. Angira fell where he stood, bathed in blood, in the middle of the field.

The fire-gods stared at their fallen leader. Then the four among them who are the sons of Brahma turned, and with them the whole host, and they fled — back to Bana's city, carrying the news that the king's protection had burned out in a single exchange of arrows.

Garuda spread his wings, and the three Yadavas went on across the last stretch of sky toward Sonitpura, the air behind them empty and quiet where the fires had burned.
stories.reflection: Krishna's smile before the battle is the story's strangest note — anger without rage, the calm of someone who has already seen the end of the matter. The fire that had paled the travellers' skin was itself only a servant of the city, and it scattered the moment its chief fell.
stories.content_note: Mild battle violence: Angira is struck down by an arrow and falls bathed in blood; described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But in Bana's city, in the women's quarters, his daughter Usha was already dreaming of a man she had never met.

stories.title: Chitralekha Comes for Aniruddha
stories.story:
She came to Dwaraka with a theft on her mind and a name on her lips: Aniruddha.

Chitralekha made her way to the city and settled near the palace of Vasudeva, turning over the question of how she might find Pradyumna's son and carry him away. While she sat thinking, she saw the ascetic Narada meditating in the water. Her eyes widened with joy. She approached him, saluted him, and stood before him with her head bowed. Narada blessed her, and then asked, gently, what she had come for.

With folded hands she told him everything. She was a messenger, she said, come to take Aniruddha with her. In the city of Sonitpura lived the great asura Bana, and Bana had a daughter, Usha, the most beautiful of maidens. By the boon of a goddess, Usha had chosen Aniruddha as her husband — a man she had never met except in a dream. The dream had claimed her utterly, and Chitralekha meant to take him to her. But after she had carried Aniruddha to Sonitpura, Krishna must learn the truth, for a great encounter would follow: Bana was too powerful for Aniruddha to defeat, yet the large-armed Krishna would vanquish the thousand-armed asura. And that was what she feared. Krishna, when angered, could consume even the three worlds with a curse; she begged Narada to arrange matters so that Usha might have her husband and she herself might not be burned by that wrath.

Narada gave his answer. “I offer you protection,” he said. “Shorn of fear, hear what I say. If any encounter takes place while you steal away Aniruddha to the apartments of the maidens, remember me — I am fond of seeing battles, and take great pleasure in them. And accept the Tamasika learning, which I have mastered by hard austerities, that can infatuate all the worlds.”

“So be it,” said Chitralekha. She saluted the sage, and set out through the sky, searching for Aniruddha's house.

She found it in the centre of Dwaraka: the palace of Kama, the god of love, and beside it the palace where Aniruddha lived — golden altars, pillars of gold and sapphire, garlands hanging along the walls, jars of cool water set at the doors, peacocks carved on the turrets, and rows of celestial buildings set with jewels and coral, filled with the music of the Gandharvas. And there she saw Aniruddha, playing in the midst of the most beautiful women of the court as the moon shines among the stars. Hundreds of women attended on him. Seated like Kubera on a fine seat, he was drinking Madhvika wine; sweet songs rose and fell in time; accomplished dancers moved before him. But Chitralekha saw no pleasure in him. His mind was not on the wine; he showed dislike even for drinking. She watched, and understood: surely his mind is busy with the dream. And her anxiety fell away.

Hiding herself in the sky above the palace, she spoke to him in sweet words, asking whether all was well with him, and then delivered her message. “I have come to you from Usha,” she said, “the maiden whom you saw in a dream and married, and who cherishes you at her heart. She is weeping, and yawning, and sighing, for she cannot see you. She will live if you go to her; forsooth, in your absence she will die.”

The words found their mark. By the power of her Tamasika illusion Chitralekha overpowered everyone in the palace except the prince himself, and carried Aniruddha away through the sky to Sonitpura — to a maiden's rooms where Usha was waiting for the man of her dream.
stories.reflection: The whole errand runs on illusion — the dream that joined Usha to a man she had never met, the Tamasika learning that lets Chitralekha move unseen through a city — yet every deception serves a genuine longing. Narada's blessing is characteristic: he helps gladly, and asks only to be remembered when the fighting begins.
stories.next_story_tease: But Vana's city would not keep its secret long, and the thousand-armed king had soldiers enough to answer it.
stories.hero_scene: Chitralekha, hidden in the sky above Aniruddha's jewelled palace in Dwaraka, speaking down to the prince as he sits among dancers and musicians, his mind elsewhere — the moon among stars, and the messenger who moves like thought.

stories.title: One Club Against Vana's Host
stories.story:
The king of Sonitpura learned of his daughter's guest the way kings learn such things — late, and from other mouths.

Aniruddha had come to Bana's city the way he had come to Usha's dream: without warning, and utterly. The princess had seen him in a vision, chosen him as her husband by the boon of a goddess, and pined for him so sorely that her friend Chitralekha had crossed the sky to Dwaraka, received the sage Narada's blessing and his Tamasika learning, and stolen the sleeping prince out of his own palace. Chitralekha had found him where the moon sits among stars — surrounded by the most beautiful women of his court, wine in his hand and his mind far away — and she had known at once that his heart was busy with the dream. She had spoken to him of Usha: how the maiden wept, and yawned, and sighed, for she could not see him; how she would live if he came to her, and die in his absence. Then, by the power of her illusion, she had carried him through the sky to Sonitpura, to a maiden's rooms where Usha was waiting.

Now the dream had a body. In the women's quarters of the city, Usha lived with Aniruddha as a bride with her husband, and for a little while the city of the thousand-armed king kept its secret.

But no secret survives long among the watchful. Word reached Bana that his daughter was living with a Yadava prince, Pradyumna's son, who had come unbidden into his house and into his daughter's chambers. The king did not go himself, and he did not ask questions. He sent his soldiers — the Daityas and the Danavas of his host — with a single order: kill the intruder.

They found Aniruddha at ease, and they paid for the surprise. The young prince seized a dreadful parigha, a great iron club, and fell upon them. He killed the Daityas who pressed closest, and then, single-handed, he drove the whole Danava host from the field. The soldiers of Sonitpura broke and scattered before one man, as though the city had sent its army against a single storm.

When the field was empty, Aniruddha stood among the fallen, raised his voice in delight, and set up a leonine shout — the long cry of a victor who has enjoyed his fight — that rang across the rooftops of Sonitpura.

The shout carried into the king's palace, and Bana understood what his soldiers could not do. But the king of a thousand arms had other instruments than an army, and before long the Yadava prince would find himself a prisoner in the city he had just emptied of its host.
stories.reflection: Aniruddha, brought to Sonitpura by illusion and dream, meets his first trial with an iron club and open force. The story keeps him young — few words, quick action, and a shout of pure delight when the field is his — which makes the coming imprisonment all the sharper a turn.
stories.content_note: Mild battle violence: Aniruddha kills Daityas with an iron club and drives the demon host from the field; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Vana had another answer than soldiers, and in his prison the prince would find himself bound by nooses of serpents.

stories.title: The Goddess Cuts the Serpent-Noose
stories.story:
In the dark of Bana's prison, the young man who had routed an army had nothing left but his voice.

He had come to Sonitpura in the night, stolen from Dwaraka by illusion to marry a princess he had only ever seen in a dream — and the dream had kept its promise for a little while. Usha had chosen him by the boon of a goddess, her friend Chitralekha had carried him across the sky in secret, and for a few days the two had lived together as husband and wife in the women's quarters of the city. But when Bana, Bali's son, learned that his daughter was living with the Yadava prince, he had answered the leonine shout in the only way left to him: he seized Aniruddha and threw him into chains, there in his own city, together with Usha, who would not be parted from him. The hero of the field was now a prisoner, held by a strong noose of serpents, his strength useless and his club far away.

And it was there, in that darkness, that Aniruddha did the one thing left to him: he sought refuge with the goddess Kaumari, the maiden goddess, and sang her a hymn.

It was a careful song, and a knowing one. Saluting the endless, undecaying, eternal prime deity, the Lord Narayana, he chanted the glories of Chandi — the worshipful goddess Katyayani, whom all the gods and all the worlds worship, whom the gods, the rishis and the rakshasas alike adore, singing the very names that Hari sings. For his own well-being he bowed to her, the sister of Indra and of Vishnu, she who bestows honour and answers the prayers of her devotees. Cleansed and with a purified mind, his hands folded, he asked one thing only: “Release me from my bonds, and give me life and health.”

The goddess, fond of her votaries, heard him. Durga herself came to the place where Aniruddha lay in chains. She appeared before the young hero in the gloom of the cell, and consoled him; he saluted her, and then — with her own fingers, as easily as a mother loosens a knot — she cut the strong noose of serpents that held him.

And then she spoke. “O Aniruddha, wait here for a few days more. The holder of the discus, the slayer of the Daityas, will cut off the thousand arms of Vana, release you from your fetters, and take you to his own city.”

She did not carry him out of the prison. She cut his bonds, gave him a promise, and left him with something stronger than freedom: the certainty of rescue. Aniruddha waited — and across the sky, already flying toward Sonitpura on Garuda's back, came Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna to make the goddess's words good.
stories.reflection: The hymn is a prisoner's prayer that calls the goddess by her family — sister of Indra and of Vishnu — as though asking kin to remember one of their own. And Durga's answer is exact: she frees Aniruddha from despair, not from the prison, because Krishna's arrival is what will set him truly free.
stories.next_story_tease: The goddess's promise pointed one way: across the sky, Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna were already flying to Sonitpura on Garuda.
stories.hero_scene: In the shadowy prison of Sonitpura, the great goddess Durga bends over the chained Aniruddha and, with her own fingers, cuts the strong noose of serpents that binds him, light breaking around her in the dark cell.

stories.title: Garuda Bears Them to Bana's City
stories.story:
The city of Dwaraka sent its warriors to war with music. Conch-shells and bugles sounded, bards sang the praises of the heroes, and crowds shouted blessings for victory as Krishna made ready to leave. Aniruddha, his grandson, the young son of Pradyumna, had been carried off to the city of the demon Bana and lay captive there, and the Yadava chiefs had resolved to bring him home.

But when it was time to go, Krishna did not call for chariots or mustering armies. He thought of Garuda in his mind, and the great bird was there at once, wings folded, waiting. The son of Vinata rose into the sky, and his beauty, touched by the radiance of the one who rode him, became immense.

That day Krishna chose to go to war as a god goes, not as a man. Desiring to kill Bana, he assumed a form with eight arms, towering like a mountain, crowned with innumerable heads. In his four right hands he carried the sword, the discus, the club and arrows; in his left hands, the shield, the Sharanga bow, the thunderbolt and the conch. Behind him on Garuda's back sat Balarama, holding a thousand forms, white-armed and white-weaponed, shining like the rising moon over Mount Kailasa. And Pradyumna, eager to display his prowess in battle, had taken a form radiant as the sage Sanatkumara.

Then Garuda flew. The beating of his wings shook innumerable mountains and checked the very course of the wind. With the speed of the mind he crossed the sacred path of the Siddhas and Charanas, the sky itself seeming to part before him.

Halfway across the world, Balarama looked down at his own arms and frowned. "Krishna," he said, "what wonder is this? We have all on a sudden lost our radiance. We have turned golden, every one of us. What is the cause? Have we come to the side of Mount Sumeru?"

Krishna smiled. "I think Bana's city is near at hand. To protect it, a fire is blazing out of the city, and its glow has fallen on us. The effulgence of that fire of oblation has changed our colour."

"Then if approaching Bana's city costs us the lustre of our bodies," said Balarama, "do what you think proper afterwards."

Krishna turned to Garuda. "Son of Vinata, do what you think proper. When you have found a way, I will do what is proper."

So Garuda, who could take any form he wished, assumed a thousand mouths. He leaped up to the celestial Ganga, the river of heaven, drank deep of its water, and came back showering it down upon the fire. The blazing guardian of the city hissed and died out. Even Garuda was astonished at its power. "How strong is this fire," he said, "like the fire at the end of an age. It changed the colour of even Krishna himself."

And then the servants of that fire came out against them. The fire-gods, followers of Rudra, saw three dreadful men of many forms riding on a giant bird, and asked one another who they were and why they had come. They could not settle the matter, and so they attacked. A great uproar rose as the fire-gods and their armies fell upon the three Yadus.

Their chief, the fire-god Angira, ascended a blazing chariot and lifted his mace, burning bright in the middle of the field. Krishna, angered, smiled again and again. "Fire-gods," he called to them, "wait patiently a few moments. The time of your destruction is drawing near. Within a moment, consumed by the energy of my weapons, you will fly away on all sides."

But Angira rushed at him with a burning trident, as if to take his life. Krishna cut down his mace with crescent-shaped arrows and struck him in the breast with an arrow like death itself. Angira fell, bathed in blood. And the other fire-gods, the sons of Brahma and their hosts, fled headlong toward Bana's city.

The sky fell quiet again. Far ahead, over the edge of the world, the towers of Sonitpura rose into view, the city where Aniruddha lay bound and waiting to be rescued. Garuda gathered his wings for the descent, and the three riders of the sky looked down at the city of the demon king.
stories.reflection: Krishna's eight arms and countless heads are described matter-of-factly, as equipment for the journey rather than spectacle: the divine form is not an ornament but a readiness. The golden stain of the city's fire is a stranger touch still, the protectors of the world themselves marked by what they approach.
stories.next_story_tease: Even as Garuda flew, Dwaraka had fallen into mourning for its vanished prince.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, eight-armed and crowned with innumerable heads, seated on Garuda's back high above the clouds — Balarama radiant with white weapons behind him and Pradyumna beside — while Garuda's vast wings shake the mountains below and the towers of Bana's city glimmer far ahead.

stories.title: Where Has Aniruddha Gone?
stories.story:
The weeping began in Aniruddha's palace and did not stop. His wives and their companions cried in his empty rooms, like ewes crying for a lost lamb. "Even under the protection of Krishna," they said, "we are weeping, stricken with fear and grief. He under the shade of whose arms the gods themselves live without anxiety, in the celestial region — his heroic grandson has been carried off. Who has stolen him away? Whoever has excited this unbearable fire of Vasudeva's anger has no fear in this world, and yet he stands before the open teeth of Death. Our husband is gone; on account of this separation we are brought under the sway of death itself."

Their cries rose over the palace like the noise of thousands of ospreys crying in the sky, and the whole city heard. The Yadu chiefs rushed out of their houses as lions rush from their caves when assailed. "Krishna protects us completely," they said. "Whence is this fear, then? Why is such a noise heard in Aniruddha's house?" The great bugle of Krishna's court was brought and sounded, and at its call the Yadavas assembled. They asked one another what had happened, and answered one another with the little they had heard. The eyes of those dreadful warriors, reddened with anger, filled with tears; they sat and sighed, helpless.

Only one of them spoke. Viprithu looked at Krishna, who sat sighing again and again, and said: "Krishna, foremost of men, why are you possessed by anxiety? The Yadavas range freely at large under the protection of your arms. Leaving the charge of success and defeat to you, even mighty Indra sleeps happily. But your kinsmen are sunk in an unfathomable ocean of grief. Save them. What is the cause of your anxiety? Why do you not speak? You should not indulge in such idle thoughts."

Krishna sighed for a long time before he answered. "Viprithu, I have been anxiously thinking about this. Even thinking, I have not been able to settle anything — that is why I could not reply to you although you asked. Hear the truth of why I am filled with anxiety. Because of the captivity of the heroic Aniruddha, all the kings of the earth and my own friends will consider me incapable. Formerly our king Ahuka was taken captive by Shalwa, and we brought him back after a dreadful fight. Rukmini's son Pradyumna was stolen away by Shamvara in his infancy, and he, having slain his captor in battle, came home. But where has Aniruddha been exiled? I do not recollect that I ever felt such sorrow and mental agony before. And I will kill in battle, with all his people, the one who has set an ash-covered foot upon my head."

Then Satyaki spoke: "Krishna, despatch spies in every direction to find Aniruddha. Let them search the earth with its mountains and forests. Let open and secret emissaries be engaged in this work."

King Ahuka heard, and acted at once. He ordered messengers out to find Aniruddha. "Search out all the countries lying on and under the earth," he said, and he gave them horses and chariots. "Go soon on horseback. Search the mountains Rikshavan and Raivataka, covered with trees and creepers. Enter the gardens and forests without hesitation; search every creek and corner. Riding on horses and elephants, find Aniruddha, the joy of the Yadavas."

They went. They searched the mountains and the forests, the cities and the hidden places, the countries above and below the earth. And they came home with nothing. "We saw Aniruddha nowhere," the messengers said. The hall of Dwaraka fell silent again, heavier than before. The search was over; the waiting had begun.
stories.reflection: Krishna's grief here is entirely human and undecorated: he admits he cannot settle his own mind and that he has never felt such sorrow. The passage is striking because the protector of the world does not stand above his family's anguish — he sits in the middle of it, sighing like everyone else.
stories.next_story_tease: The answer would come not from the search parties, but from a visitor descending from the sky.
stories.hero_scene: The great hall of Dwaraka at dusk: the Yadava chiefs gathered in silence, their eyes red with anger and tears, while Krishna sits apart, sighing again and again, the whole city's grief resting on one bowed figure.

stories.title: Narada Brings News of Aniruddha
stories.story:
The search parties had come home empty-handed, and the great hall of Dwaraka had settled into a gloom that no one knew how to break. The messengers had searched the mountains and the forests, the cities and the hidden places, and they had said the only words they had: "We saw Aniruddha nowhere." The Yadavas asked one another the same question again and again — where was Aniruddha? — and had no answer. Then, without warning, there was an answer in the room.

Narada had arrived. The sage who wandered through all the worlds, carrying news from every court, stood before Krishna, and the assembly fell silent, because Narada always knew what others did not.

He told them what he had seen. In the city of the demon Bana, king of Sonitpura, there lived a daughter named Usha. For her sake, said the sage, the apsara Chitralekha — the enchantress of the celestial dancers, skilled in the arts of illusion — had carried off Aniruddha and brought him to the demon's city. That was the theft: not a raid of enemies, not an ambush on the road, but a girl's longing and a sorceress's art, reaching into Dwaraka itself and taking the prince away.

And Bana? When the king of Sonitpura learned that the grandson of Krishna lay in his city, he had the young man fettered with serpent-shafts, nooses strong enough to hold even a warrior, and kept him prisoner there. The Yadavas knew the king's name, and they knew his city, ringed with a guardian fire and guarded by the armies of the demons who served him. The prince who had disappeared from the middle of Dwaraka lay in the heart of the enemy's stronghold.

But there was one word in Narada's report that changed everything: Aniruddha was not deprived of life. The prince was bound, but he was alive. The serpent-nooses had not taken his breath; Bana's rage had not yet reached the point of killing him. The name of the city, the name of the demon, and the certain knowledge that the boy still breathed — the news passed through the hall like water poured on a burning house. The wives who had wept in the palace, crying that even under Krishna's protection they were lost, heard that their lord still lived. Where there had been only helpless grief, there was now a place, a name, and a hope.

Krishna heard the sage out, and the anxiety that had weighed on the court for days had somewhere to go at last. The Yadavas had searched the mountains and the forests and found nothing; Narada had walked into the palace and handed them the whole truth. Where Aniruddha was, who had taken him, and that he still lived — it was enough. Grief, when it knows where to point, becomes resolve.

Dwaraka turned its face toward Sonitpura, the distant city of the demon king, where a bound prince still breathed in his chains and waited to be brought home.
stories.reflection: Narada's gift here is not prophecy but eyewitness: he has seen with his own eyes what an army of messengers could not find. The small, precise fact that Aniruddha is not deprived of life carries the whole story — hope in this telling is not grand, but exact and practical.
stories.next_story_tease: At the gates of Sonitpura, the war-god himself would be waiting to meet them.
stories.hero_scene: The great hall of Dwaraka: the sage Narada standing before the seated Krishna, the assembled Yadavas leaning in to listen, as the gloom of the court lifts with the news that Aniruddha is still alive.

stories.title: The Discus That Blotted Out the Brahmashira
stories.story:
The war for Aniruddha had reached its strangest hour. Shiva himself — Rudra, the great god — had come to Bana's aid that day, fought against the Yadavas, and then withdrawn from the field. And now another god took his place. Kartikeya, the war-god, mounted on the chariot brought for him by the minister Kumbhanda, drove straight at Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful, sharpened arrows. Bathed in blood, the three Yadus fought back like three fires against the wind.

They struck Kartikeya with the three weapons given to them by the wind-god, the fire-god and Indra. He countered each with three weapons of his own — Shaila, Varuna and Savitri. But the Yadus, by their power of illusion, devoured every weapon the burning god hurled at them. Nothing he shot could touch them.

Then Kartikeya, blazing with rage and biting his lips, took up the dreadfullest of his arms: the Brahmashira, the head of Brahma, like the Destroyer himself. When he discharged it, the weapon blazed with the effulgence of a thousand suns, destructive of the world. Creatures lost consciousness through its warmth and fled on every side; the whole universe bewailed.

But Krishna, the slayer of Keshi, took up his discus, the weapon that destroys and counteracts all weapons. As clouds in the rainy season cover the rays of the sun, so that discus covered, with its lustre, the lustre of the Brahmashira. The world-destroying weapon was shorn of its light, its power, its energy, and hung harmless in the sky.

Kartikeya's rage blazed higher, like fire into which clarified butter is poured. He seized a dreadful golden spear, the Sakti — sure of aim, set with bells, glowing like a fire-brand, like the fire of dissolution — and with a shout that struck terror into his enemies he hurled it at Krishna. The spear rose into the sky, yawned wide, and circled above the field, as if searching for the heart of the one it was meant to kill. The watching gods despaired. "Perhaps Krishna will be consumed," they said.

Then the spear came down before him. Krishna shouted, a shout like a remonstrance, and struck it out of the air to the ground. "Well done! Well done!" rose from every side of the field. Indra and the celestials sent up a leonine roar.

Krishna lifted his discus again, to end the war with the god. But at that moment, at the mandate of Shiva, the goddess Kottavi appeared before Kartikeya, naked, shielding him with her body; the eighth portion of the goddess, Lamva, stood between them like a golden spear. Krishna stayed his hand. "Shame on you," he said. "Fly away from this place. Why do you throw obstacles in the way of certain destruction?" But the goddess would not cover herself, and would not move. "Take Kartikeya and fly away from the battlefield," Krishna said. "It will be well for us today if you do this. Or else, if I refrain from fighting, he will fight me." And the lord of Dwaraka put away his discus.

The goddess led the war-god from the field and brought him before Shiva, protected. And now the king of the demons came forward. When Bana saw Kartikeya released from Krishna's discus and retiring from the battle, he felt an inclination to fight Madhava himself. His priests chanted blessings over him, recited the mantras, and performed ceremonies of victory with herbs and sacred utterance, while the great demon commanders gathered around their king; and Bana marched out to meet the lord of Dwaraka.

Krishna, who had set aside his discus rather than strike through a goddess, turned to face the demon king, and the sky over Sonitpura darkened with the gathering of armies.
stories.reflection: Kartikeya's weapons do not fail by force but by absorption: the Yadus devour his shafts, and the discus covers the Brahmashira's light as cloud covers the sun. Power here is answered not with greater power but with a stillness that swallows it. And the duel ends not in slaughter but in deference — Krishna sets down his discus rather than strike through a goddess standing in the way.
stories.next_story_tease: But the war would end not in Bana's ruin, but in a wedding for the captive prince.

stories.title: A Kingdom for Kumbhanda
stories.subtitle: Aniruddha and Usha are wed as Bana's realm finds a new king
stories.story:
The war for Aniruddha was over, and the victors were doing something unusual with the conquered city: they were turning the enemy king's palace into a wedding hall.

Krishna had come to Sonitpura to bring home his grandson, carried off from Dwaraka in the night and bound in the women's quarters of the demon king Bana with nooses of living serpents. The campaign had ended strangely. Shiva himself had fought beside Bana and then withdrawn; Bana had been spared and honored with boons, and had departed in the company of the god who blessed him. Only one thing still weighed on Krishna: the boy he had come to save. He asked Narada again and again where Aniruddha lay, his mind overpowered with affection, and each time the sage answered that the prince was bound with serpent-nooses in the palace's inner apartments.

It was Chitralekha who opened the way, telling them plainly that this was the women's apartment of Bana. Krishna, Balarama, Pradyumna, Narada and Garuda stepped inside, and the rescue required no battle at all. At the sight of Garuda, the serpents clinging to Aniruddha's body in the shape of arrows released him at once and dropped to the floor as spent shafts. The prince, overjoyed, saluted Krishna, bowed to Balarama and to Garuda, and then approached his own father Pradyumna. Beside him Usha, encircled by her friends, saluted Krishna and the great bird, and with shyness bowed to Pradyumna as well.

Narada, smiling, showered blessings on the reunion and hailed Krishna's good fortune at being united again with Pradyumna and Aniruddha. Then the sage made a request that drew laughter from all the Yadavas: let a marriage won by prowess be celebrated for Aniruddha, he said, for he had a great desire to see the exchange of jokes between the bridegroom's party and the bride's. Krishna answered that it would soon be accomplished.

At that moment Kumbhanda arrived, carrying all the articles for a wedding, and bowed before Krishna asking for safety. He was Bana's minister, the man who had counselled mercy toward Aniruddha in the war, and Narada had quietly asked Krishna to keep him from leaving. Krishna raised him and promised him protection, saying he had been pleased by his good deeds: "You will now become the king of this kingdom. I confer this kingdom on you. Live forever under my protection, happy and self-controlled, with all your kinsmen."

Then Krishna celebrated the wedding of Aniruddha, and the regent of fire himself stood present in person at that festival. Aniruddha bathed and was adorned with ornaments, and the Apsaras cut jokes with him; the Gandharvas sang melodious, auspicious songs, and the Apsaras danced, beautifying the marriage party.

When the rites were done, Krishna honored Rudra, the giver of boons, and made ready to depart for Dwaraka with the celestials. But Kumbhanda, the new king, came forward with folded hands and offered a parting word: Bana, he said, had cows in the charge of Varuna whose milk was nectar; a man who drank it became powerful and invincible in battle. Krishna's mind filled with joy at the news, and he set the errand in his heart.

The company turned homeward. Brahma blessed Krishna and departed for his own region; Indra and the Maruts set out for Dwaraka; Usha, surrounded by her friends, started for the city of the Yadus as well. Balarama, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha mounted Garuda's back, and the foremost of birds flew on, uprooting trees and shaking the earth with the beating of his wings, carrying the rescued family and a new bride toward the city that had waited for them in anxiety.
stories.reflection: The episode rewards mercy rather than valor: the minister who counselled sparing Aniruddha receives the kingdom of the king who would not listen to him, and the war that began in a kidnapping ends in a wedding. Narada's request to hear the two families trade jests keeps the divine machinery human-sized.
stories.next_story_tease: The journey home would end in Dwaraka, where a festival was already being readied to receive the Yadu family's newest daughter-in-law.
stories.hero_scene: In the palace of Sonitpura, Krishna, one hand raised in assurance, confers Bana's kingdom on the folded-handed minister Kumbhanda, while behind them the wedding lights of Aniruddha and Usha blaze and the Apsaras dance.
