stories.title: When Balarama Came Home to Vraja
stories.story:
He went alone, and he went with Krishna's blessing, and for the first time in years Balarama took the road to Vraja by himself.

Since the two brothers had ridden out of the cowherd village — first to Mathura, then to the golden city of Dwaraka on the sea — the seasons had turned many times. The village had not forgotten them, and the news that Balarama was coming ran ahead of him like fire in dry grass. By the time he reached the cow-pens, the gopas and gopis had gathered, and they came at him all at once: the old cowherds pressing forward to embrace him, the women laughing and weeping at the same time, hands reaching for his arms as if they could not quite believe the sight.

The elders who had watched him grow up spoke first. Welcome, they said, you whom we raised among us. We have heard of your deeds — how you met the great fish Panchajana in the ocean and destroyed it; how you fought Jarasandha and the kings with him at Gomanta; how you entered Mathura, and the earth itself was steadied by it. Every tale that had reached the village, they laid before him like offerings.

Balarama answered them with something better than a list of victories. "You are dearer to us than our own kin," he told the cowherds. "We were reared in your houses. We took our meals with you and tended the cattle beside you. We spent our boyhood sporting on these very grounds. Whatever we are, we became here, among you. You are our firm friends."

Then the gopis came forward, and all their questions were of one person. Does Krishna remember his father? they asked. Does he remember his mother — the mother who held him as a child? Does he remember his friends, the boys he played with, the women who sang for him? Their voices were half teasing and half raw. He left us so suddenly, they said, cutting the thread of friendship as if it had never been woven. How do the wise ladies of Dwaraka trust the words of one so quick to charm and so quick to leave? And yet even as they spoke they could not bear to hear of anything else — when one of them tried to turn the talk to other things, the rest cried out: what other stories can we hear, when our hearts are still with him?

Balarama listened to it all, and then he gave them what they truly wanted. He carried Krishna's messages in his own heart, all the way from Dwaraka — and the words he spoke for his brother went straight to the gopis' hearts. The village learned that Krishna remembered everything: the father who had raised him, the mother who had loved him, the friends of his boyhood, the nights of song by the Yamuna. He had not forgotten; the distance was not of his choosing; the love was kept, as surely as they had kept it.

And then Balarama stayed. For two months he remained in Vraja, through the spring months of Madhu and Madhava. He sported with the gopis in the groves of the Yamuna; the days passed in play and song, and the nights in the light of the full moon, with the wind carrying the scent of flowers through the trees. For two months, Vraja had its prince back, and the women who had pined for Krishna learned that his brother carried his heart in his words. When at last the time came to leave, there was not a house in the village that did not stand at its door to watch him go.
stories.reflection: The gopis' question — does Krishna remember us? — is answered not with assurances but with messages carried in a brother's heart, and with two months of staying. Balarama's visit heals the wound of the departure not by explaining it but by showing that the love survived the distance.
stories.next_story_tease: But one night in those two months, Balarama would summon the Yamuna herself — and the river would learn what it cost to refuse him.

stories.title: The Night the Yamuna Was Dragged
stories.story:
The wine came to him from a tree.

It happened during the two months Balarama had come to spend in Vraja, in the groves along the Yamuna. Deep in the forest where he was sporting with the gopis, the goddess Varuni — sent by Varuna, the lord of the waters — flowed out of the hollow of an old tree. The fragrance of that honey-stream rode the wind to where the cowherds sat, and Balarama, who had never needed an excuse for joy, drank. Around him the gandharvas sang; overhead the sky sounded with drums, and flowers rained down on the grove. The evening had turned to gold.

By the time the moon rose, the wine had done its work, and the whole grove seemed brighter for it. Balarama wore a single earring and a garland of wildflowers; his blue cloth hung loose about him; his eyes rolled with pleasure, and the women sang his deeds back to him as he laughed among them. He was, the cowherds said, like the moon in an autumn night — all light and play.

Then he turned to the river. The Yamuna ran broad and dark through the groves, and Balarama, standing at her bank, called to her by name. He spoke to her as a man speaks to a woman he desires — "O great river, you who flow to the ocean, come in your bodily form, and let us sport together in your waters."

The river kept her silence. Perhaps she thought the words were only the wine speaking; perhaps a river that had flowed to the sea since the beginning of the world did not know how to answer a summons. He called again — "Will you not come? Will you not come?" — and when the Yamuna still gave no answer, the mood of the evening changed.

The joy in Balarama's face did not fade slowly; it simply went out, and in its place came the wrath of the plough-bearer. He seized his great plough and drove its point into the river's bank, and he dragged. The earth groaned. The bank tore open. The water, wrenched from its ancient course, followed the plough like a woman dragged by the hand — currents tangling, fish and water-creatures flung about in bewilderment, the white geese scattering in panic. The river that had chosen its own path since the beginning of time now flowed where Balarama chose.

And the Yamuna, afraid at last, begged his pardon. "Rama, Rama, mighty-armed," she said, "I did not know your valour. Forgive me — forgive the river that did not know the glory of the Blessed One."

Her words went into him like water into dry ground. His anger was gone as quickly as it had come. He released her. He stepped into her waters, bathed, and sported as he had first asked to do, at his ease in the current, and the night settled back into its old peace. The gopis and cowherds on the bank, who had watched with their hearts in their mouths, let out their breath at last. When he came out he put on blue garments and a golden garland, and the river lay quiet and restored along her course.

Long afterward, the cowherds of Vraja would point to the path where the river had been dragged — the scar in the land, the channel pulled from its old course — and say: there. That is where the Yamuna learned Balarama's name.

And of the night itself, the only thing anyone could say was this: it passed like a single moment, as all nights pass in Vraja when the heart is full.
stories.reflection: The river is dragged not out of cruelty but out of a drunkard's insistence on being answered, and the moment she names his power he lets her go. Even the wrath of the plough-bearer turns out to be a form of play — he wanted her company, and once she gave him her fear and her pardon, he was satisfied.
stories.next_story_tease: Far from the Yamuna's banks, meanwhile, a raging ape was laying waste to the land in the name of his slain friend.

stories.title: The Ape Who Avenged Narakasura
stories.story:
When Narakasura fell to Krishna's discus, he left behind a friend who would not let the world forget it.

Dvivida was an ape of the mountains, vast and powerful, and he had loved the slain demon king like a brother. Where Narakasura's other allies made their peace or hid themselves, Dvivida chose vengeance — and he had the strength to make vengeance terrible. He would repay his friend's death, he swore, with the ruin of everything Krishna loved. He was not a demon of the cities, who plots in shadows; he was a force of the wild, and he struck in the open, where everyone could see and no one could stop him.

The land he chose to punish was Anarta, the country of the Yadavas. And he began.

He set fire to the cities and the villages, and watched the flames climb. He went to the mountains and tore them up by their roots, and hurled them down upon the regions below, crushing whatever lay beneath. He waded into the middle of the ocean and stood there, scooped up the sea with his two arms, and flung it over the coastal lands until the shore drowned. The hermitages of the sages — the quiet places where holy men kept their fires and their vows — he tore apart, breaking their trees and scattering their offerings, defiling the sacred fires themselves, and the holy men were driven from the places they had kept for a lifetime. He seized men and women and hurled them into the caves of the mountains. He laid waste to the whole country, and the women of good families learned to fear the shadow of the ape.

The terror had a shape and a name. Farmers abandoned their fields; villages emptied at the first cry of alarm; the roads filled with people walking with everything they owned on their heads, not knowing which direction would be far enough. No army could catch him. He moved like a storm, and like a storm he was gone before the dust settled, leaving behind only smoke, torn earth, and the sea lying where the land had been.

For the ape, it was a kind of joy. Every village that burned was a stone laid on Narakasura's pyre; every hermitage broken was a blow struck for his friend. He was doing what the dead king would have wanted, and he meant to keep doing it until there was nothing left of Anarta to save.

And then, one day, in the middle of the country he had made his own, Dvivida came upon a sight he had not expected. Standing in the ruin — quiet, unhurried, a garland of lotuses around his neck — was the lord of the Yadavas himself. Not the one who had slain his friend. The other one. Balarama, the plough-bearer, the strongest arms in the world, come to see what had been done to his people's land.

The ape stopped. Behind him the fires still burned. His hands, which had torn up mountains, hung at his sides. The garland of lotuses swayed as Balarama stood his ground — and for the first time since Narakasura died, Dvivida looked at a man and did not see prey. For a long moment neither of them moved; only the smoke of the burning passed between them. Then the ape showed his teeth, not in fear but in the joy of a fighter who has finally found an opponent. Every creature in the country that still breathed held still, because everyone knew that the rampage had just met its reckoning.
stories.reflection: Dvivida's destruction is terrible precisely because it is faithful: he is repaying a friendship, and every act of ruin is, in his own mind, an act of love for the dead. The story sets revenge and ruin against the quiet arrival of Balarama, and the whole country holds its breath at the meeting.
stories.content_note: The ape Dvivida ravages the land: villages burn, mountains are hurled down on regions, coastal lands are flooded, and villagers are seized and assaulted. The destruction is described with restraint, but may warrant parental awareness for younger listeners.
stories.next_story_tease: The ape and the plough-bearer were about to settle everything between them.
stories.hero_scene: In the wreckage of Anarta: the vast ape Dvivida, smoke rising from burning villages behind him, faces the quiet, lotus-garlanded Balarama across the torn ground, the whole land holding its breath.

stories.title: The Ape Who Mocked Balarama
stories.story:
The hill of Raivataka had never known a stranger visitor. Balarama had brought the women of his household there for a day of ease — the wine jars open, a song on his lips, the sea breeze moving through the groves — when the leaves above him shook, a branch bent like a bow, and an ape the size of a young elephant dropped onto a limb overhead. The singing stopped.

For months this same ape had been the terror of the land. His name was Dvivida, and he had been the dearest friend of Narakasura, the demon king whom Krishna had slain; in his grief and fury he had sworn to make the whole world pay for his friend's death. He had interrupted the sacrifices and subverted the rites. He had set fire to forests, villages and towns. He had hurled rocks down upon cities, lifted up mountains and cast them into the ocean, and churned the sea until it rose over its bounds and swept away the settlements on its shores. He could change his shape at will, and he had enlarged himself until he could walk through the standing corn like a man walking through grass, crushing the harvests beneath him. The whole land, disordered by this maddened ape, had lost its peace and its sacred study. And now he had followed the Yadavas to their pleasure hill.

He did not come to fight. He came to mock. Rocking on his branch, he grinned at Balarama, rolled his eyes at the young women, flicked his brows and pulled faces at them until they drew back, half offended and half afraid. Balarama, whose head was light with the wine they called varuni, felt the anger rise, hot and sudden. He seized a stone and hurled it.

The ape caught it out of the air — and laughed.

That laugh was the turning of the day, though neither of them knew it yet. Mocked again, and worse than before, Balarama rose to his feet and took up his mace and his plough, the two weapons that had been with him since the pastures of Vrindavan. The ape, drunk on his own daring, struck at Balarama's head. The blow fell as harmlessly as red chalk flung at a mountain. And Balarama answered — with his mace, blow after blow, until the ape's great body was broken in a hundred places.

Still the beast came on. He tore up trees and rocks and hurled them in a blind rain that fell harmlessly around the plough-bearer. And Balarama, disgusted at last, cast aside his weapons and seized the ape with his bare arms, like a man taking hold of a storm. What followed was not a duel but a settling. The ape's arms, thick as palm trunks, beat uselessly against that grip. When Balarama brought him down, the earth herself shuddered — the mountains trembled, the forests swayed, as if the ground knew what had been lifted from it. The ape lay felled, vomiting blood, and did not rise again.

In the sky, voices shouted victory and homage; the gods rained flowers on the hill.

The women came out of the groves, and the songs began again, quieter than before. And down in the country, in the villages Dvivida had burned, the smoke that rose was only cooking smoke once more. The sea returned to its bed. The harvests stood. The land, which for months had lived in the shadow of a maddened animal, remembered how to be a land again.

They said afterward that the hill of Raivataka carried a scar where the great ape had fallen. But hills heal, as countries do — and the memory of that afternoon stayed longer with the Yadavas than the scar did: the day their lord, who could have been king of all the earth, stood in a grove with his mace laid by, and finished with his bare hands what no army had been able to finish in a year.
stories.reflection: Dvivida's end comes not from a weapon Balarama keeps ready but from the strength he has never needed to display: the mace and plough are laid aside before the ape is seized with bare hands. The land is freed not by armies but by one man's patience finally spent — and the hill keeps the scar, though the peace outlasts it.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells the same duel differently: there Dvivida first steals Balarama's plough and club and breaks the wine cups, and Balarama fells him with a single blow of the fist on the forehead. This account follows the Bhagavata Purana, where the ape is struck down with mace and plough and finally seized with bare arms.
stories.content_note: Mild violence — a demon-ape is slain in combat; not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the season turned, Balarama would ride out again — this time to a city that answered courtesy with insult.
stories.hero_scene: On Raivataka hill, Balarama — mace and plough cast aside — seizes the towering ape Dvivida with his bare arms and brings him crashing to earth as the hill trembles, the women of the household watching from the grove, flowers raining from a sky ringing with victory cries.

stories.title: An Envoy Answered with Mockery
stories.story:
Balarama came to Hastinapura as a peacemaker, and for a few hours it looked as though the peace would hold.

Samba, a prince of the Yadava house, lay in a Kaurava dungeon. The young warriors of Dwaraka had already strapped on their armor and were clamoring for war; Balarama had quieted them with a single word. He would go himself, he said, and bring the boy home with courtesy. Counselors like Uddhava urged restraint and the warriors urged steel, but it was Balarama who settled it: he set out alone, in a chariot radiant as the sun, and when he reached the city of the elephants he did not ride through its gates in pride. He stopped in the outer grove and sent word that he had come.

The elders came out to meet him — Dhritarashtra, son of Ambika; Bhishma; Drona; Bahlika. They were plainly glad to see him. They received him with the cow of welcome and the water of honor, and they asked after the welfare of his kinsmen, as kinsmen ask after kinsmen. Everything, so far, was grace.

Balarama delivered his errand simply. Ugrasena, king of the Yadavas, had sent him. The Kurus held one of their princes captive — seized, as the Yadavas saw it, unjustly, seized by many against one — and the Yadava king asked only that Samba be released. It was a modest request, made in a modest voice, and it was met with laughter.

Duryodhana and his brothers answered for the Kurus. The Yadavas, they said, were cowherds who had climbed above their station. Bound to the Kurus by marriage, eating at their tables, sleeping under their roofs — and now sending envoys and making demands, as if the royal insignia they had taken up were theirs by right rather than by gift. "Enough of the Yadavas' kingship," they said. "These claims fit you the way nectar fits a serpent." And even if the Yadavas took offense — what then? The Kurus named their own champions, Bhishma, Drona, Arjuna, and asked, laughing, whether even Indra, the king of the gods, could stand against them while such men stood on the field. No, they said. Samba stays.

The words were not addressed to Balarama. They were spoken about him, and past him, as though he were already gone.

Balarama heard it all. He saw the wickedness of the Kurus laid bare — their pride running in a dozen different directions, none of them toward peace — and he understood, with a sudden clarity, that these men would never release Samba for any courtesy, because they had no idea whom they were insulting. They mocked the house of Ugrasena, the Yadava king, before whose seat fortune herself waited, upon whose feet the guardians of the world set their crowns. "The Vrishnis eat land given by the Kurus!" they jeered. And Balarama looked at them, and thought: alas for the pride of men mad with wealth, stumbling like drunkards down a road they cannot see.

But he said nothing of it. He had come with open hands, and he would not answer mockery with steel — not here, not yet. He rose, and the laughter died in the hall, and the elders watched the great plough-bearer walk out past them without another word.

The chariot rolled out of the grove, and the gates of Hastinapura shut behind it on a peace that had never really begun. Behind him the mockery was already being retold with relish, in the very halls that had honored him that morning. Balarama carried one thing out of Hastinapura that day, and it did not cool on the long road home: the anger of a man who has been laughed at in front of the people he loves.
stories.reflection: The insult cuts deeper because it comes after a true welcome — the cow and the water of honor are offered before the mockery begins. The Kauravas measure the Yadavas by birth and borrowed land; Balarama measures them by a kingship they cannot see. The two sides are not even arguing about the same thing.
stories.next_story_tease: The anger he carried out of Hastinapura was not the kind that cools.

stories.title: The City Dragged Toward the Ganga
stories.story:
Hastinapura was still laughing when the earth began to groan.

Balarama had been mocked out of the city that day — mocked for the cowherds he came from, mocked for the peace he had come to make, mocked in front of elders who had welcomed him and then let the mockery stand. He had not gone far. The anger that had banked itself since morning came up at last, and his eyes went red with it. He turned back toward the city, carrying with him the one thing a city cannot withstand: a man who has stopped caring about the cost.

He drove the blade of his plough deep into the earth, beneath the very ramparts of Hastinapura. "Today," he said, "I will make the earth free of the Kauravas." And he leaned into the plough and pulled.

The city moved.

Walled and towered, gate and street and all, Hastinapura — the city of the elephant — tilted, swayed, and began to slide toward the Ganga like a boat torn loose from its mooring. Inside the walls the streets tipped, the houses groaned, and the great hall where the Yadavas had been mocked an hour before pitched like a deck. The river waited below, patient and deep, and it was plain to every soul in the city that in a few more paces Hastinapura would plunge into it like a stone into a well.

Then the gates flew open, and the Kurus came out — not in war-array, but with their families, terrified, clutching children, scrambling over one another, the great gates standing open and empty behind them. They ran to Balarama and fell at his feet and poured out their hearts: "Rama, Rama, support of all, we did not know your power. You are the one cause of creation and preservation and destruction; you yourself bear this earth upon your head, O thousand-headed one. Your anger is for the instruction of the world, not born of hatred or envy. Homage to you, soul of all beings."

Duryodhana himself came forward and yielded. Samba was brought up out of his cell, and with him Lakshmana — the bride for whose sake the whole trouble had begun — and both were placed in Balarama's keeping. Then the Kuru king, humbled as he had never been, made his peace in the coin of kings: a herd of elephants, every one of them sixty years old, and six thousand golden chariots blazing like the sun. He even asked, he who was proud of his skill with the mace, to be taken as Balarama's pupil in club-fighting; and Balarama accepted him. An odd peace, sealed between the man who had mocked and the man he had mocked, on the tilted ground of a city that had almost drowned.

Balarama accepted the gifts, released the city, and set it back upon its foundations. Then he turned for home, and in Dwaraka, in the assembly of the Yadus, among kinsmen who loved him, he told the whole tale — how he had gone for peace and been answered with pride, and how the pride had been answered with the plough.

And Hastinapura — they say its walls have leaned toward the river ever since that day, the way a man leans after a blow. The city was set back, but it never stood quite straight again. Some marks a city carries the way a body carries a scar: for as long as it stands, and it shows them to every traveler who comes up by the river, as proof of what one man with a plough could do when he was pushed past patience.
stories.reflection: What frees Samba is not the argument that failed the day before but the visible proof of what Balarama is: the city is not conquered but lifted, and the Kurus' surrender takes the form of recognition — they call his anger instruction, not vengeance. Even Duryodhana's pride finds a way to bend, becoming a pupil's humility before the very mace he had mocked.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha records that Duryodhana, after surrendering Samba, became Balarama's pupil in club-fighting; that detail is included here. The Vishnu Purana has Balarama plunge the ploughshare beneath the city's ramparts with eyes red with rage, and the city drawn toward him.
stories.next_story_tease: The plough had saved a city — but a blade of grass would soon cost its wielder more than any war.

stories.title: The Suta Who Would Not Rise
stories.story:
The talk in Dwaraka had turned to the coming war — the Kurus and the Pandavas, cousins sharpening blades against each other — and Balarama, who had no taste for what was coming, went walking.

He was a pilgrim in those days. He bathed at Prabhasa, and made his offerings to the gods, the seers and the ancestors. He visited the holy waters one after another — Prithudaka, Bindu-saras, Tritakupa, Sudarshana — and the tirthas strung along the Yamuna and the Ganga like beads on a thread. At last he came to the forest of Naimisha, where the sages were holding a long sacrifice, a satra that ran on season after season.

The sages saw him coming and rose to meet him, every one of them, like a field of grass bending to the wind. They honored him, seated him with his company, and made him welcome among them. It was then that Balarama's eyes found the one man in that whole assembly who had not risen.

He was a suta — a bard of the charioteer line, born of a mixed union — and he sat among the brahmanas on a seat of honor, unmoving. He had not stirred when Balarama arrived. He had not offered the folded hands of greeting. His name was Romaharshana, and the long sacrifice had made him great: he had been a pupil of the blessed seer Vyasa himself, and he had learned much, and he sat there full of his learning, in the seat the sages had given him, and rose for no one.

Balarama looked at him, and the anger came up like a tide. A suta — however learned, however honored — seated above the brahmanas, refusing to rise in their own sacrifice, before the very sages who had raised him. Untamed, undisciplined, vainly proud of his scholarship. Balarama spoke so that all could hear: "This is the very purpose for which I was born into this world." He bent, plucked a single blade of kusha grass from the earth, charged it with his power, and struck the suta down.

Romaharshana fell, and did not rise.

Then the cry went up — "Ha! Ha!" — a sound of grief that ran through the forest like wind through dry leaves. The sages came crowding around the fallen man, and they turned to Balarama with faces he had not expected. Not anger. Grief, and dismay. "O prince of the Yadus," they said, "we ourselves gave him this seat. It was we who raised him to the brahmana's seat; it was our gift that made him what he was. What you have done, you have done without knowledge. You have slain a brahmana. This is brahma-hatya — the killing of a brahmana — and there is no heavier sin."

Balarama stood over the man he had struck down and heard them. He had been certain — he had said so aloud, that this was the very purpose of his birth. And the sages, who had honored him to his face, told him that in that single stroke, done without knowledge, he had committed the one sin that stains even the stain-removers.

"If there is any purifier of this sin," they said, "O purifier of the worlds, tell us — and we will show you the way to it."

The forest was quiet. The long sacrifice had stopped. Balarama, who had come to Naimisha for peace and for purity, stood in the middle of it over the body of a man he had been certain it was right to kill — and heard, from the mouths of the sages, that the certainty itself had been his error.
stories.reflection: The episode keeps two judgments alive at once: Balarama sees a suta who will not rise, while the sages see a brahmana they themselves raised up. What is striking is that the slaying is called "done without knowledge" — the sin is real, yet the certainty that produced it was the error. Even the purifier of worlds can act from ignorance, and must be purified in turn.
stories.content_note: Mild violence: a man is struck dead (with a blade of grass, no gore). The episode turns on caste and honor, and the sages themselves dispute the act.
stories.next_story_tease: The sages would show him the penance for his unwitting sin — and it began with a demon who defiled their sacrifice.
stories.hero_scene: In the Naimisha forest, among the gathered sages, Balarama holds a single blade of kusha grass as the suta Romaharshana lies struck down at his feet and the sages cry out with grief around them.

stories.title: The Sages Prescribe Balarama's Penance
stories.story:
At Naimisha the grove had gone quiet. The suta Romaharshana lay where he had fallen, cut down by a blade of kusha grass in the very enclosure where he had been reciting the ancient tales, and the cry the sages had raised still hung in the air like smoke: brahma-hatya — the slaying of a brahmana. And the man who had struck the blow stood before them, waiting.

Balarama had come to the Naimisha forest as a pilgrim, and the sages were gathered there for their great sacrifice, with the suta holding the whole assembly through his recitation of the sacred lore. When the plough-bearer arrived among them, Romaharshana remained seated — failing to rise and honor the sages — and the answer had been terrible and swift: a single blade of kusha grass, and the voice that had filled the grove fell silent forever. The suta had been dear to them, a voice that had carried the ancient lore across the years, and the sages had cried out at the deed. Now the heaviest sin of the old law lay on Balarama, and every man in that grove knew its weight, for the killing of a brahmana is the sin that even the gods are said to fear.

The sages did not rage at him. They had cried out at the deed; now they drew together and spoke of atonement, as elders speak to one who has failed, and what they prescribed was no small thing. They told him of the demon Balvala, son of Ilvala, who had plagued their sacrifice for as long as any of them could remember. At every parvan — at the close of each cycle of rites, at the time of the new moon and of the full — the demon came down from the sky and rained filth and impurity upon the fire, defiling what years of penance had made pure, so that the sacrifice had to be begun again from the first offering. Year after year their rites had been broken by him, and they had been powerless to stop it. "Slay that cruel one," the sages said, "and that shall be the first part of your penance." Then they spoke the second part: for twelve months Balarama must wander through all of Bharatavarsha, the sacred land, bathing at its holy fords and washing the stain from himself in its waters, until the turning of the year had cleansed him.

Balarama heard the whole of it without flinching. He might have argued that the suta had dishonored the sages first, that respect had been broken before his blade was drawn; he said none of it. The killing had been his; the cleansing would be his as well. He stood before the sages and accepted — the slaying of the demon and the year of wandering both — and the old text is careful to say that he undertook the expiation for the benefit of the world, not only for himself.

So the penance was set, and the grove settled back toward its long rite with a new understanding: the man who had broken the silence of Naimisha would answer for it at the next parvan, when Balvala came again to rain his filth upon the fire. The sages returned to their seats. Balarama remained among them, watching the flame that the demon had defiled so many times, waiting for the season of his atonement to begin.
stories.reflection: The sages answer bloodshed not with punishment but with a task: the sin is to be washed out in action — by facing the demon who has plagued their rites, and by a year of walking the sacred land. Balarama accepts without defense or argument, and the old text says he did it for the benefit of the world; the burden, once accepted, turns outward and becomes service.
stories.next_story_tease: At the next parvan the demon would come again to defile the fire — and Balarama's penance would meet him.

stories.title: Balarama Slays the Demon Balvala
stories.story:
The morning of the parvan rose clear over Naimisha, and the sages fed their fire and offered the day's oblations as they had done a hundred times before. Then, without warning, the sky above the sacrificial hall turned dark — not with cloud, but with a shape. From that darkness a rain began to fall, hissing into the fire and soiling the offerings: a rain of filth and impurity. The demon Balvala had come again.

It was exactly what the sages had described when they set Balarama's penance. The son of Ilvala, cruel and ancient, a rover of the sky who at every parvan descended to defile their sacrifice at the very moment of its completion. For years they had endured him, powerless, watching their rites broken time and again by a hand they could not reach — the fire smothered, the offerings spoiled, the work of penance undone and begun again. And now they had in their midst the man whose penance was this demon's end. Every eye in the grove turned to Balarama, and he understood at once: this was the first half of his atonement, coming to meet him.

He saw the demon clearly — a body huge and black, like a mountain of crushed collyrium, drifting over the enclosure while the defilement rained down from him. And at the sight Balarama remembered his weapons, the plough and the mace that had torn apart the armies of the demons, and he did not wait. He raised the plough, and with its tip he caught the sky-roaming Balvala and dragged him down out of the air, and the demon fell to the earth before the fire — his forehead split, blood streaming from the wound — and Balarama finished the work with his mace, crushing his skull. The defiler of Naimisha lay still at last, and the rain of impurity stopped as suddenly as it had begun.

The grove filled with the sages' joy, and it was a joy with years of helplessness behind it. They crowded around Balarama, praising him and calling down blessings that never fail; they laid upon him the vaijayanti, the celestial garland strung with lotuses that do not fade, and gave him garments from heaven itself. The fire that had been defiled so many times burned clean and bright above the demon's body, and the sacrifice went on as it had always been meant to go on.

With the sages' leave, Balarama set out from Naimisha the next morning, walking with the brahmanas toward the river Kaushiki — the first steps of the twelve-month pilgrimage that would carry him through all the sacred fords of Bharatavarsha. The demon was dead. The penance had begun.
stories.reflection: There is a strange economy in the episode: the same hands that committed brahma-hatya at Naimisha are the hands that free the sages' sacrifice, as if the penance and the service were one act. The sages' gift of the unfading garland and their unfailing blessings suggest that in their eyes the cleansing had already begun with the deed.
stories.content_note: Demon-slaying: Balvala is dragged from the sky by the plough and his skull is crushed by the mace; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: Far away, on the slope of Govardhana hill, the king of the gods was descending to ask a favour of Krishna.

stories.title: Indra Asks Krishna to Befriend Arjuna
stories.story:
The rain that had lashed Vrindavan for seven nights had ceased, and Govardhana hill stood again in the valley where it had always stood — lifted, held, and set down by a cowherd's hand. The cattle were safe beneath it, and the village was drying in the sun. Then the sky over Govardhana opened a second time, and what descended was no storm: an elephant, vast as a cloud that holds its water, with the king of the gods upon its back.

Indra had watched the mountain rise with his own eyes, and wonder had overcome his anger. He had seen the worship offered to him set aside, and the village turn instead to the hill; he had answered with a deluge meant to break the cowherds — seven nights of rain that even gods and demons could not withstand. But the boy had held up the mountain through all of it, and the cows had sheltered and survived, and Purandara, the lord of the celestials, had felt his fury turn to awe. He desired to see this Krishna.

He left his elephant at the foot of the hill, and Airavata stood patient as a rainless cloud, the rut-juice trickling down its temples. Indra approached the boy seated at ease beneath the mountain — playing in the forest, the old text says, engaged in human actions. What he saw shook the king of heaven: the cowherd with the Srivatsa mark upon his breast, dark as a blue lotus, a crown bright as the sun above his brow, celestial earrings at his ears and a necklace of jewels on his chest; and above his head the great bird Garuda, invisible to mortal eyes, spreading his wings to shade him from the sun. The god who had come to humble a village stood before the protector of all the worlds in the guise of a milkman, and he was ashamed, and then he was glad.

He spoke with a voice deep as thunder, and he did not pretend. He had been enraged when his worship was set aside, he said, and he had sent the rain — but Krishna had put it down by his own power, in Indra's very presence, holding the weight of the mountain like a house in the sky. "Whose mind would not fill with wonder?" the king of the gods asked. "As gold is the foremost of metals, so you are the foremost of the celestials; you alone are eternal among the gods, and I see no second who could carry what you have carried." Then, standing on the green ground of Vrindavan, Indra asked something stranger than praise: he spoke of a son.

A portion of himself, he said, had been born on earth as Arjuna, the son of Pritha — Krishna's own cousin, of the same line of kings. In the coming war of the Bharatas, Arjuna would be his friend and his help in battle. "Befriend him," Indra said. "Instruct him in spiritual knowledge. Always regard him and take care of him as you take care of me."

Krishna heard him out, and his answer was simple and final: he knew Arjuna, and he would befriend him as long as he continued upon the earth.

So the king of the gods returned to heaven with his anger spent and a promise carried in his heart, and the cowherds of Vrindavan went back to their herds under a clean sky. None of them knew that on the green slope of Govardhana the friendship of the two greatest warriors of the coming age had been sealed.
stories.reflection: Indra comes down to praise, but the heart of the visit is a request — that Krishna befriend a boy he has never met. The king of heaven asks the cowherd to love his son as he himself is loved, and Krishna's flat promise, "as long as I continue upon the earth," quietly measures the whole span of the friendship that follows.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana adds that Indra first bathed Krishna with water from Airavata and installed him as Govinda, king of the cows, while the cattle poured out their milk in celebration; the Harivamsha version, followed here, moves directly from praise to the request concerning Arjuna.
stories.next_story_tease: Years later, in the amphitheatre of Panchala, a young brahmana would rise to string a bow no king could bend — and Krishna would remember the promise.

stories.title: Krishna Rejoices as Arjuna Wins Draupadi
stories.story:
In the amphitheatre of Panchala, the bow lay on its stand in the middle of the ground, and it had already beaten every king in the land. One after another the monarchs had risen, strained, and sat down again in failure; the bow would not bend for them. The target wheel turned high overhead, and through the hole in its rim a mark hung waiting for the one man in the world who could send an arrow through it.

Draupadi, the daughter of Drupada, was to be won that day by the man who could string the bow and shoot the mark, and the amphitheatre held half the kings of the earth. Rukma had failed, and Sunitha, and Vakra; Karna, the son of Radha, had failed; Duryodhana had failed; Salya, mighty among the kings, had failed. The brahmanas who had come as guests watched the royal suitors in their disappointment, and the hall was heavy with it.

Then a young man rose from among the brahmanas seated in the assembly, and a clamor went up. Some of the priests tried to stop him — how could a brahmana stripling, unpracticed in arms, string a bow that the great Kshatriyas could not? If he failed, the whole body of brahmanas would be mocked before the assembled kings. But others spoke for him: did not Rama, son of Jamadagni, defeat all the Kshatriyas? Did not the sage Agastya drink the fathomless ocean with his spiritual power? Never despise a brahmana's strength, they said, for brahmanas are strong in their own energy. Let the youth bend the bow. And the brahmanas, in their hundreds, blessed him on his way.

The young man was Arjuna, disguised as a priest — Jishnu to the watching world, the middle Pandava, possessing the complexion of Indra's banner. He walked around the bow, bent his head to Ishana, the giver of boons, and remembered Krishna. Then he took up the bow that the kings of the earth could not string — and strung it in the twinkling of an eye, he who was like the younger brother of Indra in might. He took the five arrows and shot the mark through the hole in the wheel, and the mark fell to the ground.

The sky itself applauded. The gods showered celestial flowers on the head of the slayer of foes; thousands of brahmanas waved their upper garments in joy; the musicians struck up in concert and the bards chanted his praises; and all around the hall, the kings who had failed cried out in grief and despair. Drupada, watching, was filled with joy and ready to lend his armies to the victor. In the uproar, Yudhishthira and the twins slipped quietly away to their lodging.

And Krishna, who had watched it all from among the crowd, beheld the mark fallen and Partha shining like Indra himself — and his heart filled with joy. He moved through the celebrating throng and approached the son of Kunti with a white robe and a garland of flowers, the honors of a victor, and placed them on him. No one in that hall understood the gesture; no one needed to.

Arjuna, having won Draupadi by his deed in the amphitheatre, was saluted with reverence by all the brahmanas, and soon after he left the lists, followed closely by the woman who had become his wife — while behind him the defeated kings of the earth watched the young brahmana walk out of the hall with the prize.
stories.reflection: Krishna's joy is different from the amphitheatre's roar: everyone else marvels at the feat or grieves over it, but Krishna moves through the crowd carrying a white robe and a garland — not celebrating the deed but honoring the man, with a private gesture in the middle of a public triumph. It is the first gift of a friendship promised years before on the slope of Govardhana, and the promise has begun to keep itself.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the day was out, Krishna would whisper the truth of the disguised Pandavas to Balarama.

stories.title: Krishna Names the Disguised Pandavas
stories.story:
Krishna saw them the moment they crossed the floor of the amphitheatre: five young Brahmins in a hall full of kings who had eyes only for Draupadi. Where the other princes saw ascetics in deerskins, he saw mighty elephants moving toward a lake overgrown with lotuses, or fire lying under ashes, alive and unspent.

It was the svayamvara of Drupada's daughter. Every royal house had come to Panchala, and one after another the kings had failed to string the great bow, tossed to the ground and left panting, their crowns loosened and garlands disordered. Karna had strung it easily, but Draupadi's voice had rung through the hall, "I will not select a Suta for my lord," and the son of the sun had thrown the drawn bow aside, laughing in vexation. Then a Brahmana seated among the priests had risen, strung the stiff bow as if it were a reed, and put an arrow through the golden mark; and Krishna, filled with joy, had gone to greet him with a white robe and a garland of flowers. That was only moments ago. Now Drupada stood to give his daughter to that Brahmana, and the kings of the earth were on their feet in fury.

"Passing us by and treating the assembled monarchs as straw," they cried, "this Drupada desires to bestow his daughter on a Brahmana! Let us slay him!" They seized their weapons and rushed at the king of Panchala, who, pale with fear, sought the protection of the Brahmins. Then the mighty Bhima, of the strength of thunder, tore up a large tree like an elephant and divested it of its leaves, and stood with it near Arjuna like the mace-bearing king of the dead armed with his fierce mace. And Arjuna, shaking off all fear, stood with his bow ready to receive the assailants.

And it was then, in the middle of the uproar, that Krishna turned to his brother Balarama and began, very quietly, to name the five Brahmins.

"That hero there, of tread like that of a mighty lion, who draws the large bow in his hand four full cubits in length, is Arjuna! There is no doubt about this, if I am Vasudeva. That other hero who, having speedily torn up the tree, has suddenly become ready to drive off the monarchs is Vrikodara! For no one in the world, except Vrikodara, could today perform such a feat in the field of battle. And that other youth of eyes like lotus-petals, of full four cubits height, of gait like that of a mighty lion, humble withal, of fair complexion and prominent and shining nose, who had a little before left the amphitheatre, is Dharma's son, Yudhishthira. The two other youths, like unto Kartikeya, are, I suspect, the sons of the twin Aswins. I had heard that the sons of Pandu along with their mother Pritha had all escaped from the conflagration of the house of lac."

Balarama, of complexion like a cloud uncharged with rain, looked where his brother pointed, and his face cleared. "O, I am happy to hear, from sheer good fortune," he said, "that our father's sister Pritha and the foremost of the Kaurava princes have all escaped from death!"

Krishna had in fact known since the five first came into view. Beholding them drawn toward Draupadi like elephants toward a lake, he had murmured to Balarama, "That is Yudhishthira; that is Bhima with Jishnu; and those are the twin heroes," and Balarama, surveying them slowly, had cast a glance of quiet satisfaction at his brother. The feat with the tree had only confirmed what his eyes had already told him. The two Yadava princes watched the uprooted tree and the drawn bow with the calm of men who had just found a lost family.

Around them the amphitheatre seethed. The monarchs, biting their nether lips in wrath, saw only two insolent Brahmins. They did not see five princes of the Kuru line who had escaped a burning house, survived the wilderness, and walked into the heart of the world's greatest gathering in borrowed robes. The kings saw what they expected to see. Krishna saw what was.

And for now, he said nothing.
stories.reflection: Krishna's recognition is a private gift, not an announcement: he names each brother to Balarama in the middle of a roaring hall and then keeps the secret, so the Pandavas can remain hidden until they choose to be seen. The scene turns on restraint — knowing who someone is, and letting them stay disguised, is its own act of friendship.
stories.next_story_tease: But the insulted kings were not ready to let the matter end in a bride given to a Brahmana.
stories.hero_scene: In the roaring amphitheatre of Panchala, a young Brahmana stands immovable with a drawn bow while a giant beside him holds an uprooted tree like a mace; in the crowd of furious kings, Krishna leans toward Balarama and quietly names the disguised heroes, the two Yadava princes calm amid the storm.

stories.title: Krishna Stills the Angry Kings
stories.story:
"Slay him!" The cry rose from the kings of the earth as one voice. Drupada had risen to give his daughter to the Brahmana who had strung the great bow and shot the mark, and the monarchs he had invited and feasted felt the insult like a wound. "Passing us by and treating the assembled monarchs as straw," they said, "this Drupada desires to bestow his daughter on a Brahmana! The svayamvara is for the Kshatriyas; the Brahmanas have no claim in the choice of a Kshatriya damsel. Let us slay him, along with his son!" They took up their weapons and rushed at the king of Panchala, who, pale with fear, sought the protection of the Brahmins.

The Brahmins, for their part, were not afraid. They shook their deer-skins and their water-pots of cocoanut shell and shouted back, "Fear not — we will fight the foe!" Arjuna, still in his Brahmana's robes, smiled at them and raised his hand. "Stand aside as spectators of the fray," he said. "Showering hundreds of arrows furnished with straight points, even I shall check, like snakes with mantras, all these angry monarchs." And taking up the great bow he had won, he stood immovable as a mountain, with Bhima at his side.

Karna came at him first, rushing against Jishnu with all his fire, while Salya the king of Madra charged Bhima like a great elephant against another for the sake of a she-elephant in heat. Arjuna drew his tough bow and pierced the son of the sun with sharp arrows until Karna fainted; and when Karna recovered, he fought with greater care than before, and the two champions raged at each other until each, enveloped in the other's shower of arrows, became invisible to the watching crowd. Only heroes could read the words they flung at each other — "Behold the strength of my arms!" — "Mark how I have counteracted that feat!" Then Karna paused and called across the field. "O foremost of Brahmanas, I am gratified by the energy of thy arms. Art thou the science of weapons embodied, or Rama the best of Brahmanas, or Indra himself, or Vishnu, who has taken the form of a Brahmana to fight with me?" And Arjuna answered, "O Karna, I am neither the science of arms nor Rama. I am only a Brahmana who is the foremost of all warriors and all wielders of weapons. By the grace of my preceptor I have become accomplished in the Brahma and the Paurandara weapons. I am here to vanquish thee in battle. Therefore wait a little." And Karna, reflecting that Brahma energy is ever invincible, desisted from the fight.

On the other side of the field, Salya and Bhima had locked together like two elephants in rut, striking with clenched fists and knees, throwing each other down and lifting each other up, until the lists rang with the clash of their bodies like the meeting of two masses of granite. Then Bhima took the king of Madra up in his arms and hurled him to the ground — yet set him down so gently that Salya was not much hurt, a feat of strength and mercy together that amazed all who saw it. The monarchs drew back, alarmed, and crowded around the two Brahmins. "Surely these bulls amongst Brahmanas are excellent warriors!" they murmured. "Who can encounter Karna in fight, except Rama or Drona, or Kiriti the son of Pandu? Who also can encounter Duryodhana in battle, except Krishna?"

And it was at that moment that Krishna himself rose. He had beheld Bhima's feat, and he believed now, beyond doubt, that these two were the sons of Kunti. Gently, addressing the assembled monarchs, he said one thing: "This maiden hath been justly acquired." And the monarchs, accomplished in battle, desisted from the fight. The storm that had risen over the amphitheatre broke apart, the kings lowered their weapons, and the unknown Brahmana walked out of the hall with the daughter of Drupada beside him — while in the crowd, the two Yadava princes exchanged a glance and said nothing at all.
stories.reflection: The duel proves what the brothers are; only Krishna's word settles what they are not — a threat. Strength wins the field with bows and an uprooted tree, but the peace is won with a single sentence spoken gently at the right moment, and the monarchs accept it. There is a kind of power that consists in knowing when not to fight.
stories.content_note: Battle violence, described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: That evening the five brothers carried their bride back to the potter's house — but someone had already guessed who they were.

stories.title: Fire, Even Covered, Can Be Known
stories.story:
"Enjoy ye all," Kunti called from the inner room, without looking out. The five brothers had come home to the potter's house in the evening and told their mother they had brought alms that day; and Kunti, who had not yet seen her sons, answered as the mother of Brahmanas should. "Enjoy ye all what ye have obtained."

The moment after, she saw Draupadi — and cried out, "Oh, what have I said?"

She had told five sons to enjoy, together, the alms they had brought; and the alms was the daughter of the king of Panchala. Anxious from fear of sin, Kunti took the cheerful princess by the hand and went to Yudhishthira. "The daughter of king Yajnasena was represented to me by thy younger brothers as the alms they had obtained," she said, "and from ignorance, O king, I said, 'Enjoy ye all what hath been obtained.' Tell me, O bull of the Kuru race, how my speech may not become untrue, how sin may not touch the daughter of the king of Panchala, and how she may not become uneasy."

Yudhishthira reflected for a moment and consoled his mother; then he turned to Arjuna. "By thee, O Phalguna, hath Yajnasena's daughter been won. It is proper, therefore, that thou shouldst wed her. Igniting the sacred fire, take thou her hand with due rites."

But Arjuna shook his head. "O king, do not make me a participator in sin. Thy behest is not conformable to virtue; that is the path followed by the sinful. Thou shouldst wed first, then the strong-armed Bhima, then myself, then Nakula, and last of all Sahadeva. All of us are obedient to thee; command us as thou likest."

The brothers looked at one another, and at Draupadi; and the beauty of Panchali, fashioned by the Creator himself, entered their hearts, and the god of desire pressed upon their senses. Yudhishthira, watching his younger brothers, understood what was passing in their minds, and remembered the words of the sage Krishna-Dwaipayana. From fear of a division amongst the brothers, he spoke: "The auspicious Draupadi shall be the common wife of us all."

It was then that two more visitors came to the potter's house. Krishna, suspecting that the five men he had seen at the svayamvara were none other than the heroes of the Kuru race, had come with Balarama; and entering, they beheld Yudhishthira of the well-developed long arms seated there, and his younger brothers passing the splendour of fire sitting around him. Vasudeva approached the foremost of virtuous men, touched the feet of the son of Kunti, and said, "I am Krishna." And Balarama did the same. The Pandavas, beholding Krishna and Balarama, expressed great delight; and the two heroes of the Yadu race touched also the feet of Kunti, their father's sister.

Then Yudhishthira, gazing at Krishna, asked the question that had been burning in him. "How, O Vasudeva, hast thou been able to trace us, as we are living in disguise?"

Krishna smiled. "Fire, even if it is covered, can be known. Who else among men than the Pandavas could exhibit such might? Ye sons of Pandu, by sheer good fortune have ye escaped from that fierce fire; and by sheer good fortune the wicked son of Dhritarashtra and his counsellors have not succeeded in accomplishing their wishes. Blest be ye, and grow ye in prosperity like a fire in a cave, gradually growing and spreading itself all around. And lest any of the monarchs recognise ye, let us return."

And the two Yadava princes went out again into the evening, as quietly as they had come, leaving the potter's house to keep its secret a little longer.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer — that fire, even covered, can be known — cuts both ways. The disguise holds not because the brothers are invisible, but because the people who see through it choose to protect the secret instead of revealing it. Recognition and restraint are both acts of friendship, and the visit ends the moment it might betray them.
stories.next_story_tease: In the days that followed, the potter's house prepared for a wedding — and Krishna prepared a gift.

stories.title: Krishna's Wedding Gifts
stories.story:
After the wedding, the fear left Drupada entirely; the king of Panchala no longer stood in fear even of the gods, for his daughter was married into a line that the world believed dead, and all that had seemed lost to his house had returned in a single season. The ladies of his household went to Kunti and worshipped her feet, naming themselves one by one, and Draupadi, attired in red silk with the auspicious thread still encircling her wrists, saluted her mother-in-law with reverence and stood before her with joined palms.

Kunti looked at her daughter-in-law and blessed her. "Be thou unto thy husband as Sachi unto Indra, Swaha unto Vibhavasu, Rohini unto Soma, Damayanti unto Nala, Arundhati unto Vasishtha, Lakshmi unto Narayana," she said. "Be thou the mother of long-lived and heroic children, and be installed as the queen of the kingdom and capital of Kurujangala with thy husband Yudhishthira the just. And as I rejoice today beholding thee attired in red silk, so shall I rejoice again when I behold thee the mother of a son."

Then the gifts began to arrive, and the courtyards of Drupada's palace slowly filled. After the sons of Pandu had been married, Krishna sent unto them presents: various gold ornaments set with pearls and black gems, lapis lazuli; costly robes manufactured in various countries; beautiful and soft blankets, and hides of great value; costly beds and carpets and vehicles; vessels by the hundreds, set with gems and diamonds; female servants by the thousands, brought from various countries, endued with beauty, youth, and accomplishments, and decked with every ornament; well-trained elephants brought from the country of Madra; excellent horses in costly harness; and cars drawn by horses of excellent colours and large teeth. And the slayer of Madhu, of immeasurable soul, sent them coins of pure gold by crores upon crores, laid out in separate heaps.

It was a royal fortune, sent to men who had come to Panchala with nothing but their bows and their disguises — the wealth of an alliance declared openly, at last, after years of hiding. The brothers who had escaped a burning house and begged their bread as Brahmins stood among mountains of gold and gifts sent by a cousin who had recognised them in a crowd and never once said their names aloud. Gift followed gift, and still the heaps of gold stood apart, each mound its own small treasury.

And Yudhishthira the just, desirous of gratifying Govinda, accepted all those presents with great joy — taking them as they were meant: not payment, not dowry, but the welcome of one house laid at the feet of another, and a promise that the hidden princes would not be hidden much longer.
stories.reflection: The catalogue of gifts is almost excessive — gold by crores, servants by thousands — yet the source records no message sent with them, only the presents themselves. The wealth says what Krishna cannot say aloud in a hall of spies: these are my people. And Yudhishthira's joy in accepting, desirous of gratifying Govinda, completes the exchange — the pleasure of receiving is itself the gift returned.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna knew the brothers could not stay hidden forever — and he would soon counsel them toward a kingdom of their own.

stories.title: The Counsel at Panchala
stories.subtitle: Vidura brings word from Hastinapura, and Krishna's opinion decides the Pandavas' next move.
stories.story:
Vidura came to Panchala as the messenger no one could dismiss, and the message he carried had been waiting in the air ever since the wedding fires died down. The Pandavas had found a refuge, a father-in-law, and a wife in King Drupada's house. But Vidura spoke now of their ancestral kingdom — of the throne of Hastinapura that was theirs by right, and of the question that would not stay buried: would the sons of Pandu press that claim?

Drupada heard him out, and his answer was careful. The princes should return to their ancestral kingdom, he said; it was highly proper. But it was not proper for him, their host, to say so himself. If Yudhishthira and Bhima and Arjuna and the twins themselves desired to go, and if Balarama and Krishna — both acquainted with every rule of morality — were of the same mind, then let the Pandavas go. For those two, he added, were ever engaged in doing what was agreeable and beneficial to Pandu's sons.

Yudhishthira answered with all the warmth of a son: "We are now, O monarch, with all our younger brothers, dependent on thee. We shall cheerfully do what thou art pleased to command."

Then Krishna spoke, and his words settled the room. "I am of opinion that the Pandavas should go. But we should all abide by the opinion of king Drupada, who is conversant with every rule of morality."

It was a rare sentence: an opinion given, and then set aside for another man's judgment. Drupada received it as the honour it was. He agreed with what this foremost of men thought, having regard to the circumstances — for the sons of Pandu were now as dear to him as they were to Vasudeva. And then he said the thing that has been remembered about this quiet council ever since: "Kunti's son Yudhishthira himself doth not seek the welfare of the Pandavas so earnestly as Kesava, that tiger among men."

That was the decision, and it moved with the speed of a command. At Drupada's bidding the Pandavas, with Krishna and Vidura, set out — taking Draupadi and the renowned Kunti with them — journeying toward the city called after the elephant, and stopping along the way for pleasure and enjoyment, as though the road itself wanted to delay a homecoming that had been too long coming.

Word of their approach raced ahead of them. King Dhritarashtra sent the Kauravas out to receive the heroes: Vikarna of the great bow, Chitrasena, Drona the foremost of warriors, and Kripa of Gautama's line. Surrounded by that honour guard, the brothers entered Hastinapura, and the whole city became radiant with the gay throng of sight-seers. The citizens called out as they passed. "Here returns that tiger among men, conversant with all the rules of morality, who always protects us as if we were his nearest relatives," some cried. And others, with the fierce love of a city for its own, said: "If we have ever given away in charity, if we have ever poured libations of clarified butter on the fire, if we have any ascetic merit, let the Pandavas, by virtue of all those acts, stay in our town for a hundred years."

At the palace, the brothers worshipped the feet of Dhritarashtra and of the illustrious Bhishma, and of everyone else who deserved that honour, and enquired after the welfare of every citizen present. They rested, and were summoned to the court. There Dhritarashtra gave them what no one had dared hope for — not a welcome merely, but a settlement. "Repair ye to Khandavaprastha so that no difference may arise again between you and your cousins. If you take up your quarters there, no one will be able to do you any injury. Protected by Arjuna, like the celestials by the thunderbolt, reside ye at Khandavaprastha, taking half of the kingdom."

The brothers agreed. Content with half a kingdom, they worshipped the king and set out from Hastinapura toward a stretch of unreclaimed desert that they would have to turn into a home. It did not look like much of a throne. But Krishna had said they should go — and Krishna, who had left the desert only after them, was already thinking of what the land could become.
stories.reflection: Drupada's parting tribute is striking: he measures Krishna's care for the Pandavas against the love of their own eldest brother and finds it no less. In a court where everyone has an interest in the brothers — the Kauravas, the citizens, even their new father-in-law — Krishna alone wants for them exactly what they would want for themselves, and gives his opinion in a form that leaves the final word to others.
stories.next_story_tease: The unreclaimed desert was a strange gift — and Krishna would not leave the Pandavas to it until it had become a city.

stories.title: Founding Indraprastha
stories.subtitle: Krishna helps raise a capital from the wilds of Khandavaprastha, and then takes his leave.
stories.story:
Half a kingdom sounds like a fortune until you stand on it. The land Dhritarashtra had granted the Pandavas — Khandavaprastha — was unreclaimed desert: thorn and dust and emptiness, no walls, no palace, no street that could be called a street. The brothers had come there content, asking only that no difference should arise again between them and their cousins. But contentment does not build cities. Work does.

Krishna had not gone home. Of all those who had pressed the brothers toward Hastinapura, he was the one who came with them into the wilderness, and he stayed. With Krishna at their head, the Pandavas began to make the desert theirs. They called in the sage Vyasa — Dwaipayana — and with his assistance selected a sacred and auspicious region for the settlement. There they performed propitiatory ceremonies to hallow the ground, and measured out the piece of land on which their city would stand. Every step was deliberate: first the ground made holy, then the ground made level, then the ground made home.

What rose from that measuring was not a camp but a capital. A trench was dug around it, wide as the sea. Walls rose over it, reaching high up toward the heavens, white as fleecy clouds or the rays of the moon. The city stood resplendent, and those who saw it said it gleamed like Bhogavati, the jewelled capital of the nether kingdom decked with its Nagas — so bright and finished did it shine against the desert it had replaced. Beautifying the place as they went, the Pandavas had made what the storytellers would call a second heaven. And the city on that measured ground came to be known as Indraprastha. The name itself sounded like a promise to men who had grown up depending on the goodwill of others: not a refuge, not a guest-house, but a capital. The brothers who had been schooled in Hastinapura on sufferance, sheltered in Panchala as refugees, now had a place that answered to their name alone.

It was the first thing in many years that belonged wholly to the Pandavas. Since their father's death they had been guests and wanderers — schooled in Hastinapura as dependents, sheltered in Panchala as refugees, then sent off with half a kingdom in the desert. Now, at last, they had walls of their own, and a trench wide as the sea, and gates that opened on a city that bore their name.

And when the walls stood, Krishna took his leave. Having settled the Pandavas there — having seen the ground hallowed and measured, the city raised, his friends standing inside their own gates — he obtained their leave and set out for the west, with Balarama beside him, toward Dwaraka. There is little recorded of the parting itself; there was little to say. The work was done, and a friendship like that one does not need speeches. The brothers stood at the gate and watched the two cousins drive away, the dust settling slowly on the road west — and what they carried back into their new city was not the emptiness of guests left behind, but the ease of men who had been settled in their own home.

The Pandavas watched the two cousins go, the men of Dwaraka who had ever been engaged in doing what was agreeable and beneficial to Pandu's sons. Behind the brothers, the white walls of Indraprastha threw long shadows across the desert that used to be empty. Ahead of them, the road home.

But Dwaraka was not so far, and Krishna's heart was not the kind that stayed in one place. The city was built. The friendship would keep the road busy.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not merely wish the Pandavas well — he stays until the city stands, helping choose the ground, hallow it, measure it, raise its walls, and only then takes his leave. The gift of the kingdom was Dhritarashtra's, but the gift of a home worth ruling was made together, and the parting that follows is confident precisely because the work is complete.
stories.next_story_tease: In the years that followed, Arjuna would leave the new city for a long wandering through the holy places — and Krishna would hear of it before any word was sent.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna standing with the Pandavas on the raw ground of Khandavaprastha, pointing across the measured land as the white walls of the new city rise behind them — a trench wide as the sea ringing the site, towers white as fleecy clouds, while Balarama waits at the roadside for the journey home.

stories.title: Reunion at Prabhasa
stories.subtitle: In the middle of his exile, Arjuna is met on the western shore by the friend of his oldest story — the two who were Nara and Narayana of old.
stories.story:
Somewhere along the shores of the western ocean, a wanderer came to a place that felt like home though he had never been there.

Arjuna was in the middle of his exile — the long forest years of wandering through the holy places of the earth — and he had made his way from one sacred water to the next, bathing where the old stories said the gods had bathed. At last he reached Prabhasa, a sacred and delightful region on the coast. He had told no one, sent no word ahead. He was, the old account says, the invisible Arjuna, moving through the world quietly, asking nothing of anyone.

But Krishna heard of it.

The slayer of Madhu, in Dwaraka, learned that his friend had arrived at Prabhasa, and he went at once — across the land, down to the shore, to the place where the wanderer stood. They met and embraced, there on the sacred ground, two friends enquiring after each other's welfare with the easy closeness of men who had never needed distance. The storyteller adds a strange and beautiful note: these dear friends, he says, were none other than the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old — the two ancient sages of legend, bound to each other through the ages. Anyone watching the pair on that shore would have understood why the tale was told.

They sat down together, and Krishna asked the question that mattered. "Why, O Pandava, art thou wandering over the earth, beholding all the sacred waters and other holy places?"

Arjuna told him everything — the long roads, the rivers, the reasons that had sent him out into the world. Krishna heard him out, and answered only: "This is as it should be." No lecture, no plan to shorten the exile, no argument. His friend had chosen a hard road, and Krishna honoured the choice.

They spent their time at Prabhasa as they pleased, the two of them sporting together by the sea. Then Krishna drew him onward, to the Raivataka mountain, where they would pass some days. Krishna had seen to everything beforehand: at his command, artificers had adorned the mountain, and food had been collected in abundance. Arjuna enjoyed the performances of the actors and the dancers, dismissed them all with proper respect, and laid himself down on an excellent bed that had been prepared for him. As he lay there, he described to Krishna everything he had seen in his wandering — the sacred waters, the lakes, the mountains, the rivers, the forests — while his friend listened in the dark. And in the middle of his telling, sleep stole upon him.

He woke in the morning to sweet songs and the melodious notes of the vina, and the panegyrics and benedictions of the bards — a king's morning, arranged for a guest who had been living like a pilgrim. After the necessary acts and ceremonies, Krishna accosted him affectionately, and Arjuna rode out on a golden car toward Dwaraka, the capital of the Yadavas.

The city had dressed itself for him. At Krishna's command, every garden and house had been adorned, and the citizens, desirous of beholding the son of Kunti, poured into the public thoroughfares by hundreds of thousands. In the squares, hundreds and thousands of women mixed with the men in the great crowd of the Bhojas, the Vrishnis, and the Andhakas. Arjuna was welcomed with respect by all the sons of those tribes, and he in turn worshipped those who deserved his worship and received their blessings. The young men of the Yadava tribe gave him an affectionate welcome, and he embraced again and again all who were equal to him in age — old friends meeting the wanderer returned.

Then he went to Krishna's mansion, filled with gems and every article of enjoyment, and took up his abode there — and there he stayed, with Krishna, for many days. No one hurried him. The exile would resume; the road was still waiting. But for those days, the invisible Arjuna was simply the guest of his oldest friend, in the most beautiful house in Dwaraka.
stories.reflection: The storyteller names Krishna and Arjuna as Nara and Narayana of old, and the embrace at Prabhasa carries that weight: the friendship is older than either man's fame. Krishna asks why his friend wanders, listens to everything, and answers only, "This is as it should be" — acceptance rather than rescue, which is exactly what Arjuna, in the middle of his own long exile, most needed.
stories.next_story_tease: At the festival on Raivataka, Krishna would notice where his friend's gaze kept lingering — and would counsel him to act.
stories.hero_scene: On the sacred seashore at Prabhasa, Krishna and Arjuna embrace in greeting, the western ocean stretching behind them — two friends who were said to be the Rishis Nara and Narayana of old, meeting again in the middle of the wanderer's exile.

stories.title: Krishna Counsels Arjuna to Abduct Subhadra
stories.story:
The festival on Raivataka had everything a festival should have, and more of it than anyone could take in at once.

The Vrishnis and the Andhakas had gathered on the mountain to make merry, and they threw themselves into it completely. Musicians struck up and dancers danced and singers sang, and the young men of the Vrishni race, brilliant with ornaments, rode about in cars decked with gold. Mansions set with gems and artificial trees of bright color rose around the hill, and citizens came by the hundreds and thousands, some on foot and some in fine chariots, with their wives and their followers. Balarama roved at will, cheerful with drink, with Revati beside him and musicians trailing after. Pradyumna and Samba, ever eager for battle, roamed the ground flushed and garlanded with bright flowers, disporting themselves like a pair of celestials. King Ugrasena moved through it all with his thousand wives, and Akrura and Sarana and Gada and Satyaki and Uddhava and a hundred other heroes, each with his own train, adorned the mountain. It was a festival loud enough to forget yourself in. Both clans had turned out for it, and no one thought of anything but the day.

Through all of it two friends walked together, seeing everything: Krishna and Arjuna, who was there in his wandering years, far from his brothers, and whom Krishna had made welcome. And as they wandered, they came upon a young woman in the midst of her maids — Subhadra, the daughter of Vasudeva, Krishna's own sister, decked with every ornament and lovely to look upon.

Arjuna stopped. The great archer, the man who had ranged the wilds and faced a hundred dangers without flinching, stood still as a struck bell. The battle-hardened warrior, who had never once flinched at an enemy, could not look away. The god of desire had taken him, and it showed all over his face. The drums and the singing went on around them, but Arjuna no longer heard them; the whole bright festival had narrowed to a single figure.

Krishna noticed at once, because Krishna noticed everything. He looked at his friend — this tiger among men, suddenly struck dumb — and smiled.

'How is this?' he asked. 'Can the heart of one who ranges the woods be agitated by the god of desire?' It was the smile more than the words that undid Arjuna. 'This is my sister, Partha, the sister of Sarana and the favourite daughter of my father. Tell me if your heart is fixed upon her, and I shall speak to my father myself.'

Arjuna answered as a man in his condition must, and his answer was honest. She was Vasudeva's daughter and Krishna's sister, he said, and with so much beauty, whom could she not fascinate? What heart would not be stirred?

And so, warm and unhurried, Krishna turned matchmaker. Rather than leave the matter to the slow formality of self-choice, he counseled Arjuna to carry Subhadra away by force — the celebrated Kshatriya form of marriage. It was counsel given with a smile, between friends, and it set in motion everything that followed. There was nothing solemn about it; Krishna made the matter sound as simple as it was bold. The seed of the plan was planted there in the noise of the festival, and it would not take long to grow.

Subhadra, meanwhile, knew nothing of the two men who had stopped to look at her, or of the plan already taking shape behind Krishna's easy manner. She stood among her maids at the bright center of the festival, and the day went on around her.
stories.reflection: The comedy sits beside the warmth: the mightiest archer of his age stopped still by a glance, and Krishna too fond of him to leave him stranded there. Friendship here looks like a knowing smile and an offer to manage everything — and a nudge toward a bolder path than waiting.
stories.hero_scene: Arjuna stopped in the middle of the Raivataka festival, gazing at Subhadra decked in ornaments among her maids, while Krishna stands beside him watching with a knowing smile.
