stories.title: Nuptial Gifts for Indraprastha
stories.subtitle: Krishna brings the Yadava host to honour Subhadra's new home.
stories.story:
When the twelve years of his exile were complete, Arjuna came back to Khandavaprastha — and he did not come back alone. Beside him was Subhadra, the sister of Krishna, whom he had carried away from Dwaraka and married there. It was a homecoming with two edges: the city gained a prince returned, and the household gained a new bride.

Arjuna went first to the king. He approached Yudhishthira, then worshipped the brahmanas with respectful attention, and at last went in to Draupadi. She met him with the sharpness of a woman who had waited twelve years and heard where her husband had been. "Why tarriest thou here, O son of Kunti?" she said. "Go where the daughter of the Satwata race is! A second tie always relaxeth the first one upon a faggot!"

It was the old fear, put plainly: a new bond loosening the old one, the way a second rope loosens the first on a bundle of wood. Arjuna pacified her, and asked her forgiveness, again and again. And then Subhadra herself finished what his words had begun.

She came into the inner apartments dressed not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman — Arjuna's own doing, a way of saying she came as a sister to the household, not a rival for its crown. She looked, the account says, handsomer in that dress. The celebrated Bhadra, of large and slightly red eyes, first worshipped Pritha — Kunti — and Kunti, from excess of affection, smelt the head of that faultless girl and pronounced infinite blessings upon her. Then Subhadra hastened to Draupadi, and worshipped her, and said: "I am thy maid."

Draupadi rose quickly and embraced her — the sister of Madhava — from pure affection, and blessed her: "Let thy husband be without a foe!"

"So be it!" said Subhadra, with a delighted heart.

From that time, the Pandavas began to live happily, and Kunti too became very happy. And when Krishna heard that Arjuna had reached Indraprastha with his sister — that the household had made its peace — he came thither himself, to make the marriage an alliance the whole world could see.

He came with Balarama and the heroes of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes, with his brothers and his sons and many brave warriors, and a large army protected him on the road. Akrura came, the exceedingly liberal generalissimo of the brave Vrishni host; Uddhava of great renown; Satyaka, Kritavarman, Pradyumna, Gada, and many more of the Bhojas and the Andhakas. And they brought with them many nuptial presents, in the manner of a family celebrating a wedding it had not been able to attend.

King Yudhishthira, hearing that Madhava had arrived, sent the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, out to receive him. And the Vrishni host entered Khandavaprastha in splendour. The city had dressed for the occasion: the streets were well-swept and watered, decked with floral wreaths and bunches, and sprinkled with sandalwood water that was fragrant and cooling. Flags and ensigns flew over the gates. Every part of the town filled with the sweet scent of the day.

Then the gifts were given. Krishna gave to the Pandavas a thousand cars of gold, furnished with rows of bells; ten thousand cows; mares and mules; and damsels, presented as is fitting when a daughter of the house goes to a new family. It was generosity on the scale of Dwaraka itself — not the payment of a debt, but the celebration of a bond.

The Pandavas received their kinsman's gifts, and the household that had been uneasy for one bright afternoon settled into the happiness that would carry it for years. The city of Indraprastha stood fragrant and adorned, its streets full of Yadavas and Kurus mingling like one family. And at the heart of it all was the small, true thing the whole procession had come to honour: a bride who had said, "I am thy maid," and a blessing that answered, "Let thy husband be without a foe."
stories.reflection: Subhadra's answer to Draupadi — "I am thy maid" — dissolves the jealousy in a moment, and Draupadi's blessing follows at once: "Let thy husband be without a foe." The household's peace is made not by Krishna's gifts but by the two women's grace; the great procession of cars and cows that follows only makes the alliance visible to the world.
stories.tradition_note: The nuptial gifts in this episode are for Subhadra's marriage and are distinct from the wedding presents Krishna earlier sent after Draupadi's wedding (Mahabharata 1.201). The Bhagavata Purana tells the Subhadra episode more briefly.
stories.next_story_tease: Before long the new household would welcome a child — and Krishna would be there for the rites.

stories.title: Birth Rites for Abhimanyu
stories.story:
The rites of infancy are a family's quiet business, but for the son Subhadra bore at Indraprastha, they were performed by Krishna's own hands. He had come to the city with all the pomp of the Vrishni host — Balarama and Akrura and Uddhava, Satyaka and Kritavarman, his own sons and brothers, a great company of heroes riding in with nuptial presents, their coming made festival by streets swept and watered and decked with floral wreaths, sprinkled with cool, fragrant sandalwood water. And when the celebration was over, he stayed. The high-souled Vasudeva remained there with Arjuna in the delightful city, and the two friends were in no hurry to part.

The palace was still learning its own harmony, for it had not always been easy. When Arjuna first brought Subhadra home, Draupadi had met him with the sharpness of a woman who feels her place taken. "Why do you tarry here, son of Kunti?" she had asked. "Go where the daughter of the Satwata race is! A second tie always relaxes the first one upon a faggot." Arjuna had pacified her and asked her forgiveness, and Subhadra, sent into the inner apartments not as a queen but in the simple garb of a cowherd woman, had gone straight to Draupadi and bowed. "I am thy maid," she said. Draupadi herself had risen and embraced her — the sister of Madhava — and blessed the marriage: "Let thy husband be without a foe!" From that time, the text says, the household had lived happily, and Kunti also became very happy.

Now the household was growing. Subhadra, the favourite sister of Kesava, gave birth to an illustrious son. The news ran through Indraprastha, and among all who came to see the child, none was awaited more eagerly than his mother's brother. The son that Subhadra brought forth was called Abhimanyu, and from the first hour the child's name was spoken with pride in both houses — the name of the Yadavas' own blood now running in the line of the Pandavas.

Upon his birth, Krishna performed the usual rites of infancy. It was the plainest of services — the ceremonies that welcome a child into the world, mark his naming, and set the first blessing on his days — and Krishna performed them himself, as an uncle does who loves a child before the child can know him. No vision was seen and no miracle recorded; the passage simply tells that the rites were done, and the child began to grow up like the Moon of the bright fortnight.

And the child grew dear to Krishna. The boy who would one day be remembered as a warrior of the Pandavas was, in those first years, simply his uncle's joy — a brightening in the palace that no one could miss, growing night by night as the moon grows, without haste and without shadow. Indraprastha had many splendours in those days — the wealth of the new capital, the court of the five brothers, the friendship between the Yadavas and the sons of Pandu — but this small one was watched over most closely of all. In the boy's laughter, in his first steps, in the way he reached for his uncle, the two houses that had joined at Subhadra's wedding were joined again, in the most ordinary and lasting way.

Krishna lingered in the city through the child's earliest years, and when at last he spoke of returning to Dwaraka, the parting was a real one. He left behind a sister happy in her new home, a friend in Arjuna, and a nephew whose first rites had been performed by his own hand — a bond that would be remembered every time the boy's name was spoken in the years to come.
stories.reflection: The rites are performed without spectacle — no prophecy, no miracle — and that is the point: Krishna gives the child the most ordinary of services, the welcome a family gives a new life. The story's devotion lives in the uncle's plain attendance, not in any display.
stories.next_story_tease: That summer, Krishna was still at Indraprastha when Arjuna proposed an outing to the banks of the Yamuna.

stories.title: The Stranger on the Yamuna
stories.story:
The summer days have set in, Arjuna told Krishna one morning at Indraprastha. Let us go to the banks of the Yamuna; sporting there in the company of friends, we will return in the evening. Krishna answered that this was his wish too. And so, with Yudhishthira's leave, the two set out with their friends, leaving behind a city that was thriving as never before.

The Pandavas, settled at Indraprastha at the command of Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, had brought the neighbouring kings under their sway, and the people lived most happily depending upon Yudhishthira the just, like a soul living happily in a body blest with auspicious marks. Yudhishthira paid homage to virtue, pleasure and profit in judicious proportion, as if each were a friend dear to him as his own self, and it seemed as if the three pursuits became personified on earth, with the king shining among them as a fourth. He was devoted to the study of the Vedas, performer of the great sacrifices, protector of all good people; and the people took delight in him not only because he was their king but from sincere affection. Under such a king, the brothers could be easy with one another, and Krishna, visiting as he did, was more brother than guest.

They chose a fine spot on the Yamuna, overgrown with numerous tall trees and covered with high mansions that made the place look like the celestial city. Everything had been gathered there for pleasure: costly and well-flavoured viands and drinks, floral wreaths, various perfumes, and inner apartments adorned with precious gems of pure rays. The women of the party sported as they liked — some in the woods, some in the waters, some within the mansions, as directed by Partha and Govinda. Draupadi and Subhadra, exhilarated with wine, gave away their costly robes and ornaments to the women who sported about them. Some danced, some sang, some laughed and jested, some drank excellent wines and some obstructed one another's progress in play; flutes and guitars and kettledrums filled the groves, and the whole place, the text says, became the scene of Prosperity personified. For a day in high summer, the world seemed to have arranged itself purely for enjoyment.

In the midst of it all, Arjuna and Vasudeva slipped away to a charming spot a little apart from the others, and sat down upon two very costly seats. There, discoursing upon their past achievements of prowess and other such topics, the two friends passed the afternoon like the Aswins seated in heaven, while the music and laughter of the grove came to them from a distance, softened. It was the talk of two men who had fought side by side and trusted each other with their lives — old campaigns retold, old enemies remembered, the easy silences between.

And then a Brahmana came to them. He was still some distance off when the two friends felt the change — the day's noise seemed to fall back from him, and the grove grew quieter as he walked. He stood like a tall Sala tree; his complexion was like molten gold; his beard was bright yellow, tinged with green; the height and thickness of his body were in just proportion; and his locks were matted. He came toward the two heroes as they sat talking of old victories — a figure blazing with splendour, the foremost of Brahmanas, and his coming put an end to the idleness of the day. He did not look like a man who had come to share their sport. The music of the grove seemed, suddenly, very far away.
stories.reflection: The day is all brightness and ease — music, wine, generosity, two friends at their leisure — and the stranger cuts across it like a shadow at noon. The story lets pleasure stand at its full height before the omen walks into the grove, as if to say that the world's golden hours are exactly when the unknown arrives.
stories.next_story_tease: But the Brahmana who approached them had not come for sport — he had come hungry.
stories.hero_scene: On a grassy bank of the Yamuna under tall trees, Krishna and Arjuna sit on two costly seats deep in conversation, while behind them the pleasure mansions rise and the river sparkles — and a towering Brahmana with molten-gold skin and a yellow-green beard walks toward them through the grove.

stories.title: Agni Asks for the Khandava Forest
stories.story:
The Brahmana stood before them and asked for food — not politely, but as a starving man asks. "I am a voracious Brahmana that always eateth much," he said to Arjuna and Vasudeva. "O thou of the Vrishni race, and O Partha, I solicit you to gratify me by giving me sufficient food." Krishna and the son of Pandu answered that they would: tell us what kind of food will gratify you, and we will endeavour to give it to you.

"I do not desire to eat ordinary food," the Brahmana said. "Know that I am Agni! Give me that food which suiteth me. This forest of Khandava is always protected by Indra, and as it is protected by the illustrious one, I always fail to consume it. In that forest dwelleth, with his followers and family, a Naga called Takshaka, who is the friend of Indra. It is for him that the wielder of the thunderbolt protecteth this forest; many other creatures are protected here for Takshaka's sake. Desiring to consume the forest, I succeed not in my attempts, in consequence of Indra's prowess — beholding me blazing forth, he always poureth upon me water from the clouds. I have now come to you, who are both skilled in weapons. If you help me, I will surely consume this forest, for even this is the food that is desired by me. Prevent those showers from descending, and prevent any of the creatures from escaping, when I begin to consume this forest!"

The request hung in the summer air. The matted locks were the same locks the stranger had worn when he approached them on the Yamuna's bank; but now the talk of blazing seemed to kindle something behind his eyes. Two men who had fed armies and cities stood before a god who asked to be fed with a forest.

To understand why the fire-god hungered so, Vaisampayana said, one must hear the tale as the sages told it — and the tale goes back to a king named Swetaki, endued with strength and prowess, equal unto Indra himself, whom no one on earth has equalled in sacrifices, charity and intelligence. Swetaki performed the five great sacrifices and many others, with large presents unto the Brahmanas, year after year, until the sacrificial priests, their eyes afflicted by the continued smoke and their bodies grown weak, left the monarch, wishing never more to assist at his sacrifices. The king asked them to return; they would not, because of the painful state of their eyes. So he invited others like them, and completed the sacrifice he had begun. Then he desired to perform another sacrifice that should extend for a hundred years — and obtained not a single priest to assist him. He courted them with bowing, with conciliatory speeches, with gifts of wealth; all of them refused. At last the royal sage grew angry, and told the Brahmanas plainly: if he were a fallen person, or wanting in homage and service to them, he would deserve to be abandoned — but he was neither degraded nor wanting in homage, and they had no adequate reason to obstruct his sacrifice. "If you abandon me from enmity alone, or any improper motive," he warned, "I shall go unto other priests for their assistance in this sacrifice of mine, and conciliating them by sweet words and gifts, I shall represent unto them the business I have on hand."

The priests, who knew well that they could not assist at the king's sacrifice, pretended to be angry in their turn. "Thy sacrifices are incessant," they told him. And there the old tale pauses at the edge of the forest's memory.

On the bank of the Yamuna, Krishna and Arjuna looked at the blazing Brahmana, and then at the great dark forest across the water, which the friend of Indra had kept unburned for so long. The fire-god was asking them to stand between him and the rain. To refuse was possible; the request was only a request. But Agni had called them the two foremost of heroes on earth, and he had asked them for food.
stories.reflection: Agni comes not as a god commanding but as a guest asking, and in that framing the heroes' weapons become an answer to hunger. The fiercest event in the story — the burning of a forest — begins with a request, the oldest courtesy of the world.
stories.tradition_note: The tale of King Swetaki, told here to explain Agni's craving for the Khandava forest, continues in the source beyond the passage excerpted here.

stories.title: The Earth Shall Drink Their Blood
stories.story:
The forest of Kamyaka had never seen such an assembly of wrathful kin. When the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas heard that the Pandavas had been banished from their kingdom, they went to the great forest where the brothers lived in affliction; with them came the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, and Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and the celebrated and powerful Kaikeya brothers, their hearts fired with wrath. They reproached the sons of Dhritarashtra in the hearing of all, and asked the only question there was to ask: "What should we do?" Then the bulls of the Kshatriya race, with Vasudeva at their head, sat themselves down in a ring around Yudhishthira the just.

Kesava saluted the foremost of the Kurus with respect, and then he spoke mournfully — and the words were a vow. "The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni! Slaying these in battle and defeating their followers along with their royal allies, will we all install Yudhishthira the just on the throne! The wicked deserve to be slain! Verily, this is eternal morality."

The forest listened. When Krishna spoke of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, he had got into a passion, and he seemed bent upon consuming all created things; and in that moment Arjuna, who loved him, exerted himself to pacify him. He began to recite the feats Krishna had achieved in his former lives — for he who stood wrathful in the exiles' camp was, Arjuna said, the soul of all things, himself immeasurable, the eternal one of infinite energy, the lord of Prajapati himself, the supreme ruler of the worlds: Vishnu of profound wisdom. Had not Krishna wandered on the Gandhamadana mountains for ten thousand years as a muni whose home was wherever evening fell? Had he not lived upon water alone for eleven thousand years by the lake of Pushkara? On the high hills of Vadari he had stood on one leg for a hundred years, living all the while upon air; on the banks of the Saraswati he had passed twelve years in sacrifice, his body emaciated and looking like a bundle of veins; on the plains of Prabhasa he had stood on one leg for a thousand years of the celestials. All asceticism rested in him, and he was the embodiment of all sacrifices.

He had slain the Asura Naraka, offspring of the Earth, and taken his ear-rings, and performed the first horse-sacrifice, offering up that Asura as the sacrificial horse; he had slain all the Daityas and Danavas mustered in battle, and given Indra the sovereignty of the universe, taking his own birth among men. He had slain Ahvriti at Jaruthi, and Kratha, and Sisupala with his adherents, and Jarasandha, and Saivya, and Satadhanwan; on a car roaring like clouds and effulgent like the sun, he had defeated Rukmi in battle and obtained the daughter of Bhoja for his queen; he had slain Indradyumna and the Yavana called Kaseruman, and Salwa the lord of Saubha, and destroyed the city of Saubha itself. And even as a child, in consequence of his energy, he had filled the heaven, the firmament and the earth in three steps.

Arjuna's voice went on, reciting the old deeds as one recites a litany — and as he spoke, the wrath of Janardana, which had seemed bent on consuming all created things, began to be held, like a fire held in the hands of a friend. The kinsmen sat silent in their ring; the vow stood spoken, heard by every leaf of the forest. But the anger in Krishna was not yet turned aside, and Arjuna's words had not yet done their full work.
stories.reflection: The vow is spoken for the sake of the just king in exile, and Krishna's wrath is inseparable from his friendship: the same heart that delights in his friends burns at their wrongs. Arjuna's answer is not argument but remembrance — he recites who Krishna is, holding the fire in the vessel of a thousand lifetimes.
stories.tradition_note: Krishna's vow here is echoed later, before the war of Kurukshetra, in a similar promise.
stories.next_story_tease: But Arjuna's recitation had only begun to do its work on the wrathful Krishna.

stories.title: Nara and Narayana
stories.subtitle: Arjuna soothes Krishna's wrath with the tale of his own ancient deeds
stories.story:
Krishna heard what had been done to the Pandavas, and the anger that rose in him frightened his own kinsmen. By the time the riders reached the Kamyaka forest, that anger had grown into something terrible — a heat that seemed ready to burn the world down around the wrongs that had been done to it.

The Pandavas had lost their kingdom at dice and were living in the great forest in affliction. Their friends came to them in grief and in wrath: the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the consanguineous relatives of Panchala, Dhrishtaketu the king of Chedi, and the Kaikeya brothers, their hearts fired with anger against the sons of Dhritarashtra. "What should we do?" they asked one another, and they sat down in a wide circle around Yudhishthira the just, with Vasudeva at their head.

Respectfully saluting the foremost of the Kurus, Krishna spoke, and his voice was heavy with mourning. "The earth shall drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni," he said. "Slaying these in battle and defeating their followers along with their royal allies, we shall install Yudhishthira the just on the throne. The wicked deserve to be slain. Verily, this is eternal morality."

But the vow did not cool his blood. On account of the wrongs of Pritha's sons, Janardana had fallen into such a passion that he seemed bent upon consuming all created things; those nearest him could feel it, like standing close to a fire. Then Arjuna exerted himself to pacify him.

Beholding Kesava angry, Arjuna began to recite the feats achieved in his former lives by that soul of all things — immeasurable, eternal, of infinite energy, the lord of the Prajapatis themselves, the supreme ruler of the worlds, Vishnu of profound wisdom. He spoke of the ten thousand years Krishna had wandered on the Gandhamadana mountains as a muni whose home was wherever evening fell; of the eleven thousand years lived on water alone by the lake of Pushkara; of the hundred years on the high hills of Vadari, standing on one leg with arms upraised, living upon air; of the twelve-year sacrifice kept on the banks of the Saraswati until his body, stripped of its upper garment, looked like a bundle of veins; of the thousand celestial years stood on one leg on the plains of Prabhasa. He spoke of the slaying of Naraka, offspring of the Earth, and of the first horse-sacrifice that followed it; of the Daityas and Danavas destroyed in battle until the sovereignty of the universe was placed in Indra's hands; of the three steps by which, even as a child, Krishna had filled heaven, the firmament and the earth; of the sinful Asuras slain by the hundred in each of his thousand incarnations.

"All asceticism rests in thee," Arjuna said, "and thou art the embodiment of all sacrifices — the cause of creation and its course, the mover of all minds, the beginning and end of all things. Thou art mine and I am thine, and all that is mine is thine also. O thou irrepressible one, thou art Nara and I am Narayana."

Krishna answered him. The fire in his eyes sank, and the wrath that had seemed ready to consume creation gathered itself back into the shape of a man sitting among friends. He did not unsay the vow — the earth would still drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, and Yudhishthira would still be crowned — but he spoke of it now without fury, as a thing already accomplished. And those who had watched the storm pass looked at Arjuna with wonder. He had not argued with Krishna, nor pleaded with him. He had simply told Krishna who Krishna was — and it had been enough.
stories.reflection: Arjuna does not argue Krishna out of his anger; he reminds him of his own identity. The catalogue of ancient feats — penances of ten thousand years, three steps that filled the three worlds — is a way of saying that the power now blazing in wrath has always existed and has always been used with purpose. And the claim goes deeper than comfort: if the two friends are Nara and Narayana, one soul in two bodies, then an injury to Arjuna is literally an injury to Krishna, which is why the vow follows so naturally.
stories.next_story_tease: But the day's work was not done: Draupadi still wept, and Krishna had yet to speak to her.

stories.title: A Promise for a Weeping Queen
stories.subtitle: What Krishna swore to Draupadi in the Kamyaka forest
stories.story:
Some sorrows cannot be answered with plans for war. In the Kamyaka forest, while the kinsmen talked of vengeance, Draupadi sat apart and wept.

Her husbands had lost everything at dice — kingdom, wealth, dignity — and were living in exile in the great forest, far from the comforts of their old life. The whole morning the clearing had been full of their friends, come from near and far with hearts fired with wrath against the sons of Dhritarashtra: the Bhojas, the Vrishnis and the Andhakas, the relatives of Panchala, the king of Chedi, the Kaikeya brothers. They had sat in a wide circle around Yudhishthira, and Krishna at their head had vowed that the earth would drink the blood of Duryodhana and Karna, of Dussasana and the wicked Sakuni, and that Yudhishthira would sit on the throne again. But that was talk of battles yet to come, and it is cold comfort to a woman who has already lost. She was the princess of Panchala, the shared wife of the five brothers, and she had tasted enough of the Kauravas' cruelty to know that vows and battles are cheap until they are kept. Her anger had names, and each of them sat safely in Hastinapura while she sat weeping on forest grass.

Krishna saw her tears, and he did not offer her patience or philosophy. Vasudeva spoke to the weeping Draupadi, and his words were a promise laid against the future like a stone.

"O fair lady," he said, "the wives of those with whom thou art angry shall weep even like thee, beholding their husbands dead on the ground, weltering in blood."

Then he went further — much further. "I promise thou shalt once more be the queen of kings! The heavens might fall, or the Himavat might split, the earth might be rent, or the waters of the ocean might dry up, but my words shall never prove futile."

For a moment the forest seemed to hold its breath. It was an odd comfort, to a woman who had been wronged before a court: not "bear it patiently," but "they will weep as you weep now, and you will sit on a throne again." Krishna did not soften the wrong or blur the memory of it. He swore that it would be answered, measure for measure, and he staked the order of nature itself on his word — the heavens might fall, the Himavat split, the earth be rent, the oceans dry up, before that promise would break. And this, the forest knew, was not the language of a man comforting a woman; it was the language of a king giving his word before witnesses.

The weeping Draupadi heard him, and her tears slowed on her face. Those who knew Krishna knew that his word, once given, was firmer than the ground under their feet. Even Arjuna, standing among the allies, said nothing; there was nothing to add to a vow that had made the sky its surety.

In the evening, the talk among the gathered kings turned from grief to plans — of armies and alliances, and of the war that waited at the end of thirteen years. But those who had heard Krishna's words to Draupadi carried something else away with them: the memory of a queen weeping in exile, and the man who had promised her a throne with the fall of heaven as the only price of his failing. She, for her part, began that evening to believe it — because she knew, as everyone in that camp knew, that Krishna had never in his life spoken a word that the world had not, in the end, been forced to keep.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not tell Draupadi to be patient or to forget. He answers grief with a counter-vow, matching the wrong done to her with a future so certain that he stakes the order of nature on it — heaven falling, oceans drying up — before he will let his word fail. Consolation here is not softness; it is the same iron promise that will later be kept on the battlefield.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Krishna turned to Yudhishthira with a confession that had been burning in him since Dwaraka.

stories.title: Had I Been at Dwaraka
stories.story:
"If I had been present at Dwaraka," Krishna told Yudhishthira, "this evil would not have befallen thee."

The words came out of him like a confession, there in the Kamyaka forest where the exiled Pandavas sat with their allies around them. Everyone in that circle knew the story: how Yudhishthira had been drawn into a gambling match at Hastinapura, how the dice had been loaded, how he had staked and lost his wealth, his brothers, himself, and at last the queen herself — and how the Pandavas had been sent into exile for thirteen years. And everyone knew, too, that Krishna had not been there to stop it. He had been away from the Anarta country, the region of his own city Dwaraka, engaged against the forces of Salwa.

"Coming unto the gambling-match even if uninvited by the son of Amvika, or by Duryodhana, or by the other Kauravas," he went on, "I would have prevented the game from taking place, by showing its many evils — summoning to my aid Bhishma and Drona and Kripa, and Vahlika."

He laid out for Yudhishthira exactly what he would have done, as if the scene still played out behind his eyes. He would have stood before Dhritarashtra and told him plainly that his sons should have nothing to do with dice. He would have shown the evils through which the son of Virasena had formerly been deprived of his kingdom; he would have described how a man once engaged in the game continues to play, from the mere desire of victory, until ruin takes him — how through dice men in a single day lose their possessions, fall into distress, are deprived of their untasted wealth, and exchange harsh words with those they love. "Women, dice, hunting and drinking," he said, "to which people become addicted in consequence of temptation, have been regarded as the four evils that deprive a man of prosperity. Those versed in the Shastras hold that evils attend upon all these."

And he did not stop at counsel. If Dhritarashtra had accepted his words, he said, the welfare of the Kurus and virtue itself would both have been secured. But if the old king had rejected his gentle counsel, offered like medicine, Krishna would have compelled him by force. And if the men who waited at his court — professing to be his friends but in reality his foes — had supported him in the folly, Krishna would have slain them all, along with those gamblers, there in the hall itself.

"O Kauravya," he said, and his voice was rough with grief, "it is owing to my absence from the Anarta country at that time that thou hast fallen into such distress begot of dice."

Then he told Yudhishthira how he had learned of the calamity: on arriving at Dwaraka he had heard it all from Yuyudhana, and with his heart sore and agitated by grief he had come at speed, wishing only to see his friend. "Alas! O bull of the Bharata race," he said, "ye have all fallen into dire distress. I see thee with thy brothers plunged in misfortune."

It was strange, the Pandavas thought, to hear the man who had just sworn that the earth would drink their enemies' blood speak now like a man shouldering blame. He did not console them with assurances; he grieved with them, and he grieved for his own absence — for the single moment when his friends had needed him and he had been elsewhere, fighting his own war at Saubha, and the dice had fallen without him there to catch them. But the lament, for all its grief, was also a promise in disguise: whatever game came next, he would not be absent from it.
stories.reflection: Krishna's lament is both grief and claim. He names the four evils — women, dice, hunting, drinking — as the root of the ruin, but he also insists that his own presence would have changed everything, by counsel or by force. It is a friend's confession of where power truly lies: not in being everywhere, but in the one moment a friend is absent and disaster slips in.
stories.next_story_tease: And the forest would soon test that friendship again, when a furious sage and ten thousand disciples arrived without warning.

stories.title: A Prayer Heard in Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: How Draupadi's prayer crossed the miles to Krishna's side
stories.story:
In Dwaraka, Krishna lay asleep with Rukmini resting by his side. In the Kamyaka forest, far away, Draupadi's heart was failing her. And at that very moment ten thousand ascetics were walking toward the Pandavas' hermitage.

The sage Durvasa had timed his visit carefully. He had first ascertained that the Pandavas were all seated at their ease and that Draupadi had finished her meal and was reposing; then, surrounded by ten thousand disciples, he repaired to the forest. Yudhishthira, seeing such a guest arrive, went forward to receive him, joined his palms, pointed to an excellent seat, and gave the rishis a fit and respectful welcome. "Return quick, O adorable sir," he said, "after performing thy diurnal ablutions and observances." And the sinless muni, not troubling himself to wonder how the king would provide a feast for him and his disciples, went with them to the stream to bathe.

But Draupadi, devoted to her husbands, was in great anxiety about the food. The vessel that fed the Pandavas was a gift of the sun: it remained full until she had finished her meal, and empty after. She had already eaten. There was no food in it now, and no way of filling it — and a guest like Durvasa could not be turned away with apologies.

After much anxious thought, she came to the conclusion that there were no means of providing a feast. And so she did what she had done in her darkest hour before: she prayed. Inwardly, to Krishna, the slayer of Kamsa. "Krishna, O Krishna, of mighty arms, O son of Devaki, whose power is inexhaustible," she said in her heart, "thou art the soul, the creator and the destroyer of the universe, the saviour of the afflicted, ever kindly disposed towards those that take refuge in thee — thou with a complexion dark as the leaves of the blue lotus, eyes red as the corolla of the lily, attired in yellow robes, with the bright Kaustubha gem in thy bosom. As thou didst protect me before from Dussasana, do thou extricate me now from this difficulty."

The great and sovereign God, lord of the earth, of mysterious movements, ever kind to those who depend on him, heard her. Perceiving her difficulty, he instantly repaired to that place — leaving the bed of Rukmini, who slept on unaware.

Draupadi bowed down to him in great joy and told him everything: the arrival of the munis, the empty vessel, her fear of the sage's wrath. And Krishna, who had crossed half the world at the thought of her trouble, said only: "I am very much afflicted with hunger. Do thou give me some food without delay, and then thou mayst go about thy work."

She was confused. "The sun-given vessel remains full till I finish my meal," she said. "But I have already taken my meal today; there is no food in it now."

"This is no time for jest," said Krishna. "I am much distressed with hunger. Go thou quickly, fetch the vessel, and show it to me."

She had the vessel brought, and he looked into it and saw a particle of rice and vegetable sticking at its rim. He took it and swallowed it. "May it please the god Hari, the soul of the universe," he said, "and may that god who partaketh at sacrifices be satiated with this."

Then the long-armed Krishna, the soother of miseries, said to Bhimasena: "Do thou speedily invite the munis to dinner." And Bhima went quickly to the nearest stream of transparent, cool water — where Durvasa and his disciples, having plunged in, were rubbing their bodies and finding, to their astonishment, that their stomachs were full to the throat. They came out of the water and stared at one another. "Having bade the king make our meals ready, we have come hither for a bath," they said. "But how can we eat anything now? The repast hath been uselessly prepared for us."

And Durvasa, understanding at last, said: "By spoiling the repast, we have done a great wrong to that royal sage, king Yudhishthira."
stories.reflection: The story's hinge is that Draupadi's prayer is answered before it finishes: Krishna leaves Rukmini's bed in Dwaraka the instant the thought forms in the forest. And the miracle is rendered with almost comic smallness — not a feast conjured from the sky, but one leftover grain swallowed at the rim of an empty pot, after which the world quietly rearranges itself. Krishna's protection here is not spectacle; it is presence, arriving exactly when there was no other help.
stories.tradition_note: The sun-given vessel that fed the Pandavas until Draupadi had eaten is the same vessel the epic elsewhere calls the Akshaya-patra, and Durvasa's visit is one of several episodes that turn on its power.
stories.next_story_tease: Now Durvasa and his disciples had to face the king whose feast their own bellies had already consumed.

stories.title: A Single Grain for Ten Thousand
stories.subtitle: How Krishna fed the sage Durvasa and his ten thousand disciples with one grain of rice.
stories.story:
Ten thousand guests, and nothing to set before them.

It happened in the years the Pandavas spent in exile. One day the sage Durvasa arrived at their hermitage in the Kamyaka forest, and behind him came ten thousand disciples. He had not been expected, and there was no time to prepare. Ten thousand is not a number a household forgets; it is a number that empties a granary and breaks a cook's heart. Yudhishthira, the king without a kingdom, came forward with his mothers to receive him. He joined his palms, offered the sage an excellent seat, and spoke with perfect courtesy. Perform your ablutions in the river, he said, and return quickly, and the food will be ready.

It was a gracious invitation and a desperate one. There was no food to be had, and to send such a guest away unfed was unthinkable. A feast of any size was beyond them now; a feast for ten thousand was a thing to laugh or weep at. Draupadi, devoted to her husbands, had already finished the day's meal, and the cooking vessel was nearly bare. Durvasa, suspecting nothing of how the king would feed him and his host of followers, went down to the stream to bathe, and the ten thousand went with him.

Draupadi was in agony. She turned the problem over and over and found no way to provide a feast for ten thousand men. At last she did the only thing left to her: she prayed. Inwardly she called on Krishna, the son of Devaki, whose power was inexhaustible, the lord of the Universe, the saviour of the afflicted and the refuge of the helpless. She called on him whose face was dark as the leaves of the blue lotus and whose eyes were red as the lily, who wore yellow robes and the bright Kaustubha gem at his breast. And she begged him to cherish her with his kindness.

And Krishna came. He brought no carts of provisions and no army of cooks. He asked simply for whatever there was to eat, and Draupadi brought him the vessel. He looked into it, and there, sticking to its rim, was a single grain of rice and a scrap of vegetable. One grain — not even a mouthful. He swallowed it, and he spoke: 'May it please the god Hari, the soul of the Universe, and may the god who partakes at sacrifices be satisfied with this.'

That was all. A single grain, offered and accepted, and nothing more.

Down at the river something strange happened. Durvasa and his ten thousand disciples had plunged into the water and were rubbing their bodies, when one by one they stopped and looked about them. Every one of them felt, suddenly and unmistakably, that his stomach was full — completely, comfortably full, as after a rich feast. There was nothing more to ask for and nothing more to want. A man who is already full cannot in courtesy sit down to a meal, and a guest who is already satisfied cannot ask for more. To return now and ask for a feast they could not eat would be absurd, almost a small shame. So the sage and his ten thousand disciples did not return to the hermitage at all. They went on their way, and the Pandavas' nearly empty vessel had been enough.

Quietly, with no display, Krishna had met ten thousand hungers with a single grain of rice. Or, more truly, he had taken what little they had to give and made it more than enough. And the ten thousand, full and uncomprehending, went away none the wiser.
stories.reflection: The humor is quiet and exact — a sage with ten thousand disciples slipping away rather than admit he is already full. But the heart of it is the single grain: Krishna does not multiply abundance so much as accept what is offered with complete trust, and the scarcity simply stops being scarcity.

stories.title: Virtuous Men Never Suffer
stories.story:
The ten thousand disciples of Durvasa went down to the stream to bathe, and when they came out of the water they were full. Not full of the feast they had been promised — full in a way none of them could explain, their stomachs heavy to the throat. The great sage looked at his followers, and his followers looked at one another. Durvasa understood first. A feast had been promised them and they could not touch it — what king would forgive such an insult to his hospitality? The wrath of the royal sage Yudhishthira, they feared, would fall on them like fire. And so, without a word of farewell, the whole company slipped away from the Kamyaka forest as quietly as it had come, fleeing the anger they believed they had earned.

The Pandavas were left standing in the sudden quiet. A little while earlier the forest had been loud with the arrival of ten thousand ascetics, and Yudhishthira had gone forward with joined palms to welcome them, promising a meal for all of them. But the sun-given vessel from which the Pandavas ate each day held nothing, for Draupadi had already taken her food, and not a grain remained for a feast. Draupadi, alone with her worry, had done the only thing she could: she had called on Krishna, far away in Dwaraka, and he had heard her. She had reminded him of the other time she had needed him — the day in the assembly of the Kurus, when Dussasana had dragged her by the hair and the whole court had sat silent. "As you protected me then," she had prayed, "extricate me now from this difficulty." And Krishna had left the bed of Rukmini and come to her in an instant. He had looked into the empty vessel and found what a desperate eye could not: a single grain of rice and a leaf of vegetable clinging to its rim. That grain he had eaten. And in that same hour the sages bathing in the stream felt their hunger die in their stomachs.

Now Krishna stood before the Pandavas, and the brothers did not know how to thank him. He spoke first, and his words were simple. Knowing their danger from that wrathful sage, he said, he had been implored by Draupadi to come, and therefore he had come speedily. There was no need for fear now; the Rishi Durvasa was gone. And then he gave them the deeper assurance, the one they would carry long after the forest grew quiet again: virtuous men never suffer.

It was a strange comfort to hold, because their lives had been full of suffering — the poisoned feast, the lost kingdom, the exile, their wife dragged before an assembly of enemies who had shamed her. Yet the words came from someone who had crossed the whole distance from Dwaraka in the time it takes to say a name, and standing in his presence the brothers found that they could believe them.

The sages were gone. The feast that could not have been made had somehow been served. The danger that had filled the afternoon had dissolved like mist on the river. Krishna asked only one thing of them: their permission to return home. The Pandavas gave it freely, and watched him go.

When he had disappeared among the trees, the forest seemed to breathe again. Yudhishthira looked at the empty vessel, at the stream where the ascetics had bathed, at a sky that had never seemed so mild, and understood that the protection they had prayed for had been with them all along — nearer than the next breath, quicker than fear.
stories.reflection: Krishna's reassurance is striking for what it does not say: no rebuke of the sage, no drama about the miracle, only the quiet certainty that virtuous men never suffer. The relief comes not from Durvasa's retreat but from the discovery of who had been standing behind them all along.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Mathura, Krishna would soon send a trusted friend to Hastinapura to learn the truth of the Pandavas' suffering.

stories.title: An Errand for Akrura
stories.story:
Krishna walked through the streets of Mathura and stopped at the house of Akrura, and with him came Balarama and Uddhava. He did not send for his old friend, nor summon him to the palace; he came himself, on foot, to the door of the man who had once carried Kamsa's message and had come back carrying Krishna's grace instead.

When Akrura saw them approaching, he went out to meet them and bowed low before Krishna and Balarama, and they received his reverence and returned it. With his own hands he washed their feet, and held that water to his head as if it were the holiest thing he would ever touch, and then he seated them and sat at their feet, stroking them with the tenderness of a man who had waited a long time for this visit. "Blessed are our dwellings," he said, "that the teacher of the world has entered them."

"By good fortune," he said, "Kamsa is slain with all his followers, and this family is yours." Then his praise poured out like a river that had been dammed too long. These two, he said, were the foremost of persons, the cause and the substance of the world. Krishna creates, sustains and dissolves the universe with his own powers; whenever the ancient path of the Vedas is lost among men, he restores it for the good of all; and now he had come down into the house of Vasudeva to lighten the burden of the earth, spreading glory over his own family. Even the kings of the gods, he said, found Krishna's way hard to reach — and yet here he stood, inside the walls of a devotee's house. "What wise man," Akrura asked, "would seek refuge anywhere but in you — dear to your devotees, true in speech, a friend who remembers a kindness and grants every wish?" He spoke of the bonds that hold a man — son, wife, wealth, house, the body itself — and begged Krishna to cut them all, as if the lord's presence were a blade and his devotee's heart the rope.

Krishna heard him out, and then answered. Great souls like Akrura, he said, are the ones to be served, the most worthy of all. The holy places are not made of water, nor are the gods made of clay and stone. The true sacred presence lives in people — in a friend who wishes you well, in a heart that has bowed to the good. He might have said more, but he had come on other business, and now he spoke of it.

After their father Pandu died, Krishna told him, his children had been left with their mother, deep in sorrow, and the blind king of Hastinapura — the son of Ambika — dealt with his brother's sons out of a mean and troubled mind, guided by his wicked son. The boys had been brought to the capital after their father's death; they were there not by choice, and the king's house was not their home. "Go to Hastinapura," Krishna said, "and learn how the Pandavas fare — whether things go well with them or ill." Learn, and come back and tell me, was the meaning of it: not a war, not a proclamation, but a friend sent to look with his own eyes and report honestly.

Akrura bowed his head. He asked for no guard, no retinue, no letter of authority; a friend's eyes were the only credential he needed. He would go, and he would watch, and he would remember everything. Krishna, Balarama and Uddhava left him standing at his own door, and the house that had held the lord of the world felt, for a moment, like the center of the earth.
stories.reflection: The episode's quiet teaching is in Krishna's praise: holiness lives in people, not in things, and Akrura's bowed heart is a truer sacred place than any shrine of water or stone. The errand that follows shows the same instinct — the protection Krishna offers the Pandavas begins with one friend sent to look, and to tell the truth of what he sees.
stories.next_story_tease: In Hastinapura, a sorrowful woman waited to hear that someone from home still remembered her.

stories.title: A Doe Among Wolves
stories.story:
Hastinapura was full of eyes, and Kunti had learned to live under them. The palace of the Kurus was a place of whispers and rivalries, and in the years since Pandu's death she had felt herself watched from every side — the widow of the dead king, the mother of five boys the court had never wanted. Then word came that her brother Akrura had arrived from Mathura, and for the first time in many months, Kunti let herself hope.

Akrura did what courtesy required, and more. He greeted the elders of the house — Bahlika with his son, the sage Bharadvaja, Gautama, the old friends of the family — and then he settled in and watched. He stayed for months, asking little, seeing everything. He marked how the sons of Pandu shone: their brilliance, their strength, their courage, their humility, every good quality that had survived their father's death. And he marked, too, what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done to them — the poison mixed into their food, the cruelties that had no name in the law but were known to every whisper in the palace.

Then Kunti came to him, and she did not come composed. She was weeping. In the months of Akrura's stay she had kept her composure, as a queen of the Kurus must, but this was her brother, and with him the composure failed. Among her rivals, she told him, she was like a doe among wolves; every day she measured her children's danger by the faces that surrounded them. Then she asked the question that had pressed on her heart since the day she learned her brother was in the city. "Do they still remember us?" she said — her parents, her brothers, the home she had left behind in Mathura. "Do my father and brothers still think of me?" She did not ask for wealth or power or a return to favor; she asked only to be remembered, to know that the world she had left behind still held her name.

And then, as if the question had carried her to the edge of a deeper need, she turned from the messenger to the one he had come from. "The blessed Krishna, my brother's son," she said, "is the refuge, dear to his devotees. Krishna, Krishna," she cried, "great yogin, soul of the universe, protector of all beings! I see no refuge for us but your lotus feet." She spoke of him as her nephew, the boy of Mathura who was, she knew, more than any boy. "Salutation to Krishna, the pure one, the supreme self." If her parents had forgotten her, Krishna had not. If the wolves of Hastinapura closed in, the refuge was still there, as close as a name spoken through tears.

Akrura and Vidura stood with her, sharing her sorrow, taking it into themselves. Vidura — the wise uncle of the Kurus who had always loved the Pandavas — and Akrura, who had come straight from Krishna's side. Between the two of them they could give her what the palace never would: the assurance that she was not alone. The doe among wolves had spoken her grief aloud and been heard; and when she was heard, the wolves seemed a little further off.

That night, perhaps, Kunti slept more peacefully than she had in months. The prayer had gone out of her, carried on a friend's memory, and something in her knew that it had reached its destination — and that it had been answered, in the form of a friend's promise to carry her words back to Mathura, and in the shape of events that had not yet begun to stir.
stories.reflection: Kunti's grief is doubled: she is a widow among enemies, and her only refuge is a nephew far away. The story does not soften this — her prayer is said through tears, in the middle of a hostile court — and that is exactly why it is moving: the doe among wolves has nothing but her devotion, and the devotion is enough.
stories.next_story_tease: Before he left the city, Akrura had one more word for the blind king.
stories.hero_scene: In a quiet corner of the Hastinapura palace, Kunti weeping before Akrura — a doe among wolves — while Vidura stands beside them, sharing her sorrow.

stories.title: No One Dwells Here Forever
stories.story:
Before he left Hastinapura, Akrura asked to see the king. He had come to the city to learn how the Pandavas fared, and he had learned it — the poison, the cruelties, the slow grinding-down of five boys and their mother. Now, with that knowledge sitting in him like a stone, he went to the one man who could change it: the blind king Dhritarashtra, who sat on the throne his brother had left empty, and loved his own sons with a love that had gone crooked.

Akrura did not flatter him. He spoke as a friend of the house, plainly. "Rule the earth by righteousness," he said, "and win your subjects by good conduct. Act otherwise, and you will be blamed in every mouth and walk into darkness." Then he said the thing that kings rarely hear: no one dwells in this world forever with anyone. A being is born alone, and dies alone; no retinue follows a man out of the world, and the guards who surround a throne cannot surround a grave. The wealth a man gathers by wrong means is carried off by others of little wit; the man who nourishes his sons on unrighteousness, thinking himself clever, takes the guilt onto his own shoulders and is finally abandoned by those very sons. "Therefore this world, O king," Akrura said, "is a dream, a waking illusion, a fantasy of the mind. Do not anchor your soul to it."

Dhritarashtra heard him out. The truth of it was undeniable, and the old king admitted as much. "Even so, gentle one," he said, "your sweet words do not rest in my heart, because my heart is unsteady." He knew what was right; he loved his sons more than he could hold to what was right. His love for them sat on his mind like a weight, and the truth could not move it. And then he spoke the deeper helplessness, the one that makes counsel useless: "What man can undo the ordinance of the Lord?" The lord who, entering his own creation through his inscrutable power, sets in motion the wheel of the world — who could stand against that wheel, and who could call a man guilty for being crushed beneath it? He bowed to that power, unknowable in its play, and fell silent.

Akrura left the city as he had come, and the blind king remained on his throne, the truth ringing in his ears and no room for it in his heart. The counsel had been given; whether it would be kept was another matter, and Akrura knew better than to wait for the answer.

Back in Mathura, he went straight to Krishna and Balarama and told them everything — what he had seen of the Pandavas, what the sons of Dhritarashtra had done, and what the blind king had confessed when the truth was set before him. He told them how the king had heard every word of the counsel, and acknowledged the truth of every word, and how the acknowledgment had changed nothing in his heart. He reported it all without softening a word. Krishna listened. Balarama listened. The news did not surprise them, but it was news that had to be carried, and it had been carried by a friend's eyes and a friend's honesty.

The kingdom of the Kurus went on as it had. But from that day, nothing between Hastinapura and Mathura was quite what it had been. A message had passed between the two cities — not of war, not yet — and the road that carried it ran both ways.
stories.reflection: Dhritarashtra hears the truth and agrees with it, yet cannot act on it — the story's most honest moment. Akrura's counsel fails in the usual sense, and the failure is recorded without judgment: some truths find no hold in a heart that loves wrongly, and the wise know better than to wait for the answer.
stories.next_story_tease: Before long, Krishna himself would walk into the Pandavas' court at Indraprastha.

stories.title: A Visit That Made Them Whole
stories.story:
The city of Indraprastha was not expecting a guest that day, and that may be why the news ran through it like a wind. Krishna, who ruled on the far coast at Dwaraka, had come to see the Pandavas. He did not arrive with an army or a summons. He came, the old telling says, simply to see them; and the five brothers, who had known him longest in exile and danger, went out to him before any court ceremony could be arranged.

The Pandavas were kings now, settled in the capital they had built on the banks of the Yamuna, and Yudhishthira's rule had already made the kingdom prosperous. But none of that ceremony mattered the moment Krishna stepped down. Yudhishthira rose at once, and Bhima with him, and they embraced him with both arms, the way men embrace a brother who has crossed a hundred lands to stand in their doorway. The touch of him, the tellers say, seemed to wash away the weariness of every hard year they had carried. Krishna paid his respects first to Yudhishthira and Bhima, then to the others as they pressed forward, and Draupadi led him herself to the finest seat in the hall. Satyaki, who had ridden with him from Dwaraka, was received with the same warmth, honored and greeted by each of the brothers in turn.

But it was Kunti who spoke for them all. She had been mother to these boys through the years of wandering and want, when Krishna had been the one cousin who remembered them, who came to them, who wrote to them in their exile. Now she stood before him, the queen of a great house, and her composure broke. Weeping, her voice choked with love, she said, "Now we are safe, for you have remembered us."

They understood what she meant. Safety, for Kunti, was not walls or armies. It was being remembered by the one person in the world whose friendship could not be bought, threatened, or worn out. The boy who had come to their forest hut in the years of hiding was now the master of Dwaraka, and he was still the same friend. Her tears were not grief. They were the relief of a woman who had watched her sons survive everything, and had only ever asked one thing of the world: that they not be forgotten.

Yudhishthira asked him to stay through the rains, and Krishna stayed. Four months he remained at Indraprastha, through the slow green season when the roads dissolved and the world turned inward. He did not come as a king to be entertained. He lived among them, at ease — sitting with Yudhishthira over the long questions of kingship, testing grips with Bhima, walking the gardens with Arjuna, letting the twins argue with him about horses and swords. The old telling closes the account with a plain sentence: he delighted them all.

In those four months he was simply what he had always been to them: a cousin visiting, a friend at leisure, the one ally who had never once asked what the friendship was worth. The palace of Indraprastha, so often a stage for plots and prophecies, became for a season only a house where someone beloved was staying — and no one in it wanted the rains to end.

When at last he left, he took nothing with him but their goodbyes, and left behind a household that had been, for a little while, whole.
stories.reflection: Kunti's words — "now we are safe, for you have remembered us" — define the Pandavas' bond with Krishna more exactly than any treaty: safety as being remembered. The story's quiet power is that nothing is accomplished in it; a visit, an embrace, a season of joy — and that is precisely the point.
stories.next_story_tease: But the friendship was about to be tested in fire: the forest of Khandava was waiting, and Agni would not be denied.

stories.title: Krishna Grants the Khadava Forest to Agni
stories.story:
There came a time when Agni, the god of fire, set his desire on the Khadava forest. It was an ancient woodland, thick and deep, older than memory, and he wished to consume it — to feed on it as fire feeds, until nothing was left but ash. Agni is not a god who begs, and he is not a god who is refused. And the strange thing was this: the forest was not torn from him or taken by force. It was given, freely, by the two men who stood at its edge. And the giving of it would change the fortunes of the Pandavas forever.

Krishna was dwelling then among the Pandavas, not as a guest but as a friend and kinsman, wishing only to do them good. When the moment came, it was Krishna who stood beside Arjuna, and who took up the reins of Arjuna's chariot with his own hands, to serve as his charioteer. It was a small thing to watch, a friend taking the reins; but it placed Krishna exactly where the moment needed him.

For this task Arjuna would need a steady hand. To give a forest to fire meant to let the fire have its way — to watch the great woodland, tree by tree, turn to flame, the smoke rising in a black column over the land, the heat rolling out across the plain until it pressed against the face. There is no sound quite like a forest burning in earnest: the crack of sap, the hiss of green wood surrendering, the long sigh of a trunk giving way. And so it happened. With Krishna holding the reins and Arjuna at the bow, the Khadava forest was given over to Agni. The god of fire fell upon it and consumed it, until the ancient trees were gone and only ash remained, glowing faintly where the forest had stood.

Krishna asked for nothing in all of this. He did not fight for his own sake, and he claimed no share of what was given. He simply held the reins, so that his friend could give the forest to the god who asked for it. The whole deed was an act of friendship — between Krishna and the Pandavas, and between Arjuna and the fire.

Agni was pleased, and a pleased god does not leave empty-handed those who served him. To Arjuna he gave the great bow called Gandiva, a weapon whose name would be spoken with awe for generations. He gave him white horses, swift and gleaming, and a chariot that no enemy could stop. And he gave him quivers that would never run empty — however many arrows Arjuna drew, there would always be another waiting at his fingertips. Each gift was a piece of what the Pandavas would become.

Out of the burning itself came one more gift. Maya, the master builder, had been caught in the forest as the fire swept through it, and his life was spared. In gratitude he would raise for the Pandavas their great assembly hall — a hall so beautiful that those who entered it could not say whether it had been built by human hands or by something finer.

It was a strange bargain: an ancient forest gone in a season, and in its place the beginnings of a kingdom's strength. So the forest's destruction became the Pandavas' founding. From the ash came the bow and the horses, the unstoppable chariot and the endless quivers, and a hall that kings would come to envy. The fire had taken much; but what it left behind would arm and shelter a dynasty.
stories.reflection: The Khadava forest is one of those episodes where destruction and founding turn out to be the same thing. Agni consumed an ancient woodland, and from the ash the Pandavas received the weapons and the hall on which their power would rest — while Krishna's whole part was simply to hold the reins.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana condenses this episode to a few verses; the Mahabharata tells the burning of the Khadava forest at far greater length.
stories.next_story_tease: The hall Maya built for the Pandavas would soon host the great Rajasuya sacrifice.

stories.title: The City That Rose to Meet Him
stories.story:
News traveled ahead of the chariots. Krishna was coming — not for a visit this time, but for the Rajasuya, the great sacrifice through which Yudhishthira meant to be acknowledged as a king of kings. And the city of Indraprastha met him the way a festival meets the sun.

The streets had been swept and sprinkled with water fragrant with elephant musk. Banners streamed from every rooftop, golden arches stood at the crossings, and at each doorway sat the full pitchers that are the auspicious vessels of welcome. From the palace, Yudhishthira came out to meet him with his preceptors and his friends, and the sound that went before them was music and the chanting of the Vedas at once. When Krishna stepped down, the heart of the king of the Pandavas melted. Yudhishthira took him in both arms and held him, and the embrace said everything a court could not.

Bhima embraced him next, smiling through eyes blurred with love — Krishna was his mother's sister's son, his own cousin. Arjuna folded him in his arms. The twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, bowed and touched his feet. Around them the bards and panegyrists sang his praises, and the whole assembly seemed to press inward, each person wanting to be nearer to him. Of the welcome, the old telling notes simply that Krishna stood at the center of it like the jewel crowning a hundred good reputations.

The women of the city had abandoned their household work the moment the news came. Down the king's road they hurried, hair-braids coming loose and garments slipping in their eagerness, to stand where they could watch him pass. From the rooftops they showered flowers on him and welcomed him with smiles, embracing him in their minds. Those who caught sight of Krishna's queens — Rukmini, Satyabhama, Bhadra, Jambavati — murmured to one another that the ladies of the Vrishni house moved among them like the stars around the moon. What had those women done, they asked, to be looked on by one whose glance made a festival of the eyes of all the world?

In the palace, Kunti rose from her couch and went to meet her sister's son. Krishna bowed to his aunt and to the elder women of the household, and Kunti brought Govinda home with her own hands, honoring him as the lord of the three worlds. At her mother-in-law's bidding, Draupadi welcomed each of Krishna's queens — Kalindi, Mitravinda, Saibya, Nagnajiti, and the rest — and settled them in the women's quarters with every honor.

Yudhishthira settled Janardana himself, giving him the best of the palace. And when Krishna was seated at ease, the king spoke, and in the Mahabharata's telling his words are plain. "It is because of you that the whole earth is under my sway," he said. "It is through your grace that I have gathered this wealth. I desire to give it away according to the ordinance, to the brahmanas and to the fire. Grant me permission to perform the sacrifice with you and my brothers — install yourself at it, for if you perform it, I shall be cleansed of sin."

Krishna answered with the affection of a friend who wants nothing from the friendship. "You deserve imperial dignity. Let the great sacrifice be performed by you; if you perform it and obtain its fruit, we shall all regard ourselves as crowned with success. I am always engaged in seeking your good. Perform the sacrifice you desire — and employ me in some office for it, for I should obey all your commands."

"Then my resolve is already crowned with fruit," Yudhishthira said, "since you have arrived here just as I wished."

So the son of Pandu set himself, with his brothers, to gathering the materials for the Rajasuya, and the arrival that had begun in embraces and showers of flowers became the beginning of the greatest sacrifice the age would see. For a few days more, though, there was only this: a king's city gladdened by the presence of its truest friend, like a dark region made bright by the sun.
stories.reflection: The Rajasuya is often remembered as the summit of Yudhishthira's glory, but this story records the arrival as pure affection — a city that empties its households to see one man pass. The political begins as the personal: the king who would conquer the world first asks his cousin to bless the undertaking.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata frames the same arrival differently — Krishna coming with a mass of treasure for Yudhishthira and a Yadava army under Vasudeva's command. This account follows the Bhagavata's framing of the arrival as a reunion of love.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet not long before this day of glory, the same friendship had nearly been broken by an elopement — Arjuna had carried off Krishna's sister from the very heart of Dwaraka.

stories.title: The Renunciant Who Carried Off a Bride
stories.story:
The rumor reached Arjuna on the pilgrim road, and it turned his wandering into a rescue. At Dwaraka, it was said, Balarama had decided to give their sister Subhadra in marriage to Duryodhana. The plan had been kept close — no one outside the house knew of it — but Arjuna, walking the holy places during his long exile from Indraprastha, heard it anyway; and the thought of it burned in him.

He knew Subhadra. He had seen her the way a man sees a name written in light, and he was not about to let her be given to the cousin who hated his brothers. And so the second son of Pandu, who had faced armies without blinking, did a strange thing: he put aside the warrior's dress and went to Dwaraka as a wandering renunciant, carrying the triple staff of a mendicant, and entered the city where the Yadavas — his own mother's kin, his friends — would never think to look for him in that garb.

It was the rainy season, and he stayed in Dwaraka through its months, patient, waiting for his moment. The Yadavas took the young ascetic in without question, as hospitality is given to the wandering holy man. One day Arjuna was brought into a house and offered guest-offerings, and there he saw her — Subhadra, the great-hearted maiden, the one who stole the hearts of heroes. And she, seeing him, desired him; the old telling says it plainly, that he was the one who stole the hearts of women. Neither of them spoke of it aloud. They did not need to.

Then came the day of a great festival procession, when the image of the gods was carried out of the city. The chariots rolled through the gate, the crowds followed, and Subhadra rode in one of them. In the joyful confusion — when the guards' eyes were on the procession and no one was watching the quiet renunciant — Arjuna saw his chance. He seized his bow, took the chariot's reins, and carried her off, curbing the brave warriors who rushed to stop him.

The news ran back to Dwaraka before the wheels had settled. And Balarama — the elder, the mighty, the one who had raised his hand against kings — broke. His anger rose like the ocean at full moon, sudden and immense. The warriors of the Vrishni race spoke of pursuit and punishment, of the insult done to their house, and for a while it seemed the road behind Arjuna would fill with armed men.

Then Krishna spoke — he whom the old telling also calls Vasudeva — and his words turned the storm. What Arjuna had done, they argued, was not an insult but an honor. The house of Vrishni was not for sale: no daughter of theirs was to be given in marriage like an animal, no one was to be sold like goods, and a self-choice was a gamble no father should make for his daughter. Arjuna had seen the faults in every gentler method and had taken the maiden by force, according to the ordinance of warriors — and who could fault him? He was the son of Kunti, born of the line of Bharata, and there was no one in all the worlds who could vanquish Partha in battle except the three-eyed god himself. "Go to him," Krishna said, "and by conciliation stop him and bring him back. If he rides home after defeating us, our fame is gone. There is no disgrace in friendship."

The Yadavas went out and stopped Arjuna — with words, not weapons. He turned his chariot back to Dwaraka, and there, welcomed and honored by the sons of Vrishni, he was united in marriage with Subhadra. And the anger that had risen like a tide went out again: Balarama, appeased, sent rich wedding gifts for the bride and the groom, and the house of Vrishni made the marriage its own.

When at last Arjuna brought his bride to Indraprastha, the welcome there was warmer than the road had been long. Draupadi, who had waited through his travels, met her new rival with a jealousy that dissolved within the day: Subhadra came to her and said, "I am your maid," and Draupadi rose and embraced her and answered, "Let your husband be without a foe." Kunti, from excess of affection, blessed the girl who had become her daughter. And from that day, the old telling says, the Pandavas' household lived happily.
stories.reflection: Krishna's defense of the elopement is remarkable for what it protects: not Arjuna's honor but his family's. The argument that a bride must not be given like an animal or sold like goods turns a scandal into a principle — the Yadavas did not lose face, they gained the alliance of the Pandavas, and the anger that might have ended in war ended in wedding gifts.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata gives the decisive speech for the alliance to Vasudeva, Krishna's father, and adds the full story of Subhadra's welcome at Indraprastha; the Bhagavata condenses the episode and credits Krishna himself with pacifying Balarama. This account follows the Bhagavata's shape.
stories.next_story_tease: At the great sacrifice that followed, the man who had stolen Subhadra would watch Krishna take the humblest office in the hall.

stories.title: The Highest Hands at the Lowest Work
stories.story:
On the last day of the Rajasuya, when the king himself was to be sprinkled with the consecrating waters, the inner enclosure of the sacrificial ground held the most extraordinary assembly the age had gathered. The great brahmana seers had come with the invited kings — rishis who had lived on mountain air and silence, seated now at ease beside thrones, with Narada at their head, he who had seen more ages begin and end than the kings there had counted years. They talked, they debated, they argued philosophy like hawks darting at meat thrown into the air; the enclosure, crowded with gods and seers and kings, shone like the sky thick with stars. No one without vows was near that platform. Yudhishthira's sacrifice had drawn the whole world, and the whole world had come in its best.

Narada looked at the king's prosperity, born of the sacrifice, and was glad. Then he looked at the vast concourse of Kshatriyas — the warriors of a hundred kingdoms, the pride of every royal house in the land — and he grew thoughtful. He remembered words he had heard of old in the mansion of Brahma, when the celestials had been commanded to be born on earth, to meet one another in the field of war, and to return. He knew that this assembly was no mere gathering of princes. It was a concourse of incarnate gods, and the one who moved among them as a man was the one he had known as the source of all things, Narayana, the lord of all, who had taken birth in the line of the Yadavas. The seer sat at the sacrifice of the wise king with feelings of awe, and he saw what no one else in that brilliant hall could see: that this shining gathering was a field being sown for a harvest no one wanted to name.

And into the middle of that glory came the moment the tellers have never forgotten.

Krishna — he who was himself the centre of all worlds, round whom every creature moved — was engaged at his own will in washing the feet of the brahmanas.

He did it himself. The one whom the seers knew as the Self-Create took up the menial office of the sacrifice — the office no proud man would take — and washed the feet of the priests, desirous of excellent fruits, at his own will. No one had asked him. No one could have commanded him. He chose it: the highest bending to the lowest service, and the gesture was so quiet that the old telling records it without fuss, as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Then Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, rose and addressed Yudhishthira. "Let the arghya be offered to the kings, each as he deserves," he said. "There are six who deserve honor — the preceptor, the sacrificial priest, the relative, the Snataka, the friend, the king. But let the first arghya be offered to the foremost among those present. As the sun among all luminous objects, so is this one among us, in energy, in strength, in prowess. This sacrificial mansion is illuminated and gladdened by him as a sunless region is by the sun, as still air by a breeze."

Yudhishthira asked whom he meant, and Bhishma judged by his intelligence and named Krishna. And at the grandsire's command, Sahadeva duly presented the first arghya of excellent ingredients to Krishna of the Vrishni race, and Krishna accepted it according to the forms of the ordinance.

The hall had seen the lord of all worlds wash the feet of servants; now it saw him raised above all kings. The two honors belonged to the same act, and the whole assembly knew it: the one who served all was fit to be honored by all. For a moment the sacrifice held both images together — the bent back at the water, the raised vessel of honor — and that was the truest thing the Rajasuya showed that day.

But among the seated kings, one had watched the first arghya with a face like a closed fist. His grievance was older than the sacrifice, and it would not wait for the consecration.
stories.reflection: The juxtaposition is the meaning: the same man takes the lowest office in the sacrifice and then receives its highest honor, and no one finds the two in tension. Narada's vision — that the assembly was a concourse of gods gathered to thin the burdened earth — gives the scene its quiet weight: the one serving at the feet of priests is the one who set the whole gathering in motion.
stories.next_story_tease: One king's old grievance, smoldering through the honors, was about to turn the assembly to battle.
