stories.title: Shishupala Incites the Kings to Battle
stories.story:
Krishna had received the first worship of the Rajasuya, and the great hall of Indraprastha changed in a single breath from a place of ceremony into a place of war. The kings of the earth had come to Yudhishthira's sacrifice from every direction, to witness the rite, to share in its glory, to be counted among its guests. And when the first offering of honor went to Krishna, before any of them, the assembly had felt the sting of it. They had carried that sting through the long rites, and the air of the hall had grown thick with it.

Then Shishupala, king of Chedi, rose and gave the anger a voice. "When I am here to head you all," he cried out, "what are you thinking of now? Arrayed, let us stand in battle against the assembled Vrishnis and the Pandavas!"

The words found their mark at once. The vast assembly of kings, already agitated with wrath, stirred like the terrific sea when the winds that blow at the time of universal dissolution whip it into frenzy. All around the hall, the countless waves of troops that had ridden in with their masters seemed to gather themselves for a rush. It was the moment the ceremonies had been building toward without anyone daring to name it.

Krishna saw it before anyone else. Seated in his place, he understood that the vast sea of monarchs, with its countless waves of troops, was preparing for a terrific rush, and he did not move. He neither rose nor reached for a weapon nor called for his chariot. He waited, as a man waits when he has already seen the end of a thing.

Yudhishthira saw the same storm and read it differently. This was his sacrifice, his city, his guests, and the ruin of any one of them would be his. He leaned toward Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, who sat near him like a mountain among men. "This vast ocean of kings has been agitated by wrath," he said. "Tell me, O Grandsire, what I should do, so that my sacrifice may not be obstructed and my subjects may not be injured."

Bhishma answered as though the matter were already settled. "Fear not, O tiger of the Kurus. Can the dog slay the lion? As dogs in a pack approach the lion that is asleep and bark together, so are all these lords of earth. Before the sleeping lion of the Vrishni race, these monarchs are only barking in rage. Achyuta now is like a lion asleep. Until he wakes, this chief of the Chedis makes these monarchs look like lions."

The old man's voice did not rise, and the hall leaned in to hear him. "This Shishupala, possessed of little intelligence, is desirous of taking all these kings along with him, through the agency of him who is the soul of the universe, to the regions of Yama. Assuredly, Vishnu has been desirous of taking back unto himself the energy that exists in this Shishupala. The intelligence of this wicked-minded king of the Chedis, as also of all these monarchs, has become perverse. Indeed, the intelligence of all those whom this tiger among men desires to take unto himself becomes perverse, even like that of the king of the Chedis. O Yudhishthira, Madhava is the progenitor as also the destroyer of all created beings of the four species existing in the three worlds."

He fell silent, and the silence was heavier than the shouting had been. Kings glanced at one another, uncertain whether the rage they felt was their own or something placed in them.

But the ruler of Chedis had heard every word, and it had not cooled him. He turned on the grandsire, and when he spoke, his words were stern and rough, the words of a man who means to answer a prophecy with a war.
stories.reflection: Bhishma's calm before a hall of furious kings is not a dismissal of their numbers; it is a reading of their anger as a prelude. The more the monarchs rage, the closer he knows the end to be — the fury of the hall is not the danger but the sign.
stories.next_story_tease: Shishupala, however, had heard every word — and his answer was already forming on his lips.

stories.title: Bhishma Foretells That Krishna Will Destroy Shishupala
stories.story:
The hall of Indraprastha balanced on a single moment. Shishupala, king of Chedi, had called the assembled monarchs to war, and the rage he had spoken for had not subsided; it had gathered. Yudhishthira, whose sacrifice this was, looked across the sea of angry kings at Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, as though the old man were the only fixed thing left in the room.

"Tell me, O Grandsire," he said, "what I should do, so that my sacrifice may not be obstructed and my subjects may not be injured."

Bhishma answered without hesitation. "Fear not, O tiger of the Kurus. Can the dog slay the lion? As dogs in a pack approach the lion that is asleep and bark together, so are all these lords of earth. Before the sleeping lion of the Vrishni race, these monarchs bark in rage. Achyuta now is like a lion asleep. Until he wakes, this chief of the Chedis makes these monarchs look like lions."

Then the grandsire spoke of what he truly saw in the commotion. "This Shishupala, possessed of little intelligence, is desirous of taking all these kings along with him, through the agency of him who is the soul of the universe, to the regions of Yama. Assuredly, O Bharata, Vishnu has been desirous of taking back unto himself the energy that exists in this Shishupala. The intelligence of this wicked-minded king of the Chedis, as also of all these monarchs, has become perverse; for the intelligence of all those whom this tiger among men desires to take unto himself becomes perverse, even like that of the king of the Chedis. O Yudhishthira, Madhava is the progenitor as also the destroyer of all created beings of the four species existing in the three worlds."

It was the kind of speech that should have silenced a hall; it silenced everyone except Shishupala.

"Old and infamous wretch of your race," the king of Chedis said, turning on the grandsire, "are you not ashamed of affrighting all these monarchs with these numerous false terrors? You are the foremost of the Kurus, and living as you do in the third state, celibacy, it is but fit for you to give counsel so wide of morality. Like a boat tied to another boat, like the blind following the blind, are the Kurus who have you for their guide."

He was not done with Bhishma's praise of Krishna. "You have simply pained our hearts by reciting the deeds of this one, the slaying of Putana and others. If Krishna in his infancy slew a vulture, what is there remarkable in that? What of his slaughter of Aswa and Vrishava, both unskilled in battle? If he threw down by a kick an inanimate piece of wood, a car, what is there wonderful in that? What is remarkable in his having supported for a week the Govardhan mount, which is like an anthill? 'While sporting on the top of a mountain, he ate a large quantity of food' — hearing these words of yours, many have wondered exceedingly. But is not this still more wrongful, that Kamsa, whose food this one ate, has been slain by him?"

Then the king of Chedis turned from the deeds to the law. "The virtuous and the wise always instruct the honest that weapons must never be made to descend upon women, kine, and Brahmanas, upon those whose food has been taken, and upon those whose shelter has been enjoyed. It seems all these teachings have been thrown away by you. Desiring to praise Kesava, you describe him before me as great and superior in knowledge and age, as if I knew nothing. If at your word one who has slain women and kine is worshipped, what is to become of this great lesson? How can one who is such deserve praise?"

Then he turned on the man himself. "If you know the ways of morality, if your mind is guided by wisdom, blessed be you. Then why, O Bhishma, was that virtuous girl Amva, who had set her heart upon another, carried off by you, so proud of wisdom and virtue? Your brother Vichitravirya, knowing her condition, did not marry her though she was brought by you. Boasting of virtue as you do, in your very sight sons were begotten upon the widow of your brother by another, according to the ways of the honest. Where is your virtue, O Bhishma? This celibacy of yours, led either from ignorance or from impotence, is fruitless. Worship, gift, study, sacrifices distinguished by large gifts to the Brahmanas — all these equal not even one-sixteenth part of that which is obtained by the possession of a son. You are childless and old, the expounder of false morality."

The hall had gone very still. When Shishupala spoke again, his voice had dropped, and what came next was not an insult but a sentence. "Like the swan in the story," he said, "you shall now die at the hands of your relatives. Other men possessed of knowledge have said this of old, and I will presently recite it fully in your hearing."

And he began the tale of the old swan on the sea-coast, a bird forever preaching virtue to the feathery tribe while its own conduct fell short. The kings leaned forward, understanding what was being promised — and what was being dared.
stories.reflection: Shishupala's mockery dismisses as ordinary the very deeds the tradition treasures — Govardhan, Putana, Kamsa — while his attack on Bhishma carries its own prophecy. He names the grandsire's death at the hands of his relatives without seeing that his own fate has already been named, in the same breath, by Bhishma.
stories.next_story_tease: Behind Shishupala's rage lay an old story of a mother's plea and a promise that was nearly spent.
stories.hero_scene: Bhishma, white-haired and unflinching, addresses the furious assembly with one hand raised in reassurance — comparing the raging kings to dogs before a sleeping lion — while Shishupala stands opposite with burning eyes, about to answer.

stories.title: Krishna Grants Shishupala's Mother the Boon of a Hundred Offences
stories.story:
To understand the king who now stood raging in the hall at Indraprastha, Bhishma said, one had to go back to his birth, in the city of Chedi.

The child born to the king of Chedi had three eyes and four hands. The moment he drew breath, he screamed and brayed like an ass, and the sound of it struck fear into his father, his mother, and all their kin. Such omens were not to be borne; his parents resolved to abandon him.

Then an incorporeal voice spoke to the king and his wife, with their ministers and priests, all with hearts paralyzed by anxiety. "This son of yours, O king," the voice said, "will become both fortunate and superior in strength. Therefore you have no fear from him. Cherish the child without anxiety. He will not die in childhood; his time is not yet come. He that will slay him with weapons has also been born."

The mother, rendered anxious by affection for her son, bowed and asked the invisible being: "I desire to hear who will be the slayer of this my son." And the voice answered: "He upon whose lap this child, being placed, his superfluous arms fall down upon the ground like a pair of five-headed snakes, and at the sight of whom the third eye on his forehead disappears — he will be his slayer."

Hearing of the child with three eyes and four arms, and of the words of the invisible being, all the kings of the earth went to Chedi to behold him. The king of Chedi, worshipping the monarchs as each deserved, placed his child upon their laps one after another. And though the child passed through the laps of a thousand kings, the sign that the voice had promised did not come to pass.

Word of the wonder reached Dwaravati, and the mighty Yadava heroes, Balarama and Krishna, set out to see their father's sister, that daughter of the Yadavas who was queen of Chedi. They saluted everyone according to his rank, and the king and queen, and asked after everyone's welfare; and when the heroes had been worshipped, the queen, with great pleasure, herself placed the child on the lap of Krishna.

As soon as the child was placed on his lap, the superfluous arms fell to the ground, and the eye on his forehead disappeared. And the queen, beholding it, was filled with alarm and anxiety, and begged Krishna for a boon. "O mighty-armed Krishna," she said, "I am afflicted with fear. Grant me a boon. You are the assurer of all afflicted ones, the dispeller of everyone's fear."

Krishna said: "Fear not, O respected one. You are acquainted with morality; you need have no fear from me. What boon shall I give you? What shall I do, O aunt? Whether able or not, I shall do your bidding."

The queen said: "You will have to pardon the offences of Shishupala for my sake. O tiger of the Yadu race, know that even this is the boon I ask."

And Krishna said: "O aunt, even when he will deserve to be slain, I will pardon a hundred offences of his. Grieve not."

So the old story ran, told that day in the hall at Indraprastha while the king of Chedi stood before the assembly, burning with pride in that very promise. "Even thus, O Bhima," Bhishma said, turning to the sons of Pandu, "is this wretch of a king, Shishupala of wicked heart, who, proud of the boon granted by Govinda, summons you to battle."

The hundred offences had been counted out over the years, in slights and mockeries and open insults. And the count, Bhishma did not need to say, was nearly spent.
stories.reflection: A mother's plea converts an omen of death into a hundred pardons, and the child's own body marks his slayer the moment Krishna touches him. The boon does not erase the sign; it only postpones it — and the hundred offences, counted out over a lifetime, are what make the final reckoning possible.
stories.next_story_tease: The hundred pardons were nearly spent — and the sacrifice that had gathered them all to Indraprastha had first been announced, long before, in Dwaraka.

stories.title: Narada Announces the Rajasuya
stories.story:
The sage Narada appeared in Krishna's hall at Dwaraka like a light entering a room. The divine sage who travels between the worlds, messenger of the gods and known in every court, came in radiant, his matted locks the color of tawny flame, and the whole assembly stirred at his coming.

Krishna rose and received him as a sage must be received. He honored Narada with the rites, saw that a seat was set for him, and waited until the sage was at ease before he spoke, for a guest who had crossed the three worlds deserved every courtesy. "Is there any fear today in the three worlds?" Krishna asked him. "For nothing is hidden from you among the worlds and those who rule them."

Narada bowed and answered. "Who is able to know your doings rightly?" he said. "You create this world through your own power of illusion and draw it back again; you bring release to the soul that wanders, ignorant, through the body that carries it toward misfortune. What you do, who can measure it?"

Those who sat in the hall knew better than to take the sage's words for idle courtesy. Narada did not travel between the worlds to pass the time; when he spoke, courts listened, because his news always carried weight. And this day, everyone present felt, his news would be of a different order entirely.

"But," the sage said, and his tone changed from praise to announcement, "I will proclaim before the world this play within the world of mortals. The Pandava Yudhishthira, your cousin, desiring imperial sovereignty, will worship you with the Rajasuya, the sacrifice of emperors. In that best of rites, O God, even the gods themselves and all who dwell near you are purified — by hearing of you, by chanting your name, by meditating upon you."

Narada went on, and the hall listened to him speak of Krishna as it had never quite heard anyone speak. "Your fame is spotless in heaven, and it is spread through the lower worlds and upon the earth — a blessing to the worlds, a canopy over the quarters. The water that has washed your feet purifies the universe: in heaven it is called Mandakini, in the worlds below Bhogavati, and here upon the earth, Ganga."

Narada fell silent, and the words hung in the air like a stone dropped into still water. Then the sage delivered his request. Yudhishthira would perform the Rajasuya, and Krishna should consent to it; he should come to the sacrifice, and his presence would be its heart. The announcement hung in the hall like a summons: a king of the world, asking through the messenger of the gods, that Krishna come and be worshipped at the sacrifice of emperors. The assembled Yadavas stirred, for a request carried by Narada was a request that would not go unanswered.

Krishna heard all of it, he who knows everything before it is spoken — and he received it as though it were news, as though he were a man who needed counsel. He turned to Uddhava, his friend and his minister, and asked him what he thought, like one playfully seeking advice on a matter already decided.

The question hung in the air after the sage had gone: how the lord of Dwaraka would answer the summons, and what the emperor's sacrifice would bring. But Uddhava would not be long in answering. Krishna's question to his friend had been a decision already made, and the road from Dwaraka to Indraprastha would be traveled again, bearing the Yadavas and their lord to the sacrifice of emperors.
stories.reflection: Narada's announcement frames the Rajasuya as more than a king's ambition: the rite is a world-event, its very telling a purification, its heart Krishna's consent. And Krishna, who knows everything, receives it as though it were news — a god playfully asking counsel, so that the world's great rites may proceed as friendship, not as command.
stories.next_story_tease: Uddhava's counsel would shape how the Yadavas answered the summons to Indraprastha.

stories.title: Yudhishthira Asks Krishna's Blessing
stories.story:
The treasury of Indraprastha had grown so heavy that no one imagined it could be emptied in a hundred years. Yet no one thought of that wealth as greed made visible. In those days of Yudhishthira's rule, clouds poured exactly as much rain as the people wished, fields and herds and trade flourished, and the kingdom knew no drought, flood, plague, or fire. Even thieves and cheats, it was said, gave up lying when they dealt with each other, and foreign kings came to the court only to serve, to worship, or to offer tribute that would not impoverish them — never to fight.

It was this kingdom, prosperous beyond dreaming, that Yudhishthira's friends and ministers approached, each separately and all together. "The time has come, exalted one, for your sacrifice," they said. "Let arrangements be made without delay." And the son of Pandu, weighing the fullness of his treasury, fixed his heart on the Rajasuya, the sacrifice that belonged to emperors — a rite so great that it was said to purify everything it touched.

It was then that Krishna came to Indraprastha. He came as a friend comes to a celebration: not alone, but at the head of a great host, chariot wheels rattling over the roads, bringing with him a large mass of treasure for the king — an inexhaustible ocean of gems, the chronicle says — and leaving the Yadava army in Vasudeva's command, as a man does who means to stay. The capital was gladdened by his presence the way a dark region is gladdened by the sun, or still air by a gentle breeze.

Yudhishthira received him with joy and all due honor, and when Krishna had been seated at ease, the king stood before him with Dhaumya and Dwaipayana and the other sacrificial priests, and with Bhima and Arjuna and the twins.

"Krishna," he said, "it is for you that the whole earth is under my sway. Through your grace this vast wealth has come to me, and I desire to devote it according to the ordinance to the brahmanas and to the fire that carries the offerings. Grant me permission, then, to celebrate a sacrifice with you and with my younger brothers. Better still, install yourself at that sacrifice. For if you perform it, I shall be cleansed of sin. Or, if you will, permit me to be installed at it with my brothers, and by your permission I shall enjoy the fruit of an excellent rite."

There was no ceremony in his voice, no king's formality. What the son of Pandu asked for, before the whole court, was Krishna's blessing on the grandest ambition of his life.

Krishna, extolling his virtues, answered him. "You, O tiger among kings, deserve imperial dignity. Let the great sacrifice be performed by you. When you have conquered all the kings and gathered the requisites, the rite should be performed — and once it is, none can surpass you in splendor, not even the gods. If you perform the sacrifice and obtain its fruit, we shall all regard ourselves as crowned with success. I am always engaged in seeking your good. Perform, then, the sacrifice you desire, and employ me also in some office for the purpose, for I should obey all your commands."

The king found no words for a moment. Then he said, "O Krishna, my resolve is already crowned with fruit, and success is surely mine, when you have arrived here agreeably to my wish."

Commanded by Krishna, Yudhishthira and his brothers set themselves to collecting the materials for the Rajasuya. And the first order that went out was to Sahadeva and to all his ministers: let persons be appointed, without loss of time, to gather everything the great rite would need.

The sacrifice had not yet begun, but the work of empire had already turned toward it. For the first time the brothers looked outward from Indraprastha — toward the four quarters of the earth — and measured what the world owed them.
stories.reflection: Yudhishthira's request is striking because the most powerful king of the age does not presume to begin the world's greatest rite on his own authority; he waits on Krishna's word. And Krishna's answer inverts the court's order of power entirely — the emperor-elect is told to employ the lord of the universe in some office.
stories.next_story_tease: With Krishna's blessing given, Yudhishthira sent his brothers to the four quarters of the earth to make the world ready for the sacrifice.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna's chariot rolls into Indraprastha before a vast host, wheels rattling and wagons of treasure behind him, as the city turns out to greet him and Yudhishthira waits at the gate with his brothers and priests.

stories.title: Four Brothers, Four Directions
stories.story:
Yudhishthira did not delay. The moment Krishna's permission was given, the king turned from the council to the horizon: before a single fire could be lit for the Rajasuya, the four quarters of the earth had to be made ready. An emperor's sacrifice draws its splendor from the tribute of kings, and tribute follows strength.

So he called his four brothers before him and gave each a direction of the world.

Sahadeva, the youngest, he sent to the south, and with him the Srijnayas, his allied warriors — toward the hot lands where the southern kings kept their ancient thrones. Nakula he sent to the west, toward the sea kingdoms and the sunset. Arjuna, the great archer, he sent to the north, where the mountain kings watched from their passes. And Bhima, whose strength was the dread of every court, he sent to the east, the quarter of the rising sun.

Four brothers. Four roads out of Indraprastha. The city watched them go, banners bright in the morning light, and understood that the empire was reaching out its hands to gather the world.

And while they were away, Indraprastha waited as a city waits for its armies. The priests rehearsed the rites of the Rajasuya; the craftsmen raised the halls that would hold the kings of the earth; the treasury counted what it had and made room for what was coming. Every report from the roads — a messenger, a merchant, a returning soldier — was met at the gate and questioned for news of the four brothers and their wars.

The chronicles do not linger over those campaigns. No single battle of that season earned a name in the telling; what the poets record is simpler and more astonishing. The heroes marched to the ends of their directions, vanquished the kings who ruled there, and carried back abundant wealth for the sacrifice. King after king of the four quarters was overcome by their might, and from every direction the tribute began to move toward Indraprastha.

Then came the returns, and the city began to fill. Sahadeva came up from the south, his wagons heavy. Nakula rode in from the west with the wealth of the sea kingdoms. Arjuna descended from the north with the treasure of the mountain lords. Bhima arrived from the east, and the ground itself seemed to shake under the weight of his train. Coins and gems, cloth and horses, gold beyond counting — the abundance of four directions — poured into a treasury that had once seemed inexhaustible, and still it grew.

Yudhishthira received each brother as a king receives a returning army, and Indraprastha prepared. For now the sacrifice had its wealth and its tribute, its proof of empire — and only the great rite itself remained.
stories.reflection: The fourfold conquest is told in a handful of verses because its purpose is not war but gathering: the brothers conquer the directions the way farmers reap, to feed a rite that will crown their brother emperor. Here empire is only the road by which the tribute travels to the sacrifice.
stories.next_story_tease: When the tribute of the world had gathered in Indraprastha, the Rajasuya began — and its first honor would divide the assembly.

stories.title: Krishna Receives the First Honor
stories.subtitle: At the Rajasuya, the assembly must decide who is honored first.
stories.story:
The question hung over the great hall the way such a question hangs over any gathering of the powerful: of all the men present, who deserved to be honored first?

Yudhishthira had just performed the Rajasuya, the great royal sacrifice that declared him emperor, and kings and sages from across the land had come to Indraprastha for it. They sat in a vast assembly — monarchs in their finest, learned men marked by long study, warriors whose names were already legend. The sacrifice was done, and one honor remained: the arghya, the first offering of welcome, the water and garlands and silk with which a host set his most worthy guest apart. To be honored first at such a sacrifice was no small thing; it declared, before all the world, who mattered most. But who should receive it? There were kings in that hall who had conquered kingdoms, sages who had read every scripture, teachers and warriors and men grown old in dignity. The members of the assembly weighed the matter among themselves, and the question did not settle itself.

Then Sahadeva rose. He was the youngest of the Pandava brothers, and in that company he commanded no army and wore no great crown. What he had was certainty. The honor, he said, belonged to Krishna alone. Not because Krishna held a throne — he was the lord of the Satvatas, and the hall held greater crowns than his. Not because he was the oldest or the most learned. Because in Krishna all the deities and every sacrifice had their being. The whole universe was in him, and he was one, without a second. Let the highest honor be given to Krishna, the soul of all beings, whose sight was undivided. And having said it, Sahadeva fell silent, because he knew what he knew.

The assembly did not argue. Hearing him, and reading in the faces around them that the choice was right, the gathered company approved. Then Yudhishthira himself rose, and what he did next stilled the hall. Overwhelmed with love, he knelt and washed Krishna's feet. He lifted the water that had touched those feet and carried it to his own head, as a son might do. And he worshipped Krishna with yellow silk and garments and jewels of great worth. Around him the whole assembly stood with hands joined, and no one spoke, because there was nothing left to say.

Krishna accepted it quietly, in the manner the ordinance required, as one who receives what has been freely given.

But one man in that hall could not bear what he saw. Shishupala watched the worship and felt his fury rise. To him it was an insult to every king present. He pointed around the hall at the worthier men: there sat Bhishma, there Drona, there the old seer Dwaipayana, there Karna the mighty. What was Krishna beside these? He was not even a king, Shishupala insisted — neither a sacrificial priest nor a preceptor, not the oldest among them, not the most learned. Why should he, of all of them, be worshipped first? The objection poured out of him, a tide of wounded pride, and in it the seeds of something far worse were already sown. He could not bear to see that worship offered to Krishna, and he would not let it pass.

But that is another story. For this one it is enough to hold the image: the youngest Pandava speaking a truth he had not reasoned his way to, and the eldest kneeling to wash the feet of a man who was, in that moment, the only one worth honoring.
stories.reflection: Two things stand side by side here: Sahadeva's declaration that the universe and every sacrifice abide in Krishna, and Yudhishthira's act of washing a guest's feet and lifting the water to his own head. The honor is not political; it is devotion made visible, and it divides the hall between those who bow and one man who cannot bear to watch.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata has Bhishma judge Krishna foremost and Sahadeva present the offering; the Bhagavata, followed here, has Sahadeva himself make the declaration.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shishupala could not contain his fury, and before the assembly ended he would let it speak.
stories.hero_scene: Yudhishthira kneeling before Krishna in the crowded assembly, washing his feet and lifting the water to his own head, while kings and sages stand around with joined palms and Shishupala's face darkens at the sight.

stories.title: Shishupala's Outburst
stories.story:
The first honor had been offered, and the assembly was still settling back into its seats, when one king rose.

The moment had come earlier in the day, when Krishna received the arghya — the first worship of the Rajasuya, the choice that had pleased nearly every guest and enraged exactly one. Now Shishupala, son of Damaghosha, king of Chedi, rose from his seat, raised his arm, and spoke so that the whole great hall could hear him: harsh words, fearless words, his face black with the fury that hearing Krishna's praises had kindled in him.

"You call yourselves the best of judges of what deserves honor," he said. "Do not take this for the babble of a child. Here sit men of austerity and learning, whose sins have been burned away by knowledge — and before them, this cowherd has been given the first worship! A cowherd who abandoned his own order, cast out of every duty of caste and stage of life, stripped of all dharma. The line of Yayati was cursed by the good and driven out; these men left the lands where the great sages dwelled and lost the splendor that belongs to the priestly virtue they have thrown away."

He went on, and the hall grew very still. He mocked the deeds themselves. "If Krishna slew a vulture in his infancy, what is remarkable in that?" he cried. "If he held up Govardhan for a week — what is a mountain but an anthill to a strong man?" And he spoke of Jarasandha, the great king slain in his own city, and called the slayer a wretch of the Vrishni race who had killed him unrighteously. Praise of Krishna he answered with sneers; honor he answered with contempt.

The assembly could not bear it. The sages sitting in the hall stopped their ears, unable to listen to the blasphemy, and curses fell from their lips. And the Pandavas rose — Bhima blazing with anger among them — and with them their allies, the Matsyas, the Kaikayas, the Srijnayas, weapons drawn, ready to kill the man who had defiled the assembly.

Yudhishthira strove to hold the moment back. "What you have said is scarcely proper for you, O lord of earth," he said. "It is sinful and needlessly cruel. Do not insult Bhishma by saying he does not know what virtue is. These kings before you, older than you, all approve of the worship offered to Krishna. Bear it patiently, as they do. Bhishma knows Krishna truly; you do not know him so well."

Then Bhishma spoke, and his voice carried the weight of the eldest of the Kurus. He who disapproves the worship offered to Krishna, the oldest one in the universe, deserves neither soft words nor conciliation. "I do not behold in this assembly of kings even one ruler who has not been vanquished in battle by the energy of this son of the Satwata race," he said. "This one of undefiled glory deserves to be worshipped not by ourselves alone, but by the three worlds. We have offered him the first worship for his fame, his heroism, his success. This Shishupala is a mere boy, and he does not know Krishna."

And the mighty-armed Bhishma caught hold of Shishupala, as Mahadeva seizes his own son, holding him back from the fight that was gathering around him.

But the king of Chedi stood unperturbed, as though the drawn weapons and the curses were nothing to him. He had already seized sword and shield, and he stood ready in the middle of the hall — one man against a storm of honor, refusing to feel its weight. And over his head, in that stopped and waiting silence, the storm hung gathered around the one figure it could not touch.
stories.reflection: Shishupala's fury attacks Krishna for being a cowherd — for the very lowliness the tradition places at the heart of Krishna's mystery. His insults measure him, not Krishna: envy, unable to reach its object, spends itself on the air of the assembly and only exposes the one who speaks.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata and the Mahabharata tell the same assembly scene; the Bhagavata stresses the sages' curse and Shishupala's sword and shield, while the Mahabharata gives fuller speeches to Bhishma and Yudhishthira.
stories.next_story_tease: The king of Chedi had spent a hundred offenses in that hall — and Krishna had counted every one.

stories.title: Krishna Slays Shishupala
stories.story:
In the palace of the kings of Chedi, a child was born with three eyes and four arms, and the moment he entered the world he screamed like an ass. His parents were terrified, and would have given him up. But a voice without a body spoke from the sky and told them not to fear: their son would grow fortunate and superior in strength, and the man who would one day kill him had already been born.

The voice said more. The extra arms and the extra eye would vanish the day the child was placed on the lap of the one who was destined to slay him. So the kings of the earth came one by one to Chedi, curious to behold so strange a child, and one by one the boy was laid upon their laps — a thousand of them — and nothing happened. The arms remained, and the eye upon his forehead watched them all, as if it were waiting for one particular face. And so the boy grew up under a prophecy that everyone remembered and no one could explain.

Then Krishna came to Chedi with his brother Balarama, to see their father's sister, who was the queen there. When the queen herself, with great tenderness, set her son upon Krishna's lap, the extra arms fell away like a pair of snakes, and the third eye upon his forehead disappeared. The queen was seized with fear, for she understood now who would take her son's life — she had watched the sign the voice promised come true before her own eyes.

She begged a boon of Krishna, and Krishna, who loved his aunt, granted it. He promised that he would bear with this boy, Shishupala, through a hundred offences before he raised a hand against him. A hundred. To a grieving mother it must have seemed a long reprieve, almost a lifetime of mercy. And so the matter was settled, and the child was cherished, and the years began to pass.

Shishupala grew into a king, and the old hatred in him never cooled. At the great Rajasuya sacrifice of Yudhishthira in Indraprastha, when Krishna was honoured before the assembled kings, Shishupala could not contain himself. He rose and poured out abuse against Krishna in full view of the court, one insult after another, while the elders shifted in their seats and the other kings looked from one to another. Everyone in that hall knew the story of the boon, and many had wondered how long Krishna would keep it. The offences mounted, and mounted, until the hundredth came, and the promise was spent.

Krishna's own followers moved to answer the insult, but Krishna held them back. He rose himself, and with the razor-edged discus he severed Shishupala's head as the king rushed at him. A great uproar broke out in the assembly. There was no second blow, and no need of one.

Then, before the eyes of everyone present, something astonishing happened. A brilliant light rose from Shishupala's body and passed into Krishna, and the two became one. For Shishupala had fixed his mind on Krishna through three births — not in love, but in enmity — and that constant, burning attention had been enough. The enemy who could not stop thinking of Krishna came at last to the very place he had spent his whole life opposing. The hatred of three births, gathered and released, had carried him home.

The assembly fell quiet. The promise had been kept to the letter, and the enmity of three lifetimes came to rest, not in destruction, but in the light it had always, without knowing it, been seeking.
stories.reflection: Shishupala's story turns on a paradox: the sources say he attained oneness with Krishna not through devotion but through three lifetimes of enmity, because his mind never left its object. The hundredth offence is also the hundredth proof of how completely, even in hatred, he was absorbed in Krishna.
stories.content_note: Shishupala is beheaded with the discus; the violence is described with restraint.

stories.title: The Rajasuya Completed
stories.story:
The great fire that had burned for the Rajasuya was at last allowed to grow quiet.

Months had passed since the tribute of the four quarters had poured into Indraprastha, since the kings of the earth had gathered in the hall, since the first honor had been given and the storm around it weathered. The sacrifice had been fed with offerings day after day, its rites performed by the priests in their appointed order, its splendor witnessed by gods and men alike. A rite of that scale does not close itself; it has to be carried through to its end by someone whose will can hold it there, and the chronicle is plain about whose will that was. And through it all, it was Krishna — the lord of the lords of yoga, as the chronicle names him — who completed the great rite for the king.

When the final oblations were done, Krishna bestowed the fees of the sacrifice: ample gifts, given without stint, to the officiating priests and to all who had sat in the assembly. The gifts were as generous as the rite itself had been, measured out to every priest who had served the fire and every learned man who had kept the assembly company. No one who had served the rite went away empty-handed. Then came the avabhritha, the concluding bath, and Yudhishthira stepped down into the water and was cleansed — the emperor washed clean of the great rite, the Rajasuya finished and its fruit secured. The emperor came out of the water an emperor; the rite had done what rites are for, and the kingdom had its crowning.

Yet Krishna did not leave. He stayed on in Indraprastha, month after month, as a friend stays past the hour of his departure because the house does not want him to go. They were quiet months after the great noise of the rite — the city still full of its guests, the king still warm from the honour that had crowned him, and Krishna among them not as a visiting lord but as one of the household. And when at last he asked leave of the king, Yudhishthira was reluctant to give it, and could hardly bear the asking. But Krishna took leave all the same, and turned his face toward his own city, and the road to Dwaraka received him.

Then the guests departed, and Indraprastha began to empty. Gods and men and the beings of the air, every one of them honored by the king as they went, carried away from that city nothing but praise — praise of Krishna, and praise of the sacrifice he had completed, and the memory of a rite that had crowned a king of the earth. They left with the king's honours on them and good words in their mouths; a feast of that size is meant to be remembered, and this one was, by everyone who had shared it.

Almost every one of them.

One guest of the Kurus left Indraprastha in a different temper entirely. Duryodhana, the wicked one — the strife itself, the disease of the Kuru line, as the tellers of the tale name him — could not endure the Pandavas' prosperity. Where the other guests carried praise home, he carried the sight of their splendor like a coal pressed to the palm, and the pain of it did not cool on the road. He came to it grudging and left it burning, and what stayed with him was the fact of their greatness itself — a fact he would spend the coming months trying to undo.

The fires of the Rajasuya were out. The treasury stood full, the emperor was crowned, the guests had scattered to their kingdoms. Only that one burning grievance remained, traveling back to Hastinapura in the heart of a prince who had shared in none of the joy — and it arrived there before any of the praise did.
stories.reflection: The Rajasuya ends in harmony, leave-taking, and praise — and the only discord is carried out by a guest who took no part in any of it. Duryodhana's envy does not touch the sacrifice itself, but it plants a wound in him that the coming months will only deepen.
stories.next_story_tease: The grievance Duryodhana carried out of Indraprastha would find its wound soon after, in the mirrored hall that Maya had built.

stories.title: Duryodhana Falls in Maya's Hall
stories.story:
The wonder of Indraprastha was its new hall, and the wonder of the hall was that no one could trust it. Maya, the great architect, had built it for the Pandavas, and every surface in it seemed to be something it was not. Light lay on polished crystal in sheets so smooth they looked like standing water; pools lay so perfectly clear they looked like solid floor. The guests who had come for the Rajasuya walked through it slowly, testing each step, and those who watched them smiled.

Duryodhana, king of Hastinapura, walked through it like a man who refused to be impressed. He had come to Yudhishthira's sacrifice with his brothers, and he had not liked what he saw. The palace rose around him like a second heaven, and its splendor seemed gathered from every treasury at once, as if the wealth of earthly kings, of the lords of demons, of Indra himself had been poured into one building. Envy sat in his heart and burned there, and he let it show in nothing but the set of his jaw. He was proud, and pride was exactly the wrong companion for Maya's floor.

He came to a stretch of crystal so clear and so still that it seemed a sheet of water had been laid across the hall. The pillars reflected in it. Duryodhana, seeing water where the careful had learned to look twice, gathered the hem of his garment in his hand to keep it dry and stepped forward, the way a man steps into a pool. The floor met his foot, hard and flawless and dry. Somewhere behind him a servant bowed quickly to hide a smile.

Duryodhana lowered his garment and walked on, his color high. Then the hall played its second trick, crueler than the first. A little further on lay a real pool, sunk in the stone, so clear that the floor seemed to continue across it without a break. Duryodhana, this time certain of his footing, walked straight into the water and fell.

The laugh that broke out was Bhima's, first and loudest — Bhima, who could no more have held it in than he could have held a storm. The women of the court laughed, and the kings who stood about laughed with them, though Yudhishthira, the host, made a sign for restraint and would have stopped them if he could. It was no use. The hall had given them a king of Hastinapura stumbling in a pool with his dignity in tatters, and the laughter passed through the assembly like wind through a grove.

Duryodhana rose from the water. He said nothing. That was the frightening part, for those who knew him: no threat, no retort, no feigned good humor. He stood, dripping and burning — burning with shame, and with a hatred that fed on the shame — and he walked out of the hall in silence, out of the city, and back to Hastinapura, carrying the laughter with him all the way. He would remember it, and the hatred would wait for its own time.

Krishna watched it all and said nothing. He saw Duryodhana's silence, and he saw further, to what that silence would become. The earth was heavy with the pride of its kings, and Krishna sat silent in that hall, intent on one thing alone: relieving the burden the earth carried. He did not soften the moment. He let the laughter ring out and let Duryodhana carry it home, because the time had not yet come, and the pride of kings was doing its slow, certain work.
stories.reflection: The hall does not humiliate Duryodhana on purpose; it merely mirrors what is already in him. A proud man shown up before kings does not forget — he converts shame into grievance, and grievance into a score to settle. Krishna's silence is the quiet center of the scene: he lets the enmity ripen, because the events that must follow cannot be hurried.
stories.next_story_tease: Far from the laughter of the hall, Shishupala's friend Shalva was already making a vow that would bring war to the Yadavas.
stories.hero_scene: Inside Maya's mirrored hall, proud Duryodhana gathers the hem of his robe before what he takes to be a sheet of water, while behind him Bhima's laughter breaks out and Krishna watches in stillness from his seat.

stories.title: Shalva Wins the Flying City Saubha
stories.story:
The kings of the earth had not all gone home from the Rajasuya when a man stood up among them and made an oath that turned every head. His name was Shalva, and he was the friend of Shishupala, the king of Chedi whom Krishna had struck down at the sacrifice. Shalva had also been at Rukmini's wedding, in that company which had come to claim her and had gone away defeated; the Yadavas had humbled him once, and now they had killed his friend. In the hearing of all the kings he vowed: the earth would be made empty of Yadavas.

The kings heard it, and some were glad, for it is easier to applaud a vow than to keep one. Others shook their heads, remembering how many oaths had been spoken at that sacrifice and how few had survived the journey home. Shalva meant his. He turned away from courts and went up into the Himalayas, seeking the lord Shiva, the Pasupati, the husband of Uma, and he set himself to win Shiva as an ally.

The penance he took up was terrible. Day after day, in the cold and the silence of the mountains, he ate nothing but a handful of dust. That was his whole austerity — not fire, not staged fasts, not chants — dust, a single handful each day, taken like a man who had forgotten that food was a thing of the world he had left behind. The seasons turned above him, and he did not turn with them. The snows came and went on the ridges; the king who had made the vow grew thin, then thinner, until he was a shadow kneeling before a shrine, and still the handful of dust was his only meal.

Shiva is easily pleased. The old accounts say it almost with affection: quickly contented, swift to give. At the year's end the lord of the mountains appeared before Shalva and offered him a boon. Shalva asked for a citadel that nothing could destroy: a city that would move through the sky at its master's will, a fortress that no god, no demon, no man, no gandharva, no serpent, no rakshasa could overcome or even approach. It was a request that named every power in the three worlds — and set itself above them all. Shiva heard him out and nodded once, for a year of dust deserved a straight answer, and the request was granted.

Shiva said yes, as he does to those who give him everything, and he gave the making of the thing to Maya. Maya was the architect whose works had stood against the gods themselves, the one they called the conqueror of enemy cities. At the mountain-lord's command he built Saubha: an iron city, dark as a storm, hard to assail, moving wherever its master willed it. It rose from the mountain into the sky like a piece of night that had decided to travel, and the world looked up at it and felt fear, because a fortress that can move is a fortress that can arrive. The wise named it the abode of darkness, for it sailed wrapped in a gloom of its own, and no weapon of god or demon could assail it.

Shalva climbed into his city. He had his fortress, his weapon, his flying home, and an army gathered beneath its shadow. He stood at the iron ramparts and watched the earth fall away below him, the rivers turning to threads, the ranges to wrinkles. And in the long silences of that flying iron, with the world turning far beneath his feet, his thought went where it had been pointed from the beginning: toward Dwaraka, and the house of the Yadavas.
stories.reflection: Shalva's vow is the mirror-image of Krishna's silence in the crystal hall: where Krishna waits, Shalva converts grief into a single purpose and gives it a year of his life. The penance buys him power, not wisdom — Shiva grants what is asked, and Shalva asks for war, and the universe politely supplies the weapon.
stories.next_story_tease: In the flying city, Shalva set his course for Dwaraka and the enmity of the Vrishnis.
stories.hero_scene: On a Himalayan ridge, the emaciated king Shalva kneels before the lord Shiva, a single handful of dust raised to his lips, while behind him in the sky the iron city Saubha rises like a piece of traveling night.

stories.title: Shalva Besieges Dwaraka
stories.story:
The noon sky over Dwaraka turned dark, and the people looked up to see a thing no one could name. It was not a cloud. It hung above their city — an iron city, dark as a storm, vast, moving slowly of its own will, with ramparts and towers and gates of its own. A piece of the night had come visiting in the middle of the day. Around it and behind it, the sky filled with the shapes of an army.

Shalva had come. He remembered the enmity of the Vrishnis: his friend Shishupala dead at the Rajasuya, his own defeat at Rukmini's wedding. He had brought his vengeance home in the form of Maya's city. Saubha moved over Dwaraka and opened itself, and everything it carried came down at once.

Weapons first, in their hundreds. Then stones, and whole trees torn up by the roots and flung, and thunderbolts that struck the towers and split them, and serpents that rained hissing out of the sky, and showers of gravel that rattled on the roofs like hail. The gardens of Dwaraka, the famous groves and pleasure grounds where the city walked in the evening, were shredded. The gates were shattered, the walls dented, the palaces and ramparts and upper terraces cracked and smoking. The golden city by the sea was being pounded from above, and its people ran through the streets looking up at a doom that would not come down to fight them — only to torment them from the sky, where no arrow could reach and no wall could answer. What Shalva wanted was not the city but its courage, and he meant to break that too.

Terror was Shalva's real weapon. A city can stand a siege on the ground, can man its walls and count its enemies and wait. It cannot easily stand a siege that hangs overhead and will not be reached — a moving mountain of iron that chose its spot in the sky and opened itself again and again. There was no front line to hold and no enemy to charge; only a darkness overhead that went on dropping ruin.

Then a voice cut through the panic. Pradyumna, Krishna's son by Rukmini, had seen his people afflicted — seen his own people tormented — and he would not watch them break. He mounted his chariot and rode out into the open, and his cry rang over the streets: "Do not fear!" The cry passed from street to street, and where it passed, panic began to turn back into purpose.

The Yadava warriors heard it and rallied. Satyaki came out, and Charudeshna, and Samba, and Akrura with his younger brothers; and behind them the great archers, the leaders of the chariot troops, all those who had built Dwaraka's name in battle. They poured through the broken gates, horses straining, bows ready, and arrayed themselves against the iron city and the host that moved beneath it. The two hosts met in the shadow of the flying city, and the clash of it rolled over the sea like thunder.

The battle that followed was unlike any Dwaraka had fought, because the enemy did not stand on the earth. Saubha wheeled above them, loosing weapons and magic at will, now high, now low, and the Yadavas answered from below, chasing a foe that had no fixed place. Pradyumna, the son of Rukmini, met the illusions of the lord of Saubha with divine weapons of his own, arrow for illusion, until the sky over the city was a snarl of light and iron, and the ground beneath it was littered with the wreckage of the morning.

And their lord was not among them. Krishna had gone to Indraprastha, summoned by Yudhishthira for the sacrifice, and the news of what hung over his city had not yet reached him. His people fought on without him, under a sky that would not stop falling.
stories.reflection: Shalva's siege works precisely because it cannot be answered: terror from above has no face, no line of battle, no place to be met. The people's salvation is not a miracle but the courage of their own princes — Pradyumna's "Do not fear" is leadership as pure action, spoken only after he has already ridden into the open.
stories.content_note: Siege warfare with weapons, stones, trees and serpents raining on the city; described with restraint and no graphic detail.

stories.title: Krishna Returns to the Battle
stories.story:
In Indraprastha, in the middle of the honors and ceremonies of the Rajasuya, Krishna grew restless with omens he did not need explained twice. He had come there at Yudhishthira's summons — the sacrifice of emperors, whose heart was his presence — and the elders of the Kurus had honored him, and the sages, and Pritha his aunt, with her sons. It had been good to be among them. But the signs turned bad, and he read them without difficulty: his own people were in danger, far away by the sea.

He took his leave with courtesy, as he did everything — from the elders of the Kurus, from the sages, from Pritha and her sons. He had come when they called; now the road called him home. No one pressed him to stay, for those who knew him read the haste in his calm. And he set out for Dwaraka with all speed, the omens hurrying him, the dust of the road rising behind his chariot before the farewells were done. The road from Indraprastha to the sea was long, and Krishna took it at speed, for the omens did not ease as the miles fell away.

What he found when he reached the city confirmed every sign. The gardens were wreckage. The gates hung broken, their leaves torn from the hinges. The marks of a long assault were everywhere — scarred walls, fallen towers, the streets still full of the debris of the morning — and the sky above Dwaraka still carried the dark shape of the flying city. Krishna saw the ruin of his own people, and he understood at once: the allies of the Chaidya, the friends of the slain Shishupala, had attacked his city while he was away.

He wasted no time on anger. He called to Daruka, his charioteer: "Bring my chariot. Quickly. Straight to Shalva."

Daruka did not ask twice. He readied the chariot and drove it out at speed, straight at the iron city and the army that hung beneath it.

Shalva saw Krishna coming, and he knew what it meant. His army was already near to broken by the Yadava princes, and now the one man he had built his vengeance around had arrived. He answered with his best weapon. From the heights of Saubha he hurled a spear at the chariot — aimed not at Krishna but at Daruka, the charioteer. A blazing spear it was, and it came down through the sky like a great meteor falling, trailing fire, so fast that the eye could barely follow it.

Krishna's bow was already up. His arrows met the spear in mid-air and cut it to pieces — a hundred pieces — so that what reached the chariot was only sparks and splinters raining down.

Then he turned the answer on the thrower. Sixteen shafts he drove into Shalva, fast and deep, and the flying city reeled through the sky, knocked off its course by the assault from below. Saubha staggered like a struck ship, and for the first time since the siege began, its barrage faltered.

Shalva was not finished. His own bow came up, and his arrow struck Krishna's left arm — the arm that held Sharnga, his great bow — and bit deep, so that for a moment the bow wavered in the hand that carried it. A great cry of lamentation went up from the beings who watched: from the armies on both sides, from the people of Dwaraka who saw their lord struck. It was a sound like the sky itself grieving, a long wail that hung in the air over the ruined city. But the hand that held Sharnga did not let it fall, and Krishna's answer to the cry was to press the chariot closer.

But the wound did not end it. Krishna pressed forward, and the battle that had begun in the fields of Dwaraka rose into the sky, and Saubha staggered under his assault. Krishna had come home to a war — and he had brought the war its answer.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not rush home because he doubts his people; the omens tell him his presence is the turning point, and he obeys them without ceremony. Shalva's spear, aimed at the charioteer rather than the warrior, is his most honest blow — strike the hands that carry a god into battle — and Krishna cuts it down mid-air, an answer that says: whatever comes at those he loves must pass through him first.
stories.content_note: Battle scenes with spears, arrows and a wounding; described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shalva had not spent his last deception — he would soon show Krishna a vision of Vasudeva's death.

stories.title: Shalva's Illusion of Vasudeva's Death
stories.story:
In the middle of the battle, a man came running to Krishna's chariot, weeping and calling his name.

Krishna had hurried back from Indraprastha, where omens of danger at Dwaraka had reached him in the midst of his cousin's great sacrifice, and had found his own sky occupied by an enemy. Shalva, king of Saubha, had brought his flying city down upon the coast while Krishna was away, and since his return the two had fought a running duel across the sea — Shalva striking from his city of metal, Krishna answering from the ground, the air between them thick with arrows. Shalva hurled iron javelins, flaming lances and heavy clubs down from his height, and Krishna cut each one into two or three pieces before it could reach him, so that the sea beneath them rained splinters. The duel had now reached its strangest pass. Krishna hurled his mace at the king of Saubha with a force that would have felled a mountain, and when the mace came spinning back to his hand, the sky where Shalva had stood was empty. The king had vanished; his war-cries came from everywhere and nowhere at once.

And then the weeping man was there, stumbling among the chariots, his clothes torn, his voice broken. 'Krishna, Krishna, mighty-armed one!' he cried. 'Your father — you who love your father!' He had come from Dwaraka, he said, though he gave no name, and Krishna, in the press of battle, did not think to ask for one. Shalva, the man sobbed, had broken into the city and carried off Vasudeva like an animal; the tyrant had him now, and only Krishna could save him. Every man in that host knew the report was possible: behind them lay Dwaraka, undefended while Krishna fought.

And then Shalva himself stood before Krishna, and in his grip was an old man in the robes of Vasudeva. 'Here is your father!' Shalva shouted, holding his captive up for Krishna to see. 'The man you live for! Save him, if you can!' And before Krishna could move, the demon's sword came down, and the head of the old man fell into the dust.

For one moment, Krishna's face was any son's face who has watched his father die. The Bhagavata says that he took on the human mood, and in that instant he was wholly, painfully human. He was not thinking of war, or of sorcery, or of the city in the sky; he was thinking only of the old man in the dust — he, whom the text calls fond of his father — and the grief came over him like a wave, and for a second his eyes lost the battle.

Then he looked again.

There was no messenger. There was no body, no head, no blood — only the sky, and Saubha wheeling in it, and Shalva's laughter ringing down. It was Maya, the demon's sorcery, woven out of the great illusion. The grief left Krishna's face as mist leaves a field at sunrise, and the calm that replaced it was more terrible than any anger. The father he had mourned was safe; the death he had watched had never happened. He had been shown his own heart, and the showing had failed. Shalva had staked the war on the one blow that could shake him, and it had not landed.

Krishna turned back to the sky where Saubha drifted, his face utterly calm. The sorcery had spent itself; nothing it could show him now would move him. He raised his bow again, and the real battle began.
stories.reflection: Krishna's moment of grief is the hinge of the scene: the sorcery works, and then it fails. The Bhagavata's sages note that bewilderment cannot truly touch him, but the story lets the human mood stand first — a son's grief worn for an instant and then seen through, which is what makes the recovery feel like a return to himself.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata tells the same scene with a stronger effect: Krishna swoons and the bow Sharanga slips from his hand before he recognizes the illusion. This story follows the Bhagavata Purana, where his bewilderment lasts only a moment.
stories.next_story_tease: But Shalva's flying city still wheeled above Dwaraka, and the war was not yet over.

stories.title: Krishna Destroys the Flying City Saubha and Slays Shalva
stories.story:
For one more hour, the flying city Saubha hung over the sea like a slow storm — the last storm the coast of Dwaraka would ever fear.

It had been a war unlike any Dwaraka knew: no army to meet, no gate to storm, only an enemy that drifted with the wind and rained destruction from above. Saubha was not a fortress; it was a flying capital, a kingdom with wings, the one place in the world that no army had ever taken, and Shalva had ruled it for years from above the reach of every enemy, his grudge festering there like a wound. Krishna had answered it for days from the ground, and the duel with Shalva had now narrowed to its end. His sorcery had failed him; his weapons had been shattered one by one; and the king of Saubha, who had fought from an unreachable sky, was running out of sky.

He came down one final time, rushing at Krishna with everything he had left, and Krishna met him with arrows that struck true through pride and armor alike. The shafts pierced his guard, cut through his war-plate, snapped his bow, and tore the jewel from his crest. Even Krishna's own chariot had not been spared that day — his horses and his charioteer Daruka stood thick with shafts, and the driver, pierced and enfeebled, had confessed he could barely hold the reins. Krishna had cheered him and told him to hold on — the driver's duty was to stay at the reins, and he himself would not fail him; the battle, he said, would not last forever.

And in that moment of weakness Krishna did what he had come to do. He took up his mace and turned it on the city itself. The blow that might have been saved for a king was spent on a kingdom: the mace struck Saubha's hull, and the flying city — the wonder of the age, the terror of the coast, the thing no army could ever reach — came apart. The Bhagavata says it fell into the water in a thousand fragments, and the sea swallowed it like rain. Men would say afterwards that it went down as Tripura had gone down of old, the triple city shaken from the sky by the great god's shafts.

Where a city had floated, there was only sky — and Shalva. City gone, weapons gone, the king of Saubha came at Krishna on foot, mace in hand, with nothing left but his fury. Fury, for all its weight, was not enough. As he rushed in, Krishna severed the arm that held the mace. The weapon fell beside its owner, and the king of Saubha stood weaponless at last.

Then Krishna raised the discus — the wondrous weapon that blazed like the sun at the end of the world — and for a moment it hung in the air like a second sun, and every eye on the field followed it. Then it fell, and in one clean sweep it cut off Shalva's crowned head; where it passed, the enemy burned. The king who had lived above the world was gathered into it at last.

The war was over. The sea smoothed itself over the scattered stones of Saubha; the sky above Dwaraka was only sky again; and the grudge that had darkened it was ended. The king who had raided the coast, who had conjured a dead father before his son's eyes, who had fought from a city no army could reach, lay in the dust at last, where his enmity could trouble no one anymore.
stories.reflection: The fall of Saubha is total: city, weapons, and king gone in a single hour, and the Bhagavata gives each its own instrument — the mace for the kingdom, the discus for the king. The image of the discus blazing like the sun at the world's end turns the end of a tyrant into a kind of sunrise: destruction, but destruction that clears the sky.
stories.tradition_note: In the Mahabharata, the discus alone finishes the war: it cuts Saubha in two like a saw through a tall tree, then cleaves Shalva as he raises his mace. The Bhagavata Purana gives the mace the task of shattering the city and the discus the beheading; this story follows the Bhagavata.
stories.content_note: Mild violence: Shalva's arm is severed and he is beheaded; described without gore.
stories.next_story_tease: The news of Shalva's end would not travel far before another enemy rose to answer for it.

stories.title: Krishna Slays Dantavakra and Viduratha
stories.story:
Krishna was on the road home from the war with Shalva, the dust of one victory still settling, when the road began to shake — and the men who rode with him looked up to see a single figure approaching on foot.

It was a lonely stretch of road, Dwaraka's walls still a day's march ahead, and no one on it but the returning war-party and the single figure coming to meet them. It was Dantavakra, kin to the slain Shishupala and friend to the slain Shalva, and he had not come to talk. The news of both deaths had reached his kingdom of Karusha, and he had taken up his mace and walked out to settle the debt himself — alone, on foot, the grudge in his hand.

Krishna saw him coming and knew what the day would be. He took up his own mace, Kaumodaki, and waited.

Dantavakra came on, and the ground trembled under his steps. Rage had made him careless of everything — no chariot, no army, no counsel, only the mace and the debt. He was one of those warriors the world had learned to fear, the sort of man who settles his friendships with a weapon, and the weapon he carried had never once failed him. When he was close enough to be heard, he raised it and shouted at Krishna.

'You are our own cousin, Krishna,' he called, 'and yet you turn on your own kin! You are the betrayer of friends. You killed Shishupala at his own kinsmen's sacrifice; you killed Shalva in the ruin of his city. Do you think I will let that stand? I owe my friends a debt, and I am kind to my friends — I have come to pay it with your head.'

His words were harsh as goads on an elephant, the text says, and Krishna heard them all without a word. Dantavakra came within reach, and for a moment the two stood facing each other — the mace-man and the chariot-lord — while the dust settled around them. Then Dantavakra swung.

The mace came down on Krishna's head with all the strength of that huge body behind it — a blow that would have felled a fortress wall. Krishna did not move. The Bhagavata is exact about it: struck by the mace in the very press of the fight, he did not stir, as though the blow had fallen on a mountain.

And then Kaumodaki answered. Krishna's mace struck Dantavakra square in the chest and crushed it. The king of Karusha staggered, blood pouring from his mouth, and fell — and as he fell, those who watched saw a wonder: a subtle light rose out of him and entered Krishna, a thing too fine for the eye to hold, and gone before anyone could say what it was.

Before the field could take breath, Viduratha came rushing onto the road — Dantavakra's brother, his heart drowned in grief for the brother he had just lost. He had no plan and no weapon to match the moment, only rage and sorrow. Krishna met him with the discus, razor-edged, and took his crowned head.

The road was quiet. Two brothers lay where they had fallen, and the vengeance they had come to take had ended the way vengeance usually does — in two graves instead of one. The men who rode with Krishna gathered in silence, and no one spoke of victory. They would speak for years, though, of the light they had seen leave the fallen king, uncertain of what they had witnessed.

Then Krishna turned his chariot toward Dwaraka, and the dust settled behind him.
stories.reflection: The text passes over the violence to dwell on one detail: a subtle light leaving Dantavakra and entering Krishna. It is the strangest moment in the scene, and the most tender — the enemy who had walked out to kill his cousin returning, at the last, into the one he fought, as if the long feud had been a homecoming all along.
stories.content_note: Mild violence: Dantavakra's chest is crushed and Viduratha is beheaded; described without gore.

stories.title: Draupadi's Cry as She Is Dragged and Disrobed
stories.story:
One throw of the dice had cost Yudhishthira his kingdom, his brothers, and himself — and then, in the madness of the game, his wife.

It had happened at Hastinapura, in the hall of the Kurus, where Yudhishthira had been drawn into a game he could not win. He had staked his wealth and his kingdom; he had staked his brothers, one by one; he had staked himself. And when nothing was left to stake, he had staked Draupadi — and lost her too.

Now Duryodhana, flushed with winning, commanded the herald: 'Go, bring Draupadi here. You have nothing to fear from the sons of Pandu.'

The herald went unwillingly, like a dog entering a lion's den, and told the queen that she had been won in the game and must come to the house of Dhritarashtra to do menial work.

Draupadi looked at him. 'What prince is there,' she asked, 'who stakes his wife? The king was certainly mad with the game. Could he find nothing else to stake?'

'When he had nothing else,' said the herald, 'he staked you. First his brothers, then himself, then you.'

'Then go back to that gambler in the assembly and ask him one question,' said Draupadi. 'Whom did he lose first — himself, or me? Find that out, and then come and take me.'

The question was not a delay; it was the hinge of everything. If Yudhishthira had lost himself before he lost her, then he was no longer his own master — and a man who does not own himself cannot stake his wife. The whole right of the Kauravas' claim turned on the answer.

The herald carried the question to the hall, where Yudhishthira sat among the kings like a man robbed of his wits and gave no answer, good or ill.

'Let the princess of Panchala come here and put her question herself,' said Duryodhana. 'Let everyone in this assembly hear the words that pass between her and Yudhishthira.'

So the herald went back a second time, more distressed than before. And Draupadi answered with what she had always held: 'Morality is the one highest object in the world,' she said. 'If it is cherished, it will bless us. Let it not abandon the Kauravas. Tell them I will do whatever the elders, who are virtuous and conversant with what is right, tell me.'

The herald repeated her words in the assembly. And the kings and elders sat with their faces downward, and not one of them spoke — for they all knew the eagerness and the resolution of Dhritarashtra's son. Yudhishthira, bound by his own promise, sent word that she should go before her father-in-law and weep; but that was not a rescue, and everyone in the room knew it.

Duryodhana had no use for questions or for morality. 'Dussasana,' he said, 'this herald fears Bhima. Go yourself, and bring the daughter of Yajnasena here by force. Our enemies are in our power now. What can they do to you?'

So Dussasana rose, his eyes red as blood, and went into the dwelling of those great warriors. 'Come, come,' he told the princess, 'you have been won by us, and won rightly. Accept the Kurus for your lords, and come to the assembly.'

And when she would not come, he seized her and dragged her into the hall before the gathered kings — before her husbands, before the elders who had lowered their faces — and in the sight of all of them, he began to strip her.

And it was then that Draupadi cried out. Not to the assembly, which had chosen silence. Not to her husbands, who sat bound and helpless. But past all of them, to the one name that could cross the distance:

'O Govinda, who dwells in Dwaraka! O Krishna, who is fond of the cowherds of Vrindavan! O Kesava, do you not see how the Kauravas humiliate me? O Lord, husband of Lakshmi, lord of Vraja, destroyer of all afflictions, O Janardana — rescue me, who am sinking in the Kaurava ocean!'

The cry rose through the hall and out of it, past the walls of Hastinapura, toward a city by the sea. The assembly heard it; the sky heard it. Whether anyone in Dwaraka heard it, the hall could not know — but the cry had gone out, and some cries are not finished when they end.
stories.reflection: Draupadi's question — whether Yudhishthira had lost himself before he lost her — is the one true test the assembly is offered, and the kings fail it in silence. Her cry that follows is not argument but address: she stops pleading with men and names the one who can cross the distance, and the naming itself is the whole of her faith.
stories.next_story_tease: But the cry had not gone unheard — in Dwaraka, the one who heard it had already begun to move.

stories.title: Krishna Protects Draupadi with Endless Robes
stories.story:
In the great assembly hall of Hastinapura, the queen of the Pandavas called out a single name, and her voice filled the silence. It was the only thing she had left. She called on Krishna.

Draupadi had been brought there because her husband Yudhishthira had lost everything at dice. He had staked his kingdom and lost it, staked his brothers and lost them, and then staked himself. And when there was nothing else left to wager, in the madness of the game, he had staked his own wife. Now the court had sent for her, and she stood among the kings and elders who had watched it all happen and said nothing. Only Vidura had spoken against it, warning that the house was calling ruin down on itself, and his warning had been brushed aside.

The messenger had come to her rooms like a dog into a lion's den, as the old text puts it, and told her she had been won, and that she was to be brought before the assembly. Draupadi had answered him with a question no one in the court could answer. When Yudhishthira had nothing left, had he staked himself first, or her? If he had already lost himself, how could he stake anyone at all? The question was carried back to the assembly, and her own husband, the king, sat there like a man demented, and gave no answer, good or ill. He could not say whether he had lost himself before he lost her, and so he said nothing, and his silence hung over the hall like a judgement.

So she was brought before them, and Dussasana laid his hands on her garment and began to pull, to strip her of her honour in front of the whole assembly. The elders looked away. The fathers and grandfathers of the house sat with lowered eyes, and not one of them rose. And Draupadi, alone in that crowded hall, raised her voice and called out to Krishna, pouring out her heart to the one who had never failed her.

Krishna heard her. The text says plainly that, hearing her words, he was deeply moved, and that, leaving his seat, out of compassion he came to her there. He did not thunder, and he did not break down the door. He came the way mercy comes.

And then something the assembly could not explain began to happen. The illustrious Dharma — the very principle of righteousness — remained there unseen, and covered her. As each garment was drawn away, another of the same kind appeared in its place, covering her again. One after another the robes came, without end, of many bright hues, hundreds upon hundreds of them, so that no matter how long Dussasana pulled, Draupadi remained covered. The harder he pulled, the more the robes came, as if the cloth itself had set its mind to keeping her covered. Her honour could not be taken from her.

The pile of cloth rose and rose until Dussasana, spent and disgraced, let go and fell back, and could pull no more. He sank down amid the very heap of robes he had tried to tear from her, and the heap itself stood as a witness against him. Draupadi stood unharmed, wrapped in an endless garment that was not cloth so much as the answer to a prayer. The court sat stunned before the proof of something they had refused to admit.

The protector never showed a face and never spoke a word. But every new robe was a word, and together they said what no one in that hall had been willing to say: the woman who calls on Krishna is never left alone.
stories.reflection: The text does not say Krishna struck anyone or even raised his voice; it says he was moved, and that the unseen Dharma covered her. The miracle is a quiet one — not a display of power but an answer to a call, given so that honour and dignity could not be torn away.
stories.content_note: Describes the attempted public humiliation of Draupadi, whose garment is seized before the assembly; the scene is handled with restraint, and she is protected.
stories.hero_scene: Draupadi standing in the crowded Kuru assembly, calling out to Krishna as Dussasana pulls at her garment, while robe after robe of many hues appears around her, covering her again and again, the elders looking on in silence.
