stories.title: Draupadi Demands Vengeance
stories.story:
The talk in the Pandava camp at Upaplavya had turned, as it so often did in those last days before war, to peace. Yudhishthira had just spoken for it, his words fraught with virtue and profit, and Sahadeva and the mighty car-warrior Satyaki had warmly approved. Even Bhima — whose answer to every grievance was a raised mace — had declared for peace. Then Draupadi rose, and the counsel of peace fell silent.

Her hair hung loose about her shoulders, and she held the dishevelled tresses in her hands as she spoke, as though she could not put them down. Her eyes, black and large as lotus leaves, were wet with tears. She addressed Krishna directly, and the whole gathering heard her out.

"You know," she said, "by what deceitful means the son of Dhritarashtra and his counsellors robbed the Pandavas of their happiness. You know the message that was privately delivered to Sanjaya — that we asked only for five villages: Avishthala, Vrikasthala, Makandi, Varanavata, and any fifth besides. Yudhishthira, modest and anxious for peace, asked for that much, and Duryodhana would not grant even that."

She went on, her voice growing firm. If Duryodhana wanted peace only on condition that the kingdom be surrendered, there was no need for Krishna to travel to Hastinapura at all; the Pandavas, with the Srinjayas at their side, could stand against the Dhritarashtra host. When men could not be won by conciliation or by gifts, they had to be met with severity. A Kshatriya true to the duties of his own order struck down the covetous — the scriptures excepting only a Brahmana, the preceptor of all orders — and there was as much sin in sparing one who deserved to die as in slaying one who did not. Let Krishna, then, inflict the punishment that was due, and let him do it with the Pandavas and the Srinjayas behind him — for such a deed would become the son of Pritha, add to Krishna's glory, and be a source of great happiness to the whole Kshatriya race.

"Whatever woman on earth is like me?" she asked. "I am the daughter of king Drupada, who rose from the sacrificial altar. I am the sister of Dhrishtadyumna, your dear friend. I am the daughter-in-law of the illustrious Pandu, the queen of his five sons, and the mother of five sons who are bound to you as Abhimanyu is. And being such, I was seized by the hair, dragged into the assembly, and insulted before the very eyes of the sons of Pandu — in your own lifetime, Krishna. With the Pandavas, the Panchalas and the Vrishnis all alive, I was treated as a slave before the gaze of that gathering."

The assembly hall of that terrible day hung in the room with them. She reminded him how the brothers had sat silent, and how, in that silence, she had called upon him in her heart: "Save me, O save me!" How Dhritarashtra, her father-in-law, had offered her a boon, and she had asked only that the Pandavas be made free men with their cars and weapons — and how they had been freed, only to be exiled to the woods. Morally, she said, she was the daughter-in-law of both Bhishma and Dhritarashtra; being such, she had still been made a slave. "Rescue me, O lotus-eyed one," she pleaded, "with my husbands, my kinsmen, and my relatives, from this grief."

"Fie to Arjuna's bowmanship," she said, her voice breaking, "and fie to Bhima's might, since Duryodhana lives even for a moment. If I deserve any favour at your hands, if you have any compassion for me, let your wrath be directed towards the sons of Dhritarashtra."

She wept as she finished, tears running down her face, and then, walking like a cow-elephant, heavy and slow, the queen of the Pandavas came and stood before Krishna, waiting for his answer. The camp was very still.
stories.reflection: Draupadi's appeal rests her entire case on who she is — daughter of the altar, sister of a dear friend, daughter-in-law of two houses, mother of five — and yet none of that standing protected her in the assembly. Her grief is not only for the insult but for the silence of the men who loved her, which is why she does not ask them to avenge her; she asks Krishna, the one she called to in her heart.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna's answer, when it came, would be a vow.

stories.title: Krishna Vows the Kuru Women Will Weep
stories.story:
For a long moment Krishna said nothing.

Draupadi's appeal still hung in the air of the tent at Upaplavya — the tale of the assembly hall, the hair seized by Dussasana's hand, the plea for vengeance — and her tears had not stopped. She stood before him with her unbound hair in her hands, waiting, and everyone who watched held their breath to hear what the lotus-eyed one would answer. She had told it all again, as she had told it a hundred times: how the brothers had asked for nothing but five villages — Avishthala, Vrikasthala, Makandi, Varanavata, and any fifth — and even that much had been refused; how she had been seized by the hair and dragged into the assembly, insulted in the sight of her husbands and in Krishna's own lifetime, while she called on him from the floor of that hall — save me, O save me; how the freedom she was finally granted had ended in exile anyway. She was the daughter of a king risen from the sacrificial altar, the queen of five heroes, the mother of five mighty warrior sons bound to Krishna as Abhimanyu was — and she had been treated as a slave in the hall of her own father-in-law.

When Krishna spoke, his voice was gentle, but it carried the certainty of something settled long ago. "Soon, Draupadi," he said, "you will behold the ladies of Bharata's race weeping as you weep now. Their husbands and their kinsmen will lie slain, and they will know the grief you know tonight."

She made as if to speak, and he raised his hand. "The mountains of Himavat might shift from their place," he went on. "The earth herself might split into a hundred fragments. But my words can never be futile. Dry your tears. I swear to you: soon you will see your husbands, with their enemies slain."

It was a strange comfort, to be promised weeping — but not her weeping alone. The women of the Kuru house would mourn as she had mourned, in the very city where her humiliation had been staged before a packed assembly. What had been done to her would be answered not in words or treaties but in the fate of the whole Kuru line. The men of the house that had wagered her like a stake would fall, and their wives would sit with loosened hair, as she had sat, and weep.

Those who heard him knew what kind of promise this was. Krishna did not swear lightly; when he spoke of mountains shifting and the earth splitting, he was not reaching for poetry. He was saying that the order of the world would break before his word would. And these men had seen his word hold before — in that very assembly hall, when her robes had streamed out endlessly and no hand could strip her. The man who had answered her cry with cloth now answered it with an oath, and the two were of the same fabric. In that tent, among the Pandavas who had sat silent in the assembly and the Panchalas who had raged since, the vow settled like a stone dropped into still water.

Draupadi's tears did not stop all at once, but something in her shoulders eased. She had been heard; the long waiting was over, and the answer was an oath. Whatever the mountains might do, and whatever became of the earth itself, what Krishna swore that night in Upaplavya would come to pass. And he had sworn it to her by name, as a friend swears to a friend: not to a queen, not to a grievance, but to the woman who had cried out to him in that hall. The promise was made; the rest was time.
stories.reflection: Krishna comforts Draupadi not by softening her grief but by taking it into his own vow: her weeping will be matched, measure for measure, by the women of the house that wronged her. The oath's power lies in its quiet finality — he does not argue with her demand for vengeance, he simply guarantees it, with the earth itself offered as the lesser thing that might break first.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet before war came, the brothers would make one last appeal for peace — and charge Krishna to carry it.
stories.hero_scene: In the lamplit tent at Upaplavya, Krishna speaks gently to the weeping Draupadi, one hand raised as he swears his vow, while the Pandavas watch in silence and her tears fall unheeded.

stories.title: The Pandavas Entrust the Peace Mission
stories.story:
The vow was spoken, but the question of peace would not die with it. Krishna had come to Upaplavya as the Pandavas' friend, and for days the tent had argued the one question that divided the house: whether to stretch out a hand to Hastinapura or to raise weapons against it. Now, in the lamplight, the brothers gathered around Krishna and pressed the last great plea of their house upon him: carry our cause to Hastinapura, and bring back either the kingdom or an answer that ends this waiting. One after another they spoke for the mission, Bhima and Nakula each entrusting the family's hope to him, until Arjuna rose, and the night's argument took its final shape.

"Yudhishthira has already said what should be said," Arjuna began. "But it seems to me, Krishna, that you do not think peace can be easily obtained — whether because of Dhritarashtra's covetousness or because of our present weakness. You think that human prowess alone is fruitless, and that without putting forth one's prowess nothing can be achieved. That may be true, and it may not always be true. Nothing, however, should be regarded as impracticable."

He leaned forward, and his voice changed from argument to entreaty. "If peace is properly proposed, it may be concluded. Strive, therefore, to bring about peace with the foe. You are the foremost friend of both the Pandavas and the Kurus, even as Prajapati is the friend of both the gods and the Asuras. Accomplish what is good for both houses. The accomplishment of our good is not difficult for you — as soon as you go there, it will be accomplished."

Then the harder edge of the night surfaced. Whatever Krishna wished — peace or war — his wish would be honoured by the Pandavas, Arjuna said; the choice was his. But let him remember what had brought them to this pass. Duryodhana, unable to bear the sight of Yudhishthira's prosperity and finding no honest expedient, had deprived them of their kingdom by the sinful expedient of deceitful dice. "What bowman," Arjuna asked, "born in the Kshatriya order and invited to combat, turns away from the fight even if he is sure to die? When I saw us vanquished by sinful means and banished to the woods, I thought that Suyodhana deserved death at my hands."

Yet he did not press that course. If Krishna judged their immediate destruction preferable, let it be done soon and without further deliberation. But if the road of peace remained open, then Krishna alone could walk it, for he was related to both houses and trusted in both courts.

"Surely you know," Arjuna said, "how Draupadi was insulted in the midst of the assembly by Duryodhana of sinful soul, and how we bore it with patience. That Duryodhana will behave with justice towards the Pandavas, I cannot believe. Wise counsels will be lost on him like seed sown in barren soil. Therefore do without delay what you think proper and beneficial for the Pandavas — what should next be done."

He fell silent. The mission had been entrusted: the kingdom's last claim, the family's dignity, and the question of war or peace were all placed in Krishna's hands. Every eye in the tent turned to him, waiting for the answer that would set the road to Hastinapura — or to battle. Outside, the night pressed against the canvas, and the camp settled into its watch. Inside, the brothers waited, and the waiting itself had become a kind of faith: whatever Krishna decided, they would follow it, to the Kuru city or to the field of arms.
stories.reflection: Arjuna's speech carries both directions of the Pandavas' hope: he entreats Krishna to win peace and in the same breath reminds him that Duryodhana cannot be trusted, that wise counsel will fall on him like seed in barren soil. The brothers are not naive — they simply believe that whatever Krishna chooses will be right, which is why the night ends not with a decision but with an expectation.
stories.next_story_tease: It remained for Krishna to answer whether he would carry the Pandavas' plea to Hastinapura.

stories.title: Krishna Accepts the Peace Mission
stories.story:
When the brothers had finished, Arjuna spoke once more, and this time his words were few and direct. "You are now the best friend of all the Kurus," he said. "Related to both parties, you are the dear friend of both. It behoves you to bring about peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra — you are competent, and therefore it behoves you to bring about reconciliation. Going hence for peace, say to our ever-wrathful brother Suyodhana what should be said: if the foolish Duryodhana does not accept your auspicious and beneficial counsels, fraught with virtue and profit, he will surely then be the victim of his fate."

Krishna answered without hesitation. "Yes, I will go to king Dhritarashtra," he said, "desirous of accomplishing what is consistent with righteousness, what may be beneficial to us, and what also is for the good of the Kurus."

The night passed. A bright sun rose in the east, the hour called Maitra set in, and the rays of the sun were still mild. It was the month of Kartika, under the constellation Revati; the season of dew had come, autumn having departed, and the earth was covered with abundant crops on every side. Krishna performed the customary rites of the morning, purified himself by a bath, and decked his person with unguents and ornaments. He worshipped the Sun and Fire, touched the tail of a bull, bowed reverently to the Brahmanas, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious articles placed in view.

Then he recollected Yudhishthira's words and called to Satyaki, seated near. "Let my car be made ready," he said, "and let my conch and discus, along with my mace, my quivers and darts, and all kinds of weapons, offensive and defensive, be placed on it. For Duryodhana and Karna and Suvala's son are all of wicked souls — and foes, however contemptible, should never be disregarded by even a powerful person."

His attendants understood and set to work. The chariot they readied blazed like the fire of universal dissolution, and its speed matched the thought of the rider. Its two wheels resembled the sun and the moon in lustre; it bore emblazonments of moons both crescent and full, of fishes, animals and birds, and was adorned with garlands of flowers and with pearls and gems on every side. A tall flagstaff rose from it, bearing beautiful pennons, and tiger-skins covered its frame. Incapable of being resisted by any foe, capable of robbing the fame of every enemy, it was a chariot that enhanced the joy of the Yadavas. To it they yoked the great horses Saivya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa and Valahaka, bathed and attired in beautiful harness. And as Krishna's dignity grew still greater, Garuda, lord of the feathered creation, came and perched on the flagstaff, producing a terrible rattle.

Krishna mounted the car — high as the summit of Meru, sounding deep and loud as a kettle-drum or thunder — and, taking Satyaki up beside him, set out, filling the earth and the sky with the rattle of his chariot-wheels. The sky was cloudless, auspicious winds began to blow, and the atmosphere, freed from dust, turned pure. Auspicious animals and birds, whirling by the right side, began to follow him; cranes and peacocks and swans cried out good omens, and the fire fed with homa libations blazed up cheerfully, sending its flames towards the right. Great seers — Vasishtha and Vamadeva among them — stood on Krishna's right as he passed. Yudhishthira followed his cousin, and with him Bhima, Arjuna, and the twins, and behind them the valiant Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu the ruler of the Chedis, Drupada, and the king of Kasi. They accompanied the car for a little way and then let it go, watching as the last chance for peace rolled northward towards the residence of the Kurus, its wheels thundering under the bright Kartika sky.
stories.reflection: Krishna accepts the mission in three clauses — what is righteous, what is beneficial, and what is good for the Kurus — as if the three could be one. And then he arms his chariot for a peace mission, because he knows whom he is going to meet: the same Krishna who promises reconciliation also tells Satyaki that no foe, however contemptible, should ever be disregarded.
stories.next_story_tease: The road to Hastinapura lay open before him, and in the Kuru city the brothers waited to receive their guest.

stories.title: The Chariot Krishna Rode to Hastinapura
stories.story:
It was the month of Kartika, under the star Revati; autumn had gone and the season of dew had come, and the earth around Upaplavya lay covered with abundant crops. The night had passed, a bright sun rose in the east, and on such a morning everyone in the camp understood what the day would bring, for Krishna had promised to ride out on the road to Hastinapura and ask for peace. For months the Pandavas had lived on borrowed hope, and all of that hope now rested on a single journey. Arjuna had begged him to go; Yudhishthira had weighed every word; and Krishna had given his word to the Kurus that he would come.

Before the sun was high he finished his morning rites: bathed and anointed, he worshipped both the Sun and Fire, touched the tail of a bull, bowed to the brahmanas who blessed his going, walked round the sacred fire, and cast his eyes on the auspicious articles set before him. Then he remembered Yudhishthira's request and called to Satyaki, Sini's grandson, who sat near him.

"Let my car be made ready," he said, "and let my conch and discus, along with my mace, my quivers and darts, and every weapon of offence and defence be placed upon it. For Duryodhana and Karna and Suvala's son are all of wicked soul, and even a contemptible foe should never be disregarded by a powerful man."

His attendants understood the wishes of Kesava and went to work at once. The car they yoked was a marvel: its two wheels shone like the sun and the moon, its sides were emblazoned with moons both crescent and full, and with fishes, beasts and birds, and it was hung with garlands of many flowers and studded with pearls and gems. Gold covered it, and a fine flagstaff carried bright pennons; tiger-skins lay across it; and the very sight of it raised the hearts of the Yadavas. To it they brought the four great horses, Saivya and Sugriva and Meghapushpa and Valahaka, bathed and harnessed in beautiful gear.

Then, as if the sky itself had answered, Garuda, the lord of all winged creatures, came down and perched on the flagstaff of that car, and the flagstaff rattled terribly under his weight. Krishna mounted the high chariot, tall as the summit of Meru, and its wheels turned with a sound deep as a kettle-drum, loud as thunder, like a celestial car coursing at the will of its rider. He took Satyaki up beside him, and the chariot set out, filling the earth and the sky with the rattle of its wheels.

The sky above him was cloudless, and auspicious winds blew round him, and the air, freed of dust, grew pure. Auspicious beasts and birds wheeled past on his right hand and followed him, and cranes and peacocks and swans cried out in good omen. The fire of the altar, fed with offerings and mantras, blazed up cheerfully toward the right, free of smoke. And on his right side stood the great sages, Vasishtha and Vamadeva, Bhuridyumna and Gaya, Kratha and Sukra, Kusika and Bhrigu, and many another brahmarishi and celestial sage, to honour his going.

Behind the chariot came the Pandavas: Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, and Bhima, and Arjuna, and the twin sons of Madri. And with them walked Chekitana, and Dhrishtaketu the ruler of the Chedis, and Drupada, and the king of Kasi, and the mighty car-warrior Sikhandin. It seemed the whole earth was moving with that one chariot, and the sound of its wheels rolled ahead of it like a promise, all the way to the gates of Hastinapura.
stories.reflection: Krishna rides out for peace with every weapon laid on the chariot: he will offer peace with open hands, but he will not go unarmed into a court where Duryodhana, Karna and Shakuni hold the king's ear. The preparation is not a contradiction of the mission; it is its honesty.
stories.next_story_tease: Before the chariot had gone far, Yudhishthira came walking behind it, carrying messages for the ones he loved.

stories.title: Messages for Kunti and the Elders
stories.story:
Krishna had not ridden far when he heard Yudhishthira's voice behind him and reined in. The eldest Pandava had followed the chariot some distance on foot, and now he came up beside it, carrying the weight of everything he had not managed to say at parting.

He had not followed alone, though the others were gone by now. When the chariot rolled out of Upaplavya, the whole camp had gone a little way with it — Bhima and Arjuna and the twins of Madri, and after them the allied kings, Chekitana and Dhrishtaketu, Drupada and the king of Kasi and the mighty car-warrior Sikhandin. One by one they had fallen back and turned for home, until only the eldest Pandava was left on the road, still walking after the chariot.

"The lady who brought us from our infancy," Yudhishthira began, and Krishna knew at once whom he meant. Kunti, their mother, had remained in Hastinapura when her five sons went out to the world of exile and danger, and she had grieved for them every day since. Whatever was said in councils about kingdoms and armies, this was the message that had to travel first.

"Ask after her welfare," Yudhishthira said. "Salute her and embrace her, and comfort her over and over, for she is overwhelmed with grief on account of her sons."

Krishna waited, for the eldest Pandava had not finished. And indeed Yudhishthira went on, naming the elders of the Kuru house one by one, and each name carried its own weight. "Salute the Kuru king Dhritarashtra for me," he said, the blind father who had watched his own son swallow a kingdom and done nothing to stop it. "And Bhishma," the grandfather who had taught them the use of arms and was bound now to the other side by his vow. "And Drona, and Kripa," the teachers who had shaped them as warriors. "And salute Vidura," Yudhishthira said, and his voice changed, "who is endued with great wisdom" — the wise uncle who had stood by the Pandavas in that cold court when no one else dared.

Krishna took the messages into his keeping, one by one, and promised that each would be delivered exactly as it had been given: the embrace for the mother, the salutations for the king, the honours for the elders, the warm regard for Vidura. Nothing had been asked for himself; Yudhishthira had sent no demand, no warning, no word of his own rights. Only the grief of his mother and the courtesy owed to the old.

Then Yudhishthira stepped back from the chariot and stood in the road, and Krishna drove on. Behind him the eldest Pandava remained where he was, watching the chariot shrink toward the horizon, and the messages he had entrusted to it went ahead of him like a small, careful map of everything the coming days might break: a mother who stood to lose her sons whichever way the war went, teachers bound by oath to the wrong side, a wise uncle who could see the catastrophe and could not prevent it. The chariot carried all of it with it, rolling on toward Hastinapura.

It carried one thing more. Krishna had his own word to keep on that road. To Arjuna, who had pleaded that he carry peace between the two houses, he had answered that he would go to king Dhritarashtra — desirous of accomplishing what was consistent with righteousness, what might be beneficial to the Pandavas, and what was also for the good of the Kurus. The private messages and that public errand rode together now, in the same chariot, toward the same city.
stories.reflection: At the moment when war hangs in the balance, Yudhishthira's first thought is not for his claim to a throne but for his mother's grief and for the elders he still honours. The messages are a small map of the tragedy to come: a mother who loses either way, teachers bound to the side they cannot leave, a wise uncle powerless to stop what he can foresee.
stories.next_story_tease: But there was one more parting word to come, from Arjuna, and it carried the weight of everything the mission stood against.

stories.title: Arjuna's Warning and Bhima's Roar
stories.story:
Arjuna walked a few more steps beside the chariot, and then he spoke again, in a voice that carried over the rattle of the wheels. The morning was still early, and the chariot had not yet cleared the camp.

Krishna turned to listen. Everything Arjuna had said before, urging the peace mission, had been a plea: the words of a friend who wanted reconciliation, who called Krishna the best friend of both the houses and begged him to bring peace between the Pandavas and the sons of Dhritarashtra. He had asked Krishna to carry one more word to their ever-wrathful brother Suyodhana: that if he refused counsels fraught with virtue and profit, he would be the victim of his own fate. This was a different kind of word. This was what a man says when he has finished asking.

"If Dhritarashtra's son," Arjuna said, "who always adopts improper means, acts otherwise, then I shall surely, O Janardana, annihilate the whole race of the Kshatriyas."

There was no heat in the words, and that made them heavier. He did not name Duryodhana's crimes or rehearse the wrongs of thirteen years. He said simply that if the man who always chose the crooked path chose it once more, then the warrior race itself would be ended — by his hand, in a war that would leave no one to boast of victory. The warning was exact, and it was total: peace was being offered, and refusal had been priced. Krishna had already accepted the errand. To the plea he had answered that he would go to king Dhritarashtra, desirous of accomplishing what was consistent with righteousness, what might be beneficial to the Pandavas, and what was also for the good of the Kurus. The warning did not change the errand; it only made plain what the errand was riding against.

Then Bhima heard it, and Bhima answered in his own way. He set his feet on the earth, drew a breath that seemed to draw in half the morning, and set forth a terrible shout. It went out across the camp and the fields and the road, a sound with no words in it and no need of them, the whole of the promise Arjuna had just spoken given a body and a voice.

The bowmen who heard it trembled where they stood, their hands unsteady on their bows. And the steeds and the elephants, it was said, lost all control of their bodies in that moment of fear, standing shaking on the ground as the sound rolled over them. Some who stood near felt the very ground tremble with it, and for a moment the air carried nothing else. Even the birds of omen that had followed the chariot scattered. It was the sound of the war that had not yet begun — the war itself announcing its presence at the edge of the camp, so that every man who heard it knew, without being told, what a refusal would sound like. The shout hung in the air long after the sound of it had died, and the camp behind Krishna fell silent in its wake.

Krishna drove on. He carried the plea for peace, and now he carried the shape of its failure too: the mother's messages, the king's claim, the warrior's warning, and the roar that would be the first sound of the war if the crooked path was chosen again. They rode with him, side by side, all the way to Hastinapura — and Duryodhana, when he chose, would be choosing in the hearing of that shout. Behind him the brothers stood on the road and watched the chariot go, and between them and it the morning still trembled with the sound of what Bhima had said.
stories.reflection: The warning and the plea travel in the same chariot. Arjuna's words are not the opposite of the peace mission but its shadow: Duryodhana must hear what refusal will cost before his choice can mean anything. Peace is being offered not as a favour he may take for granted, but as a choice he is still free to refuse — and the refusal has been priced.
stories.next_story_tease: Farther along the road, a company of sages waited to greet the envoy of peace.

stories.title: When Krishna Met Parashurama
stories.story:
Ahead of him on the road, Krishna saw a company of sages, and even from a distance they seemed to burn with a light of their own, the radiance of men who had worn away the world's desires in austerity. He reined in the chariot, and before the horses had fully stopped he had alighted and gone to worship them, for though he travelled as the envoy of kings, before sages every envoy of kings bows first.

The rishis stood in the road blazing with that Brahmic lustre, and among them Krishna recognised Narada, the tireless traveller of the three worlds, whose presence carried its own meaning: whatever happened here would be known everywhere. And there were others whose names the road would carry all the way back to Upaplavya. It was an honour beyond any court's, and Krishna offered it as it was due: he worshipped them, and waited for their word.

Then one of the sages came forward, and the air seemed to change around him. It was Parashurama, Jamadagni's son, whose name every warrior in the world knew. He approached Govinda, the slayer of Madhu, and embraced him, and the embrace was not a formality between two great men; it was the greeting of an elder who had come a long way on purpose.

"We are desirous," Parashurama said, "of beholding all the Kshatriyas of the earth assembled from every side." The peace conclave at Hastinapura would draw every king and every warrior of the world to one gathering, and the sages had not wanted to miss it. But they had not come only to watch. "And we are anxious," the sage went on, "to listen to those words fraught with virtue and profit, which will be spoken by you unto the Kurus, in the presence of all."

There was something in the words that made the moment larger than a roadside courtesy. These were men who had renounced the world, yet they had journeyed to hear a speech about peace. They would not take sides in the quarrel; they had come to witness it, to stand as listeners at the place where the fate of the earth would be spoken aloud. And it was Parashurama, Jamadagni's son, who said it — the ancient sage, feared by warriors since before the fathers of the men now gathering, standing on the open road to say that what mattered was the word Krishna would speak.

Krishna received the blessing and the embrace, and the sages stood on the roadside as he remounted the chariot and gathered the reins. The chariot rolled on toward Hastinapura, and behind him the rishis remained where they were, a company of witnesses in the dust of the road, their presence a kind of promise: whatever words were spoken at the conclave of the Kurus, they would not be spoken unheard. The light of their austerity faded behind the chariot, and ahead lay the city, and the assembly, and the words that everyone had come to hear.
stories.reflection: The sages come as witnesses, not as advisors: they want to see the warriors of the earth gathered and to hear the words of peace spoken before them. That the ancient Parashurama, Jamadagni's son, should journey to listen rather than to act is its own quiet argument that in the coming days, the words spoken at Hastinapura may matter more than any sword.
stories.next_story_tease: With the sages' blessings behind him, Krishna turned his face toward the city of the Kurus.

stories.title: Krishna's Auspicious Journey to Hastinapura
stories.story:
When Krishna set out from Upaplavya on the errand Yudhishthira had asked of him, ten car-warriors rode behind his chariot, fully armed and able to cut down hostile heroes; a thousand foot-soldiers and a thousand horsemen followed, with attendants by the hundred carrying provisions in abundance. The road to Hastinapura, the Kuru capital, lay ahead. And for those who watched him go, the sky began to speak in signs.

Janamejaya, the king to whom this tale was told long afterward, asked how Krishna had made his journey and what omens were seen when he set out. The answer came: though there were no clouds, thunder rolled and lightning flashed. Fleecy clouds in a clear sky rained down behind him. The seven great rivers, the Sindhu among them, that flow eastward, turned and ran the other way. The directions themselves seemed reversed, and nothing could be told apart. Fires blazed up from the earth, and the earth trembled again and again. The contents of wells and water jars by the hundred swelled up and ran over. The whole universe was enveloped in darkness; dust filled the air until neither the cardinal nor the subsidiary points of the horizon could be distinguished. Loud roars rolled through the sky with no being visible from whom they came. And a south-westerly wind, harsh with thunder, uprooting trees by the thousands, crushed the city of Hastinapura.

But in the places through which Krishna passed, the same world turned gentle. Delicious breezes blew, and everything became auspicious. Showers of lotuses and fragrant flowers fell there. The very road grew delightful, free from prickly grass and thorns. Wherever he stayed, Brahmanas by the thousand glorified the giver of wealth and worshipped him with dishes of curds, ghee, and honey and presents of wealth. The women, coming out onto the road, strewed wild flowers of great fragrance upon the person of the hero devoted to the welfare of all creatures. The same departure was ruin for the Kuru capital and blessing for every place his chariot touched.

He passed through villages abounding in bees, picturesque to the eye and delightful to the heart, and through diverse cities and kingdoms, until he came upon a delightful spot called Salibhavana, filled with every kind of crop, delicious and sacred. The citizens of Upaplavya — always cheerful, well protected by the Bharatas, free from all anxiety on account of invaders — came out of their town and stood together on the way, desirous of beholding Krishna. And when that one who resembled a blazing fire arrived, they worshipped him with all the honours of a guest arrived in their abode.

At last, when Kesava came to Vrikasthala, the sun reddened the sky with straggling rays of light. Alighting from his car, he duly went through the usual purificatory rites, and ordering the steeds to be unharnessed, he set himself to say his evening prayers. Daruka, his charioteer, freed the horses and tended them according to the rules of equine science, taking off the yokes and traces and letting them loose. Then the slayer of Madhu said, "Here we must pass the night, for the sake of Yudhishthira's mission."

Ascertaining his intention, the attendants soon raised a temporary abode and prepared in a trice excellent food and drink. The Brahmanas of the village — noble and high-born, modest, obedient to the injunctions of the Vedas — approached that chastiser of foes and honoured him with their benedictions and auspicious speeches, placing their houses, abounding in wealth, at his disposal. Saying "Enough," Krishna paid them proper homage, each according to his rank, wended with them to their houses, and returned in their company to his own tent. And feeding all the Brahmanas with sweetmeats and taking his meals with them, Kesava passed the night happily there, at the threshold of the city whose sky had darkened at his coming.
stories.reflection: The omens at Krishna's departure split the world in two: ruin gathers over Hastinapura while his own path turns auspicious, as though the sky itself chose sides. The same journey is disaster for one city and blessing for every village along the way — his presence, not the weather, decides what happens where.
stories.next_story_tease: In Hastinapura, Duryodhana was already raising a reception fit for a king — pavilions, gems, and garlands meant to dazzle the arriving guest.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna's chariot rolls along a road free of thorns as showers of lotuses fall from a clear sky and women strew wildflowers in his path, while the sky over distant Hastinapura churns with darkness, lightning, and dust.

stories.title: Duryodhana's Lavish Pavilions That Krishna Ignores
stories.story:
News of Krishna's journey reached the Kuru palace before Krishna did. Dhritarashtra, the blind king, learned from his spies that the slayer of Madhu had set out, and his hair stood on end. He called Bhishma, Drona, Sanjaya, and the wise Vidura, and spoke to Duryodhana and his counsellors.

"Strange and wonderful is the news we hear," he said. "Men, women, and children are talking of it, in the houses where men congregate and in open spots. All say that Dasarha of great prowess will come here for the sake of the Pandavas. The slayer of Madhu deserves honour and worship at our hands. He is the Lord of all creatures; on him rests the course of everything in the universe. Intelligence, prowess, wisdom, and energy — all reside in Madhava. Worthy of honour at the hands of all righteous persons, he is the foremost of all men, eternal Virtue itself. If worshipped, he is sure to bestow happiness; if not worshipped, he is sure to inflict misery. If Dasarha is gratified with our offerings, all our wishes may be obtained through his grace in the midst of the kings. Make every arrangement for his reception without loss of time. Let pavilions be set up on the road, furnished with every object of enjoyment. Make such arrangements that he may be gratified with you. What does Bhishma think in this matter?"

Bhishma and the others applauded the king's words. "Excellent," they said.

And Duryodhana, understanding their wishes, ordered delightful sites to be chosen for the erection of pavilions. Many pavilions were thereupon constructed, abounding with gems of every kind, at proper intervals and at delightful spots along the route. The king sent handsome seats of excellent quality, beautiful girls, scents and ornaments, fine robes, excellent viands, drinks of diverse qualities, and fragrant garlands of many kinds. He took especial care to erect, for Krishna's reception, one highly beautiful pavilion at Vrikasthala, full of precious gems. When all was done — arrangements godlike, far above the capacity of human beings — Duryodhana informed Dhritarashtra that everything was ready.

The road from Vrikasthala to the capital had been turned into a pageant. Pavilions rose at proper intervals, each one a small palace of gems, and the air along the way carried the weight of garlands, scents, and vessels of drink laid out for a king's welcome. Travellers and citizens alike slowed to look at what Duryodhana had built, and the talk was all of the wealth being spent to receive one man.

Then Kesava arrived at the capital of the Kurus.

And he passed all of it by: the gem-studded pavilions, the seats, the garlands, the viands, the whole costly display raised in his honour — without casting a single glance at it. Not one of the gems of diverse kinds drew his eyes. The contrast was there for the whole city to see. Duryodhana had built as though the visitor could be dazzled into alliance, as though magnificence itself were the language in which the Kurus and the Pandavas could still be reconciled. Krishna, who needed nothing, made the whole architecture of the welcome irrelevant as his chariot rolled past the last pavilion and on toward the city — and a court that had measured him in gold was left, at his silent passing, to wonder what measure would have been right.
stories.reflection: The reception is measured entirely in riches, and Krishna's answer is perfect indifference: the gifts say everything about the giver and nothing about the guest. A man who needs nothing cannot be won by display — only by the truthfulness of the one who receives him.
stories.next_story_tease: When Dhritarashtra began planning gifts meant to bind Krishna, Vidura would name the deception openly.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna's chariot passes gem-studded pavilions hung with garlands along the road to Hastinapura, his eyes fixed straight ahead, while the assembled display of seats, vessels, and ornaments stands ignored and unused.

stories.title: Vidura Exposes the Plan to Bribe Krishna
stories.story:
When Dhritarashtra began to speak of the lavish gifts he would heap upon Krishna, Vidura could hold his peace no longer. The blind king, anxious to please the visitor the whole court called the lord of the three worlds, planned to shower him with wealth; and most of the assembly took this for wisdom. Vidura heard it, and answered with the one thing no one else in that room would say — the truth.

"O monarch, best of men," he said, "you are respected by the three worlds and loved and regarded by everybody. Venerable in years, what you say at this age can never be against the dictates of the scriptures or the conclusions of well-directed reason, for your mind is ever calm. Your subjects are well-assured that, like characters on stone, like light in the sun, like billows in the ocean, virtue resides in you permanently. Every one is honoured and made happy by your numerous virtues. Strive, therefore, with your friends and kinsmen to retain those virtues. Adopt sincerity of behaviour. Do not, from folly, cause the wholesale destruction of your sons, your grandsons, your friends, your kinsmen, and all that are dear to you."

Then he came to the point. "It is much that you wish to give to Kesava as your guest. Know, however, that Kesava deserves all this and much more — aye, the whole earth itself. But I truly swear by my own soul that you do not wish to give him all this either from motives of virtue or for the sake of doing what is agreeable to him. O giver of great wealth, all this betrays only deception, falsehood, and insincerity."

The words fell on the court like a stone into still water. Vidura went on, unsparing. "By your external acts, O king, I know your secret purpose. The five Pandavas desire only five villages. You do not wish to give them even that; you are therefore unwilling to make peace. You seek to make the mighty-armed hero of Vrishni's race your own by means of your wealth — and in this way you seek to separate Kesava from the Pandavas. But I tell you that you are unable, by wealth or attention or worship, to separate Krishna from Dhananjaya. I know the magnanimity of Krishna; I know the firm devotion of Arjuna towards him; I know that Dhananjaya, who is Kesava's very life, is incapable of being given up by him."

And then he told the king what Krishna would actually accept. "Save only a vessel of water, save only the washing of his feet, save only the usual enquiries after the welfare of those he will see — Janardana will not accept any other hospitality, nor set his eyes on any other thing. Offer him, O king, the hospitality that is most agreeable to that illustrious one deserving of every respect, for there is no respect that may not be offered to Janardana. Give unto Kesava that object in expectation of which, from desire of benefiting both parties, he comes to the Kurus. Kesava desires peace between you and Duryodhana on one side and the Pandavas on the other. Follow his counsels, O monarch. You are their father, O king, and the Pandavas are your sons. You are old and they are children to you in years. Behave as a father towards them, who are disposed to pay you filial regard."

Vidura had named the plan and the heart beneath it in the same breath. The gifts were not generosity but a strategy to prise Krishna loose from the Pandavas; the peace Krishna had come to offer was real; and the guest who had crossed half the country to save the house of Kuru could not be bought at any price. The question that hung in the air of the Kuru hall was whether anyone there was willing to hear it.
stories.reflection: Vidura's service is to name what everyone else politely ignored: the king's gifts are not generosity but an attempt to separate Krishna from the Pandavas. His certainty rests on character, not suspicion — he knows Krishna's magnanimity and Arjuna's devotion, so he knows no price exists that could come between them.
stories.next_story_tease: But Duryodhana had already formed a resolution of his own — to imprison the ambassador who was coming to make peace.

stories.title: Duryodhana Resolves to Imprison Krishna
stories.subtitle: Bhishma Departs in Anger
stories.story:
Duryodhana listened to the debate over Krishna's welcome, and when he finally spoke, he agreed with Vidura on one point alone: that Janardana could never be separated from the Pandavas. "All that Vidura has said about Krishna has been truly said," he declared. "Janardana is greatly devoted to the Pandavas and can never be separated from them. The diverse kinds of wealth proposed to be bestowed upon him ought never to be bestowed. Kesava is, of course, not unworthy of our worship — but both time and place are against it, for on receiving our worship he will very likely think that we are worshipping him out of fear. It is my certain conviction that an intelligent Kshatriya must not do that which may bring disgrace upon him. The large-eyed Krishna deserves the most reverential worship of the three worlds. It is quite out of place, therefore, to give him anything now — for war having been decided upon, it should never be put off by hospitality."

So much for the gifts. What replaced them was worse. The Grandsire, Bhishma, answered in his deep old voice: "Worshipped or not worshipped, Janardana never becomes angry. None, however, can treat him with disrespect, for Kesava is not contemptible. Whatever he purposes to do is incapable of being frustrated by anybody, by every means in his power. Do without hesitation what Krishna of mighty arms says, and bring about peace with the Pandavas through Vasudeva as the means. Janardana, possessed of a virtuous soul, will say what is consistent with religion and profit. It behooves you, therefore, with all your friends, to tell him only what is agreeable to him."

Duryodhana's answer came like a blow. "O Grandsire, I can by no means live by sharing this swelling prosperity of mine with the Pandavas. Listen — this is a great resolution which I have formed. I will imprison Janardana, who is the refuge of the Pandavas. He will come here tomorrow morning; and when he is confined, the Vrishnis and the Pandavas — aye, the whole earth — will submit to me. What may be the means for accomplishing it, so that Janardana may not guess our purpose, and so that no danger may overtake us, it behooves you to say."

A silence fell over the hall. Even Dhritarashtra, who had yielded to his son in so much, recoiled. Hearing these fearful words about imprisoning Krishna, the king and all his counsellors were very much pained and became deeply afflicted. "O ruler of men," he said to Duryodhana, "never say this again. This is not immemorial custom. Hrishikesa comes here as an ambassador. He is, besides, related to us and dear to us. He has done us no wrong. How then does he deserve imprisonment?"

But the old king's protest only released the older man's wrath. Bhishma rose from his seat. "This wicked son of yours, O Dhritarashtra, has his hour come," he said. "He chooses evil, not good, though entreated by his well-wishers. You also follow in the wake of this wicked wretch of sinful surroundings, who treads a thorny path, setting at naught the words of his well-wisher. This exceedingly wicked son of yours, with all his counsellors, coming in contact with Krishna of unstained acts, will be destroyed in a moment. I dare not listen to the words of this sinful and wicked wretch that has abandoned all virtue."

And having said this, the aged chief of the Bharata race, Bhishma of unbaffled prowess, inflamed with rage, rose and left that place — the assembly staring after him, the blind king stricken, the prince unmoved, and the plan to imprison the ambassador left standing in the middle of the hall like a storm that had not yet broken.
stories.reflection: Duryodhana's resolution turns diplomacy into a siege: he will imprison the ambassador who came to make peace, confident that holding one man will bend the whole earth. Bhishma's rage is the measure of the folly — he walks out rather than listen, naming the ruin he already sees coming.
stories.next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would enter Hastinapura and walk into the middle of that broken council to meet Dhritarashtra.

stories.title: A City Rises to Receive Krishna
stories.story:
Every street of Hastinapura was adorned as though for a festival when Krishna came. The principal avenues were decorated with jewels and gems, and no one, man, woman or child, remained indoors, so eager were the citizens to see him. Even before he reached the gates the welcome had begun: all the Dhartarashtras except Duryodhana, attired in their finest robes, had gone out to meet him, together with Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and the other elders, and the people followed by thousands, on cars of diverse kinds and many on foot.

Krishna had risen at day-dawn, gone through his morning rites, and taken leave of the Bharatas before setting out for the city of the Kurus; the inhabitants of Vrikasthala came out to bid farewell to that mighty one of long arms, and only when he was gone did they return to their homes. Now, meeting Bhishma of spotless deed, and Drona, and Dhritarashtra's sons on the way, he entered the city surrounded by them all. The citizens lined the streets and bent their heads down to the ground, singing eulogies in his honour as he passed through. Substantial mansions, filled with high-born ladies, seemed about to fall down under their living weight, so thickly did the women lean from the windows to see him. And although Krishna's steeds were endued with great speed, yet they moved very slowly through that dense mass of human beings.

He came at last to Dhritarashtra's ash-coloured palace, enriched with numerous buildings, and passed through the first three chambers. There he came upon the royal son of Vichitravirya, the blind king Dhritarashtra himself. At Krishna's approach, the blind monarch of great fame stood up, and with him rose Drona and Bhishma, Kripa and Somadatta, and king Vahlika also: all of them stood up to honour him. Krishna approached the king, worshipped him and Bhishma with proper words and without losing any time, then greeted the other kings according to their seniority in years, and accosted Drona and his son, Vahlika, Kripa and Somadatta.

In the chamber lay a spacious seat of beautiful workmanship, made of gold and set with jewels. At Dhritarashtra's request, Krishna took that seat, and the king's priests duly offered him a cow, honey and curds and water, the rites of hospitality performed with care. When the rites were over, Krishna remained there for a while among the Kurus, laughing and jesting with them according to his relationship with each, honoured and worshipped by the blind king. Then, with Dhritarashtra's permission, he came out, greeted all the Kurus in their assembly, and went on to the delightful abode of Vidura.

Vidura received him with every auspicious and desirable offering. What use, he said, in telling Krishna of the joy he felt at this advent of his, for he was the inner soul of all embodied creatures. When the hospitable reception was over, Vidura, conversant with all the principles of morality, honest and learned and free of wrath, enquired about the welfare of the Pandavas. And Krishna, to whom the past and the future were as the present, knowing that Vidura was loved by the Pandavas and friendly towards them, learned and firm in morality, honest and harbouring no wrath, began to tell him everything in detail about the doings of the sons of Pandu.

The day had begun with a city pouring out of doors to see one arrival, and it ended with Krishna speaking of his cousins in the forest, in the lamplight of Vidura's quiet house. Everyone in Hastinapura had risen to honour him, and still the true purpose of his coming, the errand of peace, waited to be spoken aloud.
stories.reflection: The whole city rises to honour Krishna, and he returns the honour in exact order of age and standing, paying the court its due before a single word of his mission is spoken. His first night in Hastinapura is spent not among kings but with Vidura, the one man in the palace who loves the Pandavas; even his welcome is a quiet alignment.
stories.next_story_tease: The same afternoon, Krishna went to the house of his aunt Kunti, who had not seen her sons in a long time.

stories.title: Kunti Pours Out Her Grief
stories.story:
Kunti had not seen Krishna in a long time, and when he came to her house that afternoon, after his meeting with Vidura, his countenance beaming like the radiant sun, she could not hold back. She threw her arms around his neck and began to pour forth her lamentations, remembering her sons; the tears of Pritha flowed fast at the sight, after so long, of Govinda of the Vrishni race, the companion of those mighty children of hers. Krishna received the rites of hospitality and took his seat, and only then did Kunti speak, with a woe-begone face and a voice choked with tears.

Her sons, she said, had from their earliest years always waited with reverence on their superiors; they were attached to one another in friendship; deprived deceitfully of their kingdom, they had gone to seclusion, though they were worthy of living in the midst of friends and attendants. They had subjugated both wrath and joy, were devoted to Brahmans and truthful in speech. Those children of hers, who had abandoned kingdom and enjoyments, leaving their miserable mother behind, and gone to the woods, plucking the very roots of her heart, how, she asked, did they live in the deep forest abounding with lions and tigers and elephants?

They had been deprived of their father in infancy and brought up tenderly by her. At home they had slept in high palatial chambers on soft blankets and the skins of the Runku deer, waked in the morning by the grunt of elephants, the neighing of steeds, the clatter of car-wheels and the music of conchs and cymbals, with flutes and lyres, the honeyed strains of songstresses and the eulogies chanted by bards and professional reciters, blessed at early dawn by the sacred hymns of Brahmans. That such sons should sleep in the deep woods resounding with the shrill and dissonant cries of beasts of prey could hardly be believed. How could those who were roused from their beds by music and eulogies be waked in the wild by the yells of beasts?

Then, one by one, she asked after them. How was Yudhishthira, of virtuous soul and complexion like pure gold, the foremost of all the Kurus in learning and disposition, handsome and mighty-armed and without an enemy, who bore the heavy burden that royal sages of old had borne, fit to become the monarch of the three worlds? How was Bhimasena, with the strength of ten thousand elephants and the speed of the wind, the slayer of Hidimva and Vaka, he who slew Kichaka with all his relatives, terrible in wrath yet obedient to the commands of his elder brother? How was Arjuna, who at one stretch shot five hundred arrows, equal in the use of weapons to king Kartavirya, in energy to the sun, in restraint of senses to a great sage, in forgiveness to the Earth itself, and in prowess to Indra himself? So her questions went, and her grief with them.

Krishna answered her gently. What woman is there in the world, he asked, who is like her? Endued with every virtue and with great wisdom, it behooved her to bear with patience both happiness and misery. The Pandavas, with Krishna, saluted her through him. And she would soon behold them become the lords of the whole world, with their foe slain and themselves invested with prosperity.

The words were spoken softly, but they carried the weight of a certainty. Kunti had poured out her sorrow to the one person who could answer it as a promise, and she let her tears fall, knowing that her sons would come back to her.
stories.reflection: Kunti's lament is unbearable precisely because it is concrete: she remembers the music her sons woke to and the beds they slept in, and measures their suffering against it. Krishna does not scold her out of her grief; he answers it with a certainty, that her sons will return as lords of the world, consolation grounded in what will come to pass rather than in hope.
stories.next_story_tease: That same day Krishna came to Duryodhana's palace, where a feast had been prepared for him.

stories.title: Krishna Refuses Duryodhana's Feast
stories.story:
With Pritha's leave, and having walked around her in farewell, Krishna went to the palace of Duryodhana. It was furnished with great wealth and adorned with beautiful seats, like unto the abode of Indra himself; unhindered by the orderlies-in-waiting, Krishna crossed three spacious yards and entered the mansion, which looked like a mass of clouds, high as the summit of a hill and blazing forth in splendour. There, in the midst of a thousand kings and surrounded by all the Kurus, sat Dhritarashtra's son of mighty arms on his throne, with Dussasana and Karna and Sakuni, the son of Suvala, on their seats beside him.

At Krishna's entry, Duryodhana rose from his seat with his counsellors to honour him. Krishna greeted the sons of Dhritarashtra, and all his counsellors, and every king present, according to their respective ages, and took his seat on a beautiful throne of gold overlaid with a carpet embroidered with gold. The Kuru king offered him a cow, and honey and curds and water, and placed at his service palaces and mansions and the whole kingdom. The Kauravas, with all the kings there present, worshipped him as he sat there, resembling the sun itself in splendour.

Then, the worship being over, king Duryodhana invited Krishna to eat at his house. Krishna did not accept the invitation.

The king pressed him, in a gentle voice with deception lurking behind his words, eyeing Karna as he spoke. Why did Janardana not accept the diverse kinds of viands and drinks, the robes and beds, all prepared and kept ready for him? He had granted aid to both sides; he was engaged in the good of both parties; he was the foremost of Dhritarashtra's relations and much loved by him. I desire to hear, Duryodhana said, what the true reason is of this refusal.

Krishna raised his mighty right arm, and in a voice deep as that of the clouds replied, in words clear and distinct and without a single letter dropped: envoys, O king, eat and accept worship only after the success of their missions. Therefore, O Bharata, after his mission became successful, Duryodhana might entertain him and his attendants.

It behooved him not, the king answered, to behave towards them in this way; whether he became successful or unsuccessful, they were endeavouring to please him because of his relationship with them. With Krishna they had no hostility, no war; on reflection, words such as these scarcely became him.

But Krishna had not finished. Not from desire, nor from wrath, nor from malice, nor for gain, nor for the sake of argument, nor from temptation, would he abandon virtue. One takes another's food when one is in distress; at present Duryodhana had not inspired love in him by any act, nor had Krishna himself been plunged into distress. Without any reason, O king, he said, you hate, from the moment of their birth, your dear and gentle brothers, the Pandavas, endued with every virtue. This unreasonable hatred of yours for the sons of Pritha ill becomes you. The sons of Pandu are devoted to virtue; who, indeed, can do them the least injury? He who hates them hates me; he who loves them loves me. Know that the virtuous Pandavas and my own self have but a common soul. And the food of that house, defiled by wickedness, did not deserve to be eaten by him; the food supplied by Vidura alone, he said, should be eaten by him.

In a palace furnished for a thousand kings, Krishna had chosen the table of a minister's house. The refusal was not discourtesy; it was a line drawn. A guest may eat where he is welcomed, but a friend of the Pandavas could not sit down at the table of the man who had spent his life hating them.
stories.reflection: Krishna's refusal of Duryodhana's food is not a diplomatic slight but a statement of identity: he and the Pandavas, he says, have but a common soul, and one does not eat at the table of a man who hates one's own self. It is also a quiet correction of Duryodhana's arithmetic, which counts feasts and favours where Krishna counts only love and virtue.
stories.next_story_tease: That night, at the table Krishna had chosen, Vidura would tell him the truth about the court he had come to save.

stories.title: Vidura's Warning in the Night
stories.story:
It was at Vidura's table that Krishna had eaten that day, as he had told Duryodhana's court he would. And now, the meal over and the house quiet, the meaning of that choice became clear. After Krishna had dined and been refreshed, Vidura spoke to him during the night, and the man who had welcomed him with joy spoke now with dread.

This advent of yours, O Kesava, he said, has not been a well-judged one. Dhritarashtra's son transgresses the rules of both profit and religion; he is wicked and wrathful, insults others though himself desirous of honours, and disobeys the commands of the aged. He is a transgressor of the scriptures, ignorant and of wicked soul, already overtaken by fate, untractable, disposed to do evil to those who seek his good. His soul is possessed by desire and lust; he foolishly regards himself as very wise; he is the enemy of all his true friends, ever-suspicious, without any control over his soul, ungrateful, he has abandoned all virtue and is in love with sin. A slave of his senses, ever obedient to the impulses of lust and avarice, irresolute in every act that should be done, he is endued with these and many other vices. Although Krishna would point out to him what is for his good, he would disregard it all, moved by pride and anger. He has great faith in Bhishma and Drona and Kripa and Karna and Drona's son and Jayadratha, and therefore he never sets his heart on peace.

Krishna listened, and Vidura went on. The sons of Dhritarashtra, with Karna, firmly believed that the Pandavas were incapable of even looking at Bhishma and Drona, not to speak of fighting against them. The foolish Duryodhana of limited sight, having assembled a huge army, regarded his purposes as already achieved; he had arrived at the conclusion that Karna, single-handed, was competent to vanquish his foes. He will, therefore, never make peace. Krishna desired to establish peace and brotherly feelings between the two parties, but all the sons of Dhritarashtra had come to the conclusion that they would not give the Pandavas what they had a right to. With those who are so resolved, his words would certainly prove vain. Where words, good or bad, are of the same effect, no wise man would spend his breath for nothing, like a singer before the deaf. As a Brahmana before a conclave of Chandalas, Krishna's words would command no respect among those ignorant and wicked wretches that have no reverence for all that deserves reverence.

It did not seem proper to Vidura that Krishna should go into the midst of those wicked-minded wretches seated together, and utter words against them. They had mustered a strong force and had suspicions of Krishna himself; they were inspired with the firm belief that Indra at the head of all the celestials was incapable of defeating them in battle. Staying in the midst of his ranks of elephants and his army of cars and heroic infantry, the foolish and wicked Duryodhana, with all fears dispelled, regarded the whole earth as already subjugated; he coveted extensive empire on the earth without any rivals. Peace, therefore, with him was unattainable. That which he has in his possession he regards as unalterably his. Alas, Vidura said, the destruction of the earth seems to be at hand for Duryodhana's sake, for, impelled by fate, the kings of the earth, with all the Kshatriya warriors, have assembled together, desirous of battling with the Pandavas. All those kings are in enmity with Krishna and have all been deprived of their possessions before this by him; through fear of him they have joined together with Karna and made an alliance with Dhritarashtra's sons. Reckless of their very lives, all those warriors have united with Duryodhana and are filled with delight at the prospect of fighting the Pandavas. It does not commend itself to me, Vidura said, that you should enter into their midst.

The night was still. Krishna had heard every word, the catalogue of Duryodhana's vices, the certainty of war, the plea that he not walk into that assembly. He did not argue with any of it. Vidura knew this court as no one else did, and Krishna had not come to Hastinapura to be persuaded out of listening.
stories.reflection: Vidura's warning is a portrait of a man already overtaken by fate: every vice he names is a reason Duryodhana cannot be persuaded, and every reason is also a prophecy of war. Krishna listens without argument, because the value of the warning is not that it changes his purpose, but that it is true.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna would answer Vidura's warning with a resolve of his own.
stories.hero_scene: Late at night in Vidura's quiet house, the lamp burning low, Vidura leans forward with a grave face as he warns Krishna, who sits in calm stillness listening to every word.

stories.title: The Merit of Striving for Peace
stories.story:
The lamps in Vidura's house burned low, and the city of Hastinapura slept. But the two men in that quiet room knew that the sleep of the city would not last. Krishna had come to the Kuru capital as a messenger of peace, and Vidura, the wisest of the Kurus, had just told him plainly what waited in the court: Duryodhana's wickedness, and the hostility of every Kshatriya who had sided with him.

Krishna listened to all of it without surprise. Then he answered, and his answer was not a defense of his plan but a statement of why he had come at all.

"Everything you have said is true, Vidura," he said. "You have spoken to me as a father and mother speak, and your words are worthy of you, consistent with virtue and profit and truth. But listen now to the reason for my coming. Well do I know the wickedness of Dhritarashtra's son, and the hostility of the Kshatriyas who stand with him. I have still come to the Kurus. Great will be the merit earned by him who frees the whole earth from the meshes of death — the earth, with its elephants, its chariots, and its steeds, overwhelmed by a dreadful calamity."

He spoke of merit as a man speaks of something he has weighed. If a man strives with all his might to perform a virtuous act and meets with failure, Krishna said, the merit of that act is still his — of that he had not the least doubt. And just as truly, if a person only intends a sinful act in his mind but never commits it, the demerit can never touch him. The scales of the world were not read by outcomes alone.

"I will sincerely endeavor, Vidura, to bring about peace between the Kurus and the Srinjayas, who are about to be slaughtered in battle. That terrible calamity which hangs over them all has its origin in the conduct of the Kurus — it is directly due to the actions of Duryodhana and Karna, and the other Kshatriyas only follow where these two lead. The learned call a man a wretch who will not, by his own solicitation, seek to save a friend about to sink in calamity. Striving with all his might, even to the extent of seizing his friend by the hair, one should dissuade him from an improper act. He who acts so reaps praise, not blame."

So it was that Krishna had come: not because he expected the court to listen, but because a true friend takes on the work of an intercessor when dissension breaks out between kinsmen. If Duryodhana judged him wrongly, he would still have the satisfaction of his own conscience. He had come, he said, so that no unrighteous, foolish, and inimical person might later say that Krishna, though competent, had made no attempt to restrain the angry Kurus and Pandavas from slaughtering one another. He had come to serve both parties. Having striven for peace, he would escape the censure of all the kings.

"If the foolish Duryodhana will not accept my words, he will only invite his fate. But if I can bring about peace among the Kurus without sacrificing the interests of the Pandavas, my conduct will be highly meritorious, and the Kauravas themselves will be liberated from the meshes of death. If the sons of Dhritarashtra reflect coolly on what I shall say — words fraught with wisdom and consistent with righteousness — then peace will be brought about, and the Kauravas will honor me as its agent."

And then, with the calm of a man who has settled a long argument in his own heart, he added what Vidura was meant to carry back into the night with him. "If, on the other hand, they seek to injure me, I tell you this: all the kings of the earth, united together, are no match for me — like a herd of deer incapable of standing before an enraged lion."

There was nothing more to say. The lamps flickered, the city slept on, and Krishna, the delighter of the Yadavas, laid himself down on his soft bed for the night. Whatever the morning brought, he would meet it having done the one thing that lay within his power: he had come, and he would speak.

Vidura remained wakeful long after, weighing the words of the man who had come to plead for peace and, in the same breath, had told him that he could not be harmed if the plea was refused. Somewhere between those two truths lay the whole of what was about to happen to the world.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer to Vidura turns the peace mission into a matter of conscience: merit belongs to the striving itself, not to the outcome. He does not come to the Kurus expecting to be heard — he comes so that the attempt is made, and so that no one, least of all himself, can later say it was not.
stories.next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would ride out into the streets of Hastinapura toward the Kuru assembly.
stories.hero_scene: In the lamplight of Vidura's house in Hastinapura, Krishna sits across from Vidura in the small hours of the night, one hand raised as he explains why he has come to a court he knows will not listen, while the sleeping city lies beyond the shuttered windows.

stories.title: Krishna Enters the Kuru Assembly
stories.story:
Before the sun was fully up, the sound of conchs and cymbals drifted into Vidura's house, where Krishna had passed the night in talk. A band of choristers and bards with melodious voices had gathered at the door to wake Kesava with music, and the city of Hastinapura, which had slept through the darkest hours of the night, stirred with the first news that the messenger of peace was awake.

Krishna rose and went through the customary acts of the morning: the cleansing bath, the sacred mantras, the libations of clarified butter poured on the sacrificial fire. He decked his person and began his worship of the rising sun, and while he was still at his devotions, Duryodhana and Sakuni, the son of Suvala, came to him.

"Dhritarashtra is seated in his court," they said, "with all the Kurus headed by Bhishma, and with all the kings of the earth. They are all soliciting your presence, O Govinda, like the celestials in heaven desiring the presence of Indra himself."

Krishna greeted them both with sweet and courteous enquiries, and when the sun had climbed a little higher, he summoned a number of Brahmanas and made them presents of gold, robes, kine, and steeds. Then his driver Daruka came and saluted him, and soon returned with his master's car: a large, blazing car furnished with rows of tinkling bells and harnessed with excellent steeds, producing a rattle deep as the rumbling of mighty masses of clouds.

Krishna walked round the sacred fire and the band of Brahmanas, put on the gem known as the Kaustubha, and mounted the car, blazing with beauty, surrounded by the Kurus and well protected by the Vrishnis. Vidura, conversant with every precept of religion, followed on his own car; Duryodhana and Sakuni followed on one car; and Satyaki, Kritavarman, and the other mighty car-warriors of the Vrishni race rode behind on cars, on steeds, and on elephants.

They came out upon a broad street that had been swept and watered, fit for the highest of kings. Cymbals began to play, conchs were blown, and other instruments poured forth their music. A great number of youthful heroes, foremost in the world for heroism and possessed of lion-like prowess, surrounded the car of Sauri. Thousands of soldiers in variegated dresses, bearing swords, lances, and axes, marched in advance of Kesava. Full five hundred elephants followed, and chariots by thousands. All the citizens of the capital, of every age and both sexes, came out into the streets, desiring to behold Janardana; the terraces and balconies of the houses were so thronged by ladies that the houses seemed ready to fall down with the weight. Worshipped by the Kurus, listening to sweet speeches, and returning the greetings of all as each deserved, Kesava went along the street, casting his eyes on all.

At last he reached the Kuru court, and his attendants loudly blew their conchs and trumpets and filled the sky with the blare. The whole assembly of kings trembled with delight at the expectation of soon setting eyes on Krishna. Hearing the rattle of his car, rumbling like the deep roll of rain-charged clouds, the monarchs understood that Krishna was near, and the hair of their bodies stood erect with joy.

At the gate of the court, Krishna alighted from his car, which resembled the summit of Kailasa, and entered the court — a place that looked like a mass of newly risen clouds, blazing with beauty, like the very abode of great Indra. And that illustrious hero entered arm-in-arm with Vidura and Satyaki on either side, overshadowing with his own the splendour of all the Kurus. The kings made way; the Rishis who had come to the assembly were given their seats; and Krishna, the guest for whom the whole city had poured into the streets, took his seat in the midst of the assembly.

There he sat, the calm centre of a court that had dressed itself in all its glory to receive him — a glory that seemed, in that moment, borrowed from his presence rather than lent to it.
stories.reflection: The procession into the Kuru court is honor laid on like cloth of gold, and Krishna accepts all of it — the music, the crowds, the trembling delight of the kings — without once bending toward its vanity. He is the guest the whole city turned out to see, yet the calm at the center of that splendour belongs to a man who has come on other business entirely.
stories.next_story_tease: Once the assembly had settled into silence, Krishna rose to make his plea for peace.
stories.hero_scene: At the gate of the Kuru court in Hastinapura, Krishna, wearing the Kaustubha gem, alights from his blazing car and enters the cloud-like hall arm-in-arm with Vidura and Satyaki on either side, his radiance overshadowing the splendour of all the assembled Kurus.
