stories.title: Krishna's Plea Before the Assembly
stories.story:
Silence fell over the Kuru assembly as the last of the kings took his seat, and into that silence Krishna's voice came — low and full, deep as a drum, deep as the roll of clouds in the rainy season. Though he addressed Dhritarashtra, he spoke so that the whole assembly heard him, every king leaning forward into his words.

"In order that peace may be established between the Kurus and the Pandavas without a slaughter of the heroes, I have come here," Krishna said. "I have no other words to offer, O king. Everything that should be learnt in this world is already known to you."

He reminded Dhritarashtra what his race was. The Kuru dynasty, he said, was distinguished among all royal dynasties for its learning, its behaviour, its accomplishments. Joy in the happiness of others, grief at the sight of misery, the desire to relieve distress, abstention from injury, sincerity, forgiveness, and truth — these prevailed among the Kurus. "It would be a pity if anything improper were done by any one belonging to such a race," Krishna said, "and a greater pity still if it were done by you. You are the first of those who should restrain the Kurus if they behave deceitfully toward strangers or toward their own kin."

Then he came to the point, and the assembly heard the name it had been waiting for. "Know that your wicked sons, headed by Duryodhana, abandoning both virtue and profit, disregarding morality, and deprived of their senses by avarice, are acting most unrighteously toward their foremost of kinsmen. The terrible danger that threatens all has its origin in the conduct of the Kurus. If you become indifferent to it, it will produce a universal slaughter. But if you are willing, you may allay that danger even yet — peace is not difficult of acquisition."

The establishment of peace, Krishna said, depended on two men: the king and himself. "Set right your sons, O king, and I will set the Pandavas right. Whatever you command, it behooves your sons with their followers to obey. If they live in obedience to you, that would be the very best they could do. If you strive for peace by restraining your sons, it will be to your profit, as also to the benefit of the Pandavas. Let the sons of Pandu be your allies. Protected by the illustrious sons of Pandu, Indra himself at the head of the celestials will not be able to vanquish you — how, then, could mere earthly kings withstand your prowess?"

He drew the king a picture of a world that did not have to burn. With Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, Aswatthaman, Vikarna, Somadatta, Vahlika, the chief of the Sindhus, the ruler of the Kalingas, and Sudakshina of the Kamvojas on one side — and with Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Savyasachin, the twins, Satyaki, and Yuyutsu on the other — who, Krishna asked, of such misdirected intelligence would fight such a host? With both the Kurus and the Pandavas at his back, the sovereignty of the whole world and invincibility before all foes would be his. All the rulers of the earth would seek alliance with him. Protected by sons, grandsons, fathers, brothers, and friends, he would live in exceeding happiness.

"In battle, O great king, nothing but wholesale destruction is visible. In the destruction of both parties, what merit do you see? If the Pandavas are slaughtered in battle, or if your own mighty sons fall, tell me what happiness you will enjoy. All of them are brave and skilled in weapons; all of them are desirous of battle — the Pandavas as also your sons. Save them from the terrible danger that threatens them. After the battle you will not behold all the Kurus or all the Pandavas. Car-warriors slain by car-warriors, you will see the heroes of both parties reduced in numbers and strength. All the rulers of the earth have been assembled here, and inflamed with wrath, they will not stop short of destroying one another."

When Krishna finished, the assembly was stiller than it had been at his first word. He had laid before the blind king the whole arithmetic of war: every warrior counted, every alliance weighed, every happiness that would survive the slaughter set against the one that would not — and the choice, plainly, was Dhritarashtra's to make.
stories.reflection: Krishna's plea is built on a single repeated question: in the ruin of both houses, what happiness would remain to the king? He offers Dhritarashtra sovereignty won by alliance instead of battle, and leaves the choice entirely in his hands — the peace mission succeeds or fails on whether the blind king can see what has been put before him.
stories.next_story_tease: Into that silence, the sage Parashurama rose to tell the assembly a story from the age of the world.

stories.title: Parashurama Reveals Nara and Narayana
stories.subtitle: The legend of Dambhodbhava
stories.story:
When Krishna finished speaking, the whole assembly sat silent, the hair on their bodies standing on end. Every king there thought the same thing: there was no man who could dare reply to that speech. And as the silence stretched on, a voice rose from among them — the voice of the sage Parashurama, the son of Jamadagni, addressing Duryodhana directly.

"Listen confidingly to my words, illustrated by an example," Parashurama said, "and seek your own good if my speech recommends itself to you."

And he told the assembly the story of a king of yore named Dambhodbhava, who was the head of the earth and whose sovereignty extended over the whole world. Every morning, after the night had passed away, that mighty car-warrior called the Brahmanas and the Kshatriyas to him and asked the same question: "Be he a Sudra, a Vaisya, a Kshatriya, or a Brahmana, is there any one who is superior or even equal to me in battle?" And uttering those words, the king wandered over the earth, intoxicated with pride and thinking of nothing else.

Certain high-souled Brahmanas, conversant with the Vedas and fearing nothing on earth, counselled the monarch to curb his pride. But though they forbade him, the king went on asking the same question day after day. At last some Brahmanas, endued with ascetic merit and inflamed with anger, answered him plainly. "There are two persons," they said, "who are foremost of all men and always victorious in battle. You will by no means be equal to them if you seek an encounter with either one."

The king asked where those two heroes might be found, in what race they were born, and what feats they had achieved. "They are ascetics called Nara and Narayana," the Brahmanas replied. "They have both taken their births in the race of man. Go and fight with them if you will. That illustrious pair are even now practising the severest of penances in some hidden region of the mountains of Gandhamadana."

Unable to bear even the reputation of such rivals, the king speedily mustered his great army, of the six kinds of forces, and marched to the rugged and frightful mountains of Gandhamadana. He searched among the woods and at last came upon the two ascetics, concealed in the forest, emaciated with hunger and thirst, their veins swollen and visible, much afflicted by the cold winds and the hot rays of the sun. The king approached them, touched their feet, and enquired after their welfare. The two Rishis received him hospitably, with fruits and roots, a seat and water, and then asked his business. "Let it be done," they said.

The king spoke the words he was in the habit of speaking to all. "The whole earth has been conquered by the might of my arms," he said. "All my foes have been slain. Desiring a battle with you both, I have come to this mountain. Offer me this hospitality — I have cherished this wish for a long time."

"O best of kings," Nara and Narayana replied, "wrath and covetousness have no place in this retreat. How can a battle be possible here? There are no weapons here, and nothing of unrighteousness and malice. Seek battle elsewhere — there are many Kshatriyas on earth."

But the king pressed them, and the Rishis soothed him and overlooked his importunity. Still he repeated his summons to battle, again and again. At last Nara took up a handful of grass-blades and said, "Desirous of battle as you are, come, O Kshatriya, and fight! Take up all your arms and array your troops. I will curb your eagerness for battle hereafter!"

Dambhodbhava answered that he had come desiring to fight and would fight even against such a weapon; and with all his troops he covered every side with a shower of arrows. That ascetic, however, by means of those blades of grass, baffled all the terrible shafts capable of mangling the bodies of hostile warriors. Then the invincible Rishi let off toward the king his own terrible weapon made of grass-blades, incapable of being counteracted — and what followed was so wonderful that it silenced every boast that had ever been made in Dambhodbhava's court. The king who had measured himself against the whole world found his measure at last.

Parashurama paused, and let the assembly understand the point of his tale before he spoke it aloud. "They that were Nara and Narayana in days of yore," he said, "are now Arjuna and Kesava. Know then, O great king, who these brave and foremost of persons are. If you believe in this and do not mistrust me, adopt a virtuous resolution and make peace with the sons of Pandu."

The kings of the earth sat in that assembly and looked at the two men among them — the charioteer-brother and the prince who had come to plead — and heard, in Parashurama's words, the oldest names in the world laid over their newest faces.
stories.reflection: The tale of Dambhodbhava is a lesson in misplaced pride delivered through the oldest of mirrors: the king who measured himself against every man on earth never once thought to ask what the gods' own companions might be. Parashurama leaves the assembly in no doubt about who sits before them — the question now is whether Duryodhana will believe it.
stories.next_story_tease: The appeal would be carried one step further, directly to Duryodhana himself.
stories.hero_scene: On the hidden slopes of Mount Gandhamadana, the emaciated ascetic Nara stands calmly holding up a handful of grass-blades while King Dambhodbhava's army looses a shower of arrows that the blades turn aside, the king's pride breaking at last before the weapon that cannot be counteracted.

stories.title: Krishna's Appeal to Duryodhana
stories.story:
Of all the doors Krishna knocked on during his peace mission to Hastinapura, the hardest was Duryodhana's. Bhishma had listened, and Drona, and the wise Vidura had never needed persuading. Even the old king, Dhritarashtra, found everything Krishna said true, reasonable, and good for the world — except that it demanded a resolve he did not possess.

"I am not independent," he confessed to Krishna. "Duryodhana never does what pleases me. He does not listen to the words of Gandhari, or of wise Vidura, or of friends headed by Bhishma, all of whom seek his good. Do you yourself, O Krishna, counsel that crooked, senseless prince. By doing this you will have done the noble act that a friend should ever do."

So Krishna, who understood both virtue and what was practical, went and stood before the ever-wrathful Duryodhana and spoke to him in sweet words, meant especially for his good and for the good of all who followed him.

"You are born in a race distinguished for its wisdom," he began. "It behooves you to act righteously as I will indicate. You have learning and excellent behavior; you are adorned with every good quality. It is only the wicked-souled, the cruel, and the shameless who act in the way that seems acceptable to you. The inclinations of the righteous stay consistent with virtue and profit; the inclinations of the unrighteous turn perverse. The disposition you keep showing, O bull of Bharata's race, is of that perverse kind. Persistence in such behavior is sinful, frightful, and capable of leading to death itself — and it is causeless, for you cannot even hold to it for long."

He did not scold. He reasoned, the way one reasons with a kinsman whose ruin one can already see. If Duryodhana avoided what was productive only of woe, Krishna said, he would escape the sinful and disreputable deeds of his brothers, his followers, his counsellors. "Make peace with the sons of Pandu," he urged. "They are endued with great wisdom and great bravery, with great exertion and great learning, and all of them have their souls under complete control. Such conduct will be agreeable to your father, who is endued with great wisdom; to the grandsire Bhishma; to Drona; to the high-souled Kripa; to Somadatta; to wise Vahlika; to Ashwatthama; to Vikarna; to Sanjaya; to Vivinsati; and to many of your kinsmen and friends. The whole world will derive benefit from that peace."

Then the sweet words grew weightier, and the whole assembly heard what a friend was willing to say. "You are modest, born in a noble race, learned, kind of heart. Be obedient to the commands of your father and of your mother. Good sons always regard as beneficial what their fathers command; when calamity overtakes a man, he recollects his father's injunctions. Peace with the Pandavas recommends itself to your father. Let it recommend itself to you also, with your counsellors. That mortal who listens to the counsels of friends and does not act on them is consumed at the end by the consequences of his disregard, like him who swallows the fruit called Kimpaka. He who from folly does not accept beneficial counsel, unnerved by procrastination and unable to attain his object, is obliged to repent at last. But he who, having listened, accepts at once, abandoning his own opinion, always wins happiness in the world."

He ended where he had begun, on kinship. "He who rejects the words of well-meaning friends is soon subjugated by his foes. Disregarding the opinions of the righteous, he abides by the opinions of the wicked and makes his friends weep for him. Forsaking superior counsellors, he seeks the advice of inferior ones and falls into great distress. That companion of the sinful, who behaves falsely and never listens to good friends, who honors strangers but hates his own — he is soon cast off by the Earth. You have quarrelled with your own kin and seek protection from those who are sinful, incapable, and foolish. What other man on earth is there who would do this?"

Krishna fell silent, and the court of the Kurus held its breath around the two of them: the guest who had spoken like a friend, and the prince who had been asked, at last, to choose.
stories.reflection: Krishna's appeal never leaves the ground of kinship and self-interest: he argues for peace as the path of wisdom, obedience, and survival, not as surrender. The tragedy of the scene is that the strongest argument in the hall is addressed to a man who has already decided, and everyone present knows it.
stories.next_story_tease: But Duryodhana was already shaping his answer, and it would fit on the point of a needle.
stories.hero_scene: In the crowded Kuru assembly, Krishna stands close before the seated Duryodhana, one hand raised in earnest counsel, while Dhritarashtra watches from his throne and the court falls silent around them.

stories.title: Duryodhana's Refusal: Not a Needle-Point of Land
stories.story:
Krishna's words had barely settled in the assembly before Duryodhana rose to answer them. He had listened to the sweet counsel with a face like stone, and now the court of the Kurus heard, in reply, not a rebuttal but a declaration.

"It behooves you, O Kesava, to speak after reflecting on all circumstances," he began, and the formality of the address did not hide its edge. "You find fault with me alone — you, and Vidura, and the king, and the preceptor, and the grandsire. Yet I do not find the least fault in myself, not even after reflection, not even a minute one. In the game at dice that was joyfully accepted by them, the Pandavas were vanquished and their kingdom was won by Shakuni. What blame can be mine as regards that? The wealth that was won from them then, I ordered returned. And that they were defeated once again at dice and had to go to the woods — can that be any fault of ours?"

He spread his hands, the picture of a man unfairly accused. "Imputing what fault to us do they regard us as enemies? Though really weak, why do the Pandavas so cheerfully seek a quarrel with us, as if they were strong? What have we done to them?"

Then the defensive tone hardened into pride. "We shall not, in consequence of any fierce deed or alarming word of theirs, bow down to them in fear, deprived of our senses. We cannot bow down to Indra himself, let alone the sons of Pandu. I do not see the man, observant of Kshatriya virtues, who can venture to conquer us in battle. Let alone the Pandavas — the very gods are not competent to vanquish Bhishma, Kripa, Drona, and Karna in battle."

And now the assembly heard the heart of it, spoken plainly. "If, in the observance of the practices of our order, we are cut off with weapons in battle when our end comes, even that will lead us to heaven. Even this is our highest duty as Kshatriyas: that we should lay ourselves down on the field of battle on a bed of arrows. If, without bowing to our enemies, ours be that bed of arrows, it will never grieve us. Who is there, born in a noble race and conforming to Kshatriya practices, who would from fear bow to an enemy, desiring only to save his life?"

He invoked the old saying of Matanga, and the words rang through the hall like a sword drawn from its sheath. "A Kshatriya should always keep himself erect, and never bow down, for exertion alone is manliness. One should rather break at the knots than bend. A person like me bows only to the Brahmanas, for the sake of piety, and regards nobody else."

Then came the closing, delivered slowly, each clause a door shut. "That share in the kingdom which was formerly given to them by my father shall never again be obtainable by them as long as I live. As long as king Dhritarashtra lives, both ourselves and they, sheathing our weapons, should live in dependence on him. Given away formerly from ignorance or fear, when I was a child and dependent on others, the kingdom — incapable of being given away again — shall not be obtainable by the Pandavas."

Duryodhana paused, and looked directly at Krishna, and the court heard the words that would be remembered for as long as the Bharatas told this story. "At present, O Kesava of mighty arms, as long as I live, even that much of our land which may be covered by the point of a sharp needle shall not be given by us unto the Pandavas."

There it was. Not a province, not a village, not a field — a needle's point. The peace mission had asked for five villages, for a token, for anything that would let the cousins live without war; and the answer measured out the whole earth in terms of a needle's point and found it too much. The assembly sat in silence, and even those who had long expected this refusal felt the finality of it settle over the hall like dust.
stories.reflection: Duryodhana's refusal is not stammered but recited — an argument with its own logic, grounded in pride and a warrior's code of never bending. What makes it chilling is its clarity: he genuinely believes the dice game was not his fault, and he genuinely believes a bed of arrows is a happy fate. Pride here speaks fluently in the language of honor.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's patience had limits, and the needle's point had just crossed them.

stories.title: Krishna's Rebuke of Duryodhana's Crimes
stories.story:
For a long moment after Duryodhana finished, Krishna said nothing. When he spoke, the court saw that his eyes were red with anger, and the sweet counsel of the morning was gone.

"Wishest thou for a bed of heroes?" he asked, and the formal thou was colder than any shout. "Verily, thou shalt have it, with thy counsellors. Wait but a short while — a great slaughter will ensue."

Then he turned to the claim that had just been made before them all. "Thou thinkest, O thou of little understanding, that thou hast committed no offence against the Pandavas? Let the assembled monarchs judge. Grieved at the prosperity of the high-souled Pandavas, thou conspiredst with Suvala's son about the gambling match. How could those virtuous, honest, and superior kinsmen of thine otherwise have engaged in such a wicked act with the deceitful Shakuni? Gambling robs even the good of their understanding, and for the wicked, disunion and dire consequence spring from it. It was thou who devisedst, with thy wicked counsellors, that terrible source of calamity, without consulting persons of righteous behavior."

Krishna's voice did not rise; it gathered. "Who else is there capable of insulting a brother's wife in the way thou didst — of dragging her into the assembly and addressing her in the language thou hadst used towards Draupadi? Of noble parentage and excellent behavior, dearer to them than their very lives, the queen-consort of Pandu's sons was treated even thus by thee. All the Kauravas know what words were addressed in their assembly by Dussasana unto the sons of Kunti when they were about to set out for the woods. Language such as becomes only the heartless and the despicable was frequently repeated by Karna, and by Dussasana, and by thee."

He moved through the crimes one by one, as though turning over stones. "Thou hadst taken great pains to burn to death, at Varanavata, the sons of Pandu with their mother, while they were children — though that effort of thine was not crowned with success. After this, the Pandavas with their mother were obliged to live for a long while concealed in the town of Ekachakra, in the abode of a brahmana. With poison, with snakes, with cords, thou hadst by every means sought the destruction of the Pandavas, and none of thy designs was successful. With such feelings, having always acted towards them so deceitfully, how canst thou say that thou hast not offended against the high-souled Pandavas?"

Now the rebuke turned to prophecy. "Thou art not willing to give them their paternal share in the kingdom, although they are begging it of thee. Thou shalt have to give it them — this, when, divested of prosperity, thou shalt be laid low. Having done innumerable wrongs to the Pandavas, thou seekest now to appear in a different garb. Though repeatedly solicited by thy parents, by Bhishma, by Drona, and by Vidura to make peace, thou dost not make peace. Great is the advantage in peace, O king, both to thyself and to Yudhishthira. Peace, however, does not recommend itself to thee. To what else can it be due but to thy loss of understanding? Sinful and disreputable is that act which thou art about to do."

While Krishna was still speaking, Dussasana rose and turned on his own brother. "If, O king, thou dost not willingly make peace with the Pandavas, verily the Kauravas will bind thee hand and foot and make thee over to the son of Kunti. Bhishma, and Drona, and thy own father will make over us three — Vikartana's son, thyself, and myself — to the Pandavas."

Hearing this, Duryodhana rose from his seat in anger, breathing heavily like a great snake. He disregarded Vidura, and Dhritarashtra, and the great king Vahlika, and Kripa, and Somadatta, and Bhishma, and Drona, and Krishna himself — all of them — and walked out of the court. His brother and all his counsellors rose and followed him, and the kings followed after, and the assembly emptied in his wake.

Bhishma watched him go, and said to those who remained: "The enemies of that person who, abandoning both virtue and profit, follows the impulses of wrath, rejoice on beholding him plunged into distress at no distant date. This wicked son of Dhritarashtra obeys only the dictates of wrath and avarice. I see, O Janardana, that the hour of all those Kshatriyas is arrived."
stories.reflection: Krishna's anger here is the anger of a witness: he lists the offences one by one — the dice, the assembly, the burning house, the poison — not to win an argument but to fix the record before the war begins. And Bhishma, who will himself fall in that war, is the one who names the hour already arrived.
stories.next_story_tease: When the hall had emptied, Krishna turned to the elders who had let him go.
stories.hero_scene: In the Kuru assembly, Krishna stands with eyes red in anger, one hand extended towards Duryodhana as he enumerates his crimes, while the seated kings and elders listen in frozen silence.

stories.title: Krishna Urges the Elders to Bind Duryodhana
stories.story:
The Kuru court emptied in Duryodhana's wake, and when the last of his followers had gone, Krishna stood before the elders who remained. His eyes were still red, but his voice was quiet, and what he said was not counsel any more. It was an indictment.

"Even this is great transgression," he said, "of which all the elders of the Kuru race are becoming guilty — for they do not forcibly seize and bind this wicked king."

The words fell on the old men of the court like a stone into still water. Bhishma had spoken of the hour of the Kshatriyas; Krishna now named who bore the blame for letting it arrive. The king's counsellors had watched Duryodhana refuse peace, insult a brother's wife, plot murder by fire and poison — and they had stood, and let him walk out. In Krishna's telling, standing by was itself a crime.

Then he gave them the example they could not answer, and it was his own. "Kansa, the son of Ugrasena, abandoned by his relatives, was slain by me in a great encounter, from desire of benefiting my kinsmen."

He did not need to explain it. The old kings in that hall knew the story: Kamsa, the tyrant of Mathura, who had imprisoned his own sister and murdered her children, who had hunted his nephew across the countryside — and who had at last been struck down, not by an army, not by the gods, but by the kinsman he had wronged, acting for the sake of his kin. The wicked had been seized, bound, and ended, and the family had survived. That was what a kinsman did, Krishna said, when a kinsman turned tyrant. That was the standard by which the elders of the Kurus would now be judged.

"Binding Duryodhana fast," he said, "make peace with the Pandavas."

The assembly heard the two halves of it, and understood that they were one command. Bind the wicked king — that was the necessary act. Make peace with the Pandavas — that was its purpose. The peace that had been begged for, pleaded for, offered in sweet words and reasonable arguments, had come to this: it could only be achieved by the elders laying hands on their own king. Krishna had come to Hastinapura asking for five villages and a chance for the cousins to live; he left the elders of the Kurus with a harder question than any he had brought. Would they seize Duryodhana to save him from himself? Or would they stand by, guiltless in their own eyes, and watch the slaughter that would follow?

The silence that answered him stretched through the hall. No elder stepped forward. No hand was laid on the king who had already left the court. And Krishna, who had done what a friend could do — who had spoken sweet words, and plain words, and terrible words — had nothing left to say to men who would not act. He had urged them to bind the wicked king, and they had not, and the hour Bhishma had seen was nearer now than it had been that morning.
stories.reflection: Krishna's appeal to the elders rests on a startling precedent — his own killing of Kamsa, a kinsman turned tyrant, done for the sake of his kin. The charge is that the elders' inaction is itself a crime: peace is not merely advised but demanded, and the demand exposes how far the Kurus have fallen from what kinship requires.
stories.next_story_tease: But the elders' silence was not the last word — plans were already being laid to seize Krishna himself.
stories.hero_scene: In the nearly empty Kuru assembly, Krishna stands facing the elders — Bhishma, Drona and the rest — with one hand extended in accusation, urging them to bind the wicked king who has just stormed out.

stories.title: The Plot to Seize Krishna; Satyaki's Alarm
stories.story:
Some conspiracies are born in such low whispers that the walls themselves seem to lean in to listen. The one that took shape in Hastinapura that day began when Duryodhana rose from the Kuru assembly, deaf to the grave words his mother had just spoken to him, and walked out in anger to the company of men who would tell him only what he wanted to hear.

The Pandavas' messenger, Krishna, had come to the Kuru court seeking peace, and every elder who still had influence — the king, the grandsire, the wise Vidura — had urged Duryodhana to accept it. He would not. And now, outside the assembly, with the dust of the court still settling behind him, he set his mind to the other way of ending the matter.

He consulted with Sakuni, Suvala's son, the man most clever in dice, who had once gambled the Pandavas' kingdom away from them. Karna joined them, and Dussasana made the fourth. And this was the resolution they arrived at: 'This Janardana, quick in action, seeks, with king Dhritarashtra and Bhishma the son of Santanu, to seize us first. We, however, shall forcibly seize this tiger among men, Hrishikesa, before he can move against us — as Indra once forcibly seized Vali, the son of Virochana.'

Each of them supplied reasons, and each reason sounded, to their own ears, like wisdom. Once Krishna was bound, they told one another, the Pandavas would lose heart and become incapable of exertion, like snakes whose fangs have been broken. He was the refuge and the protection of them all — the grantor of wishes, the bull of all the Satwatas. Confine him, and the Pandavas with the Somakas would sit depressed and helpless. Therefore, disregarding Dhritarashtra's cries, they would seize Kesava even here, in the heart of the Kuru court, and then fight with the foe.

What the four conspirators did not know was that they had already been read. Satyaki, Krishna's companion, possessed the gift of knowing a man's heart by his signs — the too-quick glance, the careful lowering of a voice, the way Duryodhana's fingers worked at the hilt of his sword as he spoke of seizure. He knew the plot before the plotters had finished shaping it, and he rose quietly and left the court, with Kritavarman, Hridika's son, at his side.

At the entrance he stopped and turned. 'Array the troops,' he said. 'Accoutred in mail, with your men drawn up for battle, wait here at the entrance of the court until I have represented this matter to Krishna.'

Then Satyaki went back into the hall, like a lion entering a mountain cave. He informed the high-souled Kesava first, then king Dhritarashtra, then Vidura. And having told them the whole resolution, he laughed.

'These wicked men intend to commit an act here that is disapproved by the good, from consideration of virtue, profit, and desire,' he said. 'They will never be able to achieve it. These fools of sinful souls, overwhelmed by lust and anger, these wretches desiring to seize the lotus-eyed one, are like idiots and children trying to seize a blazing fire with their garments.'

Vidura, who foresaw all things, turned to Dhritarashtra in the midst of the Kurus. 'O king, the hour of all your sons is come,' he said, 'for they strive to perpetrate a highly infamous act, however incapable they are of accomplishing it. United, they desire to vanquish this younger brother of Vasava and seize the lotus-eyed one. Encountering this tiger among men, they will all perish like insects in a blazing fire. If Janardana wishes, he can send all of them, even if they fight in a body, to the abode of Yama, like an enraged lion dispatching a herd of elephants. But he will never do any such sinful and censurable act. This best of persons, of unfading glory, will never deviate from virtue.'

In the doorway stood Kritavarman's mail-clad ranks, silent and ready. In the middle of the hall sat the man they had meant to seize, untouched, unhurried, listening. And everyone present understood, in the hush that followed Vidura's words, what kind of quarry the four had chosen — and that the conspiracy was dead before it had ever been allowed to move.
stories.reflection: The conspiracy fails at the moment of its forming, and not because the plotters were careless: they simply misjudged the company they kept. Duryodhana counted on deceiving everyone in the court, but he sat within reach of a man who could read hearts by signs, and he plotted against someone who did not need an army to be unseizable.
stories.next_story_tease: When Krishna heard the warning, his answer would be neither fear nor anger, but a calm permission that unsettled the conspirators more than any threat.

stories.title: Krishna Defies the Conspirators
stories.story:
Every eye in the Kuru assembly turned to Krishna, and the hall, crowded with kings, fell so quiet that the breathing of the mailed men at the door could be heard. Satyaki's warning was out. The plot of Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni, and Dussasana stood exposed — and the man they had planned to seize had heard of it, it seemed, without moving a muscle of his face. The four who had resolved on the seizure were not in the court to hear it — they had gone away from the assembly to shape their plot in secret, and their certainty would first waver only later, when Vidura brought the unwilling Duryodhana back before Krishna. What they had planned in whispers had been carried into the open by Satyaki's warning, under the eyes of the whole court.

Krishna cast his eyes on Dhritarashtra and spoke, in the midst of those who listen to others' words.

'O king,' he said, 'if these men desire to chastise me by using violence, permit them to chastise me. As for my chastising them — I dare chastise all of them together, so excited are they with rage. But I will not perpetrate any sinful and censurable act.'

He paused, and the court felt the whole meaning of what he had said settle over it: he had not asked for protection, had not called on the arrayed troops, had not even risen from his seat. Threats had been hurled across that hall for months, but no one had ever spoken like this — with the calm of a man describing the weather while holding the outcome in his hand.

'Coveting the possessions of the Pandavas, your sons will lose their own,' he went on. 'If they desire to perpetrate such a deed, Yudhishthira's object will then be easily accomplished — for, this very day, seizing these men with all that follow them, I can make them over to the sons of Pritha. What is there that is difficult of attainment by me? But I will not, in your presence, O great monarch, commit any such censurable deed as can proceed only from wrath and a sinful understanding. Let it be, O king, as this Duryodhana desires. I give permission to all your sons to do it.'

A sound went through the hall that was half wonder and half fear. The Pandavas' messenger had come to Hastinapura speaking of peace, and the court had grown used to thinking of Krishna as a negotiator — a voice, a supplicant for an agreement. But the man who sat before them now spoke as one who could end the argument between the two houses with a single motion, and who chose, instead, to withhold himself. He was not refusing the conspiracy because he feared it. He was refusing to meet it on its own ground. And in that refusal, something became clear to everyone present: the conspiracy had not failed because it had been discovered. It had failed because it was impossible, and had been impossible from the moment it was conceived.

Dhritarashtra sat blind and silent, his face turned toward the voice. Then the old king found his answer. 'Kshattri,' he said to Vidura, 'quickly bring here sinful Duryodhana, who is so covetous of sovereignty, with his friends, counsellors, brothers, and followers. I shall see if, indeed, making one more effort, I can bring him to the right path.'

So Vidura went out once more and caused the unwilling Duryodhana to enter the court, surrounded by Karna and Dussasana and the kings who followed him. The son of Dhritarashtra came back into the hall with his face set, and the kings who crowded in after him filled the aisles, so that the court, which had been hushed, grew restless again — men shifting, weapons clinking, every face turned toward the father and the son.

The defiance hung in the air of the assembly like a drawn blade. Krishna had given his permission — the calmest, most terrible permission ever spoken in that court. And Dhritarashtra, grasping at his son, was making one last attempt to keep the peace from breaking. Whether the attempt would hold, no one in that hall could say.
stories.reflection: The striking thing about Krishna's answer is what it refuses to do: he does not rage at the plot, does not threaten the plotters, does not even protect himself. He grants them permission to try, and names his own restraint — not his power — as the only boundary he will not cross. Power held in check, he suggests, is the greater demonstration.
stories.next_story_tease: Duryodhana's answer to that permission would draw from Krishna a sight no one in the court had ever seen.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, calm and unmoved in the midst of the Kuru assembly, looks directly at blind Dhritarashtra and gives his sons permission to try to seize him, while the court holds its breath.

stories.title: Krishna Reveals His Universal Form
stories.story:
Duryodhana had been brought back into the assembly, and he stood before his father and the assembled kings still stiff with defiance. It was then that Krishna turned to him, and the tone of the court changed.

'From delusion, O Duryodhana, you regard me as alone,' Krishna said. 'It is for this, O you of little understanding, that you seek to make me a captive after vanquishing me by violence. Here, however, are all the Pandavas, and all the Vrishnis and Andhakas. Here are all the Adityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus, with all the great Rishis.'

And with that, the slayer of hostile heroes burst into loud laughter. It began as the laugh of a man amused by a child's boast, and it grew until the air of the hall seemed to thicken with it.

And as he laughed, the laughter became something else. From his body, which blazed like a fire, issued myriads of gods, each of lightning effulgence, each no bigger than a thumb. On his forehead appeared Brahman; on his breast, Rudra. On his arms appeared the regents of the world. From his mouth issued Agni, the Adityas, the Sadhyas, the Vasus, the Aswins, the Marutas, with Indra and the Viswedevas. Myriads of Yakshas, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas also came forth from him, of the same measure and form. From his two arms issued Sankarshana and Dhananjaya — and Arjuna stood on his right, bow in hand, while Balarama stood on his left, armed with the plough. Behind him stood Bhima and Yudhishthira and the two sons of Madri; before him were all the Andhakas and the Vrishnis, with Pradyumna and other chiefs, bearing mighty weapons upraised. On his countless arms were seen the conch, the discus, the mace, the bow Saranga, the plough, the javelin, the Nandaka — every weapon that is named, all shining with effulgence and upraised for striking. From his eyes and nose and ears, from every part of his body, issued fierce sparks of fire mixed with smoke; from the pores of his skin, sparks like the rays of the sun.

And these were not signs or symbols. They were there — gods and yakshas and heroes and weapons filling the assembly — so that the court of the Kurus became, for that moment, the meeting-place of all the worlds at once.

And the court of the Kurus beheld what no court of men had beheld. All the kings closed their eyes, their hearts affrighted — all except Drona, and Bhishma, and Vidura, and the greatly blessed Sanjaya, and the Rishis possessed of the wealth of asceticism, for the divine Janardana gave them divine sight on that occasion, so that they could bear to look. Many of the kings hid their faces; some covered their eyes with their hands; even the bravest among them could not raise their gaze.

In the sky above the hall, celestial drums beat, and a shower of flowers fell upon him. The whole Earth trembled, and the oceans were agitated. The wonder did not stay within the hall; it reached outward, to earth and ocean, as though the whole world had been summoned to witness what the court of the Kurus had provoked. And all the denizens of the earth were filled with great wonder, though few of them knew why.

Duryodhana had wanted to seize a man. What stood before him now, blazing from every pore, filling the hall with gods and weapons and fire, was what the four conspirators had proposed to bind with their hands. The boast had been answered not with a threat but with a revelation — the disclosure of what, all along, had sat before them through the peace negotiations, patient, and had been mistaken for a negotiator.

Then the vision withdrew. That tiger among men, that chastiser of foes, drew back the divine and highly wonderful and auspicious form, and was himself again — Krishna, the messenger of the Pandavas, seated quietly in the assembly of the Kurus, as though nothing at all had happened. The gods, the weapons, the fire — all of it had come from him, and all of it had returned to him, and what remained was the quiet figure the court had grown accustomed to, as though the two could not be the same person, and yet were.

In the ringing silence, the kings slowly opened their eyes.
stories.reflection: Krishna answers a threat of capture not with a display of power aimed at the plotters, but with the simple truth of what he is. The vision is not a weapon; it is an unveiling. And it is telling that only those with some purity — Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Sanjaya, the Rishis — could bear to look, as though the sight itself demanded something of the seer.
stories.next_story_tease: The court was still reeling when Krishna rose to go, and the blind king, shaken, hurried to protest that he was powerless.

stories.title: Krishna Departs as Dhritarashtra Pleads Powerlessness
stories.story:
Krishna rose from the assembly, and no one moved to stop him. Arm-in-arm with Satyaki on one side and Kritavarman, Hridika's son, on the other, and with the permission of the Rishis, the slayer of Madhu walked out of the Kuru court. During the uproar that followed his going, the Rishis — Narada and others — vanished, repairing each to his own place, as though the wonder they had witnessed had been enough for one world for one day.

The Kauravas, with all the kings, rose and followed him, like the gods following Indra. But Sauri, of immeasurable soul, did not bestow a single thought on those who followed; he went out of the court like a blazing fire mixed with smoke, and the mail-clad ranks of Kritavarman closed behind him. He walked unhurried, and the kings who streamed after him kept a careful distance, none of them willing to come near the fire that had just gone out of the hall.

At the gate waited his charioteer Daruka with the great white car: furnished with rows of tinkling bells, decked with golden ornaments, endued with great speed, the clatter of its wheels resounding like the rumbling of clouds, covered all over with white tiger-skins, and harnessed with the steeds Saivya and her fellows. The car stood ready, as though its master's departure had been expected from the beginning, the horses shifting, the bells chiming softly as the kings pressed out behind him. There, too, mounted on his own car, waited Kritavarman, the favourite hero of the Vrishnis, the mighty car-warrior.

Krishna was about to depart when king Dhritarashtra addressed him once more.

'O grinder of foes,' the blind king said, 'you have seen the power I wield over my sons. You have witnessed all with your own eyes. Nothing now is unknown to you. Seeing me endeavour to bring about peace between the Kurus and the Pandavas — knowing the state in which I am — it behooves you not to entertain any suspicion regarding me. O Kesava, I have no sinful feelings toward the Pandavas. You know what words I spoke to Suyodhana. The Kauravas and all the kings of the earth know that I have made every endeavour to bring about peace.'

It was a plea, and everyone heard it as one — the plea of a father who had just watched his son defy the entire assembly, watched the universe itself blaze out of the guest he had failed to protect, and who could offer, in his own defence, nothing but the record of his good intentions. The blind king had seen nothing with his own eyes; he had heard of wonders and heard of his son's folly, and could only protest that he had tried. He had summoned the conspirators back, had spoken to his son once more, had pleaded for peace before the whole court — and still the decision had slipped from his hands. The power he confessed to Krishna was real, and it was precisely this: that he had none.

The mighty-armed Janardana turned to Dhritarashtra, and to Drona, and to grandsire Bhishma, and to Kshattri Vidura, and to Vahlika and Kripa, and said: 'You have yourselves witnessed all that has happened in the assembly of the Kurus — how wicked Duryodhana, like an uneducated wretch, left the court from anger, and how king Dhritarashtra describes himself as powerless. With the permission of you all, I shall now go back to Yudhishthira.'

He saluted them, that bull among men, and mounted his car. And as he drove away from Hastinapura, the message he carried was not the peace he had come to arrange, but the report of what the Kurus had chosen. The chariot gathered speed, the white tiger-skins streaming behind, and the city of the Kurus fell away. Behind him, the blind king stood at the door of his court, having witnessed everything and prevented nothing.

The war was no longer a question. It was only a matter of travel.
stories.reflection: Dhritarashtra's final protest is the story of his whole reign in miniature: he has witnessed everything and prevented nothing, and in the end can only plead that his intentions were good. Krishna does not accuse him of ill will — he simply confirms what the blind king himself has admitted, that he is powerless — and leaves carrying the truth of what was chosen.
stories.next_story_tease: The journey back to the Pandavas carried another voice as well: Kunti's words, kept for years, would soon find their way to her sons.

stories.title: Kunti's Charge: The Duty of a Kshatriya
stories.story:
In the quiet of her abode in Hastinapura, the mother of the five Pandavas waited to hear how the world had answered her sons' plea for peace. Krishna came to her straight from the assembly of the Kurus, entered and worshipped her feet; and sitting before her, he laid the whole embassy before her, briefly, as one lays down a burden.

Both he and the Rishis who had sat with him had spoken words worthy of being accepted, words fraught with reason. Duryodhana had accepted none of them. "As regards Duryodhana and his followers, their hour is come," Krishna said. Now, with her leave, he would speed to the Pandavas. What should he carry to them as her instructions?

Kunti answered as a mother of kings, and her answer was not soft. "Say unto king Yudhishthira of virtuous soul these words," she began. "Thy virtue, O son, is decreasing greatly. Do not act vainly, like a reader of the Vedas who catches their words but never their real meaning. Thy understanding, affected by the words of the Vedas alone, vieweth virtue only. Cast thy eyes on the duties of thy own order, as ordained by the Self-create. For all ruthless deeds and for the protection of the people, the Kshatriya was created from the arms of the Brahmana, and he is to depend upon the prowess of his own arms."

Then she gave Krishna a story to carry, an instance heard by her from the aged. In days of yore, Vaisravana, filled with gratification, made a gift of the Earth to the royal sage Muchukunda. The sage would not accept it. "I desire to enjoy that sovereignty which is won by the prowess of arms," he said. At this, Vaisravana was filled with wonder and delight; and Muchukunda, fully observing the duties of the Kshatriya order, ruled the earth, having conquered it by the prowess of his arms.

The king's place in the world, Kunti went on, is not a matter of comfort but of cause. A sixth part of the virtue practised by subjects well protected by their king is obtained by that king. The virtue a king practises confers godhead on him; if he perpetrates sin, he goes to hell. The penal code, properly applied, keeps the four orders at their own duties. And it is the king who creates the age: he who causes the Krita age to reign enjoys heaven exceedingly, and he who causes the Kali age to reign earns sin exceedingly and resides in hell for countless years. "The king's sins affect the world," she said, "and the world's sins affect him."

"Observe, therefore, those kingly duties that befit thy ancestry. That is not the conduct of a royal sage in which thou wishest to abide. He that is stained by weakness of heart, that adheres to compassion and is unsteady, never obtaineth the merit born of cherishing his subjects with love."

The understanding by which Yudhishthira was now acting, she said, was never wished for him by Pandu, or by herself, or by his grandsire. Sacrifice, gift, merit, bravery, subjects and children, greatness of soul, might, energy — these were what she had prayed for him, while well-wishing Brahmanas gratified the gods and the Pitris with Swaha and Swadha for his long life, wealth and children. "The mother and the father, as also the gods, always desire for their children liberality and gift and study and sacrifice and sway over subjects. Whether all this be righteous or unrighteous, you are to practise it, in consequence of your very birth."

And then her voice found its hardest edge, for she spoke of what her sons now were. Though born in a high race, they were destitute of the very means of support, afflicted with misery. Hungry men, approaching a brave and bountiful monarch, are gratified and live by his side. "What virtue can be superior to this?" A virtuous person, upon acquiring a kingdom, should make all persons his own — some by gift, some by force, some by sweet words. A Brahmana should adopt mendicancy; a Vaisya should earn wealth; a Sudra should serve the other three. "Mendicancy, therefore, is forbidden to thee. Nor is agriculture suited to thee. Thou art a Kshatriya and therefore the protector of all in distress. Thou art to live by the prowess of thy arms. O thou of mighty arms, recover thy paternal share of the kingdom which thou hast lost, by conciliation or by war."

Krishna received the words. They would be carried unaltered to the camp at Upaplavya, where the eldest Pandava, who had staked everything on peace, would hear his mother tell him that peace was a luxury he could no longer afford.
stories.reflection: Kunti's message never mentions revenge. She frames Yudhishthira's patience as a failure of kingship: the Kshatriya is created to protect, and a ruler who chooses compassion over his order's duty abandons the people who depend on him. The story of Muchukunda makes the same point in reverse — refusal of a gift becomes the highest kingly act, because sovereignty is only real when it is won.
stories.next_story_tease: Kunti had not finished; she pressed one more tale into Krishna's keeping before he could leave.
stories.hero_scene: In Kunti's dim chamber in Hastinapura, the aged queen, one hand raised in emphasis, delivers her charge to Krishna, who sits at her feet — a mother sending her sons to war through the mouth of a god.

stories.title: Vidula's Rebuke: Rise, O Coward
stories.story:
Kunti had not finished with Krishna. When he had received her charge for Yudhishthira, she drew him into an older story — the tale of a mother who would not let her son lie defeated.

"In this connection, O chastiser of foes, is cited an old story of the conversation between Vidula and her son," she said. "It behoveth thee to say unto Yudhishthira anything that can be gathered from this, or anything more beneficial than that."

There was a high-born dame of great foresight named Vidula. She was famous, slightly wrathful, of crooked disposition, and devoted to Kshatriya virtues. Well educated, she was known to all the kings of the earth, and she had listened to the speeches and instructions of teachers of diverse minds. One day the princess Vidula rebuked her own son — who, after his defeat by the king of the Sindhus, lay prostrate, his heart depressed with despair.

Her first words were chosen to cut. "Thou art not my son, O enhancer of the joys of foes. Begotten thou hast not been by myself and thy father! Whence hast thou come? Without wrath as thou art, thou canst not be counted as a man. Thy features betray thee to be a eunuch. Sinkest thou in despair as long as thou livest? If thou art desirous of thy own welfare, bear the burden of thy affairs on thy shoulders. Do not disgrace thy soul. Do not suffer it to be gratified with a little. Set thy heart on thy welfare, and be not afraid. Abandon thy fears. Rise, O coward. Do not lie down thus after thy defeat, delighting all thy foes and grieving thy friends, reft of all sense of honour."

Then the rebuke turned to proverb-making, and the proverbs were fierce. Little streams are filled with only a quantity of water; the palms of a mouse are filled with only a small quantity. A coward is soon gratified with acquisitions that are small. "Rather perish in plucking the fangs of a snake than die miserable like a dog. Put forth thy prowess even at the risk of thy life. Like a hawk that fearlessly rangeth the sky, do thou also wander fearlessly, or put forth thy prowess, or silently watch thy foes for an opportunity."

"Why dost thou lie down like a carcass, or like one smitten by thunder? Rise, O coward; do not slumber after having been vanquished by the foe. Do not disappear from the sight of all so miserably. Make thyself known by thy deeds. Never occupy the intermediate, the low, or the lowest station. Blaze up like a well-fed fire. Like a brand of Tinduka wood, blaze up even for a moment, but never smoulder from desire, like a flameless fire of paddy chaff. It is better to blaze up for a moment than smoke for ever and ever."

She spoke of what a royal son owes his race. "Let no son be born in a royal race who is either exceedingly fierce or exceedingly mild. Repairing to the field of battle and achieving every great feat that is possible for man to achieve, a brave man is freed from the debt he oweth to the duties of the Kshatriya order. Such a person never disgraceth his own self. Whether he gaineth his object or not, he that is possessed of sense never indulgeth in grief."

"If fall and sink one must, he should seize the foe by the hips and fall with the foe. Even if one's roots are cut off, he should not yet give way to despair. Horses of high mettle put forth all their prowess for dragging or bearing heavy weights. Remembering their behaviour, muster all thy strength and sense of honour. Know also in what thy manliness consists. Exert thyself in raising that race which hath sunk in consequence of thee."

And the naming of what a coward is became almost unbearable. "He that hath not achieved a great feat forming the subject of men's conversation only increaseth the number of population. He is neither man nor woman. He whose fame is not founded in respect of charity, asceticism, truth, learning and acquisition of wealth is only his mother's excreta." The idle, wretched profession of mendicancy, worthy only of a coward, was not for him; friends find no happiness in the weak man at whose sight foes are delighted.

"Alas," Vidula cried at last, "exiled from our kingdom, driven from home, deprived of all means of enjoyment and pleasure, destitute of resources, we shall have to perish from want of the very means of life! Misbehaving in the midst of those that are good, and the destroyer of thy race and family — by bringing thee forth, O Sanjaya, I have brought forth Kali himself in the shape of a son. Oh, let no woman bring forth such a son as thou, without wrath, without exertion, without energy, the joy of foes. Do not smoulder. Blaze thou up, effectively displaying thy prowess."

So the tale ended, and Kunti looked at Krishna. The message for Yudhishthira was plain: a mother's love, when her son has been defeated, may take the shape of a fury that will not let him lie down. If Vidula could say such things of her own Sanjaya, the Pandavas' mother expected Krishna to repeat them all.
stories.reflection: Kunti chooses, as her exemplar for Yudhishthira, a mother shaming her own defeated son — the harshest form of love. Vidula's fury is never cruel for its own sake: every insult is an argument that the son still owes his race the effort of rising, and that the coward's quiet is a kind of death already chosen.
stories.next_story_tease: Before Krishna left, Kunti had parting words for every one of her sons.

stories.title: Kunti's Parting Words to Her Sons
stories.story:
Krishna's farewell to Kunti was not a matter of one message but of five — parting words for each of her sons, and for the daughter-in-law she held dear as her own.

For Arjuna she had a memory that had never dimmed. "Say unto Arjuna these words," she said. "When thou wert brought forth in the lying-in room, and when I was sitting in the hermitage surrounded by ladies, a celestial and delightful voice was heard in the sky, saying: 'O Kunti, this thy son will rival the deity of a thousand eyes. This one will vanquish in battle all the assembled Kurus. Aided by Bhima, he will conquer the whole Earth, and his fame will touch the very heavens. With Vasudeva as his ally, he will slay the Kurus in battle and recover his lost paternal share in the kingdom. Endued with great prosperity, he will, with his brothers, perform three great sacrifices.'"

She had never doubted that voice. "Thou knowest how steady, in truth, is Vibhatsu, otherwise called Savyasachin, how irresistible he is. Let it be as that celestial voice said. If there is anything like righteousness, those words will be true — for then, Krishna, thou wilt thyself accomplish it all. I do not doubt what that voice said. I bow to righteousness, which is superior to all. It is righteousness that supports all creatures."

For Bhima, always ready for exertion, the message was short and hard. "The time hath come for that in view of which a Kshatriya lady bringeth forth a son! They that are foremost among men never become cheerless when they have hostilities to wage." Krishna knew the state of Bhima's mind: that grinder of foes is never pacified until he exterminates his foes.

For Draupadi, the daughter-in-law of the high-souled Pandu, there was praise. "Say unto Draupadi, the auspicious Krishna of great fame, who is conversant with the details of every virtue, these words: 'O thou that art highly blessed, of noble parentage, endued with great fame, that becoming behaviour which thou always showest towards my sons is, indeed, worthy of thee.'"

For the sons of Madri, always devoted to Kshatriya virtues, Kunti's message was a call to remember what had been done to their family. "Covet ye more than life itself those enjoyments that are acquired by prowess. Objects won by prowess always please the heart of a person that liveth according to Kshatriya practices. Engaged as ye are in acquiring every kind of virtue, before your eyes the princess of Panchala was addressed in cruel and abusive epithets. Who is there that can forgive that insult? The deprivation of their kingdom grieved me not. Their defeat at dice grieved me not. But that noble and fair Draupadi, while weeping in the midst of the assembly, had to hear those cruel and insulting words — that is what grieveth me most. Alas, exceedingly beautiful Krishna, ever devoted to Kshatriya virtues, found no protector on that occasion, though she was wedded to such powerful protectors."

And to Arjuna once more, the final instruction: he should always tread in the path that may be pointed out by Draupadi. "Thou knowest it very well, Kesava, that Bhima and Arjuna — that pair of fierce and all-destroying Yamas — are capable of making the very gods go the way of all creatures. Is not this an insult to them, that their wife was dragged into the assembly? Recall to their remembrance all those cruel and harsh words that Dushasana said unto Bhima in the very presence of all the warriors of Kuru's race."

Then she asked for her own remembrance. "Enquire in my name after the welfare of the Pandavas with their children, and of Draupadi. Say unto them, O Janardana, that I am well. Go thou on thy auspicious way, and protect my sons."

Krishna rose. He saluted her, walked round her in farewell, and issued out of her abode, carrying his last messages out of the city — and the road to Upaplavya lay open before him.
stories.reflection: Kunti's parting words map her love precisely: a prophecy for Arjuna, a summons for Bhima, praise for Draupadi, and for the twins a reminder of the one insult she could never forgive. What grieved her was not exile or the lost dice game, but Draupadi weeping in the assembly with no protector — and she binds Krishna himself to righteousness as the guarantee that the celestial voice will prove true.
stories.next_story_tease: Out of the city, Krishna's chariot carried one more passenger — Karna.

stories.title: Karna Upon Krishna's Chariot
stories.story:
The court of Hastinapura watched Krishna take Karna onto his chariot, and the wonder of it followed him out of the city.

He had come to the Kuru capital as a messenger of peace, and the embassy had failed: Duryodhana had refused every word that Krishna and the Rishis had spoken, and the earth now stood on the edge of war. From Kunti's abode Krishna had carried away a mother's charge to her sons — parting words, a prophecy, a demand that her children live by the prowess of their arms. He had saluted her and walked round her before issuing out of her abode, the mighty-armed Krishna whose gait resembled the majestic gait of the lion. Now, at the edge of the royal quarter, he dismissed the chiefs of the Kurus, with Bhishma at their head, who had followed him through the city. Then he took Karna upon his chariot, called Satyaki to his side, and drove out through the gates.

After he had departed, the Kurus gathered and talked among themselves of that highly wonderful and marvellous incident connected with him, and their talk was not of hope. "Overcome with ignorance," they said, "the whole earth hath been entangled in the meshes of death!" And they said also, "Through Duryodhana's folly, all this is doomed to destruction."

On the road, Krishna and Karna spoke together at length. What passed between them on that stretch of dusty ground is not set down in this telling; the source records only that the foremost of persons proceeded, deliberating with Karna for a long time, and that the chariot kept pace with the conversation. Krishna had come to Hastinapura carrying a secret about Karna's birth — a secret he had chosen this road to begin telling, and one that would be carried to its end on a later road, when the charioteer's son would learn who he truly was. That revelation, with all it would offer and all it would cost, belongs to another telling; here, the two men rode side by side through the fading day, the one who knew and the one who did not.

For now, the road itself was the story. When Krishna had said what he had come to say, he dismissed Karna and urged his steeds to greater speed. Daruka held the reins, and the swift coursers, endued with the speed of the tempest of the mind, went on as if drinking the skies. They traversed a long way like fleet hawks and reached Upaplavya very soon, bearing the wielder of Saranga — Krishna — back to the camp of the Pandavas, where the brothers waited to hear what peace had come to. The messenger of peace rode in alone, having left behind him the one man of the Kuru side he had chosen to ride beside, and a city that already knew itself doomed.
stories.reflection: Krishna leaves Hastinapura with Karna beside him — the one warrior of the Kuru side he treats as a companion rather than a foe — and returns alone, at the speed of the mind, as if the conversation had given him everything and nothing. The Kurus' parting words frame the whole embassy: the earth already entangled in the meshes of death, not by the gods, but by Duryodhana's folly.
stories.tradition_note: The fuller account of the private conversation between Krishna and Karna — in which Karna's birth is revealed and the kingdom offered to him — follows in the sequel (Udyoga Parva 5.138–141); the present story follows the compressed reference in 5.137.
stories.next_story_tease: But the secret Krishna had begun on that road — the truth of Karna's birth — had yet to be spoken aloud.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna's chariot thunders out of Hastinapura with Karna seated beside him and Satyaki behind, the dust of the road rising as Bhishma and the Kuru chiefs stand watching at the city gates.

stories.title: Krishna Offers Karna the Kingdom
stories.subtitle: Karna learns he is Kunti's firstborn son.
stories.story:
Krishna had come to Hastinapura to speak for peace, and as he was leaving he did something stranger than any of his speeches. In the sight of all the princes and their servants, he took Karna — the man the whole court knew as a charioteer's son, the Suta's son — up onto his own chariot, and drove out through the city gate with him alone, leaving the court to its whispering. The whole court had watched them go, and no one there could have said what the two of them had to say to each other; even the king who had seen them leave would later beg to be told every word of it.

On the road beyond the walls he turned to the man beside him, and his voice was deep as clouds newly risen in the season of rain. What he said was mild and intimidating at once, agreeable and consistent with virtue, true and beneficial, pleasing to the heart. "You have worshipped the Brahmans," he said, "and with a concentrated mind, free of envy, you have questioned them after truth. You know the eternal sayings of the Vedas, and the subtle conclusions of the scriptures. So you know what the wise say of sons born of a maiden: that the man who weds the maiden is their father. You, Karna, were born in this way. You are, therefore, morally the son of Pandu."

He did not stop there. "Know that on your father's side you have the sons of Pritha, and on your mother's side the Vrishnis. These are your own people. Come, be a king, as the scriptures allow. Ride with me from here this very day, and let the Pandavas know you as a son of Kunti, born before even Yudhishthira."

Then Krishna laid out what that offer meant, detail by detail, and each detail was a weight. The five Pandava brothers would embrace his feet. The son of Draupadi and the son of Subhadra would embrace his feet. Every king and prince gathered for the Pandava cause, and all the Andhakas and the Vrishnis, would do the same. Queens and princesses would come bearing jars of gold and silver and clay, full of water, with delicious herbs and every kind of seed and gem and creeper, for his consecration. Draupadi herself would come to him as a wife in time. And Dhaumya, the restrained priest of the Pandavas, would pour the libations of clarified butter on the sacred fire while the Brahmans who regarded all four Vedas as authoritative performed the ceremony of his installation.

Krishna fell silent. The road was quiet, and the words hung between the two men on the chariot, heavier than anything either of them carried.

The man the world called the son of Radha listened while a kingdom was spread before him like a feast. Everything that had ever been denied him — a father's name, a mother's sons, a throne, a rightful place — was being offered in one sentence, on an empty road, outside a city that had never once called him its own. To be crowned a king, he who had been denied even a father's name. To be called the eldest of the Pandavas, he who had spent his whole life on the other side of that very name. Karna had built everything he was on the name of a charioteer's son, and now he was being told that his name, his place, his whole history, rested on a secret he had never once been told. The chariot stood still. And the offer stood waiting, unanswered.
stories.reflection: Krishna's gift is devastating precisely because it is true: in a single breath he hands Karna the birthright he was denied and, with it, a choice he never asked to face — to claim a kingdom at the cost of the life and loyalties he had already built. The passage does not record an answer, and that silence is its own weight.

stories.title: Karna Refuses, Pledging Loyalty to Duryodhana
stories.story:
The road outside Hastinapura lay quiet in the late light when Krishna drew his chariot to a halt and called Karna over. Krishna had come to the Kuru capital as a messenger of peace; he had stood before the assembly and spoken, and been heard in silence. But on the open road, with only the evening between them, he told Karna what no one in that city had ever told him plainly. Kunti had borne him before her marriage, through her union with Surya the sun god. He was her firstborn, the eldest of the Pandavas, older than Yudhishthira himself. The kingdom, by right, could be his, and Krishna offered it to him.

Karna listened without moving. When he answered, his voice was steady. He knew that Krishna spoke from love and friendship, from a desire to do him good, and he did not doubt a word of it. "Morally," he said, "I am the son of Pandu, as the scriptures hold. My mother, while a maiden, bore me through her connection with Surya, and at Surya's own command she abandoned me as soon as I was born, without thinking of my welfare."

That was all his birth mother had ever done for him, and he said it without bitterness, as a fact. Then he spoke of the people who had raised him. The charioteer Adhiratha, finding the abandoned child, had taken him home, and Radha's breasts had filled with milk that very day. She had washed him and raised him; Adhiratha had performed every rite of infancy upon him according to the scriptures, and had caused the Brahmanas to bestow the name Vasushena. When he came of age, Adhiratha chose his wives, and through them his sons and grandsons were born. His heart, and every bond of affection in it, was fixed on them. "From joy or fear, Govinda," he said, "I cannot break those bonds, not for the whole earth, not for heaps of gold."

He had known for years that he was not of the Suta class by birth, and it had changed nothing. With the Sutas he had performed his sacrifices; with the Sutas all his family rites and his marriages had been conducted. Through his friendship with Duryodhana he had enjoyed sovereignty for thirteen years without a thorn at his side. It was Duryodhana who, having won him, had prepared for war and provoked hostilities with the Pandavas, and it was Karna who had been chosen as the great antagonist of Arjuna, to advance against him in single combat. "For the sake of death, or the ties of blood, or fear, or temptation," he said, "I cannot behave falsely toward the intelligent son of Dhritarashtra. If I do not meet Arjuna in single combat, it will be inglorious for us both."

Then he made one request: that Krishna keep this conversation secret. "If Yudhishthira, virtuous and self-controlled, comes to know me as Kunti's firstborn son, he will never accept the kingdom. And if this empire were somehow mine," he said, "I would make it over to Duryodhana alone. Let Yudhishthira be king forever. He who has you for his guide, Arjuna and Bhima for his champions, Nakula and Sahadeva and the sons of Draupadi for his own, is fit to rule the whole earth."

He went on, naming the great warriors of the Pandava host, Dhrishtadyumna of the Panchalas, the mighty Satyaki, Chekitana, the invincible Sikhandin, the Kekaya brothers, Kuntibhoja with his rainbow-colored steeds, and Krishna himself, like an ocean. His voice, reciting them, sounded almost like praise. The kingdom celebrated among all the kings of the earth was already won in all but name; he was telling Krishna that he knew it, and that he would stand against it anyway.

Krishna did not argue. The offer had been made in good faith and refused in good faith, and there was nothing left to say on that road. In a single afternoon Karna had been given the truth of his birth and the crown of the world, and he had answered with the life he had actually lived. As Krishna urged his chariot on toward Upaplavya, Karna stood in the dust and watched him go, a man who had refused a kingdom to keep his word.
stories.reflection: Karna's refusal is not stubbornness but a claim about where a life is actually made: the mother who abandoned him before she knew him, and the parents and friend who took him in afterwards. Krishna's offer of a kingdom could not undo the shape of a life built on gratitude, and Karna knew that accepting it would betray everyone who had ever been loyal to him.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Karna turned from the offer to the war ahead, and spoke of it as a sacrifice with Krishna as its witness.
stories.hero_scene: On the empty road outside Hastinapura, Krishna stands beside his halted chariot facing Karna, one hand raised in appeal, while Karna listens with a still, unmoved face as the evening light slants across the dust.

stories.title: Karna's Prophecy of the Coming War as a Sacrifice
stories.story:
The refusal had been spoken, and still Karna did not step toward his chariot. Krishna had offered him the world, and he had declined it for the sake of the people who had raised him and the friend who had stood by him. But there was one more thing he wanted Krishna to know, and he said so plainly first: the words had been spoken for his good, and the Pandavas, obedient to Krishna, would do all that Krishna had said. Then he turned to what was coming.

Duryodhana, he said, was preparing a great sacrifice, a sacrifice of arms. And he described it the way a priest describes a rite already fixed on the calendar, with certainty and with composure.

Krishna himself would stand in that rite as the Upadrashtri, the witness who oversees the ceremony, and the office of Adhyaryu, the priest who chants the hymns, would be his as well. The ape-bannered Arjuna, accoutred in mail, would be the Hotri, the chief priest who pours the oblation. Gandiva, his great bow, would be the sacrificial ladle, and the prowess of the warriors the clarified butter consumed in the fire. The celestial weapons Arjuna would release, the Aindra, the Pasupata, the Brahma, the Sthunakarna, would be the mantras of that sacrifice. Abhimanyu, resembling his father or perhaps excelling him in prowess, would be the chief Vedic hymn chanted as the rite proceeded. And when mighty Bhima struck Duryodhana down, the sacrifice of Dhritarashtra's son would be concluded.

He did not ask for the war to be stopped. He had already chosen his place in it, and he knew, naming the parts of the rite, exactly what his own part would cost. What he asked was only this: that Krishna conceal the discourse, for therein lay their benefit. If Yudhishthira ever learned the truth of his birth, the king would never accept the kingdom. And he asked one thing more, a request that from any other man would have sounded like a challenge and from Karna sounded like a prayer: "Bring Kunti's son before me for battle."

The phrase hung in the air, and its weight had changed in the last hour. Kunti's son. All his life Karna had used those words of Arjuna, the rival who had everything that had been denied to him. Now he had just learned that he himself was Kunti's son, the firstborn, older than the man he was asking to meet. He did not take the revelation back. He did not trade it for the kingdom. He simply folded it into his request: bring Kunti's son before me, and let the two of us meet in the rite we have both been appointed to.

Krishna listened to the whole prophecy without interrupting. A war that would cover the earth with bloody mire, a rite in which every hero had a priestly office, a sacrifice that would end only when Bhima closed it, Karna had looked at the coming catastrophe and found in it a shape, and the shape gave him composure. He was not asking Krishna to save him. He was asking Krishna to witness.

He had spoken of the war to come, of his own place in it, and of the secrecy that would keep Yudhishthira from a kingdom he could not in conscience accept, and he had done it all in the calm voice of a man settling his accounts before a long journey. When he had finished, the evening lay quiet around them. The prophecy hung in the air like smoke from an altar already lit, and the two men stood on the road in silence, each knowing exactly what the other would do when the rite began.
stories.reflection: Karna's image of the coming war as a sacrifice gives the catastrophe a shape and, with it, a kind of composure: every hero has a priestly office, Krishna himself will stand as witness, and the rite ends only when Bhima closes it. He describes the war not as something to escape but as a ceremony already fixed, in which he has already accepted his part.
stories.next_story_tease: And before they parted, Karna told Krishna of the omens he had seen.
