stories.title: Karna Worships Krishna and Takes His Leave
stories.story:
"Knowing everything, why do you still seek to beguile me?"

Karna had listened to all of Krishna's words, the revelation of his birth, the offer of a kingdom, the plea to change course, and he had worshipped Krishna before he answered, honoring the man who had spoken them. Now he gave his answer, and it was not the answer of a man who could be turned. The destruction of the whole earth was at hand, he said, and its causes were Sakuni, and Dussasana, and king Duryodhana. A great and fierce battle was coming between the Pandavas and the Kurus, a battle that would cover the earth with bloody mire, and all the kings and princes following Duryodhana, consumed by the fire of weapons, would proceed to the abode of Yama.

And then, because he wanted Krishna to understand that he spoke with open eyes, he told him what he had seen. The omens were everywhere, and they all pointed one way. Saturn was afflicting the constellation Rohini; Mars was wheeling toward Jyeshtha and Anuradhas, sign of a great slaughter of friends; the planet Mahapat lay heavy on Chitra. The spot on the moon's disc had shifted, and Rahu approached the sun. Meteors fell from the sky with loud noise and trembling motion. Elephants sent forth frightful cries, while the horses shed tears and refused their food and drink. In every division of Duryodhana's army the soldiers ate little and passed much, a sign the wise called a defect, while the elephants and steeds of the Pandavas were cheerful, and the animals wheeled to their right, an omen of success. The same animals passed to the left of Duryodhana's army, and incorporeal voices were heard over their heads. Auspicious birds, peacocks, swans, cranes, followed the Pandavas, while vultures and kankas and hawks, wolves and bees, followed the Kauravas. The drums in Duryodhana's camp yielded no sound, while the drums of the Pandavas sounded without being struck. The wells in the Kaurava encampment roared like bulls. The gods showered flesh and blood on Duryodhana's soldiers, vapoury edifices with high walls and porches appeared in the sky over their camp, and a black circle surrounded the solar disc. Both twilights were terrible, and the jackals yelled. Birds with one wing, one eye, and one leg cried out in the dark, and fierce birds with black wings and red legs hovered over the camp at nightfall. Duryodhana's soldiers had begun to hate the Brahmanas first, then their preceptors, then their own servants. The eastern horizon was red, the southern the hue of weapons, the western earthy, and all the quarters around the encampment seemed ablaze. "In all these portents," Karna said, "great is the danger that is indicated."

And he had seen more than omens; he had seen a vision. Yudhishthira was ascending with his brothers a palace supported by a thousand columns, all of them in white robes and white head-gear, seated on white seats. Krishna himself was enveloping the blood-dyed earth with weapons. Yudhishthira, of immeasurable energy, stood upon a heap of bones and gladly ate buttered payasa from a golden cup, and he swallowed the earth that Krishna handed to him, which meant that he would rule it. And Bhima, fierce Vrikodara, stood on a summit, mace in hand, devouring the earth, which meant that he would slay them all in battle. Karna recited all of it without flinching, every sign of the ruin of his own side, as a man might recite a verdict already delivered.

Krishna heard him to the end. His answer was short, and it was the most terrible thing Karna would hear that day. "Indeed, the destruction of the earth is at hand," he said, "when my words do not become acceptable to your heart."

Then Karna pressed Krishna to his bosom, holding him once, as a man holds a friend he may never see again. Dismissed by Kesava, he descended from the chariot. The two parted on the road, each knowing what the other knew, each having said everything that could be said, and the earth went on toward its destruction.
stories.reflection: Karna's catalogue of omens is the testimony of a man who sees his own side's ruin and refuses to look away; he does not read the portents as a warning to flee but as a truth to accept. Krishna's reply, that the destruction of the earth is at hand when even his words cannot reach Karna's heart, turns the omens inward: the deepest sign lies not in the sky but in the failure of persuasion.

stories.title: Krishna Reports the Failure of Peace
stories.story:
Krishna's chariot rolled into Upaplavya, and the report of the peace mission came with it. He had gone to Hastinapura to ask for peace in the name of the Pandavas, and now he told them everything that had happened there, and sat long in consultation with them. Then, wearied, he went to his own quarters for rest.

The Pandavas dismissed the kings who had gathered around them, with Virata at their head. When the sun had set, they said their evening prayers, their hearts fixed on Krishna, thinking of him. At last they brought him into their midst again and deliberated once more on what they should do. It was Yudhishthira who spoke first, addressing him as one addresses a refuge: "O you of lotus-petal eyes, tell us all that you said to Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly of the Kurus."

Krishna's answer was brief and final. "Having gone to the city of Hastinapura," he said, "I addressed Dhritarashtra's son in the assembly with words that were true, reasonable, and beneficial. That wicked-minded fellow did not accept them."

The mission had failed. But Yudhishthira did not want the summary; he wanted everything. When Duryodhana chose the wrong path, what had the aged grandsire said? What had the preceptor Drona, the son of Bharadwaja, said? What had Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, his own parents, said? What had Kshattri, Vidura, their junior father, foremost of all who knew virtue, always afflicted with sorrow for them, whom he regarded as his own sons, said? And what had all the kings who sat in that assembly said? "Tell us all of it exactly as it happened," Yudhishthira said. "You have already told us the disagreeable words of the Kuru chiefs, but they have flitted from my memory. I want to hear them again. You are our refuge, our lord, our guide."

So Krishna began, and the night closed over Upaplavya while he spoke. "Hear, O king, the words that were addressed to Duryodhana in the midst of the assembly of the Kurus, and bear them in mind. After my words were ended, Dhritarashtra's son laughed aloud."

That laugh had decided more than the assembly knew. Highly incensed, Bhishma had risen and spoken for the preservation of their race. He reminded Duryodhana of the vow he himself had taken, how for his father Santanu's sake he had procured Kali to become his mother and had renounced the throne, so that an only son might not be the end of the line; how Vichitravirya had been born and installed as king while Bhishma served under him; how, when Vichitravirya died and anarchy seized the realm, the chief of the gods withheld rain until the starving subjects, afflicted with frightful maladies, begged Bhishma to take the throne for their sake, and he had refused, keeping his vow. And now, Bhishma said, the line he had sacrificed his own kingship to preserve was being led toward ruin by the very prince who carried it.

And the recounting had only begun. The night stretched on, and Krishna's voice carried that assembly into the quiet camp, the laughter, the anger, the pleadings of parents and preceptor and grandsire, all the words that peace had been unable to make true. The Pandavas knew now, in full, what they had known in outline: nothing remained to be said about peace, and they would carry this story with them onto the field of Kurukshetra.
stories.reflection: Yudhishthira's insistence on hearing the assembly's words exactly, even a second time, shows how much the telling matters on the eve of war: the brothers cannot move forward until they know precisely what was said and who said it. The failure of the mission becomes, in Krishna's retelling, a story the Pandavas will carry with them to the battlefield.
stories.next_story_tease: Peace had failed, and the battles to come would bring Krishna to Arjuna's side once more.

stories.title: The Weapon Only Krishna Could Name
stories.story:
The war was over, and that was when the killing happened.

In the dark hours after the armies had stopped fighting, Ashvatthama, Drona's son, slipped into the sleeping camp of the Pandavas. He moved through the tents meaning to do what would please his master, and he came to the quarters where Draupadi's sons lay asleep. He killed them where they lay. The camp woke to the worst news a camp can wake to, and Draupadi heard of the death of her sons and grieved as a mother grieves.

Krishna went to her and comforted her. "I will wipe away this sorrow of yours, good lady," he said, "with the head of that unworthy son of a brahmin, the assailant who struck without warning." And a promise, once spoken, is a thing that must be carried out.

Arjuna took up the pursuit at once, Krishna himself driving his chariot. The chase ran long across the darkening plain, and the horses were failing, their strength spent, when Arjuna saw the man he hunted stop at last and turn to face him from far off. Ashvatthama was not the kind of man to be cornered without recourse. He was Drona's son, schooled in the secret science of weapons, and he had one weapon left that no arrow could answer. He released it.

The night came apart. A terrible fire blazed up in every direction at once, not a flame to be aimed at or dodged but a burning that filled the sky from horizon to horizon, so that the whole field stood in glare. In that light Arjuna saw himself for what he was: a man without refuge, his horses spent, his weapons useless against a fire that no steel could stop.

He did not reach for another arrow. He turned to the friend beside him, as a man turns in the last extremity, and his cry went up out of the burning: "Krishna, Krishna, mighty-armed one, giver of fearlessness to your devotees — you alone are the rescue of those being burned!" And more than that, in the terror of the moment, he said what his heart had always known: that Krishna was the primal person, the Lord himself, beyond the nature he had made; that the living world was deluded by his power of illusion; that this very descent of his was for the lifting of the earth's burden. "What is this, and from where does it come?" he cried. "O God of gods, I do not know."

Krishna answered calmly, as though the sky were not on fire. "Know this to be the brahma weapon of Drona's son," he said. "He does not know how to recall it. Only an astra can quell an astra."

So Arjuna, touching water as the rite requires, discharged his own weapon to meet it. The two fires met in the middle of the field, wrapped in a storm of arrows, and their meeting was more terrible than either alone. Together they blazed so fiercely that the three worlds stood in peril — the creatures of the earth and the dwellers of heaven alike threatened by that burning, the very order of the worlds about to be consumed.

And then, at Krishna's word, Arjuna withdrew both weapons — his own and the one that had been loosed against him. The two fires sank, the glare drained out of the sky, and the field was night again, quiet in the way a place is quiet after lightning.

Arjuna stood a long while in the dark, trembling from a terror he would not forget. In the camp behind him a mother still wept, and a promise still waited to be kept.
stories.reflection: In the glare of a weapon no arrow could answer, Arjuna's fear turns naturally into worship: he does not ask for a technique but for refuge, and names Krishna the rescue of those being burned. And the rescue comes as Krishna's rescues often do — not by abolishing the crisis but by giving one clear instruction, and then the strength to draw back a fire no one else could recall.
stories.content_note: References Ashvatthama's night killing of Draupadi's sleeping sons and the blazing of divine weapons; the violence is recalled without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But the camp had not yet delivered its judgment on Ashvatthama.

stories.title: Krishna's Verdict on Ashvatthama
stories.story:
The son of Drona was brought in bound, and the camp came out to see him.

Arjuna led him up with a rope about him, dragging him along like an animal, his face averted, and the man who had captured him looked away from his own errand in disgust. It was an uncomfortable sight for everyone: the warrior who had crept into the camp by night and killed Draupadi's sleeping sons, now brought low before the very people he had wronged.

Bhima saw him and could not contain himself. "Do not spare him, Arjuna!" he cried. "This unworthy son of a brahmin — kill him! For what is he but the kind of man who would strike the mad, the careless, the sleeping, children, women, the helpless — who feeds his own life on the lives of others? Such a one is a cruel wretch, and his death is the only good thing left in him." And Bhima reminded them all of the promise. "You swore to Panchali that you would bring his head," he said, "and I was listening when you swore it. Let this sinner die — this assailant, this slayer of his own kindred."

Krishna heard it all — Bhima's fury and the vow he recalled, Draupadi's grief and what it demanded — and the tent waited for him to speak.

But Draupadi, who had more right than anyone to demand that death, could not bear the sight of him bound and dragged like cattle. She spoke, and her voice unsettled the certainties of the tent. Drona, she reminded them, had been the master of the secret science of weapons, the whole art of discharging and recalling them; and that blessed teacher lived on, she said, in the form of his son. "Honor his family," she pleaded. "Let his mother Gautami, devoted as she is to her husband, not weep for this."

The tent fell into the silence of two truths pulling against each other. Nakula and Sahadeva stood by, Satyaki and Arjuna waited, and Bhima, still burning, insisted that for such a man death itself was the only mercy. What was owed to the children who lay dead? What was owed to the mother who lived?

Then Krishna, the four-armed one, who had heard Bhima's words and Draupadi's both, gave his judgment. "A brahmin's unworthy son is not to be slain," he said, "yet an assailant deserves punishment. Both are my ordinances; uphold them. Keep the promise you made to your beloved, and satisfy Bhima, Panchali, and me."

Arjuna understood what Krishna's heart intended. He stepped forward and, with his own hand, cut the jewel away from the head of Drona's son — the jewel along with the hair, so that the man who had thought to wear a warrior's glory walked away shorn and stripped of his treasure. Then Arjuna released him from his bonds and drove him from the camp.

The promise had asked for his head. What the camp saw was the jewel from that head, taken; the shaven scalp of a man who would never again be mistaken for a warrior; and a life, spared. The splendor of the child-killer was gone, struck down — as the old tellers would say — by the very children he had killed.

The camp watched him go, and no one cheered. Bhima's fury had its answer, Draupadi's tears had theirs, and the vow that had sent Arjuna riding into the night had been kept in the only way that could keep them all: a punishment that took everything but life.
stories.reflection: Krishna's judgment holds two ordinances together — the law that forbids slaying even an unworthy brahmin's son, and the law that an assailant must not go unpunished — and resolves them by making the punishment public and complete without making it fatal. The promise is kept in a way no one had imagined: not the head, but the honor the head carried, forfeited.
stories.content_note: The episode turns on Ashvatthama's killing of the sleeping children, recalled without detail; his punishment is humiliation rather than violence.

stories.title: Bhishma's Passing in Krishna's Presence
stories.story:
Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows and would not die until the sky gave him his hour.

He had fallen in the war he had foreseen and refused to leave, holding his life in his hands through the last of the fighting, waiting for the sun to enter the northern course — the auspicious solstice on which those who give up the body pass to what does not pass away. The war ended. The field fell silent. The survivors came and sat by him, and still he waited, and taught, and watched the sky.

Then Krishna came to the field, and the sight of him walking toward the bed of arrows undid something in the old warrior that the arrows had never touched. "See," Bhishma said to the kings around him, "the compassion of the Lord toward his unalloyed devotees. This very Krishna has come to me as I give up my life, out of love for those who love him without reserve. May he be my refuge." And he asked one thing only: "Merging my mind in him with devotion, chanting his name with my voice, may that God of gods, the Lord, wait until I give up this body."

So Krishna stood before him, and Bhishma, with the Pandavas and the gathered sages looking on, gave what remained of his strength to the teaching he had carried all his life — the duties of charity and of kings, the duties of those who seek release, and the four ends of a human life, each in its place, each with its means, spoken according to the rank and stage of the one who heard it. He spoke of dharma the way a man speaks who is about to leave it behind, and while he spoke, the hour he had waited for came and stood at his shoulder.

Then Bhishma gathered in his speech and let the words go. He fixed his unblinking gaze upon the four-armed Krishna standing before him in yellow robes, and his last prayer went up like a flame finding the sky: "May my love rest on Krishna —" and the praise poured out of him, the long remembrance of a lifetime of watching.

He remembered Krishna dark as the tamala tree, his garments bright as the rays of the sun, driving the chariot through the dust of the battlefield with his locks disheveled and sweat on his face. He remembered how, at the height of the war, Krishna had placed the chariot between the two armies; how, hearing his friend's plea, he had set aside his own word and leapt down from the chariot — Krishna, who had sworn he would not fight — striding out to make true the vow of the old warrior who had pressed him to it, his armor shattered by sharp arrows, bathed in blood, glorious to behold. He remembered the great assembly at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya, crowded with sages and kings, where the same Lord had moved among them with his gentle smile and his loving glance. And at the end of the remembering: "Him, the unborn, dwelling in the heart of every embodied being — on him let my love rest."

The gaze did not waver. With pure concentration, his mind freed from attachment and fixed on the Primal Person, his sins burned away by that one sight, the weariness of a hundred wounds fell from him as a garment falls — gone, as the old tellers would say, by the very look of the Lord.

And when the sages around him knew that Bhishma was merging into the attributeless Brahman, the drums sounded — played by gods and men together, a roll of thunder over the field where he lay. The rites for the departed were performed, and the old warrior who had waited so long for his hour passed from the field, his mind in Krishna and Krishna's name on his lips, into the silence from which no one returns.
stories.reflection: Bhishma's death completes his life's discipline: the man who spent his strength in waiting spends his last hour in praise, and the gaze he fixes on Krishna does what no art could — the weariness of the war falls from him by that sight alone. He does not cling to life; he looks at the Lord, and the looking is the release.
stories.next_story_tease: That field would be remembered for the trembling of the earth beneath the gathered armies.

stories.title: The Field Where the Earth Trembled
stories.story:
The earth itself trembled at Kurukshetra.

Uddhava, speaking long afterward of Krishna's deeds, came at last to that field, and the telling of it still made him pause. He had been Krishna's companion and messenger across the years, carrying the Lord's words from court to court, and he had seen many wonders. But when he remembered the plain at Kurukshetra, what came back to him first was the trembling — the ground shuddering beneath the armies of the cousins, the sons of two brothers drawn up against each other, the kings of the land ranged on either side until the field grew dark with men and horses and raised standards. So much war had gathered in one place that the earth beneath it had seemed to know what was coming.

And what was coming, in the end, was the thing Krishna had descended to accomplish. The burden that had pressed on the earth for so long — the weight of kings and armies, of pride and endless quarrels — was to be lifted at last, and Kurukshetra was the place appointed for the lifting. That, too, was Krishna's design: the war was his instrument, and the earth would be lighter when it was done.

The war ran its course, and the kings fell on either side, so many that the field seemed to be made of them. Every house had sent its sons, and every kingdom its king, and the plain that had trembled under the gathering lay heaped with the fallen. Those who had counseled the ruin — Karna, Dushasana, Shakuni — were destroyed in fortune and in life by the ripening of their own evil counsel; the schemes they had spun so carefully ripened into the harvest that reaped them. And at the last, Duryodhana himself, Suyodhana, lay on the field with his thigh broken, his followers fallen about him, the long quarrel of the cousins ended in a way no throw of dice could have foretold.

Uddhava, telling of it, did not rejoice. There was no triumph in the memory, no satisfaction in the tally of the fallen, and he never spoke of that field as a victory. The earth had been relieved of its burden — that was the purpose, and the purpose had been accomplished. But the plain that had trembled under the armies lay quiet now, and the quiet had cost more than anyone who had called for the war had imagined paying.

So he remembered it: the trembling at the beginning, the silence at the end, and between them the long burning of a quarrel that should never have been settled in blood. The cousins' enmity was finished; the earth stood lighter; and the one who had come to lift the burden had done what he came to do.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's memory of Kurukshetra holds no triumph, and that is the point of the telling: the earth's relief was accomplished, but at a cost that silences the one who remembers it. The war's meaning lies in its ending — a burden lifted, a quarrel finished — and in the quiet that follows, which no one who called for the war had counted on.
stories.content_note: Recalls the scale of the Kurukshetra war and the fallen; no combat is depicted in detail.

stories.title: The Commander of the Seven Hosts
stories.subtitle: Krishna Names Dhrishtadyumna Generalissimo of the Pandava Army
stories.story:
Seven armies had gathered at Upaplavya, and the whole war had narrowed to a single question: who would lead them?

The Pandavas had heard everything that had happened in the court of the assembled Kurus, and Krishna's account of the failed peace had made the shape of things clear. Now, in Krishna's presence, Yudhishthira addressed his brothers. Seven Akshauhinis of troops stood ready for victory, and seven celebrated warriors would lead them: Drupada, and Virata, and Dhrishtadyumna, and Sikhandin, and Satyaki, and Chekitana, and Bhimasena of great energy. All of them knew the Vedas, all had practised excellent vows, all were conversant with policy and accomplished in war. One name was still missing. Tell us now, Yudhishthira said, who that warrior is, conversant with all kinds of battle-array, that may become the leader of these seven, and may also withstand in battle Bhishma, who is like unto a fire having arrows for its flames.

Sahadeva answered first, and he named Virata, the king of the Matsyas: closely related to them, sympathising with them in distress, endued with great might, skilled in weapons, irresistible in battle. Relying upon him we hope to recover our share of the kingdom, Sahadeva said. He will be able to bear in battle both Bhishma and all those mighty car-warriors.

Then Nakula spoke, and he named Drupada, their father-in-law. The king of Panchala was respectable in years, in knowledge of the scriptures, in perseverance, in family and birth; he had studied the science of weapons with the sage Bharadwaja; he was one who always challenged Drona and mighty Bhishma; and he had once performed, moved by wrath, the austerest of penances for the destruction of Drona. That bull among monarchs always cherishes us like a father, Nakula said. He will be able to withstand both Drona and Bhishma rushing to battle.

Then Arjuna rose, and he did not describe a statesman or an ally. He described a man who had not been born like other men. Dhrishtadyumna had sprung into life through the power of ascetic penances and the gratification of sages, issuing from the sacrificial fire-hole armed with bow and sword, accoutred in armour of steel, mounted on a car unto which were yoked excellent steeds, and the clatter of his car-wheels was as deep as the roar of mighty masses of clouds. He was like a lion in his frame and his prowess, with leonine shoulders, arms, chest, and a voice like a lion's roar; he was incapable of being penetrated by weapons of any kind; he looked like an elephant with rent temples; he was truthful in speech, his passions under control. This Dhrishtadyumna was born for the destruction of Drona, Arjuna said. I do not see the man except Dhrishtadyumna who is able to withstand Bhishma of great vows, whose arrows strike with the vehemence of the thunderbolt and fall like flames of fire.

The brothers fell silent, and every eye turned to Krishna, who sat among them. The lotus-eyed one looked toward Arjuna and spoke. O king, I fully approve of all those powerful warriors whom ye have named for becoming the leaders of thy troops. As regards our leader, I would name that chastiser of foes, Dhrishtadyumna.

The matter was settled, and the camp had its answer. The fire-born prince of Panchala would stand at the head of the seven divisions, in the first rank against the man whose arrows no one else could bear. Drupada's son, who had come into the world armed and ready, would now carry the hopes of seven hosts, and before the war was over, the purpose for which the sages said he was born would meet him on the field.

That night the question that had hung over the camp was gone. The Pandavas had their generalissimo, and the war had its shape.
stories.reflection: Yudhishthira asked his brothers for a name, but the choice belonged in the end to Krishna, as if an army's fate could only be settled by the one who already saw the whole war. And the man chosen was the one born, the sages said, for Drona's destruction, which gave the appointment the weight of destiny rather than mere strategy.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet naming a commander was not the same as choosing war — the decision itself still hung in the air.
stories.hero_scene: In the tent at Upaplavya, Krishna sits among the Pandavas and raises a hand toward Arjuna as he speaks; the five brothers lean forward, and in the doorway the ranks of the seven divisions wait in the dusk, banners stirring.

stories.title: The Two Decisions
stories.subtitle: Krishna Declares That War Is Now Inevitable
stories.story:
Yudhishthira had marched out with the desire of battle and now lay encamped on Kurukshetra itself, protected by Vasudeva, aided by Virata and Drupada with their sons, surrounded by the Kekayas, the Vrishnis, and other kings by hundreds, and watched over by numerous mighty car-warriors, like the great Indra surrounded by the Adityas. In the Kuru capital the news of that camp brought a swift answer. Krishna had left the court without achieving his object, and the king of the Kurus wasted no time in marking what that meant. Calling Karna, Dussasana, and Sakuni to him, Duryodhana read out the shape of things to come. Kesava hath gone to the sons of Pritha without having been able to achieve his object, he said. Filled with wrath as he is, he will surely stimulate the Pandavas. A battle between myself and the Pandavas is much desired by Vasudeva. Bhimasena and Arjuna were ever of the same mind with Krishna, and Yudhishthira himself was very much under the influence of Bhimasena. Virata and Drupada, against whom Duryodhana had once waged hostilities, had both become leaders of Yudhishthira's host. The battle, therefore, that will take place will be a fierce and terrific one. Casting off all sloth, cause every preparation to be made for the encounter.

His orders were precise, and they were obeyed. The allied kings were to pitch their tents by hundreds and thousands on Kurukshetra, spacious tents, near enough to places abounding with water and fuel, so placed that the enemy could never stop the roads by which supplies travelled. The road from the city to the camp was to be levelled for the march. And it was to be proclaimed that very day, without loss of time, that the march would commence tomorrow.

The Kuru capital became a city preparing for war as for a festival. The monarchs rose from their costly seats, with wrath burning in them for their foes, and rubbed their mace-like arms, blazing with bracelets of gold and decked with the paste of sandal and other fragrant substances. They put on their head-gears, their lower and upper garments, their ornaments. Foremost car-warriors superintended the furnishing of their cars; men conversant with horse-lore harnessed their steeds; those versed in matters relating to elephants equipped the huge animals; foot-soldiers took up arms and eased their bodies in armour decorated with gold. Filled with rejoicing millions, the city of Duryodhana wore the bright aspect of a festive occasion. At the prospect of battle the Kuru capital looked like the ocean on the appearance of the moon: the vast crowds of humanity its waters, the cars, elephants, and horses its fishes, the tumult of conchs and drums its roar, the bright weapons its white foam, the rows of houses the mountains on its beach.

On the other side of the same plain, the Pandava camp was asking the last question that remained. Krishna had gone to the Kuru court with words of peace, and the prince of the Kurus had met them with deceit; now Yudhishthira pressed him for guidance, and Krishna answered in a voice deep as that of the clouds or cymbals. That wicked-souled wight beareth no good will towards thee, he said. As regards ourselves, we do not desire to make peace with the Kauravas by abandoning our property. War, therefore, is that which should now take place.

Two decisions, made on opposite sides of Kurukshetra, now faced each other across the field. One city had readied itself with the joy of a festival; one camp had heard the words that made the fight certain. Neither king had blinked. Nothing was left now but to draw up the armies and let the plain decide.
stories.reflection: The war begins twice, in the same moment, on both sides of the field: Duryodhana's city turns toward battle with the joy of a festival, while Krishna names the choice plainly — the Pandavas will not buy peace by giving up what is theirs. Neither camp hesitates at the edge; both have already decided, which is what makes the coming war feel less like a choice than a gathering tide.
stories.content_note: War preparations and the acceptance of war; no combat depicted.
stories.next_story_tease: With war now certain, the Pandavas turned to arraying their host — and to choosing who would drive Arjuna's chariot.
stories.hero_scene: In the lamplit tent at Upaplavya, Krishna speaks to Yudhishthira with one hand open toward the field beyond the canvas, while across the plain the Kuru capital glitters with the lights of a city arming itself for war as for a festival.

stories.title: The Charioteer
stories.subtitle: Krishna Is Chosen as Arjuna's Guide and Driver of His Steeds
stories.story:
How, O Kesava, could wicked Duryodhana say it? Recollecting the words that Vasudeva had spoken, Yudhishthira pressed Krishna once more, in the camp at Upaplavya, seeking guidance for what had now to be done. He reminded Krishna of all that he knew: the views of Duryodhana, of Karna, of Sakuni the son of Suvala; the views of the Pandavas themselves; the words of Vidura and of Bhishma; the words of wisdom spoken by Kunti. Overlooking all these, Yudhishthira said, tell us, after reflection, and without hesitation, what is for our good.

And Krishna answered in a voice deep as that of the clouds or cymbals. In the Kuru court he had spoken words consistent with both virtue and profit, and they had found no response in Duryodhana, in whom deceit supplied the place of wisdom. That wretch of wicked understanding listened not in the least to the counsels of Bhishma or Vidura or Krishna himself; he transgressed everybody; he wished neither to earn virtue nor to win fame. Relying upon Karna, he regarded everything as already won. He had even ordered Krishna's incarceration, though he had not obtained the fruition of that wish, and neither Bhishma nor Drona had said anything on the subject, for all of them followed Duryodhana except Vidura. Sakuni, Karna, and Dussasana, all equally foolish, had given foolish and vindictive Duryodhana much improper advice regarding the Pandavas. In brief, Krishna said, that wicked-souled wight beareth no good will towards thee. Not even in all these kings together that form thy army is that measure of sinfulness and wickedness which resideth in Duryodhana alone. As regards ourselves, we do not desire to make peace with the Kauravas by abandoning our property. War, therefore, is that which should now take place.

When he had finished, all the kings there present, without saying anything, looked at Yudhishthira's face. And Yudhishthira understood their intention and, with Bhima and Arjuna and the twins, gave the word: draw up the troops in battle array. The command passed through the army; a great uproar rose amongst the Pandava host, and all the soldiers were filled with joy.

King Yudhishthira the Just, however, beholding the impending slaughter of those that deserved not to be slain, began to sigh deeply. That for the sake of which I accepted an exile into the woods, and for which I suffered so much misery, that great calamity overtaketh us of a set purpose, he said. How shall we fight with those reverend superiors of ours whom we on no account can slay? What kind of victory shall we achieve by slaying our preceptors of venerable age?

Arjuna repeated to his elder brother all the words that Krishna had said. Thou hast certainly understood all the words spoken by Kunti and Vidura, that were repeated to thee by Devaki's son, he said. I know it for certain that neither Vidura nor Kunti would say anything that is sinful. Besides this, we cannot withdraw without engaging in battle. And Krishna said to Arjuna, it is even so.

That night the sons of Pandu made up their minds for war and passed the hours with their soldiers in great happiness. And when the army was drawn up and Arjuna took his place for the war that was coming, he did not stand alone: handsome Janardana, endued with great intelligence, the younger brother of Sankarshana, was chosen as the guide of Arjuna and the driver of his steeds. The counsellor of the war would now drive the chariot into it, and the friend who had carried the words of peace would stand closest to the man who had to fight.
stories.reflection: Yudhishthira gives the order for battle and grieves in the same breath, accepting the war even as he mourns what it will cost. And Arjuna answers that grief the only way he can: not by doubting the war, but by placing himself beside Krishna, trusting the words that came from Kunti and Vidura and were carried by Devaki's son.
stories.content_note: The acceptance of war and anticipation of battle; no combat depicted.
stories.next_story_tease: But one man would not march with them — Balarama, who refused to raise his hand against either side.
stories.hero_scene: At dawn on the plain, Arjuna stands beside his war-chariot with the reins being settled in Krishna's hands; behind them the Pandava host stretches to the horizon, while Arjuna looks back once toward the grieving king who gave the order.

stories.title: The Man Who Walked to the River
stories.subtitle: Balarama Refuses to Take Sides and Departs for the Saraswati Tirthas
stories.story:
While the Pandava camp rang with the order to draw up for battle, one man among the Vrishnis would take no part in it, and he was Krishna's own elder brother.

The decision had been made. When Krishna had finished speaking, all the kings there present had looked at Yudhishthira's face, and Yudhishthira, understanding them, had given the word with Bhima and Arjuna and the twins: draw up the troops in battle array. A great uproar rose amongst the Pandava army, and all the soldiers were filled with joy. King Yudhishthira the Just, however, beholding the impending slaughter of those that deserved not to be slain, began to sigh deeply. That for the sake of which I accepted an exile into the woods, he said, and for which I suffered so much misery, that great calamity overtaketh us of a set purpose. How shall we fight with those reverend superiors whom we on no account can slay? Kings rose from their seats and took up their arms; the two great hosts arranged themselves across Kurukshetra. In the middle of that gathering of warriors, Balarama stood apart.

He was unwilling to fight against either the Pandavas or Duryodhana. Both armies held men he had known all his life, and he would raise his arm against neither. Yet his refusal was not a withdrawal from the quarrel of his own heart. As regards myself, he declared, I dare not cast my eyes on the world without Krishna on my side. It is for this that I follow whatever Krishna seeketh to achieve.

He followed Krishna's cause, then, without reservation, and the words he left behind were not the words of a man washing his hands of the quarrel. But following it was not the same as standing on the field to watch it carried out. I shall now repair to the tirtha of the Saraswati for ablutions, Balarama said, for I shall not be able to behold with indifference the destruction of the Kauravas.

So, while the kings armed themselves and the soldiers raised their joyful uproar and the two hosts settled into their places, Balarama turned his back on the field. He walked to the Saraswati, the sacred river of the sages, to its holy fords, places of ablution and prayer where pilgrims came to be cleansed, and there he would bathe and pray. A warrior leaving the war he could neither join nor watch: his refusal to fight was no judgment against either army, but the only position left to a man who loved both sides and could not bear to see one of them destroyed.

The war would be fought without him, and the brothers of the Vrishni race would part at the edge of it. Behind Balarama, the greatest war of the age gathered itself. Before him lay the quiet fords of the Saraswati, where the water asked nothing of any man. He had chosen the only side left to him: the side of neither army, and of the one cause he could not abandon.
stories.reflection: Balarama's withdrawal is not indifference — he follows Krishna's cause even as he refuses to witness its cost. The story is a quiet acknowledgment that devotion and kinship can pull in different directions, and that sometimes the honest answer to an unbearable war is to walk away from it and let the water carry what the field cannot.
stories.next_story_tease: On the morning of battle, Krishna would bid Arjuna hymn Durga for victory.

stories.title: Durga's Promise Before the Battle
stories.story:
The night before the battle, Krishna gave Arjuna an order that sounded less like war counsel than like ritual. "Cleanse yourself, mighty-armed one," he said, "and on the eve of this battle recite your hymn to Durga, so that the defeat of the foe may be assured."

At dawn the armies of the Pandavas and the Kauravas would meet on the field of Kurukshetra. For years the cousins had been pushed toward this plain — by insult, by exile, by a game of dice that should never have been played — and now there was nothing left to settle but the war itself. Yet on the last night, the charioteer's first command was not about formations or weapons. It was about a hymn.

Arjuna did not ask why. He stepped down from his car, and there in the quiet of the camp, with his hands joined, he recited the hymn as he had been taught. He praised the goddess in her many names: the leader of the yogins, she who is identical with Brahman; Kali of the black and tawny hue; Mahakali, who brings benefits to her devotees; the fierce giver of victory, who bears a banner of peacock plumes and holds spear, sword, and shield; the younger sister of the chief of cowherds, born in the race of the cowherd Nanda; she who is fond of buffalo's blood and dresses in yellow robes; she who devoured the Asuras with the face of a wolf; the slayer of Kaitabha; the mother of Skanda; she who dwells in inaccessible places and in the houses of her worshippers. He named her Swaha and Swadha, Saraswati and Savitri, the twilight and the day, the sleep of creatures and their beauty. He praised her as the Vedas and the Srutis, the highest virtue, propitious to Brahmanas engaged in sacrifice; as the science of Brahma among the sciences; as contentment and growth and light, she who supports the Sun and the Moon and makes them shine; she who dwells in inaccessible regions, in places of difficulty, in the abodes of her worshippers, and in the nether regions, always defeating the Danavas; she whom the Siddhas and the Charanas behold in contemplation. And with his inner soul cleansed, he prayed: "Let victory always attend me through your grace on the field of battle."

Perhaps it was that last line that was heard. For Durga, who is always graciously inclined toward mankind, understood the measure of Partha's devotion and appeared in the sky — and she spoke in the presence of Govinda himself. "Within a short time you shall conquer your foes, O Pandava," the goddess said. "You are invincible, O Pandava, for you have Narayana again to aid you. You cannot be defeated by your enemies — not even by the wielder of the thunderbolt himself."

Having said this, the boon-giving goddess disappeared as suddenly as she had come. Arjuna stood a moment holding the promise, then mounted his own excellent car. And Krishna and Arjuna, seated on the same chariot, blew their celestial conches, and the sound of them rolled out over the sleeping armies like the first note of the war that would begin at dawn.

Sanjaya, telling all this to the blind king Dhritarashtra, added that a man who recites this hymn at dawn has nothing to fear — not from Yakshas, Rakshasas, or Pisachas, not from snakes or any creature of fang and tooth, not even from kings. He is victorious in every dispute and freed from every bond, and he lives a hundred years in health and strength. But the Kauravas, Sanjaya said, entangled in the meshes of death, did not know that Nara and Narayana stood before them on a single chariot, and that the hour of their kingdom had already arrived. Dwaipayana and Narada, Kanwa and the sinless Rama had all tried to turn Dhritarashtra's son from this course, Sanjaya said, but the prince would not accept their words; there where righteousness is, there victory would be.
stories.reflection: Krishna's first preparation for the war is an act of worship, not a tactic: before Arjuna is taught to fight, he is sent to bow. And the goddess's promise — that the invincible one has Narayana to aid him — names what the hymn has accomplished: the charioteer and the goddess are already on Arjuna's side, and the battle is blessed before a single arrow is loosed.
stories.next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would drive the chariot between the two armies.

stories.title: A Chariot Between Two Armies
stories.story:
Somewhere on the field of Kurukshetra there were hundreds of thousands of men, but what Arjuna asked to see was only their faces.

It began with a question from a blind king. Seated in his palace, Dhritarashtra asked Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas had done, assembled together on the sacred plain from desire of fighting. And Sanjaya answered as he saw it, moment by moment, from the first arraying of the armies.

King Duryodhana walked the lines with his preceptor Drona, reviewing the might he had gathered. He pointed out the enemy's champions — Yuyudhana, Virata, Drupada, Dhrishtadyumna, the ruler of Kasi, Subhadra's son Abhimanyu, the sons of Draupadi — and then named his own: Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashwatthaman, Vikarna, Jayadratha, and the many heroes ready to lay down their lives for his sake. Our army, protected by Bhishma, is insufficient, he said; theirs, protected by Bhima, is sufficient. He asked his captains to station themselves at the entrances of their divisions and protect Bhishma alone.

Then the valiant grandsire of the Kurus, giving Duryodhana great joy, roared like a lion and blew his conch. At once conches, drums, cymbals, and horns sounded together, and the noise became a great uproar. Krishna and Arjuna, stationed on their great car yoked with white steeds, blew their celestial conches — Krishna blew Panchajanya, and Arjuna blew Devadatta. Bhima blew his huge conch Paundra; Yudhishthira blew Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosa and Manipushpaka. The ruler of Kasi, Sikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, the unvanquished Satyaki, Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra — all blew their conches. The blare reverberated through the sky, and it rent the hearts of the Kauravas.

Then Arjuna, whose banner bore the ape, raised his bow and spoke to Krishna as the throwing of missiles was about to begin. "Place my car between the two armies, O one who knows no deterioration," he said, "so that I may observe these men who stand here desirous of battle, and with whom I must contend in the labours of this struggle. I want to see those who have assembled to fight for the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra."

Krishna drove the excellent car between the two armies, in full view of Bhishma and Drona and all the kings of the earth, and said, "Behold, O Partha, these assembled Kurus."

And there the son of Pritha beheld, standing on both sides, his sires and grandsons, his friends, his father-in-law, his well-wishers — his preceptors and his teachers, his sons and his grandsires, his maternal uncles and his brothers-in-law, his kinsmen, the men who had raised him. And as he looked at them, something in him gave way. "Beholding these kinsmen, O Krishna," he said, and his voice failed him. His limbs grew languid, his mouth went dry; his body trembled, and his hair stood on end. Gandiva slipped from his hand. "I do not desire victory, O Krishna," he said, "nor sovereignty, nor pleasures. Of what use is a kingdom, or enjoyment, or even life, since those for whose sake we desired them stand here arrayed against us, ready to give up life and wealth? I wish not to slay these, though they slay me, not even for the sovereignty of the three worlds — what, then, for the sake of this earth?"

The car stood between the armies, the white horses still, and the whole field waited — the conches silent, the banners still — while the finest archer in the world looked at the men he loved and found he could not fight them. And Sanjaya's voice, telling it all to the blind king, fell silent too, for the charioteer had not yet spoken.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not drive the chariot where Arjuna can admire the spectacle; he drives it where Arjuna must see that both armies are his family. The survey before battle is no scouting mission — it is the moment the war becomes unbearable, and every word of the Gita will grow out of that unbearable sight.
stories.next_story_tease: In that moment of pity, Arjuna would set down his bow and refuse the war.

stories.title: Arjuna's Despair and Collapse
stories.story:
The two armies had drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, and the war everyone had dreaded and prepared for was about to begin. Years of grievance and humiliation had been folded into this single hour. Every man on that field was someone's father, son, or brother; almost all of them shared the same blood. Then, before a single arrow flew, the man at its center lost the will to fight.

The Kauravas and the Pandavas stood facing each other, and the sound of their conches and drums and cymbals and horns filled the field. Duryodhana had walked the length of his own army naming its warriors to his preceptor Drona — Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Aswatthaman — and the venerable old grandsire Bhishma had raised his conch and blown a lion's roar. On the other side, standing on a great chariot yoked to white steeds, Krishna blew the conch Panchajanya and Arjuna blew Devadatta. The terrible Bhima blew his great conch Paundra, Yudhishthira blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosa and Manipushpaka. The answering horns went up, and for a moment the whole plain was one vast, brazen noise.

And then Arjuna looked across the field, and everything stopped.

He saw the men arrayed before him, his own kinsmen on both sides. There was his grandsire Bhishma, the venerable old warrior who had presided over his whole life. There was his preceptor Drona, who had taught him the bow. There was Karna and Kripa and Aswatthaman, and beyond them cousins and kinsmen he had grown up beside, uncles and nephews and the sons of old friends. And behind him, in his own ranks, stood Subhadra's son, his own boy, and the sons of Draupadi. These were the men the war had gathered — and the men he was about to kill.

The pity came on him all at once, and it was not a small thing. His body began to tremble, and the hair stood on end along his skin, and his skin burned. It was not fear that did this; it was something nearer to love, and it was stronger than either. The great bow Gandiva, which had never failed him, slipped from his fingers — and with it slipped everything he had prepared for this day. He could not hold it. A man who cannot raise his bow cannot fight a war, and this man had been the hope of an entire side of it.

He spoke, despondent, to Krishna beside him. His voice, which had carried across a hundred battlefields, was low. 'I wish not to slay these though they slay me,' he said. 'O slayer of Madhu.' What kind of victory, he was asking without quite asking, would be bought with the deaths of his own people?

He did not wait for an answer, or perhaps he could not. His mind troubled with grief, he cast aside his bow and his arrows and sat down in the chariot, right there on the field of battle, between two armies that were waiting for him. The conches that had roared a moment before were silent; the field held its breath. The noise of the day fell away, and the man who was supposed to lead them all sat slumped and still.

Krishna did not speak yet. He held the reins, and he waited. There would be time for words soon, and the words would change everything. But for now there was only this: the strongest man on the field, undone not by any enemy but by the sight of the people he loved standing where he would have to kill them.
stories.reflection: The Gita does not begin with philosophy; it begins with a man falling apart. Before Krishna can teach Arjuna anything, Arjuna has to be honest about what he feels — and what he feels is that the victory he has spent his life preparing for is not worth the faces in front of him.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna had not yet spoken — and what he was about to say would become the heart of the teaching.
stories.hero_scene: Arjuna slumped in his chariot on the field of Kurukshetra, the great bow Gandiva slipped from his hand and his arrows cast aside, while Krishna stands quietly at the reins against the hush of two waiting armies.

stories.title: Teach Me, I Am Your Disciple
stories.story:
On the field between the armies, with both hosts looking on, Krishna told the finest archer of his age to stop grieving.

"Whence has this despondency come upon you at such a crisis, O Arjuna?" he said. "It is unbecoming of noble birth; it shuts one out from heaven and earns infamy. Let no weakness be yours, son of Kunti — this does not suit you. Shake off this vile feebleness of heart and arise, chastiser of foes."

But Arjuna could not rise. "How can I fight Bhishma and Drona with arrows," he asked, "men who deserve my worship? It is better to live on alms in this world than to slay my preceptors. Even if they are greedy for wealth, killing them would leave me pleasures that are bloodstained. I do not know which is of greater moment — that we conquer them, or that they conquer us. The very men by whose death I would not wish to live stand before me. My nature is affected by the taint of compassion; my mind is unsettled about my duty. I ask you: tell me what is assuredly good for me. I am your disciple. Instruct me, I seek your aid. I cannot see anything that would dispel the grief that blasts my senses — not a prosperous kingdom without a foe, not even the sovereignty of the gods."

Then he said plainly: "I will not fight." And he fell silent.

It was not a surrender of arms only. Standing on a battlefield with two armies waiting, Arjuna had handed over the thing he had trusted most — his own judgment about right and wrong — and asked for it back, instructed. The disciple's plea and the refusal sat side by side, and the whole field, Sanjaya would later say, seemed to hold its breath.

Krishna looked at him in the midst of the two armies and began to answer. "You mourn those who deserve no mourning, and you speak like a man of learning," he said, "yet those who are truly wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living. It is not that I, or you, or these rulers of men never were; nor that we shall not all be hereafter. As childhood, youth, and old age come to the body, so the embodied soul acquires another body, and the wise are never deluded by this. The contacts of the senses with their objects — heat and cold, pleasure and pain — come and go; they are not permanent. Endure them, O Bharata. The man whom they do not disturb, who is the same in pain and in pleasure, who is firm of mind, is fit for freedom.

Know that by which all this universe is pervaded to be immortal: no one can compass the destruction of the imperishable. The bodies of the eternal, indestructible, infinite soul have an end; therefore fight, O Bharata. He who thinks the soul is the slayer, and he who thinks it is the slain, both know nothing; it neither slays nor is slain. It is never born and never dies; it has not come into being and will not cease to be. Unborn, unchangeable, eternal, ancient — it is not slain when the body perishes. As a man casts off worn-out robes and puts on new ones, so the embodied soul casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones. Weapons cleave it not, fire consumes it not; the waters do not drench it, nor does the wind waste it. It cannot be cut, burned, drenched, or dried. It is unchanging, all-pervading, stable, firm, eternal. Therefore it does not behoove you to mourn.

And even if you were to regard the soul as constantly born and constantly dying, still you must not mourn. Of one who is born, death is certain; of one who has died, birth is certain. All beings were unmanifest before birth, manifest during the interval of life, and unmanifest again at death. What grief is there in this?"

The charioteer's voice went on across the field, and the armies stood silent. The war would wait; something else had begun. The disciple had asked what was truly good, and the answer was opening like a door into a room neither army could see.
stories.reflection: Arjuna's surrender is the true hinge of the field: he does not ask to be spared the battle but to be told what is good. The Gita begins because a warrior lays down not only his bow but his certainty — and it is to that humility that Krishna answers with the nature of the self.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's answer would grow until it revealed the whole universe gathered in his form.
stories.hero_scene: Between the two waiting armies, Arjuna stands with joined hands before the chariot, his bow set aside, asking Krishna to instruct him, while Krishna looks at him with the first words of the teaching already forming.

stories.title: Krishna Reveals the Vishvarupa
stories.story:
The armies of the Kauravas and the Pandavas stood drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, waiting, and in the long pause before the first blow Krishna had been teaching. The despair that had brought Arjuna to his knees at the sight of his own kinsmen drawn up against him was gone. What Krishna had called the supreme mystery — the knowledge of the Self, spoken for his welfare — had dispelled his delusion. But in its place stood a hunger no teaching had yet satisfied. He had heard, at length, of how all beings come into being and pass away again, and of a greatness in Krishna that never diminished. He believed it. Believing was no longer enough. He had been taught the whole of it, and the teaching had left him with one thing still unfulfilled: he wanted to see, with his own eyes, the being who had been speaking to him.

"What you have said of yourself is true," Arjuna said at last. It was not a demand; it was trust. "I desire to behold your sovereign form. If you think that I am able to bear it, show me your eternal Self."

Krishna looked at him with eyes like lotus petals, and did not refuse. "Behold my forms by hundreds and thousands," he said, "divine, of many hues and many shapes. Behold the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aswins, the Maruts. Behold innumerable marvels never seen before. Behold, you of the curly hair, the entire universe — everything that moves and everything that does not — gathered together in this body of mine, and whatever else you may wish to see. But you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you celestial sight. Behold my sovereign, mystic nature."

And then he showed him.

The form that rose before Arjuna had many mouths and many eyes, many wondrous aspects, celestial ornaments and weapons uplifted, garlands and robes of heaven, anointed with a fragrance that belonged to no earth. It was full of every wonder, resplendent, without end, its faces turned in every direction at once. Arjuna had known light his whole life — the sun, the fire, the lamps of evening — but nothing he had ever seen came near this. If the light of a thousand suns were to burst forth together in the sky, it would only resemble the light of that Mighty One.

In that single body Arjuna saw the entire universe, divided and subdivided into its many parts, all collected together. His hair stood on end, and he bowed his head and joined his hands, filled with amazement. When he spoke again his voice had changed. "I see all the gods," he said, "and all the varied hosts of creatures, and Brahman seated upon his lotus, and the rishis and the celestial serpents. I see you with arms and stomachs and mouths and eyes beyond counting, on every side, O you of infinite forms. Neither end nor middle nor beginning can I find in you, Lord of the universe, Lord of the universal form."

Still the vision pressed on him, and he looked and looked, unable to turn away. "Bearing your diadem, your mace and your discus," he said, "a mass of energy glowing on every side, I behold you — hard to look upon, blazing like fire at its full height."

There, between two armies that had not yet begun to fight, the man who held the reins of Arjuna's chariot stood revealed as the ground of everything. And the warrior who had asked to see it could only bow before what he had been shown.
stories.reflection: The vision is granted because Arjuna asks for it, and it overwhelms him not with threat but with scale: the whole of creation gathered into one form that has no end, middle, or beginning. What silences him is not fear of the form's power but the sight of every thing he has ever known held, at once, in a single body.
stories.next_story_tease: But the war would not wait long on vision; harder counsel lay ahead on that same field.

stories.title: I Am Death, Destroyer of Worlds
stories.story:
Arjuna looked into the mouth of the universe and saw his own family entering it.

Krishna had given him celestial sight, and what it revealed stood before him like a second sky: a form with a thousand faces and a thousand arms, mouths that blazed like the fire at the end of the ages, bearing diadem, mace, and discus, glowing on every side. The whole universe — gods and beasts, heaven and earth — was gathered into that one body. He saw Brahman seated on his lotus seat, the Rishis and the celestial serpents, the Rudras, the Adityas, the Vasus, the Ashwins and the Maruts; he saw hosts of gods entering the form while others, afraid, prayed with joined hands, and the great Rishis and Siddhas praising it with hymns. The space between heaven and earth, and every point of the horizon, was pervaded by that body; the sun and the moon were its eyes, the blazing fire its mouth. The form was hard to look at — a mass of energy glowing on all sides, touching the very skies, many-hued, with blazing, enormous eyes and its mouth wide open. It had no beginning, no middle, no end; it was indestructible, the supreme object of the universe, heating the whole creation with its own radiance. At the sight of it the triple world trembled, and the hosts of great Rishis and Siddhas praised it with cries of hail, while Gandharvas, Yakshas, and Asuras stared, amazed. "Neither end, nor middle, nor beginning of you do I behold," Arjuna said, with his hair standing on end.

And then he saw what was happening at the mouths. "The sons of Dhritarashtra," he said, "together with the hosts of kings, and Bhishma, and Drona, and Karna the son of the charioteer, with the principal warriors of our own side — all of them are quickly entering your terrible mouths, made fierce by your tusks. Some, with their heads crushed, are caught between the interstices of your teeth. As rivers of many currents roll swiftly toward the ocean, so these heroes of the world of men enter your flaming mouths. As moths rush with increasing speed to the blazing fire for their own destruction, so do these men rush to their doom in you. I can no longer command courage or peace of mind. Be gracious, O God of gods, O refuge of the universe."

And from within that blaze a voice answered — the same voice that had driven the chariot, the same voice that had spoken of the immortal soul. "I am Death," it said, "the destroyer of the worlds, fully developed. I am now engaged in slaying the race of men. By me have all these been already slain. Be only my instrument."

The words fell on Arjuna like a second revelation. The war he had dreaded, the killing he had refused, the kinsmen he could not bear to face — all of it had already happened, in the will of the one who stood before him. The warriors he had seen streaming into those mouths were not about to die; they were already gone. What remained was only whether Arjuna would be the willing instrument, or something less.

The vision blazed around him — mouths and tusks and flame, the splendour of a hundred suns — and Arjuna, trembling, bowed his head in the middle of the blaze. He had asked to see the truth, and the truth was this: the battle was not his to begin or to refuse. It was his to serve, or his to watch in helplessness — and the whole difference between those two, the whole war, lay in that single choice. Still the voice waited for his answer.
stories.reflection: The terrible form is the kindest thing Krishna could have shown him: the war Arjuna fears to cause has already happened — the warriors are already gone. His choice is not whether they die but whether he will be the willing instrument or the helpless witness, and the whole of the Gita's call to action rests on that strange, liberating knowledge.
stories.content_note: Contains imagery of warriors being drawn into the cosmic form's flaming mouths; intense but not graphic.

stories.hero_scene: Within the blazing cosmic form, the warriors of both armies stream like rivers into Krishna's flaming, tusk-fierce mouths, while a small Arjuna stands before the vision with joined hands, his hair standing on end.

stories.title: The Return of the Gentle Form
stories.story:
Show me the form I know, Arjuna said, and his voice trembled as he spoke.

Moments earlier Krishna had given him celestial sight and shown him the sovereign form: the body of the universe itself, with a thousand faces and a thousand arms, the sun and moon for eyes, the blazing fire at the end of the ages for a mouth. Arjuna had seen the whole creation gathered into that one body. He had seen gods and serpents, Rishis and Siddhas, the hosts of the Rudras, the Adityas, the Vasus and the Ashwins, some entering the form, others praying with joined hands before it. And he had seen the most terrible thing of all: the warriors of both armies, Bhishma and Drona and Karna, the sons of Dhritarashtra and all their kings, rushing into those flaming mouths like rivers streaming into the sea.

The wonder of it had lifted him. The fear of it had nearly undone him. His hair had stood on end, his inner soul had trembled, and even now, with the vision folded away, he could not be still.

Beholding your form, unseen before, he said, I have been joyful, and yet my mind is troubled with fear. Show me that other form, the ordinary one. Show me the face of my friend, the face of my charioteer.

Krishna heard the plea and answered it. Once more he showed Arjuna his own ordinary form. The thousand faces folded back into one face. The mouths that blazed like the fire at the end of the ages became a smile. The diadem, the mace, the discus faded, and there stood the Krishna Arjuna knew: the friend who had driven his chariot, who had sat with him and counselled him, whose voice he had heard all his life. Assuming once more his gentle form, the high-souled one comforted the man he had afflicted.

Krishna said nothing of the vision. He simply waited, as a friend waits, while Arjuna found his footing again.

And comfort, in that presence, was not a word but a work. The trembling in Arjuna's hands began to ease. His scattered thoughts gathered themselves and settled. He breathed, and the breath no longer caught in his chest. The field that had seemed, for a moment, to be the mouth of the end of all things became again a stretch of grass and dust, with two armies waiting across from one another and the morning light lying quietly between them.

Then Arjuna spoke, and this time his voice was his own. Beholding this gentle human form of yours, he said, I am composed once more. My senses have returned to me. I am myself again.

That was Krishna's gift to him: not merely a vision withdrawn, but a friend returned. The one who had shown him the body of the universe had chosen, for the sake of a trembling friend, to fold himself back into the shape of a charioteer. The terrible form was truth; the gentle form was mercy, and both wore the same face.

Arjuna stood, restored to himself, and looked across the field. The war still waited. So did the last of his questions, the one about duty and renunciation and what it truly meant to act without clinging to the fruit. But that was for the morning. For this moment, it was enough that his friend was beside him again, in the form he could bear.
stories.reflection: The return to the gentle form is the other half of the revelation. Arjuna could carry the truth of who Krishna is only because Krishna was willing to be small for him: mercy here is not an abstract quality but a shape, the familiar face and the charioteer's hands. The terrible form revealed the universe; the gentle form revealed what the universe's lord chooses, again and again, to become.
stories.next_story_tease: Restored to himself, Arjuna still carried one question about duty and renunciation that only Krishna could answer.
stories.hero_scene: On the battlefield at Kurukshetra, the blazing cosmic form with a thousand faces folds back into the familiar figure of Krishna the charioteer, who reaches out to comfort Arjuna as the trembling archer bows before him, the morning light returning to the field.

stories.title: What the True Renouncer Gives Up
stories.story:
Arjuna had one question left, and it was the question of a man who had nearly walked away from everything.

He had come to the field of Kurukshetra ready to lay down his bow, sickened by the thought of killing his own kin. Krishna had answered him from the heart of the war itself, until Arjuna's delusion had begun to loosen. Then the universe had opened before him, and closed again, and his friend had returned to his gentle form. Now, standing in the chariot with the armies waiting, Arjuna asked the question that still burned in him.

Of renunciation, he said, I desire to know the true nature. And of abandonment, tell me distinctly what it means.

Krishna answered as one who had been asked this before, by every man who ever stood where the road divides. The rejection of works done with desire, he said, the learned call renunciation. The abandonment of the fruit of all works, the discerning call abandonment. Some wise men say that work itself is evil and should be cast off entirely. Others say the works of sacrifice, gift, and penance should never be abandoned. Listen to my decision.

The works of sacrifice, gift, and penance should not be abandoned, he said. They purify the wise. But they should be done abandoning attachment, abandoning the fruit. The renunciation of an act prescribed in the scriptures is not proper. To drop a duty from delusion is abandonment of the quality of darkness; to drop it from fear of bodily pain is abandonment of the quality of passion, and it earns no fruit. But the work that is done because it should be done, without attachment and without longing for its fruit, that abandonment is of the quality of goodness. And since no embodied being can truly give up action altogether, the real renouncer is the one who gives up the fruit of action, not the action itself.

Then Krishna spoke of the five causes that stand behind every deed: the substratum on which it rests, the agent, the organs that carry it out, the efforts they make, and the deities presiding over them. With body, speech, or mind, whatever a man undertakes, these five are its causes. So the man of dull understanding who sees his own self as the sole agent, who says, I alone did this, sees wrongly. But he who has no feeling of egoism, whose mind is not sullied, even killing all these people, kills not, nor is fettered by the deed.

Knowledge itself is threefold, Krishna went on. The knowledge that sees one eternal essence in all things, undivided in the divided, is of the quality of goodness. The knowledge that sees all things as separate essences, each closed in its own kind, is of the quality of passion. And the knowledge that clings to a single object as if it were the whole, without reason and without truth, is of the quality of darkness. So too with action: the act done without attachment, without desire and aversion, by one who longs not for its fruit, is good; the act done for objects of desire, heavy with egoism and attended with great trouble, is passionate; the act undertaken from delusion, without regard to consequence or one's own power, is dark. And so too with the agent: the agent of goodness is free from attachment, never speaks of himself, is constant and energetic, unmoved by success and defeat. The agent of passion is full of affection, covetous of fruit, cruel, impure, tossed between joy and sorrow. The agent of darkness is without application, obstinate, deceitful, malicious, slothful, always putting things off.

The chariot stood still on the field, and the two armies held their breath without knowing it. Then Arjuna spoke, and this time his words were not a question.

My delusion is destroyed, he said. Through your favour, I have gained the recollection of what I am. I am firm. My doubts are dispelled. I will do your bidding.

It was not the answer of a man who had been persuaded. It was the answer of a man who had finally seen the shape of his own life: that he was never the sole author of his deeds, that the fruit was never his to hoard, and that the work itself, done without clinging, was its own purity. The bow that he had been ready to drop was in his hands again, and the battle that had seemed impossible was now simply the thing he would do.
stories.reflection: Arjuna's question about renunciation is the question of every person about to act greatly: how does one move without being consumed by attachment? Krishna's answer gives the warrior his footing, not by promising success but by relocating the self: he is not the sole agent, and the fruit is not his to guard. The man who abandons the fruit, not the work, is the one who can finally act without fear.
stories.next_story_tease: With Arjuna resolved, Krishna turned his attention to the one warrior on the enemy side who could still change the war.
stories.hero_scene: Standing in the chariot between the two waiting armies, Krishna speaks of renunciation with one hand raised, while Arjuna, bow in hand and doubts gone, bows his head in the firm declaration: I will do your bidding.

stories.title: The Offer to Karna
stories.story:
Of all the men on that field, the one Krishna sought out was the one who could still change the war.

The Gita had been spoken and Arjuna's doubts had fallen away. When the son of Pandu took up his arrows and Gandiva once more, the mighty car-warriors of the Pandava host raised a tremendous shout. The Pandavas and the Somakas blew their sea-born conches, drums and cow-horns sounded together, and the uproar was very loud. The gods themselves came to watch, with the Gandharvas and the Pitris, the hosts of Siddhas and Charanas, and the blessed Rishis in a body with Indra of the hundred sacrifices at their head, all gathered to witness the great slaughter that was to come.

Then, before the armies met, the king of the Pandavas did a strange thing. Yudhishthira the Just put off his coat of mail, cast aside his weapon, descended from his car, and walked on foot, with joined hands and restrained speech, toward the hostile host, facing east. His brothers followed him, alarmed. What is this act of yours, Arjuna called after him, that you abandon your brothers and walk on foot toward the foe? Where will you go without your armor, Bhima demanded, leaving your brothers behind? Nakula and Sahadeva too pleaded with him. But Yudhishthira said nothing and kept walking.

Krishna smiled and explained what the others could not see. His object is known to me, he said. He has gone to pay his respects to his elders, Bhishma and Drona and Kripa and Shalya. It is heard in the histories of old that he who honors his preceptors and his revered kinsmen before battle is sure to obtain victory.

Among the Kaurava ranks a loud uproar rose. The warriors of Dhritarashtra's son jeered and waved their garments, calling Yudhishthira an infamous wretch of his race, a king come in terror to seek Bhishma's shelter, and they censured him and his brothers and Kesava alike. Yudhishthira walked through the shower of insults as though through rain, penetrated the array bristling with arrows, and stood before the grandsire. Seizing Bhishma's feet with both hands, he said, I salute you, O invincible one. With you we will do battle. Grant us your permission, and give us your blessing.

Bhishma's answer silenced the jeering ranks. If you had not come to me thus, he said, I would have cursed you for bringing about your own defeat. I am gratified with you, my son. Do battle, and obtain victory. Ask also whatever boon you desire.

And then, when that courtesy was done, Krishna went to Radha's son on the field of battle. For the sake of the Pandavas he said to Karna, I have heard it said, O Karna, that out of hatred of Bhishma you will not fight. Come to our side, son of Radha, and stay with us as long as Bhishma is not slain.

It was a strange offer, made in the open field between two armies: the finest warrior of the enemy, invited across, and spared the one fight that burned in him. Karna heard it to the end. Then he gave his answer, and there was no hesitation in it. I will not do anything that is disagreeable to Dhritarashtra's son, he said. However the war goes, whatever Bhishma thinks of me, Duryodhana is my friend and my king, and I will not be disloyal to him.

Krishna had come for the sake of the Pandavas, and he returned to them with the answer he had carried out with him: some loyalties are not bought, even with justice, even with the throne. The offer was made, and refused, and the war would be fought with Karna on the side he had chosen. The conches had sounded, the gods had gathered, and there was nothing left to do but begin.
stories.reflection: Krishna's offer to Karna is war strategy in its purest form, but Karna's refusal is something rarer: a loyalty that no grievance could bend. He knows Bhishma despises him and that the Pandava cause is just, and still he will not do anything disagreeable to the man who stood by him when no one else would. Some bonds are chosen before they are reasoned about, and Karna honors his to the end.
stories.tradition_note: This is the second offer Krishna makes to Karna; an earlier and fuller offer before the war is told elsewhere in the Mahabharata, when Karna's reasons for refusing are given at greater length.
stories.next_story_tease: The war began, and by evening Bhishma's arrows would bring Yudhishthira to the edge of despair.
stories.hero_scene: On the open field between the two armies, Krishna stands before Karna making his offer with an open hand, while Karna, tall and unbending in his armor, refuses with folded arms as the conches of both armies sound in the distance.
