stories.title: The Name of Bhishma's Slayer
stories.story:
The first day had taught Yudhishthira what war with Bhishma meant, and the lesson had nearly broken him.

When the troops withdrew at evening, Duryodhana was filled with delight, for Bhishma had raged through the Pandava ranks like a storm. King Yudhishthira the Just came to Krishna with all his brothers and all the kings of his side, and his grief was plain on his face. He had seen his army burning, and he could not see how it would end.

Behold, O Krishna, that mighty bowman Bhishma of terrible prowess, he said. He consumes my troops with his arrows like fire consuming dry grass. He licks up my army like a flame fed with clarified butter. My soldiers fly away, pierced and afflicted, and I cannot blame them. Enraged Yama himself might be vanquished, or Indra armed with the thunderbolt, Varuna with his noose, Kuvera with his mace, but the mighty car-warrior Bhishma of great energy cannot be vanquished. I am sinking in the fathomless ocean that is Bhishma, and there is no boat to carry me.

His voice grew heavier as he went on. Out of the weakness of my understanding, he said, having gotten Bhishma for a foe, I will retire into the woods. To live there is preferable to devoting these lords of earth to Death in the form of Bhishma. My brothers are pained and pierced with arrows for my sake, having given up sovereignty and happiness out of love for their eldest brother. During the remainder of my days I will practise the severest austerities. I will not cause these friends of mine to be slain.

Then he looked at his own camp and found it wanting. Arjuna, he said, is an indifferent spectator in this battle. Only Bhima fights, remembering the duty of a Kshatriya, achieving the most difficult feats with his mace among foot-soldiers and steeds and cars and elephants, and even he cannot destroy the hostile host in fair fight in a century. Bhishma and Drona, their celestial weapons applied without rest, are consuming all the Kshatriyas. Tell me, O Krishna, without delay, what should be done. Look for that great bowman, that mighty car-warrior, who will give Bhishma his quietus, like rain-charged clouds quenching a forest conflagration. Then, through your grace, we may recover our kingdom and be happy with our kinsmen.

And the son of Pandu, his heart afflicted, fell silent and remained so for a long while, his mind turned inward.

Krishna looked at the king who had spoken of leaving the war, and he answered the grief before he answered the argument. Do not grieve, O chief of the Bharatas, he said. It does not behove you to grieve when your brothers are all heroes and renowned bowmen in the world. I am employed in doing you good, and so are the mighty car-warrior Satyaki, and Virata and Drupada, both reverend in years, and Dhrishtadyumna of Prishata's line. All these monarchs with their troops are devoted to you and expectant of your favour. Your commander, Dhrishtadyumna, is always desirous of your welfare.

Then Krishna spoke the words that changed the king's night. And this Sikhandin, he said, O mighty-armed one, is certainly the slayer of Bhishma.

The name fell into the silence like a stone into still water. Sikhandin. The one warrior on earth appointed to bring the grandsire down. Krishna did not say how, or when, or by what means; he said only that it was so, and Yudhishthira, who had been ready to trade his crown for a hermit's bowl, felt the despair in his chest begin to ease. If Bhishma had a slayer, then the war had an end, and the end was not the annihilation he had seen all day.

In that very assembly, in the hearing of Vasudeva, the king turned to his commander. O Dhrishtadyumna, he said, mark these words that I say to you. My words should not be transgressed. Approved by Vasudeva, you have been the commander of our forces.

An hour before, he had been speaking of the woods. Now he was giving orders for the war. The despair had not vanished, but it had found its limit, and the king who had been sinking had been handed a boat.
stories.reflection: Yudhishthira's despair is the particular weight of leadership: he watches his brothers and allies burn for his sake and cannot bear to spend them. Krishna does not argue him out of his grief; he hands him a single fact, that Bhishma's fall has a name, and the fact is enough. Knowing that the end is already appointed, and that it will come through Sikhandin, is what lets the king sleep and stand again.
stories.content_note: Depicts the aftermath of a day of battle, with descriptions of an army being devastated by arrows; intense but not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: The next morning, Krishna would drive Arjuna's chariot straight at Bhishma.

stories.title: The Chariot Against the Grandsire
stories.subtitle: Krishna drives Arjuna straight at Bhishma
stories.story:
Of all the arrows shot at Kurukshetra that morning, three were aimed at the man who did not fight.

The day had opened with the armies already locked in battle. At Duryodhana's word the combatants, cased in mail and with standards upraised, had rushed against the Pandavas, and the battle that followed made the hair stand on end. Cars and elephants churned together; shafts with beautiful feathers and sharp points fell upon horses and upon men. And at the head of the Kaurava host came Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, mighty-armed, cased in mail, his bow in hand, showering an arrowy downpour on the heroes of the other side — on Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra, on Arjuna himself, on the ruler of the Kekayas, on Virata and Dhrishtadyumna of Prishata's race, on the Chedi and the Matsya warriors. The Pandava array wavered at his onset; horsemen and car-warriors and foremost of steeds fell fast, and the car-divisions of the Pandavas began to fly away.

Arjuna, beholding the grandsire, turned in anger to the man who held the reins. "Proceed to the place where the grandsire is," he said. "It is evident that this Bhishma, with wrath excited, will annihilate my host for Duryodhana's benefit. And Drona, and Kripa, and Salya, and Vikarna, united with Dhritarashtra's sons and protected by this firm bowman, will slaughter the Panchalas. Even I, therefore, shall slay Bhishma for the sake of my troops."

Krishna's answer was a warning and a promise in one breath. "Be careful, O Dhananjaya," he said, "for I will soon take thee, O hero, towards the grandsire's car." And he took that car — the car celebrated over the world, its numerous banners waving, its steeds handsome as a flight of white cranes, the ape roaring fiercely on its standard, of solar effulgence, its rattle like the roar of clouds — and drove it straight through the Kaurava divisions and the Surasenas, slaughtering the ranks in his path. The son of Pandu came speedily to the encounter, rushing like an infuriate elephant, frightening brave combatants and felling them with his shafts. And Bhishma, protected by the warriors headed by Saindhava, by the combatants of the East, by the Sauviras and the Kekayas, met him with great impetuosity.

So the great car swept before the car of Bhishma, and the duel began. Then Bhishma, that foremost of smiters, struck Vasudeva himself — three arrows, between his two breasts. The charioteer, who had driven his friend into the teeth of the enemy, took the shafts and did not flinch, and held the car steady.

Then the arrows flew between the champions. Bhishma pierced the son of Pandu with seventy-seven arrows; Drona with twenty-five, Kripa with fifty, Duryodhana with four and sixty, Salya with nine, Drona's son with sixty, Vikarna with three, Saindhava with nine, Sakuni with five, and Artayani with three broad-headed shafts. Pierced on all sides, that great bowman wavered not, like a mountain pierced with arrows. In return the diadem-decked Arjuna pierced Bhishma with twenty-five arrows, Kripa with nine, Drona with sixty, Vikarna with three, Artayani with three, and Duryodhana with five. And Satyaki, Virata, Dhrishtadyumna of Prishata's race, the sons of Draupadi, and Abhimanyu all surrounded him in support, while the prince of the Panchalas advanced against Drona.

Then Bhishma pierced the son of Pandu with eighty sharp arrows, and the combatants on Duryodhana's side were much gratified. But Arjuna, hearing the shouts of those lions among car-warriors, entered cheerfully into their midst and sported with his bow, aiming at the mighty car-warriors one after another. And king Duryodhana, beholding his own troops afflicted in battle, turned to Bhishma and spoke. Who else save the Kuru grandsire, and Drona, and Karna, could have advanced against the bearer of Gandiva? The question hung over the field. And between the two armies, the car of solar effulgence stood where Krishna had driven it — before the grandsire's car — with three arrows still standing in the breast of the man who held the reins, who had not once turned it away.
stories.reflection: Krishna drives the car not away from the enemy but straight at the strongest bow on the field, and takes the arrows meant for the warrior — the charioteer shields the fighter with his own body. The image of the divine driver pierced between the breasts and unmoved is the story's quiet center: protection that asks nothing back.
stories.content_note: Battle scene with heavy casualties and arrow exchanges, described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Bhishma's fury was only gathering, and soon it would bring a moment when Krishna himself left the chariot.

stories.title: Stopped at the Tenth Step
stories.subtitle: Arjuna holds Krishna back from the fight
stories.story:
Krishna stepped down from the chariot in the middle of a battle, though the grandsire's shafts had already struck him that day.

The Pandavas had won the forenoon of the day. The sun had passed a portion of his westward course when Bhishma, the grandsire, bound by the dreadful vow he had sworn at Duryodhana's words, rushed with his fleetest steeds at the army of the Pandavas, protected by a large force and by all of Dhritarashtra's sons. And a battle began such as had never been seen or heard before.

The twang of bows and the flapping of bowstrings against the leathern guards made an uproar like the splitting of hills. "Stay — here I stand — know this one — turn back — stand — I wait for thee — strike": these were the words heard everywhere. Coats of mail of gold, crowns and diadems and standards fell with the sound of stones falling on stony ground, and heads and arms decked with ornaments fell by hundreds and thousands. A dreadful river of blood began to flow, impetuous, miry with flesh and blood, with the bodies of dead elephants for its rocks, running toward the ocean that is the next world, delightful to vultures and jackals. Cars could not make their way for the bodies of the slain. Some, wounded almost to death, still rushed cheerfully and proudly upon the foe; others cried aloud for father, brother, friend, and kinsman not to abandon them.

And at the heart of it moved Bhishma. With his bow drawn into a circle he shot shafts of blazing points, like snakes of virulent poison, and smote the Pandava car-warriors, naming each one beforehand. Such was the lightness of his hands that he seemed to be everywhere at once — dancing along the track of his car like a circle of fire, seen now on the east, the next moment on the west, multiplied a thousand-fold, so that every man there regarded him as having multiplied himself by illusion. No one among the Pandavas was capable of even looking at him. Kings in thousands fell upon that fire like senseless insects; with one straight shaft he despatched a single elephant as if a hill were riven by the thunderbolt; two or three elephant-riders at a time he pierced with one arrow. Whoever approached him, seen for a moment, was next beheld to fall. The vast host of Yudhishthira the just gave way in a thousand directions, trembling in the very presence of Vasudeva and the high-souled Partha.

And then — worse than Bhishma's arrows for the watching army — Krishna rose in the chariot. No one had ever seen the charioteer leave his car; the conch had always called others to war. But he had watched the host of his friends reaped before his eyes, and his wrath kindled at the sight, and he made to end it himself, stepping down from the car onto the blood-soaked earth and striding toward the grandsire.

Arjuna jumped down from his own car and ran on foot after the chief of Yadu's race, his long arms outstretched, and seized him by his two hands. It took all his strength; he succeeded, O king, in stopping him with difficulty at the tenth step. "Quell this wrath of thine," he said. "Thou art the refuge of the Pandavas, O Krishna. I swear to thee that I will not withdraw from the acts to which I have pledged myself."

Hearing that promise, Krishna was gratified. His anger left him like a held breath released. He returned to the chariot, gathered the reins, and raised the conch Panchajanya to his lips and sounded it — the long, familiar blast that carried across the field and told both armies that the war would go on, and that the charioteer was still at his post. Of all the steps Krishna ever took on that field, the tenth was the one Arjuna never forgot — the step he had not taken, because a friend had asked him not to.
stories.reflection: Arjuna's restraint of Krishna is the war's strangest reversal — the student holding back the lord, not by force but by a vow. What stops Krishna is not Arjuna's strength but his pledge not to withdraw, and that is the kind of promise that keeps a war, or a life, on its course.
stories.content_note: Battle imagery includes a river of blood and severed heads and limbs, kept at a level suitable for reading aloud.
stories.next_story_tease: The war was far from over, and Karna was still waiting for his hour.

stories.title: Let Karna Pass
stories.subtitle: Krishna holds Arjuna back from the son of Radha
stories.story:
The ruler of the Sindhus had just been slain by Arjuna when the field turned on him again.

Kripa, son of Saradwat, enraged at the fall of Jayadratha, covered Arjuna with a dense shower of arrows, and Drona's son rushed against him from his car as well. The two foremost of car-warriors poured their keen arrows upon the son of Pandu from opposite directions, and Arjuna, afflicted, felt great pain. But he had no desire to slay his preceptor — Kripa had taught him the science of arms — nor Drona's son. So he acted like a preceptor in arms himself: he baffled their weapons with his own and sped shafts that coursed mildly, not meant to kill, though their number caused great pain. Kripa lost all strength and swooned away on the terrace of his car, and his driver, believing him dead, bore him away from the fight. Drona's son, from fear, fled from the son of Pandu.

Then Arjuna, beholding his preceptor thus afflicted and senseless, began to lament on his car, his face tearful and his heart in dejection. "Alas," he said, "the words of the truth-telling Vidura have come true. On the birth of the wretched Suyodhana, that exterminator of his race, Vidura said to Dhritarashtra, 'Let this wretch of his race be soon killed; owing to him, a great calamity will overtake the foremost ones of Kuru's race.' It is for him that I behold my preceptor today lying on a bed of arrows. Fie on the practices of kshatriya! Fie on my might and prowess! Who else like me would fight with a brahmana who is besides his preceptor? Kripa is the son of a rishi; he is my preceptor; he is the dear friend of Drona. Though not wishing it, I have still been the means of crushing him with my shafts. Those who give desirable objects unto their preceptors attain to godhead; those who strike their preceptors go to hell. Without doubt, this act of mine will lead me to hell. While I studied the science of arms at his feet, Kripa told me, 'Do not ever strike thy preceptor.' That command of my righteous preceptor I have not obeyed. Fie on me, O Krishna, since I have struck even him."

While Arjuna was still lamenting, Karna, beholding the ruler of the Sindhus slain, rushed toward him. Seeing the son of Radha rushing at Arjuna, the two Panchala princes and Satyaki suddenly rushed at Karna. And Arjuna, seeing Karna advancing, smiled and said to Krishna: "Yonder comes the son of Adhiratha against the car of Satyaki. Without doubt he is unable to bear the slaughter of Bhurisravas in battle. Urge my steeds, O Krishna, toward the spot whither Karna comes. Let not Vrisha cause the Satwata hero to follow in the wake of Bhurisravas."

But Krishna replied in opportune words, holding him back. "The mighty-armed Satyaki is singly a match for Karna, O son of Pandu. How much superior, then, will this bull among the Satwatas be when he is united with the two sons of Drupada! For the present, O Arjuna, it is not proper for thee to fight with Karna. The latter hath with him the blazing dart, like a fierce meteor, that Vasava — Indra — gave him. O slayer of hostile heroes, he hath kept it for thee."

The words fell like a hand on a bowstring. Satyaki was enough; the dart was the reason. Karna had carried that meteor across the war, through every battle, spending nothing, saving it for the one enemy he meant to destroy. And Krishna, who knew what was kept and what was coming, would not let Arjuna walk into it that day.

So the chariot did not move, and Karna swept past toward Satyaki and the Panchalas — and the blazing dart stayed unspent, kept, as it had always been kept, for the man it was meant for.
stories.reflection: Krishna's counsel is pure foresight: he does not doubt Satyaki's courage, only the weapon Karna carries. He lets the fight happen on terms that cost the Pandavas nothing — and keeps Arjuna's life out of the reach of a dart that was never meant to miss.
stories.next_story_tease: But Krishna had already seen what Satyaki would need.

stories.title: A Chariot for Satyaki
stories.subtitle: Krishna lends his own car to the Satwata hero
stories.story:
Some gifts are given a day before they are needed, and only the giver knows why.

The afternoon of that battle had turned on the death of the ruler of the Sindhus. Karna, unable to bear the slaughter of Bhurisravas, had rushed toward Arjuna, and Satyaki, with the two Panchala princes, had rushed to meet him. Arjuna had wanted to drive into the fight himself; Krishna had held him back, speaking of the blazing dart that Karna kept for him. Then the field had taken its own course: the Satwata hero closed with the son of Radha, and the duel began.

What Krishna knew, he had known since before the encounter began. Janardana knows both the past and the future, and in his heart he had already seen what was coming: the heroic Satyaki would be vanquished in that fight. It was not that Krishna doubted the Satwata hero — only that morning, when Arjuna had wanted to charge into the fight himself, Krishna had said that the mighty-armed Satyaki was singly a match for Karna. But being a match was not the same as winning; the blazing dart that Karna carried changed every reckoning, and Krishna had done the only thing that could not be argued with.

And so, beforehand, he had done a strange thing. The blast of his conch had carried over the camp, and when his charioteer Daruka came, Krishna had commanded him: "Let my car be kept equipped tomorrow."

Daruka had obeyed. While the armies slept, the great car stood ready — the car that resembled the blazing fire or the sun in effulgence, the car of the friend of the Pandavas, harnessed and gleaming, its armor in place and its banners furled, waiting for a morning no one else had seen coming.

Now the hour Krishna had foreseen arrived. Satyaki's fight against Karna went against him, as it had always been going to; the Satwata hero was pressed and vanquished, his own car unable to save him. And then, across the field, came the car that had been readied for this moment: Krishna's own celestial car, guided by Daruka, blazing like fire, like the sun. With Krishna's permission, Satyaki mounted it.

Think of what that meant on a battlefield where every chariot was a fortress: the friend of the Pandavas, who had driven Arjuna through the wars, handing over his own car — the one he rode in, the one whose rattle the Kauravas had learned to fear — to a warrior who was not even one of the five brothers. He did not ask what Satyaki had done to deserve it. He had seen the fight coming, and he had prepared for it while the armies slept, quietly, as if help were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Satyaki, upon that blazing car guided by Daruka, turned again toward Karna. And the son of Radha, who had come to settle the account of Bhurisravas, found himself facing not the failing car of a tired warrior, but the car of the charioteer of the Pandavas himself, driven by Krishna's own hands' servant, gleaming like the sun over the field.

Krishna watched him go — the warrior he had armed with his own hands, in his own car, with his own driver. It was the kind of help that cannot be returned: not a weapon given, but the chariot itself, and with it the knowledge that someone had seen the danger coming long before and had already made the road ready.
stories.reflection: The gift is prepared before the need appears — the car readied and equipped while the armies slept — because Krishna knows the future without needing to see it. It is the quietest kind of divine aid: help that was already on the road, so that when Satyaki's hour came, help and need arrived together.
stories.next_story_tease: That night, when the field fell quiet, Krishna would embrace Arjuna and praise him before the army.

stories.title: This Is Your Victory, O Lord
stories.story:
Karna had stripped Bhima of his chariot, and the taunts were still ringing in his ears. Standing on the bare ground with his bow in his hand, Bhima shouted across the din to Arjuna: Karna had called him eunuch, fool, glutton, unskilled in weapons, and had done it in Arjuna's very sight. "You know the vow I made along with you," he cried. "Remember the words I spoke then. Do not let my vow, or yours, be falsified. Do what will make my vow true."

To be made carless was to be left standing on the open field, horses and driver gone, an easy mark for the next charge. And this was a day already heavy with vows. That morning Arjuna had sworn to slay Jayadratha — who had helped cut his son Abhimanyu down — before the sun set. That vow was spent: Jayadratha lay dead, and Vriddhakshatra, his father, had died with him. But now a second oath hung in the air.

Arjuna rode up to Karna, and his words came cold and exact. "You fight falsely," he said, "and you applaud yourself. A hero meets one of two things in battle, victory or defeat, and both are uncertain even when Indra himself fights. When Yuyudhana made you carless, your senses left you and you stood at the very point of death. Remembering the vow I had made to slay you, that hero dismissed you without taking your life. The truly righteous, having vanquished a foe, never boast and never speak ill of anyone. You did deprive Bhima of his car, it is true; but your abuse of him was sinful. Since you have spoken so harshly of him, and since you with others slew the son of Subhadra out of my sight, you shall reap the fruit of it this very day. I will slay Vrishasena before your eyes, and every king who advances against me I will send to Yama's abode. Accomplish now whatever you must, for a great calamity is hanging over you."

A loud and tremendous uproar rose among the car-warriors at those words. And at that frightful time, when confusion was everywhere, the thousand-rayed sun dimmed its rays and went down behind the Asta hill.

Then Krishna, stationed in the van of battle, took Arjuna in his arms. "By good luck, your great vow is accomplished," he said. "By good luck, Vriddhakshatra is slain along with his son. Even the commander of the celestial army, meeting this host of Dhritarashtra's, would lose his senses in battle — there is no doubt of it. Except you, I do not see in all the three worlds the man who could fight this force. Many royal warriors equal to you, or greater, have joined together at Duryodhana's command; clad in mail, they could not come near you, meeting your angry self in battle. Your energy and your might are equal to Rudra's, to the Destroyer's own. None else could put forth such prowess as you, alone and unsupported, put forth today. And I shall applaud you again, in the same words, when Karna of wicked soul is slain along with his followers; I shall glorify you when that enemy of yours lies vanquished."

Arjuna answered with a humility the field had seldom seen from him. "Through your grace," he said, "this vow, which even the gods could accomplish only with difficulty, has been accomplished by me. It is no wonder that those who have you for their lord win. Through your grace, Yudhishthira will obtain the whole earth. All this is your power. This is your victory, my lord. Our prosperity is your victory."

The two stood together in the van while the last light drained out of the sky — the warrior who had kept his word, and the friend who had driven him to it. The vow was spent, and the day was done. In the dark that was gathering, the war would go on.
stories.reflection: Arjuna's answer is the heart of the scene: at the peak of his powers, having done what even the gods found difficult, he gives the victory entirely to Krishna. The praise never reaches his head because he understands the deed as Krishna's — devotion carried by an act, not by adjectives.
stories.next_story_tease: As the chariot bore them back across the field, Krishna turned Arjuna's gaze to what his shafts had left behind.

stories.title: The Field of Fallen Kings
stories.story:
The chariot turned back across the field, and the wheels had to pick their way. The sun was gone. What light remained was grey and spent, and under it the plain of Kurukshetra lay covered with the work of a single day of war.

That morning the same ground had been loud — conches and war-cries, the thunder of chariot wheels, the long drums of the elephants. Now it was quiet in a way that pressed on the ears, and the quiet was its own kind of noise. Dust still hung in the air where the fighting had been thickest. A stray horse stood over its fallen rider, not knowing where to go, and here and there a chariot lay on its side. The field had become a place that answered no one.

Krishna spoke first, and as he spoke he pointed. "Desirous of victory in battle, or of world-wide fame," he said, "many heroic kings are lying on the earth, struck down by your shafts. Behold, O hero, those huge creatures, afflicted with shafts, lying on the ground in convulsions."

Arjuna followed the pointing hand. The kings lay where they had fallen — kings of great kingdoms and kings of small ones alike — each of them come to this field wanting one of two things: victory, or a fame that would outlive them. The field had settled both desires in the same dust. The great elephants and the horses lay among them, struck and struck again, still shuddering on the ground. Krishna did not hurry him past any of it. The accounting, his pointing hand seemed to say, was complete: every warrior who had ridden out that morning was being counted in the dust.

His arrows had done this from a distance, shaft after shaft loosed at moving shapes, at chariots and banners and men. From the chariot's platform it had been a task, a sequence of targets. Here, at walking pace, it wore a different shape, and Krishna was not letting him look away from it.

He did not ask why Krishna was showing him this. Perhaps he understood without asking. Victory, seen close, is not a banner raised over a field; it is a field full of the men who came to win or to be remembered. Krishna had not let him ride past it in the failing light. He had made him look at the sum of the day before the night covered it.

"This fame-enhancing and mighty feat on the field of battle," Krishna said, "is capable of being achieved by you only, O puissant one." The praise came in the same breath as the pointing, and the two belonged together in Krishna's telling: the deed and its cost, the glory and the ground it lay on. His hand moved slowly, as if the field were a text and he was teaching Arjuna to read it.

Arjuna said nothing. The wheels turned, and the chariot picked its way between the fallen. Behind them, under the grey light, the field lay like a ledger kept in the open, and Krishna had made him read every line of it. Somewhere ahead, the war was still waiting.
stories.reflection: Krishna shows Arjuna the field not to humble him but to make the victory honest: the same hand that points at the fallen kings names the deed as one only Arjuna could have done. Praise and price are held together, and that is what turns triumph into reflection.
stories.content_note: Describes a battlefield strewn with the slain, including elephants and horses; handled without gore.
stories.next_story_tease: But that night, Drona and Karna fell upon the broken Pandava host.

stories.title: Cast Away Your Fears
stories.story:
The night battle had begun with reproach. Duryodhana, watching his army die, had ridden to Karna and Drona and spoken the words that stung: this war had been set on foot by the two of them, in rage, after the ruler of the Sindhus fell to Arjuna's arrows; they were watching the slaughter of his army with indifference, though they were fully competent to vanquish it. "If you meant to abandon me," he said, "you should have told me at the beginning. You told me you two would vanquish the sons of Pandu, and I believed you. I would never have provoked these hostilities if you had told me otherwise."

Pierced by the goad of his speech, the two heroes went back into battle like snakes vexed with sticks. They rushed at the Pandavas, and the Pandavas, uniting, advanced to meet them with all their troops. Drona pierced Satyaki with ten arrows; Karna pierced him with ten more, Duryodhana with seven, Vrishasena with ten, and Suvala's son with seven, until the grandson of Sini stood walled in by the enemy. The Somakas answered by piercing Drona from every side with showers of arrows. And Drona, enraged, began to take the lives of the Kshatriyas the way the sun destroys the darkness around him with his rays.

A loud uproar rose among the Panchalas as he slaughtered them. Some abandoned their sons, some their fathers, some their brothers and uncles and kinsmen, and fled for their lives; others, out of their senses, ran straight at Drona himself. That night the Pandava host fled, throwing down their blazing torches all around, in the very sight of Bhima and Arjuna and Krishna and the twins and Yudhishthira and Dhrishtadyumna. The world was swallowed in darkness; only the light among the Kaurava troops showed where the fugitives ran. And Drona and Karna pursued the flying host, scattering shafts.

Seeing the Panchalas slaughtered and routed, Krishna grew cheerless, and he spoke to Arjuna. "Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki, with the Panchalas, went against those great bowmen Drona and Karna, shooting many shafts," he said. "This great host of ours has been broken and routed by them. Their flight is being checked, but they cannot be rallied. Seeing the host fly away through fear — you Pandava warriors, cast away your fears! With all the forces arrayed in good order, the two of us, with uplifted weapons, are even now proceeding against Drona and the son of the Suta, to withstand them."

Then Krishna saw Bhima advancing, and he spoke again, as if to gladden Arjuna. "Yonder Bhima, who delights in battle, is coming against those mighty car-warriors, Drona and Karna, surrounded by the Somakas and the Pandavas. Supported by him, and by the many mighty car-warriors among the Pandavas, fight now, son of Pandu, to assure all your troops."

The two tigers among men — the son of Pandu and he of Madhu's race — approached Drona and Karna and took their station at the head of battle. And the vast force of Yudhishthira, seeing them, turned and came back, returning to the place where Drona and Karna were grinding their foes. At dead of night a fierce encounter took place, like two oceans swelling at moon-rise. The warriors of the Kaurava host threw away the blazing lamps they held and fought the Pandavas fearlessly and madly, while the world lay under gloom and dust.

Krishna's voice had done what shouting could not: the fear went out of the Pandava host, and the night went back to being a battle. But even as the two chariots stood at the head of the field, Krishna was looking past Drona and Karna — at something else in the dark, and at a time that had not come yet.
stories.reflection: The rally works because Krishna does not shame the fleeing host; he names the fear and sets his own courage beside it. Leadership here is standing at the head of the battle with the frightened, not above them.
stories.content_note: Night battle with a routed host and heavy casualties; violence is kept restrained but parents may want to know the episode is set in the war's bloodiest stretch.
stories.next_story_tease: Yet even as the night raged, Krishna still held Arjuna back from Karna.
stories.hero_scene: In the darkness of the night battle, Krishna stands tall in the chariot, one hand raised with his bow, rallying Arjuna as the Pandava host turns back toward Drona and Karna, torches scattered and burning on the ground.

stories.title: The Time Has Not Come
stories.story:
The night had not cooled Karna. He struck Dhrishtadyumna on the chest with ten shafts that pierced to the very vitals, and the Panchala prince pierced him back with five, crying, "Wait! Wait!" The two great bowmen shrouded each other in that dreadful combat with showers of arrows, sped from bows drawn to their fullest stretch.

Then Karna despatched the driver and the four steeds of Dhrishtadyumna to Yama's abode, cut his foremost bow with keen arrows, and felled his driver from the car with a broad-headed shaft. Dhrishtadyumna, deprived of car, steeds, and driver, jumped down, seized a mace, and — though struck all the while by Karna's straight shafts — approached and slew Karna's four steeds in turn. Then he turned and climbed onto Arjuna's car, and would have gone back at Karna, but Yudhishthira bade him desist.

Karna mingled his leonine shouts with the twang of his bow and blew his conch with great force. The Panchalas and the Somakas, seeing their prince vanquished, took up every kind of weapon and rushed at him, making death itself their goal. But Karna's driver had yoked fresh steeds, white as conchs, of the Sindhu breed, well broken and swift, and Karna, sure of aim, afflicted the Panchala warriors like a cloud pouring torrents of rain on a mountain. The Panchala host fled in fear, like a doe frightened by a lion.

Horsemen fell from their horses, elephant-riders from their elephants, car-warriors from their cars, all around. With razor-faced arrows Karna cut off the arms of flying combatants and heads decked with ear-rings; he cut the thighs of men on elephants, on horseback, and on the earth. Many fled without even feeling the loss of their limbs, and in their fright they took the motion of a straw for Karna himself; deprived of their senses, they fled from their own flying friends, mistaking them for him. And Karna pursued the broken, retreating host, shooting shafts on all sides.

Then king Yudhishthira, beholding his army flying, addressed Arjuna. "Behold that mighty bowman, Karna, stationed there like Rudra armed with his bow," he said, "scorching everything around him like the blazing sun at this dead of night. These wails you hear are the cries of your helpless friends, mangled by his shafts. He aims and looses with no interval between the two acts. He will annihilate all our friends. Do now, Dhananjaya, what you judge should next be done about the slaughter of Karna, for the time may have come."

Arjuna turned to Krishna. "The son of Dharma is frightened today by the prowess of Karna," he said. "Our army is flying away, broken and mangled by Drona's shafts and frightened by Karna. I see him careering fearlessly, and I cannot bear it, like a snake that cannot put up with the tread of a man upon its body. Take me to the spot where that mighty car-warrior stands. I will either kill him — or let him slay me."

But Krishna, looking out across the field, held him back. "I behold Karna, that tiger among men, careering in battle like the chief of the celestials himself," he said. "There is none else who could stand against him. But I do not regard the time as come, O mighty-armed one, for you to encounter the son of the Suta. The blazing dart given to him by Vasava is still with him — the weapon Indra gave him, still unused. Let the mighty Ghatotkacha proceed against the son of Radha instead."

And Krishna, turning, addressed Hidimva's son. Ghatotkacha, the Rakshasa, stood in the dark like a storm waiting to be loosed. "Slay Karna in battle," Krishna told him, "at this dead of night." The command was simple. The purpose behind it was not: the dart that had been saved for Arjuna was still burning in Karna's keeping, and Krishna meant for it to be spent on Ghatotkacha before the time ever came for the two of them to meet.
stories.reflection: Krishna's refusal to let Arjuna meet Karna is strategy wearing the face of grace: he sends another to draw the weapon that was saved for his friend, so that when the time does come, Karna will face Arjuna with his one infallible dart spent. The plan protects Arjuna and asks everything of Ghatotkacha in return.
stories.content_note: Depicts Karna's night-time slaughter of fleeing warriors, including severed limbs; softened here but the episode is the war's most violent stretch.
stories.next_story_tease: But another Rakshasa, Alayudha, had come to fight beside Karna that night.

stories.title: A Detour That Was No Detour
stories.subtitle: Krishna sends Ghatotkacha against Alayudha
stories.story:
By the light of a thousand torches the night battle raged on, and in the thick of it Krishna saw something that needed correcting: Bhima, his great mace swinging, was being overwhelmed by a Rakshasa taller than his chariot.

The giant was Alayudha, brother of Vaka — the same Vaka Bhima had slain in the forest years before — and he had come to the Kaurava side with a grudge and with strength to match it. Bhima held his ground, but the fight was going out of him. Krishna, watching from his chariot, did not ride to Bhima's aid. He rode instead to Ghatotkacha.

Ghatotkacha was Bhima's own son, born of the Rakshasa woman Hidimva, and that night he was locked in combat with Karna, holding back the greatest of the Kaurava warriors. Krishna reined in beside him and spoke. "Behold, O mighty-armed one," he said, "Bhima is violently assailed by the Rakshasa in battle, in the sight of all the troops and of yourself. Abandon Karna for the present and quickly slay Alayudha. You can afterwards slay Karna."

It was an order that looked like a detour. Ghatotkacha obeyed it without a question: he broke away from Karna, turned, and met Alayudha in the middle of the field. The two Rakshasas closed with each other, and the night rang with a duel of giants such as that plain had not seen.

While they fought, the battle went on around them in its separate currents. Satyaki, Nakula, and Sahadeva drove their arrows through Alayudha's Rakshasa warriors; Arjuna, the diadem-decked, loosed shafts on every side and overthrew whole ranks of Kshatriyas. Karna, still furious at being abandoned, fell upon the Panchalas under Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandin, and Bhima, seeing his comrades cut down, rushed at him in turn. Nakula, Sahadeva, and Satyaki, their first work done, rode to join that fight, while the Panchalas turned to face Drona. Only the two Rakshasas fought alone, and the whole field seemed to pause around them.

Alayudha struck the first telling blow: a gigantic iron club crashed down on Ghatotkacha's head. The son of Bhima staggered, sat down motionless, and for a moment the watching armies thought the night was over. But he shook himself awake, seized a mace decked with gold and hung with a hundred bells, blazing like fire, and hurled it. The mace smashed through Alayudha's horses, his driver, and his loud-rattling chariot, crushing them all to pieces.

Then Alayudha did what Rakshasas do when their strength fails them: he turned to illusion. Leaping from the wreck of his car, he poured out a copious shower of blood until the sky itself seemed a mass of black clouds torn by lightning, with thunder rolling and strange cries filling the air. Ghatotkacha rose into the sky and destroyed the illusion with one of his own. Alayudha answered with a heavy shower of stones; Ghatotkacha met it with a shower of arrows. Spears, maces, swords, clubs, and battle-axes flew between them; they tore up great trees — sami and pilu and champaka, banian and peepul — and hurled mountain-summits at each other until the clash of wood and rock was like rolling thunder. Men who watched said it was like the old combat between Vali and Sugriva, the monkey kings.

At last, stripped of every weapon, the two giants rushed at each other and seized each other by the hair. Wounded and bleeding, with blood and sweat streaming down them, they looked like two mighty storm clouds pouring rain. Then Ghatotkacha whirled his enemy high overhead, dashed him down upon the earth, and cut off his great head. Lifting it by the earrings, he roared.

The Panchalas and the Pandavas answered with leonine shouts. Thousands of drums were beaten, ten thousands of conches blown, and the night — illumined with torches all around and resounding with music — declared the victory of the Pandavas. Krishna had sent Ghatotkacha to kill Alayudha, and Ghatotkacha had done it, exactly as told, before turning back to the greater fight that waited for him.
stories.reflection: Krishna's command looks like a detour — leave Karna, kill the other giant first — but it is the shortest road to the same end. Ghatotkacha is trusted not with one enemy but with the whole shape of the night's work, and he carries it out without asking why.
stories.content_note: A night battle between two Rakshasas described with restraint; ends with Alayudha beheaded, without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But Karna's infallible dart was still waiting in his quiver.
stories.hero_scene: By torchlight on the night battlefield, the giant Ghatotkacha whirls the wounded Alayudha overhead and dashes him down, while Krishna watches from his chariot and the armies pause around them.

stories.title: The Dance of the Spent Dart
stories.subtitle: Krishna rejoices while the Pandavas mourn
stories.story:
The Pandavas stood grieving over Ghatotkacha's fallen body — and Krishna danced.

The son of Bhima and Hidimva lay like a mountain riven in two, slain at last by the dart Karna had saved for Arjuna. All the Pandavas wept, and the troops, seeing their champion fall, began to fly away in panic. But Krishna, alone among them, was filled with delight. He uttered leonine shouts. He embraced Arjuna. He tied up the horses, roared aloud, and began to dance in a transport of joy, like a tree shaken by a tempest, slapping his own armpits and shouting from the terrace of the chariot.

Arjuna, whose heart was full of grief, could hardly bear the sight. "O slayer of Madhu," he said, "you show great joy at a time scarcely fit for it — an occasion for sorrow, caused by the death of Hidimva's son. Our troops are flying away, beholding Ghatotkacha slain. We too are filled with anxiety. The cause must be very grave indeed when at such a time you feel such joy. If it is not a secret, tell me truly what has removed your gravity. This lightness of heart seems to me like the drying up of the ocean, or Mount Meru itself learning to move."

Krishna's answer came without hesitation. "Great is the joy I feel," he said. "Listen, Dhananjaya, and what I tell you will dispel your sorrow and infuse delight into your heart. Know that Karna, his dart being baffled through Ghatotkacha, is already slain in battle."

And then he explained. No man existed who could stand before Karna armed with that dart, looking like Kartikeya himself in battle. With his natural armour and his ear-rings, Karna could have vanquished the three worlds single-handed — neither Indra nor Varuna nor Yama would have dared approach him. Even Arjuna bending the Gandiva, even Krishna himself uplifting the Sudarshana discus, could not have conquered him. But by good luck the armour had been taken away; by good luck the ear-rings had been taken away; and now, by good luck, the infallible dart itself was spent — through Ghatotkacha. Long ago Karna had cut off his natural armour and his brilliant ear-rings and given them to Indra in exchange for the dart, and for that he was called Vaikartana. From that day he had carried the weapon that never missed, always regarding Arjuna as already slain.

"But now," said Krishna, "that dart has slain Ghatotkacha, and it is gone. Karna is like an angry snake of virulent poison stupefied by incantation, or a fire of mild flames. Deprived of his armour, his ear-rings, and the dart given him by Vasava, he is now like a man — no longer like a god."

Yet Krishna would not let Arjuna grow careless. Even without the dart, Karna could be slain by no one else; he was devoted to Brahmanas, truthful in speech, engaged in penances, kind even to foes — that was why he was called Vrisha. Heroic as a lion, blazing like the mid-day sun, he could not be vanquished by the gods themselves, and would mangle them so that their flesh and blood would fall copiously on the field. "But there will occur one opportunity for his slaughter," Krishna said. "When his car-wheels sink in the earth, avail yourself of that opportunity and slay him in that distressful situation. I will make you a sign beforehand. Warned by it, you should act."

So the night ended with the Pandavas weeping for Ghatotkacha and Arjuna suddenly understanding: the grief and the joy were the same event. The boy who had fought so fiercely had spent the one weapon that could have killed Arjuna, and his death had bought the war. When Krishna had danced, he had danced because he saw Arjuna standing alive — and because he already saw Karna, shorn of his armour and his charm, walking toward the moment when his chariot wheel would sink into the earth.
stories.reflection: Krishna's joy is not callousness but recognition: Ghatotkacha's death has already done its work before the body has fallen. The episode shows how Krishna counts costs the Pandavas cannot yet count — and it lets Arjuna's grief stand, answered rather than erased.
stories.content_note: The episode turns on the death of Ghatotkacha, described as a fallen mountain with no graphic detail; the focus is on Krishna's unexplained joy.
stories.next_story_tease: In the same chariot, Arjuna would ask how such enemies had ever been slain.

stories.title: The Deaths Krishna Arranged
stories.subtitle: How Jarasandha, Ekalavya, and Sisupala fell
stories.story:
On the night when his own troops were fleeing, Krishna sat in the chariot and answered a question that had been pressing on Arjuna. "How, O Janardana, for our good and by what means, were those lords of the earth — Jarasandha and the others — slain?"

Krishna's answer began with what would have happened if they had lived. If Jarasandha, and the ruler of the Chedis, and the mighty son of the Nishada king had not been slain, they would have become terrible. Duryodhana would certainly have chosen them; they had always been hostile to the Pandavas, and they would all have adopted the side of the Kauravas. All of them were heroes and mighty bowmen, accomplished in weapons and firm in battle, and they would have protected Dhritarashtra's sons like the celestials themselves. With Karna and Jarasandha and the Chedi king and the Nishada's son together, they would have succeeded in conquering the whole earth. "Listen, Dhananjaya, to the means by which they were slain," Krishna said. "Without the employment of means, the very gods could not have conquered them in battle. Each of them could fight the whole celestial host protected by the Regents of the world."

Jarasandha first. Once, assailed by Balarama, he had hurled a mace capable of slaying all creatures, blazing like fire, coursing toward them like the parting line of a woman's tresses, with the impetus of Indra's thunder. Balarama met it with the weapon called Sthunakarna, and the mace, its force destroyed, fell to the earth and split her open, making the very mountains tremble. In that blow the Rakshasa woman Jara — she who had long ago joined the two halves of the child and so given him his name, Jarasandha — was slain with her son and her kinsmen. Deprived of his mace, Jarasandha was afterwards slain by Bhimasena in Arjuna's own presence. "If the valiant Jarasandha had stood armed with his mace," Krishna said, "the very gods with Indra at their head could not have slain him in battle."

Then the Nishada's son, Ekalavya. His prowess could not be baffled; he was deprived of his thumb by Drona, by an act of guile, with Drona assuming the position of his preceptor. Proud and steady, with his fingers cased in leathern gloves, he had shone like a second Rama. Undeprived of his thumb, he was incapable of being vanquished by the gods, the Danavas, the Rakshasas, and the Uragas together — a man of firm grasp, accomplished in weapons, able to shoot incessantly day and night, one at whom mere men could not look. "For your good," Krishna said simply, "he was slain by me on the field of battle."

And the ruler of the Chedis, Sisupala. He too was incapable of being vanquished by the gods and the Asuras together, and he was slain by Krishna before Arjuna's eyes. "I was born to slay him, as also the other enemies of the gods, with your assistance, from desire of benefiting the world."

Then Krishna widened the account until it took in the whole war. Hidimva and Vaka and Kirmira — Rakshasas of might equal to Ravana's, destroyers of Brahmanas and of sacrifices — had all been slain by Bhimasena. Alayudha, possessed of great powers of illusion, had been slain by Hidimva's son. And Hidimva's son himself — Ghatotkacha, whose body still lay on the field — Krishna had slain by the employment of means, through Karna with his dart. "If Karna had not slain him with his dart in the great battle, I myself would have had to slay Bhima's son Ghatotkacha. From desire of benefiting you, I did not slay him before." The Rakshasa had been inimical to Brahmanas and sacrifices; because he was a destroyer of sacrifices and of a sinful soul, he had been slain. And by that same act, the dart given by Indra had been rendered futile.

"They that are destroyers of righteousness are all slayable by me," Krishna said. "Even that is the vow made by me, for establishing righteousness. Whither the Vedas and truth and self-restraint and purity and righteousness and modesty and prosperity and wisdom and forgiveness are always to be met with, thither I myself always remain."

Then he returned to the field. "You need not be at all anxious about Karna's slaughter; I will tell you the means by which you will slay him. Vrikodara also will succeed in slaying Suyodhana." But the uproar of the hostile army was increasing, and the troops were flying away on all sides. Having achieved their objects, the chariot had to move again.
stories.reflection: Krishna's list of slain kings is also an account of his own vow: he stands wherever righteousness stands, and he will use any means — guile, a preceptor's ruse, a Rakshasa's dart — to clear the field for it. The hardest sentence is the quietest: Ghatotkacha's death was never an accident of war but a price Krishna had already agreed to pay.
stories.tradition_note: The epic's account of Ekalavya's end — a thumb taken by Drona's guile and death on the battlefield — differs from later folk retellings; this story follows the Mahabharata as excerpted in the evidence pack.
stories.content_note: Recounts the deaths of several kings and Rakshasas, all described without graphic detail; one episode involves a thumb cut off by guile.
stories.next_story_tease: Then Krishna spoke of a protection Arjuna had never known he had.

stories.title: The Protection Arjuna Never Knew
stories.subtitle: Why Karna's dart never found its mark
stories.story:
Karna had carried the dart through the whole war without once hurling it at Arjuna. Krishna, speaking to Satyaki as the night's uproar died down, finally explained why.

Everyone knew the dart. Indra had given it to Karna long ago, in exchange for the natural armour that grew from his body and the ear-rings that were part of it — and from that day it had been meant for Arjuna. It was the weapon that never failed, the one thing that could end the war in a single stroke. Karna had kept it through every battle, waiting for the moment when Arjuna would come within reach. That moment had come many times. And every time, something had gone wrong.

"I, however, O foremost of warriors," Krishna said to Satyaki, "always used to stupefy the son of Radha. It was for this that he did not hurl the dart at Pandu's son."

That was the whole secret: not armour, not luck, not a vow. Whenever Karna's hand closed on the dart and his eyes found Arjuna, Krishna clouded his mind, and the moment slipped away. The perfect weapon waited in its quiver while its owner's thoughts wandered, and the danger passed before anyone on the Pandava side even knew it had come. That was the protection — invisible, unfelt, working in the instant between the drawing of a bow and the loosing of an arrow.

And then Krishna went further, and said something that had no strategy in it at all. "I do not regard my sire, my mother, yourselves, my brothers — ay, my very life — so worthy of protection as Vibhatsu in battle."

His father. His mother. His brothers. His own life. He set Arjuna above all of them. Satyaki heard the words and understood, at last, why Krishna had danced on the chariot while the whole army wept: not because he was unmoved by Ghatotkacha, but because he had seen Dhananjaya, like one returned from the dead, still standing alive on the field. "Beholding Dhananjaya, therefore, like one returned from the dead," Krishna said, "these transports of delight, O Yuyudhana, have seized me."

The night made sense then as one long act of protection. Karna had been stupefied at every critical moment, so that the dart that could have killed Arjuna was held back until the one night it was spent on another — spent, through Ghatotkacha, and gone forever. The armour, the ear-rings, the dart: each had been stripped away in its turn, and the last of the three had been taken from Karna's hands on the night Krishna had chosen. Arjuna had never known how close the war had come to ending in a single instant, because the danger had never been allowed to arrive.

On the dark field, with the enemy's uproar growing and the troops still scattered, Krishna sat in the chariot with Arjuna alive beside him. He had protected what he valued most in the world, by means no one could see, at a cost he had already counted. And somewhere on the battlefield, Karna still carried his bow, not yet knowing that the weapon he trusted was gone — and that he himself, stripped of armour and charm, had become mortal at last.
stories.reflection: Krishna's protection of Arjuna is almost invisible: it works by clouding Karna's mind at the exact instant of the throw, so the danger dissolves before anyone knows it existed. His confession to Satyaki — Arjuna above father, mother, brothers, his own life — turns the night's strategy into a statement of love.
stories.next_story_tease: Dawn would bring its own griefs, and Krishna would console the eldest Pandava.
stories.hero_scene: On the dark battlefield, Krishna sits in the chariot with Arjuna alive beside him, while in the distance the faint figure of Karna stands at his chariot, one hand resting on the spent quiver that no longer holds the dart.

stories.title: Rise, O King, and Fight
stories.subtitle: Krishna consoles the grieving Yudhishthira
stories.story:
The dart that Karna had carried through the war like a held breath was gone. It had been saved, all those months, for Krishna or for Arjuna — a weapon that could slay any one person in battle and that not even the gods could bear or baffle. And it had been spent, in the darkness of that night, on Ghatotkacha, the son of Bhima and the rakshasa princess Hidimba — a death that Dhritarashtra would later call as insignificant as the crushing of straw.

Now the Kaurava troops, filled with joy at the slaughter of the rakshasa, raised loud shouts in the black hour of night and fell impetuously upon the Pandava ranks. King Yudhishthira watched the field begin to give way, and something in him gave way too. He turned to Bhima. "Resist the Dhartarashtra host," he said, "for in consequence of the slaughter of Hidimba's son, a great stupefaction overwhelms me." Having ordered Bhimasena thus, he sat down on his car. With a tearful face and sighing repeatedly, the king who had borne exile and loss without flinching sat staring at Karna's prowess, utterly cheerless.

Beholding him so afflicted, Krishna spoke. "O son of Kunti, let not such grief be thine. Such cheerlessness does not become thee, O chief of the Bharatas, as it does an ordinary person. Rise, O king, and fight. Bear the heavy burden, O lord! If cheerlessness overtakes thee, our victory becomes uncertain."

The words reached the king through the noise of the night, and he wiped his eyes with his hands and answered. The excellent path of duty was not unknown to him, he said. Then he spoke of Ghatotkacha. While the Pandavas lived in the woods, the high-souled son of Hidimba — then a mere child — had done them many services. When Arjuna had departed for the acquisition of weapons, Ghatotkacha had come to him at Kamyaka and dwelt with them until Dhananjaya's reappearance. Over many inaccessible fastnesses he had carried on his back the tired princess of Panchala. The feats he achieved showed that he was skilled in all modes of warfare; the high-souled one had accomplished many difficult feats for the king's benefit. "My affection for Ghatotkacha," Yudhishthira said, "is twice that which I naturally bear towards Sahadeva. That mighty-armed one was devoted to me. I was dear to him and he was dear to me. It is for this that, scorched by grief, O thou of Vrishni's race, I have become so cheerless. Behold our troops afflicted and routed by the Kauravas. Behold those mighty car-warriors broken before Karna's shafts."

His voice broke off, and the night held its silence. All around them the battle pressed on — Karna's shafts still darkening the air, the Pandava host still reeling from the shock of the rakshasa's fall — but in that circle of the chariot there was only the king's grief and the charioteer who had come to answer it. Krishna had not asked the king to forget. He had asked him to stand, to bear the heavy burden, to keep the victory from becoming uncertain. So he waited, letting the grief speak itself out, for he knew the king's love for the dead boy was not something to be argued away. The war did not stop for Yudhishthira's sorrow; the Kaurava shouts still rang across the dark field, and the Pandava line still had to hold. But the counsel had been spoken — cheerlessness becomes not the chief of the Bharatas — and the king who had wiped his eyes with his own hands had answered with the weight of his love rather than with despair. That, in the dark of that night, was the first step of bearing the burden again.
stories.reflection: Krishna does not belittle the king's grief; he refuses to let it become despair. Yudhishthira's answer matters because he does not deny his sorrow — he measures it openly, weighing Ghatotkacha's services against his own duty — and that honest accounting is what lets him stand again.
stories.next_story_tease: But on the field where the night was still loud, Krishna had already begun to think of other means against Drona.

stories.title: The Ashvatthama Stratagem
stories.story:
Drona was cutting through the Pandava army, and nothing could stand before him. The Panchalas and the Srinjayas rushed at him in waves, yelling loud and fierce as they came, and his shafts and darts struck them down as fast as they arrived. They were mighty car-warriors, full of might and energy, and though he slaughtered them they were not yet afraid of him; still they came on, and still they fell. The carnage of steeds and men went on like the slaughter of the gods' enemies in some older age, and the sons of Kunti, afflicted with his shafts, felt fear enter their hearts and hope drain out of them. Drona alone seemed enough to undo them all. The day was theirs to lose, and Drona was taking it from them hour by hour.

"He will consume us all," they said to one another, "like a raging fire eating a heap of straw in the season of spring. There is no one who can even look at him in battle. And Arjuna — the one man who is a match for him — will not fight him." For Drona, conversant with the mightiest of weapons, had been Arjuna's own teacher, and Arjuna, who knew the ways of morality, would not raise his bow against the man who had taught him the bow.

It was Krishna who answered their despair — Krishna, endued with great intelligence and devoted to their welfare. "This foremost of all bowmen cannot be vanquished by force," he said, "not even by the gods with Indra at their head. But when he lays aside his weapons, he can be slain even by men. Cast aside virtue, sons of Pandu, and find some contrivance, before Drona of the golden car destroys us all. When his son Ashvatthaman has fallen, he will cease to fight. Let some man tell him that Ashvatthaman has been slain."

It was not the kind of counsel the brothers had expected from him, and it landed among them like a stone thrown into still water. Arjuna would not approve it; he heard the plan and rejected it. Others approved it. And Yudhishthira — the eldest, the one whose word was truth itself — accepted it only with the greatest difficulty. To save his brothers, he would have to become, for a little while, the instrument of a falsehood, and he agreed to carry it. It was the hardest thing he had yet agreed to in the whole war, and he accepted it with his head bowed.

So it was done, in a way that cut the truth down the middle. Bhima, the mighty-armed, took up his mace and slew a huge, terrible, foe-crushing elephant named Ashvatthaman, one that belonged to their own army, to Indravarman, the chief of the Malavas — their own war-elephant, struck down by their own mace, not to win any fight but to make a single sentence true. Then he approached Drona in the midst of the battle, and with some bashfulness cried aloud, "Ashvatthaman has been slain."

The words were true of the elephant that lay dead behind them. They were spoken to a father who would hear them as his son. There is a difference between a lie and a truth told to deceive, and the whole weight of that difference sat in Bhima's voice. Drona had heard a thousand war-cries that day and never once turned from his work, but this one name, spoken low, would do what no weapon on the field could. On the width of a name shared between a man and a beast, the whole battle was about to turn.
stories.reflection: The man who taught Arjuna the way of dharma on this same field now counsels him to lay that virtue aside, and the text refuses to smooth it over: Arjuna rejects the plan, Yudhishthira accepts it only with great difficulty, and the lie is built out of something technically true. The episode leaves the reader standing in exactly that discomfort, without a verdict.
stories.content_note: Battle violence and a wartime deception.
stories.next_story_tease: The battle did not end with Drona; ahead waited Karna, and an arrow meant for Arjuna alone.
stories.hero_scene: In the dust and noise of the battlefield, Bhima lowers his mace beside the fallen elephant named Ashvatthaman while, at a distance, the chariot of the aged Drona waits as the words of his son's death are carried toward him.

stories.title: The Untruth That Was Nearly True
stories.subtitle: Krishna urges Yudhishthira to speak the lie that would stop Drona
stories.story:
Drona came on like a springtime fire through dry straw, and no one could stand before him. The preceptor of both armies, wrathful at the slaughter of Bhurishravas and Jayadratha, had turned his full fury upon the Panchalas and the Srinjayas. He slew them with shafts and darts; the great car-warriors of the Pandava army rushed at him again and again and were cut down, and the earth grew miry with flesh and blood. Fear entered the hearts of the Pandavas, and they despaired of victory. There was none competent to even look at him in battle, and Arjuna — the one man who was his match — would not fight his teacher, for he was conversant with the ways of morality.

Beholding the sons of Kunti afflicted and afraid, Krishna, devoted to their welfare, spoke. This foremost of all bowmen, he said, was incapable of being vanquished by force in battle, not even by the very gods with Vasava at their head. But when he lays aside his weapons, he becomes capable of being slain on the field even by human beings. "Casting aside virtue, ye sons of Pandu, adopt now some contrivance for gaining the victory, so that Drona of the golden car may not slay us all in battle. Upon the fall of his son Ashvatthama he will cease to fight, I think. Let some man, therefore, tell him that Ashvatthama hath been slain in battle."

To Yudhishthira, the truth-loving king, Krishna said it even more plainly: "If Drona fighteth, filled with rage, for even half-a-day, I tell thee truly, thy army will then be annihilated. Save us, then, from Drona. Under such circumstances, falsehood is better than truth."

The advice was not approved by Arjuna. Others approved of it. But Yudhishthira — Dharma's son, whose whole life had been the keeping of his word — accepted it with great difficulty.

Then the mighty-armed Bhima slew with his mace a foe-crushing, terrible and huge elephant of their own army, one named Ashvatthama, that belonged to Indravarman, the chief of the Malavas. It was a beast built for the front of a charge, and its fall shook the ground where it stood. And approaching Drona in that battle with some bashfulness, Bhimasena began to exclaim aloud, "Ashvatthama hath been slain!" The words carried across the field to where the preceptor fought, and Bhima, keeping the true fact within his mind, said what was untrue.

Hearing those highly disagreeable words, Drona's limbs seemed to dissolve like sands in water. But recollecting the prowess of his son, he soon came to regard the intelligence as false, and recovering his senses he was comforted, remembering that his son was incapable of being resisted by foes. Rushing towards Dhrishtadyumna, the son of Prishata, he covered him with a thousand keen shafts, and twenty thousand Panchala car-warriors covered him in turn. Then, filled with wrath, Drona invoked the Brahma weapon, and he looked resplendent like a smokeless, blazing fire. He felled the heads of the Panchalas and cut off their massive arms, decked with golden ornaments, and the Kshatriyas lay scattered like trees uprooted by the tempest. He slew twenty thousand Panchala car-warriors, cut off the head of Vasudana with a broad-headed arrow, slew five hundred Matsyas and six thousand elephants and ten thousand steeds.

The lie that was meant to end him had only fed his fury. Beholding Drona stationed on the field as if for the extermination of the Kshatriya race, the Rishis — Viswamitra, Jamadagni, Bharadwaja, Gautama, Vasishtha, Kasyapa, Atri — gathered to look upon him, and even they could not turn the great teacher from his course.
stories.reflection: The half-truth is told with almost unbearable care: Bhima keeps the true fact within his mind, Yudhishthira accepts the plan only with great difficulty, and Arjuna refuses it outright. What the episode makes visible is the cost of the lie — Drona's doubt lasts only a moment, and the deception that was meant to disarm him releases instead his full, terrible power.
stories.content_note: Depicts the heavy carnage of Drona's onslaught (described with restraint) and the moral cost of the Ashvatthama deception; may warrant parental awareness for younger children.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's stratagem had not ended Drona's fury, and on the other side of the field Karna was already tearing the Pandava divisions apart.
stories.hero_scene: Before the towering, blazing figure of Drona on his golden car, Bhima calls out with downcast, bashful face the words 'Ashvatthama is slain,' while behind him the huge slain elephant lies on the miry field and Krishna watches from the Pandava chariot.

stories.title: The Field Seen From Krishna's Chariot
stories.subtitle: Krishna points out Karna's rampage and urges Arjuna forward
stories.story:
From the chariot where the two of them stood, Krishna showed Arjuna the field as only he could see it. "Yonder," he said, pointing, "your brother Yudhishthira is being pursued by many mighty and great bowmen of the Dhartarashtras, all inspired with the desire of slaughtering him. The mighty Panchalas, difficult of defeat in battle, are proceeding after the high-souled king from desire of rescuing him."

Arjuna looked, and Krishna went on, reading the confusion of the battle like a text. Duryodhana himself, the king of the whole world, clad in mail and accompanied by a large car force, was pursuing the Pandava king, together with his brothers, the touch of whose weapons was as fatal as that of poisonous snakes. The Dhartarashtra elephants and horses and car-warriors and foot-soldiers were advancing to seize Yudhishthira like poor men after a precious gem. They had been checked for a moment by Satyaki and Bhima, stupefied like the Daityas that desired to take away the Amrita, made motionless by Sakra and Agni. But in consequence of the vastness of their numbers they were again proceeding towards the king, like a vast quantity of water in the season of rains rushing towards the ocean, uttering leonine roars, blowing their conchs, and shaking their bows.

"I regard Kunti's son Yudhishthira," Krishna said, "thus brought under the influence of Duryodhana, to be already within the jaws of Death, or already poured as a libation on the sacrificial fire." The army of Dhritarashtra's son was arrayed and equipped duly; Sakra himself, coming within the range of its arrows, could scarcely escape. Who, in battle, could bear the impetuosity of the heroic Duryodhana, who shot showers of arrows with the greatest celerity and who, when angry, resembled the Destroyer himself? The force of Duryodhana's shafts, or Drona's son's, or Kripa's, or Karna's, would break down the very mountains.

And then Krishna came to what he had been leading towards all along. That scorcher of foes, king Yudhishthira, had once been compelled by Karna to turn his back upon the field. The son of Radha was endued with great might and great lightness of hand; possessed of great skill, he was competent to afflict the eldest son of Pandu, especially when united with the mighty and brave son of Dhritarashtra. The king was exceedingly emaciated in consequence of his fasts; he was endued with Brahma-force, but the puissant one was not endued with much of Kshatriya-might. Assailed by Karna, the royal son of Pandu had been placed in a situation of great peril. "I think, O Partha, that king Yudhishthira has fallen," Krishna said. "Indeed, since that chastiser of foes, the wrathful Bhimasena, coolly heareth the leonine roars of the frequently shouting Dhartarashtras longing for victory and blowing their conchs, I think, O bull among men, that Pandu's son is dead."

Yonder, Krishna pointed, Karna was urging forward the mighty car-warriors of the Dhartarashtras towards the son of Pritha with the weapons called Sthunakarna, Indrasjaha and Pasupata, and with clubs and other weapons. The king's standard was no longer visible; it had probably been struck down by Karna with his shafts. In the very sight of the twins, of Satyaki and Shikhandi, of Dhrishtadyumna and Bhima and Satanika, of all the Panchalas and the Cedis, Karna was destroying the Pandava division with his arrows, like an elephant destroying an assemblage of lotuses. There, those car-warriors of Arjuna's army were flying away; those elephants, assailed by Karna, were flying in all directions, uttering cries of pain. The foremost standard of the Suta's son, bearing the device of the elephant's rope, moved all over the field, and there the son of Radha was rushing against Bhimasena, scattering hundreds of shafts as he proceeded and slaughtering the army, routing the Panchala car-warriors even as the Daityas had been routed by Sakra.

"Righteously setting thy heart on battle," Krishna said, "advance against that leader of car-warriors."
stories.reflection: Krishna's words do not merely report the battle; they arrange it — first the pursued king, then the overwhelming numbers, then Karna's particular menace — until Arjuna can see with his charioteer's eyes that hesitation has become the only real enemy. The urgency is built entirely from what is visible on the field, not from exhortation.
stories.next_story_tease: But before Arjuna could advance, the field rose up against him in the person of Drona's son.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna, standing in the chariot beside Arjuna, points across the battlefield towards the distant figure of king Yudhishthira, while on the far side Karna's standard bearing the elephant's rope moves over the field, scattering the Pandava division like an elephant destroying an assemblage of lotuses.

stories.title: Comfort the King First
stories.subtitle: Krishna advises Arjuna to see the wounded Yudhishthira before facing Karna
stories.story:
Before Arjuna could advance against Karna, the field put another enemy in his path. Drona's son Ashvatthama, surrounded by a large car-force, suddenly proceeded to the spot where Partha was. Like a continent withstanding the surging ocean, the heroic Partha, with Krishna at his side, withstood the impetuously rushing Ashvatthama. Then the valiant son of Drona, filled with rage, covered both Arjuna and Vasudeva with his shafts, and the warriors who witnessed the two Krishnas shrouded with arrows wondered exceedingly.

Arjuna, as if smiling, invoked a celestial weapon; the brahmana Ashvatthama baffled it. All the weapons that Arjuna sped from desire of slaying the son of Drona were baffled by that great bowman. During that awful encounter the son of Drona resembled the Destroyer himself with gaping mouth. Having covered all the points of the compass, cardinal and subsidiary, with straight arrows, he pierced Vasudeva with three arrows in the right arm.

Then Arjuna, slaying all the steeds of his high-souled assailant, covered the earth with a river of blood; the car-warriors of Ashvatthama's division were slain and destroyed by the arrows sped from Partha's bow. Ashvatthama in turn caused a terrible river of blood to flow to Yama's domains. The two fought without showing any regard for one another, rushing hither and thither. Ashvatthama approached Arjuna, shook his formidable bow decked with gold, and pierced him from every side with many sharp arrows, and once more bent his bow and struck Arjuna cruelly at the chest with a winged arrow. Deeply pierced, the wielder of Gandiva forcibly covered the son of Drona with showers of arrows and cut off his bow. Taking up a spiked mace whose touch resembled that of thunder, Ashvatthama hurled it at the diadem-decked Arjuna; the son of Pandu, as if smiling the while, suddenly cut off the mace as it advanced, and it fell to the earth like a mountain broken by the thunderbolt.

Filled with rage, Drona's son covered Vibhatsu with the Aindra weapon, a shower of arrows spread over the welkin. Partha, taking up Gandiva and fixing on his bowstring a mighty weapon created by Indra, destroyed that arrowy shower and covered the car of Drona's son with his own shafts. Through that shower of arrows the son of Drona penetrated, and approaching Arjuna invoked a mighty weapon and pierced Krishna with a hundred shafts and Arjuna with three hundred small arrows. Then Arjuna pierced the son of his preceptor with a hundred arrows in all his vital limbs, poured arrows on his steeds and driver and bowstring, and felled his adversary's driver with a broad-headed arrow. Drona's son, himself taking up the reins, covered Krishna with many arrows, guiding his steeds while he fought with Phalguni — a feat of activity and prowess that all the warriors applauded. Then Vibhatsu, otherwise called Jaya, smiling the while, quickly cut off the traces of Ashvatthama's steeds with a razor-faced arrow, and the steeds of Drona's son ran away, and a loud noise arose from the troops.

The duel was over. The field that had been a storm around them fell suddenly quiet, and the two Krishnas stood together on the car, the charioteer's right arm still marked by Ashvatthama's arrows. Arjuna, his bow still humming, turned to Krishna — and asked, as the field around him demanded, to be taken against Karna, who had done this to their army and their king, whose standard with the elephant's rope still moved yonder over the host. But Krishna answered: "The royal son of Kunti hath been deeply wounded and mangled by Karna. Having seen him first and comforted him, thou wilt then, O Partha, slay Karna."
stories.reflection: The order is revealing: Krishna does not deny Arjuna the duel with Karna — he only insists that the wounded king comes first. In the middle of the war's worst carnage, the charioteer's counsel is still that the brothers should see each other's faces before the last great battle is joined.
stories.content_note: Depicts the intense single combat between Arjuna and Ashvatthama, including arrow wounds to Krishna; described with restraint and no gore.
stories.next_story_tease: And Krishna, taking up the reins, drove Arjuna straight to the side of the wounded king.
stories.hero_scene: On the battlefield, Arjuna and Krishna stand together in the chariot — Krishna with three arrows piercing his right arm — while Ashvatthama's riderless, trace-cut steeds bolt away across the field, and beyond them the distant standard of Karna moves over the host.
