stories.title: Krishna Drives Arjuna to Yudhishthira's Side
stories.story:
The battle had just given Arjuna a feat few warriors could claim — victory over the son of Drona — and he should have been the happiest man on the field. Instead he stood in his chariot, bow still outspread in his hands, and searched his own troops for a face he could not find.

Yudhishthira was gone.

Arjuna turned his car toward Bhima. "Tell me, where is the king?" Bhima's answer was blunt: King Yudhishthira had left the field, his limbs scorched by Karna's shafts, and whether he still lived was doubtful.

The words struck Arjuna like a blow. He remembered how the king, though deeply pierced by Drona's arrows, had stayed in the battle, expecting victory, until Drona himself was slain. Now Karna had done what Drona could not, and driven the king from the field, wounded and alone. "Without doubt he has gone to the camp," Arjuna said. "Go quickly, Bhima, and bring me news of him. I will stay here and hold back all our foes."

Bhima shook his head. "Go yourself, Arjuna. If I leave now, every hero on this field will say I ran from the battle." Arjuna gestured at the ranks before his division. "The samsaptakas stand in my way. I cannot stir until they are slain." Then Bhima did what only Bhima could promise: "Rely on my strength. I will fight all the samsaptakas myself. You go, Dhananjaya, and see the king."

So Arjuna, surrounded by enemies, turned to the one who held the reins and asked for the one thing he had never asked before — to be taken out of the battle. "Urge the steeds, O Hrishikesha," he said. "Leave this sea of troops. I desire to see king Ajatasatru."

Krishna looked at Bhima, and his voice carried the warmth of a man who had watched these brothers all their lives. "This feat is not at all wonderful for you, Bhima. I am about to go. Slay these assembled foes of Partha."

Then he shook the reins.

The chariot flew. The horses, swift as Garuda himself, carried Krishna and Arjuna across the field at a speed that turned the sea of war into a blur — past the standards, past the shouting, past the last scattered fights — until the noise fell away and the chariot drew up beside a quiet place where a king lay alone on his bed.

Yudhishthira lay there, the marks of Karna's shafts upon him, alone as a man is alone when he has sent his brothers into danger and paid for it with his own body. And then the two of them — the one who held the reins and the one who drew the bow, the pair the old text calls the two Krishnas — stepped down from the chariot.

They did not stand at a distance. They did not wait to be greeted. Krishna and Arjuna walked to the king's bed, and both of them worshipped his feet.

That is the picture the old text leaves us: the charioteer of the war, the one who had guided every battle, bowing to the man who had carried the war's heaviest weight. Seeing the king safe and sound, the two were filled with joy, like men who had braced for the worst and found the one they loved alive.

The king raised his head, and his voice was choked with delight. He believed Karna had fallen. He believed the war had turned at last, and he congratulated them both as a man congratulates those who have done the impossible.

He was wrong. But for that moment, on the bed where he lay wounded, the king was happy.
stories.reflection: Krishna, who held the reins through every battle of the war, steps down to worship the feet of the wounded king — reverence flowing upward, not downward. The moment marks the war's real hierarchy: the one who guided it honours the one who carried it.
stories.next_story_tease: But the king rejoiced too soon — Karna was still on the field, and the worst of the day lay ahead.
stories.hero_scene: On the quiet edge of the battlefield, Krishna and Arjuna — the two Krishnas — step down from the chariot and bow to worship the feet of Yudhishthira as he lies wounded on his bed, while the war's noise fades behind them.

stories.title: Krishna Offers Sudarsana to Slay Karna
stories.story:
The two champions were alike in the way of two mountains: both white-steeded, both at the height of their power, and now they came together in the duel the whole war had been building toward. Arjuna and Karna met like two infuriated elephants of full-grown tusks fighting for a she-elephant in her season, and the field trembled.

Like a mass of clouds meeting another mass, or a mountain meeting a mountain, they poured showers of arrows at each other — their bows twanging, their bow-strings and palms ringing, the wheels of their cars clattering — while the armies of both sides watched in silence. Karna struck first, piercing Arjuna with ten mighty shafts; Arjuna answered with ten of his own, driven into the centre of Karna's chest. The fight left nothing unhurt: the limbs of the two heroes, of their charioteers, of their horses, were mangled, and the blood ran like a river whose water no one would drink.

Arjuna rubbed his two arms and the string of Gandiva, and then the arrows came in floods. He sped cloth-yard shafts, nalikas, arrows headed like a boar's ear, razors, anjalikas, crescent-headed arrows — and they filled the sky like birds coming home to roost in the evening. Every one of them, every successive shower, Karna cut off with his own arrows.

Both armies, and the beings gathered in the welkin, were struck with fear at the sight of that wonderful encounter; and some among the spectators, filled with joy, raised their arms and uttered leonine shouts, waving their fingers and the cloths they held, whenever Arjuna rushed against the son of Adhiratha.

The duel went on until the sun itself seemed to disappear. Arjuna, furious now, drew Gandiva and loosed a weapon of fire — a blazing thing that covered the earth, the welkin, and the ten points of the compass, that hid the very course of the sun and set his own body alight with its glow. The robes of the watching warriors caught fire and they fled, and the sky roared like a bamboo forest burning.

Karna did not flinch. He answered with the weapon of the waters, the varunastra, and great clouds, dark as mountains, gathered on every side and flooded the field. The conflagration, fierce as it was, was quenched in a trice.

The two looked at each other across the wreckage of their arrows, and the armies of both sides shouted — the Somakas urging Arjuna to pierce Karna and cut off his head, the Kauravas urging Karna to slay Arjuna and send the sons of Pritha back to the woods forever.

It was Krishna who broke the silence. He had watched every exchange from the driver's seat of the chariot, and now his patience ran out. "What is this, O diadem-decked Arjuna," he said, "that Karna should succeed in crushing your weapons today?"

The calm of the charioteer had become the wrath of a friend who had watched enough. Krishna held out his hand, and in it turned the Sudarsana — the discus, its edge keen as a razor, the weapon that had felled demons and kings. "Putting forth your might," he said, "strike off the head of this foe of yours with this Sudarsana that I give you — as Indra struck off the head of his foe Namuci with the thunderbolt."

The discus blazed in the air between them, offered like an answer to a question no one had dared to ask. Through every battle of the war, Krishna had held nothing but the reins; now he offered his own weapon, and the duel hung, waiting.
stories.reflection: Krishna, who came to the war holding nothing but reins, offers his own discus at the moment Arjuna's weapons fail — the wrath of a friend who has watched enough. The offer measures what the war has cost even the one who never lifted a weapon in it.
stories.content_note: Fierce single combat with showers of arrows and a blazing weapon; blood is mentioned without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: But the duel was not to be settled by the discus, and the earth itself would soon swallow the chariot's wheels.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna stands in the chariot holding out the blazing Sudarsana discus to Arjuna, whose exhausted bow-arm hangs low, while Karna's distant chariot waits amid the wreckage of arrows on the darkened field.

stories.title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot
stories.story:
The duel Karna and Arjuna had been waiting for all their lives came at last, and for a long time no one could say who was winning. Everything hung on this duel, and both armies knew it. Arjuna's weapon had been swelling with energy and careering through the sky like lightning, consuming the Kauravas, and the broken divisions of their army had drawn back to a distance to watch it — until Karna crushed it with shafts winged with gold, using the great foe-killing weapon he had obtained from Rama, and turned it back. Then he bent his own loud-sounding bow, whose string could not be broken, and sent showers of shafts that pierced Arjuna again and again.

So the two of them closed with each other, and the sky went dark. They struck like two fierce elephants locking tusks. The points of the compass vanished behind their weapons, and the sun itself disappeared beneath the downpour of arrows, until the whole welkin was one vast web of shafts with no space between. The men watching from both armies could see nothing but arrows, and no one on either side could tell where the next one would come from. Two warriors, both accomplished in the use of weapons, wove every kind of beautiful manoeuvre, each of them watching for the other's single lapse — the one opening that would end it.

Now the son of the charioteer would press his rival back, now the diademed Arjuna would drive him in turn. The beings gathered in the sky shouted first "Excellent, O Karna!" and then "Excellent, O Arjuna!" while the earth was pressed deep beneath the weight of the cars and the trampling of steeds and elephants. It was a passage of arms so dreadful that the other warriors on the field could only stand and wonder.

And in that darkness of arrows, something else was waiting for its opening too. The snake Aswasena had long been hostile to Arjuna, and he had been sheltering in the arrow-net above the field, biding his time. Now he let himself be fitted to a shaft, and Karna, bending his loud-sounding bow, loosed him at Arjuna's head.

The shaft blazed as it flew through the welkin, alive and burning, aimed to end the duel at a stroke.

Krishna saw it coming — the way a man who has driven a thousand chariots sees the one arrow among ten thousand that matters.

With great speed and the greatest ease, he pressed down the chariot with his feet. The excellent car sank about a cubit into the earth, and the white steeds, white as the rays of the moon, bent their knees and laid themselves down on the ground.

The burning arrow passed low over Arjuna's head, close enough to graze it — and swept away only his diadem.

The crown fell to the earth, and the man who had worn it was still standing. The diadem was the mark by which the whole field knew Arjuna, and Karna's deadliest shaft had torn it from his head and left the head itself untouched. It had met a charioteer who would sink the very ground beneath his friend to keep that head upon his shoulders. In the middle of the greatest battle the world had ever seen, the moment that saved Arjuna came down to a man setting his feet a cubit deeper into the earth. The chariot rose again, the moon-white horses came back to their feet, and the duel went on — but the opening had passed, and it had passed because of the man holding the reins. Krishna had raised no weapon that day. He had not needed one.
stories.reflection: The episode makes Krishna's loyalty literal: he is not fighting, not speaking, only driving, and yet the whole outcome turns on his feet pressing a chariot into the earth. The divine protection here is not a weapon or a miracle of light but a quick, precise act of a charioteer who will not let his friend be taken.
stories.content_note: Battle violence; an arrow narrowly misses Arjuna.
stories.next_story_tease: But the duel between Karna and Arjuna was not yet decided.

stories.title: Krishna Identifies the Snake Aswasena
stories.subtitle: The snake of Khandava returns as Karna's arrow
stories.story:
The broken divisions of the Kauravas had fled before the falling of Arjuna's arrows, and now they stood at a distance, gazing at the weapon that careered around the field with the effulgence of lightning. Karna and Arjuna struck each other like two fierce elephants striking with their tusks; their arrows met in mid-air until the sun was invisible and the welkin was one vast expanse of shafts with no space between. All the warriors on the field watched with wonder, and the beings of the sky applauded, crying now "Excellent, O Karna!" and now "Excellent, O Arjuna!"

Karna had already baffled the burning weapon Arjuna loosed at him, crushing it with showers of shafts and destroying it with the foe-killing weapon he had received from Rama, a thing like an Atharvan rite. But his own wounds were many. Scorched by Arjuna's arrows, his limbs mangled, Karna found he could not prevail — and in that hour he reached for the one shaft he had kept for years, lying alone in its quiver.

He did not know what it was. No one on the field knew.

For there was a snake beneath the earth who had been waiting for this day. His name was Aswasena, and his hatred of Arjuna was older than the war. Years before, when Arjuna fought for the god Agni in the burning of the Khandava forest, Aswasena had been in the sky, hidden within his mother's body. Arjuna's arrow slew the mother. The son escaped the conflagration, pierced the earth in his fury, and hid in the nether region, nursing the death of his mother and the enmity it planted in him. Now, beholding the fight between Karna and Arjuna, he rose from the lower world, soared up on the power that let him climb the skies, and slipped into Karna's quiver — a living snake in the form of an arrow.

When Karna set his heart on the single shaft and lifted it out, it was a snake-mouthed arrow, blazing and fierce, that he strung: the weapon he had long kept for Partha's destruction, born of the serpent race, polished according to rule and kept in a golden quiver amid sandal dust. He drew it to his ear and aimed it at the head of Phalguna.

And in that instant the Regents of the world raised their voices and wailed — Sakra himself among them, and the guardians of the directions — for they saw what no man on the field could see.

Fatigued with their exertions, the two heroes looked at each other, fanned by apsaras in the sky with waving fans of young palm leaves sprinkled with fragrant sandal-water, while Sakra and Surya themselves gently brushed the faces of the two warriors. The chariot stood sunk in the earth, where Krishna had pressed it down in the moment the arrow flew. And Krishna, who had seen everything from the first, spoke. "While you, armed with your bow, were engaged at Khandava in gratifying the god Agni," he said, "this snake was in the sky, his body hidden within his mother's. You slew her. He escaped the flames, and remembering that act of hostility, he comes toward you today for your destruction."

He named him: Aswasena.

Then Krishna bade Arjuna slay the snake, and Arjuna did not ask how. The shaft that Karna had loosed was met and cut down, the snake cut off, the vengeance of Khandava ended on the field of Kurukshetra.

Afterward, when the sky was clear again and the duel stood still, Krishna himself stepped down from the car, put his arms beneath it, and raised it from the earth with his own strength. The chariot that had carried them through every battle of the war stood level once more, as if the ground had never swallowed it.

Karna's last weapon was gone. But Karna himself still stood on the field, wounded and failing — and the duel was not over.
stories.reflection: The snake hides in an enemy's quiver and comes for the archer who slew his mother years before — old griefs find their way back to the field in whatever shape they can. Krishna alone reads the arrow for what it is, because he alone remembers the whole history; discernment is memory made present.
stories.content_note: Fierce single combat and a vengeful snake-arrow; described without graphic detail.
stories.next_story_tease: Wounded and failing, Karna still stood on the field — and the end of the duel was yet to come.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna stands beside the chariot sunk in the earth, one arm beneath it lifting the car free, while the severed form of the snake Aswasena falls from the sky and Arjuna lowers his bow on the battlefield.

stories.title: Krishna Urges Arjuna to Slay the Distressed Karna
stories.story:
It was the war at Kurukshetra, and all through that long afternoon the sky had been turning into a net of arrows. Arjuna and Karna, the son of the charioteer Adhiratha, had been searching for each other's one lapse, and neither had yet given it. The two hosts had fallen back to watch, for it seemed the whole long war had narrowed at last to these two men alone, each of whom was desirous of availing himself of the other's lapses.

Arjuna had loosed a weapon that swelled with energy and went careering through the air with the effulgence of lightning, consuming the Kuru ranks, and the broken divisions of the Kauravas fled and stood at a distance, gazing at it. Karna alone held his ground. With showers of shafts winged with gold he baffled that burning weapon while it was still in the sky, and with a foe-killing weapon of his own, the great weapon he had obtained from Rama and which resembled in its efficacy an Atharvan rite, he crushed it and pierced Arjuna with keen shafts. Bending his own loud-sounding bow of unbreakable string, he shot showers of arrows, and the two of them closed.

They struck at each other like two fierce elephants striking with their tusks. The points of the compass became shrouded with weapons and the very sun went invisible. The sky turned into one vast arrowy net with no space between, and all the Kauravas and the Somakas beheld that wide-spread arrowy net, and in that dense darkness caused by arrows the two armies could make out nothing else. Those two foremost of men, both accomplished in weapons, kept aiming and shooting, and displayed diverse kinds of beautiful manoeuvres. Sometimes the Suta's son prevailed over his rival, sometimes the diadem-decked Arjuna prevailed, in prowess and weapons and lightness of hands, and every warrior on the field was filled with wonder. Even the beings in the welkin applauded, crying sometimes, Excellent, O Karna, and sometimes, Excellent, O Arjuna. And a serpent named Aswasena, who nursed an old hatred of Arjuna, had slipped into that arrowy darkness and was waiting there for his moment.

Then the turn came. The earth had been pressed deep all day with the weight of cars and the tread of steeds and elephants, and now it seemed to turn against one of its own. Karna's chariot wheel sank into the earth, and the ground held it, as though it had at last chosen its side. Karna stood stupefied. The man who had never shown his back in battle was held motionless in the open, in the sight of both hosts, and he could not draw his car free.

He called out to Arjuna and appealed to his righteousness. He was in distress, he said; he had been brought low not by his enemy's hand but by the ground itself. He did not ask for mercy, only for time, the chance to free his wheel and face Arjuna as an equal, as the dharma of warriors required. Let Arjuna remember dharma, he urged. Grant him one moment's respite, the bare moment that a warrior in his place could rightly claim.

Krishna, the younger brother of Indra, did not let the moment pass. Why, O son of Pandu, dost thou become so forgetful? he addressed him, with great excitement. They that are truly wise never spare their foes, however weak, even for a moment. Slay him, therefore, like Indra slaying the Asura Namuci.

Arjuna's arrow answered, and the warrior who had asked for a moment received none. The wheel stayed where the earth held it, and the duel was over.
stories.reflection: The two pleas stand side by side and the account does not step in to say which was right. Karna asks for what dharma owes a man brought low; Krishna answers that a war is no place for such debts, and names Indra and Namuci as the precedent. That the episode ends without resolving the argument is, perhaps, the point: the hardest questions are the ones the source leaves open.
stories.content_note: A warrior is slain in battle; the death is described with restraint.
stories.next_story_tease: But the war's grief was not finished; a mother's curse was about to fall upon Krishna.
stories.hero_scene: Karna standing motionless beside his chariot, its wheel sunk into the earth, calling out to Arjuna while Krishna urges Arjuna to strike, the sky above them dark with a net of arrows.

stories.title: Balarama Tries to Halt the Mace-Duel
stories.story:
The news reached Balarama from the mouths of brahmins, telling of the great war of the Kurus and the Pandavas and the slaughter of the warrior kings. He listened, and he understood: the burden the earth had carried so long — the weight of kings grown too heavy for the world — was being lifted at last, king by king, on the field of Kurukshetra. The brahmins brought the tale as it had come to them, name by name, and Balarama heard in it the ending of an age.

But one duel remained.

Bhima and Duryodhana, the two mightiest mace-fighters of their age, had met in their final combat and were beating each other toward death with their iron clubs, the blows ringing out across the field. Balarama set out for Kurukshetra at once, for the slaughter of the kings was done, and he would not see two more lives spent on what was already decided. He had been journeying through the holy places when the news reached him, and as he rode, the news was still turning in his mind — the war done, the kings fallen, and two champions yet beating each other to death. He drove on with the sound of those iron blows in his ears.

Yudhishthira saw him coming and went to greet him, and the twins and Krishna and Arjuna with him. But Balarama had not come for greetings. His eyes were on the centre of the field, where the two champions stood, maces in hand, enraged, each bent on victory — Bhima of the Pandavas and Duryodhana of the Kurus, the last two fighters of a war that had consumed the kings of the earth. All around them lay the silence of a finished slaughter; the great armies were gone, the banners down, and only these two still stood, one against the other, settling what the war had not settled.

"O king!" he called, and his voice carried across the field. "O Vrikodara! The two of you are of equal strength, equal heroes. Neither of you can win this fight. Desist."

It was the counsel of an honest man, and it was the truth. The two were matched so evenly that victory could be claimed by neither; at the end of such a duel, ruin waited for both. Balarama had no stake in the quarrel of the cousins — he had come only to say what any onlooker with clear eyes could see — and the words he flung across the field were meant to save the lives of both of them.

But the champions did not heed his words. They were bound by enmity, the way kings are bound by the greed of a kingdom; they remembered the insults they had exchanged across the years, and memory held them tighter than any counsel. What Balarama said was reasonable, and neither of them had come to Kurukshetra to be reasonable.

Balarama waited, watching the maces rise and fall, and saw that he could not part them. He was not a man to force his will upon destiny. Accepting what he saw — two champions locked in their duel, deaf to everything but their own hatred — he turned away without another word.

He returned to Dwaraka, leaving the field to the mace and the men who swung it. Behind him, the maces rose and fell, and the last duel of the war went on without him. He had spoken, and been heard, and refused; there was nothing left for a witness to do but leave the field to the two who had chosen it.
stories.reflection: Balarama comes to the last duel as an impartial witness, speaks the truth over the field, and leaves when it is not heard — even the greatest can offer counsel, not compel. The war's ending belongs to the men who chose it and to the hatred that binds them.
stories.next_story_tease: Only the duel of the maces stood between the field and the end of the war.
stories.hero_scene: Balarama stands at the edge of the field, one hand raised, calling to the two mace-wielding champions locked in combat in the centre, while the Pandavas watch and the dust of the duel rises around them.

stories.title: Kunti Asks Only for Remembrance
stories.subtitle: A queen's farewell hymn as Krishna turns toward Dwaraka
stories.story:
The brahma weapon of Ashvatthama had been spent that night and turned back, and the sons of Pandu stood alive in the wreckage of it. Krishna had stayed only long enough to see them safe. Now he was turning toward Dwaraka, his own city, and Kunti — who had thanked him in her heart through a lifetime of dangers — knew she might not see him again like this, with the world grown quiet. She had watched him save her sons so many times that the court had lost count of the rescues.

She came forward as he turned to depart, and she spoke. The mother of kings, Yudhishthira and his brothers standing silent behind her, addressed him in the hearing of the whole court; and what poured out of her was not a plea but a hymn.

She bowed to the primal Person, veiled by his own play, unknowable to the ignorant, imperishable; the goal of the pure-hearted sages. She bowed to Krishna, son of Vasudeva, son of Devaki, lotus-navelled, garlanded with lotuses. She remembered his mother shut away for years in Kamsa's prison, given over to sorrow — and freed at last. Then she remembered herself. Poison had come to her sons, and the great fire, and the cruel assembly of the dice hall, and the long hardships of forest exile, and the weapons of the mightiest warriors of the age. From all of these, again and again, he had freed her and her children.

And then Kunti said the thing that made the court go still. "May those dangers remain with me forever, teacher of the world," she said, "for it was in danger that I saw you. A man puffed up by birth, by wealth, by learning, by beauty, does not see you at all." She bowed again — to him who is the wealth of those who own nothing, who stands beyond the pull of the world's moods. "I consider you Time itself," she said, "the lord without beginning and without end. No one can read your intention, for you move among us in the guise of a man. Your birth, your deeds — though you are unborn and do nothing. Even the rope with which a gopi of Vrindavan bound you as a child, when you had misbehaved, your eyes blurred with tears and running collyrium — even that was your play."

People argued about why he had come at all, she said. Some held that the unborn one took birth to give glory to the virtuous. Others said Vasudeva had prayed for him, and he came to Devaki. Others said he came to lift the earth's burden, as a boat is lowered onto a drowning sea. Whatever the truth — and the wise could not agree — the troubled of this world heard of his deeds and sang them, chanted them, remembered them, and took joy in them.

Then the hymn found its wound. "Will you abandon us today, lord?" she asked. "Will you leave your friends, your servants? What are we, Pandavas and Yadavas alike, without you, but name and form? This land will not shine as it shines now, bearer of the mace, once you are gone." And she named him as the verses name him — Shri Krishna, friend of Arjuna, bull of the Vrishnis, whose valor has no end.

The court was silent. And Kunti, who in all those years had asked nothing for herself — no kingdom, no wealth, no safety — asked the one thing she wanted. "May my mind be fixed on you alone, lord of Madhu," she said. "Again and again, on you alone."

Krishna, whose every glory she had praised, smiled gently. "So be it," he answered her. And he turned back toward the city.
stories.reflection: Kunti's hymn is one of the strangest farewells in the tradition: she does not ask Krishna to stay, only that her remembrance of him stay. Her prayer that dangers might remain forever is not a love of suffering but a confession that it was in danger that she knew him most clearly — gratitude so complete that it can thank even misfortune.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna granted her prayer, but he would not leave the city that day — there were months of leave-taking still ahead.
stories.hero_scene: Queen Kunti, hands folded in salutation, stands before Krishna in the morning light of Hastinapura as he turns toward his chariot; the Pandava court silent behind her, and Krishna smiling gently as he answers her hymn.

stories.title: Krishna Departs Hastinapura
stories.subtitle: A city watches its friend leave
stories.story:
It was months before Krishna could bring himself to leave Hastinapura.

He had stayed on after the great war — to gladden his friends, to comfort his sister Subhadra, who mourned the dead of two houses, to let a broken city begin to heal in the presence of someone it trusted completely. The months passed, the wounds of the Kuru house began to close, and still the parting was put off. At last it could be delayed no longer. He took leave of everyone, embraced them one by one, bowed to the elders, and mounted his chariot. The morning was clear, and every person in the city knew this was the last they would see of him from their own streets for a long while.

And the city could not let him go.

Subhadra, Draupadi, Kunti — Gandhari, Dhritarashtra, all of them — could not bear the thought of his going. Their eyes followed him and would not turn away. The wise, the verses say, once they have tasted true company, cannot give it up again; how then could the Pandavas, whose minds were fixed on Krishna, endure his absence? Tears rose in their eyes and were held back, from sheer longing for Devaki's son. No one wanted to be the first to look away.

The whole city came out to see him go. The mridangas sounded and the conches, the bheris and the vinas; drums and horns answered down the length of the royal road. The women of the Kuru house climbed to the roofs of the palaces, desperate for one more sight of him, and the children of the city ran beside the chariot wheels until the road turned. A white umbrella sewn with pearl garlands was raised over his head, and Uddhava and Satyaki walked beside his chariot, waving the great chauris. Here and there along the way, the blessings of the brahmins rose over the noise and were heard.

And as the chariot moved through the streets, the people spoke to one another of the one who was leaving. "This is he, surely," they said — "the ancient Person, who alone existed before all distinctions, who by his own power sets creation turning again. His are the feet the sages seek; his deeds are sung in the hidden places of the Vedas. When kings grow dark with unrighteousness, he comes down." "How praiseworthy is the clan of Yadu," others said, "how holy the forest of Madhu that raised him. And Kushasthali, his city — it dims the glory of heaven itself and makes the earth famous. The women who won him by the price of valor, carrying off the fierce king of Chedi and the rest at the svayamvara, make womanhood itself glorious." So the women of the city talked as he passed. The verses set it down that these were the words heard along the royal road that morning — a whole city praising, as one, the one it loved.

Yudhishthira rode with him part of the way, for the protection of the army and the escort. And there at the edge of the city, the Kurus stood at a distance, tormented by separation, their eyes unblinking on the figure growing smaller down the road.

Krishna passed on. He travelled through Kuru-jangala and Panchala, through Shurasena and the lands along the Yamuna, across the Maru desert, through the far reaches of Sauvira and Abhira. And at every kingdom he crossed, the people came out to meet him and did him honor, pressing gifts upon him as he passed — for the road to Dwaraka, though long, ran through a country that had been waiting to see him.
stories.reflection: The verses pause to note that those who have known such company cannot bear to lose it, and the Pandavas, whose minds were fixed on Krishna, could hardly endure the parting. What makes the scene moving is that the grief is not for a king or a deity but for a friend: the city grieves him as a presence that will simply be gone.
stories.next_story_tease: Ahead lay the desert road — and a sea-girt city already decking its gates for his return.

stories.title: Dwaraka Welcomes Krishna Home
stories.subtitle: A conch brings the whole city running
stories.story:
The city of Dwaraka heard its lord returning before it saw him.

Krishna was still some way out, crossing into his own prosperous land of Anarta, when he lifted his conch and blew. The white-bellied shell, reddened by his lips, sent out a sound that carried ahead of him like light — a sound that, as the verses say, removes the fear of the world. And Dwaraka, hearing it, rose and ran to meet him.

The citizens poured through the gates, their faces blooming with joy, their voices choked with delight. "We bow to your lotus feet, lord," they cried, "feet worshipped by Brahma and Shiva and the kings of the gods. Be our welfare — for you alone are our mother, our friend, our husband, our father. When you went away to the Kurus, or to the Madhus, to see your friends, how could we live? How could we bear it, with your glance far off — the glance that dries up every sorrow?" So the people spoke, and Krishna, who is tender to his devotees, heard them all. And the joy ran through the city like a tide, from the swept avenues to the humblest doorway with its pot of curds.

The city had been made ready for him as for a festival. Arches of welcome stood raised at the gates and along the roads; the great avenues had been swept clean, the lanes and markets and squares freshened; at every door were set pots of curds and unbroken rice, fruits and sugarcane. And out of the gates came his own people to meet him: his father Vasudeva, great-hearted; Akrura; Ugrasena, the king he had restored; and Balarama, the wondrous Rama, his brother — with Pradyumna and Charudeshna and Samba, Jambavati's son, riding behind them. The foremost elephant led the procession, and the brahmins chanted auspicious blessings; courtesans by the hundred rode out in their vehicles, eager for his sight; actors and dancers, bards and panegyrists filled the road with song.

Krishna moved among them and did not hurry past. He bowed to the elders and to the brahmins with their wives; he took the hands of his relatives, returned embrace for embrace, smile for smile, glance for glance — the whole long welcome answered in kind. The noble women of Dwaraka watched from the terraces along the royal road: the sight of him was the drinking vessel of their eyes, and his chest, they said, the very home of fortune. He passed beneath the white umbrella and the waving fans, showered with flowers from the balconies all the way to his father's house.

There his mothers were waiting — the wives of Vasudeva, Devaki at their head. He bowed to them, and they lifted him onto their laps and held him like a child again, their eyes wet with the tears of love. For a long moment the courtyard held only the sound of their weeping.

Only then did he enter his own palace, the house that fulfilled every desire. His wives, who had watched the road for his return all the months he was gone, saw their husband come home and their minds broke into festival; with their children about them, with their eyes and their very hearts, they embraced their lord. And the verses close the scene with a quiet marvel: even to those who lived beside him, who saw him in the next room and alone, his two feet were always new.

Dwaraka had him back. The sea-girt city, which had been decked and swept and kept awake while he was away, settled into the long happiness of his presence.
stories.reflection: The citizens' words — 'you alone are our mother, our friend, our husband, our father' — are striking because they come from an entire city, not from a single devotee; a whole people measures its safety by one presence. And the closing marvel, that his feet were always new even to those who lived beside him, says something quiet about devotion: nearness does not exhaust wonder.
stories.next_story_tease: But the wheel of time was turning, and the years of peace were numbered.
stories.hero_scene: Krishna sounding his conch at the approach to Dwaraka, the white sea-girt city rising ahead of him, while citizens stream through the decorated gates with garlands, pots of curds and flowers to welcome him home.

stories.title: Time's Answer to Arjuna
stories.subtitle: Vyasa consoles the grieving archer, and Parikshit is enthroned
stories.story:
When the news reached him, Arjuna went to Dwaraka alone.

Krishna and Balarama had left the world, and their city was a city of the dead. Arjuna performed the last rites for the two brothers and for all the slain. The eight queens of Krishna, Rukmini at their head, embraced the body of their lord and entered the funeral fire; Revati, holding the body of Rama, entered the blazing pile, and the fire, the verses say, was cool to her, happy in her contact with her lord. Hearing this, Ugrasena and Vasudeva, with Devaki and Rohini, gave themselves to the flames. Arjuna performed their rites too, then made the whole city rise and leave. He took Vajra, the young prince of the Yadus, and led the thousands of Krishna's wives and all the people of Dwaraka slowly away with tenderness and care.

Behind them, the Sudharman palace and the Parijata tree, which Krishna had brought down to earth, rose and went back to heaven. On the same day Hari left the earth, the dark-bodied Kali age descended. And the ocean rose and submerged all of Dwaraka, save one small temple of the Yadu deity, which the sea has never washed away; there, they say, Kesava still abides, and whoever visits it is freed from sins.

Arjuna halted the great company in the Panchanada country, a rich and fertile land. But the robbers of the region saw a single warrior in charge of so many widowed women and so much treasure, and their greed woke. They gathered the lawless Abhiras to them. "Here is Arjuna," they said, "rich, and proud of slaying Bhishma and Drona and Karna. He does not know the prowess of simple villagers. Up! Take your staves! Why should we not lift our arms?" And they rushed at the people with cudgels and clods of earth.

Arjuna faced them. "Retire, wretches," he said, "unless you wish to die." They paid him no heed; they seized the treasure and the women. Arjuna reached for his heavenly bow, Gandiva — and it would not brace. The string stayed slack in his hands, however he strained. The incantations of the superhuman weapons would not come back to his memory. He loosed arrows as best he could, and they merely scratched skin; even the shafts Agni had given him were themselves destroyed. He beat at the bandits with the horn of his bow, and they laughed. And in the sight of Arjuna, the barbarians carried off the women of the Vrishni and Andhaka tribes and went their way.

Then the greatest archer of the age broke down. "Alas, alas!" he wept. "I am deserted by my lord!" And in that instant Gandiva and the heavenly weapons, his chariot and his horses, perished before his eyes. "Resistless are the decrees of fate," he said, "who gave feebleness to me and victory to the base. These arms are mine; this fist is mine; I am Arjuna. But without that righteous aid all of it is pithless — and without him I am overcome by peasants."

He went on to Mathura and installed the young Yadava prince Vajra as its king. And there, in a wood, he found the sage Vyasa and prostrated himself at his feet. Vyasa looked at him for a long time. "How is it, Arjuna," he asked, "that I see you shorn of your lustre? Have you been beaten by your inferiors in battle?"

Arjuna sighed deeply and told him everything. "Hari, who was our strength, our heroism, our very brightness, has left us," he said. "Without him we are as weak as straw. Gandiva, famed through the three worlds, is foiled by the sticks of peasants; the household of Krishna is carried off by thieves with cudgels. It is not that my lustre is gone — it is a wonder that I live."

Vyasa's answer was gentle, and it was absolute. "Think no more of your disgrace, my son," he said. "Know that time subjects all beings to the same vicissitudes. Rivers, seas, mountains, gods, men, trees, insects — all are created by time and destroyed by time. Krishna came down to lift the burden of the earth; that object is accomplished. All the kings are slain, the Vrishni race is destroyed; nothing remained for him to do, and so the lord has departed, his ends fulfilled. At creation he creates, in duration he preserves, at the end he destroys. Your defeat by miserable thieves was as much his work as your victories over Bhishma and Karna. It is only the sport of the universal Hari."

Then Vyasa told him a story. Once, a brahman named Ashtavakra — a great ascetic, crooked in eight places — stood in water for years, meditating. After the Asuras were overthrown, the nymphs of heaven passed that way to a festival on Mount Meru; seeing the sage, they praised him. "Ask what you wish," he said. Some asked for the best of husbands, a sovereign of the Brahmans. "So be it," he said, and rose from the water — and when the nymphs saw how crooked his body was, they laughed. The sage cursed them: "You shall have the first of males for your husband, but because you laughed at my deformity, you shall afterwards fall into the hands of thieves." They begged his pardon, and he softened: in time, he said, they would return to the sphere of the gods.

"It is because of that curse," Vyasa said, "that the wives of Kesava have now fallen into the hands of the barbarians. Do not grieve for it. All this destruction was effected by the lord of all — and your end, too, is near, since he has withdrawn your strength and your splendour. Death is the doom of everyone born; fall is the end of exaltation; union ends in separation; growth tends to decay. Knowing this, wise men are touched by neither grief nor joy. Relinquish everything, and repair to the holy forest. Go and tell Yudhishthira that tomorrow, with his brothers, he must tread the path of heroes."

Arjuna went back and told his brothers all that he had seen and heard. And the sons of Pandu placed Parikshit on the throne, and went to the forest.
stories.reflection: Vyasa's consolation rests on a single recognition: Krishna's coming and going alike were the working of time, which gives and takes away without partiality. The Ashtavakra story makes the point gently — even heavenly nymphs were promised to thieves by an old curse — so that Arjuna's defeat loses its sting: it was never his to keep, and never his loss alone.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana gives a somewhat different account of Dwaraka's end and the deaths of the elders; this story follows the Vishnu Purana, as cited in the evidence pack.
stories.content_note: Contains the funeral-pyre deaths of Krishna's queens and family elders after his death, and an attack by robbers; may warrant parental awareness for younger readers.

stories.title: The Pilgrimage to Samanta-panchaka
stories.story:
When the sun went dark over Dwaraka in the middle of the day, the Yadavas did not read it as a bad omen. A solar eclipse is a summons, not a warning: a day when the pious go down to the sacred waters, bathe away the dust of their years, and give cows and gifts to the worthy. Every family in the city knew the day's arithmetic — the dark sun above, the sacred water ahead, and the merit to be won by those who came with open hands.

The road led to Samanta-panchaka, the field of the Kurus where the warrior Rama, best of weapon-bearers, had once made lakes of the kings' blood. It was a field the blessed Rama himself had hallowed with his great sacrifice — Rama, untouched by any deed's stain — and the water there was counted among the holiest in the land. Krishna went, and Balarama, and Vasudeva, and Akrura, and the chief men of the Yadava houses, and behind them half the city. The road filled with chariots that gleamed like the dwellings of the gods, drawn by swift horses and hung with garlands of gold, so that the whole procession shone as it crossed the plain beneath the darkened sky. It seemed that all the people of the land were on the road as well, streaming toward the same field, each pilgrim hoping to leave a lifetime of sins behind in the sacred water.

At the tirtha they bathed in Rama's five pools, fasting with their minds gathered close, and then, as the rite required, bathed a second time. They gave cows and gifts and performed what the day demanded. And only then did the field show them what the eclipse had truly gathered.

Kings had come from every quarter — from Kamboja and Kaikaya, from Madra and Kunti, from Anarta and Kerala — and with them, kinsmen and friends the Yadavas had not seen in years. Men who had been parted by wars and reigns and the long business of kingdoms fell on one another's necks. Their faces opened like lotuses in the joy of meeting, and tears ran down unchecked. The women of the two houses embraced as well, arm crossing arm, the red kumkuma of festival dress marking each other's shoulders, tears of love bright in their eyes. The youngest bowed to the eldest and were blessed in return, and the elders gave the blessings with both hands, as if they could not let go.

By evening the field had turned into something rarer than a festival: a reunion of half the world's families. Tents had gone up everywhere; the plain had become a city of its own. Old quarrels were forgotten at the sight of a familiar face. News was exchanged at every campfire; children born since the last meeting were shown to relatives who wept over them; men who had last met on a battlefield found they could laugh together. The eclipse that had darkened the sky at noon had become the excuse for a homecoming no one had dared to arrange.

And then, toward the end of the day, a new dust rose on the road — not the fine dust of chariots but the slower, thicker dust of ox-carts and walking herds. A caravan of cowherds came up out of the haze, men in the rough cloth of the countryside, and a stir ran through the Vrishni camp. For among all the kings and kinsmen the field had gathered, these were the faces from the oldest years of Krishna's life: Nanda, and Yashoda, and the cowherds of Gokula.

The pilgrimage had saved its best gift for last.
stories.reflection: The eclipse gathers what the years have scattered: a day that begins in darkness becomes the occasion for half the world's families to find one another again. Krishna travels to the tirtha like everyone else, and the story's weight falls not on anything he does but on the reunion that his presence draws together.
stories.next_story_tease: Nanda and Yashoda had come to Samanta-panchaka — and the Vrishnis rushed to meet them as if life itself had returned.
stories.hero_scene: Under the eclipsed sun, a long procession of golden chariots crosses the plain toward the five pools of Samanta-panchaka, where kings from many realms and long-separated kinsmen embrace one another with tears of joy.

stories.title: Reunion with Nanda and Yashoda
stories.story:
The caravan of the cowherds came slowly up the road — ox-carts, dusty men, the lowing of herds — and the Vrishnis who went out to meet it came back changed. In the middle of the crowd walked Nanda, older than when they had last seen him, and the Yadavas fell on him as if life itself had returned to their bodies. Vasudeva was the first to reach him. He embraced his old friend, pleased past all words, overwhelmed with love, holding on as a man holds on to something he thought he had lost. Around them the whole clan pressed close, hands reaching out, voices rising and falling, everyone talking at once and no one listening.

Then Krishna and Balarama came forward and bowed low to the two parents of their boyhood, to Nanda and Yashoda. With their own hands they seated the two parents on the seats of honor, and then, speechless with love, embraced them with both arms — the sons of Dwaraka holding the father and mother of Gokula, grown men who had commanded armies pressing their faces into shoulders they had not felt in years.

Yashoda took her two sons onto her lap. They were men now, broad-shouldered and scarred, princes of a city by the sea; on her lap they became again the boys who had crawled after the calves in her courtyard. She held them and said nothing, and the two of them let themselves be held. Around them the cowherds of Gokula stood smiling and wiping their eyes, as if they too had come home.

Then Devaki and Rohini came to Yashoda. The three women stood a moment, remembering. Devaki, who had given her sons into other hands when they were smaller than her arm, and Rohini, who had shared those first years of waiting — they embraced the queen of Vraja and spoke of the love she had shown the boys in Gokula. "Who could forget that friendship, queen of Vraja?" they said. "Who could forget what you gave them — the years of tending, the childhood you made safe and bright while we could only wait?" The boys, who had never known their parents' care until this day, had rested in her hands the way the eyelash rests on the eye — placed there, and safe, and afraid of nothing.

Yashoda answered them the way she had always answered: she gave them back their sons, sitting there on her lap, whole and grown. The two mothers of Dwaraka looked at the two boys of Gokula — at the princes everyone else in the field saw — and what they saw was the milkmaid's courtyard, the dust of the calf-pens, the little feet running in the sun. Nothing needed to be said about it. The embrace said it.

Vasudeva watched from a little way off and said nothing. Somewhere in his chest a debt he had never been able to name was being counted again, and he knew that before this gathering ended, he would have to speak of it. But not yet. Not while Yashoda's arms were still around her sons.

For the rest of that day, the eclipse field became a small Gokula again. The boys were back on their mother's lap; the years of separation had shrunk to nothing. The pilgrimage, which had begun as a duty under a darkened sun, ended with the oldest, simplest thing in the world: a mother holding her children, and the years falling away from her face. It was the kind of day the elders would tell about for years afterward — the day the whole family was whole again.
stories.reflection: The quiet heart of the reunion is the meeting of the four mothers: Devaki and Rohini, who could not raise the boys, honour Yashoda, who did, and no one needs to say whose claim is greater. The embrace dissolves the old division between the two families in a single gesture.
stories.next_story_tease: But the women of Vraja had come to the field too, and they had waited longest of all to see him.

stories.title: Krishna's Counsel to the Gopis
stories.story:
The gopis had come to Samanta-panchaka like everyone else — to bathe at the eclipse, to see the great gathering — but they had come for one face. They had not seen Krishna in years, and in all that time they had measured the days by his absence: the nights when the flute stayed silent, the mornings when the road to the forest was just a road. They had grown older in his absence, and would not have traded the waiting for anything, because the waiting had kept him near. When at last they stood where he could see them, they did not rush forward. They embraced him in their hearts, and in that inward embrace they attained a state that even the ever-yoked, the ascetics who have bound their minds for lifetimes, can hardly reach. Their eyes had once cursed their own eyelids for blinking and stealing him from their sight; now their eyes held him, and would not let him go.

Krishna saw them and came to them, drawing them aside to a quiet place away from the crowds — he came to them alone, the way he had come to them in the old days in Vraja, without fanfare and without warning. And he asked them, gently: "Do you remember our friendship?" And then: "Or do you think ill of me — do you suspect that I am ungrateful?"

It was not a question they expected. They had come with their longing, not their grievances; in all the years of waiting they had asked nothing of him, only waited. But he did not wait for an answer; he gave them the answer instead.

"As the wind gathers the clouds and scatters them," he said, "as it lifts the dry grass, the cotton, the dust, and lets them fall where it wills, so I bring beings together and carry them apart. I am the one who joins, and I am the one who separates. No meeting lasts by its own strength; every parting that grieves you is woven into the world I wind and unwind. But there is one bond that is not broken — devotion to me. Devotion is what grants immortality to beings. Hold to that, and no separation can touch you. I am the beginning of all beings and their end; I am inside them and outside them; there is nowhere you can go where I am not."

The gopis heard him in the quiet place, with the eclipse-darkened sky above the camp, and their bondage dissolved. The years of longing, the nights of calling his name to the moon, the fear that he had forgotten them — all of it fell away, and they attained him then, in that moment, in a way that no practice could have given them. What he had told them was not that they would never be parted, but that parting itself was his weaving, and that their love of him ran deeper than the weave.

Before they rose, they spoke their answer as a prayer: "O lotus-naveled one, may your lotus feet — which the lords of yoga contemplate in their hearts with their profound wisdom, the one support for those fallen into the well of this world — always rise in our minds, even for us who dwell at home."

He had given them back their friendship, and then he had given them something larger: the knowledge that the friendship had never left them. The gopis returned to their camp walking lightly, as if the road were not there. For the rest of the pilgrimage they moved among the other pilgrims like women who had been shown the end of a long road — having gained, in a single hour, what even the ever-yoked can hardly gain.
stories.reflection: Krishna answers the gopis' longing not with a promise that they will never be parted, but with the truth that no being is ever really parted from him — he is the beginning, the end, and the inside of all things. Their love, which had looked like grief, turns out to be the one thing that cannot be lost.
stories.next_story_tease: The reunion at Samanta-panchaka could not last forever — soon Nanda would take the road back to Mathura.

stories.title: Nanda's Farewell
stories.story:
The pilgrimage had wound down, camp by camp, and the field of Samanta-panchaka was emptying the way it had filled — in dust and shouting and the slow creak of carts. Only one farewell remained, and it had been going on for three months. Nanda had stayed all that time, honored with great worship by the Yadavas, feasts and gifts and the attendance of princes. It was, everyone agreed, a farewell without end. Some of the cowherds joked of settling at the tirtha for good, but Nanda knew the road home was waiting. And still the leaving had to come.

On the last day, Vasudeva stood before his old friend, and the words he had carried inside him for three months came out wet. The snare called affection, he said, is hard to cast off — harder still when it is weighted with guilt. He told Nanda what he had never told anyone: that blinded by royal splendor, by crowns and palaces and the endless business of a kingdom, he had neglected his oldest friend, the man in whose house his sons had grown up, safe and loved, through all the years he himself could not be there. In the years when it had been in his power, brother, he said, he had done nothing for him — nothing at all, while Nanda had done everything for his sons. He wept as he spoke, and Nanda saw that these were tears the old friend had been saving for years. For Vasudeva, the great ocean of his longing had at last been crossed, and he was not sure he deserved to have crossed it.

"May royal splendor never befall a man who desires his own good," he said, "for it steals the eyes." And yet, he said, wiping his face, the eyes had been given back to him now.

Nanda answered him the way he had answered everything in his long life — not with a speech, but with an embrace. He had done what a friend does: he had raised the boys, kept the friendship, and asked for nothing. That, Vasudeva understood, was the gift that could not be repaid, only honored.

Then came the farewell itself. Nanda's carts were loaded with riches — gifts from Vasudeva and from Ugrasena, from Krishna and Uddhava and Balarama — so that the caravan that had arrived in the plain cloth of the countryside left carrying the wealth of a kingdom. The cowherds and the cowherdesses of Vraja made ready; the oxen were yoked; children were lifted into the carts; the dust began to rise. Every Yadava family pressed something on the departing guests — cloth, ornaments, cattle — until the carts could hold no more, and Krishna himself walked beside Nanda's cart as far as the edge of the camp.

Nanda climbed up onto his cart, and his heart, better than any gold, stayed behind — fixed on Govinda's lotus feet, which he carried with him always. The caravan moved off down the road to Mathura, and Krishna and Balarama stood watching until the carts were small against the sky, until the dust settled back into the road.

When the kinsmen had gone, the Vrishnis, whose deity is Krishna, turned homeward themselves. But for a long while no one spoke. The eclipse had come and gone; the pilgrims had bathed; the gifts had been given. What the field of Samanta-panchaka had truly given them could not be bathed away or loaded onto carts. It stayed in the memory of embraces given and received, and in the sight of an old friend's back moving down the road to Mathura, carrying home a heart that would never leave.
stories.reflection: Vasudeva's lament is a confession that royal splendor can blind a man to his oldest debts, and Nanda's silent reply — the embrace, the refusal to count the cost — is the friendship itself. The riches on the carts matter less than the heart Nanda carried home, fixed on Govinda's lotus feet.
stories.next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, the city's sixteen thousand queens were waiting for their lord to come home.

stories.title: Sixteen Thousand Wives, One Beloved
stories.story:
On the edge of Dwaraka, in lakes ringed with blossoming groves, the water itself seemed to be laughing. And in the water was Krishna.

The city had settled back into pleasure after the long years of exile and war: elephants wandered the scented streets, gardens hung heavy with flowers, and music never quite stopped. In the middle of all this abundance, the city's single most beloved man was at play. He had sixteen thousand wives, queens of every great household of Dwaraka, and he was the one beloved of them all. That morning they were in the lakes, and Krishna with them.

The water sports began the way such things always begin: someone splashed, someone shrieked, and in a moment everyone was in the game. The queens surrounded him in a ring, their fine clothes clinging, their wet hair loosened and strung with flowers, and tried to douse him; he answered in kind, laughing, until the spray rose like rain. He stood among them as an elephant-lord stands among his cows, towering and playful at once, letting himself be caught and then slipping away. Musicians played on the bank — drums, flutes, small cymbals — and the dancers moved with the beat.

To each of the sixteen thousand, the sport felt like a secret. Every woman there was certain of one thing: he is sporting only with me. Each looked at his smile and believed she alone held it. Strange to say, there was no jealousy among them, for their minds and eyes were fixed on one man, and where the heart is wholly given, there is no room left for envy.

Some of the queens cried out in mock terror and clung to him: "O Hari, I am being drowned — save me!" Others rowed small boats shaped like herons and serpents and sea-monsters across the bright water, and some swam on their own strength, and some with water jars, all of them trying to please him. The water itself seemed to enter the game, standing at the knee of one, the thigh of another, the breast of a third, so that each was met exactly as she came. His garland was streaked with saffron, his hair fell loose about his face, and he gave himself to each game as though it were the only one.

Then, as the afternoon cooled, the play changed. The queens, still in the water, began to sing — songs of longing, strange for women who had been laughing with their lord only moments before, as though he were far away. One sang to the osprey crying over the lake: you call all night and cannot sleep — has love pierced you too, as it has pierced us? Another sang to the shelduck parted from her mate: you weep in the dark, and we weep, for we too have given ourselves wholly to his feet. They sang to the thin moon: are you, too, wasting away from remembering him? They sang to the southern breeze: what have we done that you bring us his memory and nothing else? They sang to the clouds, heavy with rain: you, like us, are bound to the lord of the Yadavas by love, and you spill your tears remembering him. And they sang to a swan as to a messenger: Welcome, swan; drink the water, and tell us of Shauri. Is the Unconquered One well? Does he, whose friendship moves so quickly, remember us? For a woman, the songs ended again and again, there is no refuge but him.

The drums and flutes answered from the bank, and Krishna listened. He was the water they stood in, the breeze they sang to, the one they called to; in his presence they sang of his absence, and their longing was itself the closest embrace. The old scripture says that by such love — constant, single-hearted, poured out in song — those queens attained the supreme state, for the heart that gives everything receives everything.

Evening came down over the lakes, and the queens rose from the water, their wet clothes and loosened hair and smiling faces bright as lotuses. The game ended where it had begun: in laughter, in water, in the middle of Dwaraka, where the lord of sixteen thousand hearts was, that day and every day, the single beloved of them all.
stories.reflection: The strangest, most moving thing in this story is that the songs of longing are sung by women who are not separated from Krishna at all — the absence is imagined, and imagining it lets their love pour itself out completely. The story's quiet miracle is that each of the sixteen thousand is given the whole of Krishna, and none of them is diminished.
stories.tradition_note: The Harivamsha sets the same sport in the ocean, whose waters Krishna frees from salt, and adds that the water rose only to the height each woman wished; this account follows the Bhagavata Purana, which places the play in the lakes of Dwaraka.
stories.next_story_tease: Krishna's watchfulness would be tested again soon — on the banks of the Ganga, where a grieving king was coming to meet the Pandavas.

stories.title: Krishna Substitutes an Iron Statue for Bhima
stories.story:
The blind king of Hastinapura was coming to meet the men who had killed his sons — and he was coming with open arms.

The war was over. King Dhritarashtra, whose hundred sons lay dead on the field of Kurukshetra, had set out from his city, grief weighing on him like a stone. It should have been a simple meeting — a nephew going to comfort an uncle — but the whole court watched it with a dread no one spoke aloud. Yudhishthira, now king in his place, heard that his uncle was coming and went out to meet him, taking his brothers and Krishna of Dasharha's race with him, and Yuyudhana and Yuyutsu; and the princess Draupadi, burning with grief, followed her lord. On the banks of the Ganga they found the ladies of the Bharata court, weeping like a flight of ospreys, their arms raised in anguish: where is the righteousness of the king, where is truth and compassion, that he has slain sires and brothers and preceptors and sons and friends? Yudhishthira passed through them in silence and saluted his uncle's feet, and his brothers announced themselves, each giving his own name.

Dhritarashtra embraced Yudhishthira — a reluctant embrace, brief, with a few words of comfort — and then he asked for Bhima. His grief had kindled into something else: a fire, the story says, fanned by the wind of his sorrow, ready to burn everything that came near it, and ready above all to consume the forest that was Bhima. He wanted the man who had killed Duryodhana. He wanted to hold Bhima in his arms.

And Krishna knew it. He had known it from the very outset — that was why an iron statue of Bhima, made long ago at Duryodhana's order, had been kept ready. Before the embrace could happen, Krishna quietly drew the real Bhima away and set the statue in his place. The blind king, told that the second son of Pandu stood before him, seized it with both arms, thinking it to be Bhima himself in flesh and blood.

The strength of Dhritarashtra was the strength of ten thousand elephants. He crushed the iron Bhima as if it were a reed, shattering it into fragments. But the blow recoiled on him: his own breast was bruised and broken, and blood poured from his mouth. Covered in blood, he fell to the ground like a parijata tree brought down under the weight of its flowers. His charioteer Sanjaya, the son of Gavalgana, ran to him, raised him, and steadied him. "Do not act so," Sanjaya said. And the old king, his wrath spent at last, wept aloud: "Alas, oh Bhima — alas, oh Bhima!"

Only then did Krishna speak. "Do not grieve, Dhritarashtra," he said. "You have not slain Bhimasena. That was an iron statue you broke. I saw the rage in you, and I dragged the son of Kunti out of the jaws of Death. There is none equal to you in bodily strength — what man could endure the pressure of your arms? As no one escapes the Destroyer himself with his life, so no one comes out safe from your embrace. That statue, made by your son, had been kept ready for this moment. Grief for your sons has pulled your mind away from righteousness, and in that darkness you sought to slay Bhima. But what good would his death have done you? Your sons will not be revived by it. Accept what we have done for the sake of peace, and do not set your heart on grief."

Bhima, who had stood within an arm's length of death, was alive. And on the banks of the Ganga he stood among his brothers — the real Bhima, in flesh and blood — while the blind king wept out his grief and his wrath together.
stories.reflection: Krishna's mercy here works in two steps: he lets the king's rage spend itself against iron rather than flesh, and only then tells the truth. The substitution saves Bhima; the timing saves Dhritarashtra, who is allowed to discover that he is not a murderer and that his grief is not, in the end, a weapon.
stories.content_note: A grieving king crushes an iron statue in his embrace, wounding his own breast and vomiting blood; intense but not graphic.
stories.next_story_tease: The old king's wrath was spent, but his grief still needed one more word from Krishna.

stories.title: Krishna Counsels Dhritarashtra to Govern His Wrath
stories.story:
The blind king had been washed of his own blood, and now he sat in silence, with nothing left to him but grief.

An hour earlier he had crushed what he believed was Bhima in his arms. It had been an iron statue — Krishna had drawn the real Bhima away and set it in the blind king's embrace, and the strength that had shattered iron had broken the king's own breast and sent blood pouring from his mouth. Only when the wrath had burned itself out had Krishna told him the truth: you have not slain Bhimasena. Now the maid-servants had washed the king and dressed his wounds, and Krishna came to him again.

Yudhishthira and his brothers stood a little apart, watching. Krishna did not let the silence soften into comfort. "You have read the Vedas and the scriptures," he said. "You have heard the old histories and everything about the duties of kings. You are learned, possessed of great wisdom, indifferent to strength and weakness. Why, then, do you cherish such wrath, when everything that has overtaken you is the result of your own fault?"

He reminded the king of what had been said to him before the war. Krishna himself had counselled him; so had Bhishma and Drona, Vidura and Sanjaya. The king had not followed a word of it, though they had told him plainly that the Pandavas were superior to his own sons in strength and courage. "A king who can see his own faults, and knows the distinctions of place and time, obtains great prosperity," Krishna said. "But the man who will not accept the counsel of well-wishers, good or bad, meets with distress, and grieves over the policy he chose himself. You did not keep your soul under restraint; you let Duryodhana rule you. What has come upon you came through your own fault. Observe a different course of life now. Why do you seek to slay Bhima? Recollect your own faults, and govern your wrath."

And then, in the same breath, Krishna turned to the old king's tenderness. He reminded him of the day Duryodhana, from pride, had caused the princess of Pancala to be brought into the assembly. "That mean wretch has been slain by Bhimasena in just revenge," Krishna said. "Look at your own evil acts, and at the acts of your wicked-souled son. The sons of Pandu are perfectly innocent, and yet you and your son treated them most cruelly."

It is a hard thing to be told, at the end of one's life, that one's sorrow is one's own doing. But Dhritarashtra did not argue. "It is even so, O mighty-armed one," he said. "What you say is perfectly true. It was parental affection, O thou of righteous soul, that caused me to fall away from righteousness — love for my own sons, Madhava. By good luck, that tiger among men, the mighty Bhima of true prowess, protected by you, never came within my embrace. Now I am free of wrath and fever. I desire eagerly to embrace that hero, the second son of Pandu. When all the kings are dead, when my children are no more, upon the sons of Pandu depend my welfare and my happiness."

And then the old king did what grief had made impossible an hour before. He rose and embraced those princes of excellent frames: Bhima, and Dhananjaya, and the two sons of Madri — the young men he had been ready, an hour before, to destroy. He wept over them, comforted them, and pronounced blessings upon them. The king who had come to the river with murder in his grief left it with his arms around the sons of Pandu.
stories.reflection: Krishna's counsel works because it separates the two things the old king was carrying: the grief, which is real and never rebuked, and the wrath, which is chosen and can be set down. He names Dhritarashtra's fault not to shame him but to give him back the one thing sorrow takes away — the sense that his own choices still matter.
stories.next_story_tease: But beside that same river, another grief was gathering — one that would not answer to counsel.

stories.title: Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile
stories.story:
The war was over, and the field at Kurukshetra lay strewn with the dead, and Gandhari walked among them and saw what a mother sees when the war is over. Her own sons lay dead among the rest, and with them it seemed she had lost everyone's sons, and she poured it all out to Krishna, who stood beside her.

Behold, she said, the ruler of the Kambojas, that bull-necked hero, lying in the dust though he deserved to rest at ease on soft Kamboja blankets. His wife is weeping bitterly at the sight of his blood-stained arms, those arms that once were smeared with sandal-paste; even now, adorned with beautiful palms and graceful fingers, they resemble a couple of spiked maces, and within their clasp joy never left her for a moment. What will be my end, the beauteous one cries, O ruler of men, when I am deprived of thee? Endued with a melodious voice, the Kamboja queen weeps helplessly and quivers with emotion.

Behold the ruler of the Kalingas, lying on the ground with his mighty arms adorned with angadas. Behold the ladies of Magadha, crying around their lord Jayatsena, their ornaments displaced, the long-eyed and sweet-voiced girls whose wails were stupefying her heart exceedingly, ladies worthy of costly beds lying now on the bare ground. Behold that bevy of fair ladies there; though tired with exertion and worn out with heat, beauty leaves not their forms, like the sightliness of the wreaths worn by the celestials though exposed to the sun, and their faces, through toil and the rays of the sun, look like faded lotuses. Behold the Kosala prince Brihadbala, his women plucking from his body the shafts with which Abhimanyu pierced him, losing their senses again and again.

There were the young sons of Dhrishtadyumna, of tender years, adorned with garlands of gold, fallen upon Drona like insects on a blazing fire, Drona whose car was a chamber of fire, his bow the flame and his shafts and darts and maces the fuel. And the five Kekaya brothers lay with their faces still turned toward the man who slew them, their coats of mail, of the splendour of heated gold, and their tall standards and cars and garlands, all of the same metal, shedding a bright light on the earth.

These wails, Gandhari said, were stupefying her heart exceedingly. And then she turned from the dead to the one who might have stopped it all. Since thou wert indifferent to the Kurus and the Pandavas whilst they slew each other, she said, therefore, O Govinda, thou shalt be the slayer of thy own kinsmen. In the thirty-sixth year from this day, thou shalt perish by disgusting means in the wilderness.

Krishna, the high-souled one, heard her out, and there was a faint smile on his face as he answered. There is none in the world, save myself, he said, that is capable of destroying the Vrishnis. Which was another way of saying that the end she spoke of was not something to be argued with or feared, for it was already written, and it would come from their own hands.

And so the curse was received, not resisted.
stories.reflection: Gandhari speaks from the raw center of grief, and her curse is grief given a shape and a date. Krishna does not defend himself or dispute the blame; he smiles, because he already knows how the Vrishnis will end, and he is not afraid of it.

stories.title: Krishna Rebukes Gandhari
stories.story:
She had just cursed him, and he had accepted the curse with a smile. Now Krishna stood before Gandhari, and the grief of a hundred dead sons hung between them like weather.

Gandhari, the mother of the Kauravas, had raised her hands over the field of Kurukshetra and pronounced her curse on the man she held responsible for the slaughter — that he would die, as her sons had died, by the hands of his own kinsmen. Krishna had taken the words as one takes a blessing. And now, with the pyres not yet built, he spoke.

"Arise, arise, Gandhari," he said. "Do not set your heart on grief. Through your own fault this vast carnage has taken place. Your son Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious, and exceedingly arrogant. You applauded his wicked acts and regarded them as good. He was cruel, the very embodiment of hostility, disobedient to the counsel of the elders. And you — why do you wish to ascribe your own faults to me?"

It is worth sitting with what he did not say. He did not say that the war was fate, or that the gods had willed it. He said: this is yours. And then he said something stranger still about grief itself. "The person who grieves for what has already occurred obtains more grief. By indulging in grief, one increases it two-fold." Mourning, he told the mother of the dead, is a fire that feeds on itself.

Then came the harshest words of all. He spoke of the children that different women bear: the woman of the priestly class bears sons for austerities, the cow bears for burdens, the mare for speed, the servant-woman for servitors, the herdsman's wife for keepers of cattle. "But a princess," Krishna said, "bears sons for being slaughtered."

Gandhari said nothing. The story records that her heart was exceedingly agitated by grief, and that she remained silent. Whatever she had expected from Krishna — comfort, apology, the name of the guilty — she received the truth instead, and the truth left her no reply.

Her husband, Dhritarashtra, had been listening at her side, and it was he who broke the silence, turning to Yudhishthira with a question that sounds, after everything, almost impossible: how many have fallen? Yudhishthira answered with a number so vast it reads like the census of a small country — one billion, six hundred and sixty million, and twenty thousand men, the story says, and two hundred and forty thousand, one hundred and sixty-five who escaped. And the blind king asked where the fallen had gone.

Yudhishthira, who had received the gift of spiritual sight from the sage Lomasa during his years of wandering, answered: those who cast off their bodies gladly in fierce battle have reached the worlds of Indra; those who met death without joy have found the company of the celestial musicians; those who fell while turning away from the field or begging quarter have reached the world of the hidden ones; the high-souled warriors who, scorning flight, advanced unarmed against armed foes have attained the bright regions of Brahman; and all the rest who died on the field have gone to the world of the Uttara-Kurus. To every death, a place.

Then the work of the living began. Dhritarashtra asked about the friendless dead — those with no one to light their pyres — and Yudhishthira gave his order: let no one perish for want of someone to care for them. And so the pyres were built, of sandalwood and aloe and gathered wood, with ghee and oil and perfumes, silken robes, broken chariots, and heaps of weapons for fuel; and the fires were lit. Duryodhana and his hundred brothers were burned with due rites, and Shalya, and Jayadratha, and Abhimanyu, Arjuna's boy; Duhshasana's son, and Bhurishrava, and Drupada, and Virata, and Shikhandi, and Dhrishtadyumna, and the thousands of the Srinjayas. The smoke of the pyres rose over Kurukshetra, and the field of the great war became, at last, a place of burning and of farewell.
stories.reflection: Krishna's rebuke comes to a woman who has just cursed him, and it refuses to let her grief become a weapon that rewrites what happened. 'A princess bears sons for being slaughtered' is brutal — and it is also the one sentence that could make a queen of the dead stop and hear that her sorrow, however vast, is not the whole story.
stories.next_story_tease: On the road back to Hastinapura, Arjuna would ask Krishna to speak again the teaching he had heard before the war began.
