stories.title: Arjuna Asks Krishna to Repeat the Gita
stories.subtitle: Krishna offers the Anugita in its place
stories.story:
Years later, when people asked what Krishna and Arjuna spoke of in the days after the war, the answer began with a confession: everything Krishna had told him on the battlefield, Arjuna had forgotten.

The war was over. Arjuna had recovered his kingdom and was spending his days in pure joy, doing nothing but keeping company with Krishna in the palace at Hastinapura, in rooms that seemed a piece of heaven, surrounded by relatives and attendants. And yet one thing had begun to trouble him. One day, as the two friends wandered together through that beautiful mansion, Arjuna turned to Krishna. It was on the approach of battle, he said, that Krishna's greatness had become known to him; on that field he had also seen Krishna's form as the Lord of the universe. But everything Krishna had spoken to him then, out of affection, had slipped away from him, because of the fickleness of his mind. He had been curious about those truths again and again, he said — and Krishna would soon be leaving for Dwaraka. Would Krishna tell him once more?

Krishna embraced him before he answered. It was exceedingly disagreeable to him, he said, to learn that Arjuna had not, from folly, received what was imparted. The recollection of all he had told him on that occasion would not come to him now; that teaching was more than sufficient for understanding Brahma, and he could not discourse on it again in detail, for he had spoken of Supreme Brahma while concentrated in yoga. But then his voice softened into a promise: he would recite an old history upon the same topic, and if Arjuna listened with an understanding shaped by his teaching, he might yet attain the highest end.

And so Krishna began the old history. Once, he said, a Brahmana had come to them from the regions of Heaven, from the presence of the Grandsire, a being of irresistible energy, and they had reverenced him duly. When they asked him about the religion of Emancipation — asked, the Brahmana observed, out of compassion for all creatures and not for his own good — he agreed to speak, asking only that they listen with concentrated attention.

The old history concerned a Brahmana named Kasyapa, foremost of all persons conversant with duties. Kasyapa had heard of another Brahmana, one who had become conversant with all the mysteries of religion. This second sage had mastered all the knowledge the scriptures teach about the departure and reappearance of beings, and possessed that direct knowledge of all things which yoga gives. He was skilled in the truths of every topic relating to the world; he knew the truth about pleasure and pain, understood the distinctions between merit and demerit, and had beheld the ends attained by embodied creatures high and low in consequence of their acts. He lived like one already emancipated, crowned with ascetic success and perfectly tranquil, all his senses under complete control. He seemed to blaze with the resplendence of Brahma, could go everywhere at will, and knew the science of disappearing at will from before the eyes of all. He roved in the company of invisible Siddhas and celestial musicians, conversing with them in spots retired from the bustle of humanity, and he was as unattached to all things as the wind.

Kasyapa, having heard of him truly, desired to see him. The foremost of Brahmanas approached the sage, and when he had seen all those wonderful attributes he fell with a rapt heart at the sage's feet, filled with wonder, and began to wait upon that master with dutiful reverence.

So Krishna spoke, in the palace of celestial beauty, with Arjuna before him — and the old history he had promised, the tale the Brahmana of Heaven told to Kasyapa, would unroll through the days that followed into the teaching known as the Anugita.
stories.reflection: Krishna's answer to forgotten truth is not a repetition but a story: he cannot summon back the words of the Gita, so he begins an old history, and the Anugita is born from that refusal. Arjuna's fickleness of mind becomes, in a strange way, the occasion for the teaching to be given again in a new form.
stories.tradition_note: The Anugita is the Mahabharata's own sequel to the Gita, and within the text Krishna explains that he cannot repeat the original discourse; the full old history unfolds through the chapters of the Anugita Parva that follow.
stories.next_story_tease: Before long, Krishna would speak his final teaching to a different disciple, at the foot of an ashvattha tree.

stories.title: Krishna's Final Instruction to Uddhava
stories.story:
By the time the Yadava clan had all but destroyed itself, there was almost no one left at Krishna's side. He had watched the course of his own maya run out to its end, and now he walked to the bank of the Sarasvati, sipped the water of the river, and sat down at the foot of an ashvattha tree.

There he told Uddhava to go to Badari, the hermitage in the north. Uddhava, who had followed Krishna his whole life, found that he could not leave his feet. It was not that he defied the command; it was that the road north led away from Krishna, and that was the one road Uddhava had never learned to take. He lingered. He followed at a distance, waiting. And Krishna, who takes away the sorrow of all who surrender to him, found him there and said: I know your heart's desire. I grant you what is hard for others to attain.

Uddhava has left us his own account of that hour. He saw his Lord seated alone, contemplating — the beloved one he had always sought. Krishna was dark and radiant, free of all passion, his eyes peaceful and touched with red, his right foot resting upon his left thigh. He was the refuge of the great devotee, and when Krishna spoke, Uddhava — the great devotee, the friend of Vyasa himself — bowed with joy, his head bent low.

This is the last of your births, Krishna told him. My grace has come to you. What I spoke long ago to Brahma, seated on the lotus born from my navel at the beginning of creation — that is what I give you now.

Uddhava could barely take it in. He had asked for nothing; he had only failed to walk away when he was told to go. And now he was to receive what the Lord had spoken to Brahma at the dawn of the universe. He praised Krishna — the one who acts without desire, whose birth and non-birth alike are beyond telling, the refuge of the distressed, whom the frightened reach by fleeing from every fear; the one who is invoked in mantras, whose knowledge of the self is unbroken, complete, eternal; the one who, knowing the secret of the self, could unfold that knowledge fully. All his life Uddhava had been blessed, moment by moment, by the grace of that Supreme Person, and only now did he understand how much had already been given. To whom else would the Lord teach it, he wondered, but to one whose heart was laid open? For those who serve the lotus of his feet, what could be hard to obtain, even among the four aims of life?

And so, to Uddhava whose heart had been opened, the supreme Lord taught the supreme knowledge — the knowledge that illuminates the secret of the self — and granted him the state that is hard for others to attain.

It was the final teaching, given at the foot of a tree on the bank of a river, to the one man who could not make himself leave Krishna's feet. The world would long remember the words spoken at Kurukshetra; what Uddhava carried away that day was what came after them — the knowledge of the self, granted in a whisper by a river.
stories.reflection: Uddhava is told to go, and his reward is that he cannot; he receives the supreme state not for asking but for refusing to leave Krishna's feet. The episode quietly suggests that the last grace comes to those who cannot bear separation, even when the Lord himself sends them away.
stories.tradition_note: The account in the third canto is Uddhava's own recollection of the moment; the fuller exposition of the teaching he received is traditionally known as the Uddhava Gita.
locations: the foot of an ashvattha tree

stories.title: Krishna Sends Uddhava to Vrindavan
stories.story:
In the palace at Mathura there were kings and counselors, kinsmen and crowds — but when Krishna wanted comfort carried to the people of his boyhood, he did not look to any of them. He looked to Uddhava, his beloved devotee, his friend whose heart was fixed on him alone.

Uddhava held no office and no rank. What he had was rarer: he had been at Krishna's side through the long years in Mathura, and he had seen how the young hero of the city grew quiet whenever the talk turned to Vrindavan — how a single mention of the village could stop him mid-sentence. Krishna's heart was still there, among the cowherds who had raised him and the women who had loved him, and Uddhava knew it.

One day Krishna called Uddhava to him and gave him a journey. Go to Vraja, he said. Bring joy to my parents. Nanda and Yashoda had raised him in the village of his childhood; the summons of Kamsa's court had carried him away to Mathura, and the years since had been long for the people who still loved him there. But it was not only his parents that Krishna spoke of.

The women of Gokula, he told Uddhava, had their minds fixed on him; their very lives were given up for his sake; for his sake they had abandoned everything — comfort, standing, even their own bodies. To them he was the dearest of all dear ones, and he was far away. They were keeping themselves alive, he said, with great difficulty, somehow, only just.

Uddhava understood what was being asked of him. Krishna was not sending a herald to deliver orders, or a prince to settle accounts. He was sending his own affection into the village that still sang his name — and he was sending Uddhava of all people, because Uddhava could speak of him most truly. The women who had given up everything for Krishna were pining, and Krishna, who could have sent anyone, was sending the one friend who would say the words the way they needed to be said.

Uddhava accepted the charge. He would go to Vrindavan, he promised, and he would tell Nanda and Yashoda of their son, and he would carry Krishna's love to the women of Gokula, and he would not rest until he had done all that could be done to console them.

So he made ready to leave Mathura, carrying the strangest of royal messages: that Krishna, far away, remembered — remembered their songs and their meadows and their faces — and had sent the dearest of his friends to say so. He carried no army and no gifts, only words that would have to be worth the years of waiting. The road to Vrindavan lay open before him, and he set out.
stories.reflection: The message Krishna entrusts to Uddhava is not doctrine but a description of love — minds fixed on him, lives given up for his sake. In sending his dearest friend to console Vrindavan, Krishna sends a part of himself, and comfort travels in both directions.
stories.next_story_tease: He reached Vrindavan as the sun went down, to a welcome he had not expected.

stories.title: Uddhava Arrives in Vrindavan
stories.subtitle: Nanda longs for Krishna as Yashoda weeps
stories.story:
Uddhava reached Nanda's Vraja as the sun went down.

The village at dusk was a thing alive. Powerful bulls, scenting the cows, bellowed and fought in the lanes; white calves leaped this way and that, so that the whole settlement seemed dressed in them; and the women sang as they worked, singing the auspicious deeds of Bala and Krishna, the two brothers the village had raised and lost. Every home bore the marks of worship — the fire, the sun, the guest, the cow, the Brahmana, the ancestors, the gods, each honored in its turn — and around the settlement the forests stood in full flower, loud with the calling of birds.

Uddhava walked through the lanes slowly, taking it all in — the smoke of the evening fires, the lowing of the cows coming home, the songs rising and falling. So this was the world Krishna spoke of in his quiet moments; no wonder his heart had never quite left it.

When Nanda learned who had come, he hurried out to meet him: Krishna's own companion, his beloved attendant, a traveler from the city that had taken his son. He embraced Uddhava and honored him as he would have honored Vasudeva himself, and pressed upon him the finest food the house could offer, and seated him comfortably on a couch. Only then, with his guest at rest, did the old man's questions begin to spill out.

Is our friend well, he asked — the son of Shura, our Krishna? By good fortune, he said, the sinner Kamsa had been killed, with all his followers, by the very evil he had done. But does Krishna remember us? Does he remember his mother, his friends, his playmates? Will Govinda ever come back, even once, to look upon his own people?

Before Uddhava could answer, Nanda was already answering himself, the memories crowding in. He remembered how Krishna had sheltered them from the forest fire, and from wind and rain, from the great bull and from the serpent. He remembered his heroic deeds, and the playful sidelong glance of him. He remembered the rivers, the mountains, the forests — every one of them adorned by the touch of Krishna's feet. The more he remembered, the more he wondered: surely Krishna and Rama were the best of the gods, come down to walk among men. Who else could have broken the great bow, tall as three palm trees, as an elephant king snaps a staff? Who else could have brought down Kamsa, strong as ten thousand elephants, together with the two wrestlers and the royal elephant? And the demons of Krishna's boyhood — Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arishta, Trinavarta, Baka — one after another they had fallen to the two brothers in the very fields where Nanda's cattle still grazed.

And as Nanda spoke, Yashoda listened — and wept. She had held herself steady while the messenger spoke of Mathura; it was the boyhood deeds that undid her, the demon fights in the pastures and the fire in the forest, because those were the years when he had still been hers to hold.

So the evening passed in Nanda's house: the honored guest upon the couch, the old cowherd recounting wonders, and the mother of Krishna weeping quietly at the sound of her son's name.
stories.reflection: Nanda's questions run straight to the only thing that matters to him: not what Krishna has conquered, but whether Krishna remembers — his mother, his friends, his playmates. The village keeps Krishna alive by singing his deeds, and the measure of its love is remembrance.
stories.next_story_tease: Only then did Uddhava find the words to speak the message Krishna had entrusted to him.

stories.title: Uddhava Begs Krishna Not to Leave Him Behind
stories.story:
The omens had begun to appear in Dwaraka — small ones at first, a strange bird on a rooftop, a vessel of milk soured before its time — and then signs that made the city speak in low voices. Krishna read them all, and grew quiet.

Uddhava had lately returned from Vrindavan, carrying Krishna's message to the cowherds and bringing back their longing in his heart. Nanda's grief, the gopis' tears, the old villagers who pressed his hand as if touching Krishna himself — he had carried all of it home with him. And now, in Dwaraka, he read the omens for what they were. The work Krishna had come to do was done. He meant to leave the world.

Dwaraka felt it before anyone said a word. The city had grown rich and proud, and its pride had begun to work like a slow fever: feasts that lasted too long, quarrels that flared over a look, young men of the Yadu clans who had forgotten how to fear anything. The elders whispered that the family had grown too great for the earth to hold it, and the omens seemed to say the same thing. Only Krishna moved through it all untroubled — speaking gently, settling disputes, smiling at children — and Uddhava, watching him, understood that this calm was itself a kind of farewell.

Uddhava found him alone and fell at his feet, and for a long moment could not speak. At last he said: "Even for half a moment, Keshava, I cannot bear to leave your lotus feet. Wherever you go, carry me also to your abode."

And then, with Krishna's hand resting on his head, everything he had stored up in silence came out. Krishna's pastimes, he said, were the supreme good fortune of human beings; there was nothing in the three worlds to set beside them. The bed he had slept in, the seat he had sat on, the roads he had walked, the river pools he had bathed in, his games and his meals, the garlands that had lain on his chest, the scents he wore, his clothes, his ornaments — Uddhava had kept each of them like a secret treasure, and how could he give up the source of them all? Even the ascetics who renounce everything, who throw away wealth and home and name and wear only the wind for clothing, wander the paths of action with nothing, remembering and singing Krishna's deeds. They never touched his hand, and they cannot let him go. If the memory of Krishna keeps a man alive who has given up the whole world, what holds the man who has held nothing back — who has poured his entire life into that one friendship, and been trusted with Krishna's deepest errands in return?

He said all of it with his face against the ground, and when he had finished he lay still, waiting.

Krishna raised him up with his own hands. "What you have said is exactly my own intent," he said. "Brahma, Shiva, and the guardians of the worlds long for my return to heaven. The time has come." He spoke of the gods' longing simply, without triumph, the way one mentions an old appointment kept at last. And he granted Uddhava his prayer — he would not be left behind.

But that was not all he granted. In the quiet of that hour, with the troubled city beyond the walls, Krishna began to instruct him, as a teacher speaks to a disciple he loves — about the self, the world, and the way to freedom. Uddhava had begged to be carried; he received instead something harder and greater: the teaching that would let him stand, and stand alone, after Krishna had gone.
stories.reflection: Uddhava's plea measures devotion not by what a devotee has done but by how near the beloved is: even the sages who have renounced everything cling to the memory of Krishna's deeds, so how could the man who lived beside him bear a moment's separation? And Krishna's answer transforms the request — he grants Uddhava's wish to be carried along, and then gives him something that makes the wish unnecessary: the teaching that lets him stand alone.
stories.next_story_tease: And he began his teaching with a story — of a king who met a wandering sage on a forest road.

stories.title: Yadu Meets the Wandering Avadhuta
stories.story:
"Listen," Krishna said, "and I will tell you what freedom looks like." Uddhava had asked for teaching, and Krishna answered as he often did — with a story.

There was once a king named Yadu, of the line of Nahusha, who ruled a great kingdom and knew its burdens: the ministers who angled for favor, the endless petitions, the wars that had to be fought to keep the peace. One day his party halted in a forest, and down the road came a wandering brahmin — an avadhuta, a renunciate who had put aside everything: home, family, ritual, even the marks of his order.

The king could not take his eyes off him. The man owned nothing and feared nothing. He moved without hurry, laughed like a child at a falling leaf, wandered like one possessed, stood as still as a ghost — and yet there was a serenity in him that Yadu had never seen at court. At court everyone wore his rank like armor; here was a man who wore nothing at all and needed no armor, and the difference struck the king like a blow.

The world around them was burning, and the king thought of it constantly: people everywhere consumed by the forest fire of desire and greed, each one running after what the next one had. His own ministers would have cut each other's throats for the succession to a district; the neighboring kings measured friendship in brides and borders; even the ascetics who came to the palace asked for something — a cow, a village, an audience. This man asked for nothing and was afraid of no one, and he walked through the middle of the burning world untouched, clear-eyed, sweet-spoken, at ease in his own skin.

Yadu dismounted and approached him. "Men spend their lives in dharma, wealth, pleasure, and the itch of curiosity, and burn in that fire all the same," he said. "But you are capable, wise, skilled, fortunate; your speech is like nectar; for those who ask, you are the very cause of joy. You act like a child, a madman, a ghost — and yet you are a sage. How did you gain such wisdom?"

The brahmin smiled, the way a man smiles who has been taught by everything he ever met. "O king, I have many gurus. Twenty-four of them. From each one I learn whatever I learn."

And he named them, one after another: earth, wind, sky, water, fire, the moon, the sun; the pigeon, the python, the ocean; the moth, the bee, the elephant, the honey-gatherer; the deer, the fish, Pingala, the osprey; the child, the maiden, the arrow-maker, the serpent, the spider, the cricket.

Yadu stared. Twenty-four teachers, and not one of them a scholar or a sage. Some of the names were familiar — every child knew the sun and the moon were holy — but a python? A fish? A maiden? And Pingala — the name sounded like a woman's, and the king's curiosity sharpened at the thought that she too had taught this man something. He had paid the finest brahmins in the land to instruct him, had mastered the texts and the rituals, and here was a penniless wanderer who had studied with rivers and birds.

"Then teach me," Yadu said.

The avadhuta looked at him for a long moment — at the king's ornaments, the armed guard, the fine horse cropping the grass — and it seemed to Yadu that the man was not judging him but weighing something far older: whether the question had come from the king's boredom or from his hunger. Then he nodded, as if he had been waiting for it all along. And he began with the first of his teachers: the earth itself.
stories.reflection: The wonder of the avadhuta is that his wisdom has no human source at all: a king who spent his life being taught by the best of men finds that the deepest freedom was being taught, all along, by the simplest things. The list of twenty-four gurus — rivers and pigeons and a woman named Pingala — quietly reverses the order of the world: the lowliest teacher may hold the greatest lesson.
stories.next_story_tease: And his first lesson came from the earth beneath their feet.

stories.title: The Avadhuta's Lessons from the Elements
stories.story:
"The earth taught me forbearance," the avadhuta said. "Every being walks upon her — beasts and men, armies in their thousands, the hooves of cattle, the wheels of carts. She is trampled by all of them, morning and evening, and she never once strays from her course. So the wise one, though the world treads on him, does not leave his path."

He had been wronged a hundred times, Yadu thought — by rivals, by fate, by his own temper — and he had never once stayed on the path because of it; he had veered off it in fury. The first lesson had already found its mark.

"The wind taught me detachment," the avadhuta said. "It moves everywhere — through palaces and market streets, through the trees, into every corner of every house — and it clings to nothing it touches. So the yogi moves among the objects of the senses and remains unattached, passing through the world without being caught by it."

The wind, the king realized, had taught this man what he had spent his life failing to learn: to be in the middle of things and not be caught by them.

"The sky taught me to remain unaffected. The clouds sail through it, the rain falls from it, the smoke of a thousand hearths rises into it, the birds cross it — and none of them leaves a mark. In the same way the wise one dwells among all the bodies of the world, moving and unmoving, hidden in each one and touched by none; the sky is everywhere, and nowhere is it held, and so he sees the one self in all things and knows himself in everything."

"The water taught me purity. It is clear by nature and sweet to the taste, and wherever it flows it becomes a holy place — a tirtha for men to bathe in. So the sage, pure in himself, makes everything around him sacred; people come to him as they come to a river, and the dirt they carry falls from them in his presence."

"The fire taught me to be untainted. Whatever it is given — wood, refuse, offerings, filth — it burns, and takes no stain from any of it. It shines by its own heat; it is brilliant, and hard to approach. So the sage, whatever he consumes, is not polluted by it. His light is his own, and the world's dirt does not reach it."

"The moon taught me to wax and to wane. It swells to fullness and thins to a sliver, and both are its own nature. So the body rises and falls — birth, youth, age, death, all the states from the first to the cremation ground — and these belong to the body, not to the self. The wise one watches them as the moon watches its own phases, taking what time brings and letting it go when time takes it."

"The sun taught me the one soul in many bodies. One sun rises on the palace and on the hut, on the king and on the beggar, and illumines them all. So the one self appears in every body, and when a body ends, nothing of the light is lost; the wise one lives in that single sight, seeing himself in every face."

The king was silent. Seven lessons, each one drawn from a thing that had never spoken a word — and each one clear as water. He had filled his court with the learned, and none of them had ever told him anything so simply. The avadhuta paused, and when the king leaned forward, he went on — to the eighth of his teachers, the pigeon, and to what love had cost it.
stories.reflection: The seven elemental lessons are striking because each is drawn from a teacher that never spoke: forbearance from the trampled earth, detachment from the wind, purity from water, radiance that takes no stain from fire. And the sun's lesson gathers them all — the one self in many bodies — showing that the elements were never teaching about themselves, but about the single reality reflected in all of them.
stories.next_story_tease: Then he spoke of the pigeon, the eighth of his teachers — and of what love cost it.

stories.title: The Pigeon and the Hunter's Net
stories.story:
A pigeon built his nest in a forest tree, and there, with his mate, he raised a family. The two birds were bound to one another by a love that showed in everything they did. They were, in the way of birds, a single household, and the tree was their home.

They shared one bed and one seat. Where they roosted, they roosted together; where they walked, they walked side by side; what they said, they said to one another. They played together and ate together, and whatever one wanted, the other gave without being asked. It was a small life and a complete one, and they asked for nothing beyond it.

In time the hen laid her first eggs, and when the chicks hatched the two birds loved them with a tenderness that filled the nest with soft feathers and low, contented cooing. They fed them and kept them warm and watched over them, devoted to their children, and their days became nothing but the feeding and the keeping and the watching of those small, downy, open-beaked lives. The nest was all their world, and their world was warm.

The chicks grew, and their feathers came in soft as silk, and their cooing and their clumsy, innocent antics were the parents' whole delight. Watching them, the two birds felt that no harm could ever reach this tree, this nest, this small bright world they had made. Everything they had was in that nest — their young, their days, their whole reason for flying out and returning. They wanted for nothing, and they feared nothing, and they did not see the snare that their own tenderness was quietly weaving around them.

One day the two of them flew out together to gather food for the chicks. While they were gone, a hunter came through the forest, and he saw the young birds in the nest, alone and unguarded. He spread his net, and he caught them all.

The hen came home first. She saw her chicks struggling in the mesh, and love moved faster in her than fear. She did not pause, did not call out, did not think of herself. She flew straight into the net and settled down among her young. She did not try to pull them free; she only wanted to be with them.

Then the pigeon came home and saw them — his chicks, his mate, all of them tangled in the hunter's cords. He cried out: “Alas, what has my poor, misguided mind brought down upon us? My home is destroyed, my wife and children are caught — what use is my life now?” He could not bear to be the only one left free, to sit in an empty nest while those he loved were taken from him. Better, he thought, to share their fate than to outlive them in an empty home. The net that held them held everything he had. So he too flew into the net.

The hunter, finding them all gathered there for him, gathered them up and went on his way. And the nest stood empty in the tree, its soft lining stirring once in the wind and then going still. And so the very love that had made the nest a home became the thing that left it empty. The story was kept as a caution: a householder who clings to home and family as that bird did, bound to them and without peace, comes in the end to ruin — a human life, the one birth that stands with its door open to freedom, shut upon itself.
stories.reflection: The tale is offered as a warning, but it does not condemn love — it shows love without distance, a tenderness so total that it cannot let the lost stay lost. The pigeon is not wicked; he simply cannot bear to be the one left outside the net. What undoes him is not the hunter's cruelty but the completeness of his devotion.

stories.title: The Python's Contentment and the Ocean's Depth
stories.story:
"The python taught me contentment," the avadhuta said. "He lies where he happens to be, and whatever comes within his reach — fine food or foul, much or little — he takes. If nothing comes, he lies still for days on end, without effort, without pursuit, without complaint. He does not hunt, he does not plan, he does not grieve the meal that passed him by; hunger comes and goes, and he is still the python either way. So the sage accepts what chance brings and does not run after more. He carries a body full of vigor and strength, yet he does not spend it on striving; his hands do what needs doing, but his acts leave no trace on him, because they are not born of desire."

The king, whose days were a long argument with appetite — the next campaign, the next pleasure, the next proof of his greatness — heard this and felt the strangest lightness, as if a knot had been loosened inside him.

"The ocean taught me depth," the avadhuta said. "The rivers pour into it, and it does not swell; the rivers dry up, and it does not sink. The rivers may rage in flood or fail in drought; the sea receives both without preference, because its depth is not borrowed from them. It stays deep, full, and serene — so deep that no one can fathom it, so still that no one can stir it. Whatever pours in, whatever is withheld, its fullness is its own. So the sage remains the same whether the world pours gifts upon him or leaves him empty-handed. Whether his desires are fulfilled or he is left destitute, he is fixed on Narayana alone; that is his fullness, and it does not rise or fall with fortune."

Yadu looked at the wanderer — at the man who owned nothing and had just described the ocean as if it lived inside him. And slowly he understood that the python's stillness and the ocean's depth were one teaching: freedom does not come from having enough; it comes from not needing anything. The sage is not the man who has everything — he is the man who is complete without anything, like the sea that no river can fill and no drought can empty.

A wind moved through the forest, and the avadhuta sat in the middle of it, unmoved, like his teachers. The king, who had come to the forest to escape his court for a day, found that he had wandered into a school greater than any he had built. And the sage, seeing that the lesson had landed, spoke again — of the moth, and of the flame it cannot resist.
stories.reflection: The python and the ocean teach the same freedom at two scales: the python accepts what comes without striving, the ocean stays full whether rivers come or not — and the two together show that contentment is not a matter of how much one has but of where one's center is. The sage's fullness is fixed on Narayana, so fortune can neither add to it nor take from it.
stories.next_story_tease: Then he told of the moth, which cannot resist the flame.

stories.title: The Moth and the Bee
stories.story:
A lamp flame is a small thing, and yet the moth flies straight into it. It circles the light once, twice, drawn by a brightness that promises nothing but itself, and in a moment it is gone — a scorched thread of a body dropping onto the ledge below the flame. The light did not hunt it; the moth did all the hunting itself. The flame burned on as if nothing had happened.

It was by a lamp in a wayside rest-house, at night, that the wandering teacher watched this happen, and he counted the moth among his teachers. He was an avadhuta — a brahmin who had put aside home, name, and belongings — and he walked the forest roads taking lessons from everything he met. He had no guru but the world, and the world never ran out of lessons. He learned to read the smallest things this way: a drop of water, a bent blade of grass, a sparrow's quarrel — each one a page of some teaching. Nothing was too small to teach him, and nothing, he said, was too small to destroy a man.

The moth's lesson was desire. The flame asks nothing of the moth; it is the moth that gives everything, and for what? A little brightness. So it is, he said, with a man who is not master of his senses. Bewitched by a woman's beauty — by the gold of her ornaments, the fine weave of her clothes, the thousand small enchantments that the world spins around itself — he follows the brightness wherever it leads, and falls into blinding darkness, exactly as the moth falls into the flame. He had seen it happen to men he knew — sensible men, undone by a face. It is not that beauty is false. It is that desire cannot stop at looking. It must draw nearer, and then nearer, until the light that seemed so lovely is the fire that burns it.

The bee taught him the other way. In the mornings he would sit where the bees worked, among the wild flowers at the road's edge, and watch them go about their business: nothing in haste, nothing in excess, each blossom left able to bloom again. The bee visits many flowers and takes from each only a little — a sip of nectar, a dusting of pollen — and carries nothing away to hoard. So the wise man, said the avadhuta, gathers the essence from every teaching, great and small, from the longest scripture to the humblest creature's way of living, the way the bee gathers from every flower: he takes what is good from each and clings to none. He eats a little at a time, just enough to keep the body alive, and what is begged for the day is used that same day; he never lays it up for the evening or the morning. The flower is not the enemy. The hoard is the enemy.

Two small creatures, two ways of being alive. One dies of wanting everything; the other lives by taking a little and letting the rest go. The avadhuta said he had made himself the bee: he tasted the world's sweetness without needing to own it, listened to great teachings and small ones without becoming the servant of any, and slept each night with empty hands, having kept nothing for a day that had not yet come. He was not cold, he said; he was only free of the need that makes men hold on.

He used to say that the two insects together were one complete teaching. The moth shows what appetite costs; the bee shows what appetite is for. Between the two, a man may choose how to want. It is a quiet discipline — and a hard one. The flame is so bright, and the flowers are so many.
stories.reflection: The two lessons work by contrast: the moth dies of wanting everything, the bee lives by taking a little from each flower and keeping nothing. The point is not that beauty is false but that grasping is fatal — the same hunger destroys when it must own, and sustains when it only takes enough.
stories.next_story_tease: The wandering teacher's next gurus were wilder still — an elephant led by desire, a honey-gatherer stung for his hoard, a deer caught by song, and a fish taken by the tongue.

stories.title: The Elephant, the Honey-Gatherer, the Deer and the Fish
stories.story:
The elephant is the strongest thing in the forest. It can uproot a tree and scatter a hunting party like dry leaves, and yet it is caught by something soft — a she-elephant. The hunters know this well. They send the cow out as a decoy, and the great male, all his strength forgotten, follows her step by step into the clearing where the rope and the stake wait. He is not conquered; he is led. And he goes willingly.

The avadhuta, the wandering brahmin who took the world itself as his guru, watched this and learned from it. If desire can bind an elephant, he said, what will it do to a man? The senses are not weak, but they are hungry, and hunger does not bargain. Strength counts for nothing against desire; the elephant could have broken every rope in the forest, and instead it stood quietly while the rope was tied. He said that a renunciate should not touch a woman even of wood, so strictly did he fence himself away from desire; the wise, he said, do not go near what brings the death of the self. The only safety from the snare is not to follow the decoy, however sweet she seems.

The honey-gatherer taught him about hoarding. A man climbs to the wild hive in the rocks, and the bees swarm and sting him for every comb he takes; he comes down aching and half-blinded, carrying the honey — and who eats it? Others. The sweetness is enjoyed by hands that never felt the stings, while the gatherer keeps the scars. The gatherer's hands were swollen, and still he climbed again the next season, because the honey was sweet and the memory of the pain was short. So it is with wealth painfully hoarded, said the avadhuta: a man gathers it in sleeplessness and worry, and in the end others enjoy what he spent his life clutching. The sage does not pile up what was gathered in suffering.

The deer taught him about the ear. The deer is swift and watchful, and no hunter can run it down; but it is caught by song. He had seen the hunters lure the deer with a flute, the animal stopping mid-step, ears turned to the music, forgetting everything that had kept it safe. The ear, said the avadhuta, is a door that cannot see. A wandering renunciate should not listen to the music and dancing of the village, the songs that please the senses; the sweetest sound can be the snare.

The fish taught him about the tongue. The fish is caught by the mouth and hooked through the tongue, and it is the taste of the bait that undoes it. Of all the senses, said the avadhuta, the tongue is the hardest to master. A man may close his eyes and stop his ears, but the craving for taste follows him everywhere, and it is the craving that pulls the hook. A man may refuse the cup and the plate, he said, and still be undone by the memory of a taste.

So the avadhuta walked his road with his senses held in check, like a man fasting. He said the senses are conquered quickly when they are not fed — the whole secret is to stop feeding them. And he warned that it must be all of them together: a man who has mastered one sense while another rules him is not yet master of anything. When the village music drifted out to the road at dusk, he walked on past it; when the markets offered their sweets, he did not turn. He had seen where each road ended — in the rope, in the stings, in the bow, in the hook. The elephant was stronger than the rope that held it, and it was led anyway.
stories.reflection: Three of the four teachers are caught through a single sense — the elephant by sight, the deer by hearing, the fish by taste — and the honey-gatherer shows what comes of clutching what one has gathered. The senses are not evil, only hungry, and the avadhuta's point is that hunger, indulged, becomes a trap: restraint is not poverty but freedom.
stories.next_story_tease: Among his teachers the avadhuta counted a woman he had never met — Pingala, the courtesan of Videha.

stories.title: Pingala the Courtesan's Renunciation
stories.story:
A wandering teacher, one of those who take their lessons from the world itself, used to say that among his teachers was a woman he had never met — a courtesan named Pingala, in the city of Videha. He spoke of her with the respect a student owes a teacher, for the lesson she had taught him had cost her a long and sleepless night.

Pingala lived by waiting. Each evening she dressed herself and adorned herself and went to the door of her house to wait for a man — a client, one who would come with money, for money was what she lived by. One night a man had promised to come to her, and so she stood at the door and watched the road. The evening fell, the lamps were lit along the street, and still he did not come. He had said he would come, but the street had emptied, and the road she watched stayed bare.

She waited, and she watched every man who passed, and with each approaching footstep her hope rose, and with each stranger who walked on by it fell. The night wore on. The lamps burned low, and the door grew cold against her shoulder. Her face grew thin and drawn, and her mind grew small and weary, and still she leaned in the doorway, holding herself together with nothing but the hope of a man who never came.

And then, in the dead of the night, something in her turned. It was not despair exactly — or if it was, it was the despair that sets a person free. She looked at herself leaning in that doorway, a woman dressed and waiting for a man who would not come, and she saw, with a sudden and terrible clarity, what she had been doing with her life, and for how many nights, and for how little.

“Look at the depth of my delusion,” she said to herself. “I have worn myself out for a man who brings a little money, when the giver of all joy, the one who grants every gift, is near me always, and I never once turned to him. What I have chased so wretchedly, let me give it up.” She saw, then, how needlessly she had tormented herself, night after night, for so small and passing a thing.

She looked down at the body she had dressed so carefully, and she saw it for what it was — a thing of bone and skin and hair, a house of nine doors that leaks and fills with what is foul. So much trouble, she thought, for a thing that would not last. And she wondered what she had been offering, and to whom, and why it had ever seemed worth a single sleepless night.

Then she cut off her hope — not the quiet hope of ordinary days, but the grasping, hungry hope that had kept her leaning at the door. She turned from the road, and she sat down, and the street that had held her eyes all night went dark and quiet behind her. and for the first time in longer than she could remember, she slept. And she slept in peace, the way a person sleeps when she owes no one anything.

The wandering teacher remembered her for this. A woman who had spent her nights waiting for what would not come, he said, had done in a single hour what the learned struggle a whole lifetime to do. And he kept her words as his own: that hope is the greatest of pains, and freedom from hope the greatest of joys.
stories.reflection: The story is careful not to make Pingala's peace a lesson for the poor or the lonely. What she gives up is not her life but her grasping — the hope that kept her leaning at a door for a man who never came, while the giver of every joy was, she realized, already near. Her “despair” is not a collapse but a release.

stories.title: The Osprey, the Child, the Maiden and the Arrow-Maker
stories.story:
The osprey had caught something — a fish, a piece of meat — and was carrying it across the sky when the stronger birds came. They mobbed it from every side, striking with beak and wing, and the osprey could not both fly and hold its prize. The avadhuta, watching from the road below, saw the bird let go. The meat fell, the attackers wheeled away after it, and the osprey flew on — free, and unhurt. Its wings never faltered; it had simply weighed the sky against the fish and chosen. It was a small drama in a wide sky, and most travelers would have walked past it; the wandering teacher stopped, watched, and took it for a lesson.

The lesson was in the letting go. It was not hunger that had endangered the bird; it was the prize. The birds that took the meat were the stronger ones — strong, and hungry, with no prey of their own — and the osprey, burdened by its prize, could not defend it against them. So it is, said the avadhuta, with a man who grips what he cannot keep. He had made himself like the osprey, he said: for him there was neither honor nor disgrace, and none of the cares that keep householders wakeful, because he had let all of them go. The moment of release looked like loss, and it was freedom.

The child taught him the same truth from the other side. A child owns nothing — no property, no reputation, no plans for tomorrow — and yet a child is not miserable. It is the freest thing alive, absorbed in the game in front of it, drowned in its own joy. A child does not hoard joy; it spends it all on the moment. The avadhuta said that only two beings are free of care: the child, who has nothing and wants nothing, and the sage, who has nothing and wants nothing. From the child he learned to be glad without possessions.

The maiden taught him about solitude. She was alone in the house one day, husking grain, and as she worked her bangles clinked against one another — a small bright sound, at every stroke of her hands. She minded it; the clinking seemed to her unbecoming, the noise of vanity, and so she broke the bangles off one by one and laid them aside, until only a single bangle remained on her wrist. And a single bangle makes no sound. When it was silent, she worked in peace. So, said the avadhuta, should the sage dwell: alone. Where many live together there is quarreling, and even two voices make a noise; strip away what clinks, and there is silence. The empty floor around her was a kind of victory, though no one was there to see it.

The arrow-maker taught him about the mind. The man sat at his work, straightening a shaft, planing and smoothing the wood with his whole attention — and a king's procession passed on the road behind him, with its music and its banners, and the arrow-maker never saw it. It was said the king himself rode in that procession, and still the man's hands never stopped their even work. His mind was fixed on the arrow and nothing else. The avadhuta said he learned from that man to fix his own mind on a single point, until nothing outside and nothing inside could pull it away; he would have it said of him what was said of the arrow-maker, that the world passed by and he did not notice. Such absorption is not laziness or dreaming; it is the whole of the mind, kept in one place.

Solitude and one-pointedness — the maiden's silence and the arrow-maker's absorption. The avadhuta said they are one discipline: empty the room until nothing clinks, and then give the whole mind to the one thing that matters.
stories.reflection: The four teachers share one thread: they are free because they want little. The osprey lets go, the child does not grasp, the maiden strips away every ornament that makes a sound, and the arrow-maker forgets the world because he is wholly given to one thing. Solitude and single-pointedness are the same discipline seen from two sides.
stories.next_story_tease: His last teachers came from the earth and the air: the serpent, the spider, and the wasp.

stories.title: The Serpent, the Spider and the Wasp
stories.story:
The serpent owns nothing — not even the hole it lives in. It does not dig; it enters a burrow another creature has abandoned, lies there without care, and moves on when the time comes, as homeless as it arrived. The burrow was never its own, and so nothing could be taken from it. It asked nothing of the earth, and the earth asked nothing of it. The avadhuta, the wandering brahmin who took the world for his guru, watched the serpent and made its way his own: he would wander alone, he said, and live in no house that he had built.

He had learned this from the serpent: building a house brings only sorrow. There is the labor of raising the walls, the worry of keeping them, the grief of leaving them — and all of it for a body that will not last. The sorrow of a house, he used to say, begins at the first brick and ends, if it ever ends, long after the walls have fallen. A man who knows the body is impermanent does not build as though he would live forever. A borrowed hole in the earth, used and left, is enough; the serpent had taught him that.

The spider taught him the deeper thing. From its own heart the spider sends out the thread; it spins from itself, the whole web drawn out of its own body and played into the air, and when it wishes it draws the thread back into itself again. It does not cling to the web; the web belongs to it, and when it withdraws the thread, nothing of the web remains. What the spider holds, it holds by its own power; nothing outside it supports the web. So it is, said the avadhuta, with the one Lord, Narayana, who alone is: the world is spun out of him by his own power, sustained by him, and in time drawn back into him, the way the web returns to the spider. Creation, preservation, dissolution — one thread, one spinner. The web is vast and beautiful, but the spider is not lost in it; it stays at the center, and the center is with the Lord always.

The wasp taught him about the mind. The wasp takes a living creature and seals it into the mud of a wall, and the creature, helpless in the dark, thinks of nothing but its captor — it broods on the wasp, its shape and its power, until it becomes like what it contemplates, and in time it is a wasp itself. So it is with the mind, said the avadhuta: it becomes what it dwells upon. A mind that dwells on the world becomes worldly; a mind that dwells on the Lord becomes like the Lord. There is no escaping that law; the only choice is what to meditate on. He would say that most men are exactly what they have been thinking of — and that they rarely choose what that is.

This was the avadhuta's last and deepest teaching, and he said it turned all his wanderings into a single practice: keep the mind fixed on the one Lord, as the wasp's captive was fixed on the wasp, and in time you become what you contemplate. He had counted twenty-four teachers in all — earth and wind and water, the pigeon and the python, the moth and the bee, the elephant and the deer, the maiden and the arrow-maker — and with the serpent, the spider, and the wasp the count was complete. And all of them, he said, had pointed to the same place: past the creatures, to the one who spins them out and draws them back. It was a strange end to a list that had begun with the earth underfoot.
stories.reflection: The wasp's captive becomes what it dwells upon, and for the avadhuta that was the heart of all his wandering: the mind given to the one Lord becomes like him, just as the world spun from the spider's heart returns to it. The last of his teachers turned his eyes from the creatures to their source.
stories.next_story_tease: The avadhuta's list of twenty-four teachers ended with the wasp, and Krishna had one more teaching for Uddhava — the story of a swan and the four Kumaras.
stories.hero_scene: In the first light of morning a spider sits at the center of its web and draws the thread back into itself, while the wandering teacher watches below, seeing in the drawn thread the world returning to its source.

stories.title: The Swan Who Answered the Kumaras
stories.subtitle: Brahma's oldest sons meet the hamsa
stories.story:
Sanaka and his brothers were the oldest minds in creation, born directly from Brahma's thought — and they carried a question that no one, not even their father, could answer.

They came to Brahma's abode and asked him for the subtle goal of yoga: the end that all practice points toward and never quite reaches. Brahma, the creator of worlds, sat with their question for a long time. He did not answer from the wealth of his own knowledge. Instead he turned his attention inward and meditated on Krishna. And Krishna, seeing what was needed, appeared before the sages in the form of a swan.

A great white hamsa came gliding into that assembly, calm as the water it had crossed. The four sages rose, walked up to it, and bowed at its feet. Who are you, they asked, that we should be answered by a bird? The swan's reply did not begin with a teaching. It began by turning the question back on them. If in truth there is no difference in the self, it said, then your question has no ground. Know that I alone am, and nothing apart from me.

Then, because they had asked, it taught them.

Look at the mind, said the swan. It runs into the qualities of nature, and the qualities run into it; the more it serves them, the deeper it sinks. Waking, dreaming, and dreamless sleep are only states of the intellect, spun out of those qualities. Bondage is nothing else: the self forgets itself and sees many where there is one. So long as the sense of difference does not turn back, the knot holds. And yet the one who enjoys the objects of waking, who recollects them in dream, who withdraws from both in deep sleep — that one is the same throughout, the knower behind the senses, untouched by what passes before it.

Cut the knot in the heart with the sword of knowledge, said the swan. See the world for what it is — the play of the mind, like the circle of fire a burning brand traces when you whirl it. One light, and the eye believes a ring of flame. So the one reality appears as many, and the dream of waking, dreaming, and sleeping is woven from nothing but the mind's own activity.

Withdraw the gaze, then. Turn from thirst. Sit in silence and taste the bliss that is simply your own self. The body is a perishable thing, put on and taken off like a garment, and the man who has woken to his own nature watches the exchange without confusion, as a drunken man hardly notices a change of clothes. Even the body's comings and goings are governed by the acts that set it in motion; the one established in awareness does not return to the dream once the reality is seen.

This, said the swan, is the secret of sankhya and yoga, the two great paths of knowledge and practice. I am the essence of yoga, the essence of sankhya, the essence of truth, of the right, of radiance. All the qualities of nature serve me, who am beyond them, wanting nothing. And the sages Sanaka and his brothers felt their doubt fall away, as a knot loosens under patient fingers. They worshipped the swan and praised it, and the praise and the worship rose in the air of Brahma's hall like a tide.

Krishna, telling all this to Uddhava long afterward, let the story rest there. That was the form his disciples had asked about, the hamsa that comes and goes upon the water of the mind. The question the Kumaras had carried from the very beginning of creation dissolved not in an answer but in the seeing of who it was that asked — and the swan, having done its work, was gone, leaving only the stillness it had pointed to.
stories.reflection: The swan's first reply is the whole teaching in miniature: before the question about the goal of yoga can be asked, the questioner must see who is asking. Krishna does not satisfy the Kumaras' curiosity so much as dissolve the position their question comes from, and the oldest sages in creation are the ones who finally learn it.
stories.next_story_tease: From the swan, Krishna turned to a man of Avanti whose loss of everything had taught him the same lesson.

stories.title: The Miserly Brahmin of Avanti
stories.subtitle: A man who lost everything sings of the mind
stories.story:
In the city of Avanti there lived a brahmin who owned more than anyone and gave away less than anyone. His wealth was a hoard, kept like a yaksha's treasure; his relatives and his guests were not honored even with a word. He was miserly by habit and cruel in manner, and one by one his own sons and kinsmen turned against him.

Then the family closed in. His relatives took part of his wealth, and thieves carried off the rest, and the brahmin who had been the richest man in Avanti sat looking at his empty rooms. He had lost both worlds at once — the comforts of this one, and the merit that might have bought him the next, worn away by the contempt he had earned.

For a long time he brooded over the ruin. Then the grief turned, and he began to speak to himself. What calamity is this, he said, that I tormented myself for nothing? Wealth never gives happiness to a miser — not once, not ever. Look what it brings: theft, violence, falsehood, deceit, desire, anger, pride, intoxication. Fifteen evils grow from a single root of gold. Brothers break with brothers over the smallest amount; fathers, wives, friends, all split apart where money is. I was given a human birth, which even the immortals pray for, and the highest station of a brahmin — the very door to heaven and to freedom — and I spent it chasing a hoard. What use are riches, or the givers of riches? What use are desires, or the givers of desires? Surely the Lord, Hari, who contains all the gods, is pleased with me, to have stripped all this away. With what life is left to me I will dry up this body, and the gods of the three worlds will rejoice in me.

So he left everything. He became a wandering mendicant, silent, his senses and his breath under control, and he walked the roads and villages of the land, begging his bread.

The townspeople did not make it easy. He was old and poor and they found him sport. Some snatched his triple staff; some grabbed his bowl and his water pot. When he sat on a riverbank to eat the alms he had gathered, they took the food from his hands. They tried to make the silent man speak, and struck him when he would not. A cheat, they said, wearing the flag of religion. A fraud. Some laughed at him; some spat insults after him; here and there a man who watched him suffer in stillness would mutter, grudgingly, that he bore it like a mountain.

And the brahmin bore it. Mocked and beaten by the base, enduring the pains that come from the world and from the body and from the gods themselves, he lifted his voice and sang a song that has been sung ever since.

It is the mind alone, he sang, that creates the qualities of nature, and from them all the varied works of men. The self does nothing — it only watches, golden and still, while the mind chases and suffers, and calls itself the doer. For a man whose mind is calm and collected, what need is there of gifts, of rites, of vows, of learning? The gods themselves fell under the mind's sway, and the mind bows to nothing else. It is an unconquerable enemy, unbearable in force, a thorn in the heart — and few there are who master it. Foolish men look at this body, which is only mind-stuff, and cry I and mine. Is it people, then, that cause our joy and sorrow? Or the gods? Or the planets? Or karma, or time? No: no one outside, anywhere, at any time, tinges the self with joy or grief. The mind alone turns the wheel of existence, and the man who knows this stands on the ground the great seers of old stood on.

When Krishna told this story to Uddhava, he ended it with a single sentence. No one gives a person joy or sorrow, he said, except his own confusion. Therefore, my son, restrain the mind with discernment — with all your strength, restrain it. And the song the mendicant sang, the song of the man of Avanti, is the song of anyone who has understood where his suffering actually comes from.
stories.reflection: The brahmin's loss of wealth is not a punishment but an unwinding: it removes the one thing that kept him from seeing himself. His song is not about poverty — it is about locating the source of joy and sorrow, and the man who could not bear to part with a coin learns to part with everything, including his own misery.
stories.content_note: The episode includes the townspeople seizing the mendicant's staff and bowl and striking him; the violence is described with restraint.
locations: the roads and villages of the land
stories.next_story_tease: A king, not a beggar, was the next to learn the same truth about the mind's delusions.

stories.title: The Emperor Who Ran After a Nymph
stories.subtitle: Pururava sings of the delusion that undid him
stories.story:
The emperor of the world was running through a forest, naked and weeping, calling a name into the trees.

His name was Pururava, son of Ila, and his fame had once covered the earth. But the nymph Urvashi had left him, and the man who had ruled an empire was now following her like a beast, mad with grief, unsatisfied, chasing a shadow through the years and the nights. When Krishna told Uddhava this story, he meant it as a mirror held up to every man who has ever handed his own mind to another and called it love.

For a long time Pururava ran. Then, in the depth of the forest, the madness broke, and he sang. His song has been remembered ever since as the song of Aila.

He no longer knew, he sang, whether the sun had risen or he had slipped deeper into darkness — he knew only that she was not there. Alas, what delusion seized me, that I, a self, a soul, made myself the plaything of a woman! I was the lord of the world, and I threw away my own majesty like a straw and ran after her. Where is her power over me, her brilliance, her sovereignty? All of it existed in my own mind. What use is learning, what use austerity, what use renunciation or scripture, to a man who does not know his own good? Shame on me — a fool who thought himself wise. For years I served the nectar of her lips, and the mind she stole from me — what power on earth could have freed it? Even when she herself spoke well-chosen words to warn me, I was too dull to hear them.

Then the song turned, and the grief turned with it.

What harm, after all, has she done me? A man sees a snake in a rope and screams — the rope never harmed him. The terror was in the seeing. And what is this body that I adorned and grieved over, this foul sack of flesh and bone, impure, made of bad smells? Whose is it — my parents', my wife's, my master's, the fire's that will take it, the dogs' and jackals' that will feed on it? In this worthless corpse the mind fastens itself, in this heap of skin and flesh and blood and sinew and marrow and bone. Let a man who knows what is good for him look at it plainly, and he will not cling to women, or to anything that belongs to the world of women, with his senses leashed to desire. From what is never seen and never heard, no attachment is born; it is born of contact, of looking and longing. Therefore let there be no contact, no clinging.

And as he sang, the delusion left him. The forest floor was only forest floor again; the name he had been calling was only a name. The emperor who had run naked and weeping rose up clothed in his own understanding, and the peace he had chased through the years and nights of his madness settled over him where he stood.

Krishna ended the tale there. If even Pururava, far-famed, lord of the whole earth, was brought so low by a mind that fastened on an object of desire, he said to Uddhava, then let anyone who hears the song of Aila look to his own heart before he lets his run.
stories.reflection: The rope-and-snake image carries the whole lament: Urvashi had done nothing — the terror and the longing were in the seeing. Pururava's peace comes the moment he stops accusing her and turns the question on his own mind. Read closely, the warning against clinging to women is a warning about attachment itself: the mind that fastens on any object of craving builds its own prison and then blames the object.
stories.tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana presents the lament as an example Krishna gives Uddhava of the danger of attachment; the language of the passage is addressed to men, but the underlying teaching concerns the mind's projections onto any object of desire.
stories.content_note: The episode includes Pururava's naked, distraught pursuit of Urvashi; described with restraint, it is a classical image of delusion rather than explicit content.
stories.next_story_tease: The teaching over, Krishna now sent his own dearest friend out of Dwaraka and onto the road.
stories.hero_scene: A king kneels in a forest glade, his robes discarded at his feet, weeping as the figure of a nymph vanishes among the trees; the first light of dawn touches the leaves around him.

stories.title: Uddhava's Road to Badari
stories.subtitle: Krishna sends his dearest friend north
stories.story:
The last teaching had been given, and there was nothing left to say. Krishna's court in Dwaraka had held the long instruction of the Uddhava Gita — the whole of what a soul needs to know, spoken by Krishna to the friend he trusted most. Now the two sat together, and the silence between them was heavier than the words had been.

Go, Uddhava, said Krishna. Go as I have commanded, to my hermitage called Badari, far in the north. Travel by the celestial route, as the blessed go, until you come to the hermitage on the bank of the Alakananda, where the very sight of the river washes away every stain. There, in that solitude sanctified by the long austerities of Narayana and Nara, dwell on what I have taught you. Patient with the pairs of opposites, gentle in conduct, your senses under control, abide there in the teaching — and meditating on me, you will come to me beyond the three paths, beyond the strands of nature that bind this world.

Uddhava heard the command and could not move. He, who had received the whole of the teaching, could not receive this one sentence. Separation from Krishna was the one thing his heart refused, and it showed in his face: the friend who had carried messages between Krishna and the Pandavas, who had been trusted with more than any other man in Dwaraka, stood stricken, unable to leave him.

But Krishna had spoken, and Uddhava was Uddhava. He walked around Krishna, once, again, and again, as if the circle of his steps could hold the moment open a little longer. Then he knelt, and took Krishna's feet and placed them upon his own head — the last honor, the last touch. And bearing Krishna's sandals in his hands, he went forth.

He placed the Lord within his own heart and set his face north. And Vidura, the wise uncle of the Pandavas, drew the story from him: how he had worshipped the sanctity of Krishna's feet, how he had learned the path of self-knowledge, how he had bowed and come away heart-torn with separation, and how he would go on to the hermitage of Badari, where Narayana and the sage Nara once performed their long austerities. Even in the telling, Uddhava's grief was fresh, and Vidura, who knew something of longing himself, let him speak.

Then Uddhava went on, north along the road that climbs toward the mountains, carrying Krishna's sandals, carrying the teaching. The city of Dwaraka fell behind him, and the life he had known there, and the friendship that had been the shape of his life. What he carried forward was stranger and stronger than either: the whole of what he had been told, and the promise that where he was going, the Lord who had sent him would be there before him — beyond the three paths, beyond everything that binds.

They say the road was long and the hermitage was high, and that the man who walked it had already left behind more than the court of Dwaraka. He had left behind himself — the self that clings and grieves — the way the teaching had shown him, step by step, until the walking itself became the teaching.
stories.reflection: The command to go to Badari is also a promise: separation from Krishna's body is not separation from Krishna. Uddhava carries the sandals — the last physical trace — but he also carries the teaching in his heart, and that is how the journey is meant to be made: the farewell that looks like an ending is, in the teaching's own terms, the beginning of the meeting.
stories.tradition_note: The Mahabharata (16.3) frames Uddhava's departure differently: he takes his leave of Krishna on the seacoast where the Vrishnis had gathered, and Krishna, saluting him with joined hands and knowing the clan's destruction was near, does not prevent him. The Bhagavata Purana places the farewell in Dwaraka at the close of the teaching, which is followed here.
stories.next_story_tease: Even as Uddhava walked north, Narada was prophesying what the ocean would one day do to Dwaraka itself.

stories.title: The Ocean That Waits for Dwaraka
stories.subtitle: Narada recites Krishna's deeds, then foretells the sea's return
stories.story:
Narada had a way of telling a man his own life back to him, and when he spoke, the years of Krishna's story came out of his mouth like a list being checked off. He stood in Dwaraka before his departure, and the wandering sage recited the deeds one by one, as if fate itself had taken dictation.

The nooses of Mura had been cut. Nisumva and Naraka lay slain, and the road to the city of Pragyotish stood clear of its terrors. The kings of the world had gone pale at the twang of Krishna's bow and the sound of the conch Panchajanya. Rukmi, protected by his chariot-warriors from the Deccan, had been vanquished, and Rukmini carried away in a car that blazed like the sun and rumbled like a cloud. In Jaruthi, Ahdriti, Kratha and Shishupala had fallen; Dantavakra and Shatadhanwa with all their soldiers; Shalwa, who flew in the city Shoubha, struck down in his fury; Dyumutsena dashed from the sky by the discus. Gopati and Talaketu, the two followers of Ravana on the summit of Mahendra, had vanished within a blink of the eye, and Hansa and Dimvaka after them. Varanasi had been burned; Maya had been killed with knotty arrows; the son of Indrasena had been set free.

The other worlds had fared no better. Varuna had been defeated beneath the sea at Lohitakuta. The Parijata tree had been carried off from Indra's own palace while the celestials looked on, forbidden to interfere. The kings of Pandya, Poundrya, Kalinga, Matsa and Banga had been swept away; Kaliya, the great serpent, had been sent from the river to the sea; and Yama himself had been forced to give back the dead son of Sandipani, restored to his teacher. Long before, in his dwarf form, Krishna had taken the three worlds back from Bali. Even the courtiers of Kamsa, Peetha, Paithika and Asitoma, had been cut down, and the Daityas Jambha, Airavata and Virupa, who came against him while he wore the semblance of a man.

Narada's voice did not rise. That was the strange part. He spoke of Arjuna crowned with success at Kurukshetra, of Drona, Bhishma, Karna and Suyodhana defeated, of the daughter of the king of Suveera carried away to please Vabhru — and it sounded less like praise than like the tally of everything the gods had asked of Krishna and received.

Then he came to the end of the list, and to what came after. Having established virtue among mortals through his sacrifices, having accomplished the great work of the gods, Krishna would return to his own region. And then, Narada said, the ocean — conversant with Krishna's desire, knowing his wish before it was spoken — would rise and devour Bhogavati, the beloved resort of the sages, and Dwaraka itself. The city of jewels and sacrificial grounds, with all its gardens, would sink into the abode of Varuna, this city built by Vasudeva that shone like the dwelling of the sun. There is none among gods, Asuras or men, said the sage, and none will be — except the slayer of Madhu himself — who will be able to live there once the sea takes it. And having set his regulations among the Dasharhas, Vishnu would be united with Narayana, with Soma and with Surya, as fire returns to fire.

The prophecy fell into the sea-bright air of the city that was not yet drowned. Krishna heard the drowning of his city and the ending of his time spoken aloud, and he did not argue. Narada took his leave, and Dwaraka went on with its day — bright above a sea that was waiting.
stories.reflection: Narada's prophecy weighs heaviest not because it announces death but because it announces completion — Krishna's work is spoken of as finished, his city as already claimed by the sea. Krishna's silence is the story's real answer: he does not dispute the design that has been traced around him.
stories.next_story_tease: Not long after, a prank played on visiting sages would give the prophecy a shape.
stories.hero_scene: Narada stands at Dwaraka's edge in the evening light, one hand raised as he speaks, while Krishna listens with folded hands and the calm golden sea stretches out behind them, patient as a held breath.

stories.title: The Prank That Cursed a Clan
stories.subtitle: Samba is dressed as a pregnant woman, and the sages answer with an iron mace
stories.story:
The joke began with a boy dressed as a bride. Samba, son of Jambavati, was wrapped in women's clothes and adorned like a young wife, and his companions led him through the city — hands folded in mock modesty — toward the sages who had come among them.

The Yadu boys were young, giddy and reckless, and the sight of holy men at their devotions struck them as an opportunity for sport. They presented the veiled Samba to the sages with exaggerated reverence. "This dark-eyed one is with child," they said. "Tell us, holy sirs — what will she give birth to?"

The sages were not deceived for an instant. They saw the dressed-up boy and the false pregnancy, and the insult of it: that the young men of the Yadava house should mock their calling to their faces. Their anger fell like a hammer. "She will bear an iron mace," they answered, "and that mace will destroy your clan."

The words were no sooner spoken than the laughter died. The mace came forth from Samba's belly then and there — iron, heavy and terrible — and the boys stood staring at the thing their joke had called into being. They had meant to play; they had brought forth their own doom. "What have we done, ill-fated as we are?" they cried to one another. "What will people say of us now?"

Terrified, they carried the mace to the assembly and laid it before the elders, their faces drained of color. Ugrasena, the Yadava king, looked at the iron bolt and understood what had happened in the city that day. He gave the order at once: the mace was ground to powder, and the powder carried to the seashore and scattered into the waves, so that nothing of the curse might remain in the hands of the clan.

But a scrap of the iron, one fragment among the dust, was swallowed by a fish in those same waters, mixed with the powder the waves had scattered. The fish grew heavy and was caught by fishermen in their nets, and when it was cut open the iron passed into other hands, passed and was worked, until at last it lay shaped as an arrow in a hunter's quiver, waiting for the day it would be needed.

Krishna, when the news reached him, was not surprised. The sages had pronounced the curse knowing the mind of the Lord: the anger of holy men had become the instrument of a design already made. He did not overturn the sentence, nor did he take the mace's coming as an accident. He gathered the Vrishnis to him, as a man gathers his household when a storm is coming — not to outrun it, but so that when it arrives, they will be found together.

The clan kept its city and its pride. The sea kept the secret of its iron dust. And somewhere the arrow waited in the hunter's quiver, while in Dwaraka the boys who had laughed at the sages grew older, and the curse settled over the Yadava house like dust settling after a blow.
stories.reflection: The curse answers a boy's prank with a clan's ruin, and the disproportion is the point: the sages punish not the joke but the arrogance behind it. Yet the sources add that they cursed knowing the mind of the Lord — so the wrath of holy men and the patience of Krishna were moving toward the same end, and the joke only opened the door that was already marked.
stories.tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana names the sages — Viswamitra, Kanwa and Narada, met at Pindaraka — and says the ground dust became rushes; the Mahabharata foretells the bolt's destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas. The Bhagavata Purana, followed here, has the last iron swallowed by a fish and later shaped into the hunter's arrow.
stories.next_story_tease: For Krishna, the curse had never been a surprise — he had weighed the Yadavas' fate long before.
stories.hero_scene: In the dusty assembly ground of Dwaraka, the terrified Yadu boys set down the iron mace born from Samba's belly while the elders stare in silence and Krishna watches, unsurprised, at the edge of the crowd.
